article_title: The Guardian view on Burnham’s Brexit reset: overdue, but proceed with care | Editorial
article_content:
The German philosopher GWF Hegel famously evoked the owl of Minerva when discussing the historical wisdom that comes through hindsight. This autumn, she has flown tirelessly over the landscape of British politics. Party conference season was dominated by conflicting Labour and Conservative accounts of the 1970s and 80s. And a decade after the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, Andy Burnham this week abandoned all equivocation over the damage – economic but also strategic – that resulted from that decision.
Having declared that it is time to “face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good”, Mr Burnham told the House of Commons on Monday that it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to explore all options for closer relations with Brussels. Though he confirmed that in this parliament he will honour the red lines in Sir Keir Starmer’s Labour manifesto, all bets will subsequently be off.
A long-delayed reset summit, Mr Burnham also announced, will take place next month with deals on food and drink and youth mobility to be negotiated. The former Labour leader Neil Kinnock asserted to an Italian newspaper on Tuesday that the prime minister’s “obvious” eventual objective was to rejoin.
That might well be contested in Downing Street. But as has become the norm in this overture phase of Mr Burnham’s premiership, his Commons statement was bracingly expansive and forthright. It also had the signal virtue of being correct in its diagnosis and prescription. Nevertheless, the reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk.
Labour’s hyper-caution over revisiting the EU relationship has increasingly been at odds with polls indicating a substantial majority of the public supports closer ties. But the devil will be in the detail. In the red wall, in particular, much will depend on the prime minister’s undoubted persuasive powers. The need to undo the economic self-harm of Brexit was not something that Mr Burnham chose to emphasise while campaigning for his seat in the leave-voting constituency of Makerfield.
For its part, the EU itself is in flux and may have new red lines of its own. Responding to a more menacing geopolitical environment, Brussels is contemplating deeper coordination in areas such as defence and economic policy. The direction of travel is already evident in the “Made in Europe” strategy, which threatens to leave British-based car manufacturers out in the cold.
As that risk illustrates, it is overwhelmingly in Britain’s interests to be acting in concert with the EU, rather than flailing in sorry isolation on the sidelines. Following the visceral mutual distrust of the Tory Brexit years, Sir Keir restored a basic if circumscribed civility to relations between the UK and the EU. Mr Burnham’s boldness can now open up new possibilities down the line for “a real reset”, to use the formulation of one EU diplomat.
It will not have escaped Mr Burnham’s notice that such a prospect would unite progressive Britain behind it, and could significantly boost Labour’s percentage vote share. His overriding early theme has been the need to rectify the political “wrong turns” of past decades. Beginning the long task of doing so on Brexit is brave, but it promises significant dividends for his premiership and, much more importantly, the country.

article_title: Why are hundreds of prisoners being released early?
article_content:
Why are hundreds of prisoners being released early?
- Published
Around 650 more prisoners in England and Wales are due to be released under the second tranche of the government's early release scheme.
Under the scheme, eligible prisoners are released after serving a third of their total custodial sentence rather than after 40% or 50% of the term.
People sentenced for manslaughter, rape, serious child sex and grooming offences are excluded.
This is not the first time a government - Conservative or Labour - has released prisoners early to make space in England and Wales' overcrowded prisons.
BBC Verify has looked at the reasons why ministers say this latest scheme is necessary.
More prisoners than prison space
The prison population in England and Wales on 12 October was 87,033, which was 97.8% of useable capacity, external.
The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has previously warned the prison population will overtake capacity as soon as this November.
In the long-term the MoJ has projected that the capacity of all prisons will rise to around 99,000 by 2032 as a result of more prisons being built by this government.
But it also projected that the prisoner population would rise to about 104,000 by 2032 if the Sentencing Act 2026 - which provides for earlier release - did not come into force.
That is why Justice Secretary Alex Norris says there is a "prison capacity crisis" which means the government has to implement the latest early release scheme.
In total 4,500 prisoners are due to be released early by June 2027, external. About 700 offenders were released from jail early on 1 October - all of whom were serving terms of less than 19 months.
The MoJ has projected that the Sentencing Act will mean the prisoner population remains below the capacity of the prison system, rising only to around 96,000 by 2032.
More people are being sent to prison for longer
The England and Wales prison population has risen significantly in recent decades with a significant uptick starting in the 1990s before reaching a record high in 2024.
The Institute for Government (IFG) think tank says this is partly the result of longer sentences.
In 2023, the average prison sentence at Crown Courts in England and Wales - which deal with more serious offences - was more than 25% longer than those handed down in 2012.
For some crimes, the increase was greater. Sentences for robbery in 2023 were 13 months longer on average than in 2012 - an increase of 36%.
Longer sentences mean more people being held in prison at any one time.
Former Conservative Justice Secretary David Gauke, who led an independent sentencing review for Sir Keir Starmer's government, argues this is the result of a "bidding war" by political parties since the 1990s over who can imprison people for longer.
Gauke also points out that the prison population has been rising at a time when overall crime in England and Wales has been falling, according to the official Crime Survey.
So despite the fall in crime more people are being sent to prison - and for longer.
Another reason for upward pressure on the prison population is that more people than before are being returned to prison for breaching the conditions of their release.
There were 51,419 licence recalls in England and Wales in the year ending March 2026, up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase.
Cassia Rowland from the IFG said most recalls are for breaches of licence conditions, such as missed appointments, rather than offenders committing further offences or posing a serious risk to the public.
"The probation service is overwhelmed, with high caseloads and lots of vacancies putting often inexperienced staff under huge pressure," she said.
Slow pace of prison building
Successive governments have pledged to increase the number of prison places - but delivery has often fallen short of those promises.
Between 2010 and 2024, when the Conservatives were in power, around 13,000 new prison places were created.
But around 12,500 places - notably those built during the Victorian era - were closed after falling into disrepair.
That means an estimated net total of only around 500 new prison places were added over 14 years.
In a 2024 report, the National Audit Office (NAO) cited the MOJ's "unrealistic timelines", and government bodies not working together to prioritise delivery, as reasons for the slow pace of prison building.
The MOJ say around 6,500 net prison places were created between 2022 and 2025, once closures are taken into consideration. These include places created in three new prisons.
However, further expansion to existing prisons has been delayed by a major supplier going into administration, according to the Prison Reform Trust.
Pia Sinha of the Prison Reform Trust told BBC Verify: "Successive governments have found it difficult to increase prison capacity because new prisons take years to plan and build, often facing planning hurdles and local opposition."
The Labour government has pledged to build 14,000 new prison places by 2031.
Analysts argue that without a major change in thinking about the appropriateness of prison as punishment, or a significant long-term increase in prison building, the system in England and Wales will remain close to capacity.
And that means governments will continue to be under pressure to implement early release schemes to avert a capacity crisis.
description: More people going to prison, and for longer, is why governments including the current one have had to release prisoners early.

article_title: The Guardian view on probation: overcrowded prisons need an outlet | Editorial
article_content:
The early release of thousands of prisoners was bound to be awkward for a new prime minister. Politically speaking, Andy Burnham’s decision to exclude those convicted of manslaughter and some other offences made sense. But with about 2,000 offenders being freed this month, the risk is that by cutting the numbers, he has added to overcrowding problems inside. With the prison and probation services under huge pressure, and a ballot on industrial action expected, there is an urgent need for moves from the government to strengthen both.
Shielded from view as prisons are, and despite the efforts of campaigners and writers such as Jimmy McGovern to draw attention to them, conditions have been allowed to deteriorate to a shocking extent. The latest annual report from the prisons watchdog drew a dismal picture of rampant drug use, organised crime and governors wasting time on form-filling. It warned that the Prison Service’s managers appear to favour crisis management over improvement.
Criticisms of the probation service of England and Wales contained in the latest report by the Institute for Government’s (IfG) appear measured, by comparison. Probation’s problems are less attention-grabbing, and senior leaders are not singled out for blame. But analysis of the impact of sentencing reforms, combined with ongoing staff shortages and tagging failures, are cause for very serious concern all the same. This is a vital public service that was already facing serious difficulties before its caseload was massively enlarged.
Problems date back to the failed part-privatisation of the service. The IfG highlights the toll of “near-constant organisational change”. One result has been de-skilling, with staff increasingly reliant on risk-management protocols rather than judgment. The number of recalls to prison due to breached conditions, rather than new offences, undermines rehabilitation and worsens overcrowding. But an overstretched workforce seems unable to break this cycle. There is simply not enough time to build relationships.
The failure to fit 45% of tags on time is obviously unacceptable; ministers need to get a grip and explain what is happening. The IfG also recommends further sentencing reforms aimed at making the system clearer. Rightly, it points out that the growing gap between jail sentences imposed in court and time actually served risks undermining trust and angering victims. Similarly, licence periods should end at the point where supervision ceases. Currently, there is a pretence that more people are serving community sentences than is actually the case. This places the probation service in a false position.
The pay dispute is the immediate challenge. As part of a settlement, ministers should pledge to rebuild capacity and fill vacancies. Looking further ahead, probation needs closer links to the local services that can help offenders to get back on their feet. The merger with the Prison Service has failed to deliver promised gains.
Managing risks to the public must remain a priority. But Enver Solomon, who leads Nacro, the criminal justice charity, is right to argue for a more “person-centred” style of probation work. No one who knows anything about prisons thinks that they are fulfilling their rehabilitation remit. A renewed focus on purposeful activity inside jails is needed. But as increased numbers of prisoners are diverted towards probation, the service needs resources to deliver what is asked of it.

article_title: One thing must now be clear to Andy Burnham. The rightwing press is on a war footing – and he’s the enemy | Jane Martinson
article_content:
While the merits of a so-called Britannia shield to protect Britain from missiles and drones are debatable, the Conservatives’ proposal did achieve one thing last week: the very idea of the shield was used to anoint a political leader.
In a significant development, little observed amid the hullaballoo of news events, Kemi Badenoch’s uncosted, pie-in-the-sky plans to build a £10bn anti-missile system were enthusiastically heralded by the rightwing press. It was not just a matter of the plans themselves being lauded, even by outlets that must know them to be ridiculous. More significant is what it said about the champion chosen by these media organisations in their offensive against the Labour government and Andy Burnham.
The Sun splashed a smiling Badenoch across its front page with a banner headline calling her the “Iron Dome Lady”; the Express paraded her in a power suit and a union jack. The Daily Mail, meanwhile, hailed the Tories for seeking to “protect the nation’s skies” and sealed the plans with its “Don’t Leave Britain Defenceless” campaign stamp. Even wartime leaders could not hope for better, unquestioning coverage from battle-aligned, nation-rallying propaganda sheets.
The slavish Badenoch coverage is significant so soon after Burnham’s first conference speech as prime minister. It marks the moment when much of the rightwing press has returned to its traditional Tory-supporting ways after years of flirting with – and outright eulogising – Nigel Farage and his now scandal-hit Reform UK party. It also suggests a back-to-basics return to the economy as the chief battleground for this fight, and not the madder excesses of the war on woke that has recently consumed them.
The praise for Badenoch, who was also recently treated to an all-expenses paid trip to Greece to meet Rupert Murdoch and executives from the Sun and Times-owning News Corp, suggests that she has cemented a position as the rightwing press’s best political hope of beating Burnham.
The search for a suitable champion has assumed a growing urgency because the prime minister has so far proved hard to leave a mark on. “Red Andy”, the early attack line, has not been widely used since the June byelection in Makerfield. The Mail may have dubbed Burnham’s first conference speech “the most Left-wing speech delivered by a modern British prime minister”, but in recent weeks only the Telegraph’s Allister Heath has fired the “Red Andy” missile in a column that called plans for pension reform, a social care system and all talk of a return to the European Union, “mad, nasty and shockingly extreme”.
This coverage reminds Alastair Campbell of his early years advising Tony Blair when he was depicted either as a “useless Bambi or Stalin”, he tells me. “They can’t decide if [Burnham] is a useless Paddington Bear or red in tooth and claw,” says Campbell. “They just can’t work him out yet.” A member of the loathed liberal elite or outright Trot?
There are a few factors that are making it difficult for the rightwing press to get the full measure of their enemy – including Burnham’s trajectory from New Labour luvvy to working-class champion, the King of the North. Labour advisers also cite the fact that Burnham’s inner circle, in contrast to his predecessors, has also been relatively leak- and conflict-free, leaving rightwing combatants with fewer vulnerabilities to exploit.
This is the calm before the storm, of course, with Burnham’s opponents gearing up for the budget and the inevitable controversies on 28 October. “The press are probing his defences,” Tom Baldwin, a former Labour party adviser, tells me. “They’ll keep trying, of course, and the chances are that one of their missiles will eventually hit a target.”
Amid rising fuel prices, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns over jobs, the back-to-the-future nature of this debate – indeed the back-to-the-Tory-future nature of it – is hardly surprising. Burnham has assaulted shibboleths. He has vowed to reverse “40 years of failure” with his pledge to repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on public ownership of water companies, to abolish the Tory version of the right-to-buy housing scheme, and to restore a sense of common good to Britain. To the right, this is unconscionable. Dan Hodges in the Mail, praising Badenoch’s “best speech yet”, wrote that the country faces a choice between Burnham’s “unashamed 1970s-style socialism” and the Tory leaders’ “bold attempt to reappropriate and recondition Margaret Thatcher’s radical conservatism”.
Although the rightwing outlets fight a similar battle against Labour, they do so for varying reasons. Some of those are ideological, but commercial imperatives also fuel their fervour. The 1970s and 80s marked a golden age for newspapers, when millions of loyal readers gave them heft and profits. With sales and readership figures now at a fraction of their peak in the late 80s, the Sun (which claimed sales of 3.8m per day in 1987) and several other titles no longer publish their numbers, focusing instead on online reach. In dwindling markets, the strategy is to stay competitive by aligning with, or perhaps exacerbating, the prevailing wave of political populism.
The Sun has struggled more than the Mail with the shift online. It has also struggled more with Burnham because of its coverage of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, in which it falsely blamed Liverpool supporters for a crush that killed 97 people. According to Baldwin, citing well-placed sources, Burnham may become the first prime minister since the Labour leader Jim Callaghan to refuse requests for exclusive interviews and articles in Rupert Murdoch’s biggest tabloid.
The right’s battle-camp has the additional problem that Burnham himself is proving quite a wily opponent. The prime minister spends 10 minutes a day with his social media team before posting to his nearly 1m followers on Instagram and more than 700,000 on TikTok. His short-form videos on fuel prices and the triple lock don’t seem to target younger voters, but they are a way of bypassing a negative narrative – or what Campbell calls “the madness of the rightwing press”.
Burnham could opt to go his own way, to ignore the hostile rightwing outlets altogether. But in a democracy, that would be no more ethical for Labour than it is for Reform UK, which has barred press critics. David Yelland, the editor of the Sun when it put Tony Blair on its front page with the headline “Is THIS the most dangerous man in Britain?”, tells me it would also be unwise. The power of the rightwing press is diminished, he says; they are “toothless tigers in a jungle full of new dangers – dangers as lethal for them as the rest of us, by which I mean AI and what comes next”. But, “the truth is the Tory press still has influence over the political and media classes … it can still set the weather”.
And as we know from famous battles past, the weather can be a decisive factor. The side that copes with it best usually wins.
-

article_title: Марко Рубио посетит Индию и Узбекистан: Госдеп США обнародовал программу поездки
article_content:
Государственный секретарь США Марко Рубио 17 октября отправится с визитами в Индию и Узбекистан. В Индии он обсудит вопросы сотрудничества в энергетической сфере, а в Узбекистане возглавит делегацию из более чем 200 руководителей бизнеса. Поездка состоится на фоне нового застоя в переговорах между Вашингтоном и Нью-Дели о торговом соглашении. Об этом сообщило информационное агентство Reuters.
Госсекретарь посетит Самарканд в Узбекистане, а также Мумбаи и Джамнагар в Индии. Поездка запланирована на 17–22 октября. В Индии Рубио встретится с представителями правительства. Стороны должны обменяться оценками региональных и глобальных процессов и обсудить возможности расширения сотрудничества в энергетической сфере.
В начале октября индийские и американские чиновники сообщили, что длительные усилия по заключению двустороннего торгового соглашения вновь зашли в тупик. Соглашение, над которым стороны работают уже длительное время, до сих пор не удалось окончательно согласовать.
В течение последнего года отношения США и Индии оставались напряжёнными из-за ряда вопросов. Среди них — повторяющиеся заявления президента Дональда Трампа о том, что именно он способствовал прекращению огня между Индией и Пакистаном. Еще одним поводом для разногласий стала американская военная атака на судно у берегов Омана. Тогда погибли трое индийских моряков.
Нью-Дели также выражал обеспокоенность американским законодательством, которое позволяет Трампу вводить пошлины до 100% в отношении стран, закупающих российские энергоносители. Этот механизм является частью усилий Вашингтона по наращиванию давления на Москву из-за её вторжения в Украину.
В начале 2026 года Индия лишь ненадолго сократила закупки энергоносителей у России. С тех пор их объемы вновь резко выросли. Особенно это стало заметно после перебоев с поставками, вызванных войной США и Израиля против Ирана. О визите Рубио объявили также на фоне протестов, продолжающихся в Индии из-за исключения 130 миллионов избирателей из списков для голосования. Вашингтон до сих пор не комментировал эти демонстрации.
В Узбекистане госсекретарь проведет двусторонние встречи с представителями Узбекистана, Казахстана, Таджикистана, Туркменистана и Кыргызстана. Он также возглавит делегацию из более чем 200 руководителей бизнеса, сообщили в Государственном департаменте США.
Напомним, что Индия предупредила США о рисках для двусторонних отношений из-за законопроекта о санкциях против России. Министерство иностранных дел Индии обнародовало соответствующее заявление 17 сентября. Документ предусматривал возможность введения пошлин до 100% в отношении крупнейших покупателей российской нефти. Нью-Дели также предостерегал от дестабилизации мировых энергетических рынков.
Кроме того, государственный секретарь США Марко Рубио и министр иностранных дел Индии Субраманьям Джайшанкар обсудили возможные санкции против стран, поддерживающих экономические связи с Россией и Ираном. Встреча состоялась в Нью-Йорке. Джайшанкар сообщил, что вновь выразил заинтересованность и озабоченность Индии в отношении санкционного закона, подписанного Дональдом Трампом.
description: Госсекретарь обсудит региональные вызовы и перспективы расширения энергетических связей.

article_title: Wednesday briefing: ​Why small boat crossings are here to stay ​
article_content:
Good morning. You’d be forgiven for missing it. Earlier this month, the government quietly scrapped its “one in, one out” deal with France. The partnership was supposed to eliminate small boat crossings by deterring asylum seekers from making the treacherous journey across the world’s busiest shipping channel.
The deal, which lasted just 423 days, was beset with problems, had a negligible impact, and now joins a long list of policies that have tried and failed to address highly visible, often tragic small boat crossings. This morning, the Home Office announced that it would be doubling the number of riot police along the French coast in lieu of the deal.
Although small boat arrivals have actually decreased over the last year, the far right continues to weaponise these crossings. In its annual threat briefing yesterday, the head of MI5 warned that extremists with anti-immigration opinions are increasingly considering carrying out terrorist attacks.
Today’s newsletter speaks to specialist reporter Diane Taylor and Daniel Trilling, author of If We Tolerate This, to situate the deal’s collapse within the wider context of policies that have exacerbated the sense of disorder they’re supposed to resolve – and asks what comes next. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories
- 
  UK news | Extremists holding anti-immigration opinions are becoming increasingly likely to consider carrying out terrorist attacks against immigration centres and asylum hotels, the head of MI5 has warned.
- 
  UK politics | Nigel Farage has denied that a Reform UK government would authorise lethal force against small boat crossings in the Channel.
- 
  Ukraine | Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump.
- 
  US politics | Kimberly Guilfoyle is stepping down as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials.
- 
  Pope Leo XIV | Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican said late on Tuesday. Leo, 71, underwent an operation and had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, with tests confirming a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said.
In depth: ‘I’ve never seen as much suffering caused to refugees by government policy’
The one in, one out policy that was announced in a joint press conference between Keir Starmer and Emmanuel Macron in July last year was supposed to render small boat crossings pointless. A person arriving in a small boat to the UK could be forcibly returned to France in exchange for another person who would be brought legally to the UK. “In effect,” Diane Taylor wrote in a moving piece about the scheme in September, asylum seekers were “used as reluctant human shields to protect our borders from others in the same predicament.”
The scheme was always limited in scale; of the 40,000 people who arrived in small boats while it was active, just 1,500 – roughly 4% – were returned to France. A report by British Future, a thinktank that championed the policy, recognised that it would have to be expanded twenty-fold to close down routes as a viable way to claim asylum. But it’s doubtful that, even at this far larger scale, it would have ever been effective. Diane reported in August that nearly 50 asylum seekers deported under the scheme returned to the UK a second time, and an unknown number arrived undetected.
The government would have liked the scheme to continue, and its official explanation was that it was scrapped because it couldn’t be effectively scaled up. But it seems likely that political concerns in France also played a role. “At a time when immigration is going to be a major issue in the French presidential election, France doesn’t want to be seen to be taking in more unwanted people from the UK,” Rajeev Syal, the Guardian’s home affairs editor, tells me.
The other side of one in, one out
The deal was partially founded on a recognition of the need for safer routes to claim asylum in Britain. Starmer acknowledged when announcing it that “it is right that we offer a haven to those in most dire need”. But this flicker of humanitarianism was outweighed by the scheme’s arbitrary cruelty. Nearly 100 children were misidentified as adults and wrongly detained under the scheme, while some asylum seekers deported back to France were beaten by people smugglers. “I’ve been writing about asylum seekers for 25 years and I’ve never seen as much suffering caused to refugees by a UK government policy,” says Diane.
It was also accompanied by the government’s fortification of security measures along the French border. To some extent, these security measures help to explain the drop in small boat crossings this year, together with an overall reduction in arrivals of asylum seekers to Europe. But they have also encouraged people to make even more unsafe crossings. The increased police presence in northern France has led to more trips in larger “mega-dinghies”, which became a subject of panicked headlines this summer, as smugglers attempt to transport more people in single crossings.
Increased security has also encouraged people to take longer routes across the channel, sailing from Normandy and Belgium rather than Calais. Earlier this summer, far-right protests spread to Portsmouth, where people arriving on small boats had sailed from Normandy. “In effect, while the security measures seem on the surface to be working, they also contribute to boat journeys becoming far more dangerous, again adding to the sense of spectacle,” Daniel Trilling tells me.
Why are so many people still crossing in small boats?
The right frames small boat crossings as a failure to control immigration. Crucially, though, they’re a manifestation of ever-more draconian attempts to crack down on people trying to claim asylum in the UK. Before people crossed the channel in dinghies, they hid in lorries, or took flights to the UK using false passports. “When I first started reporting in Calais in 2014, it was still possible for refugees to stow themselves away on lorries without paying smugglers for access,” Daniel recalls. “But the more security that was placed around ports, the harder that became, and the more refugees had to rely on smugglers who could get access to secure lorry parks.”
In 2020, when the pandemic temporarily grounded traffic between Calais and Britain, small boat crossings spiked dramatically. By the following year, these crossings had more than doubled. “There used to be really, really small numbers of boats arriving in Britain, and nobody paid attention to them,” Diane says. “And obviously, you didn’t get far-right influencers live-streaming arrivals at border control in Heathrow, or standing on the hard shoulder of the M25 waiting to film asylum seekers for their YouTube.”
What happens next
Part of the calculation behind the government’s latest decision to double the number of riot police in northern France is that, now the deal has ended, it has limited time in which to strengthen its partnership with the French government. If Marine Le Pen is elected in April next year, it’s plausible that her government could refuse to take any asylum seekers from Britain, further politicising the issue and causing a rise in crossings that would play into the hands of the far right here.
Yet the decision is also yet another manifestation of the tendency to treat migration as a security issue rather than a reflection of an increasingly unstable world. No matter the increase in security or threats of deportation, people will keep trying to claim asylum. “As long as we have wars, instability and persecution, people will be displaced, and we need to work out ways to respond to that, rather than pretending that a policy tweak here or extra security measure there will simply make it disappear,” Daniel says. “At some point, you have to make a political argument for why asylum isn’t just an act of generosity, but a necessary response to the world as it is.”

  I loved our gallery of French photographer Jean-Pierre Laffont’s work – he spent two decades capturing protests, clashes and countercultural gatherings in America, and the images to come out are stunning and empowering. Poppy
- 
  When species of birds decline, passing on the skill of singing becomes harder, even affecting their ability to breed. Rebecca Ratcliffe has this fascinating and warming look at how scientists are helping birds remember lost songs. Craille

Formula One | Formula One has confirmed Rwanda will join the calendar, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It will mark the first time F1 has raced in Africa since 1993.
The front pages
“M15 warns of rightwing shift from anti-migrant opinion to terrorism,” is the splash on the Guardian on Wednesday. “M15 chief: Russia did not sway Brexit vote,” says the Telegraph. “Putin’s Russia is biggest threat to Britain, M15 chief confirms,” says the i. “M15 chief: UK must not ‘play into hands’ of Putin,” has the Express, while the Mirror runs with: “Red Alert.”
“Tax fears eased in Burnham’s ‘pro-business’ pitch to bosses,” is the lead story over at the FT. “Online tax crackdown to boost the high street,” says the Times. “4 out of 5 new jobs went to foreigners in the past decade,” has the Daily Mail, while the Metro goes with “Toxic water spills surge.” Finally, the Star with: “Tiger’s victim a child actor.”
The Latest
‘I will not be silenced’: Trump critic Ilhan Omar defiant after home raided
Democrats have described a raid on the home of Congresswoman Ilhan Omar as “deeply disturbing” and a “rogue abuse of power” by the Trump administration. The Democratic representative for Minnesota has long been a target of highly personal attacks by Donald Trump, who claims he was not involved in ordering the raid. Lucy Hough speaks to Guardian US political reporter Shrai Popat – watch on YouTube.
Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings
The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Peter Lloyd spent most of his life unable to read or write, despite repeated attempts to learn. He struggled in school, left with no qualifications, and developed coping strategies that enabled him to work successfully as a lorry driver. During the Covid lockdowns, he found that it had become an overwhelming issue, particularly when he could not help home-school his son.
Encouraged by his wife, he contacted the charity Read Easy and began lessons with a volunteer tutor. Over three years, he learned to read and now Lloyd serves as a Read Easy ambassador.
Lloyd says: “I think it’s important to encourage others in my situation to seek help, especially men who might be too ashamed. I have three books on the go at the moment – I can’t believe how beautiful reading is!”

article_title: Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support
article_content:
Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump.
The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.”
To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect it from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones.
In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August.
Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraine to have a new leader, and announced a supposed ceasefire connected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”.
Trump is an often wayward ally for Ukraine, and Zelenskyy has expressed anger at the diesel deal, saying subsequent Russian attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine amounted to a “thanks” from Vladimir Putin.
UK governments have previously welcomed Zelenskyy after difficult experiences with Trump. He met Keir Starmer at Downing Street the day after Trump and his vice-president, JD Vance, publicly berated the Ukrainian president in the Oval Office 18 months ago.
During that trip Zelenskyy was also hosted by King Charles, who, in a pointedly personal touch, saw the Ukrainian president at Sandringham in Norfolk, which is a royal family home and rarely used for such visits.
Announcing the latest Downing Street meeting, No 10 said part of an ongoing £1.6bn package to deliver more than 5,000 LMMs to Ukraine would be sped up to help combat attacks by jet-powered drones.
These are quicker and higher-flying than the propeller-driven Shahed drones previously used, making them much harder to shoot down, allowing Russia to strike more targets in Ukraine, including in Kyiv.
The chancellor, John Healey, will separately use meetings at the ongoing International Monetary Fund summit in Bangkok to push other countries to ban Russian LNG.
In a statement before his meeting with Zelenskyy, Burnham said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.
“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer: we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe.
“It is not just the right thing to do, but it’s the necessary thing to do. Russia’s aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.”

article_title: Украина получила место в Совете ООН по правам человека
article_content:
Министр иностранных дел Андрей Сибига сообщил, что Украина была избрана на три года членом Совета ООН по правам человека (на 2027–2029 гг.). Министр подчеркнул, что Украина будет защищать своих граждан и суверенитет в условиях российской агрессии, и выразил благодарность тем членам ООН, которые поддержали кандидатуру нашей страны.
Среди приоритетов членства Украины Сибига назвал документирование и расследование преступлений РФ, привлечение страны-агрессора к ответственности за нарушение прав человека и международного гуманитарного права. Защита военнослужащих и возвращение депортированных или насильно перемещенных из Украины детей.
"Опираясь на собственный опыт, мы будем работать с партнерами, чтобы усилить привлечение к ответственности, защищать человеческое достоинство, укреплять международную архитектуру прав человека и противодействовать новым вызовам для прав человека во всем мире", — отметил министр.
Украина ранее входила в состав Совета четыре раза: в 2006–2008, 2008–2011, 2018–2020 и 2021–2023 годах.
Совет ООН по правам человека является межправительственным органом, который занимается защитой прав человека в мире, рассматривает случаи их нарушения и может создавать международные механизмы расследования. Как писало ZN.UA, работа Совета имеет практическое значение для документирования преступлений и обеспечения ответственности за них. В частности, в 2023 году Совет продлил мандат Независимой международной комиссии по расследованию событий в Украине, которая собирает доказательства возможных военных преступлений и нарушений прав человека
description: Срок членства составит три года.

article_title: Кандидат в президенти Франції назвав Трампа «корисним ідіотом» Путіна
article_content:
Кандидат в президенти Франції назвав Трампа «корисним ідіотом» Путіна
Політик також застеріг від можливого приходу до влади ультраправої Марін Ле Пен і закликав європейські країни посилити власну обороноздатність.
Французький політик Рафаель Глюксман розкритикував рішення президента США Дональда Трампа послабити обмеження на експорт російського дизельного пального. Він заявив, що така політика грає на користь Кремля та посилює загрози для Європи.
Про це повідомляє Politico.
Після перемоги на праймеріз лівоцентристського табору Глюксман виступив на Саміті з питань конкурентоспроможності в Парижі. Він різко висловився щодо політики американського президента та ролі Вашингтона в забезпеченні європейської безпеки.
«На чолі Сполучених Штатів стоїть людина, яка є або корисним ідіотом, або агентом, що підриває силу та свободу Європи. Війна Росії проти України спрямована безпосередньо проти нас, європейців, і ми залишилися наодинці», — заявив Глюксман.
Депутат Європарламенту також заявив, що перемога його ультраправої суперниці Марін Ле Пен на президентських виборах у Франції 2027 року стане вигідною для Путіна та означатиме поразку для Європи.
Politico нагадує, що раніше Ле Пен висловлювала «певну форму захоплення» Путіним. Крім того, 2014 року її партія «Національний фронт» отримала кредит від банку, пов’язаного з Росією.
Сама Ле Пен пояснювала, що її політична сила звернулася по фінансування за кордон після того, як французькі банки відмовили їй у кредитуванні. За її словами, отримана позика не вплинула на політичні позиції партії, а гроші згодом повернули.
«Хоча Ле Пен засудила тотальну війну Росії в Україні, деякі обрані представники її партії й досі категорично виступають проти надання допомоги Україні та підтримують зміцнення відносин із Росією», — йдеться у матеріалі.
За даними опитування, наведеного виданням, Ле Пен має двозначну перевагу над конкурентами в першому турі президентських виборів. Глюксман посідає четверте місце, поступаючись колишньому прем’єр-міністру Едуару Філіпу та представнику крайніх лівих Жан-Люку Меланшону.
Якщо жоден із кандидатів не набере понад 50% голосів у першому турі, у Франції відбудеться другий тур виборів.
В інтерв’ю Politico Глюксман, який виступає за поглиблення європейської інтеграції, наголосив на необхідності створення «Європейського небесного щита» для України та розвитку потужнішої й незалежнішої європейської оборонної промисловості.
Цю ініціативу також підтримав президент Франції Еммануель Макрон. За даними видання, ідея посилення європейської оборони знаходить підтримку серед представників різних політичних сил країни.
«Протягом десятиліть ми передавали наш суверенітет і нашу безпеку у руки Вашингтона, і тепер ми усвідомлюємо, якою помилкою це було», — зазначив Глюксман.
Політик також виступив за спільні запозичення країн ЄС для фінансування оборонних проєктів. Таку ідею неохоче підтримують Німеччина та інші держави, які дотримуються жорсткої бюджетної політики.
На думку Глюксмана, спільне фінансування дозволить Європі ефективніше розвивати оборонні технології, ніж реалізація окремих двосторонніх проєктів між державами. Як приклад він навів невдалу франко-німецьку програму створення винищувача нового покоління.
«Жодна європейська країна, включаючи Німеччину, не зможе в короткостроковій перспективі протистояти війні майбутнього» проти таких держав, як Китай, Росія та США, без спільних інвестицій, вважає політик.
«Це питання життя чи смерті», — наголосив Глюксман.
Раніше повідомлялося, що Трамп домовився з Путіним про постачання російського пального та вимагає від України припинити удари по російських НПЗ.
Ми раніше інформували, що президент Сполучених Штатів Дональд Трамп заявив, що «дасть знати», якщо Росія порушить енергетичне перемир’я з Україною.
description: Політик також застеріг від можливого приходу до влади ультраправої Марін Ле Пен і закликав європейські країни посилити власну обороноздатність.

article_title: «Має побачити, що від цього залежить його життя»: експерт пояснив, як змусити Путіна до переговорів
article_content:
«Має побачити, що від цього залежить його життя»: експерт пояснив, як змусити Путіна до переговорів
Щоб змусити Кремль шукати вихід із війни, необхідно забезпечити негативну для Росії динаміку на фронті, у кілзоні та в повітрі.
Диктатор Путін продовжує війну проти України, оскільки побоюється, що її завершення змусить його відповідати за скоєне. Водночас він сподівається, що зможе припинити бойові дії, не втративши життя та владу.
Про це в етері Еспресо заявив експерт Національного інституту стратегічних досліджень Олексій Їжак.
За словами експерта, Путін погодиться на переговори тоді, коли усвідомить, що від цього залежить його особисте виживання. Наразі російський диктатор, як вважає Їжак, переконаний, що продовження війни є необхідною умовою збереження його життя та влади.
«Коли Путін піде на переговори? Коли він побачить, що від цього залежить його життя. Зараз його життя залежить від того, що він продовжує війну. Йому здається, що він не може зупинити війну, інакше йому доведеться відповідати за все, що він накоїв», — пояснив Їжак.
Експерт додав, що Путін розраховує на появу обставин, які дозволять йому завершити війну без загрози для власного життя та втрати влади.
Водночас Їжак припустив, що завершення війни може відбутися і за іншого сценарію. У Росії можуть з’явитися люди, готові забезпечити передачу влади та покласти всю відповідальність за наслідки війни особисто на Путіна. У такому разі переговорний процес можуть розпочати вже вони.
«Можливо, з’являться люди в Росії, які готові будуть забезпечити спадкоємність влади при передачі всієї провини за те, що відбулося, особисто на Путіна. Можливо, інші люди підуть на переговори», — зазначив експерт.
На його думку, головне завдання — домогтися припинення війни, незалежно від того, хто саме з російського боку ухвалить відповідне рішення.
Їжак наголосив, що для наближення завершення війни необхідно змінити ситуацію на користь України та створити умови, за яких продовження бойових дій ставатиме дедалі невигіднішим для Росії.
«У будь-якому разі, щоб це наблизити, мають бути баланси. І має бути негативна для Росії динаміка і на фронті, у кілзоні, на землі та в повітрі», — наголосив експерт.
Раніше генерал-лейтенант у відставці Ігор Романенко заявив, що Путін з Трампом хочуть «дотиснути» Україну.
Ми раніше інформували, що диктатор Путін уже отримує політичні переваги від заяв Дональда Трампа про дизельну угоду з Росією.

article_title: Cryptocurrency exchange founded by Reform donor Ben Delo sued for £20m
article_content:
A cryptocurrency exchange founded by the billionaire Reform UK donor Ben Delo is being sued for £20m over claims that the company mis-sold financial products in the UK.
Lewis Barber, who is a software engineer, alleges that BitMEX offered crypto derivative products to investors in the UK, despite not being regulated or approved to do so by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
The claim filed at the high court but not yet served on BitMEX contends that under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 such contracts are void and that consumers are entitled to restitution of any bitcoin lost on those trades.
Barber claims that he lost bitcoin between 2018 and 2022 to the value of £20m through trading the derivatives offered by BitMEX, which amplified gains or losses for investors depending on the changing value of the cryptocurrency.
Barber’s lawyers allege he may be one of thousands of non-professional investors in the UK who sustained heavy losses after being sold derivative products by BitMEX in breach of FCA rules and consumer protection laws.
Barber’s claim is against HDR Global Trading Limited, the owner and operator of the BitMEX cryptocurrency derivatives exchange which has been shut down.
Barber’s statement of claim says that BitMEX “conducted promotional campaigns on a worldwide basis and did not exclude the United Kingdom from their reach”.
It goes on: “The Defendant placed at least one advertisement in the Times (published on 3 January 2019) which promoted the Defendant”.
The claim alleges that “the financial products that it was offering to [Barber] in the United Kingdom did not fall within the scope of financial services regulation in the United Kingdom”.
It adds: “On or around 3 March 2020, the FCA issued a warning that the Defendant may have been conducting trading in regulated investments in the United Kingdom without FCA authorisation.”
A spokesperson for BitMex said: “No such claim has been served on HDR Global Trading Limited.”
Gareth Keillor, a partner at Seladore Legal which is representing Barber, said: “This is a substantial claim concerning losses sustained by Lewis over a number of years.
“Lewis’s case is that BitMEX entered into these transactions without the authorisation required under UK law, and that the Financial Services and Markets Act therefore entitles him to recover the bitcoin he lost, or equivalent damages.
“The proceedings may also have wider relevance. Other UK-based persons may have entered into similar contracts with BitMEX, although whether any individual has a claim will depend on the particular facts and trading history.”
Details about the case have emerged after BitMEX’s voluntary closure on 23 September 2026, after what it described as a strategic review of the business.
The Seychelles-based company faces a number of actions internationally. In New York, investors are suing BitMEX for alleged theft of bitcoin and insider trading in a multimillion-dollar class action. The claims have been vigorously denied.
In Britain, Delo has been in the spotlight over a record-breaking £36m donation to the Reform party. Delo wrote in the Daily Telegraph that he was making the gift to Reform because he wanted a “fair fight and a level playing field”.
  Delo, alongside cofounders Arthur Hayes and Samuel Reed, pleaded guilty in 2022 to charges in the US for violating the Bank Secrecy Act due to alleged failures to comply with anti-money-laundering procedures.
They were fined and given custodial sentences, but were granted a pardon by Donald Trump in March 2025.
In 2024, BitMEX itself pleaded guilty to violations of the Bank Secrecy Act in failing to maintain adequate anti-money-laundering and know-your-customer programmes, and in January 2025 was required to pay $100m (£75m) to the US Department of Justice.
In his claim, Barber seeks the return of all bitcoin he lost in trading with BitMEX, or damages for trades going back a number of years. Should Barber be successful in his claims, the bill for BitMEX could run into hundreds of millions of pounds, it is claimed by his lawyers.
author: Daniel Boffey Chief reporter

article_title: Трамп зближується з Росією — Європа б’є на сполох: Financial Times розкрило тривожні настрої союзників
article_content:
Трамп зближується з Росією — Європа б’є на сполох: Financial Times розкрило тривожні настрої союзників
На тлі зростання напруженості через наміри Москви в Європі посилюються побоювання щодо надійності президента США Дональда Трампа та його готовності й надалі підтримувати Україну.
Домовленість між США та Росією щодо постачання російського дизельного пального викликала занепокоєння серед європейських союзників Вашингтона.
Про це пише Financial Times.
За даними видання, заяви президента України Володимира Зеленського на Варшавському форумі на адресу Дональда Трампа викликали занепокоєння серед низки європейських чиновників. У Європі побоюються, що загострення відносин між Києвом і Вашингтоном може мати негативні наслідки для безпеки регіону.
Частина європейських посадовців намагалася пояснити політику американського президента його внутрішньополітичними пріоритетами. Вони визнали, що домовленість із Росією була неприємною для європейських союзників, однак наголосили: для Білого дому краще залишатися залученим до війни в Україні, ніж повністю відмовитися від підтримки Києва.
Водночас інші чиновники вважають, що надмірне занепокоєння суперечкою навколо Трампа не має сенсу та лише демонструє чергову спробу догодити американському лідерові.
Натомість вони закликають Європу позбутися залежності від президента США, якого вважають ненадійним, і врахувати, що геополітичні цілі Вашингтона вже не збігаються з європейськими інтересами.
Італійська політологиня Наталі Точчі з Інституту європейської політики при Університеті Бокконі звернула увагу на те, що європейські лідери досі не мають спільного розуміння того, як реагувати на дії американського президента.
«Почуття реальності на індивідуальному рівні є відносно високим, але на колективному — майже нульовим. Правда в тому, що ми й досі так само збентежені (Трампом), як і два роки тому. Це не просто розгубленість, а глибший стан психологічного зриву в Європі», — зазначила Точчі.
Раніше генерал-лейтенант у відставці Ігор Романенко заявив, що Путін з Трампом хочуть «дотиснути» Україну.
Ми раніше інформували, що президент Сполучених Штатів Дональд Трамп заявив, що «дасть знати», якщо Росія порушить енергетичне перемир’я з Україною.

article_title: Judge extends White House access to banned media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico
article_content:
A federal judge ordered the White House on Tuesday to continue allowing journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to access the building as the media coalition’s lawsuit against the Trump administration plays out.
Timothy Kelly, a district court judge, had on 24 September granted a 14-day reprieve for the news organizations, which six days earlier had been banned by the president in an extraordinary move from entering the White House grounds “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”.
“Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them, shall not execute, implement, or enforce the September 18, 2026, decision to revoke the White House ‘hard pass’ press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, thereby maintaining the status quo since the Court’s entry of a temporary restraining order on September 24, 2026,” the judge wrote in granting a preliminary injunction requested by the plaintiffs.
The organizations filed a lawsuit on 21 September seeking to overturn the ban as a violation of their rights under the US constitution. But that temporary restraining order expired on Tuesday, bringing the media companies into court late last week to ask for a preliminary injunction that would lift the ban during the duration of the lawsuit, which could take months.
During arguments at the E Barrett Prettyman Federal Courthouse in Washington, Kelly seemed inclined to lift the ban indefinitely, telling a lawyer for the federal government that his side had “a notice problem” that was “probably the biggest hurdle” they had to overcome.
The Trump White House gave no advance notice to the media companies affected to say that they were at risk of losing their press badges, which the news organizations have said are essential to their ability to cover the administration. While the White House sent letters to the media companies informing them of the ban, they did so post-hoc, after building access had already been cut off, in violation of binding court precedent.
In his ruling on Tuesday, Judge Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs “are likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two First Amendment claims”. While access to the White House is not guaranteed, court precedent dictates that once it is provided to journalists, it cannot be taken away for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.
During arguments for a preliminary injunction on 8 October, media lawyer Theodore J Boutrous told the judge that Trump had offered a “confession” – in a Time magazine interview last week – that he was banning the media companies explicitly because of the content of their reporting, not because of any other considerations, such as national security.
“The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump,” Boutrous told the judge.
The judge seemed to agree. “President Trump’s own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before,” he wrote.
Although the White House has largely adhered to the judge’s prior ruling restoring access on a temporary basis, journalists for CNN and Politico have on occasion been prevented from performing “pool duty” – covering the daily activities of the president – because the administration has interpreted the judge’s temporary restraining order to solely require access to the White House complex, not smaller spaces like Air Force One or the Oval Office.
The judge required the media plaintiffs to post a bond of $1.
In a statement, Boutrous said of the judge’s ruling: “When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment. Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers.”
The court, he added, “was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future”.
