article_title: Улюблена блогерка Трампа «проїхалась» по ньому після угоди з Путіним
article_content:
Улюблена блогерка Трампа «проїхалась» по ньому після угоди з Путіним
Американська блогерка Лора Лумер, відома підтримкою Дональда Трампа, виступила на боці України після домовленостей президента США з Путіним.
Відома американська блогерка, ультраправа активістка та прихильниця Дональда Трампа Лора Лумер знову стала на бік України — цього разу після оголошених домовленостей Вашингтона з Москвою та російських ударів після заяв про «енергетичне перемир’я».
Про це Лумер написала у соцмережі X.
Блогерка заявила, що підтримує українців, і звинуватила Володимира Путіна у демонстративному ігноруванні домовленостей, про які заявляла адміністрація Трампа.
«Я підтримую народ України. Путін явно має ні за що нашу адміністрацію і нашу країну. Вчора він порушив режим припинення вогню в енергетичній сфері, що стало демонстративним і зухвалим викликом президенту Трампу», — написала Лумер.
Вона також висловила підтримку українцям, які продовжують потерпати від російських атак.
«Мої думки — з народом України, який продовжує зазнавати ударів російських балістичних ракет», — додала блогерка.
Лумер уже ставала на захист Зеленського
Це не перша за останні дні заява Лумер, яка розходиться з риторикою Трампа щодо України. Раніше американський президент заявив, що Україні нібито потрібен новий лідер. У відповідь Лумер фактично стала на захист Володимира Зеленського та пояснила, що відсутність виборів в Україні пов’язана з воєнним станом і війною, яку продовжує Росія.
За її словами, вимагати заміни Зеленського нелогічно, оскільки вибори зможуть відбутися після завершення війни.
«Путін може легко припинити атакувати Україну. Він відмовляється. Припиніть війну — і Україна проведе вибори. Чому більше людей не злі на Путіна? Він є джерелом кожної проблеми, пов’язаної з війною між Росією та Україною», — писала Лумер.
Вона також наголошувала, що українці передусім намагаються вижити в умовах війни.
Угодою з Путіним Трамп підняв проти себе «бунт»
Дизельна угода Дональда Трампа з Володимиром Путіним уже спричинила спротив як у Європі, так і всередині самих США. Союзники Вашингтона заявляють, що не збираються послаблювати санкції проти Росії, а американські політики ставлять під сумнів законність рішення президента.
Німеччина підтвердила, що й надалі повністю дотримуватиметься санкційного режиму ЄС і не планує відновлювати закупівлі російських енергоносіїв. У Берліні також наголосили, що підтримка України залишається незмінною, а країна вже кілька років не залежить від російської нафти.
Паралельно скандал спалахнув і в США. Сенатор-республіканець Том Тілліс заявив, що є «вагомі підстави» вважати, що Трамп може не дотримуватися чинного законодавства, яке після повномасштабного вторгнення РФ заборонило імпорт російської нафти.
Тілліс також дав зрозуміти, що питання дизельної угоди може вплинути на підтримку президентських ініціатив у Конгресі. Окремо він звернув увагу на співпрацю Росії з Іраном і застеріг, що додаткові доходи Москви потенційно можуть опосередковано підтримувати дії, спрямовані проти американських військових.

article_title: Республіканці повстали проти Трампа через Путіна: що і чому обурило його однопартійців
article_content:
Республіканці повстали проти Трампа через Путіна: що і чому обурило його однопартійців
У США вибухнув скандал через рішення Трампа щодо російських нафтопродуктів.
Домовленість президента США Дональда Трампа з Москвою про постачання дизельного пального з РФ на світові ринки і його схвальні заяви на адресу «фюрера» Володимира Путіна викликали нову хвилю критики з боку республіканців. За кілька тижнів до проміжних виборів до Конгресу Росія знову опинилася в центрі політичних суперечок у Вашингтоні.
Про це йдеться у матеріалі The Japan Times.
Трамп заявив, що працює з Путіним над виведенням російських запасів дизельного пального на світовий ринок. Хоч це рішення фактично послаблює багаторічні санкційні обмеження, але Білий дім пояснює цей крок прагненням знизити ціни на пальне напередодні виборів 3 листопада. Водночас у Європі попереджають, що збільшення експорту дизеля може принести Москві додаткові доходи та посилити її можливості продовжувати війну в Україні.
Дії Трампа стали небажаним сюрпризом для деяких республіканців, партія яких намагається зберегти свою незначну більшість у Палаті представників і Сенаті.
«Нам потрібен президент, який готовий очолити вільний світ. Давайте будемо чесними. Трамп є і завжди був слабким у ставленні до Путінат», — заявив представник-республіканець з Небраски Дон Бейкон.
Своєю чергою, сенаторка від штату Мен Сьюзен Коллінз приєдналася до інших республіканців і трьох демократів, які написали листа зі скаргами на Трампа, який, з їхніх слів, ігнорує закон 2022-го про заборону імпорту російської нафти.
«Сполучені Штати не повинні надавати Путіну фінансову допомогу, поки Росія продовжує вбивати українських мирних жителів», — написали сенатори.
Троє з чотирьох республіканців, які підписали лист у неділю, — Сьюзен Коллінз, сенаторка від Аляски Ліза Мурковскі і сенатор від Північної Кароліни Том Тілліс — під час першого процесу імпічменту Дональда Трампа проголосували за його виправдання. Тоді Палата представників звинуватила президента в незаконному блокуванні допомоги Україні, щоб змусити Володимира Зеленського оголосити розслідування проти колишнього лідера Джо Байдена і його сина Гантера. Коллінз, яка нині бореться за переобрання, тоді заявляла, що Трамп засвоїв «досить важливий урок».
Водночас частина республіканців, зокрема конгресмен від Пенсильванії Браян Фіцпатрік і конгресмен Дон Бейкон, планують домагатися голосування за новий законопроєкт, який має заблокувати імпорт російської нафти. Однак для подолання можливого президентського вето їм, імовірно, доведеться заручитися додатковою підтримкою.
Інші республіканці захищають Трампа, стверджуючи, що він намагається знайти спосіб завершити війну Росії проти України й водночас знизити ціни на дизельне пальне для американців.
Зауважимо, що вартість дизеля та пічного пального стала однією з болісних тем для республіканців напередодні виборів. Особливо гостро це питання стоїть у штатах, де точиться напружена боротьба за місця в Сенаті, зокрема на Алясці та в Мені, а також у сільськогосподарських регіонах Середнього Заходу, де значною мірою залежать від дизельного пального.
Напередодні дня виборів Трамп і частина республіканців розглядали й інші способи стримати ціни. Зокрема, кілька кандидатів і сенаторів пропонували тимчасово заборонити експорт дизельного пального зі США. Однак зрештою Трамп відмовився від цієї ідеї.
Зауважимо, що одним із приводів для суперечок в Америці стала інформація про весілля Дональда Трампа-молодшого, витрати на яке, за даними ProPublica, частково покрив російський олігарх Умар Кремлєв. Він витратив на це сотні тисяч доларів, зокрема оренду приватного острова в Карибському морі.
Сенатор-республіканець Джон Кертіс закликав розслідувати цю справу та викликати причетних до суду. Водночас сам президент Трамп заявив, мовляв, його син пообіцяв відшкодувати олігарху витрати.
«Тостер — це весільний подарунок. Вечірка на приватному острові, оплачена олігархом, пов’язаним із Путіним, — зовсім інша річ», — наголосив Кертіс.
Окрім того, раніше газета The New York Times повідомила, що двоє ключових політичних радників Трампа — Кріса ЛаСівіту і Джеймса Блера — перервали виборчу кампанію, щоб консультувати уряд на Балканах, який є союзником Путіна. За даними видання, уряд витратив понад 4 млн дол. на лобістів і політичних консультантів, пов’язаних із президентом США і республіканцями.
Своєю чергою, Трамп у соцмережах припустив, що може звільнити політиків, якщо в їхній роботі виникне конфлікт інтересів. Однак згодом заявив, що не бачить жодних порушень у їхній діяльності.
Як повідомлялося, Європа повстала проти курсу Трампа щодо Росії. У Європі вважають, що тиск на енергетичні доходи РФ залишається одним із головних способів змусити Кремль піти на переговори. На саміті ЄС лідери країн планують закликати до нових санкцій проти Москви і обмеження її нафтових доходів.
Окрім того, ексспецпредставник президента США з питань України Кіт Келлог заявив, що Україна повинна мати повну свободу завдавати ударів по цілях на території Росії у відповідь на агресію Кремля.
description: У США вибухнув скандал через рішення Трампа щодо російських нафтопродуктів.

article_title: We are behind you and that will not change, PM tells Zelensky
article_content:
We are behind you and that will not change, PM tells Zelensky
- Published
"We are behind you and that will not change," Andy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelensky, as he hosted the Ukrainian leader in Downing Street.
Zelensky was in London as part of efforts to reinforce backing from allies after Donald Trump called for him to go and lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.
The prime minister said Ukraine was willing to discuss an energy ceasefire proposed by the US president but said Russia's response had been "further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine".
Zelensky said: "Our people, we survived and continue to do this because we have strong partners and I'm very proud that we have one of the strongest partners in our history and it's your people, Andy."
The Ukrainian president was greeted with a hug from Burnham, cheers from civil servants and a rare honour guard as he arrived in Downing Street.
Ahead of Zelensky's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones.
- Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC 
  - Published2 days ago
Ukrainian officials have said that overnight strikes by Russian missiles and drones had left at least 600,000 people without electricity.
For the second consecutive night, Ukraine said it had not received advanced warning from its allies of a wave of missile strikes coming from Russia.
Zelensky has suggested the US had threatened to restrict intelligence-sharing unless he agreed to sign up to an energy ceasefire. Trump has denied the US is holding back information.
An adviser to the president has also said Ukraine's ability to defend itself from incoming missiles has been hindered by disruptions to its connection with the Starlink internet network, owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said the move "cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation".
Writing on X, Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".
Speaking in Downing Street, Burnham said the recent days had been "dark and difficult" for Ukraine, with the country suffering "heavy bombardment".
He told the Ukrainian leader: "You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain.
"We are behind you and that will not change."
Earlier in the day, Burnham had been invited to criticise the US decision to lift sanctions on Russia, when, at Prime Minister's Questions, Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey asked if the PM agreed there had been a "shameful Trump betrayal".
Burnham acknowledged that Zelensky was "carrying the heaviest of weights" but avoided attacking Trump, instead telling MPs that his role was to "repair bridges so that the support comes back".
"Therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together."
He added that Zelensky would not come away from his trip "empty-handed".
In a statement following the meeting, a Downing Street spokeswoman said the leaders had discussed "Russia's blatant indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure".
She said the prime minister promised that the UK would continue to develop "innovative military solutions for use on the battlefield in Ukraine, including retrofitting British capability onto equipment gifted from other partners".
On Friday, Trump shocked European allies when he announced that he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release an initial 300,000 tonnes of diesel, with more to follow.
Concerns about the cost of living are playing a key part in the US's November elections and the US president hopes his deal with Russia will reduce the cost of diesel.
The agreement runs counter to sanctions imposed on Russia by the US and its allies in a bid to choke off funds for Putin's war in Ukraine.
The deal came days after Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" and that it was time for Ukraine to "get a new president".
The criticism marks a renewal of Trump's previous hostility towards Zelensky which resulted in an infamous public row between the two men in the Oval Office.

article_title: Reform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and extreme comments
article_content:
Reform UK has been rocked by a fresh crisis after councillors and election candidates for the party were caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.
Three councillors have already stood down from the party, which said it was conducting an investigation over the first revelations from an ITV undercover investigation that aired on Wednesday.
Reform leader Nigel Farage has postponed a major announcement that was due to take place in Essex on Thursday morning as the party tries to contain the fallout expected to come from further revelations in the coming days. That will include revelations from undercover filming of senior Reform politicians and officials working at its UK headquarters.
Farage has made repeated pledges over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.
However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites,” and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.
Feeney won seats on Birmingham city council and Solihull Metropolitan borough council and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull. He has announced that he has left Reform “for personal reasons”.
Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues.
Feeney was filmed with other candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, talking about where a local mosque might be built. After they make extreme racist comments in the discussion, Feeney says: “Oh god, we’re all going to end up in the papers”.
Chris Whelan announced he had resigned from Reform on 12 October “on personal and health grounds”. Campbell is still in post.
Dean Miller, a Reform councillor for Bromley, was filmed separately making a range of comments during campaigning for the Makerfield byelection, including when he discussed what he would do with illegal immigrants crossing the Channel.
Reform has been attempting to pre-empt the impact from the ITV investigation, which will potentially be at its most damaging when footage from inside Reform’s London HQ airs.
The party used a statement issued on Wednesday night to accuse ITV and Hardcash Productions of “extreme methods of deception”.
“They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees,” it said.
The party said that this came at a time when Farage and other members of Reform were “being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation”.
“They have not included this in their report, despite being on notice since March this year. There is currently an ongoing police investigation relating to security breaches against Mr Farage, as is well known,” it added.
Reform said that not all individuals covertly recorded by ITV are members of Reform UK, adding: “Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced. In some cases, there have been suspensions and due process must be followed.”
The latest crisis to hit the party comes at a time when it has been stalling in the polls and faces problems including the fallout from a different undercover investigation which filmed senior officials discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party.
The outcome is also awaited of a parliamentary standards commissioner investigation into whether Farage should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.
Bridget Phillipson MP, chair of the Labour party, said: “The extreme racism and appalling behaviour exposed by this investigation is truly sickening. Nigel Farage can’t shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples. Every Reform councillor, council candidate or party member found to have made such despicable comments must be thrown out of Reform UK immediately.”
author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent

article_title: Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments
article_content:
Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments
- Published
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.
Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast undercover filming, gathered over a year, of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.
In the film, Undercover: A Year in Reform,, external a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites".
Labour described the investigation as "truly sickening" adding: "Nigel Farage can't shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples."
A Reform spokesman said: "Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced" and that in some cases there had been suspensions.
The spokesman added that the party had improved its procedures but some individuals who did not share their values would occasionally make it through vetting.
ITV's filming involved eight figures in Reform – the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total.
Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended.
ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.
These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, having defected from the Conservative Party in 2025.
He told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites".
Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than one per cent of British population can be non-white."
The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons," and would be continuing as an independent councillor.
Reform Party leader Nigel Farage has repeatedly said he wants to get rid of those he has called "bad apples."
Two years ago he said he didn't want Reform to be "a sectarian or racially based party in any way at all".
"I'm going to be absolutely ruthless about it," he said.
In a statement released after ITV's film was broadcast, Reform said the party "had improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting".
The Conservatives said: "Nigel Farage promised to make Reform ready for government. These sorry individuals are proof he has failed."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."
A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."
- Bigots not welcome in Reform UK, says Nigel Farage 
  - Published20 September 2024

article_title: Burnham tells Zelenskyy’s UK’s support for Ukraine ‘will not change’ – as it happened
article_content:
Burnham praises Zelenskyy for showing 'leadership' after Trump's energy ceasefire comment
Here are fuller quotes from the public statements by Andy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelenskyy before their main meeting.
Burnham said:
MrPresident, it’s a great privilege for me to welcome you to Downing Street today. And you’ve just seen the reaction [a reference to the crowd cheering as he arrived]. Obviously, you’ve seen the solidarity and the support you’ve got from everybody here in Britain. We’re behind you. And that will not change.
We know that the last few days, the last few hours, have been very dark and difficult days for Ukraine. We know that the country sustained heavy bombardments in the last 24 hours in Kyiv, particularly. And we would want to extend our condolences to all of those people in Ukraine who’ve lost loved ones as a result of what has been happening.
President Trump made a call at the weekend for an energy ceasefire. And, Volodymyr, you have shown your leadership in saying that you would be prepared to sit down and discuss what that looks like, to make sure we protect people from a very harsh winter that lies ahead in Ukraine.
Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine. It’s clear to the world, again, who the aggressor is in this conflict.
However, in these moments, Britain will continue to provide you with whatever support that we can. And today I’m announcing that we are accelerating the delivery of British-made air defences for you, and we will make sure that they’re in place as soon as possible. (See 9am.)
I’ve also asked all of our ministers here in the government to do whatever they can, extra, to support you, and they are looking at all possible avenues …
All of the people of Ukraine have our support. There are such connections between our two countries. We will forever stand by you through this difficult time.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, is holding talks with Andy Burnham in No 10 now, where he said he would be discussing with the PM “difficulties” caused by Ukraine getting less intelligence and reduced access to the Starlink internet access in the light of Washington striking a diesel deal with Russia. (See 5.31pm.)
Andy Burnham has ruled out Labour doing deals with the Green party after its conference voted for a motion saying “Zionism is racism”. (See 12.57pm.)
Dominic Cummings has not received much coverage for his appearance at the Lords constitution committee this morning, where he was talking about constitutional safeguards, and I’ve afraid I have too much other stuff on to give it much attention. But if you want to listen to a better expert on the constitution, Peter Hennessy, the historian and crossbencher peer, has given an interview to the Lord Speaker’s Corner podcast. The transcript and audio are here.
Hennessy said constitutional safeguards could quickly crumble. He said:
So much would go wrong.
If we had a government that came in, if it was a Reform government, and the first thing they did was sack the cabinet secretary, and got rid of the career officials who came in under the Northcote-Trevelyan merit, not partisanship rubric of selection, and had a go at the judges, too – it would be very easy if they had a big enough majority for them to take away the fundamentals … as the first act that they were doing week one.
We have a major competitor for power now in this country who said what they’d do. In effect, they would rip up the constitution, and the way we recruit and promote our senior civil servants, and indeed would interfere in the choice of judges.
And so much would go … We’d crumble, and it would be very hard to get it back.
Government says 900,000 people could get stronger rights under crackdown on bogus self-employment loopholes
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has told published a consultation paper on employment status reform. This sets out how the government proposes to implement plans he announced at Labour conference to close the “bogus self-employment loopholes” that deny workers basic rights.
Explaining the plans, the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade says:
Bogus self-employment is a practice whereby some businesses mislabel staff as self-employed to avoid statutory obligations.
However, the day-to-day reality is that many of these people are treated as workers, not self-employed. External estimates suggest that as many as 900,000 people may currently be affected by this and could be missing out on core employment rights.
The proposals to be consulted on could provide greater clarity to businesses and workers, levelling the playing field for those businesses who are already doing the right thing and clamping down on abuses. This could help workers such as parcel couriers, delivery drivers, hairdressers and gig economy workers.
But, in a good article on this topic for LabourList, Tom Berger points out that the plans don’t include a firm commitment to create a single status of worker in employment law – something that in opposition the party did commit to.
Meri Ahlberg, a senior policy adviser at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, a thinktank that has argued for employment status reform, said:
The measures in the government’s consultation are a step forward for making sure people have the rights and protections everyone deserves. But without putting single worker status and tax reform on the table for the near future, it will still be cheaper to employ people in less secure jobs and millions of workers will be left without sick pay and parental pay. It’s time basic protections were in place for everyone, however they work, and that existing protections are enforced properly.
Zelenskyy says he will be discussing intelligence sharing 'difficulties' and Starlink access with Burnham
And this is what Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, said in reply to Andy Burnham.
We are very thankful, all our people in Ukraine, we absolutely thankful to your nation. You are strong people, a very supportive nation …
[This is a] terrible war. Absolutely terrible as.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was being attacked by ballistic missiles and hundreds of Iranian drones.
There was no energy ceasefire, he said. It looked like “escalation from Russian side”.
He said he wanted the war to stop.
We have massive attacks today, and it’s a pity that we had also some difficulties. What I want to discuss with Andy – about Starlink and about intelligence. There are lot of different surprises on which you can’t count.
He said UK was one of Ukraine’s strongest partners.
A reporter asked Zelenskyy if he could confirm that the US had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, and if it had slowed down Starlink – meaning Ukrainian weapons lose access to the internet at very high speeds (making them inoperable). Zelenskyy did not answer.
Burnham praises Zelenskyy for showing 'leadership' after Trump's energy ceasefire comment
Here are fuller quotes from the public statements by Andy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelenskyy before their main meeting.
Burnham said:
MrPresident, it’s a great privilege for me to welcome you to Downing Street today. And you’ve just seen the reaction [a reference to the crowd cheering as he arrived]. Obviously, you’ve seen the solidarity and the support you’ve got from everybody here in Britain. We’re behind you. And that will not change.
We know that the last few days, the last few hours, have been very dark and difficult days for Ukraine. We know that the country sustained heavy bombardments in the last 24 hours in Kyiv, particularly. And we would want to extend our condolences to all of those people in Ukraine who’ve lost loved ones as a result of what has been happening.
President Trump made a call at the weekend for an energy ceasefire. And, Volodymyr, you have shown your leadership in saying that you would be prepared to sit down and discuss what that looks like, to make sure we protect people from a very harsh winter that lies ahead in Ukraine.
Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine. It’s clear to the world, again, who the aggressor is in this conflict.
However, in these moments, Britain will continue to provide you with whatever support that we can. And today I’m announcing that we are accelerating the delivery of British-made air defences for you, and we will make sure that they’re in place as soon as possible. (See 9am.)
I’ve also asked all of our ministers here in the government to do whatever they can, extra, to support you, and they are looking at all possible avenues …
All of the people of Ukraine have our support. There are such connections between our two countries. We will forever stand by you through this difficult time.
Burnham tells Zelenskyy's UK's support for Ukraine 'will not change'
Andy Burnham told Volodymyr Zelenskyy Britain’s support for Ukraine “will not change”, as he welcomed the leader to Downing Street.
In public remarks before their main meeting got under way, Burnham said:
You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change.
He added that recent days had been “dark and difficult” for Ukraine, which has suffered “heavy bombardment in the last 24 hours”, and he extending the UK’s condolences to those who had lost loved ones.
Burnham said Zelenskyy was “prepared to sit down and discuss” the energy ceasefire proposed by Donald Trump, but added: “Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine.”
He said:
In these moments, Britain will continue to provide you with whatever support we can.
Zelenskyy said he was “thankful” for British support, saying:
Our people, we survived and continue to do this because we have strong partners and I’m very proud that we have one of the strongest partners in our history and it’s your people, Andy.
Andy Burnham has welcomed President Zelenskyy to Downing Street.
As they posed for pictures outside No 10, there was a loud cheer from Foreign Office staff who were there watching. (The Foreign Office is next door to Downing Street.)
King Charles meets Zelenskyy, before Ukrainian president's meeting with Burnham
Another ‘show of support’ feature of President Zelenskyy’s visit is the fact that he was invited to meet the king at Buckingham Palace. Foreign leaders coming to Downing Street for a political visit don’t normally get to meet the king at the same time. But Charles and Zelenskyy have met many times before, and the king is a strong supporter of Ukraine.
Thank you to His Majesty King Charles III for the audience. For me, it is important to have the opportunity to personally thank him for the unwavering support of Ukraine. We appreciate all the assistance from the United Kingdom.
While Andy Burnham has been relatively guarded in what he has said in public (see 12.40pm) about Donald Trump buying diesel from Russia and declaring that Volodymyr Zelenskyy should be replaced as Ukrainian president, this is a way of using the apparatus of the state to send a visual signal that the UK is very, very firmly on Zelenskyy’s side on this one.
President Zelenskyy is expected to arrive in Downing Street shortly. Unusually, there will be a ceremonial military guard there to greet him. According to Sky News, Downing Street has not laid on one of these for a visitor since Donald Trump visited Chequers.

article_title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
article_content:
Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
- Published
Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.
The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club.
Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal.
The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up.
Separately, it has emerged that a representative from the club joined a trade mission to India this week alongside Burnham's successor as mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig.
The trade mission was organised by the business department, but as first reported in the Guardian,, external Manchester City's invitation came from the Great North, a coalition of Northern mayors and regional leaders.
The government said it played no role in approving the club's presence on the trip.
- Man City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts 
  - Published29 September
On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.
The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.
It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".
But the statement did not specify that this referred to, external two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.
A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at £300 for hospitality.
Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately £699.
Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a £150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.
But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.
BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024.
Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman.
But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount.
Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City.
"This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football."
And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners".
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.
Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester".
"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."
Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me."
With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club".
When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement.
The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned.
In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations.
The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.
Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict.
Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 - defended a decade-old deal between the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).
Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report.

article_title: The Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechanging | Editorial
article_content:
When Donald Trump pledged to end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours of re-entering the White House last year, no one with any depth of insight into the conflict believed him. But Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image as a master dealmaker. After a period when it seemed that Kyiv’s European allies had steered the US president away from pro‑Kremlin partisanship, he has reverted to the grotesque view that Ukrainian capitulation is a necessary precondition for peace.
These are the perilous circumstances in which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham on Wednesday in Downing Street. In recent days, the US president has called for a change of government in Ukraine. He claimed that a partial ceasefire had been agreed, while Russia escalated its bombardments. According to Mr Zelenskyy, the latest missile strikes have come without the intelligence warnings from the US that have, in the past, facilitated self-defence. There have been reports of Ukrainian soldiers losing access to the Starlink satellite network, controlled by Elon Musk, the US tech oligarch. This raises suspicion of coordinated pressure to tip the scales in Russia’s favour after many months when Mr Putin’s forces have failed to deliver significant advances and his country’s economy has been suffering from the effect of Ukrainian missile and drone counterstrikes.
Mr Trump is unhappy with Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries. He claims that this is the cause of high energy prices afflicting American consumers and threatening Republican prospects in next month’s midterm elections. The domestic imperative to keep pump prices down led Mr Trump to do a grubby deal to import diesel from Russia, in flagrant breach of international sanctions.
The real driver of global energy prices is not Ukraine defending itself from Russian attack, but Mr Trump’s failing war against Iran. However, the US president is incapable of admitting any fault. Blaming Mr Zelenskyy enables him to deny his own culpability and, with malevolent encouragement from Mr Putin, to revive the preposterous notion that Ukrainian intransigence rather than Russian aggression is the reason why his promise to broker a peace deal remains unfulfilled.
Disrupting Mr Trump’s pro-Russian delusions is not easy, but it has been done before. It is not a gratifying diplomatic task to indulge the monstrous vanity of the US president by trying to impress upon him a view of his country’s national interest, that Mr Putin is not an ally of his country or his personal friend, which is self-evident to any rational observer.
Mr Burnham rightly resists invitations to denounce the US president in public. He recognises that Ukraine’s cause and, by extension, also the cause of European democracy more widely, is better served by making the case in private. The best response to Mr Trump’s perfidy is for Mr Zelenskyy’s friends to reaffirm their support, as Mr Burnham has done, thereby signalling that Ukraine will not be beaten by deals between the Kremlin and the White House.
Russia is failing to achieve its war aims because the invasion was conceived in delusional hatred for the very idea of independent Ukrainian nationhood, which routinely underestimates that country’s will to resist. That is a flaw in Mr Putin’s plans that no amount of collusion with Mr Trump can fix.

article_title: UK threatens to ban Eritreans over migrant return policy
article_content:
UK threatens to ban Eritreans over migrant return policy
- Published
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders.
From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs.
Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans.
Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boats migrants in the 12 months to June - accounting for 18% of arrivals, external, according to figures from the House of Commons Library.
The Eritrean embassy in London has been contacted for comment.
"Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused," said Mahmood.
She said she would not hesitate "to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate".
The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of "abruptly" withdrawing co-operation earlier this year.
The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission.
The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara.
Earlier this year, the UK threatened bans against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
Restrictions were announced against the DRC last year, but the Home Office said these have been lifted after co-operation on returns improved.
Angola and Namibia both agreed changes before restrictions were introduced.
When announcing changes to the UK's asylum system in November, Mahmood said visa penalties would be applied to countries that failed to co-operate with returns policies.
Penalties included an "emergency brake" on visas for countries with high asylum claims until they take back citizens in the UK illegally.
According to Home Office data, more than 20,400 people have arrived in the UK by small boats so far since the beginning of this year, down 40% from the same period last year.
There were more than 40,600 returns and deportations from the UK from July 2025 to June this year - an 8% increase on the same period last year.
Of those who had been returned, less than 6,000 has been convicted of a criminal offence.

article_title: UK’s ‘incoherent’ approach to China plagued by lack of expertise, report says
article_content:
The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship.
An audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised.
“Successful UK engagement with China must always be framed by an understanding that the PRC (People’s Republic of China) is an inherently hostile authoritarian state that does not share our values,” an underlined sentence in the audit, published on Wednesday, reads.
The inherent power imbalance in the relationship with the world’s second largest economy is “further compounded by muddled policy and weak engagement”, it says.
It cites the example of a visiting Chinese delegation who had noted that no one who engaged with Beijing at a senior level in government was a Mandarin speaker, or had significant experience of living in China.
Although British expertise exists, it is often siloed and “not translated into capability”, says Ipac, pointing to budget cuts as an additional problem.
Ipac counts almost 50 MPs among its members, including from Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Scottish National party, the Greens and Reform.
Ipac member and former security minister Tom Tugendhat said the report was “a clear-eyed and realistic take on the defining foreign policy problem of this century, filling a gap left by years of policy neglect”.
A UK government spokesperson said that while working with China presented opportunities, “we are also clear-eyed about the threats China poses, and national security is the first duty of government”.
“We will cooperate with China where we can while meeting any challenges head-on,” they added.
The Chinese embassy in London said Ipac’s “sole agenda is to manufacture falsehoods, mislead the public, and undermine China’s relations with other countries”.
The report “distorts the facts” and “is not even worth refuting”, it added.
While the Ipac report accepts that “disengagement is not an option”, it advocates for clearly defined red lines around issues such as critical infrastructure, frontier technologies and human rights.
The document offers several recommendations, including better institutional coordination, the strengthened use of national security tools, and diversification of supply chains.
Emerging technologies such as AI represent “another front we’re potentially facing”, Labour’s Dame Meg Hillier said at the launch, with the report identifying areas of concern such as disinformation and surveillance capabilities.
The climate crisis is identified as a low-risk area for cooperation and alignment.
“Climate targets as set will not be met without cooperation with China, and accepting medium-term dependence. This means accepting supply chains tainted by forced labour and unfair trade practices,” the audit says.
The government conducted its own audit of the UK-China relationship in late 2024 but has said it cannot publish most of the detail for fear of damaging national interests.
But Evan Fowler, author of the Ipac report, said that a public audit was important “because engagement with China doesn’t just happen at the government level”.
It was “very welcome” that there was an understanding that better language skills were needed to deal with China, said Kerry Brown, a former diplomat and director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London.
However, he said, “the critical issue now is lived experience” in China.
“Some of the members of Ipac … are really keen on promoting this very security-oriented idea that going to China is in some ways opening you up to exposure,” he said.
“You can’t teach really important things in a classroom; you can only go and learn them through daily life … and that is the thing that is very difficult to do now, and it’s also the thing that doesn’t seem to be supported.”

article_title: The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’
article_content:
‘My mark of failure or success is whether I can get bills down or not. That’s the only thing I’m in this job to do.” So said Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, recently, bracing for the hike in energy bills that looks inevitable in January. Industry projections suggest £400-ish on an annual basis is on the way, with “stubbornly high” levels for the rest of decade even if wholesale gas prices cool down.
So, yes, one can understand why “affordability” is Fahnbulleh’s “top priority”. And, as this newspaper reported last week, there is likely to be an intervention in that direction in chancellor John Healey’s budget this month: £1bn of extra support for poorer households this winter.
But the chat in energy-land is about what comes after that – and what Fahnbulleh’s other remarks about covering the costs of the energy system in a “fairer” way seem to be hinting at.
Will the government finally get round to designing a co-called “social tariff” for energy – a way to get financial support to the most needy on a more targeted basis than the clunky warm homes discount, the mechanism Healey will be obliged to use?
Will Healey, after chopping VAT from electricity for six months, do so permanently and then shift more green levies and other “hidden taxes” of energy transition into general taxation?
And is Fahnbulleh also contemplating something very different? Welcome to the idea of the “rising block tariff” (RBT), the unwieldy name for the proposal to give every household an initial block, or allowance, of cheaper gas and electricity to cover “essential” use and then make subsequent blocks more expensive. In other words, heavier energy consumers would pay higher rates for their extra units.
Fahnbulleh has got officials in her department to explore an RBT model. And, note, the New Economics Foundation, the thinktank she used to lead, is a proponent.
The Joseph Rowntree Foundation is another backer: in its version, the government could fund an RBT with, say, £5bn of public money, allowing bills to fall for most households – but, critically, the biggest savings would flow to light users, who tend to be low-income households. “An RBT would produce greater reductions in bills lower down the income distribution,” it says.
What’s not to like? Plenty. There are at least three reasons why an RBT has few fans elsewhere, not even among charities and thinktanks that focus on fuel poverty.
First, Citizens Advice regards low energy use as a poor proxy for low income in practice. Traditional electric heaters, with high electricity usage, “are more common in social or private rented homes, where people can’t change their heating system”, it argues.
Quite: a progressive-sounding policy could end up being nothing of the sort, especially if second-home owners, by spreading their usage, are winners. If the reply is that an incomes overlay could address tricky cases in both directions, why not just do the data modelling work to design a proper social tariff in the first place?
Second, a rigid RBT would be an awkward fit with a renewables-heavy system where the most interesting innovations are “flex” tariffs to exploit very windy or sunny hours when wholesale power prices are dirt cheap. There is a danger of baffling consumers by making them mix their blocks with their flexes.
Third, a core aim of the energy transition is to drive take-up of electric vehicles, heat pumps and so on. That becomes harder if the message to consumers is that “the more electricity you use, the more you’ll be charged per unit”.
Lobby group Electrify Britain calls block tariffs “hugely counterproductive” for electrification: “You can’t ask families to go electric and then pursue a policy that would charge them more for doing so.”
That feels the killer point: an RBT model cuts across too many other goals. Fahnbulleh should keep things simple: go for a serious social tariff or discount scheme that effectively identifies “vulnerable” energy users. That idea has enjoyed wide support for years. Block tariffs are too complicated and fiddly to administer.

article_title: Burnham rules out coalition with Greens after 'Zionism is racism' motion
article_content:
Burnham rules out coalition with Greens after 'Zionism is racism' motion
- Published
Andy Burnham has said he will not support his party forming a partnership with the Green Party as long as it maintains a policy of defining Zionism as a form of racism.
Speaking in the House of Commons, the prime minister said the motion, backed by Green members at its party conference earlier this month, was "wrong" and "antisemitic" and Labour would have "nothing to do with it".
The motion said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/ or domination of the non-Jewish population".
It was criticised by Jewish groups, as well as four Green MPs and two former leaders, one of whom said it was "dangerous" and "divisive".
Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" and that he had wanted to see it amended.
However, he has defended the substantial part of the motion arguing that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
The motion, having been backed by members, has become party policy but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.
The subject was raised during Prime Minister's Questions, when Conservative MP Dame Harriett Baldwin urged Burnham to "rule out co-operating" with the Green Party.
Burnham replied: "Can I condemn the motion that was passed unequivocally.
"It is wrong, it is antisemitic, and this side of the House will have nothing to do with it.
"We will always take the right response when it comes to any partnerships we have with other parties.
"We cannot support a partnership with a party that holds the position that has recently been adopted."
In response to Burnham's comments, Polanski said: "I'm the only Jewish leader of a political party. I'm a victim of antisemitism every day and I've made it clear Jewish people are welcome in my party.
"You're a prime minister who arms a genocide and locks pensioners up for opposing it."
He added that the "blurring of challenging Israel and antisemitism" was "dangerous and irresponsible".
Labour is currently in coalition with the Green Party on local councils in Sheffield, Lewes and Warwick. In more than 10 other areas, Labour run the council with the Greens as part of a broader coalition.
A Downing Street spokesman would not confirm if the prime minister's position extended to local areas or just applied to national government level.
The adoption of the motion has prompted some Green Party figures to call for changes to the party's rules.
Last week, MP Ellie Chowns told the BBC: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."
Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the 230,000 members in the party.
Key backer of the motion Lubna Speitan has defended the motion arguing that it aimed to oppose "racist systems of oppression" adding: "We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions."

article_title: That Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything is a big help to the PM | John Crace
article_content:
Little things please little minds. And minds don’t come much smaller than some of those in Westminster. If a researcher had come up with a study that showed one element two points higher in value than countless other experiments, it would almost certainly be marked down either as an outlier or “within the margin of error”. At the very least, no conclusions would be drawn until many other experiments had been conducted which had produced similar results. Serious scientific journals would just laugh at you if you asked them to publish your findings.
And yet. In one – just one out of many – recent opinion poll, the Tories have increased their ratings by a couple of points and are now for the first time in years in second place, ahead of Reform. And all of a sudden, Kemi Badenoch is insisting this is incontrovertible proof that the Tories are back in business. All the sins of its 14 years in government have been wiped clean. All hail to Kemi, the new chief. She is the chosen one. And the Conservatives are a government-in-waiting.
You need a certain amount of self-confidence to make it as a party leader. Not to say a touch of the Panglossian. The ability to insist all is well when it is turning to shit. But you can have too much of a good thing. You must at least be within touching distance of reality. And it appears that once again Kemi has jumped the shark. The one good poll has gone to her head and she now believes she is invincible. Nothing can touch her narcissism.
In her early days as Tory leader, Kemi used to crash and burn every week at prime minister’s questions. She considered preparation and research to be beneath her. Instead, she peddled the latest conspiracy theories she had seen on X with a series of scattergun questions. She only started to improve when her minders tried to get her to concentrate for 10 minutes of sustained questions on one subject. Yet over the conference break, Kemi has undergone a brain wipe. She is back in her happy space of making it up as she goes along. No one knows better than Kemi.
Sadly for the Tory leader, Kemi’s approach is also Andy Burnham’s happy place. Much more of this and the prime minister is going to look forward to his Wednesday lunchtime encounters in the Commons. Never look an easy win in the eye. Not because he’s word perfect – there are still a lot of unanswered questions about his involvement with the Manchester City owners – but because there’s an engaging openness to him you seldom find in other politicians. A willingness to answer the questions and to appear as if he’s listening. Mr Congeniality.
It’s also a big help to Andy that Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything. Arguments are always so much simpler when your opponents are deluded. Indeed you couldn’t escape the irony of her insisting that it was Burnham who was consistently mistaken about everything. Even the head of MI5, Ken McCallum, had slapped the prime minister down for suggesting hostile actors had interfered with the Brexit referendum. Kemi can’t bear the fact she might have had the backing of the Russian state in 2016.
Burnham chose to respond to Kemi in the most hurtful way. With kindness. No anger. Just a gentle reiteration of the facts. It was incontrovertible that Russia had tried to influence both the 2019 general election and the EU referendum. The evidence was in front of our eyes. Russian bots selling misinformation all over social media. It was a non-story. And far from correcting him, McCallum had gone out of his way to confirm this.
What the MI5 boss had gone on to say was that it would be better for everyone concerned if we all just dropped the story as it would only give the Russians further encouragement. And who had been keeping the story alive for a third day by bringing it up at PMQs? Take a bow, Kemi. The Tory leader seemingly content to carry on doing the Russians’ dirty work for them. At least Nathan Gill, Reform’s former leader in Wales, had the sense to get paid for this. Kemi was doing it for free. Andy ended by saying he would be delighted to debate whether Brexit had done more harm than good. Kemi shook her head. This isn’t an argument the Tories are keen to have. Their feeling is Brexit is something we all just have to suck up.
After that, Kemi looked a bit lost. Clueless. Scouring her file for something to ask. Instead she just wasted her own and everyone else’s time. First by asking about the budget. As if Burnham was ever going to say: “You know what? Since you’ve asked I might as well give you a heads-up two weeks early.” All Kemi achieved was to make herself look half witted. She ended up sounding a bit hurt. She had hoped that Andy would have spent more time problem-solving than point-scoring. There are days with Kemi when even giving a straight answer comes across as point-scoring.
Earlier in the day, Dominic Cummings had been giving evidence to a Lords select committee on how to prevent rogue actors from entering No 10. That should have been a very short session. Just stop morons like Boris Johnson from appointing people like Dom as his special adviser. Curiously this hadn’t occurred to Dom, nor to the dopey peers interrogating him.
It was a bizarre hour and a half. The sort that gives you mild PTSD. Your mind goes back to all the damage he did to the country during the Brexit referendum and during his year in No 10 and suddenly the horror floods back. Just when your brain has done its best to forget all about him. To consider him a footnote in history. For the record, Dom is as deluded as ever. His main thesis seemed to be that Boris was right to allow him to do whatever he liked but no one else in No 10 should ever be allowed to do what he did. Some things never change. We are well rid of him.

article_title: Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham matters
article_content:
Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham matters
Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed President Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday, as the Ukrainian leader looks to shore up his European allies five years into Russia's war on Ukraine.
Burnham told Zelensky that Britain "would forever stand by you" and that he was accelerating the delivery of air defences to Ukraine.
Burnham previously told MPs that he would try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States and that Ukraine won't leave "empty-handed".
The two leaders met at No 10 Downing Street where Zelensky was welcomed with a military ceremonial guard - thought to be a first for a foreign leader.

article_title: This civil war on the British right is a charade – its politics are more united than ever | Jonathan Liew
article_content:
Kapow! In a warmly received conference speech, Kemi Badenoch turns her fire on Reform UK, describing it as “weird”, and ruling out an electoral pact. Slap! Not to be outdone, her former colleague Robert Jenrick derides Badenoch as a champion of the wealthy, which is quite rich for a guy who looks like he’s just accidentally ingested a bundle of £50 notes through his sphincter. Bosh! Reform’s Richard Tice and Restore’s Rupert Lowe clash online over the result of a council byelection in Derbyshire, in which the Greens profited from a split rightwing vote. “Vote Restore get Islamists,” Tice chides. “Vote Reform, get some random Bangladeshi bloke,” Lowe responds.
Meanwhile, the Conservatives are back. The Kemibounce is real. The Keminaissance is true. We’ve all got a severe case of the Kemirrhoids. And you may wonder why much of the media are talking about a Badenoch revival in a year where her party lost 563 councillors and 40% of its councils, remains about four points below its apparent nadir of 2024, and in which the leader herself appears incapable of doing a broadcast interview without looking like a restaurant diner who received exactly what she ordered and is inexplicably furious at it. The point is that the Conservatives are a serious party of government again, and the reason is that we all said so.
And even if we take into account Badenoch’s curiously resilient personal polling, this does feel like a largely arbitrary volte-face. There was a soft-focus interview in the Financial Times, a warm editorial in the Sun, and generally positive coverage of the Tory conference in the rest of the rightwing press. Tom Tugendhat, the new shadow foreign secretary and once regarded as a party moderate, had a sympathetic platform in the Observer to defend the party’s opposition to net zero and the European convention on human rights.
From a safe distance, it is possible to regard these realignments in a fairly optimistic light. The right is tearing itself to shreds, potentially allowing a leftwing alternative – or failing that, Labour – to clean up. And in the continuing scrap between Lowe and Nigel Farage, or the series of aggressive Telegraph editorials aimed at Restore Britain, it is tempting to glimpse a reassertion of basic, consensual values in which, for all our many disagreements, certain voices will always be beyond the pale.
Occasionally you will even hear it said on the progressive left that a strong centre-right is a necessary, welcome bulwark against the extremist far right. That while we can disagree strongly and vehemently with Badenoch’s party, we can also recognise the ways in which a moderate right can act as a kind of cordon sanitaire against the nativists, ethnonationalists and race theorists who may otherwise get their hands on the levers of government. All of which would probably be true, if that were actually what was happening. But is it?
Let’s start with the Tories, who appear to be rapidly pivoting towards a demographic that one insider has described as “Waitrose Woman”: affluent, socially liberal, turned off by culture-war rhetoric but laser-focused on tax and the economy. “We have done a ton of opinion research over the last 18 months,” a Conservative source told the Mail on Sunday. “You do have to appear reasonable.” Or, as one shadow cabinet minister told the Guardian: “We have outsourced our toxicity to Reform.”
But in the real world, beyond superficial branding, how different are the two platforms? Shadow cabinet member Nick Timothy called Islamic prayers in Trafalgar Square un-British, “an act of domination”, “straight from the Islamist playbook”, and Badenoch backed him. Badenoch advocates a ban on pro-Palestine marches, but argued Tommy Robinson should not receive the same treatment. Another shadow cabinet member, Katie Lam, advocated mass deportations of legally settled immigrants in order to make Britain a “culturally coherent group of people”.
The Conservative police and crime commissioner Donna Jones responded to the masked vigilante protests in Portsmouth by blaming the government for failing to control our borders. A former neo-Nazi activist was selected as a local election candidate for the Tories, and subsequently appointed as an adviser. In the Telegraph, Badenoch wrote that anyone committed to net zero targets is no longer welcome in the party.
As for Reform, Monday’s announcement that it would immediately suspend the UK asylum system brought the party further in line with Restore, both of whom advocate ICE-style raids, the stripping of citizenship from people who thought they were here permanently, and the cessation of aid and visas to countries who refuse to take back migrants. Suella Braverman, a former Tory, now says she can “understand why some people are drawn to Restore”, and suggests people of colour cannot be English.
Indeed, you can argue that net zero, welfare, tax cuts, Israel, Brexit, defence spending, trans rights, Donald Trump, the obsession with grooming gangs and Islam, immigration and, most importantly, their common enemies, there is barely a sheet of nori to separate the three parties. And yet at the same time we are expected to believe that these parties engaged in an eternal blood feud, rather than three heads of the same army, pursuing different strategies towards a common cause.
Naturally Westminster will fall for this narrative wholesale, focused as it is on divisions over alliances, personalities over ideas. The Conservatives will be allowed to carry on decontaminating their brand without decontaminating their platform. Farage will continue as flag bearer for the movement, sweeping up donor money and airtime. Meanwhile Restore serves an equally important role as the engine of change, the pressure group, the brains trust: shifting the rhetorical window to the right while allowing Badenoch and Farage to look reasonable in comparison.
The civil war on the right is in fact a charade, a fake fight being enacted for our benefit. The right bloc is now a single basic substance, responsive and carefully calibrated to the different audiences it needs to capture. Reform, already in informal talks with Restore, can now tailor its offering to the post-industrial north, Midlands and Wales, leaving the rehabilitated Conservatives – the acceptable face of the project – to concentrate on their southern and rural heartlands. And if, after all the bickering and infighting, a coalition should be required? Do we really expect a Conservative party founded entirely on the gain and exercise of power to suddenly turn it down?
To those on the left, the idea of a rightwing meltdown feels vaguely reassuring. But in reality nothing here is being repudiated. The personalities may butt heads for our entertainment, but the ideas and politics are largely common among them all. The parts are being divvied out, but ultimately the production remains the same.
- 
  Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist
