article_title: Burnham asks for his Widdecombe remarks to be corrected
article_content:
Burnham asks for his Widdecombe remarks to be corrected
- Published
Andy Burnham has asked for Parliament's official record to be corrected after telling MPs an "individual" was "responsible for the murder" of Ann Widdecombe.
The prime minister had faced calls to apologise for the remarks, made during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, with a senior Tory saying they breached the "presumption of innocence" in criminal cases.
A man was charged with Widdecombe's murder in July, but is yet to enter a plea for the charge and is not due to stand trial until next year.
A No 10 spokeswoman said a correction had been issued to Hansard, the official report of parliamentary debates, and would be "published in due course".
Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform spokeswoman.
A trial before a High Court judge is scheduled for 8 June next year, and a plea and case management hearing on 29 January.
Earlier this month, Kerry was also charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.
Speaking on Thursday, Conservative shadow Commons leader Jesse Norman accused Burnham of breaching Parliament's sub judice rule, which says MPs should not refer to pending court cases in order to avoid influencing the outcome.
He added that the prime minister's comments at PMQs had "breached the legal presumption of innocence".
He asked Commons leader Sir Alan Campbell, a government minister, to "correct the record, withdraw the remark and apologise on behalf of the prime minister".
In response, Sir Alan said the prime minister had "said that he misspoke, he has apologised and he has corrected the record".
"There is no excuse for misspeaking in the House and I am not trying to explain that away, but this prime minister is characterised by an authenticity and a passion in the way that he responds," he added.
"It is not unusual for prime ministers or anybody else to misspeak in the House.
"As long as they correct the record, which he has done, that should be put into perspective."
description: The prime minister had faced calls to apologise for his comments about the alleged murder of the former minister.

article_title: Repressive, secretive and highly militarised: Eritrea, the east African country facing UK visa ban threat
article_content:
Eritrea, the east African country embroiled in a row with the UK over its refusal to accept the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals, is considered one of world’s most secretive and repressive states, with reports of arbitrary detention and severe restrictions on freedom of expression, opinion and religion.
Situated in the Horn of Africa and bordering Sudan, Ethiopia and Djibouti, it became a sovereign state after gaining independence from Ethiopia in 1993 following a 30-year war.
The country is run by an authoritarian regime under Isaias Afwerki, who led separatist forces to defeat Ethiopian forces in 1991 and became president in 1993. He has served as president since independence and heads the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice, the country’s only legal political party.
Eritrea has not held a national election since independence. A constitution that was ratified in 1997 by the constituent assembly has still not been implemented nearly three decades later.
In 2001, the government shut down all independent newspapers after the publishing of an open letter by senior ruling party officials calling on the government to implement the constitution and hold elections.
A highly militarised state, Eritrea runs a compulsory national service system that requires students to study at a military training centre in their final year of secondary school. They undergo military training and political education before working in either military units or civilian national service roles that can last decades.
The repression and conscription has forced many Eritreans to risk harsh punishment for evading, deserting or escaping the military by fleeing the country. It is estimated that up to one-third of the Eritrean-born population lives abroad.
Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat to the UK in the year ending June 2026. Earlier this year, Eritrea abruptly withdrew cooperation with the UK on migrant returns, and on Thursday the UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said all Eritreans could be stopped from coming to the UK unless the country agreed to accept more rejected asylum seekers and criminals.
Eritrea’s political, economic and social framework has been defined by a doctrine of economic self-reliance, with the country notably rejecting foreign aid.
It was an Italian colony and parts of the country feature early to mid-20th-century Italian modernist architecture. The capital, Asmara, was inscribed as a world heritage site in 2017, with Unesco describing it as “an exceptional example of early modernist urbanism at the beginning of the 20th century and its application in an African context”.
A multi-ethnic country, Eritrea is mainly made up of the Tigrinya people. Its extensive Red Sea coastline (1,388 miles) gives it a strategic position along the Red Sea corridor.
The country has been in the spotlight in recent weeks because of fears of war with Ethiopia. Both countries have accused each other of aggression. Ethiopia has claimed Eritrean troops crossed up to 60km (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, while Eritrea has said the accusation is a fabrication to create a pretext for war.
The escalation is linked to renewed fighting between Ethiopian government forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), an armed opposition group, in Tigray, which borders Eritrea.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, a claim that Eritrea has denied. On Tuesday, Ethiopian forces advanced to Zalambessa, a town on the border with Eritrea that was under Tigrayan rebel control.
author: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi

article_title: The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win | Frances Ryan
article_content:
Back in 2009, months before the coalition government unleashed sweeping austerity, the then Conservative backbencher Iain Duncan Smith produced a study that would go on to lay the foundations for the rollout of universal credit. Now, nearly two decades later, Duncan Smith and his thinktank, the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), has published State of Dependency: a landmark report promising to expose “the full scale of Britain’s worklessness crisis”.
The study paints a picture of mass benefits reliance: it identifies 3,400 local areas where more than half the working-age population are on out-of-work benefits, or “economic opiates”, as the authors call them. They’ve even provided an interactive map (in the yellow and black colours of a road hazard sign, no less) so members of the public can type in their postcode to see if their neighbourhood is “a welfare hotspot”.
This is not just another ugly social policy report from a politically sidelined former minister – it is a gauntlet being thrown down ahead of Britain’s big benefits debate.
Next month, the government is expected to release two major reports into the social safety net: the Timms review on personal independence payments (Pip), which pays for some of the extra costs of disability in England and Wales, and the Milburn review into young people who are out of work.
It wouldn’t be overstating the importance of Westminster reviews to say their recommendations could shape the future of our welfare state for decades to come. With almost 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) and the disability benefits bill rising in cash terms, Andy Burnham will face immense pressure to use the proposals to launch a once-in-a-generation overhaul of the social security system.
An overhaul in itself is no bad thing. Disabled people applying for benefits face a debilitating mess of bureaucracy and barriers, while too many young people have been abandoned, facing greater obstacles and fewer services. The question is, will the overhaul actually improve conditions for the people who rely on it, or buckle to the anti-benefit sentiment that’s been bubbling up for months?
That the right is not currently in power won’t stop it from wielding significant influence on what’s to come, in large part thanks to its dominance of Britain’s media ecosystem. Legacy media are not even hiding their attempts to shape November’s reforms before they are announced, with the Times this week launching a “welfare inquiry” to investigate the impact of the benefits “crisis” on public finances.
Some of this is made up of concrete policy proposals, such as the Daily Mail’s pitch to radically means-test Pip. But increasingly much of it is just vibes, a vague sense that this disability problem is getting out of control (or having one is becoming “cool”, as the Telegraph recently put it), and that disabled people – particularly the young – are somehow grifting “perks” while everyone else struggles with rising bills.
The changes in how people consume media since the last major benefits reforms in the early 2010s mean the risks of misinformation and outright bigotry are even greater. Last week, Nigel Farage announced plans for a new video studio in Westminster for the launch of Reform TV on YouTube, with the party’s proposed £50bn benefits cuts presumably being lined up as viral content
Keep an eye out too for a revival of the striver v scrounger rhetoric as energy and housing costs are set to lead to the worst living standards in modern times by 2029-30. There are few easier ways to convince workers that the unemployed should go hungry than when they’re cutting back on their own food shop. It is telling that the CSJ study includes a section directly comparing “economically inactive claimants” with workers: someone on minimum wage would have to work six days a week to match “the security, cash and ease” a disabled person gets from a package of state benefits, it proclaims. About 1.4 million foreign nationals receive working-age benefits, it ominously adds. Divide and conquer never gets old.
A Labour government is no guarantee these divisions – worker v claimants, old v young, migrant v citizen – won’t be espoused from the cabinet table. No recommendations by Timms or Milburn have been confirmed yet, but Whitehall sources say there are potential plans to scrap a key part of universal credit for under-25s and replace it with a multi-billion pound package to get people back into work.
Sure, it’s depressing if ministers are tempted to bow to the prevailing political winds by pulling cash from young people, but it’s not exactly surprising. For decades, the right has set the boundaries for what Britain’s safety net can be, resulting in little more than subsistence-level benefit rates, an ever crueller culture of testing and a sicker population.
The conventional wisdom has always been that change can only go one way: the benefits system can repeatedly become more punitive and error-strewn, but never more compassionate or accurate. For a leader who has defined himself as someone unafraid of large-scale change, Burnham is well placed to challenge that orthodoxy – if he wants. The opportunity to transform the benefits system does not come up often, and it is rarer still for a Conservative prime minister not to be at the helm.
It’s unfashionable to say it out loud but the truth is that Labour has the power to radically improve the disability benefits system: introduce more evidence-based assessments and reduce the need for mass appeals against incorrect decisions; stop using public money to line the pockets of private companies; and end unnecessary reassessments for lifelong disabilities. Similarly, ministers can address why more people need disability benefits in the first place: by investing in threadbare mental health support; addressing NHS waiting times and poor preventive health services; fixing Access to Work; and tackling employer attitudes to disabled candidates.
The right has long believed it has a monopoly on Britain’s benefits system, as if it were still paternalistic Victorians punishing and pitying the lower orders. But check the calendar and it is 2026. There is a Labour government in office and two big wads of research coming that can at last lay the groundwork for remaking our safety net. The millions who rely on it must hold their breath to see whether that chance will be grabbed or thrown away.
- 
  Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist

article_title: Former DUP leader Donaldson sentenced to 15 years in prison for child sex abuse
article_content:
Former DUP leader Donaldson sentenced to 15 years in prison for child sex abuse
- Published
Jeffrey Donaldson has been sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences, including one count of rape.
The former DUP leader stood with his hands clasped in front of him in the dock of Newry Crown Court as his sentence was handed down.
Judge Paul Ramsey said Donaldson's crimes, which took place between 1985 and 2008, had led to a "catastrophic descent into disgrace".
He was sentenced to 11 years for his crimes against Victim B and four years for offences against Victim A.
The 63-year-old, who was convicted in June, is seeking to appeal his convictions.
Both sentences will run consecutively.
But Donaldson will spend only half his 15-year sentence behind bars.
Because the offences were committed before the Criminal Justice (Northern Ireland) Order 2008 came into effect, he qualifies for 50% remission.
Should his attempt to appeal his convictions fail, it means he will be released from prison at the end of 2033.
The remainder of his sentence will be under supervision in the community on licence.
Donaldson will also be required to sign the Sex Offenders Register for life.
The former Lagan Valley MP has been in Maghaberry Prison since then and returned to it on Thursday afternoon after being sentenced.
Donaldson spends up to 18 hours a day in his cell at the prison, which holds around 1,600 inmates.
Since being convicted, he has been held in its Moyola Unit, a part of the jail used for prisoners with health care needs, and does not share a cell.
It is thought he is in this unit for his own safety from risk of attack or verbal abuse from other prisoners.
Judge Ramsey said aggravating features include the length and protracted nature of the offending spanning many years.
He also took into account the youth of the victims and the age difference between them and Donaldson, adding that he could not accept Donaldson's lack of other convictions as a mitigating factor.
The judge said by contesting a case, a defendant avoids the reduction in sentence they would have got if they had pleaded guilty.
"It is highly significant that the defendant denied the offences to the police, he denied them in evidence and to the probation officer he continues to maintain his denials," the judge said.
"He has doubled-down in his denials.
"There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort."
Jeffrey Donaldson's wife, Eleanor Donaldson, had faced a trial of the facts on mental health grounds, meaning the jury was asked to find out if she did the acts or did not do the acts of which she was accused.
The jury found that she had done the acts in relation to five charges – including four counts of aiding and abetting her husband's offending.
She has applied to appeal the verdict.
She cannot be given a prison sentence but could be given a treatment order or an absolute discharge.
The judge is due to decide on this at a later date.
- Dawn arrest to 'descent into disgrace': How victims exposed Jeffrey Donaldson's lies 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Jeffrey Donaldson's life in politics: From DUP leader to convicted child sex abuser 
  - Published18 hours ago
Statements from both victims were released after the sentencing and read out by Det Ch Insp Leah Crothers.
Victim A said the impact of the crimes committed against her did not end when the abuse ended.
"For years I carried shame, anger and guilt, and questioned whether I was worth protecting or worthy of being loved.
"The last few years have been nothing short of a battle.
"The conviction does not erase the abuse or undo the impact of what happened to me, and I will always carry the consequences of it.
"But those responsible do not control me now. They forever changed me, but they will not take my future. The cycle is being broken and it ends with me."
Victim B said what happened to her as a child had "affected everything since then".
"What would it be like not to be afraid at night, not to wake up shaking, not to have nightmares and not to lock away every feeling I have?
"What happened took away my ability to trust people and, in all honesty, I don't think I really know what trust or love truly is. Nothing can ever change what was done to me. I wish it could.
"I stood up, many years later, because for me this is about drawing a line in the sand and knowing that the Donaldsons can no longer hurt anyone else.
"Many people get to look ahead and plan their lives with hope, I've never known what that feels like. My hope was taken away from me a long time ago."
Victims robbed of their childhood - PSNI
Det Ch Insp Crothers from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), said Donaldson's victims have "suffered immeasurably as they come to terms with what has happened to them as children".
"He robbed them both of their childhood and innocence."
She added that police "worked tirelessly" to build a "robust case against this man and his wife" whose offending "has shocked our local communities".
"The police service and our criminal justice system have sent a clear message: No-one is above the law."
The head of the Public Prosecution Service (PPS) Serious Crime Unit, Catherine Kierans, said the case "shows that sexual abuse can be hidden behind a facade of respectability".
"It also shows that no individual, irrespective of their position, status or public reputation, is beyond the reach of the law."
Kierans added that the "courage shown by the two victims in reporting the sexual abuse was the catalyst for a thorough PSNI investigation".
"I want to pay tribute to the victims in this case. We recognise that it took great courage to speak out," she said.
"Victims of sexual abuse should never feel shame for what was done to them. The shame belongs solely to those who commit these offences."
'Justice has been done' - DUP
Following the sentencing, the DUP said in a statement that Donaldson deserved "every day of the lengthy prison sentence".
"Today justice has been done with the sentencing of Jeffrey Donaldson for his vile and disgusting crimes against his victims.
"Our first thoughts are again with the innocent victims, who having suffered such evil, were re-traumatised through giving evidence at the trial.
"They deserve our compassion, support and respect. We hope they can find some measure of comfort and can look ahead to a new chapter in their lives.
"Regardless of status or position every individual must be held accountable for their actions."
Who is Jeffrey Donaldson?
Jeffrey Donaldson's time in politics began in 1985 when he was elected for the UUP as an MLA in South Down.
In 1997, Donaldson became the MP for Lagan Valley, representing the UUP. He would remain an MP until 2024.
However, in 2003, he quit the UUP and defected to the DUP.
Donaldson was awarded a knighthood in the 2016 Queen's Birthday Honours list, and, in 2021, Donaldson became leader of the DUP.
He remained leader until March 2024, when he was charged with sexual offences of a historical nature.
He was found guilty of all 18 child sex abuse charges, including one count of rape, in June 2026.
Donaldson subsequently asked for his knighthood to be forfeited and tendered his resignation from the Privy Council with immediate effect.
In July, Donaldson was stripped of his knighthood by the King.

article_title: The water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much faster | Nils Pratley
article_content:
It is strange now to recall that Thames Water had a prominent slot on what was known as “Sue’s shit list” – the internal Labour dossier, compiled by Keir Starmer’s first chief of staff, Sue Gray, of potential crises that could erupt at short notice and force the incoming administration to make some big decisions quickly.
That was July 2024. Here we are – more than two years later – and the Thames script has barely advanced. We’re still waiting to see if the financial crisis at the over-indebted, under-performing water company will be resolved by a creditor-led recapitalisation, special administration or something else.
Now Thames is seeking another £2.4bn slug of funding from creditors to stay afloat for another year and survive yet more back and forth between ministers, regulators and those same lenders. The new mystery element in the talks is what the prime minister, Andy Burnham, actually means by “greater public control”.
Still, Thames was an outlier – albeit a biggie – one might say. At least the government in 2024 cracked on with the job of deciding how to overhaul the wider water sector in England and Wales. Indeed it did: Sir Jon Cunliffe, a former deputy governor of the Bank of England, was commissioned to review what was needed and his detailed report landed in summer last year. The centrepiece was the abolition of Ofwat, the regulator.
Steve Reed, the environment secretary at the time, embraced Cunliffe’s proposals and declared the “the biggest overhaul of water regulation in a generation” via a new water bill. Game on?
Not exactly. The bill, which should have arrived this autumn, was delayed by the change of PM. Burnham has promised a “strengthened” version, which presumably will include the “public control” elements. In the meantime, Ofwat is still in place, and nobody knows which bits of the Environment Agency will be absorbed into the new super-regulator, or what the new body’s formal status will be. Will it, for example, be as formally independent as Ofwat, or will it be under a tighter ministerial leash?
Credit rating agencies have noticed the uncertainty. In dry language, Moody’s on Thursday issued a report noting that regulatory changes “appears to have stalled”, that “political scrutiny is heightened and may cause further delay” and the “potential increase in business risk will require stronger financial ratios to maintain credit quality”.
Moody’s, note, did not downgrade its assessment of the “stability and predictability” of UK water regulation, as it did in late-2024. But it did tiptoe up to the line: one of its slides at Thursday’s conference warned: “Our score could fall further.” Why does Moody’s opinion matter? Simply because rating agencies influence the price at which companies can borrow, which can itself affect the financing costs passed on to customers in bills.
The government should take the hint and decide what it actually wants from water reform. Emma Hardy, the water minister, at least indicated to the same conference that a formal transition plan to the regulator is coming soon. But that’s not the same as an actual water bill, which would reveal if the rest of the Cunliffe changes have survived.
It is, of course, entirely fair for an incoming PM to review what he wants from a bill. But the “public control” bit, if that’s delaying everything, needs to be nailed down sharpish. Is it simply the Cunliffe-compliant idea of greater powers of influence for mayors and local authorities? Or bigger changes to match the summer rhetoric? It’s impossible to tell – but it’s all taking far too long.
And make a decision one way or another on Thames. Half a parliament to address a supposedly urgent 2024 problem is extreme water torture.

article_title: «Це ганьба»: Трамп знову накинувся на Зеленського — що його розлютило
article_content:
«Це ганьба»: Трамп знову накинувся на Зеленського — що його розлютило
Американський президент заявляє, що Україна нібито має достатньо інших цілей для атак. Мовляв, не обов’язково бити саме по російській нафтовій інфраструктурі.
Президент США Дональд Трамп знову накинувся на українського лідера Володимира Зеленського і розкритикував його через відновлення ударів по російських НПЗ.
Про це він сказав в інтерв’ю телеканалу Newsmax.
Під час розмови ведучий попросив прокоментувати те, що Україна знову почала атакувати нафтопереробні заводи країни-агресорки. Трамп, відповідаючи, знову заявив про зростання цін на енергоносії.
«Якщо ви кажете мені, що Зеленський знову б’є по нафтопереробних заводах, то все, що він робить, — це підвищує світові ціни на нафту. Ну, я вважаю, що це ганьба. Є багато інших цілей… Є багато цілей, які можна вразити», — заявив Трамп.
Він наголосив, що дизельне паливо «потрібне нам і воно потрібне світові». Мовляв, так Київ «не робить доброї послуги світові».
Удари по НПЗ Росії — що відомо
Зеленський заявив Financial Times, що Україна відновила удари по НПЗ Росії після триденної паузи. Це сталося на тлі продовження російських атак на українські енергетичні об’єкти, попри оголошене Дональдом Трампом енергетичне перемир’я.
За словами глави держави, Штати висунули Україні жорстку умову щодо ударів по РФ. Чиновники вимагали припинити атаки по російських НПЗ, інакше погрожували позбавити Київ зброї і розвідданих. Як наслідок, США два вечори поспіль не попередили Україну про пуски балістики по столиці.
Своєю чергою, у Кремлі запанікували після заяви Зеленського, але водночас саме Київ звинуватили у зриві енергетичного перемир’я. Речник «фюрера» Дмитро Пєсков брехливо заявив, мовляв, Україна нічого не дотримувалася. Саме тому, каже він, «жодної новації немає».

article_title: Burnham asks for 'manual trawl' of records for former Man City links
article_content:
Burnham asks for 'manual trawl' of records for former Man City links
- Published
Andy Burnham has said he has asked for a "manual trawl" of records relating to his previous contact with Manchester City football club.
The prime minister said on Thursday he had asked the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to search "everything" to ensure "full transparency".
He continues to face questions over any relations he had with Man City while mayor of Greater Manchester for almost a decade until June. The club has been found guilty of "systematically" breaking Premier League rules.
Declarations of Burnham's contact with the club were released on Monday, but confusion grew later when it emerged records of two dinners Burnham had with Man City's chairman had been deleted.
Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday, Burnham said of the GMCA: "I've asked them to do a more manual trawl of everything, as I want everything possible to be out there."
He insisted that the occasions he dined with Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches at the Etihad in 2017 and 2018 were "included" in a statement issued by the local authority on Monday.
It comes after he was accused by his political opponents of seeking to cover up the meetings.
The GMCA statement, external mentioned a meeting Burnham had "informally" with Al Mubarak in the stands at a 2019 match, and a formal meeting the pair held at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit in October 2021, but did not specify the two dinners.
It went on: "In his capacity as Mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City FC at home matches on a small number of occasions [...]."
As mayor, Burnham previously declared the dinners from Man City, valued at a combined total of £1,000 for hospitality.
But records of them have since been deleted from the GMCA website.
The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term - but the authority has not clarified why the register dates back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024.
It also remains unclear what, if anything of significance, was discussed at the two dinners.
The BBC has asked the GMCA if it has received a request for a "manual trawl" and what this will entail.
Burnham has faced pressure since comments in a BBC interview in September, saying he would be "really concerned" if Man City's owners now sold the club, following an independent commission finding the club guilty of multiple Premier League financial rule breaches.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch told him at Prime Minister's Questions this week that the issue was not "going away".
The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period to 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into football operations.
The findings have outraged many and left the top flight of English football in limbo with its top team facing potential sanctions. Man City continues to deny any wrongdoing and has lodged an appeal.

article_title: It’s not the old two-party politics – but Labour and the Tories now know they can shun their populist challengers | Gaby Hinsliff
article_content:
Ask a straight question, get a straight answer. It’s how politics is supposed to work but almost never does, which is why on the rare occasions it happens the result can be faintly chaotic. What did Andy Burnham mean when he said – in response to a question from the Tory MP Harriett Baldwin – that Labour couldn’t partner with the Green party while it remains wedded to the “Zionism is racism” motion its members have just endorsed? Were Green MPs now barred from a future coalition government? If so, what about councils where they are currently sharing power with Labour?
Though Burnham was only confirming what ministers have been arguing privately for days, at first nobody seemed to know: tellingly, it took almost 24 hours for the Labour party chair, Bridget Phillipson, to confirm that unless local Green groups disowned that idea sharpish, “Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end”. So much for cuddly cross-party Andy, who always seemed so relaxed about rainbow coalitions. Now elected Greens in places such as Sheffield or Lewes must choose between power and members’ wrath, a useful rehearsal for what a hung parliament might feel like.
Westminster is increasingly realising that while nobody knows quite what’s in Burnham’s head except Burnham, unlike most prime ministers he is surprisingly liable just to tell you. He did it earlier this week on a podcast, pointing out that Russia tried to interfere in the Brexit vote (which is true, albeit the sort of truth that for complicated reasons prime ministers don’t generally dwell on). Now the safety catch is off again.
What did he mean with his comments about Labour and the Greens? Most likely just what he said: that the Greens crossed a line and it cannot be overlooked, especially by a party still recovering from its own battle with antisemitism. Green members did not just vote to adopt a policy that would condemn every Jew who believes in the right to a Jewish homeland, including those who simultaneously support the creation of a Palestinian state. The motion they backed advocates turning all of historic Palestine into a Palestinian state, a one-state solution wiping Israel off the map. Much as Kemi Badenoch did recently by insisting that her English-born children have every right to be considered English, no matter what the ethno-nationalists of Reform and Restore say, Burnham was simply showing that he has limits: this far, and no further.
Something has shaken loose over the party conference season. What we are seeing isn’t the return of two-party politics – things are still too volatile for that – but the return of leaders confident enough to set boundaries on what had become an almost abusive relationship with the public. They are no longer quite so terrified of naming extremism when they see it. More surprisingly, neither is behaving like a party needing to beg for coalition partners, whatever the electoral maths says.
After a period shadow boxing a prime minister who never seemed to know what he thought, Badenoch now faces one who does. That has brought drama back to the middle of politics and not just the radical edges, with genuine differences emerging between Labour and the Tories ahead of the budget over tax and spend, national security v social security, public v private ownership and the respective claims of younger and older people.
Her new strategy is not a million miles from the one outlined this week by the thinktank Bright Blue, in a paper on how the traditional European right can combat far-right populism: adopt draconian immigration policies but make the economy the actual focus of your campaign, and hold the line that citizenship can be earned rather than being determined by ethnicity (the chilling line peddled by some of those in Reform and Restore who argue openly that you have to be white to be properly English).
Though the polls still suggest the Tories can’t win without some kind of deal with Reform, the broad message of a conference speech in which Badenoch painted her rivals as aggressive weirdos who “threaten journalists, call veterans traitors and debate whether my mixed-race children are English” was that it would be a cold day in hell before that happened. That decision looks smarter with every passing journalistic exposé involving the kind of Reform councillor who thinks King Charles should be decapitated for supposedly being a secret Muslim.
Burnham didn’t go quite so studs-up on the Greens, but then he doesn’t need to. The party is already openly agonising about that anti-Zionism motion, opposed by four out of five of its elected MPs. The prospect of being politically ostracised for it may now strengthen the hand of Greens who think this freakishly hot summer might have been better spent campaigning on the climate crisis, not swerving questions about Israel’s right to exist. Yet there are risks for Burnham here, all the same.
Research by the pollster More in Common suggests that “progressive activists”, the group most commonly torn between voting Green or Labour, are significantly more likely than the average British voter to think worse of someone identifying as a Zionist. When Burnham called the Green motion antisemitic and wrong, he was confronting people whose support he may need in some Labour seats.
Sanctioning West Bank settlements, as this government has now done, isn’t enough for some of them: they want Burnham explicitly to call the Gaza war a genocide and stop proscribing Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation. (Polanski was notably quick to leap to the defence of the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, after it emerged her books are being withdrawn from sale in Britain because of her promise to donate royalties to Palestine Action: knowing where the money could be going leaves her publishers open to potential prosecution under anti-terrorism law, just for handing over her earnings.)
It’s technically possible that like some desiccated calculating machine, Burnham has crunched the numbers on all this and concluded that distancing himself from a row that has reportedly made one in three British voters less likely to vote Green (according to Opinium) is mathematically preferable.
But it’s more likely he was just doing the thing that got him here in the first place, and following his gut. If he can’t say what he thinks even now, in what passes for a honeymoon period, he never will. If basic norms are not enforced, they very quickly cease being norms. And if the Labour party can only win by sidling uncomfortably close to the kind of people it was until recently expelling for antisemitism – well, it’s not much of a Labour party. The chaos, in that sense, is probably just beginning.

article_title: Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
article_content:
Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
- Published
The UK economy's stronger than expected performance in August has been called a "sign of resilience" by Chancellor John Healey.
Healey told the BBC "it's really tough in the face of these economic global shocks" as the latest official figures showed the economy grew by 0.1% for the month, defying analysts' forecasts of a slight contraction.
It follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF) earlier this week.
Mr Healey said he wanted "to give people a bit of breathing space from the cost of living and cost of business pressures", promising to do so when he delivers his first Budget in two weeks' time.
Healey did not elaborate on what measures he will take in the Budget, but promised "where we can take action, we will".
But, vowing to keep up the government's approach to fiscal discipline, Healey said "where we want to do things we have to make sure we can pay for them within the Budget that we've got and control spending".
The latest figures from the Office for National Statistics showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August.
"It's a sign of resilience in the UK economy that some had not expected," Healey said.
The chancellor said the growth was "part of the discipline the IMF here in Bangkok this week has endorsed that they see in Britain".
Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply.
The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted.
Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period.
But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period.
August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%.
Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought".
He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs".
PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance.
"The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added.
- What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you? 
  - Published21 hours ago
- What is the Budget and what could be in it? 
  - Published21 hours ago
Healey told the BBC the "impact of AI on the economy, on productivity, is only just beginning to register".
He said the technology has "huge potential, as well as huge risks", adding that Britain's priority would be to ensure AI can be developed safely while unlocking the opportunities it presents.
The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations.
Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks."
The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget".
Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing."
He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape.
Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, Daisy Cooper, said the growth of 0.1% in August was "nothing to celebrate".
"The economy is stuck in first gear and barely crawling forward, while families are still struggling to make ends meet."
Healey went on to say the Budget would be tough and not include inflation top-ups for public sector pay.
Some experts and unions have called for extra cash for some departmental budgets, to account for the rising costs of providing public services and pay.
But, asked whether there would be extra money made available for nurses and doctors, the chancellor said: "People recognise these times that are tough for everyone, and what they do expect of a government is to manage with the budgets we've got, deliver the public services they need, and that's the challenge.
"Our departments have their spending, and the prime minister and I, being in lockstep about this, where we want to do things, we have to make sure that we can pay for them within the budgets that we've got and control spending."

article_title: The Guardian view on Stormont: voters in Northern Ireland deserve more than an endless cycle of dysfunction | Editorial
article_content:
Late last month, protesters deposited a sizable amount of foul-smelling green water on the steps of Stormont to draw attention to the appalling state of Lough Neagh, the largest freshwater lake in the British Isles. Years of agricultural pollution have created an environmental disaster in an area of huge ecological significance that once inspired the poetry of Seamus Heaney. Its plight should be a top priority for Northern Ireland’s devolved government. But the executive currently has other matters on its mind.
The sentencing of the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) Jeffrey Donaldson, after he was convicted of child sexual abuse, dominated Thursday’s headlines. Meanwhile, a cross-party political crisis continues to play out. Halfway through the financial year, Stormont has yet to set a budget. The current deadlock in negotiations with the Northern Ireland secretary, Sir Chris Bryant, could lead to one being imposed from Westminster. Cuts are already being made by default amid an atmosphere of stasis and policy drift.
An unwelcome revival of sectarian tension on the streets is further undermining the fragile political institutions established by the Good Friday agreement. On Monday, Northern Ireland assembly members debated a motion of no confidence in the first minister, Michelle O’Neill. The move followed the Sinn Féin vice-president’s participation in protests against a proposed Orange Order march on the Garvaghy Road in Portadown, controversially sanctioned by the Parades Commission for the first time in 28 years.
A prolonged standoff between unionists and mainly Catholic residents ended peacefully, after Sir Chris banned the parade on police advice. The absence of violence was a silver lining, but the episode showcased the dangers of what one politician described as “negative nostalgia”. As those seeking to revive a route notoriously associated with loyalist violence surely anticipated, the bitter row has reopened old wounds and unleashed latent animosities.
The motion of no confidence in Ms O’Neill was a performative exercise, with no chance of obtaining the necessary cross-community support. But the combination of no budget and a renewed culture-war confrontation means that Northern Ireland now risks being governed by a zombie administration until elections next May.
Given the dismal recent track record of Stormont collapses and suspensions, that should prompt some hard thinking in London and Dublin as well as Belfast. The scandalous condition of Lough Neagh symbolises the deficiencies of a polity that now seems trapped in an endless cycle of dysfunction. The steady deterioration of public services such as healthcare, education and policing can partly be attributed to underfunding. But matters have been made much worse by the existence of a political vacuum and sectarian grandstanding where effective government should be.
Power-sharing designed to reassure nationalist and unionist communities remains indispensable. But a loveless-marriage model that allows the largest party on either side of the divide to routinely bring assembly business to a halt is in urgent need of reform. Otherwise, faith in Stormont’s ability to act in the name of the common good is in danger of evaporating. Huge strides have been made in civil society since the Good Friday agreement was struck nearly three decades ago. But Northern Ireland’s voters currently do not have the politics they deserve.

article_title: 'Bring it on': Flynn challenges Burnham on independence referendum
article_content:
'Bring it on': Flynn challenges Burnham on independence referendum
- Published
SNP minister Stephen Flynn has called on the prime minister to "bring it on" and let the people of Scotland decide the country's future in an independence referendum.
Flynn, the party's former Westminster leader and now transport secretary at Holyrood, said the independence movement was facing its greatest-ever challenge.
But he insisted "we are winning the argument" and told delegates at the SNP conference in Aberdeen that "all of us should feel pride in how far our movement has come".
It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs a border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Ireland if there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed.
The PM later moved to clarify his position by telling First Minister John Swinney a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits".
Flynn told SNP members on the opening day of the conference that the party's focus was firmly on independence, with a major new campaign being announced.
He said: "Look at where we stand now – three nations of the UK whose leaders are committed to constitutional change, a British prime minister telling us we can have our independence when the people of Scotland want it.
"All of us should feel pride in how far our movement has come."
He added: "We are winning the argument, we can see that by reading the newspapers or listening to the panic of unionist politicians."
But Flynn warned there was "no shortcut" to achieving independence.
"One by one, we must persuade our families, our friends, our neighbours, of our cause. One by one, step by step," he said.
"It takes effort, it takes patient persuasion, it takes hard graft, but we can see that it is working and it is precisely because it is working that the period ahead will be the greatest challenge our movement has ever faced.
"With the weight of Scottish public opinion moving to our cause, we will see that final lap through together – for Scotland."
Swinney will bring the SNP's three-day conference to a close with a keynote speech to delegates on Saturday.
He is expected to promote his renewed push for independence, having said he wants to hold a second independence referendum by 2031.
The Supreme Court has ruled that the Scottish government is unable to do so without the consent of Westminster.

article_title: Just as Saint Nige thought it was safe to reappear, along comes pesky ITV | John Crace
article_content:
Sometimes the world can be very unfair. As though life is just one cruel joke. How else to make sense of everything? For when the history books come to be written, Nigel Farage will go down as one of the century’s unluckiest politicians.
Poor Nige. All he has ever wanted is a better Britain. A country united in a shared vision where everyone gets along with one another. Where people of all faiths and none look out for each other. Where men and women of all colours are treated as equals. Where Nige can teach the world to sing in perfect harmony.
So why do so many bad things keep happening to such a good person? Where’s the justice in that? How come Nige has been given a lead role in the rewrite of Little Britain’s Book of Job. Nige as a latter day Old Testament prophet put on Earth to show us all the value of eternal suffering. Because Nige is a decent man. The very best of us. And yet time and again he is made to feel pain. No more so than in the last few months.
First there was the money. Few would have batted an eyelid if he had been given £5m by the RNLI. For all he has done to support the work that unpaid volunteers do in rescuing all people in trouble on the sea. Let’s face it, a modern day ministry doesn’t pay for itself and no demigod-like politician can expect to get by on less than £1m a year. Those houses and bottles of champagne aren’t going to pay for themselves. Yet because the £5m came from a Thai crypto-billionaire, suddenly everyone was asking difficult questions. Anyone would think Reform might have crypto-friendly policies.
Then there was the Channel 4 sting. And yet again our Messiah was the innocent victim of an establishment plot. Compared to Nige, Jesus had it easy in Holy Week. How could he be expected to realise that two associates whom he had barely known for years might allegedly be trying to secure an illegal donation from overseas? And what were the chances that Nige might be caught on camera giving considered responses as part of a conversation he hadn’t even been listening to? Some days you just can’t buy a break.
On Thursday morning, Farage had been scheduled to host a press conference near Southend where we were promised he would spread goodwill to all men with yet another major policy announcement. Only for the event to be cancelled late on Wednesday evening. The official reason given was that Reform didn’t want to clash with the fifth anniversary of the murder of the former Southend MP David Amess. Yet more bad luck for Nige. Imagine only being given five years’ notice to plan your schedule.
Or perhaps there was another reason for the cancellation. One related to another sting, this time by ITV, that had sent undercover journalists into the Reform operations room and uncovered the only bad apples in the entire organisation. Again, what were the chances of finding racists and misogynists attracted to a party that loved women and people of all colours?
How could this ever have happened? The chances were slimmer than winning the EuroMillions lottery. And surely had nothing to do with Nige’s would-be chancellor, Honest Bob Jenrick, saying he would consider allowing soldiers to be able to blow up migrants in small boats in the Channel. What’s wrong with killing a few thousand people for the sake of a greater good? The country is just too woke for its own good sometimes. Then there’s the wannabe home secretary Zia Yusuf, who is on a one-man mission to round up all immigrants – even women and children – and send them back to countries where they may be killed. So again we are left with the question. Why are so many racists attracted to Reform?
Let’s take Dean Miller. A vetted Reform councillor from Bromley who was filmed campaigning during the Makerfield byelection. Quite how extensive the vetting process was is anyone’s guess. “Tell us, Dean. Are you in any way prejudiced against people of colour?”. “Absolutely not. I just don’t want them anywhere near me.” “That’s great. Thanks Dean. Welcome to Reform.”
Anyway, Dean was caught on camera saying that it was kill or be killed with illegal immigrants. “They’re all fucking black and they’re like animals,” he said. “I’m not a racist, but you know what I mean.” Yes, Dean. We know exactly what you mean. And he couldn’t have been clearer about his intentions towards the king. Charles was a Muslim and deserved to be beheaded. It’s a view.
When Miller was asked for a comment before the film is aired this weekend, his defence was that he had been on heavy medication at the time. And suddenly that all made sense. Because I too am on regular medication both for my psyche and for my heart. So I chose to reread the common known side effects of one of my drugs. And there among the small print about causing faster breathing, fever, muscle stiffness and drowsiness, one thing stood out. “Never take in the presence of a black person or royalty. Can make you prone to racist outbursts and in extreme cases can provoke urges to kill the monarch.” I guess I must just have been extremely lucky so far.
Miller was not the only one to have been caught out this way. Others – also apparently vetted – declared that all foreigners were parasites, that the UK should have a 1% limit on all immigrants and made disgusting comments about a female Reform councillor. Raymond Dunning said he was so far-far right it was unbelievable. Then there were those who thought it best to try to sound moderate until after they had been elected. Then the gloves would come off and they could give foreigners hell.
And in the middle of all this we have the saintly Nige. Scratching his head and wondering why all this was happening to him again. He hadn’t come in to politics to stir grievance and division. He was the god of love, the man of peace. Others among the Reform elite knew exactly where the blame lay. And it wasn’t with the innocent men who had been caught saying the only racist and sexist words they had ever said. Dicky Tice and the former Tory MP Ben Bradley were pointing the finger at ITV for daring to do its job properly. It was outrageous they had recorded Reform councillors going about their everyday jobs. Every man and woman was entitled to be as racist as they like in the comfort of their workplace.
For now, Nige was determined to rise above it. He would survive. He was doing God’s work. Just a shame that God didn’t seem to like him much.

article_title: Burnham v Swinney: will the UK PM overshadow the SNP’s conference?
article_content:
This year, even Andy Burnham is invited to the Scottish National party conference. But by the time John Swinney stands up to address members on Saturday afternoon in Aberdeen to reinvigorate the case for a second independence referendum, his party may regret giving the UK prime minister so much prominence in the conference buildup.
Burnham is expected to visit Scotland on Friday – the middle of the event – in a thinly veiled attempt to overshadow the SNP gathering. While he will be in a different venue, the former Manchester mayor’s presence in Scotland will loom large over the event. Since taking over at No 10 in July, Burnham has largely avoided direct confrontations with his political rivals, rarely attacking Nigel Farage or Kemi Badenoch. But he has taken a different approach with the Scottish first minister.
The SNP leader was the only politician from a rival party, apart from Margaret Thatcher, that Burnham mentioned in his keynote address to the Labour party conference last month. He reflected on Swinney’s prediction that he would be the last prime minister of the UK at a meeting of separatist parties Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to mark the first time all three devolved parliaments were governed by nationalists. Swinney inadvertently did so on the day Burnham’s father died.
“I quote that not to seek sympathy,” Burnham said, holding back tears. “Nor to criticise John Swinney. I relay it because I want you to know how it made me feel. Utterly determined to prove him wrong.”
Beyond ruling out a second independence referendum, recent British prime ministers have often paid little attention to Scottish internal affairs. Burnham has already said there is “no clear consensus” for another vote. But unlike his predecessors, he has decided to take on the SNP by loudly make the case for the union on Scottish soil.
Burnham presents a new challenge for the SNP as they seek to re-energise the case for Scottish independence. Swinney has said he wants a new vote before 2031. The separatists have grown used to facing off against rightwing, pro-Brexit governments in London during two decades in power in Holyrood, making it easier to argue that Scotland’s interests have been dismissed. Burnham’s devolution agenda, openness to exploring a return to the European Union and £2 bus fares are harder to confront.
Even among SNP voters, he is popular. Polling by PF Global found that 46% of Scots have a favourable view of Burnham, far higher than the Labour party itself, and double Keir Starmer’s when he left power. Only Swinney is more popular than the prime minister among SNP voters who supported yes in 2014, reaching a level not seen for a Labour leader since Jeremy Corbyn. Despite this, SNP figures have sought to capitalise on Burnham’s stance on the EU in their quest for a second independence vote.
“We are in a situation where Andy Burnham is actively and unilaterally opening up the conversation about whether we are able to go back to results of referendums and relitigate those decisions while saying that that same democratic principle does not apply to the people of Scotland,” said Lara Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry. “The idea that the union can continue to exist in its current form is absolutely farcical.”
In Aberdeen, the SNP is hoping to draw a line under a bruising few years after Nicola Sturgeon’s resignation and the subsequent fraud conviction of her estranged husband and former SNP chair Peter Murrell, who is serving a five-year prison sentence for embezzling £400,000 from the party. A proceeds of crime case against Murrell is scheduled for early December.
In May, the SNP won a fifth successive election, but only enough to form a minority government in Holyrood. Despite the victory, Sturgeon criticised a “lack of vision or big picture thinking” in the campaign in the opening to her memoir. Swinney has said they were still good friends. Some SNP figures wonder how much they owe to the unpopularity of Starmer. The party also faces challenges on multiple fronts: Reform has as many MSPs as Labour in Holyrood with 17, while the Scottish Greens won a record 15 seats. The Tories have showed that they can still win seats, defeating the SNP in Aberdeen South in June.
Despite the potential for a standoff between Swinney and Burnham, there is growing appetite in Scotland for collaboration between Westminster and Holyrood. Since the May elections, there has been a sharp rise in Scots who support a closer working relationship between the UK and Scottish governments. Polling by Ipsos has found that 42% of Scots would feel happy about the SNP-led Scottish government working with London, up 12 points since Starmer was in charge in May. Just over half of Scots believe that the country is going in the wrong direction, up six points in the same time period.
This conference, the SNP has invited speakers from other separatist and pro-independence parties. Sioned Williams, deputy first minister of Wales, will give a fraternal address on Friday. Gillian Mackay, a Scottish Green party MSP, will speak at a panel about the right pathway to independence on Saturday.
“We understand, and members of the SNP know, that this is bigger than the SNP. Obviously, I fundamentally believe that the SNP will be the party who secures independence for Scotland. But that runs so much deeper throughout the Scottish population than just those who vote for the SNP. I do think that it is important at this moment to harness and to build on that support as broadly as we can,” said Bird.

article_title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
article_content:
Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
- Published
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.
Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.
Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal.
"We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.
ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries".
The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.
The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.
It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix.
- What Sky buying ITV could mean for your favourite shows 
  - Published6 July
But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up.
In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including:
- The need for free expression of opinion in news media
- The need for a range of views in news media across the UK
- The need for a range of people controlling the media across the UK
- The need for a wide range of programmes to be offered across the UK
The letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV.
Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added.
But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV.
The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued.
This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added.
Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns.
A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."
An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process.
"This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries."
Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration.
This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes.
She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."
description: The culture secretary says the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.

article_title: Labour to break from Green council groups that back Zionism policy
article_content:
Labour to break from Green council groups that back Zionism policy
- Published
Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with the Green Party on local councils, unless its councillors disown the party's newly-adopted policy that Zionism is a form of racism.
Labour says it will give local Green groups seven days to confirm they reject the policy, which was recently approved by Green members at its party conference.
The ultimatum applies to 18 councils where it shares power with the Greens, either directly or alongside other parties.
The Greens hit back at the move, accusing Labour of meddling and arguing it would be undemocratic for the party to "tell local parties what to do".
The policy motion adopted by members of the Green Party of England and Wales said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.
It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
It has led to a backlash from Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including four of its five MPs.
Green leader Zack Polanski, who skipped the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, has said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.
He has however said that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by racist ideology", arguing this was the "substantial part" of the motion. Israel has denied committing genocide in Gaza.
The party's two deputy leaders have been at odds over the policy, with Mothin Ali backing the move and Rachel Millward voting against it.
Labour is currently in coalition with the Green Party on local councils in Sheffield, Lewes and Warwick. In other areas, it runs the council as part of a broader coalition alongside other parties.
- Burnham rules out coalition with Greens after 'Zionism is racism' motion 
  - Published1 day ago
- Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote 
  - Published5 October
On Wednesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs Labour would not partner with the Greens over the "antisemitic" policy, although Downing Street did not confirm what this meant for local government.
The party has now said it wants all local Labour groups to write to their Green counterparts, demanding "clear and unambiguous" statements rejecting the policy.
Green groups will also be asked to call on their party's "national leadership" to reconsider the policy.
"Where they are unable to provide that assurance, Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end," the party's chair Bridget Phillipson said.
In response to Burnham's comments, Polanski said: "I'm the only Jewish leader of a political party. I'm a victim of antisemitism every day and I've made it clear Jewish people are welcome in my party."
A Green Party spokesperson said: "For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong.
"Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic."
The Board of Deputies of British Jews, the UK's largest cross-community Jewish organisation, welcomed Labour's announcement.
Its vice president Karen Newman said the Greens had adopted an "antisemitic platform", adding of Labour's position: "This is a commitment we have been pressing for, and we are urging other mainstream parties to take the same clear and principled stand."
National parties exercise various levels of control over groups of local councillors who wish to do deals to govern locally.
Labour councillors require the approval of its ruling National Executive Committee before entering into local tie-ups.
According to the party's rulebook, local groups must also "stand down" from power sharing arrangements when asked to do so by their regional office.
By contrast, the Green Party of England and Wales allows local groups to make the final decision on where and whether to share power locally.
description: Labour says it will end power-sharing deals with councillors that do not disown the party's new stance.

article_title: Wes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink row
article_content:
Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort.
The British defence secretary, giving a speech before a meeting with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, argued that supporting Ukraine was in the long-term interests of Washington, and a business opportunity.
Taking questions after his address, Streeting acknowledged “the challenges of recent days”, a reference to the row over the sudden decision of the US government on Monday to limit the use of Starlink by Ukraine’s military.
He said it was “a reminder of two things – one is that American support in Ukraine has been significant and it has made, I think, a real impact in the Ukrainian war effort. And we and the Ukrainians would feel the absence of that.”
The second was that there was “an enormous opportunity for the US in terms of the support for Ukraine”, a reference to the future “defence-industrial relationship” between the countries.
Streeting was speaking at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US thinktank, before meeting Hegseth amid tensions over Ukraine, Iran and the Middle East.
Speaking to the BBC after the meeting, Streeting said he had been “reassured directly” by his US counterpart that access to the vital Starlink communications system had been restored. The defence secretary said it was not yet clear to the UK why the disruption occurred, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”
The two men were also expected to discuss the safety of US military bases in the UK, after an Iranian threat prompted the US to withdraw B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, and whether the two countries would come together to help Saudi Arabia, which has come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis.
But it is Ukraine that is the most urgent issue. A day ago, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he felt personally betrayed by Donald Trump after the US government appeared to have throttled a version of the Starlink satellite internet service used by Ukraine’s military.
Ukrainian officials have reported that the US has also threatened to cut the sharing of intelligence used by Ukraine to detect incoming missiles if it does not abandon its attacks on refineries, aimed at hurting the Russian economy.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, meeting Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday, said the UK would stand by Ukraine.
Developing the theme, Streeting made a direct appeal to the US audience, saying: “There’s rarely been a more important time for Britain and America to come together.
“The people of Ukraine are fighting for a principle that runs through the finest traditions of American political thought,” he said, which was “that a free people have a right to determine their own destiny”.
Trump has vacillated over supporting Ukraine against Russia since returning to the White House, while support among US Republicans for Kyiv has been mixed. But Streeting argued that helping Ukraine was also a matter of national self-interest for the US as well as the UK.
“Ukraine may be thousands of miles from American shores, but if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent,” he said.
The change to Starlink happened without warning at about 1am, when Ukrainian soldiers reported that terminals on drones were no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph, rendering communications inoperable.
It led to a dramatic halt to mid-strike drone attacks on targets in Russian occupied territories on the frontline, and concerns about Ukraine’s ability to intercept new Russian jet-powered attack craft that are bombing its cities.
Trump has been trying to put pressure on Ukraine to halt its bombing of Russian oil refineries in a desperate attempt to reduce world oil prices before the US midterm elections. He agreed to buy diesel from Russia earlier this month.
author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor

article_title: Repairing Brexit economic damage should be Burnham’s top priority, business chief says
article_content:
Repairing the economic damage of Brexit should be the top priority for Andy Burnham as he reconsiders Labour’s red lines on EU membership, the head of one of Britain’s leading business groups has said.
Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), said she welcomed the prime minister reopening the Brexit battle lines despite the uncertainty it could create, arguing that the UK’s current trading relationship with the EU was bad for business.
“We do think it’s right, because of what we know from the evidence of how businesses feel it’s not working,” she said.
Highlighting the continuing economic hit from Brexit, Haviland said more than half of bosses surveyed by the business lobby group believed the deal negotiated by Boris Johnson’s government and enacted in 2021 was not helping them.
“We expected it to be very difficult at the beginning, when [companies] were getting used to the new rules, and then it would sort of get easier as it went to along. But actually, that has not happened,” she said.
Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far, with national income per head between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been had the UK not left the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a long-term hit of about 4% of gross domestic product.
At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good” as he pledged to reassess Britain’s relationship with the EU. He opened the door to options including fully rejoining the bloc, and this week he said failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty”.
In an interview with the Guardian in Norwich alongside the head of the Norfolk Chambers of Commerce (NCC) chief executive, Nova Fairbanks, Haviland said the government had to take into account business frustrations with Brexit.
She said the BCC would also consult its 50,000 members, who collectively employ more than 6 million people across the UK, on a range of options for Britain’s relationship, including rejoining the EU.
“We are 10 years since the referendum,” Haviland said. “We would say the language of Brexit needs to move on. That’s gone. What businesses understand is what we had before and what we’ve got now.
“We’re apolitical, it’s not a political question. It is an economic question. So we are going to set out the options, from the where we are to the most extreme. And in consultation with our chambers, and our partners, we will see where people are.”
Fairbanks said it was clear that some Brexit-backing bosses recognised the economic damage. “It would be very interesting to see how many businesses that were very much pro-Brexit are still pro-Brexit, because I’ve certainly not heard any change of heart from those that were against Brexit. I think they are still very much: ‘We need to be closer to Europe.’”
Speaking on the sidelines of an NCC trade fair at the Norfolk Showground, the business leaders said companies were coming under growing pressure from rising energy prices and other effects of the war in the Middle East.
Haviland called on the chancellor, John Healey, to take bold action at this month’s budget to support firms despite concerns at the heart of government about the pressure on the public finances amid jitters in the bond market.
“This rumour about a sort of ‘steady as she goes’ budget, and ‘let’s not upset the apple cart’. Business don’t really want just a ‘steady as she goes’. They want to see some action that will relieve some of those costs that will drive that fly wheel [of the British economy],” she said.
“You can’t just trot along in a crouch position effectively. And surely the markets will be happy to see some spending cuts by the government, and some investment in private-sector growth?”
Haviland called for action on energy bills, business rates and taxes on employment to help companies recruit more young people. “In your energy bill, about 40% of your energy is actually energy. The other 60% is about tax. So the government can get some of that out,” she said.
“The big test for the chancellor is to put his money where his mouth is for business at the budget. Just showing that he genuinely believes that the wealth creators are the job creators – which is business.”
