article_title: «Вікно можливостей» для Путіна: що сталося зі Starlink і яка загроза нависла над Україною
article_content:
«Вікно можливостей» для Путіна: що сталося зі Starlink і яка загроза нависла над Україною
Обмеження Starshield можуть послабити українські удари по російській логістиці та ускладнити контрнаступальні дії ЗСУ на ключових ділянках фронту.
Минулої ночі, 14 жовтня, в Україні запровадили обмеження швидкості для терміналів супутникового зв’язку Starlink компанії SpaceX. Українські посадовці попередили, що це може суттєво ускладнити перехоплення російських реактивних безпілотників і роботу дронів середньої дальності.
Про це йдеться у звіті Інституту вивчення війни (ISW).
Starshield — це захищена супутникова система зв’язку, розроблена SpaceX для потреб урядових і військових структур. Вона відрізняється від звичайної мережі Starlink підвищеною стійкістю до перешкод і орієнтацією на військове використання. До запровадження обмежень військові ЗСУ могли використовувати термінали для керування безпілотниками на швидкості понад 160 км/год.
Генеральний директор SpaceX Ілон Маск заявив, що рішення щодо обмежень Starshield пов’язані з американськими військовими, а остаточна відповідальність лежить на керівництві США, зокрема президенті Дональді Трампі. Водночас він наголосив, що звичайний Starlink є комерційним сервісом, який контролює SpaceX.
Колишній міністр оборони України Михайло Федоров після цього повідомив, що SpaceX відновила роботу українських терміналів Starlink на швидкості до 160 км/год. Водночас він наголосив, що для потреб оборони України критично важливо повністю скасувати обмеження швидкості Starshield.
Аналітики Інституту зауважують — наразі невідомо, чи залишаються обмеження чинними. Звичайні тарифи Starlink уже передбачають обмеження для терміналів, які використовуються на літальних апаратах зі швидкістю понад 160 км/год.
Речник Кремля Дмитро Пєсков заявив, що Москва не отримувала офіційних повідомлень від Маска щодо обмежень роботи супутникового зв’язку для українських військових.
Ускладнення перехоплення реактивних БпЛА
В ISW зауважують, що обмеження швидкості можуть мати серйозні наслідки для української ППО — передусім у боротьбі з реактивними безпілотниками типу Geran. За словами Бескрестнова, військові використовують супутниковий зв’язок для керування дронами-перехоплювачами, які є одним із найефективніших засобів протидії швидкісним російським БпЛА.
Україна активно розвиває власне виробництво реактивних дронів-перехоплювачів. Втім, обмеження швидкості зв’язку можуть загальмувати цей процес і ускладнити захист міст та інфраструктури в Україні напередодні зими.
Водночас пов’язаний із Кремлем російський військовий блогер визнав, що обмеження можуть створити для військ РФ «вікно можливостей» для завдання ударів по українській інфраструктурі.
За даними українських Сил безпілотних систем, від 24 вересня до 14 жовтня обмеження негативно вплинули на перехоплення безпілотників.
«Це може додатково послабити спроможності української протиповітряної оборони на тактичному й оперативному рівнях», — йдеться у звіті.
Чи вплинуть обмеження на удари по РФ
Обмеження Starshield не мають вплинути на далекобійні українські удари по території РФ, адже Сили оборони не мають доступу до Starlink і Starshield над Росією, адже SpaceX обмежила роботу цих мереж у відповідній зоні.
Аналітики зауважують, що для атак по російських НПЗ, центрах обробки даних та інших стаціонарних цілях українські сили використовують альтернативні способи зв’язку й навігації.
Обмеження швидкості дронів ЗСУ
Обмеження зв’язку Starshield можуть суттєво вплинути на здатність України завдавати ударів безпілотниками середньої дальності, які протягом 2026-го допомагали ЗСУ проводити контрнаступальні операції на важливих ділянках фронту.
Безпілотники, що використовують Starshield, зокрема американські Hornet, відіграють важливу роль в українській кампанії ударів по російській логістиці. Супутниковий зв’язок дає змогу операторам керувати ними в режимі реального часу на високій швидкості, зокрема над окупованими територіями.
Однак максимальна швидкість і швидкість пікірування Hornet перевищують встановлене обмеження Starshield. Через це українським військовим стає складніше ефективно застосовувати ці дрони для ударів. Обмеження також можуть позбавити українські безпілотники можливості уражати рухомий російський транспорт та інші динамічні цілі на окупованих територіях.
За даними українських Сил безпілотних систем, 14 жовтня інтенсивність ударів по російських логістичних машинах уздовж лінії фронту суттєво знизилася. Аналітики припускають, що це, найімовірніше, пов’язано з обмеженнями Starshield.
«Кампанія ударів по наземних логістичних маршрутах російської армії була важливою складовою підготовки українських контрнаступальних дій на Олександрівському та Лиманському напрямках у 2026 році. Тепер нові обмеження можуть ускладнити для України боротьбу за оперативну ініціативу на фронті», — йдеться у звіті.
Обмеження Starlink в Україні — що відомо
Зранку 14 жовтня радник президента з питань оборонних технологій Сергій «Флеш» Бескрестнов і колишній радник міністра оборони Сергій Стерненко повідомили, що для терміналів Starshield в Україні встановили обмеження швидкості — близько 160 км/год.
Джерела Axios в американській адміністрації заявило, що у Білому домі заперечують причетність до обмежень Starlink в Україні. У Вашингтоні заявили, що не контролюють компанію SpaceX, яка забезпечує роботу супутникової системи.
Водночас асновник SpaceX Ілон Маск заявив, що рішення щодо роботи систем Starshield, зокрема швидкості та умов їх використання, ухвалюють уряд США та президент Дональд Трамп, а не приватна компанія. За словами бізнесмена, функціонування Starshield перебуває під контролем державних структур Штатів.
description: Обмеження Starshield можуть послабити українські удари по російській логістиці та ускладнити контрнаступальні дії ЗСУ на ключових ділянках фронту.

article_title: Розморозити активи Росії: США висунули нову пропозицію задля відновлення переговорів про мир — FT
article_content:
Розморозити активи Росії: США висунули нову пропозицію задля відновлення переговорів про мир — FT
Пропозиція представників Дональда Трампа щодо частини заблокованих 260 млрд євро Росії стривожила європейські столиці.
Представники президента США Дональда Трампа запропонували розморозити частину заблокованих російських активів та перевести їх під американський контроль для відновлення мирних переговорів. Така ініціатива викликала занепокоєння в Києві та була відхилена європейськими союзниками.
Про це пише Financial Times із посиланням на чотирьох обізнаних з питанням людей.
Пропозиція розморозити російські активи — що відомо
Про можливість розблокування заморожених російських активів ішлося під час переговорів у Маямі, які минулого тижня провели залучені до мирного процесу представники адміністрації Трампа та посадовці України, Франції, Німеччини, Великої Британії, ЄС і НАТО.
За даними співрозмовників видання, американська сторона представила кілька варіантів розблокування активів. Серед них, зокрема, була пропозиція перемістити кошти до нової спеціальної фінансової структури, яка перебуватиме під контролем Вашингтона.
Один із представників США підтвердив, що заморожені російські активи розглядалися в контексті потенційної всеосяжної мирної угоди. Водночас остаточного рішення щодо механізму їхнього розблокування та подальшого використання коштів наразі немає.
Американський чиновник також зазначив, що розглядалося чимало варіантів використання заморожених активів Росії після завершення війни. Водночас залучені до переговорного процесу українські представники повідомили, що це питання вже порушувалося під час попередніх контактів із США.
Реакція Європи та України на можливе розмороження активів Росії
Європейські учасники переговорів не підтримали пропозицію, яку висунули спецпредставник США Стів Віткофф і зять президента Джаред Кушнер. Ініціатива водночас викликала занепокоєння у європейських столицях і Києві та стала приводом для додаткових запитань щодо позиції Вашингтона і його значно іншого підходу до тиску на Москву задля припинення війни проти України.
Видання нагадало, що після початку повномасштабного вторгнення Росії до України 2022 року західні країни заблокували близько 260 млрд євро російських державних активів. Основна частина цих коштів перебуває на території Євросоюзу.
Країни G7 надали Україні кредит на 45 млрд євро, який залучили під відсотки, отримані від заморожених у ЄС російських активів. Водночас значна кількість європейських урядів не підтримує використання безпосередньо основної суми активів через можливі юридичні наслідки.
Наприкінці минулого року держави ЄС погодилися спрямувати ці активи на відновлення України у разі, якщо Москва відмовиться виплачувати воєнні репарації. Водночас для ухвалення рішення про розмороження коштів потрібна одностайна підтримка всіх 27 членів Євросоюзу, досягнення якої наразі видається малоймовірним.
Пропозицію щодо використання заблокованих російських активів також включали до 28-пунктового мирного плану адміністрації Трампа, представленого рік тому. Однак надалі ця ініціатива не отримала розвитку.
Київ, а також низка європейських країн, виступали за спрямування заморожених коштів на підтримку України.
За словами американського посадовця, Вашингтон попросив українську сторону підготувати пропозиції щодо використання будь-яких доступних коштів незалежно від їхнього походження. Крім того, Києву запропонували співпрацювати зі Світовим банком над реформами, покликаними посилити боротьбу з корупцією та забезпечити підзвітність.
Тим часом 14 жовтня речник Кремля Дмитро Пєсков заявив, що Москва «докладатиме всіх можливих зусиль для повернення вкрадених активів».
«Це включає юридичну роботу, судові процеси та судові переслідування», — сказав він.
За даними джерел видання, європейські представники, які брали участь у зустрічі, наголосили, що не погоджуються на втрату будь-якого контролю над замороженими активами або повернення їхньої частини Росії.
«Їм сказали, що цього просто не станеться», — сказав один зі співрозмовників.
Зауважимо, європейські лідери на саміті ЄС планують виступити проти курсу Трампа щодо Росії, який прагне послабити обмеження на дизель для зниження цін на пальне перед виборами у США. Брюссель має намір закликати до нових санкцій та обмеження нафтових доходів Москви, оскільки вважає, що лише тиск змусить Кремль до переговорів. У ЄС також скептично ставляться до оголошеного Трампом «енергетичного перемир’я», особливо на тлі продовження російських ударів по українській енергетиці.
description: Пропозиція представників Дональда Трампа щодо частини заблокованих 260 млрд євро Росії стривожила європейські столиці.

article_title: Ex-top official Robbins reaches settlement with government over sacking
article_content:
Ex-top official Robbins reaches settlement with government over sacking
- Published
Sir Olly Robbins has reached an out-of-court settlement with the government, after he was sacked as the top civil servant in the Foreign Office over the vetting of Lord Mandelson to be US ambassador.
Sir Olly was fired by then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer earlier this year, after it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.
The FDA union, which represented him in the legal action, said Sir Olly had been made a "scapegoat" to "mask the misjudgement" of Sir Keir.
How much Sir Olly received in the settlement has not been made public.
It came after he requested a judicial review over the decision to dismiss him.
A government spokesperson said Sir Olly "had a distinguished public service career over three decades".
A statement added: "The government has reached a settlement with Sir Oliver following his dismissal. We will not be commenting further on HR matters."
Lord Mandelson was announced as the UK's ambassador to the US in December 2024, before in-depth vetting had been carried out, and formally took up the role in February 2025 after being granted security clearance.
Just seven months later, he was sacked after further information emerged about his previous friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Sir Olly was sacked in April, in the wake of a Guardian story that revealed the peer's security clearance had been granted despite vetting officials raising concerns, with the prime minister later saying he was "furious" he had not been informed at the time.
Sir Keir has previously said he sacked Sir Olly after not accepting his explanation for why clearance was granted, telling MPs in April: "I did ask him, and I did not accept his explanation. That is why I sacked him."
Sir Olly has since defended his role in the process, saying that the government's vetting processes must "remain absolutely confidential".
He previously told MPs that he had not seen the documentation from UK Security Vetting, the government's in-house vetting unit, containing their vetting assessment of Lord Mandelson.
He said that instead, he was given an oral briefing, during which he was told the vetting agency considered Mandelson to be a "borderline case", but that the Foreign Office may wish to grant clearance with "appropriate risk management".
Dave Penman, head of the FDA union, said: "This settlement may bring an end to the Judicial Review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government.
"The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgement of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations - which is quite the feat.
"We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process."
Sir Olly said: "I am grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time.
"I want to thank the FDA for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life".
Sir Olly, who was appointed to the Foreign Office job in early 2025, has held a number of senior civil service roles and was previously the government's lead official during Brexit negotiations with the EU.

article_title: UK national security adviser under pressure over wife’s comment on supporting Palestine Action
article_content:
The UK’s national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, is under pressure to distance himself from a comment made by his wife, the award-winning writer Sarah Helm, in support of Palestine Action.
The post was made in defence of the critically acclaimed Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who said she had been forced to pull her books from shelves in the UK after pledging proceeds from their sales to Palestine Action.
Helm, a former Sunday Times journalist and diplomatic editor at the Independent who spent many years covering the Middle East, wrote on X indicating support for the direct action group, which was proscribed last year.
Under terror laws, this could constitute a criminal offence, carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years in prison. The ban has so far resulted in more than 3,700 arrests for backing the group, with more than 2,250 people formally charged as terrorists.
In response to comments by the broadcaster Adam Boulton that Rooney’s support for Palestine was “anti-Jewish”, Helm wrote: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action. Sounds like Adam would have all our books swept off the shelves in a jiffy.”
Police said the post was “in the process of being assessed” to determine whether an investigation was required.
Downing Street distanced itself from Helm’s post on Friday, with a spokesperson saying: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”
Helm’s works include a book about the women imprisoned by the Nazis at the Ravensbrück concentration camp, and Loyalty, a play about the Iraq war, inspired by her husband’s decade as the chief of staff to the then prime minister, Tony Blair.
The author, who is writing a book about Gaza, married Powell in 2007. He was appointed in 2024 as a national security adviser under Keir Starmer.
According to government guidance, being married to a suspected or convicted terrorist would normally result in the revocation of security clearance. Under the vetting framework for a job as national security adviser, being married to someone tied to a proscribed terrorist organisation is viewed as creating an automatic, unmitigated national security risk.
Responding to questions about Powell’s position after his wife’s comments, a government spokesperson said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”
A spokesperson for Defend Our Juries, a free speech group which supports the right for people to protest peacefully, thanked Helm for “defying this absurdly authoritarian ban”.
“How can Andy Burnham’s government possibly defend this ban in the supreme court next month when his own national security adviser’s wife has openly defied it? This unprecedented attack on free speech in our country is plainly unsustainable,” they said. “We know of 36 people who have been arrested and had their homes raided for similarly expressing support for Palestine Action on social media.
“We hope Sarah will not face the same treatment for standing up for free speech and Palestinian lives. But her defiance further exposes the absurdity of a ban that cannot be enforced against everyone who challenges it. There are simply too many of us who will continue to defy this unjust law until the government is forced to see sense and abandon it.”
However, the Campaign Against Antisemitism called for Helm to “face the full force of the law”.
A spokesperson said: “This is gobsmacking. Clearly, the police need to investigate and Sarah Helm must face the full force of the law, just like others who appear to express support for any proscribed terrorist organisation.
“But this raises extremely serious questions for Jonathan Powell and the government. Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country’s national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post.”
A Met Police spokesperson said: “We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action. It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required.
Hundreds of writers have signed an open letter in support of Rooney, whose books include Normal People and Conversations With Friends, warning that “a country that bans its writers for speaking out is not a free country”.
The letter has been signed by 419 novelists, poets, editors and illustrators including Ali Smith, Kamila Shamsie, Robert Macfarlane, Daisy Johnson, Eliza Clark, Jeanette Winterson, Alice Oseman, Derek Landy, Louise O’Neill, AM Dassu and Nikesh Shukla.
The letter states: “As authors, illustrators, poets, and editors, we stand with Sally Rooney and Faber Books, and condemn a government whose actions, and inactions, have led to her books being pulled from sale in the UK.
“Writers already face book bans worldwide and at home. It is unconscionable that a government can now effectively ban a single author for protesting that government’s own conflation of protest with terrorism. What future governments might do with this power should frighten us all.”
Rooney said she had made the decision to withdraw from the UK market with her publisher, Faber, after learning that passing earnings on to her for the sale of her books in the UK could constitute a serious criminal offence. In a letter shared with the Guardian, Rooney said she was “wholly prepared to accept the consequences”. Faber will continue to sell Rooney’s books in other countries.

article_title: Six-figure payout for senior civil servant sacked over Peter Mandelson vetting
article_content:
Olly Robbins, the former head of the Foreign Office sacked by Keir Starmer over his role in vetting Peter Mandelson, has received a six-figure payout from the government over his dismissal.
Robbins had applied to the high court for a judicial review of the prime minister’s decision to remove him as the top civil servant at the Foreign Office after he was dismissed in April.
He was removed from his post by Starmer after the Guardian’s disclosure that he had overturned a recommendation from UK Security Vetting (UKSV) to deny clearance for Mandelson.
In a statement on Friday, Robbins said he was “grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time”.
He added: “I want to thank the FDA [union] for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life.”
Dave Penman, general secretary of the FDA, which represents senior civil servants, said: “This settlement may bring an end to the judicial review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government.
“The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgment of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations – which is quite the feat.
“We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process.”
The government will ultimately have to publish how much it has given Robbins in a settlement, which is believed to be six figures but not as much as the record £860,000 given to former cabinet secretary Chris Wormald after he was forced out by Starmer after just a year in post.
At the time of his dismissal, Downing Street said Robbins had lost the confidence of Starmer and Yvette Cooper, then foreign secretary, due to his handling of the vetting of Mandelson, who was sacked over the extent of his links to the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The Guardian later revealed that Mandelson’s associations with senior figures in China, Russia and Israel had been among the concerns raised by UKSV when it concluded he should be denied clearance. His relationship with Epstein was not among the reasons.
Robbins’ legal submission had made the case that Starmer had no statutory authority to dismiss him as the head of the diplomatic service, and that there had been “no fair procedure” and “no process at all” in the dismissal. It also said Robbins had been given “irrational” reasons for being fired.
There had been strong support for Robbins within Whitehall, with senior civil servants said to believe he had in effect been sacked for doing what No 10 wanted by swiftly passing Mandelson through vetting, and that the focus should instead have been on the prime minister’s initial decision.
The Commons foreign affairs select committee has previously said that Robbins believed he was “delivering the outcome that was wanted” and concluded that his dismissal “seems to have been taken without full due process and the establishment of the facts”.
Questions remain about the defence Robbins mounted, both of his own actions and the system through which the national security establishment vets people, and the lack of mitigation put in place to get around the security concerns.
The Foreign Office refused to hand over a summary of Mandelson’s security vetting to the official tasked with compiling documents detailing his appointment as ambassador to the US, in response to a Commons motion forcing the release of documents linked to the process.

article_title: Police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser's wife
article_content:
Police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser's wife
- Published
Police are assessing a social media post by the wife of the government's national security adviser Jonathan Powell which referenced Palestine Action, a group labelled a terrorist organisation by the Home Office.
Sarah Helm wrote on the social media site X: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."
She was responding to a discussion on Sky News about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.
A No 10 spokeswoman said Helm was "an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity". The BBC has attempted to contact Helm for comment.
On Friday, a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: "We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action.
"It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required."
Reform UK MP Danny Kruger has written to the prime minister raising concerns about Helm's post.
The Campaign Against Antisemitism said the post was "gobsmacking".
"Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country's national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post," the group said.
However, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Sarah Helm is speaking absolute common sense and should be commended for her bravery."
He called for Palestine Action to be de-proscribed "immediately", calling its official labelling as a terror group "ludicrous and authoritarian".
Helm is an author and journalist, who has previously worked at the Sunday Times and as a foreign correspondent for the Independent.
Palestine Action describes itself as a "direct action movement" that uses "disruptive tactics".
Earlier this year, four of the group's activists were jailed after causing £1.2m of damage at a UK site of an Israel-based defence firm.
In 2025, the UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist group, saying it would not "tolerate" organisations that put the UK's national security at risk.
The proscription made it a criminal offence to belong to or support Palestine Action, punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
The government's decision triggered a wave of protests, which saw an estimated 3,700 people arrested in the UK for publicly expressing their support for the group.
Around 2,500 have been charged, but the cases have not gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription is due to be heard in the Supreme Court next month.
Powell began his government career as a diplomat but later served as an adviser in Tony Blair's government, where he was credited with negotiating a peace deal in Northern Ireland.
In 2024, Sir Keir Starmer appointed him as national security adviser, a position he retained when Andy Burnham became prime minister.

article_title: Target pensions or welfare, not banks, IMF tells John Healey
article_content:
The International Monetary Fund has urged John Healey to target savings on pensions and welfare, instead of taxing Britain’s banks at the budget later this month.
Helge Berger, deputy director of the IMF’s European department, was asked about bank taxes after the Guardian revealed Healey plans to tap the sector for additional revenue.
Berger replied that given the UK’s current high tax-to-GDP ratio, it might be better to “put the emphasis” on cuts.
He said if additional tax revenue were needed, reforming property taxes or VAT might be a good place to start.
He added: “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP – historically, for Britain, a high number – then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal [spending] side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”
As examples, he highlighted the pensions triple lock – which Labour has already said it will reform – and “better targeting [of] social benefits”, adding: “I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.”
Berger was speaking in Bangkok, where the IMF has held its annual meetings this week.
City lobbyists have been out in full force, warning the government that higher taxes could force banks to throttle lending, hitting the economy and even forcing some lenders to move jobs and operations abroad.
In a letter sent to Healey and copied to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on 12 October, days before news of the planned tax hike broke, the chief executive of UK Finance, David Postings, shared research commissioned by the lobby group.
It suggested that reversing Tory cuts to the bank surcharge – taking it back to 8% from 3% – would leave annual UK GDP £1.2bn lower in real terms by 2029-30 than it would have otherwise been.
He said it would also see banks issue fewer business loans and mortgages, with lending likely to be £10.4bn lower in 2029-2030 than if the surcharge was held at 3%.
“The UK’s banking sector already makes a vital contribution to the wider economy,” Postings’ letter said. “To sustain this vital contribution, the budget should avoid any increases in bank-specific taxes, as this would risk constraining the sector’s ability to lend and invest.”
However, TUC analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the Treasury has already lost out on £6bn over the three years since the surcharge cut came into force in 2023.
At the same time, banks have been reporting strong profits, largely off the back of high interest rates, with bosses subsequently increasing banker bonus pots and handing billions of pounds to shareholders.
Collectively, the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds – reported £29.2bn in profits over the first six months of the year, with almost half, £13.7bn, pledged to investors through dividends and share buybacks. Over the past five years, those banks have raked in £200bn in pre-tax profits.
Author and former banker Philip Augar said the banks were “enjoying boom conditions”, partly due to good management but partly due to economic conditions “not of their own making”. He said there was room for a “moderate increase in taxation” that would raise about £2bn to £3bn a year.
“The prime minister has said that the burden of taxation has to fall on those with the broader shoulders, and at the moment, it’s hard to think of a sector where the shoulders are much broader than the banking sector,” Augar told the BBC’s Today programme on Friday.
While banks could not expect interest rates benefits to continue forever, Augar said that banks – including those that were bailed out in the 2008 financial crisis – could not have it both ways.
“Banking is cyclical, it’s true. But when it hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out,” Augar said. “When it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment. Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.”
Some banks have threatened to pull investment, and potentially jobs, from the UK if it hikes taxes, with lobby groups noting smaller overall tax charges in rival financial centres like Frankfurt, Dublin and Amsterdam.
Jamie Dimon, who heads up the largest bank in the US, JP Morgan, said in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks.
But Augar said the government needed to see past the bluster. “There seems to have been a coordinated campaign by the big international banks who have businesses in Britain – JP Morgan, Citigroup, Santander, HSBC and others.
“But they always say this, [and] they rarely move. I think that if the chancellor judges this right, with a moderate increase in taxation or some other form of getting money from the banks, then the business will remain in the UK.”

article_title: Reform councillor quits over offensive remarks
article_content:
Reform councillor quits over offensive remarks
- Published
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.
A Reform UK councillor filmed calling Asian homeowners "parasites" has resigned from two councils and apologised for his comments.
Alan Feeney, who has since stepped down from the party, was heard making the remarks during undercover filming for an ITV News investigation, external in the run up to council elections in May.
Feeney said he had resigned every post he held on Solihull Council and Birmingham City Council, adding that his remarks "were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable".
He has also been suspended from his job with the prison service, with the Ministry of Justice [MoJ] describing the comments captured during the documentary as "despicable".
In July, his register of interests with Solihull council recorded he was employed as a custodial manager, a position described on the HM Prison and Probation Service website as "the most senior uniformed officers in a prison".
Feeney was one of several Reform members featured in the ITV investigation, which was gathered over the course of a year.
In it, while campaigning in the run-up to May's elections, Feeney described an area as "infested" with Asian families and called them "absolute parasites".
He was also recorded saying no more than 1% of the UK population should be non-white.
'Unreserved apologies'
Writing on Facebook on Friday, Feeney said he wanted "to offer my sincere and unreserved apologies for the comments I made in the recording that has recently come to light".
He added the comments did "not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report".
These were communities he had "supported countless times" over many years, he added.
He stated his true self was reflected in more than a decade of public service, but achievements "cannot reduce the impact of what has been said".
Feeney, who defected from the Conservative Party to Reform last year, was elected to the Shard End ward on Birmingham City Council in May.
A spokesperson for Reform Solihull said Feeney was briefly with the party, but spent the majority of his time as a Conservative councillor, and did not reflect "the views of the group".
The MoJ has stated the comments featured in the documentary would be investigated and action taken in line with its policy.
By-elections in Solihull
Undercover reporters also filmed with two other Reform candidates in Solihull - Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan.
On Friday, Solihull Council's leader of the opposition, Reform's Samantha Gethen, said all three councillors had now resigned, which "was the right thing to do", adding that there would now be by-elections.
Comments reported this week "were offensive, hurtful and wrong", Gethen said.
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Friday, Reform MP Robert Jenrick said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film.
He added that all parties had "bad apples" and denied it was any more of a problem in Reform than other parties.
On Thursday, the party told the BBC that Feeney had "mutually agreed" to resign from the party.

article_title: Burnham says ‘too much time is wasted in those dramas’ when asked about Scottish independence – as it happened
article_content:
Burnham on Scottish independence: 'Too much time is wasted in those dramas'
Following his speech, Burnham is taking questions from the media.
When asked by the BBC whether his approach with devolution will make him more or less likely the last prime minister of the United Kingdom, he said: “Obviously, I don’t want to be that.”
The SNP has been pushing for a path to Scottish independence, which the prime minister has repeatedly ruled out.
Burnham added:
I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions.
In my view, people in Scotland are suffering the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else. And I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people.
Right now, too much time is wasted in those dramas. It consumes too much energy.”
We’re going to wind down our UK politics coverage now, heres a quick list of some of todays top lines:
Andy Burnham has declared that he is making a “serious and genuine offer” to the Scottish government in order to put more control “in the hands of local people” through devolution. Burnham, giving a speech in Lanarkshire, stated that he was open to working with first minister John Swinney, even though the two have “a different view” on Scottish independence.
The deputy first ministers for Scotland and Wales both spoke at the SNP conference taking place in Aberdeen, with Plaid Cymru’s Sioned Williams praising the victories both parties enjoyed in May and her Scottish counterpart, Jenny Gilruth, claiming that “Westminster’s time is coming to an end”.
The Guardian understands that chancellor John Healey is poised to tax Britain’s banks in his 28 October budget to help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has labelled Andy Burnham’s devolution plans as a “waste of time”, stating Holyrood “have the powers that they need” and that they have done “absolutely nothing” with the ones that they do have. Badenoch made the comments during her own trip to Paisley in Scotland, where she posed in front of a mural for noted England enthusiast William Wallace.
The Campaign for Real Ale (Camra) has criticised Andy Burnham and Labour for their attempts to block a bill that would afford extra protections for historic pubs, calling the efforts an “absolute disgrace.”
The protections, put forward in a bill by Conservative MP Mike Wood, would have given pubs in England a “legal shield” from unlawful redevelopment, with the 2023 destruction of the Crooked House, which was located in Wood’s Kingswinford and South Staffordshire constituency, cited as an example of what can be avoided.
The bill was “talked out” on Friday, as a five-hour debate involving a group of Labour MPs prevented its second reading from taking place before the 2.30pm cut-off time.
Wood accused Labour of filibustering to prevent the bill from passing, saying, “This was Andy Burnham’s first test of whether he means what he says on pubs, and he’s flunked it.”
Paul Ainsworth, the national planning policy adviser for Camra, accused the government of blocking the bill, which he said was “an absolute disgrace”, and urged the government to “put laws in place to preserve our heritage and protect pubs from being converted or demolished against the wishes of local communities.”
Next up in Aberdeen, Gilruth’s Welsh opposite number, Sioned Williams, spoke about the connections that bind the two countries as well and claimed that they shared the same dream of independence.
Williams congratulated the SNP for their own victory in May and echoed Gilruth’s sentiment that the success of national parties in all three countries could spell the end of the UK, claiming that “the stars aligned in Wales, Scotland, and the north of Ireland, and the UK constitution now sits in a very different constellation.”
Scottish deputy first minister: 'Westminster's time is coming to an end'
Back to Scottish news, day two of the SNP conference has kicked off in Aberdeen with deputy first minister Jenny Gilruth taking the stage first.
Gilruth took the opportunity to congratulate Plaid Cymru, the SNP’s sister party, for their victory in the May Senedd elections, pointing out that it meant that “Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland are now led by first ministers who believe in independence from the UK.”
Gilruth also reminded the crowd of the meeting that took place between the three nations’ first ministers in Cardiff in September, claiming that it was “the clearest possible sign yet that Westminster’s time is coming to an end.”
In other news today, pornography that depicts strangulation and incestuous relationships will be banned in England and Wales from early November, the government has announced.
The content will be outlawed from 6 November after cross-party pressure prompted ministers to announce new legislation earlier this year.
Online pornography depicting strangulation or suffocation, sex between people who are related or pretending to be related, or when somebody is pretending to be a child under 16, will be illegal.
The justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said: “This isn’t about criminalising harmless sexual preferences. But porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people.
“Content that normalises, or even glorifies, violence against women is dangerous and can blur the line with what is acceptable in real life.”
Burnham says he accepts Swinney 'has a different view' on Scottish independence
Continuing on the theme of Scottish independence, Burnham was asked by the Daily Record whether he was categorically ruling out a second referendum during his premiership.
The prime minister said:
I think unions of countries are better because you can face a challenging world in a more confident and stronger way, in my view, when you collaborate and you work together.
That is my view, I communicated it to the [Scottish] first secretary very clearly.
He has a different view, but let’s accept there’s a different view there and then work on together what we can agree on.
My view won’t be changing, but let’s now move forward where we can make some progress.”
Burnham on Scottish independence: 'Too much time is wasted in those dramas'
Following his speech, Burnham is taking questions from the media.
When asked by the BBC whether his approach with devolution will make him more or less likely the last prime minister of the United Kingdom, he said: “Obviously, I don’t want to be that.”
The SNP has been pushing for a path to Scottish independence, which the prime minister has repeatedly ruled out.
Burnham added:
I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions.
In my view, people in Scotland are suffering the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else. And I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people.
Right now, too much time is wasted in those dramas. It consumes too much energy.”
Burnham's devolution plans 'a waste of time,' says Badenoch
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister’s plans to devolve more powers to Scottish towns and regions is a “waste of time”.
During her own visit to Scotland, at the Malcom Group near Glasgow, Badenoch said: “I think that this is yet again a waste of time discussion.
“This naval gazing about Holyrood powers and constitutional settlements and should we have another referendum and should have more councils – they all have the powers that they need.”
She said the discussion should instead be on what the Scottish government is doing with its powers, which she believed was “absolutely nothing”.
She told Sky News: “What are they doing on education? What are they doing on health? They’ve got no answers.”
Here she is standing in front of a mural of Mel Gibson’s William Wallace who famously led a rebellion against English rule:
Burham has finished his speech, which lasted about 35 minutes. I could just about hear him on the hot mic saying “sorry that went on a bit” as he shook someone’s hand off camera.
'If we don't move now, Scotland could lose out,' says Burnham
The prime minister said he is making a “serious and genuine offer” to the Scottish government to put more control “in the hands of local people”.
He said:
We need to look at the resources and decision-making powers that sit at the regional level in Scotland, so that no Scottish city regions are left behind.
I know the Scottish government has announced a long term programme for local government reform.
But if you ask me, we’ve got to move faster … if we don’t move now, Scotland could lose out.
There is a risk that some of the towns and cities become underpowered when some of the towns and cities of the north of England are going the other way and starting to power up. I don’t want to see that as prime minister.”

article_title: Housing loans granted while Burnham was mayor investigated by councillors
article_content:
Housing loans granted while Burnham was mayor investigated by councillors
- Published
Loans made to property companies - including three controlled by Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owner - while Andy Burnham was Greater Manchester mayor are being investigated by councillors.
About 50 developers have been lent more than £1bn between them from a fund managed by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) since 2015.
John Leech, the chairman of the GMCA's Overview and Scrutiny Committee, told the BBC concerns had been raised about the transparency of the process to approve the loans.
"We just want to be clear that there is a transparent rather than an opaque process," said Leech, who is the Liberal Democrat opposition leader on Manchester City Council.
He said the approval process had been criticised as "very opaque in the past and that it's not necessarily been clearly understood why X was successful and Y wasn't".
A GMCA spokesperson said it was supporting the committee with its enquiries.
Downing Street did not comment.
The money came from the Greater Manchester Housing Investment Loan Fund (GMHILF).
The fund was set up in 2015 with an initial £300m of government investment to help developers build new homes across Greater Manchester.
Three property companies ultimately controlled by Manchester City owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan were granted loans worth about £55m in total.
The decisions to approve these loans were taken in 2017, in two meetings which were both chaired by Andy Burnham when he was mayor of Greater Manchester.
The decisions to grant loans from the fund were taken publicly by all members of the GMCA, not the mayor alone.
One of Manchester's leading property developers, Renaker, has received the majority of the £1bn lent out from the fund.
Renaker has been involved in a long-running legal battle over £140m worth of loans made to the developer through the GMCA's fund.
A rival developer, Aubrey Weis, claims the the loans were unfair subsidies.
In June, the Court of Appeal found there had been "no error of law" in the GMCA's decision to provide the loans but Weis is appealing the decision.
'Out of kilter'
The Overview & Scrutiny Committee, which reviews the activities of the mayor and the GMCA, agreed to launch an inquiry into the loans earlier this year and Leech is now taking that work forward, after being elected chairman recently.
Leech, a former Lib Dem MP in Manchester, said he felt the fund was intended to be for property companies struggling to access financing.
In 2015, when the loan scheme was launched, Bill Enevoldson, the GMCA's chief investment officer, said, external: "It is not designed to finance unviable projects but can unlock currently unfundable ones."
An evaluation of the fund, external from 2025 said it was designed to provide loans for "projects which might otherwise struggle to secure financing".
Leech said it was "not unreasonable" to ask why seemingly successful businesses needed to borrow public money through this loan scheme.
"In the case of Abu Dhabi, you would imagine that they wouldn't have any problem accessing funds from elsewhere as well," Leech said.
"And so the process clearly does seem to be out of kilter with what the original stated aims were back in 2015."
Leech said the committee had asked GMCA officers to produce a report about the use of these funds.
He said the committee will ask officers questions about the fund at a private meeting, before potentially making recommendations to the Greater Manchester mayor.
The committee does not have the power to sanction the mayor but it can investigate, require answers, expose problems and challenge decisions.
The committee could call forward witnesses, such as current Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig, to give evidence as part of the inquiry.
Conservative shadow sports minister Louie French said Burnham had "serious questions to answer" about the loans.
French said "taxpayers deserve transparency over how this money was awarded".
In a statement, the GMCA said the funding for the loans had been lent "at commercial rates" and had delivered "11,000 new homes and regenerating brownfield land across the city region".
The GMCA said "not a single viable scheme was ever turned down".
A GMCA spokesperson added: "The fund is open to all developers, with lending criteria based on parameters set by the government and developed with external financial experts to reflect due diligence standards in the private sector.
"Every penny loaned from the fund is being fully repaid, delivering billions of pounds worth of development at no cost to the taxpayer."
In 2014, Manchester City Council and Abu Dhabi United Group, which owns Manchester City FC, formed a joint venture called Manchester Life.
Abu Dhabi United Group and Manchester Life were involved in three property developments that were partially financed through the GMCA's loan fund.
A Manchester Life spokesperson said: "It is standard for property development to be funded through a combination of investor equity and borrowing.
"All three sites had previously been derelict. The loans were provided on commercial terms and have been repaid in full, including interest."
The BBC asked Renaker for comment but it did not respond before publication.
Julia Hatmaker, the editor of the Place North West property news website, said viability was "always a struggle" in the development world.
She said the GMCA's loan scheme had been successful in building more homes in the city and generating a return on that investment.
But she said it's a "good time for the combined authority to re-evaluate what kind of project it wants to support with similar loan programmes and whether it wants to put stricter rules in place as to what developments can benefit from them".

article_title: No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
article_content:
No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme.
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”.
 
 
 “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

article_title: The Guardian view on the banks: too big to fail cannot mean too big to tax | Editorial
article_content:
John Healey is planning to tax British banks, the Guardian revealed, in the forthcoming budget. It’s about time for the chancellor to act. Banks have been raking it in. The campaign group Positive Money reported this summer that Britain’s four biggest banks made £29bn in the first half of this year, up a fifth on 2025. These windfalls owe more to higher interest rates than better products or services. Households and businesses pay more to borrow. Meanwhile, the Bank of England pays the banks tens of billions in interest on their reserves, with the Treasury footing the bill.
The chancellor is said to favour restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, which could raise around £2bn a year. This would recover a very modest share of the sector’s bonanza. Louis XIV’s finance minister, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, said that “the art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing”. Britain’s banks have plenty of feathers. That hasn’t stopped them hissing. The banks say that they already face higher taxes than other companies, that they won’t be able to lend as much, and that their profits won’t last.
But banks aren’t taxed on their windfall gains, and what levies they face are less than those paid by oil and gas companies. The Bank of England said banks spent £7.7bn on dividends and buying back shares in the first quarter of 2026 without affecting lending. Higher taxes might mean trimming shareholder payouts. There’s nothing to suggest productive lending must take the hit. Over the past five years Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest – which control the majority of UK personal and business accounts – made profits of £200bn. Positive Money says that households lost out on £44bn in deposit interest in 2025. Some of this paid for banking services. But that does not explain why the sum is five times the equivalent average figure for 2009-21.
The chancellor could be more radical. The precedent here is not a socialist one. Margaret Thatcher taxed banks’ windfalls in 1981. A comparable 2.5% levy on today’s interest-free deposits would, a paper by the New Economics Foundation and Positive Money suggests, raise more than £11bn. In August, Positive Money suggested looking at Spain’s success in levying a windfall tax on banks’ net income above €800m. It says that such a windfall tax – levied at the same rate as that paid by fossil fuel companies on a comparable tax base – would bring in £19bn from the UK arms of the big four banks. That would pay for a universal and comprehensive adult social care system.
Banks need to be both public utilities and good corporate citizens. Yet the sector is paying the highest bankers’ bonuses since the 2008 global financial crisis. “Most financial sector activity,” concluded a paper published in The Manchester School journal this month, “is simply negative for overall economic performance.” Politicians should stop mistaking finance lobbyists’ demands for a growth strategy. Their job is to curb a finance sector so large that it risks crises and weaker growth. Taxpayers rescued the banks after they helped crash the economy 18 years ago. Public protection carries public obligations. As Sir Philip Augar, the author and former banker, told the BBC: “Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.”

article_title: Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?
article_content:
In February 2016, days after David Cameron announced the UK would hold a referendum on leaving the EU, he told workers in Slough not to imagine they could change their minds a few years down the line if they did not like how things panned out. Voting to stay in or leave was a once in a generation thing, he said. “This is a decision that lasts for life.”
Well times change, as the last prime minister but five could testify. A decade after Britain told Brussels where to go, Brexit is back on the political agenda. After years in which many politicians avoided any mention of the B-word, Andy Burnham broke the omertà in his party conference speech last month, saying he would look again at Britain’s relationship with Europe.
This week he went further, insisting the current arrangement must change: “Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain.” Among a range of options on the table, he has been clear, is the possibility of going “all the way” and rejoining the EU.
There are pressing economic reasons Burnham has been talking up closer alignment, as the EU works out its position on the UK’s access to its protectionist “Made in Europe” legislation, which the prime minister has said could hurt British manufacturing.
But after years of bitter division and political dysfunction in the fallout from the vote, are the British public really ready to talk about Brexit again – and even to contemplate reversing it?
Polling evidence may suggest so. A “megapoll” of more than 11,000 people published this month found that half of Britons now support rejoining the EU, with only 28% opposed, and the remainder undecided. Almost 60% think it was wrong to leave.
Sliced some ways, the numbers are even more striking: a More in Common survey in June to mark a decade since the vote found that if another referendum was held today across Britain’s 632 constituencies, just 11 would vote to leave (even in Clacton, Nigel Farage’s constituency, 52% supported rejoining).
What changed? To the polling expert Rob Ford, a professor of political science at the University of Manchester, there are several key reasons, from demographic change to buyers’ remorse. Brexiters are fewer in number – “a lot of leave voters have died, bluntly” – and both young people entering the electorate and those who did not vote in 2016 skew heavily in favour of Europe. And with the project widely considered a disappointment at best, a proportion of those who opted to leave have switched positions.
“Although each is a relatively slow moving and relatively small incremental force, add them together over a decade and it adds up to quite a lot of change,” said Ford.
Given the divisiveness and turbulence of the past decade – and the fact many Labour MPs represent constituencies that voted to leave – it is little wonder that some senior Labour figures have expressed nervousness about reopening the debate. “[Burnham] definitely needs to proceed with caution because we don’t want to restoke division,” one cabinet minister told the Guardian.
But the view from formerly Brexit-supporting areas is not necessarily what it was. “Hull East voted 74% leave in the referendum, however I believe the mood has changed,” said Karl Turner, the Labour MP for the constituency since 2010 (he now sits as an independent after having the whip withdrawn).
“Constituents tell me they expected Brexit to improve their lives; instead many face higher costs and fewer opportunities.” As a result, he said, they were “increasingly ready to consider the practical benefits of rejoining the EU”.
Ford added: “Andy Burnham looks at the data and says, well, I’ve got an electoral coalition that’s 80% remain and becoming more so. The parties to my left that I need to squeeze have a [position] that is even more remain than that.
“And the overall balance of opinion in the country is now nudging up towards 60% in favour of remain, sometimes even higher in terms of how many think Brexit is a mistake. Why wouldn’t I move in a pro-remain direction? It’s the direction of travel of the country. The art of leadership is getting out ahead of the trends that are happening and using them to your advantage.”
Sara Hobolt, a professor in the department of government at London School of Economics, agrees that the polling data today suggests Brexit could be an effective general election rallying cry for Labour. “This is an issue that a lot of people were quite upset with Keir Starmer and his government for not talking about it. It is something that definitely mobilises the base.”
While Labour supporters and those the party wants to win back from other progressive parties overwhelmingly support remain, she points out, the Conservative party is now much more divided on the issue, having lost many of its hardline Brexiters to Reform. “That means that [by putting Brexit back on the agenda] you can potentially do more damage to the right than the left.
“But I think probably the main thing for Andy Burnham is that this has been seen in his electoral base as something [that has been overlooked]. ‘You talk about growth? Why are you not talking about Brexit?’ Because overwhelmingly remainers think that a lot of the economic problems we’ve faced over the last decade are due to Brexit.”
But if uniting the left before a Westminster election is one thing, winning a future Brexit referendum is a whole other challenge, as the experience of 2016 showed. “There clearly is support for rejoining the EU,” says the More in Commondirector, Luke Tryl, “the question is, how resilient would that be in the face of a referendum campaign?”
One factor is, inevitably, Brexit weariness, he says. “The British public are tired. They’ve lurched from crisis to crisis, from row to row, and I think, for some, just the idea of reopening the wounds [is unwelcome]. I think in a campaign rejoin, if it got to that, would start ahead, but I don’t think the headline polling we are seeing now would remain where it is once it was subject to a full back and forth.”
Ford agrees – noting that the EU will be resistant to serious discussions so long as there is the prospect of a wholesale reversal under a future Reform government. The risk of bringing up Brexit is not just because the subject is neuralgic to many, he says. “One of the problems during the Brexit years was it was just simply impossible to get a conversation going about all the other pressing issues that mattered.
“There is a risk for Burnham, if this thing starts to take life of its own yet again, that the big difficult conversations he wants to have about some of the longstanding structural problems in British society will be harder to have because for a lot of people in the political conversation, Brexit is like catnip – they’ll run straight to it. And then you’re not able to get them to pay attention to the issues you want them to pay attention to.”

article_title: We must save water as drought becomes new normal, says minister
article_content:
We must save water as drought becomes new normal, says minister
- Published
The government has warned action is needed to prevent water shortages becoming "the norm" after severe drought was declared across parts of southern England.
Water and flooding minister Emma Hardy told MPs current drought conditions were "something we have not experienced for decades" and urged people to "think about ways to use water wisely over the coming weeks".
Severe drought was declared across parts of southern England on Thursday after months of low rainfall, with around 50 million people now impacted.
Parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex are all affected by the move announced by the Environment Agency.
The government said supplies would not be interrupted but declaring severe drought would ensure "proactive steps are taken to safeguard water before any disruption occurs".
Speaking in the House of Commons, Hardy said the measures were down to "exceptionally low rainfall" and depleted reservoir levels.
- How we got to severe drought and what is next 
  - Published19 hours ago
- Drought permit issued in bid to secure supply 
  - Published8 October
The minister noted Yorkshire also moved into drought status last week.
"That means over 80% of England is now in drought, affecting around 50 million people," she said.
"The South East and South West, in particular, have experienced their driest April to September in over a century.
"While the record-breaking heat and lack of rainfall have put our water resources under immense pressure this year, we must take action now to prevent this situation becoming the norm."
Robbie Moore, shadow minister for environment, food and rural affairs, accused the government of being "slow to react" to the conditions.
"This is the third drought in five years, it should not have caught the government off guard," he told MPs.
Hardy insisted "we know that this the new normal when it comes to our weather", adding: "This is exactly why we are preparing for it."
The latest figures, external for Wimbleball Reservoir on Exmoor show it is at 14.9% capacity, while Ardingly in West Sussex is 19.4% full. Other major reservoirs are also low, including Roadford in Devon at 36.8%, Burrator at 33.6%, Colliford in Cornwall at 35% and Stithians at 21.9%.
Wimbleball serves about 300,000 properties across east Devon, north Devon, Somerset, west Dorset and west Somerset, while Ardingly Reservoir supplies 280,000.
As part of the severe drought conditions, water companies have been asked to conduct daily monitoring of these reservoir levels along with tougher monitoring of water quality.
The Environment Agency was also expected to increase compliance checks on businesses withdrawing water from natural sources to ensure they only take permitted quantities.
It said "small changes" including taking shorter showers, fixing leaks and turning off taps while brushing teeth could "make a real difference".
"These aren't token gestures," the agency said.
"They cut the amount of water we need to take from rivers and groundwater, protecting supplies for people and leaving more for wildlife, wetlands and the natural systems we all depend on."
The Environment Agency said further dry weather was expected for the rest of October: "The usual seasonal rainfall has yet to arrive, and 82% of England remains in drought."
In some areas, 120% of the expected rainfall was needed for the next six months or "drought conditions will continue and could worsen", it said.
Severe drought is the most serious level, and was declared "when evidence shows drought is causing, or will soon cause, serious harm, and that emergency action is needed to protect people, water supplies, the environment, farming, infrastructure or other critical services".
