article_title: ‘A direct cultural threat’: your questions on the rise of the right across Europe answered
article_content:
Support for far-right parties has been growing across Europe, with radical right, populist parties in coalition governments in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany.
The Guardian reported this year that nearly a quarter of voters in Europe voted for far-right parties in their most recent national elections, a fivefold increase since 1995.
In Germany, Alternative für Deutschland recently booked a historic state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Elsewhere, though – in the Netherlands, in Hungary and in Sweden, where the Sweden Democrats lost vote share – far-right parties have suffered defeats. But their ideas – and their influence on mainstream politics – are today clearly visible across the continent, notably on policies around immigration and law-and-order.
The coming months will see further crucial elections, beginning in Spain in November and continuing in France, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy next year.
How might these elections shape the political future of Europe? What is the impact of their policies – and what might prevent their continuing rise?
The Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley has reported for the Guardian from 23 of the EU’s 27 member states, while Europe community affairs correspondent Ashifa Kassam was on the ground in Sweden and Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state to speak with people ahead of the elections.
Jon and Ashifa answered questions about their reporting and experiences. Read the Q&A below.
One user asked: It’s no secret in Europe that Donald Trump and his allies are funding far-right parties all over the continent. Trump is unpopular enough in Europe that even the majority of people planning to vote for the AfD et al despise him. So how can so many Europeans who hate Trump still vote for the far right?
Jon Henley: You’re absolutely right about the Trump administration’s efforts to promote far right parties in Europe. That was made very plain in the US National Security Strategy policy document last year – I wrote about that here.
But while there may be an ideological affinity between European far right and nationalist voters on issues like anti-immigration, hostility toward the EU, and softer stances on Russia, Trump’s “America First” policies (demands re Greenland, tariff threats, etc.) and constant unpredictability pose major problems for far-right leaders trying to look credible in Europe, because they scare all European voters – including far-right voters.
Leaders including Giorgia Meloni in Italy and Marine Le Pen in France have openly criticised Trump and distanced themselves from his more erratic pronouncements, conspiracy claims and hostility toward European security.
European far-right voters’ support for Trump varies from country to country but is broadly low – clearly peace and security in Europe matter more than anti-immigration sentiment. Ultimately, nation-first means putting your nation first, and Trump has made clear that the US’s interests are not Europe’s interests.
The evidence would seem to suggest that many of Europe’s far-right voters think their own far-right parties will be more responsible as regards (many of) those issues – though whether they actually will be or not is moot, of course.
00000000000000000000 asked: How do you measure when a grassroots movement represents a genuine structural shift versus an isolated vocal minority?
Ashifa Kassam: Our jobs involve covering a wide range of community actions, whether it’s people fighting back against datacentres, protests against tourism, or the vandalisation of mobile phone masts by people who seemingly linked them to the coronavirus pandemic.
Oftentimes the reporting starts small and local. For example, perhaps it’s focused tightly on a protest against tourists in Barcelona or a push to restrict cruise ship dockings in Dubrovnik. From there, myself and the editors often continue to watch these movements and their reach; are politicians responding in any way? Are others joining in? Will the movements lead to policy changes? These are the kinds of questions that I tend to consider when deciding how much to make of the grassroots movements and how much coverage to give them.
At times it’s been incredible to see just where these movements will go, whether it’s the housing protests in Spain that led to snap general elections or the opposition movement that coalesced around Péter Magyar in Hungary in 2024 and which, more than a year later, saw him oust Viktor Orbán from power.
Gramoun-kal asked: Can the EU survive the rise of the extreme right? What if AfD and RN get into power at the same time?
Jon Henley: One of the very few upsides of Brexit is that hardly any European far right parties now want their countries to leave the EU. Instead, they want to “transform it from within”, turning it more into a looser “Europe of nations”.
But that’s not to say the EU would not be considerably weakened by, say, a President Le Pen, who could paralyse decision-making, challenge the supremacy of EU law and push a “France First” agenda undermining the single market and Schengen free-travel zone and opposing EU expansion, climate action, etc.
I’m not sure there’s any imminent risk of the AfD coming to national power in Germany (and if Le Pen wins France’s presidential election, which isn’t certain but looks highly plausible, she is also unlikely to have a parliamentary majority, which will limit her room for manoeuvre).
Plus, the AfD is too extreme even for the RN – Le Pen’s outfit (which kicked the AfD out of its European parliament grouping a while ago over various issues including comments to the effect that not all Nazis were bad), has repeatedly made it clear it is not an ally of the German party and does not share its views on eg. “remigration” – the mass deportation of immigrants.
But for sure – if Spain, Italy, France and Poland all see far-right parties in government after elections due over the next 12 months or so, the EU will face some major challenges. I don’t think it will collapse, but it will certainly find it even harder to reach agreement on many major issues than it already does, and so move (even) more slowly. Natalie Tocci wrote a great comment piece about this.
OrangeSpaceMan5 asked: Do you see Nato and the EU disintegrating if we see Far-Right victories across Britain, Germany and France?
Jon Henley: No, I don’t see the EU and Nato disintegrating, just becoming a lot more complicated/difficult to run … The EU could be “eroded from within” above all by far right-led governments using their veto (as Orbán did with Hungary) in major decisions like the EU budget, EU enlargement, the green deal, etc. They may well also simply ignore EU law, as Orbán also did. And for Nato, see previous answer – it would survive but become more paralysed in terms of longer term decision making.
Ashifa Kassam: I think we saw a glimpse of how complicated things can become in the European parliament after an EU vote earlier this year aimed at increasing deportations. The immediate aftermath laid bare just how deeply polarised the EU has already become, as right-wing MEPs chanted “send them back” and centre-left and left-wing MEPs shot back with “Shame on you.”
ElendX asked: Why and how have the left and centre parties failed to respond to the concerns of the electorate? How do they now need to respond?
Ashifa Kassam: What comes to mind immediately is the housing crisis in Spain and beyond. It’s been just over two weeks now since the Spanish protests and encampments over the housing crisis burst into public view, laying bare the long-simmering anger over soaring housing costs.
I think it’s an issue that has long been overlooked by many left and centre parties across Europe, even as vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected, and analysts warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. Last year I spoke to Jaume Collboni, the Socialist mayor of Barcelona, who (along with 21 mayors across Europe) are urging the EU to treat the surging housing costs as a “new pandemic” by unleashing billions in funding to boost affordable housing and give mayors a seat at the table to ensure measures capable of tackling housing speculation. Speaking to me, Collboni warned: “We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse.”
I also think left and centre parties have done little to address the precariousness of the labour market, ie. the rise of gig jobs and, in many cases, the deterioration of public services. If you keep an eye on the Eurobarometer, the cost of living constantly ranks among the top concerns for people across Europe, hinting at the idea that this could be fertile territory for politicians to focus on. Immigration, in contrast, was in 7th place in the most recent survey.
Jon Henley: I think broadly speaking mainstream parties have failed to adequately address people’s concerns about the cost of living, declining public services (healthcare, education, transport), economic/job security, etc. – as I said above, fear of/anger at some kind of “loss of status” is one of the key drivers of the far right vote. (I’m not suggesting that’s easy – it clearly isn’t, economies are struggling.)
I’d also add that far-right parties are clearly extremely effective at exploiting voters’ concerns politically, including by pointing the finger at the group they think are most to blame and promising to fix things by getting rid of them.
And I’d also note that mainstream parties really have not helped themselves by adopting far-right parties’ framing on several issues in hopes of hanging on to disillusioned voters – electoral evidence shows that almost never works, mainly because, as Marine Le Pen’s father Jean-Marie put it, people tend to prefer the original to the copy.
Dc740 asked: Did you measure any change in online activity for extremist parties like Vox in Spain after the Yandex datacentre was targeted by Ukraine?
Ashifa Kassam: Funny you should ask – earlier this week, I sent out queries on this to several research groups, so it’s something we’re looking into. It’s a really interesting question. Last week, in an interview with news site Eldiario.es, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez was asked whether he was worried about foreign interference in the elections given his high profile opposition to Israel’s war on Gaza and the US-Israeli attack on Iran. His answer: “Yes, and not only by nations, but also by non-state actors.”
Capitao_barbosa asked: How much foreign funding, especially from Russia and America, is being funnelled to these parties? And can we value how much indirect support (bots, disinformation by state actors, algorithm meddling on X, etc.) they are receiving?
Jon Henley: Our data team looked at this question a couple of years ago, before the last European parliament elections. They concluded a quarter of all private money donated to political parties in the EU was going to far-right, far-left and populist movements – aided by the fact that only a quarter of EU countries require parties to identify private donors – with €97m (about one in every seven private donation euros across the EU) going to far-right parties.
A European parliament report from 2023 estimated that about $1.18bn in funding towards organisations targeting LGBTQ+ rights and promoting traditional family policies flowed into Europe from 2019 to 2023, and a 2022 declassified US intelligence assessment found the Russian government had covertly funnelled at least $300m to foreign political parties, often in Europe, from 2014.
Ashifa Kassam: We’ve also had some recent reporting on the flow of funds from the US. In July, the Guardian reported that Donald Trump’s state department intended to allocate $12m to organisations in the UK founded by prominent conservatives. Of these funds, $7m was to go to 878, a thinktank that describes itself as being devoted to “the rediscovery of our ancient culture” and “ending mass migration.”
In July, the state department issued a notice of funding, offering grants for organisations and institutions interested in promoting what it described as “civilisational self-confidence in Europe”.
While research out of Europe, such as the Munich-based Ifo Institute, has found “no correlation” between migration and higher crime rates, the US state department notice suggested it was hoping the grants would lead to outcomes including reports on the impact of mass migration on local safety and tools to analyse impact of mass migration on democratic institutions.
One user asked: How serious would you describe the threat these far-right parties pose to democracy? And to what extent do you think there is a collaboration between them and powerful social media personalities or state sponsored online social media propaganda?
Jon Henley: Some far right parties definitely pose more of a threat to democracy than others. Political scientists divide far-right parties into those that essentially operate within basic democratic norms (“radical right” parties), and those that seek to overturn the system, to the extent even of condoning violence (“extreme right” parties).
If we take one example, AfD in Germany could be described as extreme right in some respects (and some local branches are indeed classified as such by German domestic intelligence). Some of its positions are in clear contradiction with liberal democracy: it is openly racist, homophobic, misogynistic. It believes citizens should be ranked by its own warped criteria, including ethnicity, gender and religious belief. It flirts continually with Nazi rhetoric, imagery and symbolism.
On this question I recommend this column by Cas Mudde, a top scholar of populism and the far right, after AfD won in the recent state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. He argues that mainstream parties have to wake up to the fact that they are not in a battle that’s about vote share and elections, it’s about democracy itself.
Ashifa Kassam: I would add that we’ve seen some fairly high-profile examples of collaboration, from Elon Musk’s repeated endorsements of the AfD on X to his 2025 X talk with the party’s co-leader, Alice Weidel. The Guardian has also regularly explored the interplay between the far right and social media, such as a 2025 investigation that looked at how a network of far-right Facebook groups had become an “engine of radicalisation” by exposing hundreds of thousands of people in Britain to racist and extremist disinformation.
KilmaSelth asked: Do you think the hard right parties tend to moderate as they approach power, or do they maintain their radicalism?
Jon Henley: Based on Meloni and Le Pen, I would for a long time have said yes – Meloni basically struck a bargain to get elected in which she promised to be responsible on the economy, in the EU and as regards foreign policy, as long as she could do her culture-wars stuff domestically. Le Pen has spent years “detoxifying” the National Rally and kicking out over-radical undesirables. But if you look at AfD, they haven’t moderated their language at all – if anything, they’ve hardened it – and it manifestly is not doing them any harm. And as Meloni and Le Pen have moderated their positions, we’ve started to see them being outflanked on their right, by the likes of Roberto Vannacci and his National Future in Italy and Eric Zemmour’s Reconquête in France. So I think we may be heading into a period where the former far right is effectively now part of the political landscape, like “regular” parties that will sometimes win and sometimes lose elections, and will be increasingly challenged on their right by more extreme elements.
Ashifa Kassam: Vox offers another way to look at this question, as the party was founded in 2013 by disgruntled members of the conservative People’s party (PP). Its leader, Santiago Abascal, is a career politician who was among those who saw an opportunity to push further on the right flank of Spanish politics when it came to Catalan separatism, immigration, abortion and LGBTQ+ rights. It was a hardline stance that was often (but not always) diluted when Abascal was part of the PP; now as a separate party, they’ve seized on their electoral momentum in some regions to push the party to heed their agenda.

article_title: Reform councillor calls TV report 'vote interference'
article_content:
Reform councillor calls TV report 'vote interference'
- Published
A Reform councillor has accused ITV of "electoral interference" after undercover reporters joined its Portsmouth council election campaign as part of an undercover investigation into the party.
The ITV News Exposure documentary Undercover: A Year In Reform raised questions about Reform's vetting procedures for candidates following undercover filming.
The party's Hampshire leader George Madgwick was featured voicing support for the Portsmouth Patriots anti-immigration group. He subsequently issued a statement saying the undercover reporters potentially had an "impact on the result" of council elections.
ITV News has denied accusations of electoral interference. A spokesperson said the programme was produced in accordance with broadcasting regulations and was "in the public interest".
Reform has been under pressure following the two ITV News reports, which showed undercover footage, gathered over the past year, showing some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.
It comes two years after party leader Nigel Farage promised to root out "bad apples" from his party.
ITV News said it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.
The ITV Exposure documentary was produced by Hardcash Productions. The full 90-minute documentary - Undercover: A Year in Reform - is due to be broadcast on Sunday on ITV1 and ITVX.
A second ITV News report, external broadcast on Thursday showed footage of Madgwick admitting that the Portsmouth Patriots - members of whom were shown expressing far right views - were actively helping Reform to campaign in the run up to the council elections.
In a statement, he denied being a member of the group but said he had "supported their movement over the years from the sidelines".
Madgwick said the two undercover reporters campaigned with the party in Portsmouth in March and April.
"It leads me to wonder whether their interference in an election is a potential criminal offence."
"We have no way to know whether they posted flyers they were meant to. Or whether they gave us correct door knocking information," he said.
He said they had campaigned in four seats, three of which the party narrowly lost
"Their involvement would have had an impact on the result," he said.
He also said he was a "shocked and disgusted" the party had been "infiltrated" by the reporters.
"On a personal level I allowed these men in my home. I made them drinks. They met my dogs. It's an entirely disgusting invasion of personal privacy."
The Liberal Democrats took control of the council following the elections earlier this year, holding 22 seats, with Reform as the second-biggest party on 12 seats.
An ITV spokesperson said: "ITV's programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest.
"All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme's producers."
The Electoral Commission said it sets out details of electoral offences which relate to campaigning for agents and candidates.
"Our Code of Conduct for campaigners provides a guide to what is, and is not, acceptable behaviour."
"The consideration of any potential offences would be a matter for the police."

article_title: Councils warned of risks of high street pedestrianisation
article_content:
Councils warned of risks of high street pedestrianisation
- Published
The UK government has warned councils against ill-considered plans to pedestrianise high streets in England.
In evidence submitted to an inquiry by MPs, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said pedestrianisation can make high streets "more attractive, safe and welcoming".
But the department added that "the process needs to be well considered", warning that removing traffic could make high streets less accessible and damage local economies.
"Local leaders pursuing pedestrianisation must be aware of the risks and work to mitigate them, within a broader spatial strategy," the evidence says.
The evidence was submitted, external to the Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee, which is investigating the action needed to revitalise England's high streets.
An MHCLG spokesperson said the government had not issued formal guidance to local authorities on pedestrianisation.
The government is due to publish a new strategy on high streets later this year.
"We support local leaders to make their own choices about pedestrianisation based on the needs of their communities," the spokesperson said.
"Our upcoming high streets strategy will also set out more detail on how we are bringing high streets back to life and making sure they are accessible for everyone."
Studies suggest banning cars from high streets has become increasingly common in city and town centres across the UK.
Some councils attempted pedestrianisation experiments during the Covid pandemic, which spurred debates about the use of outdoor public spaces.
But the pedestrianisation of some high streets has proved contentious, particularly in London, London Mayor Sadiq Khan has clashed with the local council over plans to make Oxford Street traffic-free.
Parts of Oxford Street will be pedestrianised from 26 October.
The London mayor's spokesperson said he was focused on making high streets "cleaner, greener and more pleasant places to spend time, and helping to drive economic growth and prosperity".
"Pedestrianisation can help reduce conflict between vehicles and pedestrians, making high streets more attractive for visitors and shoppers," the mayor's spokesperson said.
They added the Greater London Authority would use data and feedback from the Oxford Street scheme to "understand how a range of people will use the newly pedestrianised space, and help refine the design of permanent improvements".
Most pedestrianisation schemes are immediately countered by some level of local opposition, said Professor Lee Ivett, who heads the School of Architecture at the University of the Built Environment.
He told the BBC that while opposition usually focuses on short-term disruption to local businesses, evidence does suggest that pedestrianisation increases the economic viability of high streets in the long run.
But he said pedestrianisation had to be paired with improvements in public transport to realise those economic benefits.
"If you want to defeat the argument that a reduction in the amount of traffic will reduce the amount of trade, then you need to also be able to make an argument that an investment in public transport infrastructure is actually going to be the vehicle that still keeps providing accessibility to the centre," Professor Ivett said.
In urban design guidance and previous high street strategies, the UK government has supported making high streets more attractive and people-friendly.
The last high street strategy - which was published in 2021 when the Conservatives were in power - said the government wanted to see more town and city centres "designed with a sense of place and to be attractive to people walking, cycling and using public transport".
But the government's approach to date has focused on giving local authorities the tools and flexibility to make their own decisions on pedestrianisation.
Pedestrianising roads can be a long and complicated legal process, involving consultations with residents and impact assessments.
It has taken a decade for London Mayor Sadiq Khan's proposal to pedestrianise parts of Oxford Street to come to fruition, after he first suggested it in 2016.
Elsewhere some pedestrianisation trials have failed. Last month, West Berkshire Council ended Newbury's evening pedestrianisation trial, after it was opposed by 75% of respondents to a public consultation.
In contrast, the majority of Stevenson Square in Manchester's Northern Quarter has transitioned into a permanent pedestrian-friendly space, following a successful trial.

article_title: Damages for Greens deputy over false disorder claims
article_content:
Damages for Greens deputy over false disorder claims
- Published
A TV presenter and a social media commentator have apologised and will pay damages to the deputy leader of the Green Party after wrongly suggesting he participated in disorder.
Mothin Ali, a councillor on Leeds City Council, attended the 2024 Harehills unrest to assist police and appeal for calm, but posts on social media accused him of taking part in the trouble, the High Court heard.
Ali sued GB News presenter Alex Armstrong and social media commentator Bernadette Spofforth for defamation over posts on X. Both have apologised and agreed to pay "substantial damages".
Speaking outside court, Ali said: "The harm is already done. The smears leave their stench, even when proven to be false."
Trouble erupted in Harehills on the evening of 18 July 2024 after police helped social workers who were taking four children into emergency foster care.
Hundreds of people took to the streets, with a police car flipped over and a double-decker bus torched.
"I tried my absolute best to calm tensions, to protect police officers," said Ali, who has been deputy leader of the Green Party of England and Wales since 2025.
"I stayed on the scene to calm rioters and to reassure residents while buses burned. I stayed there to limit the damage, to limit the harm to my community.
"For my service to my community, I was not only accused of rioting, but something I take even more seriously - my honesty was brought into question."
As a result of the negative coverage, Ali said he was "harassed for days and weeks" and his family "lived in fear".
His car was also damaged.
"The context of this is how black and brown people are treated when they enter public life," he told reporters gathered outside the court.
Samantha Thompson, who represented Armstrong and Spofforth, a businesswoman from the Chester area, said the pair "apologise to the claimant for the serious harm to his reputation and his distress".
Green Party leader Zack Polanski said Ali was a "hero" for his actions on the night, adding: "He did exactly what an excellent councillor would do, working to calm down and heal division, and was praised across party lines at the time for doing so."

article_title: Reform faces questions over candidate vetting after undercover filming
article_content:
Reform faces questions over candidate vetting after undercover filming
- Published
Reform UK is facing further questions about its vetting procedures for candidates, after undercover filming broadcast by ITV News, external.
In the film, gathered over the course of a year, an undercover reporter is advised by a local party chairman to delete social media posts supportive of far-right activist Tommy Robinson, before being encouraged to apply to stand to be a councillor for the party.
It also shows a former Reform candidate claiming he failed the party's vetting process twice but was still allowed to stand to be a councillor. Reform denies the individual failed vetting in the first place.
Reform said the party had "improved and prioritised its vetting procedures".
In a statement, the party said that "from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting" but added: "This is the same for all organisations."
It follows undercover filming broadcast on Wednesday night, which showed some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.
Reform MP Robert Jenrick said all political parties had "bad apples".
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, he said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film.
"I don't accept this happens any more in Reform than in any other party," he added.
The party said: "There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases."
Reform also accused the ITV investigation of "extreme methods of deception" and using false information to obtain an undercover role in Reform's headquarters.
Jenrick said he believed the undercover reporters had wanted to find evidence of party leader Nigel Farage "acting in an inappropriate way" but had not succeeded.
Two years ago, Farage vowed to vet candidates more "rigorously", after the party dropped a series of candidates following reports they had made offensive or racist comments.
However, the party has continued to face questions over the strength of its vetting processes.
Speaking on Thursday, before the latest filming was broadcast, Farage told BBC Look East his party vetted "to a much higher standard than other parties" but "you can't vet for future comments".
- Reform councillor quits over offensive remarks 
  - Published10 hours ago
- Reform councillor calls TV report 'vote interference' 
  - Published12 hours ago
ITV News says one of its undercover reporters was asked if he would consider standing to be a councillor, after spending time leafleting with Reform activists.
He meets with the chairman of a local Reform branch in Chester, Ian Frost, who describes the meeting as "the first stage" of the vetting process.
After the reporter says he has previously posted in support of Robinson on social media, Frost advises him to delete the posts.
"Anything where you've got, things, Tommy Robinson or anything like that, okay, I would delete the account and I'd start again," Frost adds.
Farage has said Robinson would not be allowed to join Reform.
Frost later suggests the undercover reporter could apply to stand for the party, saying: "You might become a councillor. You might then want to go to the MP route. So, social media, yeah. And apply."
Frost told ITV News he thought the reporter was a genuine candidate and gave him the benefit of the doubt.
He added that it was not fair to judge people on a single conversation and he had since left Reform for unrelated reasons.
In another part of the film, a former Reform candidate - Alex Lomas - claims he failed the party's vetting process twice, including for sharing social media posts from Robinson.
However, Lomas says a few days after he failed for the second time he was asked to stand for the party.
"On my second application, I got declined on the Friday, I got an email from them on the Tuesday saying you've passed vetting," he is recorded as saying.
"I said, well, I think you better check with your paperwork, mate, because I've just failed on Friday. Now, you're saying I've passed it, I've not changed anything.
"And then I got a phone call a few days later. Hi, will you stand for Reform UK? I'm like, yeah okay."
He stood for Reform in local elections in Oldham in May but did not win a seat on the council.
The BBC has not been able to contact Lomas and he did not respond to requests for comment from ITV News.
Reform denies Lomas failed vetting in the first place.
ITV's undercover report also shows Farage ruling a controversial mayoral candidate Dr Chris Parry – who said the then Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy should go home to the Caribbean – should be made to apologise, but not stand down.
In a conversation at Reform's headquarters, the party's director of communications Ed Sumner suggests Farage is "protecting" Parry.
In response Farage says: "It's showing a bit of sorrow."
In a separate conversation several weeks earlier, where Farage was not present, Sumner is recorded saying Parry is "clearly a racist" and "needs to go".
After apologising to Lammy in January, Parry was allowed to remain Reform's mayoral candidate in Hampshire and the Solent until he was later suspended in March "pending investigation", following comments about a Jewish voluntary patrol service.
Parry told the BBC there was never an investigation and he has since left the party.
He said: "I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government.
"They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye, whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people."
In the report, Reform UK MP Sarah Pochin is filmed telling the undercover reporter that the party needed "women press officers".
"They are so chauvinistic... They just exclude you if you are a woman. There's a bit of a male issue going on."
Asked about her comments, Jenrick said Pochin was a "valued colleague" but added: "It is not my experience that the party has problems of that kind."
Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "These latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform UK.
"Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party.
"Time and again Farage has had every opportunity to demonstrate leadership and get Reform's house in order and every single time he has failed."
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Reform "need to sort these issues out".
She added: "Every party will have people who make mistakes and have bad apples, the difference is how you deal with it."

article_title: 'Massive challenge' to protect Donaldson from harm in jail
article_content:
'Massive challenge' to protect Donaldson from harm in jail
- Published
Protecting convicted paedophile Jeffrey Donaldson from harm inside jail will be a "massive risk-management headache" for prison bosses, according to a former governor.
The ex-Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader was given a 15-year sentence on Thursday after being convicted of 18 counts of sex abuse, including rape, against two women when they were children.
He is serving his sentence at Maghaberry Prison near Lisburn but will spend only half of his term behind bars.
Ian Acheson, who worked for HM Prison Service for about a decade, said the former Lagan Valley MP faced risks from fellow inmates.
Donaldson represents a "very complex challenge to the Northern Ireland Prison Service", Acheson added.
"There are always hierarchies within prisons - and there are even hierarchies within sex offenders - and the lowest of the low and the most vulnerable in terms of hostility from others are those who've been convicted of sexual violence against a minor," he said.
But he said it would also be necessary to "examine potential political or sectarian targeting" relating to Donaldson's leadership of the DUP and his service in the Ulster Defence Regiment, a former Army unit.
"The prison has a duty of care to protect him and he is uniquely vulnerable," Acheson told BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme.
"Maghaberry, in previous inspections, has indicated that it operates an integrated regime, where sex offenders can be safely managed in the wider prison community.
"I don't think that is remotely viable for Jeffrey Donaldson, given those offence characteristics and his background.
"So either he is kept, in effect, in conditions of solitary confinement for years and years or another solution has to be found.
"I don't think it's acceptable to keep him in conditions of solitary confinement - it may not even be legal."
Reading in his cell
Donaldson spends up to 18 hours a day in his cell at Maghaberry Prison, which holds about 1,600 inmates.
It is thought he has been put in the Moyola Unit, which primarily houses prisoners with health issues, for his own safety as it isolates him from risk of attack or verbal abuse from other prisoners.
He is believed to spend much of his day reading books from the prison library.
Acheson said the disgraced former politician was "entitled to protection but he's not entitled to special, preferential treatment".
There was a "precedent within the UK" to transfer prisoners within different jurisdictions, Acheson added - therefore Donaldson "could be potentially compulsorily transferred" to another jail.
Donaldson was convicted in June of sex offences against two females referred to in his trial as Victim A and Victim B.
He was sentenced to 11 years for his crimes against Victim B and four years for offences against Victim A.
He will also be required to sign the Sex Offenders Register for life.
During sentencing, Judge Paul Ramsey said Donaldson's crimes had led to a "catastrophic descent into disgrace".
Donaldson, who denied the charges, is seeking to appeal his convictions.
Should his attempt to appeal fail, he will be released from prison at the end of 2033.
He qualifies for a 50% remission in his sentence because the offences were committed before the Criminal Justice (Northern Ireland) Order 2008 came into effect.
The remainder of his sentence will be served under supervision in the community on licence.
Who is Jeffrey Donaldson?
Donaldson's time in politics began in 1985 when he was elected for the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) as a member of the Stormont assembly for South Down.
In 1997, Donaldson became the MP for Lagan Valley, representing the UUP. He would remain an MP until 2024.
However, in 2003 he quit the UUP and defected to the DUP.
Donaldson was awarded a knighthood in the 2016 Queen's Birthday Honours list, and, in 2021, became leader of the DUP.
He remained the party's leader until March 2024, when he was charged with a series of historical sexual offences against children.
After his conviction this year, Donaldson asked for his knighthood to be forfeited and tendered his resignation from the Privy Council with immediate effect.
In July, King Charles stripped Donaldson of his knighthood.

article_title: Labour calls for M4 relief road, seven years after axing the plan
article_content:
Labour calls for M4 relief road, seven years after axing the plan
- Published
Labour's Welsh leader has called for the Plaid Cymru administration to start work on an M4 relief road - seven years after his party had axed it.
Ken Skates told BBC Wales that there was "no other option on the table" to solve congestion in Newport, and has backed a version of the original plan with changes.
The move will be seen by some as an attempt to distance Welsh Labour from part of the legacy of former First Minister Mark Drakeford.
Labour will table a vote in the Senedd on Wednesday calling for an "appropriate relief road" to be built.
A report said the road could now cost £3bn to build. Plaid Cymru accused Labour of hypocrisy.
Skates' announcement comes weeks after the Welsh government set out some options for tackling congestion, including proposals to close junctions in Newport.
It also means that all opposition groups - Reform, Labour and the Tories - are in favour of a relief road.
Drakeford axed previous proposals for an M4 Relief Road in 2019 - on the grounds of cost and the impact on the environment.
The Welsh government has also commissioned an 18-month project to assess possible "roads-based" solutions - although it has ruled out the black route.
A report published earlier in October set out a number of alternatives to a new motorway, and said the relief road could cost around £3bn.
It also warned that the route was no longer safeguarded through the planning system.
"Over time, new development or other land use changes may occur within parts of the former corridor, making it progressively more difficult or expensive to deliver the same highway alignment in the future," it said.
But Ken Skates said the report "shows that no single or combined solution will adequately alleviate congestion on the M4 around Newport.
"That means that there is no other option on the table other than a relief road if we wish to solve the problem of congestion on that route."
He said he believed that an amended version of the original black route - the proposed motorway south of Newport that had been examined and backed by a public inquiry in 2019 - should be the road that got built.
The Welsh Labour leader said the proposed blue route alternative - using existing roads in part - was not appropriate.
"In reality, the black route remains the only appropriate route," Skates said.
"Further work would have to be undertaken to make sure that all environmental concerns today are met and adequately responded to, but something has to be done about congestion."
'We're a world away from 2019'
Asked what he would say to accusations of a U-turn, Skates added: "Well, it's a world away from where we were in 2019.
"Back then, we had come out of the EU, Brexit was causing enormous concern, we were planning for a no deal.
"We were... almost a decade into austerity. There was simply not the sort of money that was required to build the black route available to the Welsh government.
"It was right not to go ahead with it at the time because of the financial cost. I do believe firmly that had we gone ahead with it, it would have been paused or cancelled during Covid."
Skates said he wanted to know from the Welsh government what the status was now of the protected route for the relief road - which was ditched after the scheme was axed.
In a debate on 29 September, Deputy Transport Minister Mark Hooper said the black route was not achievable.
"The protected route status went when it was cancelled," he said.
"So, we're talking about decades of work to even get that off the ground."
Skates spoke ahead of the Co-operative Movement conference on Saturday, where he will say that people in the region "should be trusted, empowered and respected in deciding what affects them".
"Their need for congestion to be dealt with can only realistically be met through getting to work on a relief road.
"The debate over an appropriate solution and the balancing of environmental, human and economic concerns should be led by the people of the region, who know best what is needed in and for their communities."
Local Plaid Cymru MS, Peredur Owen Griffiths, who represents Casnewydd Islwyn, said Labour's "hypocrisy is astounding".
"It's as if they've forgotten they were in government for 27 years and scrapped plans to address the issue of congestion in and around Newport - only to now U-turn in opposition," he said.
"Plaid Cymru is clear that doing nothing isn't an option... the action we're considering could reduce traffic by 10% in just four years," he said.

article_title: Reform councillor resigns after being filmed making racist remarks
article_content:
Alan Feeney has resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after backlash over racist comments that were captured in an undercover investigation.
In a Facebook post on Friday, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”
Earlier this week, an ITV investigation revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign.
Feeney has apologised for his comments. “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said,” he wrote in a Facebook post.
“The comments do not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report. These are communities I have supported countless times in my personal and professional life over many years, many of whom I have been lucky enough to call friends.”
Earlier this year, Feeney won seats in the Shard End ward of Birmingham city council and the Castle Bromwich ward of Solihull metropolitan borough council, and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull.
Following the ITV investigation, which is part of a longer series on Reform UK, Feeney announced on Facebook that he was leaving Reform for “personal reasons”, but kept his seats as an independent councillor before resigning.
In a Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “Byelections will be held on a timescale laid out by those councils in the due course. I hope that in time these councils, and the communities they serve can heal and move on.”
Secretly filmed footage showed Feeney making racist remarks alongside two other Reform candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, while canvassing during May’s local elections. Both Campbell and Whelan have also resigned after the fallout from the investigation.
Nigel Farage has repeatedly pledged to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots”. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.
The clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Feeney calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.
In a Facebook post Feeney wrote: “I understand that my words have caused hurt and anger, particularly among those from the communities I serve. For that, I am deeply sorry. I will be undertaking intensive personal analysis to understand how these sentiments could have taken root, and ensure they can never do so again.”
Alan Feeney and Reform UK have been approached for comment.

article_title: Healey backs pro-growth case for Heathrow third runway after Burnham ducks issue
article_content:
John Healey has said there is a pro-growth case for going ahead with a third runway at Heathrow despite the prime minister declining to back it.
Healey’s predecessor as chancellor, Rachel Reeves, put approval of the long-planned runway at the heart of her “growth speech” last year, saying it would “make Britain the world’s best-connected place to do business”.
However, since arriving in No 10 in July, Andy Burnham has ducked the issue of whether the runway should go ahead, suggesting it should be “a matter for London and Londoners”.
A recent Sunday Times report suggested the prime minister had told the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, that he was “unconvinced” by arguments for the megaproject.
Asked for his views in Bangkok this week, Healey said the government would study responses to a public consultation, which recently closed. He appeared to strike a markedly more positive note than Burnham, however.
“I think in recent decades, and this is true in Heathrow and airports right across the UK, that they have been a big part of jobs and growth. And the case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth,” he said.
Healey has insisted economic growth is his and Burnham’s “number one mission” in government.
Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support.
 
 
 “Our shareholders would like to do this,” he said earlier this week. “They do think that things are taking a long time, and so far they have decided to be OK with that … But of course we cannot wait for ever.”
The airport’s owners include Qatar’s investment authority; the French private equity firm Ardian; Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, GIC. They are expected to decide in the coming months whether to apply for formal planning permission.
Healey voted in favour of the third runway when the question was put to the House of Commons in 2018.
The chancellor was in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund annual meetings but has returned to London to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.
The UK was praised by the IMF this week for taking action to cut its deficit, while other large economies have opted not to do so. The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged Healey to “stay the course” in his budget.
On Thursday, official figures showed the UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August.

article_title: Партнери України розглянуть запит Києва на 70 млрд євро для оборони — Макрон
article_content:
Партнери України розглянуть запит Києва на 70 млрд євро для оборони — Макрон
Україна просить європейських партнерів надати щонайменше 70 млрд євро додаткової допомоги у 2027 році. Йдеться про фінансування оборони, закупівлю зброї та посилення стійкості країни.
Президент Франції Еммануель Макрон заявив, що європейські партнери України розглянуть запит Києва щодо додаткового фінансування оборони у 2027 році.
Про це пише France24.
Президент Володимир Зеленський під час саміту Європейської ради у Брюсселі звернувся до лідерів ЄС із проханням знайти щонайменше 70 млрд євро додаткової підтримки.
За словами Зеленського, загальна вартість війни для України наступного року може становити близько 155 млрд євро. Додаткові кошти Київ хоче спрямувати на оборону, озброєння та підвищення стійкості держави.
Окремо президент України наголосив, що додаткове фінансування дозволило б суттєво збільшити виробництво дронів, які відіграють ключову роль у стримуванні російських атак і ударах по логістиці РФ.
Reuters повідомляє, що серед європейських лідерів є широка підтримка подальшої допомоги Україні, однак конкретний механізм нового фінансування ще мають узгодити. Серед варіантів розглядають нове кредитування та інші фінансові інструменти.
Нагадаємо, що наступного року бюджетні видатки на оборону та безпеку становитимуть майже 44% ВВП. Силам оборони знадобляться додаткові ресурси. Позабюджетну потребу військових Корецький оцінив у 45 млрд дол. (40 млрд євро).
На початку вересня прем’єр анонсував жорстку економію бюджету. Уряд знайшов 70 млрд грн, які спрямує на оборону, та попередив, що без ухвалення необхідних рішень Україна може недоотримати значну частину з 29,5 млрд дол. міжнародної допомоги цього року.

article_title: Trump in Georgia falsely claims election of Jon Ossoff was illegitimate
article_content:
At a rally in north Georgia, Donald Trump again claimed that the 2020 election in Georgia was fraudulent, alleging that the election of US senator Jon Ossoff was illegitimate.
Ossoff, who faces US congressman Mike Collins in November, does not represent Georgia’s values, Trump said.
“And he was never elected,” Trump added.
Ossoff has maintained a consistent lead against Collins, with most recent polling showing him with a nine-point lead against his Republican rival.
Trump claimed he was about to complete the “most successful” two-year run of a president in history, touting stock market gains, low unemployment and poverty rates and the establishment of “Trump accounts” for newborns. Trump again said that American voters would receive a $5,000 government check if Republicans hold the US House of Representatives, claiming that $21tn in foreign manufacturing investments pledged on his watch would offset the trillion-dollar cost.
Most of those pledges remain unfulfilled.
Trump also touted his immigration record and the overthrow of the Venezuelan government.
“Forty-eight hours, and that war was done,” Trump said.
He described the early days of the war on Iran from the perspective of Oval Office meetings and damage reports, particularly of strikes against Iranian leadership.
“They’ll blow up Israel, they’ll blow up the Middle East,” Trump said of Iran and the imperatives of launching attacks. “Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president.”
The Iran war has caused a spike in gasoline and diesel prices. Trump was dismissive of critics citing the increased cost of living on his watch, describing the term “affordability” as Democratic propaganda.
“In the past 17 months, zero illegal aliens have been admitted into the United States,” he said.
An undocumented migrant is rarely “admitted” in any official way.
Trump returned to his regular themes at the rally, which began at about 2pm. About 1,200 people packed grandstands at Dalton municipal airport. Trump took the stage at about 4.20pm, 80 minutes after his scheduled start, with about 300 people standing unshaded in the Georgia afternoon sun. His supporters were undaunted.
“Donald Trump is the greatest president of all time,” said Tracy Spencer of Chattanooga, Tennessee, as she awaited the president’s arrival in Marine One. Asked how she addresses the increasing criticism of the president from disillusioned conservatives, she scoffed.
“Well, none of my friends and family are expressing that to me, because they know better,” she said. “But I have heard the rumors that there are some people that think that, and I would say to those people that growth doesn’t happen overnight and that there are growing pains.”
Trump obliquely discussed his administration’s attacks on anti-discrimination policies he terms “DEI” while describing the “handsomeness” of a US soldier he encountered at the White House.
“Everything is based on merit,” Trump said. “I really have my difficulties with the supreme court, but … our country now is based on merit.”
Two protesters briefly unfurled a banner with an anti-ICE slogan. They were hustled out of the grandstands quickly by security. The assault of a protester in Ohio by Trump supporters in the stands on Monday was not repeated.

article_title: Трамп підписав указ про скасування частини санкцій проти Росії за "законом Грема"
article_content:
Трамп підписав указ про скасування частини санкцій проти Росії за "законом Грема"
Президент США Дональд Трамп скористався правом на винятки та призупинив застосування низки санкцій і тарифів проти Росії, передбачених "законом Грема". Сам закон при цьому залишається чинним.
Президент США Дональд Трамп підписав указ про реалізацію Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 (закон Грема - ред.), яким скасував застосування частини санкцій, обмежень і тарифів, передбачених цим законом щодо Росії.
Про це повідомляють Білий дім та Bloomberg.
Так званий "закон Грема" Трамп підписав 18 вересня 2026 року. Він передбачає масштабне посилення економічного тиску на РФ, зокрема санкції проти російських посадовців, фінансових установ, державних компаній та інших осіб і структур, пов'язаних із російською владою.
Крім того, документ передбачає можливість запровадження тарифів до 500% на російські товари, а також до 100% — проти низки країн, які є найбільшими імпортерами російських нафти й газу або допомагають Москві обходити нафтові санкції.
Водночас сам закон наділяє президента США широкими повноваженнями щодо винятків із санкційного режиму. Ще під час його розгляду адміністрація Трампа наголошувала, що глава Білого дому матиме повну дискрецію щодо таких послаблень.
Тепер Трамп скористався цим механізмом і призупинив дію низки передбачених законом заходів. За даними Bloomberg, йдеться, зокрема, про санкції та тарифи, пов'язані з російською енергетикою.
Послаблення також стосуються частини обмежень щодо російських банків, державних підприємств, чиновників, інвестицій у РФ та операцій, пов'язаних із російським енергетичним сектором. Сам "закон Грема" при цьому не скасовано, а санкції проти Росії, запроваджені на підставі інших законів і президентських указів, залишаються чинними.
Закон назвали на честь покійного сенатора-республіканця Ліндсі Грема, який був одним із головних прихильників посилення санкційного тиску на Москву. Документ Конгрес ухвалив із широкою двопартійною підтримкою.
Ситуація різко загострилася 9 жовтня. Трамп повідомив, що домовився з Путіним про постачання російського дизеля на американський та міжнародний ринки. В Україні таку заяву зустріли обуренням.

article_title: Макрон різко відповів Ле Пен щодо України: попередив про загрозу для Франції
article_content:
Макрон різко відповів Ле Пен щодо України: попередив про загрозу для Франції
Еммануель Макрон розкритикував намір Марін Ле Пен припинити фінансову допомогу Україні. Президент Франції наголосив, що підтримка Києва безпосередньо пов’язана з безпекою французів і всієї Європи.
Президент Франції Еммануель Макрон відреагував на заяву Марін Ле Пен про можливе припинення фінансової допомоги Україні після президентських виборів 2027 року.
Під час пресконференції за підсумками засідання Європейської ради у Брюсселі Макрон заявив, що підтримка України відповідає національним інтересам Франції, оскільки йдеться про безпеку самої країни та Європи, - пише Укрінформ. За його словами, відмова Парижа від допомоги Києву поставила б Францію в унікальне становище серед європейських партнерів.
Макрон наголосив, що політики, які пропонують заощадити бюджетні кошти шляхом припинення підтримки України, фактично ставлять під сумнів цінність безпеки Франції. Він також заявив, що відмова від допомоги Києву означала б загрозу для всієї європейської безпеки.
Окремо французький президент розкритикував політиків, які, за його словами, поводяться так, ніби вже перемогли на майбутніх виборах, і закликав їх поважати вибір громадян.
Раніше Марін Ле Пен заявила, що в разі перемоги на президентських виборах 2027 року Франція ще протягом шести місяців надаватиме Україні фінансову допомогу, після чого припинить її. Вона пояснила це складним фінансовим становищем Франції.
Нагадаємо, що раніше Макрон зробив різку заяву через блокаду Чорного моря
Мовляв, від агресиних дій Кремля страждає Єгипет та інші африканські держави, куди традиційно експортують українське зерно.

article_title: У Конгрес США внесли законопроєкт проти угоди Трампа з РФ: що хочуть заблокувати
article_content:
У Конгрес США внесли законопроєкт проти угоди Трампа з РФ: що хочуть заблокувати
У Палаті представників США представили двопартійний законопроєкт, який має заблокувати закупівлю та імпорт російського дизельного пального і посилити санкційний тиск на енергетичний сектор РФ.
У Конгресі США 16 жовтня представили законопроєкт, спрямований на блокування домовленостей адміністрації президента Дональда Трампа щодо закупівлі російського дизельного пального.
Ініціатором документа став старший демократ у Комітеті Палати представників із закордонних справ Грегорі Мікс. Законопроєкт отримав назву Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act. До нього долучилися представники обох партій, зокрема республіканець Дон Бейкон.
Документ передбачає заборону для Американської корпорації фінансування міжнародного розвитку інвестувати в російський енергетичний сектор. Також пропонується анулювати генеральні ліцензії, видані Управлінням з контролю за іноземними активами Мінфіну США, заборонити видавати такі дозволи надалі та зобов'язати адміністрацію запровадити санкції проти російської енергетики.
Мікс заявив, що закупівля російського дизелю, на його думку, не знизить витрати американців, натомість забезпечить Кремлю додаткові доходи для продовження війни проти України. Він закликав Конгрес підтримати законодавчу ініціативу.
Раніше демократи Комітету із закордонних справ уже виступили проти рішення адміністрації Трампа дозволити закупівлі російського дизельного пального. Вони нагадали, що ще у квітні представили окремий законопроєкт End Russian Oil Windfalls Act, який також передбачає скасування пов'язаних із російською нафтою ліцензій та санкції проти нафтових компаній РФ.
Нагадаємо, раніше Дональд Трамп знову заявив, що Володимир Путін хоче закінчити війну проти України. Водночас на запитання журналістів про Володимира Зеленського президент США чіткої відповіді так і не дав.
До того ж 13 жовтня Трамп уже заявляв, що обидва лідери хочуть зупинити війну, але не знають, як цього досягти. Тоді він пояснював глухий кут ворожнечею між президентами та запевняв, що допоможе їм дійти згоди.
