The government has said its amendments would "significantly reduce" the prospect of military veterans facing "rinse and repeat" investigations.
While some MPs have previously argued that planned protections for veterans do not go far enough, Sinn Féin has branded the amendments a "veterans' charter".
The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) has also raised concerns that MPs will not have enough time to scrutinise the proposed changes.
Sir Chris defended his plans for the attorney general to give consent to serious prosecutions, saying it was a recommendation in a recent Westminster human rights committee.
"We're not carving the Public Prosecution Service in Northern Ireland out of the process," he said.
"They're going to be working with the Crown Prosecution Service in England and Wales to make sure that they've got the same kind of rules and guidelines that apply to all of the prosecutions."
"The attorney general often exercises this kind of role. It's very different from their normal role, but it is something they do quite often."
'Control and cover up' fears
Mark Thompson from the victims' group Relatives For Justice said he feared the bill could lead to unlawful killings being covered up by the state.
"Essentially, this impacts the victims of collusion and state violence," he told the BBC's Sunday Politics programme.
He accused the government of trying to take "control" away from local courts because it did not like some of the recent rulings in Troubles-era cases.
He pointed out that judges had ruled against the Army in "dozens" of inquests into killings carried out by soldiers, including those at Ballymurphy and Springhill.
Thompson argued that local courts had provided a "level playing field" but instead the government caved under pressure from the Army veterans' lobby in London.
"What they [the government] want to do is lift it out of a rule of law process and bring it to London and have a political decision."
Veterans wanted 'Supreme Court judge'
However, lawyer Philip Barden, who has represented several ex-soldiers, claimed Army veterans were "put through the mill" in cases where there was "no evidence".
"What we want is an independent process so its not the PPS and the DPP deciding in Northern Ireland who it is who should be prosecuted," Barden told the programme.
"We wanted a Supreme Court judge as being the most independent person that we could conceive of - not being a political appointment.
"The government have come up with the attorney general of the UK, who of course makes many decisions to prosecute people."
A spokesperson for the PPS said the organisation has "considerable experience in the prosecution of legacy cases".
"We will continue to approach our decision-making with complete impartiality and independence and in accordance with our Code for Prosecutors."
They added: "The proposed role for the Advocate General for Northern Ireland in relation to legacy prosecutions is a matter of government policy and ultimately for Parliament."
Barden defended the government's choice, saying if people disagreed with the UK attorney general's decisions they could always seek a judicial review, arguing that there was "complete independence".
He added that veterans' "primary cause of concern" was the number of repeat investigations into Troubles cases, despite a lack of any new or compelling evidence.
'Too much politics'
Natasha Butler's grandfather, Paddy Butler, was killed by the Army on the Springhill estate in Belfast in July 1972.
She said she wants to "ensure victims and survivors are not lost in the politics surrounding this bill".
She added that "families have waited decades" for answers and the next generations "inherit the same silence".
David Crabbe served in the Ulster Defence Regiment and the Royal Irish Regiment during the Troubles from 1977 to 2007.
He feels "there has been too much politics at play in this" and called on the bill to be "victim-centred".
He added that "there has been a very narrow focus" on veterans.
'A work in progress'
The commissioner for victims and survivors for Northern Ireland said legislation "needs to be truly victims centred".
Speaking on Good Morning Ulster, Joe McVey described the bill as "not perfect", but added "we're very keen that the bill is progressed" as it is "still a work in progress" and needs to be scrutinised in the House of Lords.
"When you look at the Troubles' Bill, we think there's an absence on a focus on victims and survivors and I think that's the message we keep trying to make very clear."
He added: "If we don't do it this time, then I think it'll be very difficult to predict when it's going to get a hearing again."
Why is Labour bringing this bill?
It seeks to replace the previous Conservative government's contentious 2023 Legacy Act, which introduced a ban on inquests and civil actions related to Troubles-era incidents.
The act's most controversial element - offering immunity from prosecution to suspects who cooperated with an information recovery body - was disapplied after being found by the courts to be unlawful.
Labour's bill involves a legacy commission to investigate Troubles-related killings, a separate information recovery body, and a dedicated legacy unit within An Garda Síochána (Irish police).
The government said its amendments "significantly reduce" the prospect of military veterans facing "rinse and repeat" investigations.
What is the government proposing to change?
The government said:
- The legislation will make clear the commission and coroners "must not regard the lawful conduct of members of the armed forces as equivalent to the actions of paramilitaries responsible for acts of terrorism"
- The attorney general, currently Ellie Reeves, will be required to consent to all "serious" Troubles-related prosecutions
- There would be measures to prevent "cold-calling" of veterans and extending provisions for remote attendance as part of the commission's work
- Before any witness can be approached, the commission should consider if "compelling new evidence exists, or the likelihood of a witness being able to provide new information"
- The commission must consider the "context and command orders" in which military veterans were operating
- Former paramilitaries are barred from being appointed to the Victims and Survivors Advisory Group, and there is a requirement for at least one veteran or veterans' representative to be on the panel
- There is a statutory review of the measures for veterans to ensure they "deliver as intended"
Opposition parties and backbench MPs have also tabled separate amendments aimed at changing the bill, but it is up to the Commons Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle to decide whether any of them will be accepted for debate.
description: Amendments to the bill are being debated by MPs, as the long-awaited legislation returns to the House of Commons.

article_title: North Sea strikes could severely disrupt UK fuel supplies, union warns
article_content:
North Sea workers are preparing to strike at oil rigs across the ageing basin over the coming weeks in a sign of growing tensions between trade unions and oil companies.
The Unite union said on Monday that more than 160 offshore rig workers would take part in a 24-hour strike from Wednesday that could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies.
A 48-hour strike starting on Tuesday was already planned by workers at oil services company Wood Group contracted to Harbour Energy’s Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms.
Trade union leaders are scheduled to continue pay talks with the Apache energy company through the Acas mediation service on Wednesday. But Unite expects the 24-hour strike to go ahead at 6am that morning because, it says, the company has shown “no willingness” to resolve the dispute.
The strike will include workers employed at five Apache oil platforms linked to the Forties Pipeline System (FPS), which is responsible for about 30% of the UK’s oil production. Unite has claimed that a halt in production could lead to a sharp drop in pressure across the pipeline system and disrupt UK fuel supplies.
A spokesperson for Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos, the owner of the Forties pipeline, did not respond to a request for comment.
North Sea oil companies have been on a collision course with trade unions in recent years as many cut investments in their UK assets, blaming the UK’s energy policies and tax regime.
The industrial action comes ahead of the budget on 28 October and an imminent decision on the fate of the controversial Jackdaw gas project, as the UK faces fresh concerns over its energy supplies this winter because of the global fuel crisis caused by the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Texas-based Apache plans to end all its North Sea operations by the end of 2029, blaming the “onerous financial” impact of the government’s windfall tax, which means oil companies pay a total tax rate of 78% on their profits.
A spokesperson for Apache said it plans to use experienced contractors to continue production during the strike. It added that even if all five platforms were unable to operate, the company would not expect an impact on other oil companies using the Forties pipeline.
The company added: “Our offer provides a 4% pay increase for employees in the bargaining unit, whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year.”
Harbour Energy, the UK’s biggest producer of North Sea oil, has also blamed the UK’s tax regime for its decision to scale back investment in UK waters. It said late last year that it would cut 100 offshore jobs, having reduced its workforce by about 600 since 2023.
Wood Group said that only eight of the 150 employees contracted to the affected Harbour platforms took part in strike action earlier this month and that the action did not disrupt operations. A third 48-hour strike is planned for 3 November, according to Unite and trade union RMT.

article_title: Віткофф знову летить до Путіна: Axios дізналося про плани США щодо миру в Україні
article_content:
Віткофф знову летить до Путіна: Axios дізналося про плани США щодо миру в Україні
Axios повідомило про новий дипломатичний маневр США на тлі напруженості з Україною.
Спецпосланець Сполучених Штатів Америки Стів Віткофф планує відвідати Норвегію для проведення переговорів щодо припинення війни в Україні, а також Росію, де зустрінеться з диктатором Володимиром Путіним.
Про це повідомляє Axios із посиланням на неназваного американського посадовця.
За даними видання, 20 жовтня в Осло Віткофф зустрінеться з президентом України Володимиром Зеленським на тлі напруженості між Вашингтоном і Києвом через війну.
Американський посадовець також має провести переговори з прем’єром Норвегії Йонасом Гаром Стере, а також з представниками Німеччини, Великої Британії, Франції, Польщі, НАТО та інші високопосадовці з Європи.
Після цього спецпосланець США планує вирушити до Москви. За словами співрозмовника Axios, там Віткофф зустрінеться з «фюрером» Володимиром Путіним і представити йому напрацьовані ідеї.
Видання наголошує, що переговори у норвезькій столиці мають об’єднати представників України, європейських союзників і США для напрацювання мирної пропозиції, яку згодом планують передати Росії.
Мирні переговори — останні новини
Видання CBS News повідомило, що президент США Дональд Трамп готовий обговорювати завершення війни без Києва. Зазначається, що очільник Білого дому може зустрітися з російським диктатором Володимиром Путіним і лідером Китаю Сі Цзіньпіном, але без участі президента України Володимира Зеленського.
Ба більше — Трамп зухвало закликав усунути Зеленського від мирного процесу. Він накинувся з новою порцією критики на українського президента і заявив, мовляв, «давним-давно» той мав нагоду укласти «набагато вигіднішу угоду».

article_title: First minister promises to look at Welsh council powers
article_content:
First minister promises to look at Welsh council powers
- Published
The Welsh government is to examine the powers councils have and how authorities work together regionally, the first minister has announced.
At a speech at Cardiff University, Rhun ap Iorwerth announced that this could lead to new legislation after the next election in 2030.
He is due to meet Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who says ministers in Cardiff should hand more powers to local authorities, later this month.
Ap Iorwerth denied offering a quid pro quo to the prime minister, who the Plaid Cymru leader is hoping will give the Cardiff government more powers and funding.
In the same speech, he also called on the UK government to stop duplicating the Welsh government's economic development work.
"Where power can sit as closely to the people it affects, it should," the first minister said at the event at Cardiff University's Glamorgan building.
"Whilst I am clear that we should never assume that what works for England will work for Wales, and vice versa - and I hope the prime minister acknowledges this – I know that our current arrangements aren't perfect either.
"I am convinced that, over time, Wales should move towards a more coherent and more streamlined system of local and regional governance.
"But that vision cannot be imposed."
Ap Iorwerth promised a green paper by the end of the term, followed by the "option" of new legislation from the next Welsh government.
He said he wanted to be in a "good position to reflect on what is working and where change is needed" by the end of the term, but said the "conversation" had to start before then.
The first minister said it would be a "detailed, meaningful exercise reflecting on where powers and specific competences should lie, how regional working works best and what effective cooperation looks like".
Rhun ap Iorwerth has previously written to the prime minister calling for Wales to have the same powers as Scotland - including on railways, policing and justice.
Asked by BBC Wales if he was trying to offer the prime minister a "quid pro quo", ap Iorwerth said: "I don't quite see it in that way.
"As somebody who wants power close to the people in Wales, I like the fact that the UK's new prime minister is talking that kind of language, but it means different things in Wales and England.
"The devolution programme that we're hearing from Andy Burnham is largely an England programme. What I want to do is find common ground with him."
The first minister questioned whether Downing Street's "devolution agenda" was "really an England-only agenda", and whether it came to a "shuddering halt at Offa's Dyke".
Economic development in Wales is devolved to the Welsh government.
But ap Iorwerth said Wales was living with a "confused" and "increasingly fragmented system".
"A succession of UK government programmes has been layered on top of devolved responsibilities and in some cases undermining them," he said.
"Some have funded worthwhile projects. Some have brought genuine benefits. But, taken together, they have made the landscape more complicated, more fragmented and more difficult to navigate."
He listed city and growth deals, and the former Conservative UK government's levelling up and shared prosperity fund projects, as examples.
"If powers have been devolved, central government should not continue to duplicate them," he said.
He called for a "practical agreement about how our two governments work together to unlock Wales' economic potential".
Asked later to clarify, he said he was not saying he wanted to get rid of city and growth deals - agreements between the UK government, Welsh government and local councils to help fund local projects - of which there are four in Wales.
"Whatever we have, lets look at what works well and how we can improve it," the first minister said.

article_title: Ebola cases in Kenya highlight US failures amid Trump cuts to key services
article_content:
An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history has killed more than 4,300 and sickened more than 9,000 people in the region.
It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.
The US created a controversial quarantine center at Kenya’s Laikipia airbase, where Americans returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo would be required to quarantine. The center, opposed by locals, has stirred distrust in the Kenyan government, leading to protests and a Kenyan court ordering a halt to the center.
“Many Kenyans were concerned about the fact that there was no information and people did not know why the quarantine place was being set up, who was actually going to use it, and what had informed that,” said Allan Maleche, executive director of the Kenya Legal & Ethical Issues Network on HIV and Aids (Kelin). The litigation will be decided in November, he said.
In the meantime, Kenyans were “very cautious around any information that is being given by the government around Ebola”, Maleche said.
Americans who questioned whether the US has the legal authority to quarantine Americans on foreign soil and prevent them from returning home are pushing back against the quarantine center as Kenya faces its first Ebola cases.
“Is this still a viable solution for the US?” asked Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the pandemic center at Brown University school of public health. “Are we posing not only an undue burden on the Kenyan government to be able to handle this, but also is this the safest place to be bringing Americans?”
The US already has “world-class” Ebola treatment units, Nuzzo pointed out.
“American taxpayers built these units for precisely this purpose, and it’s mind-boggling to me that we’re going to leave them empty,” she said. In previous outbreaks, actively ill patients have been evacuated safely to these centers, where they have recovered without further spread of the virus.
The unease follows sweeping cuts to US health support across the world, with the demolition of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and cuts to funding and staff at health agencies like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
On 1 October, the CDC closed HIV prevention offices in Angola and South Sudan, with plans to close offices in Zimbabwe. The US has slashed programs across the world – including DR Congo, where the Ebola outbreak is centered, and other countries, like Kenya, bracing for cases as the outbreak widens.
“We have had a lot of concerns after the US first cut funding for HIV promptly without any direction,” Maleche said. “It led to clinics closing. It led to a lot of anxiety among people.”
The US is now negotiating bilateral agreements with each country, including Kenya – a process that has been mired in secrecy, Maleche said. “It’s not very clear what’s the plan, who’s rolling it out, and what will be involved.”
Cuts to decades-long programs mean the affected countries and the US have less insight into what’s happening, in addition to a lessened ability to prevent and stop outbreaks. “When you pull back on those, not only do you leave those countries less prepared to deal with that day-to-day threat, but it also means that they’re less prepared to deal with future emergencies,” Nuzzo said.
The US officially left the World Health Organization (WHO) in January, making it much harder to collaborate on the response to crises like these. When the US left the WHO, it also “pulled out a substantial amount of funding”, said Maleche. That means the WHO’s response had also been “weakened”, he said.
A Kenyan man fell ill in DRC before traveling by road to Uganda and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October, where he died in a hospital two days later. Since then, seven close contacts have tested positive.
Patrick Amoth, the director-general for health, confirmed on Sunday the total number of infections in the country was eight.
Kenya’s ministry of health pointed to the success of contact tracing and quarantine. About 108 people have been quarantined in Nairobi.
“The general feeling is that the contact tracing systems are working,” Maleche said. But Kenyans are also wondering why there were “many lapses” that resulted in a sick person traveling across countries. The border between DR Congo and Uganda has been closed since May. Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August after earlier reporting 20 cases and two deaths.
A French doctor who returned from DR Congo in June tested positive, and several Americans have been evacuated from DR Congo to Europe for Ebola treatment or monitoring.
In Kenya, “the biggest fear is around how will other countries react” to the outbreak, with travel bans a particular worry, Maleche said. The US put travel bans in place from DR Congo and neighboring Uganda and South Sudan once the outbreak was detected in May, but it would be “very ironic” if the US instituted travel bans, given its quarantine center in Kenya, Maleche said.
Raphael Warnock, a Democratic senator from Georgia, and Bill Cassidy, a Republican senator from Louisiana, penned a letter in June to the Senate appropriations committee opposing the Trump administration’s plans to cut back on HIV prevention and monitoring.
Dismantling of USAID, withdrawing from the WHO, and abruptly cutting foreign aid cuts was “degrading our outbreak preparedness” and had “seriously weakened our ability to keep Americans safe from infectious disease”, Warnock said in a statement.
“These cuts to global health funding have led to the erosion of international disease-monitoring infrastructure that helps us catch threats like Ebola before they reach our shores, at a time when the world needs American leadership most.” The US should be strengthening these systems, not abandoning them, he said.
Nuzzo agreed. “It’s about having an understanding of the systems and the conditions in other countries, and eyes and ears in those countries to detect when something out of the ordinary happens, and to get that information as early as possible,” she said. That benefits the US and the countries themselves, she said.
Work such as HIV prevention “can be repurposed”, she added. “You have connections with clinical care, the ability to move medicines, the ability to conduct laboratory tests, the ability to move specimens around – all of those capacities are things that you would use in other disease emergencies.”

article_title: Minister says Mahmood’s migration policy will ‘prolong integration’
article_content:
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, appears to have criticised Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy in a post on her constituency website, in which she suggested she had concerns that a longer settlement process could affect integration.
Fahnbulleh has since removed the critique, which appeared in a write-up of a community meeting in Peckham, her south London constituency, in September, saying it was not a true representation of her views.
In the original write-up of her comments at the town hall meeting, first highlighted by the Telegraph, Fahnbulleh was reported to have said: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.” Her office said the remarks had been paraphrased, and would be rewritten to reflect a more accurate description of what she had told residents.
The government has proposed increasing the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain from five years to 10, though it is likely to make concessions for some professions, including care workers.
The changes will also mean the pathway to permanent settlement for refugees is extended to up to 20 years, with reviews every 30 months. The government is yet to publish its long-anticipated final response to a consultation on the proposals – though the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he is committed to the bulk of the changes.
Tensions in the cabinet have already surfaced over the proposals. Last month the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, said in an interview that the proposed changes – if left unamended – would unfairly penalise care staff who had “moved their lives here to look after our loved ones”.
Fahnbulleh came to the UK as a child after fleeing the civil war in Liberia. Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast last month, she admitted her family would have found Mahmood’s changes “tough”.
“I represent a constituency which is hugely diverse, where we’ve got first, second, third-generation immigrants, and how we navigate this landscape has been tough,” she added.
With Mahmood believed to be considering changing her plans, Fahnbulleh said she wanted the government to recognise migrants’ contributions.
“I think we ultimately need to get to an immigration system that has control … but actually then recognises the contribution that people have made. And if you’re in this country and you’re working – I say this as a refugee – and you’re doing your bit, and you’re part of your community, you’re working in our health service, then actually this should be a country that welcomes you,” she said.
“I wouldn’t be here if that wasn’t the way that we structured our immigration system. It has always been the case that this country is a welcoming country, and I’m sure it will continue to be that way.”
In her address to her Peckham constituents, Fahnbulleh said the debate had become “increasingly depressing and toxic”. She said there needed to be “a more compassionate immigration system. The asylum process is broken and needs reform. Ultimately, I want to see a system based on control and compassion, with a much stronger focus on integration.”
She continued: “Peckham is a good example of what can happen when communities are built deliberately, and people are given the opportunity to integrate and participate. If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.
“We need to raise the level of the debate, challenge divisive political rhetoric and make the case for communities like the one we have in Peckham. That means talking about immigration with care, control and compassion.”

article_title: Reform MSP quits party to sit as independent
article_content:
Reform MSP quits party to sit as independent
- Published
MSP Amanda Bland has quit Reform UK Scotland to sit as an independent.
The resignation relegates the party to the third-largest group at Holyrood, with one member fewer than Labour.
A Reform UK source told BBC Scotland News that Bland was "very difficult to work with" and had been called to a meeting on Wednesday to discuss a high turnover of staff in her office.
Bland, who represents Central Scotland and Lothians West, told the BBC that her resignation was not linked to the meeting.
In a statement, she said her "principles and priorities remain unchanged" but gave no further details about her decision.
"I entered politics to champion fairness and common sense, protect women and children, improve public services, support businesses to thrive, and work towards a fairer and more effective criminal justice system," Bland said.
"As a member of the criminal justice committee, I remain committed to scrutinising legislation, holding the justice system to account and supporting practical measures that improve public safety, protect victims and ensure justice is served.
"Holding the Scottish government to account remains a key priority, and I believe I can best pursue these goals as an Independent MSP."
She said she would not be making any further statements or giving interviews about Reform, and that her focus now was on her responsibilities as an independent MSP.
A Reform spokesperson said: "Amanda Bland should reflect on her reasons for choosing to isolate herself from that team of capable individuals.
"It is incumbent on her to resign as a regional MSP for Central Scotland and Lothians West and allow her constituents to be represented by the next Reform candidate on that list."
Under Holyrood's rules, a list MSP would be replaced by their party's next candidate at the last election if they resigned.
Bland, a former primary school teacher and police officer, was among 17 Reform candidates to be returned to the Scottish Parliament in May as the party made its electoral breakthrough north of the border.
The party finished in joint second with Labour, behind the SNP on 58 seats.
Reform's cohort, led by former Conservative minister Malcolm Offord, have repeatedly invoked the condemnation of the chamber - most notably after staging a walkout during an independence debate, and by tabling a motion proposing a burka ban.
Currently, Offord is first to question John Swinney at First Minister's Questions every other week, alternating with Labour. The party is now likely to lose that privilege.
Reform UK says its goal is to disrupt a so-called "cosy consensus" in Scottish politics.
Of the 17 MSPs elected under its banner in May, only one had previous experience at Holyrood.
As party leader, Offord has only had a matter of months to try and turn them into a coherent and cohesive political force.
While Bland's resignation was sudden, some kind of fracture in the group has been widely anticipated.
Reform UK's statement on her departure claims the party has a "united team" at Holyrood - something that will attract much scrutiny and speculation.
Reform 'stunts'
Scottish Labour deputy leader Jackie Baillie said: "No-one will be surprised to see chaos at the heart of Reform."
She said the party had been "utterly useless at holding the SNP to account or getting results for the Scottish people", adding: "It's been a series of stunts, gimmicks, photo calls and precious little else."
The Scottish Conservatives said there were growing questions about Reform's ability to provide effective opposition to the SNP at Holyrood.
A spokesperson said: "With Nigel Farage's Reform being weak and ineffective at Holyrood, the Scottish Conservatives will continue standing up to the SNP and fighting for Scotland's taxpayers."
Scottish Liberal Democrat David Green MSP said that Reform had been hit by "scandal after scandal".
He added: "I'm sure more and more of its MSPs will be taking a long hard look at what they've signed up for."
The Scottish Parliament confirmed Bland's resignation and said its website, external had been updated accordingly.

article_title: Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
article_content:
Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
- Published
Bereaved families affected by severe delays paying out civil service pensions could face an "unjust" tax bill, the government has been warned.
Under HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments must be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.
Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said it was "unconscionable" some families could face a "death tax" through no fault of their own.
The Cabinet Office said that if delays caused a tax charge there were existing avenues to claim compensation, such as the Pensions Ombudsman.
However, the ombudsman is currently advising that standard complaints are only likely to be resolved within 18 months, with more complex cases facing a longer wait.
The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.
Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.
Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.
Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.
- Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says 
  - Published12 February
- Emergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensions 
  - Published29 January
- Retired civil servants left in pension limbo 
  - Published23 January
According to the latest figures up to 30 September, external, 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.
Of these, only 301 are in scope to be paid within 15 days.
The PCS union, which represents civil servants, said that while not all these cases would ultimately be affected by the two-year tax rule, there were "serious questions" over how long they would remain unresolved.
If someone dies before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit is only tax-free if it is paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value is below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.
The payment would be taxed at the same rate as the beneficiary's income tax rate.
Sir Geoffrey has written to Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh to urge the government to confirm the bereaved families affected will not face this "unjust financial penalty".
His letter came after BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live highlighted the potential tax liability.
Sir Geoffrey said "the chaos currently engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim".
He warned "a significant number" of family members "will be watching the clock quickly tick down to a year, as the maladministration of the scheme enters its tenth month".
He added: "This is an additional stress they should not have to bear."
Money Box Live: Capita, What Went Wrong?
Money Box Live looks at what is going on with Capita, which administers millions of people's pensions
Rob Wassell, 58, has been waiting almost two years for the lump sum from his brother's civil service pension, following his death.
On 22 October it will be two years since the pension scheme was notified of his death so if he does not receive the payment in just a few days times, it could face being taxed.
Rob, who contacted the BBC's Money Box programme about his case, said he had been phoning Capita with increasing "desperation" as his situation dragged on.
"It's a bitter pill to swallow to have to pay tax for something which was not my fault," he said.
"It creates unnecessary worry and anguish through the process, which is already in itself difficult."
Rob said he needed the money to cover the estate costs he had to pay for his brother and fill a £20,000 hole in his savings.
However, he said it was "heartbreaking" to hear of other cases where people needed the money just to survive.
Rob added that the idea that he might face "another battle" to recoup the tax through compensation made it feel like "you just want to give up".
Fran Heathcote, head of the PCS union, said it would be "a profound injustice" if families faced a further financial penalty because of Capita's failures.
"If that does happen, the government should be ashamed that families are being made to pay the price for failures that are entirely outside their control," she said.
A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, said: "The service levels following the move to Capita have been completely unacceptable and we are committed to ensuring no member is left financially worse off.
"We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly £10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure that individuals do not experience delays.
"If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses."
A Capita spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for the frustration that the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme has caused members and their families.
"Our teams are working tirelessly to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging personal circumstances."

article_title: No 10: Hegseth ‘wrong’ to say most non-US Nato soldiers didn’t fight in Afghanistan – as it happened
article_content:
No 10 says US defence secretary Pete Hegseth 'wrong' to say most non-US Nato soldiers in Afghanistan didn't fight
Downing Street has delivered a rare public reprimand to a member of Donald Trump’s administration, saying Pete Hegseth, the US defence secretary, was “wrong” to suggest that most non-American Nato soldiers in Afghanistan did not do any fighting.
Hegseth made the comment in a speech at the University of Tennessee, where he recalled serving in Afghanistan himself. He said:
I was a captain in Afghanistan and we would go to the headquarters in Kabul and there would be 50 flags at the headquarters. It was a beautiful thing to see, 50 different countries contributing to the Nato alliance and the Isaf [International Security Assistance Force] mission there.
Except there were maybe five that contributed. It was actually closer to one or two that by the end were actually involved in kinetic operations. In fact the patch Isaf, we joked it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting’.
Asked about Hegseth’s comment at the Downing Street lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson said Hegseth was “wrong” in what he said about the Nato operation in Afghanistan.
The spokesperson explained:
The facts speak for themselves when it comes to the UK’s and Nato’s contribution to Afghanistan. Thousands of British and Allied families made huge sacrifices to play their significant part in that war and uphold our values, and more than 450 British personnel never returned.
Their sacrifice and that of other Nato forces was made in the service of collective security and in response to an attack on our ally. We are incredibly proud of our armed forces and their service and sacrifice will never be forgotten, and it is wrong to diminish their role.
While the UK government disagrees with much of what Donald Trump and his team say and do, there is normally a reluctance to criticise them in public. However, this does not seem to apply when the reputation of British servicemen and women has been impugned. Keir Starmer tried hard to maintain a good personal relationship with the US president, but when Trump made a similar claim about Nato allies avoiding frontline fighting in Afghanistan, Starmer condemned what he said as “insulting and frankly appalling”.
Scottish Labour has become the second largest party at Holyrood after Amanda Bland, a Reform UK MSP, resigned from the party to sit as an independent. (See 12.21pm.)
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary has said the armed forces need to “live within their means” as he confirmed that some training exercises have been cancelled to save money. (See 2.54pm.)
For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.
Miatta Fahnbulleh scrubs post from website criticising Home Office plan to make migrant workers wait much longer for ILR
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, has published an article criticising the home secretary’s proposal to make immigrant workers wait much longer before they can apply for permanent residency in the UK.
In a post on the website that promotes her work as Labour MP for Peckham in south London, she said:
Ultimately, I want to see a system based on control and compassion, with a much stronger focus on integration …
If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.
We need to raise the level of the debate, challenge divisive political rhetoric and make the case for communities like the one we have in Peckham. That means talking about immigration with care, control and compassion.
According to a story by Nick Gutteridge for the Telegraph, Fahnbulleh’s team say these comments were actually written by an aide as an account of what the MP said at a meeting with consituents last month. They describe it as poorly-phrased summary, and the post has been taken down so that it can be reworded. But they do not seem to be contesting that the public version captures the gist of what she thinks.
The language is contentious because Shabana Mahmood wants to make most migrant workers wait for at least 10 years before they can apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) in the UK. Under current rules, ILR is normally available after five years.
Mahmood originally published her plans last year. Fahnbulleh, who came to the UK as a child refugee from Liberia, is not the only cabinet minister with concerns. Andy Burnham has signalled that he is unhappy about Mahmood’s plan to make foreign care workers wait 15 years for ILF (supposedly because their low earnings mean they are more likely to be a burden on the state), and Mahmood has signalled that some sort of climbdown is coming.
The latest edition of the Guardian’s Politics Weekly UK podcast is out. It features Kiran Stacey and Pippa Crerar talking about the Alan Milburn review of youth unemployment.
Welsh first minister invites Burnham to agree 'new partnership for growth' with Wales
Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, will give a speech later inviting Andy Burnham to agree to a “new partnership'” between Wales and the UK government on growth. The two governments should also avoid “duplicating activity”, he will say.
According to a report for Nation.Cymru, ap Iorwerth will say:
I will invite the prime minister to agree a new partnership for growth between our two governments – a practical agreement about how our two governments work together to unlock Wales’s economic potential …
My message to the prime minister will be a simple one – let us spend less time designing new programmes and duplicating activity. Let us spend more time unlocking opportunity and supporting investment, and more time delivering the growth we both want to see in all parts of our respective nations.
The Green party has reacted with alarm to reports suggesting the Alan Milburn review of Neets will recommend lower sickness benefits for people under the age of 25.
Pointing out that the recent review from Prof Peter Fonagy into the prevalence of mental health conditions, autism and ADHD argued cutting benefits was bad for mental health, the Green party’s co-deputy leader Mothin Ali said:
It seems that when you commission an expert like Prof Fonagy rather than a Blairite former minister, you get a far more coherent analysis of the issues affecting young people and their mental health …
The Green party has a proper jobs guarantee for young people – real jobs, with real training and rights at work. It would be funded by those who can afford to contribute, not by cutting support for those least able to cope.
Streeting rejects call from Tory MP for UK to sell Diego Garcia military base to Trump
During defence questions, Edward Leigh, the Conservative MP and father of the Commons, asked Wes Streeting about the Diego Garcia military base on the Chagos Islands. Given that it was “to all intents and purposes an American military base”, why didn’t the government just sell it to Donald Trump for £6bn, and invest the money in defence?
Streeting said that he didn’t think that was the right solution.
In an earlier answer, Streeting defended the government’s plan to transfer sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius as a response the legal doubt over the UK’s claims of ownership. He said:
Having looked at this whole issue with a fresh pair of eyes, I’ve reached the same conclusion as every prime minister since Boris Johnson, including this one, which is the capabilities provided by that base makes it extremely unwise and a risk not worth taking to have legal uncertainty. That is why efforts to negotiate a treaty continue.
Fraser Nelson, the Times columnist who is heavily involved in a project the paper is running investigating the nature of welfare spending, has written an interesting post on his Substack blog about Andy Burnham’s welfare article today. (See 9.34am.) Nelson argues that Burnham saying “benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point” is the key line. He explains:
I read this as an intention to dismantle what Whitehall officials call ‘the pipeline’ – in effect, a Neet factory. Children as young as five are categorised as disabled and a £10k package released to the parents. This ‘disability living allowance’ typically converts to adult Pip at age 16 paying about £9,000 straight to the kid.
Outcomes for such child claimants are poor: the Milburn review disclosed that the DWP holds the power to follow these kids in later life. It does not use this power lest anyone FoIs to find out the scandal (they rejected my request saying it’d cost too much to work out what happened to sickness benefit claimants, even though they could). But [Alan] Milburn used his powers to get them to publish a cohort analysis. This graph is The Pipeline.
And Nelson includes this chart showing what happens to children who have claimed DLA (disability living allowance) for children after the age of 16.
James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, reminded Streeting that, soon after being made defence secretary, he was asked in a TV interview if he would resign if the Treasury did not allocate enough for defence spending. “Absolutely,” Streeting replied. Cartlidge asked if that was still the case.
Streeting said that his answer remained the same. And he said he was confident saying that because “this government is already delivering the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the end of the cold war”.
Streeting says it is 'irresponsible' and 'inaccurate' for Reform UK to claim Britain cannot defend Falkland Islands
Back in the Commons, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, is now taking topical questions.
In response to Andrew Rosindell from Reform UK saying the UK’s “ability to protect the Falkland Islands is now in doubt”, Streeting replied:
It is simply irresponsible, not to mention inaccurate, to suggest that the UK is incapable of defending the Falkland Islands. We are perfectly capable of doing that. We had a very visible demonstration only recently. Maybe if Reform had a defence spokesperson, they might have noticed.
Israeli general election highlights flaws with PR, David Blunkett claims
This morning Daisy Cooper cited Andy Burnham’s support for proportional representation as evidence that the Liberal Democrats are “winning the battle of ideas”. (See 11am.)
But only up to a point. There are a couple of reports around this morning that show that, while Burnham may personally favour PR, he is yet to convincingly win the argument for it in the parliamentary Labour party.
In an article for PoliticsHome,Harriet Symonds and Matilda Martin point out that some of Burnham’s most senior ministers prefer first-past-the-post. They say:
PoliticsHome understands that Louise Haigh, deputy PM and Burnham’s close ally, has concerns about shifting to PR.
Other Cabinet members have previously voiced reservations about the idea.
In 2022, Angela Rayner, now secretary of state for housing, communities and local government, said she was a “first-past-the-post girl” who was “yet to be convinced by PR”, telling The News Agents podcast that it could allow extremist parties such as the British National Party (BNP) to win House of Commons seats.
And David Blunkett, the former cabinet minister who has been one of Burnham’s political mentors, has written an article for the i restating his longstanding opposition to PR. He says:
In my view, the argument can’t be that “every vote must count”. Each vote already does count, because in order to have winners and losers, people engage in the process which inevitably means that some voters’ preferences will be cancelled out by a greater number preferring another candidate.
Not everyone can have prizes in a democracy. Some candidates lose, some electors are frustrated and annoyed that their candidate didn’t succeed. Hence, the first set of questions about what it is we think this change is going to improve. The second question is why we would believe that electoral reform would change people’s interest or engagement with politics?
Later this month we will have a demonstration of what is the purest form of proportional representation in the world. Namely, the Israeli general election. If there were ever an example of how tiny minorities representing not only outlandish views, but providing a blockage on progress, compromise and long-term outcomes, it has to be this form of PR.
Streeting tells MPs that US still providing 'vital support' to Ukraine, and it 'does know which side it's on'
Wes Streeting told MPs that the US is still on the side of Ukraine in its war against Russia.
During defence questions, the Lib Dem MP James MacCleary asked about reports that the Ukrainian military were left exposed last week after President Trump reportedly intervened to restrict access to the Starlink internet service for its weapons.
Streeting replied:
It is worth pointing out, after what was unquestionably a challenging week for relations between the United States and Ukraine, that the United States has and does and will continue to provide vital support to Ukraine, whether that’s intelligence sharing or indeed the work we do on procurement with and through the United States, as well as the diplomatic track.
Referring to a meeting he had with Pete Hegseth, his US counterpart, last week, Streeting went on:
This is worth reporting to the house; Pete Hegseth, my US counterpart, was keen to thank the United Kingdom for our leadership of Ukraine.
That would suggest to me the United States does know which side it’s on.
Streeting confirms army has to had cancel some training exercises as cost-cutting measure
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, is taking questions in the Commons.
When the Reform UK MP Danny Kruger asked him if he agreed it was “absolutely scandalous” that non-essential training had been cancelled by the army, Streeting said that training exercises were taking place for the rest of this year. But he accepted that some future training had been cut.
He told MPs:
When I arrived in the Ministry of Defence, there was an in-year overspend that would have seen us overcommitted by the end of the year.
And, as I did at health, I make absolutely no apology whatsoever for sending a very strong message very early on that, while this government is delivering the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the end of the cold war, I also expect my department and our armed forces to live within their means.

article_title: Farage claim that £5m was reward for Brexit was ‘not press office line’, close aide says
article_content:
Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides.
The apparent admission came in undercover footage seen by the Guardian in which Dan Jukes says that it is “priced in” for Farage to profit from politics.
The footage raises fresh questions about the party leader’s statements that the gift was solely for security purposes.
The Reform UK leader is awaiting the outcome of a parliamentary watchdog investigation into whether or not the £5m from the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, should have been declared under parliamentary rules.
Farage told the Sun on 14 May: “And this [£5m] was given to me on an unconditional basis, completely unconditional basis. But frankly, it was given as a reward for campaigning for Brexit for 27 years.”
Now, previously unpublished footage from the undercover reporting group Verbatim, shared with the Guardian, has revealed a conversation between Jukes, a longtime close aide of Farage, and an undercover reporter.
“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said of Farage’s admission that the funds were a political reward, appearing to suggest that it was an on-air accident.
The subject of Farage’s funds arose when Jukes quipped that if a US limited liability company could not make a donation because of electoral law, perhaps the reporter posing as a donor could just make him a £5m unconditional gift instead.
After discussing if Jukes could think of any ways other than secret polling – foreign-funded polls that appeared to be orchestrated by Reform officials but which were not publicly attributed to the party – for the party to benefit from money from a US LLC, Jukes replied: “I’m happy to take a £5m personal, unconditional gift, of course.”
The undercover reporter said: “That seems like it’s [the £5m] been quite tough.”
“I’m a realist and I bat straight and it’s a little bit awkward,” Jukes said, appearing to admit that Farage was not meant to change his explanation from the £5m being intended for security costs to say it was a reward for Brexit.
“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said. “So I think now the line is it was a thank you for Brexit to pay for security so he is safe for the rest of his life.”
The undercover reporter suggested that people did not mind if Farage “makes a few bob [from politics]”.
Jukes replied: “Well it’s a bit priced in with our Nige, isn’t it, no one’s voting for him to be the pope.”
If the funds were not given unconditionally but rather as a way to circumvent donation rules, as the footage appears to suggest, it could also trigger questions about whether it was a payment for work and therefore subject to tax.
Jukes left Reform after the original Verbatim/Channel 4 investigation was aired. He had worked closely with Farage for more than a decade.
An internal Reform investigation concluded that neither Jukes nor another senior party official, James Orr, had broken laws that ban foreign donations. A police investigation is ongoing.
Harborne has previously said of the gift to Farage that it was “to support Nigel’s security not just now, but for the rest of his life”. Lawyers for the crypto-billionaire have previously said he “expected nothing in return” and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”.
The timeline for the gift is disputed.
Lawyers for Harborne have said the gift was made on 5 April 2024.
According to financial industry sources, some of the £5m was not received until the end of May, just before Farage announced on 3 June that he would stand as an MP.
The Guardian has also reported that Farage told senior Reform figures he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election.
Farage has given a wide variety of reasons for accepting the £5m including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit. He has refused to say how much, if any, of the £5m has been spent on security, adding it was nobody’s business what he did with the money and he could “spend it on Ferraris” if he wanted.
A spokesperson for Farage did not address several of the points put to them by the Guardian, including the claim that Farage had deviated from the press office line by admitting the £5m was a reward for Brexit.
Farage’s spokesperson said Jukes “accurately describes that the gift was for his security for the rest of his life”.
Lawyers for Jukes referred back to a previous statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals, using selective editing, who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK.”
They added that Jukes denied any wrongdoing and pointed to the outcome of Reform’s internal investigation.

article_title: Reform UK mayor investigated over naked photo claims
article_content:
Reform UK mayor investigated over naked photo claims
- Published
Reform UK's Hull and East Yorkshire elected mayor Luke Campbell is under police investigation for allegedly sharing naked images of himself.
A spokesperson for Hull and East Yorkshire Combined Authority (HEYCA) said: "The mayor firmly denies the allegations.
"We recognise the seriousness of the matters reported and understand the concern they have caused among our staff, partners and the wider public.
"With a police investigation ongoing, it would not be appropriate to comment further on individual allegations or speculate about the outcome."
The spokesperson added: "The combined authority has established procedures for handling complaints about members and officers, which must be conducted fairly and independently."
According to The Observer newspaper, external, the Reform UK mayor and former Olympic gold medallist boxer is accused of allegedly showing naked pictures of himself to a female member of staff.
Liberal Democrat leader of Hull City Council Mike Ross, who came second in the mayoral election last year, said that Campbell should "stand aside" during the investigation.
"I'm saying if there's an investigation taking place at the moment in any other circumstances a person in that position would be asked to stand aside while that was taking place," he said.
"And certainly if that is something that should be happening now then I believe that would be the right course of action."
Conservative leader of East Riding of Yorkshire Council Anne Handley said: "I think to look after the mayor, to look after himself, I think the best thing he could do was to just stand aside for now just until the investigation comes to a conclusion."
Humberside Police and Crime Commissioner, Conservative Jonathan Evison, also called for Campbell to step aside.
"I believe anyone in public office facing allegations of this nature should step aside while an investigation is concluded," he said.
"This is a matter of accountability and public trust, and it is essential that the appropriate authorities can carry out their work without interference.
"We must also respect due process and avoid reaching conclusions before the facts are established.
In a statement, Reform UK said: "Luke firmly denies the allegations."
"They come from a disgruntled employee attempting to leverage a settlement in a meritless workplace dispute."

article_title: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite | Gaby Hinsliff
article_content:
Another morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway.
In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to reach you right back.
And therein lies the challenge to the government’s hopes of AI helping to transform the machinery of the state on the cheap, saving not only time but billions of pounds in public money. It’s early days, but AI seems not so much to be streamlining public service delivery as gumming it up – partly because, as was once the case with email, the public is using it right back at them.
In a Substack post last week, the former civil servant Sam Freedman noted that governments around the world seem to be experiencing unusual surges in complaints, requests and responses to regulatory and official bodies since the adoption of ChatGPT. It’s the same story in the courts, with employment tribunal cases in England, Scotland and Wales reportedly rising by 39% in a year thanks in part to claimants using AI to draft claims, while magistrates and judges face a wave of people who can’t afford lawyers using ChatGPT to build cases that often don’t make sense. And all of this needs patient disentangling by a human, on the grounds that just because a defendant is citing precedents that don’t exist, it doesn’t mean there isn’t a genuine grievance buried in there somewhere.
Whitehall special advisers complain of departments drowning in AI-generated freedom of information requests, an abuse of a system originally intended to empower individuals. MPs’ offices are similarly swamped by AI-generated letters, all of which need to be read by humans for fear of missing something important from a constituent.
How long before public consultations on changing the law become so spammed by slop that they are in essence useless as a measure of what the country actually thinks? There’s a fine line between the noble aim of making it easier for individuals to interact with an otherwise remote state, and making it so easy that the result is an uncontrollable firehose of meaningless machine-generated guff.
The obvious answer to this kind of AI flooding is getting AI tools to detect or sift it, but that doesn’t always work when dealing with potentially vulnerable human beings. Constituents who use AI to express themselves in more fancy-sounding language when writing to their MP, for example, still have the right to expect a personal response from a human being.
Employers who thought they were being smart by getting AI to sift job applications, meanwhile, are reaping what they sowed, as resentful applicants automate their end of things too and spray-gun applications across the board, rather than concentrating on the jobs they really want. Now neither side can separate the wheat from an avalanche of chaff.
The risk of paralysis is likely only to increase if the public starts adopting agentic AI in the kind of numbers big tech fondly imagines. Early adopters might well find agents save them time and hassle. But shortcuts stop being shortcuts once everyone else is using them too, and risk turning into bottlenecks instead. Think of cars, which have vastly shortened journey times compared with travelling by horseback, except in cities at rush hour when too many other people are also trying to shorten theirs. By 2018, central London daytime traffic was moving on average at just over 7mph – about the same speed as a trotting pony.
Historically, humans have always learned to develop ways around problems of our own making. We have spam filters for email, congestion charges to keep cars out of cities, and in the long term we could well figure out what kind of frictions we need to put back in the system to make it possible to live with the impact of AI.
But for now a useful rule of thumb, if improbable claims start to be made for savings due to AI, will be that more isn’t always better; faster and easier isn’t always more convenient; and time saved in one section of public services has a horrible habit of popping up in another one. Let the Whac-A-Mole begin.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

article_title: ITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad apples | John Crace
article_content:
It was the dog that didn’t bark in the night. After Sunday night’s ITV exposé of widespread racism and misogyny within Reform, you might have expected one of its MPs to have taken to the airwaves on Monday morning to defend the party’s honour. To try to persuade viewers that the real problem lay with the journalists who couldn’t stop themselves from investigating Reform rather than the fact that the party’s bigotry was endemic.
Instead, we got nothing. Every Reform MP was otherwise engaged. Were too busy having breakfast. Nothing from Nigel Farage. Nothing even from Robert Jenrick. Maybe he realised he had crashed and burned a few days earlier by suggesting it was just one of those things. One of life’s little mysteries. The BBC was riddled with paedophiles and Reform was awash with racists, said Honest Bob. No big deal. Every organisation had its crosses to bear.
The only MP to post on X in the morning was Richard Tice, who was feeling decidedly grumpy, having only just got married to Isabel Oakeshott. Perhaps he had a hangover. Though his main gripe was that British Airways was yet another failing British institution because it had mislaid at least one of his bags.
Dicky’s social media post had more than a touch of the “don’t you know who I am” to it. You can only imagine the baggage handler may have known exactly who Dicky was and had taken great pleasure in diverting one of the fake Louis Vuitton suitcases from Dubai to Manila. Via Buenos Aires.
The one person out and about for Reform was the one person you would have thought the party would want to keep hidden. Step forward Matt Goodwin, the party’s failed candidate for the Gorton and Denton byelection whose own views could easily pass off as borderline racist in polite circles. Matt is going through his own personal anti-growth agenda. Working hard to deconstruct himself from low-level academic to incredibly dim primate with low social skills. Almost every day, voters in Gorton and Denton thank their lucky stars for having dodged that bullet.
Matt’s defence of Reform was … unorthodox, to put it kindly. So much so that you began to wonder whether he was even conscious. Luckily for him, he was only allowed out on Times Radio. Though that was more than enough. To try to understand Matt is to make a category error. The whole point is to not understand him. That’s the way you stay sane. Because what he wanted listeners to believe was that Nige was a buffer zone against racism. That hordes of would-be racists begged to be allowed to join Reform, only to find out that Nige was a man of peace and love. The one politician who wanted nothing but good things for all immigrants.
It got better. Because Batshit Matt also wanted us to believe that the ITV documentary had just uncovered a few bad apples in the party. So in a way it had done Reform a favour. What were the chances? The ITV journalists had managed to uncover the only seven racists in the Reform ranks. Everyone else was Team Nigel. Never had a bad word for anyone. Except, there was another way of looking at this. That ITV had filmed about 10 Reform councillors and found that seven of them had views that included beheading King Charles for being a Muslim. Some statisticians might put that down as a 70% hit rate. Not so much a few wrong ’uns but a whole army of them. Poor Nige. Always the victim.
Over in the Commons, Wes Streeting was preparing for other threats during departmental defence questions. Though John Healey was not one of them. You’d have thought that Wes might have wanted to schmooze the chancellor before next week’s budget. To try to get the best funding settlement he could. Not a bit of it. Wes began by slagging off his predecessor as defence secretary for wasting money on unnecessary training exercises and then announced he was confident that Healey would reach the necessary 3% and 3.5% targets at next year’s spending review. So, no, Wes wouldn’t be resigning any time soon. Let’s hope his confidence is well placed.
Instead, Wes seemed more interested in persuading himself that there was absolutely nothing unusual in Donald Trump switching the Starlink satellite system on and off at random moments, thereby allowing Russian drones to do untold damage on Ukraine. This was just standard procedure. The only way you could tell the system was working properly was if you turned it off from time to time. Obvious when you think about. Wes was also totally chilled about Trump trying to lower US pump prices by allowing Russian imports of diesel. Fuel that the Russians had also imported from Iran and with whom, coincidentally, the US was at war.
All of this apparently made perfect sense not just to Streeting, but also to Labour and opposition backbenchers. Wes could reassure us because he had had a personal meeting with Pete Hegseth the previous week, during with the secretary for war had reiterated Trump’s claims that Nato forces had been a waste of space in Afghanistan and that the US troops had fought alone. A nice ice breaker. After that, Pete went out of his way to say Washington was totally behind Ukraine, just so long as Russia won the war.
Curiously, the shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, didn’t use his questions to talk up the four drones of the “Britannia shield” that the Tories were sure would protect the UK from nuclear war. So it remains a mystery. Almost as if it was a bullshit party conference announcement that was designed to be forgotten within days. Highlight of the day went to Sharron Davies, the former swimmer turned Tory peer, who demanded to know why Andy Burnham hadn’t invaded France to stop the rioting. Can you explain it to her?

article_title: Shall we have another EU referendum? Maybe – but not yet | Polly Toynbee
article_content:
When I hear that word again, a shudder runs down my spine. I want to groan, hold my head in my hands and wail. The horror! No, never again, not another referendum. But the idea is back in play as Andy Burnham looks for ways to reverse a decade of economic stagnation.
As the prime minister dared to unlock the door to a Brussels reunion, you could hear Ode to Joy burst out from all remainers. But the prospect of a re-run of the most self-destructive vote in our history is dismaying.
Remember that morning a decade ago. First came Sunderland’s 12.20am result, a 61.3% vote to leave, but there was still hope for remainers … until the BBC’s 4.40am verdict that leave had won. In that second a great rift tore across the country. Remainers, dubbed remoaners, never recovered. UK politics became a circus: we who paraded as the west’s strong and stable “mother of parliaments” ran wildly through seven prime ministers in 10 years. Both Labour and Tory parties were wrecked by the most shattering event of our political lifetime. It is a wound neither has dared to reopen.
Only now Burnham has finally broken the spell of Brexit silence, aiming to rejoin, while the Tories will stay in the wilderness until they repent the Brexit disaster they inflicted on the country.
As Burnham sets out to explore all the options, outriders scout the way back in. Making the strong case for full EU membership, IPPR, the thinktank closest to Labour, has published a weighty report this week on how it can happen and why it must: we need it for prosperity, security and democracy. It has left us dangerously alone and friendless in a world of great power blocs. Our once reliable ally, the US, is never to be fully trusted again now we know what its people are capable of voting for. And so the warmth of familiar democracies across the Channel looks welcoming (at least for now). Make this bid to rejoin about who we are, bonding with where we belong, emotionally and historically. We have discovered “sovereignty” is a mirage: every treaty and trade deal requires sharing it with allies.
Within a year, a majority of people in the UK thought Brexit was a mistake (not quite the same as regretting their own vote). Now we know that Brexit has robbed us of a walloping 8% of GDP. IPPR and Persuasion UK polling finds 52% want to rejoin, 29% to stay out. Support grows by the year, partly as older people drop off their perches and young pro-Europeans join the electoral roll. As the IPPR tested every option from Keir Starmer’s slight reset to full membership, the least popular was leaving things as they are. The current Boris Johnson/Lord Frost deal is so dysfunctional that Burnham says keeping it would be a “dereliction of duty”. As ever ignoring the public mood, last year Kemi Badenoch wrote to the EU ambassador warning that, if elected, she would repeal any change, an act of near-treason that could sabotage negotiations in Brussels that start next month. Watch Michael Gove, arch-Brexit manipulator, telling the Guardian’s Aditya Chakrabortty he regrets nothing, blaming others for failing to capitalise on those illusory Brexit benefits. Would that bleating work? I think not.
But is this shift to 52% v 29% strong enough to dare throw the dice and risk everything? No, not quite yet. The IPPR admits it is still “soft”, and there are familiar echoes of what happened last time. After years in which it felt as if we could talk about nothing else, the EU now has reassuringly low salience. But that’s just as it was until Ukip and Tory Brexiters turbocharged what had been a non-issue. As before, polling figures that encouraged David Cameron to breeze arrogantly into a referendum looked sufficient to someone who assumed he would win. This time we know better. Prepare for Dominic Cummings et al rising from their coffins with Brexit defibrillators to shock new life into the issue. Nigel Farage was at it on Sunday, claiming the EU would charge Britain £42bn a year to rejoin.
Testing arguments for both sides, this report reveals traps to avoid and what people like about rejoining. Red lights flash over joining the euro, scrapping our other trade deals, giving up fishing rights and high contributions to the EU budget. Top of the most effective reasons for rejoining is passport queues. Second comes security: Ukraine has exposed this dangerous Trump/Putin world. Third is the need to bring lost foreign investment back to Britain.
But reasoned, fact-based focus groups in a calm and rational atmosphere can’t begin to replicate the monstrous lies, fabrications and devilry of a TikTok, Instagram and X referendum campaign. Remember the £350m-a-week bus, the Turks are coming, immigration will end and, best of all, “take back control”. Of what? Everything! That’s what referendums do.
So not yet. The case for joining has to be powerfully made, the argument won overwhelmingly for allied EU forces to circle the wagons against what Peter Ricketts, ex-national security adviser, along with the head of MI5, warns are “more reckless, more dangerous” cyber-attacks on vital services, such as energy, water, transport, banking or air traffic control. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, meeting with the EU home affairs commissioner today to restore data cooperation on crime and migration is a reminder of how insanely self-destructive Brexit was.
In a decade, Britain has changed. Though Brexiters will threaten floods of migrants storming the border on joining the EU, IPPR polling shows freedom of movement no longer alarms voters as it once did. The cost of living is now the top national concern, not immigration. Look how poorer countries have caught up to us: per capita income in Bucharest, Romania’s capital, is far higher than Sunderland’s.
But the EU has changed too. The question is what kind of Europe we would join if Marine Le Pen and the Alternative für Deutschland became its new axis of power. Here’s the answer: that would make joining even more urgent, to be inside to influence what we can, bolstering the democrats. Staying out leaves us powerless.
This report sets to work on the campaign Burnham ignited when he proposed going “all the way”. The goal is clear and the need is growing urgent. As the EU ambassador told the Guardian’s Patrick Wintour, the ball is in our court. Brussels, he said, is “ready to engage”, once Britain decides what it wants.
Let’s decide, but proceed with extreme caution. Would you risk the next general election by putting this into Labour’s manifesto, certain to become the right’s battle-flag? Yes, when a strong pro-EU campaign makes it winnable. But there should be no referendum until public opinion is so solid that it would be a mere rubber-stamping of the overwhelming public will.
- 
  Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist
