article_title: Andy Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drilling
article_content:
The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, signalling Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea fossil fuel industry and threatening to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs.
Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey, the energy secretary and chancellor respectively, will make the announcement from Aberdeen on Wednesday morning after more than a year of deliberations over whether doing so would violate the UK’s climate commitments.
The approval for drilling at one of the biggest undeveloped fields in the declining North Sea basin is a big boost for Britain’s oil and gas industry – and especially for Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor, which operate it.
It will be met with outrage from climate campaigners, who say it undermines Labour’s green credentials and will exacerbate the climate crisis.
Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs, as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.”
She added: “Labour’s climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.”
When fully operational, Jackdaw will account for 6% of North Sea gas production, making it one of the biggest gasfields not yet under production.
Along with the Rosebank oilfield, its status has become symbolic of the government’s commitment to the oil and gas industry, which is facing heavy job losses as reserves decline and platforms become increasingly automated.
The field was approved by the Conservative government in 2022, with ministers arguing it would help shield the UK from the volatility in the energy market caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Labour came to power in 2024 on a promise not to grant any new licences in the North Sea, not expecting to have to make a decision on Jackdaw or Rosebank.
However both fields were cast into doubt last year by a landmark ruling that said their environmental approval had been incorrectly granted.
A judge ruled that when deciding whether the two fields would violate the UK’s climate commitments, regulators should have taken into account the carbon emissions generated by burning the oil and gas they would produce.
Shell and Equinor resubmitted their application for environmental consent last September. Since then, Fahnbulleh and her predecessor, Ed Miliband, have spent months deciding whether to use their ministerial power to block it.
Both the prime minister and his predecessor, Keir Starmer, have come under heavy pressure to allow the fields to go ahead in recent months, not least from Donald Trump, who urged both men to “open up the North Sea”.
Burnham signalled he was sympathetic to the US president’s arguments earlier this summer, promising to take a “pragmatic approach” to the decision.
“There is a resource there,” he said in July. “When people are struggling – you can’t ignore that.”
He told the Commons last week: “I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas. We will set out our decisions shortly.”
Several sources have told the Guardian that Fahnbulleh has decided not to block the field, allowing the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the industry, to give the go-ahead based on financial and logistical concerns.
Making the announcement alongside Healey and the NSTA’s chief executive, Stuart Payne, they will say that granting the environmental approval does not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment because it is not a new licence.
Fahnbulleh is understood not to have made a final decision on the larger Rosebank field, but energy department officials are looking at ways the tax proceeds from the project could go to green projects if it was given. A decision is expected later this year.
The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted.
But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.
A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G and seen by the Guardian shows that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling.
That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and around half of 18- to 24-year-olds.
Ellie Mae O’Hagan, the UK energy programme lead at E3G, said: “After a summer of deadly heatwaves, the public has made up its mind: more drilling is the wrong answer.
“If the prime minister wants a decade in power to change the country, he should invest in heat pumps and solar, not tax breaks for the oil and gas companies driving up our bills and polluting the planet.”
Officials say, however, that the Rosebank decision is likely to be the more sensitive one, partly because it will produce around seven times the CO2 emissions of Jackdaw and partly because most of the oil produced there will be exported.
Khan said: “The defining test is Rosebank. Burnham must deliver on his promise and prioritise affordable bills, genuine industrial growth and a safe climate over oil profits. That means rejecting Rosebank.”

article_title: Farage vows to scrap tax on armed forces reserves
article_content:
Farage vows to scrap tax on armed forces reserves
- Published
The leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, has told a rally in Plymouth he would get rid of tax on pay for armed forces reservists.
Farage said he wanted to get more people in the reserves at the event for party supporters as part of Reform's 100 Days to Save Britain tour.
When questioned by the BBC over a Reform councillor in Plymouth who was investigated and cleared over social media posts, Farage said he was "still part of the party was because everyone believes he's a solid bloke".
About 100 protesters against Reform gathered outside the Plymouth Arena near the city centre, chanting before, during and after the event.
Farage spoke to about 300 Reform members and councillors and opened his speech by paying tribute to Ann Widdecombe, who was killed at her home in Devon.
On cutting tax for reservists, he said: "Anyone that signs up as a reservist and does their bit will face no tax on the pay they receive.
"Let's get more men and women signing up for the reserves."
When asked by the BBC about the UK deploying fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia, Farage said the UK was "not even a player any more".
He said: "Should we help with peacekeeping missions? As much as we can.
"But what we've got to face up to is the reality that we've lost our ability to be an effective player".
Plymouth Reform councillor Ben Rowe was investigated in May after being accused of sharing Islamophobic posts on social media but was then cleared.
The BBC asked Farage if Rowe's behaviour had been acceptable.
He said: "These are working class people, going into politics, venting their spleen on certain issues and maybe there's a little bit of political growing up to do.
"But let's not condemn everybody for everything they say, and the reason he's still part of the party is because everyone believes he's a solid bloke."
Outside the event, amid a significant police presence, protesters gathered with placards and joined in chants saying Farage was not welcome in the city.
Liam Condron-Farnos, from the campaign group Stand Up To Racism, said: "The way he's built his politics over the years, and still is, is on anti-immigrant hysteria.
"We need to show him that's not an uncontested view in this country."

article_title: Two men re-arrested on suspicion of aiding Iran over RAF Fairford incident
article_content:
Counter-terrorism police have re-arrested two men from central London accused of helping Iranian intelligence as part of the investigation into events at RAF Fairford last month.
A 24-year-old UK national and a 25-year-old UK/Iranian national, both from Westminster, were detained on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service in breach of the 2023 National Security Act, police said.
Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of national counter-terrorism policing, said investigators considered it highly likely there was Iranian state involvement in the incident near the airbase last month.
“Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it,” he said.
The two men were previously arrested on suspicion of terrorism offences and released on police bail. This time the arrests relate to section 3 of the National Security Act, which states that an offence is committed if a person engages in conduct “likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service”.
Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to the Gloucestershire base used by the US Air Force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September, where they were arrested.
 
 
 They were picked up after calls from members of the public as they approached the village at about 12.45am, but were released on bail a day later after no bombs or explosive devices were found.
 
 
 The prime minister, Andy Burnham, told the Commons last week that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was almost certainly behind the ambiguous episode, which led to the US withdrawing 12 B-1 bombers from the base.
The US Air Force has long used RAF Fairford, and bombers involved in the US strikes on Iran during the spring and early summer took off from there.
 
 
 One of the five men who drove to Whelford, a 24-year-old British national, was one of those re-arrested on Tuesday. The other had been initially detained on 1 October and subsequently released on bail.
Others who were involved in the late-night drive to Fairford may have not been aware what was going on, police believe, though investigations continue in an effort to establish a more definitive picture.
“Due to their sensitive nature, national security investigations can take time to progress, and I’m grateful to everyone who has given my teams the time and space needed to pursue this work thoroughly and effectively,” Taylor said.
“We know the public have unanswered questions. I want to be as transparent as possible and when we are in the position to share more, we will.”
A seventh man was arrested during subsequent investigations. Both he and the other four who drove to Whelford last month remain on bail.

article_title: Government failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds
article_content:
Government failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds
- Published
Government failures in care settings created an environment that allowed Covid to spread like wildfire, an official inquiry has said.
The sixth report from the Covid inquiry said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic and there was no "protective ring" put around homes as claimed by ministers at the time.
There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.
The 287-page report also highlighted shortages of PPE for carers and criticised the way hospital patients were discharged into care homes.
It said limits on visits caused enormous harm to residents and their loved ones, though it blamed this on care homes themselves.
Around 1.5 million adults were either living in care homes or receiving support in their own homes when Covid hit.
Action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences, the inquiry said.
Chair Baroness Hallet said a lack of testing, PPE and pre-pandemic planning combined with policy decisions early on "created an environment in which the virus could spread like wildfire".
"At the critical early stages of the pandemic, not enough was done to protect those living and working in care homes," she said.
"The overriding focus of the UK government and devolved administrations was on protecting hospitals."
- Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Covid inquiry PPE report - key findings 
  - Published14 July
Lack of PPE and financial support for carers
At the start of the pandemic, the then-Health Secretary Matt Hancock said the government had placed a protective ring around care homes.
But the report said that this claim was unfounded.
It also found:
- a lack of PPE meant staff had to resort to make-shift workarounds, including bins bags, festival waterproof ponchos and painters' overalls
- the decision to discharge hospitals patients into care homes at the start of the pandemic was understandable, but guidance should have made clear they needed to be isolated. This did not happen in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which was a significant oversight
- a lack of financial support for care workers at the start of the pandemic made it difficult to allow them to stay away from their job if they were infected
- long-standing weakness in the care sector, including financial struggles and staff shortages, exacerbated problems
- by September 2020, evidence suggested care home visitors posed only a marginal infection risk, yet many care homes failed to ease restrictions in line with updated UK guidance, contributing to a significant decline in residents' health and wellbeing.
- there was evidence of blanket do-not-resuscitate orders being put in place in some care homes, which is considered unlawful
- millions of unpaid carers were left to take on evermore complex care and struggled because of a lack of support
Jean Adamson, of the Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK, said: "Today's report is a devastating account of one of the darkest episodes in our country's history.
"It shows that the government knew the care sector was extremely vulnerable to a pandemic and yet did nothing. Failing to act until it was too late."
Totally exposed
Caroline, Abrahams, the charity director at Age UK, said the report was "devastating".
"When Covid took off, people using social care and the staff and unpaid carers providing it were left totally exposed."
She added it also demonstrated how important the overhaul of social care promised by Andy Burnham when he became prime minister was.
"If a national care service had already been in place... the various disasters that befell social care during the pandemic would have been lessened and some might have been avoided altogether."
Meanwhile, Natalie Grayson, from the GMB union, said care workers were "left vulnerable and terribly exposed" during the pandemic which saw "care homes turned into morgues".
"That cannot be allowed to happen again," she added.
Nadra Ahmed, co-chair of the National Care Association, which represents care providers in England described the findings as "really upsetting", adding that the social care workforce has "never fully recovered" from the pandemic.
She said we need to "start thinking about social care in a more constructive way" and the mantra that "we all had to protect the NHS" appears to have come at the cost of "some care home residents' lives".
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government would provide a "full response" to the report's recommendations "in due course".
Speaking in the Commons, Cooper said she agreed that social care had been "undervalued and under-recognised" for too long.
"My thoughts are with all those who lost loved ones in the pandemic, and especially those who endured the immense distress and harm of visiting restrictions in care homes, which meant they could not be with loved ones even as they died," she added.
description: The sixth report from Covid inquiry criticises the lack of PPE and the way patients were discharged from hospital.

article_title: From strife-torn France to the UK, rightwing populists win when they stir chaos while promising order  | Rafael Behr
article_content:
An election where one side represents chaos will nearly always be won by the party that promises order instead. Public fatigue after years of turbulent Tory rule accounted for Labour’s 2024 landslide victory more than any policy in Keir Starmer’s manifesto. Across the Channel, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally (RN), is currently on course to win next year’s presidential poll with a pledge of “restored authority and security” for a country that has spent years cycling between enervating stasis and explosive crisis.
Le Pen has been boosted in recent days by scenes of city centres ablaze and shops being looted as student demonstrations mutated into riots. Street confrontation is a more standard feature of the political repertoire in France than in most settled democracies, but the destruction was disturbing by any measure.
President Emmanuel Macron’s government, debilitated by the lack of a parliamentary majority, looked unprepared for the scale of the unrest. There was ample indication that something big was brewing. What began with high school students despairing at the neglected state of secondary education evolved into a general mobilisation of anger at high living costs and a lack of economic opportunities. Aggressive police tactics radicalised the crowd. As night followed day, and just as predictably, political fury gave way to opportunistic pillaging.
Prime minister Sébastien Lecornu accused “ultra-left” provocateurs of stirring disorder as part of a strategy to render the country ungovernable in the run-up to next year’s elections. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the populist left’s presidential candidate, countered that violence was the natural byproduct of a degenerate repressive state that conspires to discredit resistance, and that the protests channelled the heroic spirit of May 1968.
At 75, Mélenchon is old enough to remember that Paris spring of revolutionary fervour. He has a keen following in the current generation of activist students, but the insurrectionary rhetoric unsettles swathes of conservative France. His pungency could put Le Pen in the Élysée Palace.
In the past she has been locked out of the presidency by coalitions of moderate and left voters rallying, often without enthusiasm, behind the candidate best placed to stop her. RN’s advances in parliament have been checked in the same way, although it is currently the biggest party.
Macron has twice been the beneficiary of that dynamic, but he can’t run again, has no obvious successor and is so radioactively unpopular that the whole liberal centre ground is contaminated by his standing on it.
Current polling indicates that the “republican front” would unravel if the only names in a second-round run-off were Mélenchon and Le Pen. The centre-right would break for the RN leader. It probably wouldn’t even be close.
France’s crisis has not escaped notice across the Atlantic, where it is viewed through the warped lens of Maga ideology. Donald Trump explained that “France is burning” because the country has been overrun by immigrants “with hatred in their hearts”. JD Vance agreed that “western liberals” were to blame for opening European borders to “the third world” and advised American voters to view French misfortune as a premonition of the future if Congress is captured by Democrats in midterm elections next month.
Republican efforts to cast their rivals as catalysts of national ruin have limited traction when Trump is the obvious engine of chaos. Democrats didn’t start the war in Iran. Nor did they author a deranged trade policy that alienated the US’s friends, turning even Canada into a foe.
This is a common problem for incumbent demagogues. In opposition, simple solutions are proposed for complex problems: tariffs as the remedy for industrial decline; expelling illegal immigrants as the answer to every social and economic grievance; trusting in the leader’s judgment as the answer to everything else.
In office, those mechanisms fail to deliver the promised benefits. Someone needs to be blamed. The categories of undesirable element grow. Media, universities, courts and opposition parties are called crooked or treasonous. But purges disrupt the smooth running of a country. They are bad for the economy. This is how the insecure leader goes through the gears of tyranny. A craving for control generates dissent, which is attacked as a menace to society, requiring more draconian law enforcement. When that provokes more determined opposition, the dissenters are denounced as extremists who jeopardise public safety.
Trump has travelled some way down that road already. He might accelerate a lot further after the midterms. One option is to make bogus claims of election fraud, denying the validity of results that, if allowed to stand, would empower Democrats to hold a rogue president to account. His despotic temperament and his record of refusal to admit any electoral weakness suggest he would rather trigger a constitutional crisis of existential dimensions for American democracy than acquiesce to cohabitation with an unfriendly Congress. He will plunge the country deeper into chaos and insist that the nation rally around him as the only one capable of restoring order.
That is standard authoritarian operating procedure. The arsonists affect dismay at the conflagrations they ignite. They cavort in firefighter costumes and hose the flames with petrol.
This is the role Le Pen is readying herself for now in France. If she wins next year’s election, the backlash from the left will be ferocious. That challenge will be eagerly confronted by an incoming president likely to be looking for pretexts to declare a national emergency and remake the republic as a vehicle for her personal authority.
Britain’s radical right parties dream of an equivalent opportunity. They revel in lurid imagery of societal breakdown. Sometimes the fantasy is camouflaged as a warning about the dangers of unchecked immigration, but impatience for a violent reckoning is never far from the surface. For Rupert Lowe, leader of Restore Britain, there is seemingly no effort to conceal the relish. He told his followers on X last week that his agenda would certainly trigger “civil unrest and rioting,” and that “what needs to happen will be incredibly painful”.
Lowe is still a relatively fringe figure but he exerts disproportionate influence in the conservative digital ecosystem thanks to amplification on X by Elon Musk, the platform’s oligarch proprietor. Lowe’s candidate beat the Tories and Liberal Democrats in Manchester’s mayoral byelection earlier this year. By competing for votes with Reform UK, Restore Britain has drawn Nigel Farage into an arms race in fanatical anti-migrant rhetoric.
Farage’s status as a more serious contender in the electoral arena allows him to launder ideas that were once self-evidently extreme – mass deportations, for example – as mainstream policy. That doesn’t automatically make them popular. There is an audience for ethnically selective nationalism but it has a ceiling. The voters who are motivated by determination to thwart Farage outnumber those who want him installed in Downing Street.
That tactical coalition is easily galvanised because prominent figures on the British right wear their arsonist intent so brazenly. Also, a stable Labour government isn’t giving them opportunities to play at being firefighters.
To advance on power, Reform UK has to win over the kinds of voters that Le Pen sees heading her way through the smouldering rubble of French politics: people exhausted and bewildered by the system unravelling, without hope that incumbent authorities can get the country back on track, and amenable to the argument that fanatical leftists are the more menacing agents of chaos. Thankfully, those are not the conditions of British politics. Andy Burnham’s every step should be guided by the need to keep it that way.
- 
  Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist
author: Rafael Behr

article_title: My late wife Jo Cox was murdered in her constituency in 2016. The alleged attack on Helen Haines is a punch to the gut | Brendan Cox
article_content:
It’s never a good sign when you turn on your phone to find a dozen messages asking if you are OK. For reasons you will come to understand, I only get those messages when something awful has happened.
So on Monday, when I came out of an all-day meeting on antisemitism and picked up the messages from friends, I clicked across to check the news with real dread. The last time I’d received a similar barrage of messages was when former UK MP Ann Widdecombe was killed earlier this year.
As I read the news about the alleged attack on Australian MP Helen Haines, the dread I felt was followed by what I can best describe as a punch to the gut. A wave of shock. Deep sorrow. The despair that another elected representative had been so brutally injured.
Jo Cox MP, my late wife, was murdered in 2016 in her constituency in Yorkshire, England by a far-right extremist as she went about her constituency work.
Helen’s story reminded me of what happened to Jo. Both incidents took place in a small town far from the corridors of power. Helen, like Jo, clearly has a deep connection with her community. Even their names connected them (Jo’s first name was Helen – though she always used Jo as her main name).
When something like this happens it’s impossible not to feel yourself back in the moment of your own loss. My immediate reaction was to hope to God she survives – I remembered how I prayed the same as I heard the news about Jo’s attack.
I quickly worried about her family, the impact on them, and immediately recalled the impact on mine.
And then of course you worry about the impact on the country, its democracy and the values that underpin it.
Practically – unless you are part of her medical team – there is not much that most Australians can do to help Helen directly. Or even to comfort her family (though public solidarity really does matter). But what you can do is be part of the response.
I don’t know what motivated the alleged attack on Helen, which is still under investigation. And I’m not sure I care. Whatever the motivation, it damages democracy. And there can only be one appropriate response: to work together to strengthen it.
I know from bitter experience that moments like these can become turning points. They can reinforce our divisions, fuel our anger and make us more fearful of one another. Or they can remind us of what we stand to lose when hatred and intimidation are allowed to shape our public life and brutalise our democracy.
After Jo was killed, I saw extraordinary acts of kindness and solidarity. People who had never met her came together to celebrate her life and the values she represented. They reached across political, religious and cultural divides. They refused to let an act of hatred have the final word.
That response mattered then, and it still does today.
Across democracies, political debate is becoming more hostile. Opponents are increasingly portrayed not merely as people who are wrong, but as enemies who must be defeated at any cost. Online, contempt is rewarded, threats are normalised and people are encouraged to see the worst in one another.
We should be alarmed by that. But alarm alone is not enough.
We cannot undo what happened to Jo. We cannot take away the pain of those affected by the alleged attack in Australia. But we can decide what kind of society we build in response.
We can allow violence to make us more divided, more suspicious and more fearful. Or we can use this moment to reaffirm our commitment to democracy, decency and what we have in common.
The measure of a society is not what shocks it experiences, but how it responds. Australians cannot undo what is done, but you can still shape what it means.

article_title: UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
article_content:
UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
- Published
The UK will deploy RAF Typhoon jets to defend Saudi Arabia in response to escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks, the government has said.
The defensive mission will help defend Saudi cities and infrastructure - a move authorised by Prime Minister Andy Burnham - against aerial attacks by the Iran-backed group.
It follows Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as on energy sites on the country's coast.
"These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis," Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a written statement on Tuesday.
The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia and were ousted by the group from capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
Since September, Saudi Arabia has been struggling to defend its skies from Houthi attacks after a ceasefire of sorts in Yemen broke down.
The Houthis launched a fresh offensive against Yemen's officially recognised government and seized effective control of the crucial Bab al Mandab strait.
Government forces - backed by Saudi aircover - mounted a counter offensive and the Houthis in turn struck targets deep in Saudi territory.
The Houthis successfully hit Saudi infrastructure including the King Khalid airport, energy facilities and key ports.
Saudi authorities said last week that 19 people had been killed in Houthi attacks on the kingdom's airports.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Houthis have been retaliating for strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
More than 70 security personnel were killed earlier this week in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa.
A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city.
The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".
According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, Saudi air and artillery strikes have killed at least 141 people and injured 395 since 3 September.
The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.
Saudi Arabia has struggled to bring down incoming missiles and drones because so much of its air defence capability was used up against Iranian attacks earlier this year.
The sheer size of the country also makes it hard to provide comprehensive air defence.
The UK warplanes will not only help Saudi Arabia defend its skies, but they will also free up the country's own aircraft to carry out offensives strikes against the Houthis.
The UK will also deploy military advisers and an RAF A400M transport aircraft to support the movement of defence equipment within Saudi Arabia.
It is already providing Saudi Arabia with defence support equipment to protect against aerial attacks and air-to-air refuelling for defensive Saudi operations. The refuelling has now been extended by 90 days.
In a separate statement, Streeting said the targeting of Riyadh airport "shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region".
"That's why today I have approved further UK military support," the defence secretary added.
Streeting also pointed to violence in the Gulf disrupting energy supplies and increasing costs for families and businesses.
Earlier this month, Houthi military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia".

article_title: Nige seems tired and bored of himself as Kemi conjures a telepathic budget | John Crace
article_content:
If you’re worried about next week’s budget, then now is your time to chill out. Because Kemi Badenoch has all the answers. The chancellor, John Healey, has been living rent free in the leader of the opposition’s head for the past few weeks. Lucky man. More than that, she has been perched on his shoulder while he sits at his desk in the Treasury and tries to make the sums add up.
And – SPOILER ALERT – Kemi has now read the whole speech that hasn’t yet been written and is in a position to give her budget reply more than a week ahead of time. Opposition by telepathy. Or wish fulfilment. If things don’t work out for her in her current job she could apply to be the next Mystic Meg.
In a plush room in Westminster on a wet Tuesday morning, Kemi was giving her verdict in front of an adoring crowd of invited Tory members. They cheered every word. Which was kind. Because she won’t be getting that kind of reception next week. Nobody could be worse than Rachel Reeves, she began. Rachel had been the She-Devil who had implemented £70bn of tax rises. But wait. There was someone worse than Reeves. And that was Healey. Logic is not Kemi’s strongest point.
No matter. Healey would be worse because he would do less. Fiscal dialecticism. Yup, the chancellor was going to stand up for an hour and say absolutely nothing. Make no changes to anything. This didn’t seem very likely, but we had to take it on trust.
Kemi was John Healey’s brain. And Healey doing nothing was worse than Rachel doing something. It sounded as if Kemi rather missed the tax rises after all. But she had a further warning. The Marxist International Monetary Fund were completely wrong to praise the government for its efforts to reduce the deficit. At best, they had been duped by Healey, at worst they were trying to bankrupt the country.
Here’s what was going to happen. Labour were going to introduce some fictional cuts to benefits that would never be implemented. Because deep down what Labour MPs really wanted was for everyone to live in a country where they could pick up £80,000 a year in benefits. The sign of a functioning nirvana was a world where everyone could be paid not to work. It didn’t seem to have occurred to Kemi that the reason the benefits bill was so high was primarily because the Conservative government in which she had served had increased them substantially during her time in office. And also because many benefits, such as pensions, she was unwilling to cut herself.
Labour was doing the wrong things for the wrong reasons, she said. This opened up several philosophical lines of inquiry. Ontologically speaking, was it better to do the wrong things for the right reasons, even if the results were the same? Or what happened if you did the right things for the wrong reasons? Would you then have to negate everything regardless of the outcomes?
It turned out that I wasn’t the only one struggling with Kemi’s reasoning. When it came to the questions from the media, several reporters wondered why, if the welfare cuts that she was proposing were so easy to make, previous Tory governments hadn’t got round to making them earlier. And was it just our imagination, or were the same cuts being used to pay for several different items on the country’s balance sheet?
Kemi didn’t miss a beat. The cuts she was proposing were the ones Rishi Sunak would have made if he hadn’t been interrupted by the general election that he himself called. It was all very unfortunate. The Tories had been on the brink of success and if only they had had another couple of weeks, everything would have been hunky dory. Tax breaks for the wealthy and benefits cuts for those that need them, that was the Tory way.
Then the reverse ferret. Although she had been in previous Conservative governments, she had never inhaled. She had kept her fingers crossed and her mouth shut. Previous prime ministers had taken wrong steps. But sometimes the bravest thing a cabinet minister can do is to do and say nothing. And no one had been braver than Kemi.
“In case you hadn’t noticed,” she said patronisingly to one journalist, “we are under new management.” Only it feels very much like the old management. Kemi was still saying nothing her predecessors wouldn’t have said. It was just one of life’s sadnesses that the scales had only fallen from her eyes when the Tories had been booted out of office.
Down in Plymouth, Reform was regrouping after yet another weekend of bad headlines. And the party members who had assembled for the rally didn’t look entirely enthused when the first person sent on stage to act as cheerleader was the charisma-free Danny Kruger. The man who is meant to act as the brains of the party, despite appearing spectacularly dim.
“I don’t want to whine,” he said, before going on to do just that. The ITV exposé was just a bit unfortunate, he went on, because he was sure most Reform supporters weren’t racist. “There is no room for that kind of behaviour in the party.” Some of the audience looked a bit disappointed by that. They thought they had been guaranteed a welcome.
After a brief and entirely forgettable number from Honest Bob Jenrick – even Reform members think he seems a wrong ’un – out came Nigel Farage. He seemed like a man with the cares of the world on his shoulders. A man who could sense the tide was going out. There was no energy about him as he rolled through a collection of his greatest hits. Forgetting where he was, he even called Plymouth, Portsmouth. That drew a few boos. People like to think they matter a little bit.
Nige was just tired and bored of himself. Disappointed with a world that had promised him so much and was now crumbling before him. Hell, why hadn’t the riots even spread to this country? Then he could blame lefties and foreigners. He tried to pass off the stories of racism and financial unorthodoxy as just one offs. Every self-respecting party has a few racists. He didn’t sound as if he believed a word of it. And ITV had exposed a 70% hit rate of undesirables. Those aren’t outliers.
Come the end, Nige couldn’t wait to see the back of Portsmouth. Or wherever he was. And it felt as though for much of the audience the feeling was entirely mutual.

article_title: Після переговорів із Зеленським Віткофф везе до Путіна несподівану пропозицію: перші подробиці
article_content:
Після переговорів із Зеленським Віткофф везе до Путіна несподівану пропозицію: перші подробиці
Віткофф везе Путіну пропозиції після переговорів із Зеленським, які напередодні відбулися в Осло.
Спеціальний посланець США Стів Віткофф запропонує «фюреру» РФ Володимиру Путіну провести прямі переговори за участю американського президента Дональда Трампа і лідера України Володимира Зеленського.
Про можливість тристоронніх переговорів лідерів щодо мирної угоди оголосили після зустрічі Зеленського та Віткоффа в Норвегії, пише POLITICO.
Мета зустрічі лідерів трьох країни — спробувати домовитися про припинення вогню. Якщо саміт відбудеться, то це будуть перші переговори такого рівня від початку повномасштабного вторгнення до України 2022 року.
Своєю чергою, прем’єр-міністр Норвегії Йонас Гар Стере, який приймав учасників зустрічі в Осло, повідомив, що Віткофф вирушить до Санкт-Петербурга 21 жовтня. Він зустрінеться з керівництвом країни-агресорки та обговорить з російським умови миру. Зокрема, ідею тристоронньої зустрічі Трампа, Зеленського та Путіна.
«Сьогодні ми провели, я б сказав, добрі та конструктивні переговори — необхідні після подій минулого тижня», — сказав Стере.
За словами Стере, американський посланець передасть російській стороні напрацювання та пропозиції, «над якими опрацювали європейські та американські колеги». Це, зауважив прем’єр, може відкрити шлях до зустрічі на найвищому рівні.
Переговори в Осло — що відомо
Напередодні у столиці Норвегії Володимир Зеленський і Стів Віткофф провели переговори. Зокрема, президент України заявив, що сторони обговорили підсумки перемовин у Маямі, обговорили говорили про гарантії безпеки і «чутливі питання».
Прем’єр-міністр Норвегії Йонас Гар Стере заявив про успіх переговорів з Україною. З його слів, американські та європейські команди разом з Україною «провели змістовну роботу над ключовими питаннями».
Своєю чергою, Зеленський розкрив деталі документа про гарантії безпеки, який Віткофф повезе до Росії 21 жовтня. Відгук від росіян глава держави сподівається отримати вже за день.

article_title: Jane Dodds standing down as Welsh Liberal Democrats leader
article_content:
Jane Dodds standing down as Welsh Liberal Democrats leader
- Published
Jane Dodds has announced she will stand down as leader of the Welsh Liberal Democrats.
Dodds said she would remain the party's only Member of the Senedd (MS), but that work to increase its presence in Wales' parliament "should be led by a new generation".
"Leading the Welsh Liberal Democrats has been the honour of my life," she said in a statement on Tuesday, adding "now is the right time" to hand over the role.
Only Welsh Lib Dem MP David Chadwick is eligible to seek nomination to replace Dodds at this stage, the party said.
Relations between Dodds and the UK Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey were strained after he previously called her leadership into question.
The Liberal Democrats have been represented by just one member in Cardiff Bay since 2016, initially by former Welsh Lib Dem leader Kirsty Williams and later by Dodds since 2021.
Dodds, who represents Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd in the Senedd, is a former social worker who was made her party's Welsh leader in November 2017.
She made headlines last year by getting the previous Welsh Labour government to agree to a greyhound racing ban and £1 bus fares for under-21s in return for helping it pass its budget.
In 2024 Lib Dem leader Sir Ed asked Dodds to reflect on her position over her handling of a sexual abuse case when she worked for the Church in England.
A 2021 report found Dodds made a "grave error of judgement" by not organising a meeting to discuss a particular case of abuse by a late former bishop who sexually abused at least 18 victims over a 15-year period.
Dodds accepted there were "shortcomings", but said she would continue as leader.
After nearly two years of cool relations over the matter, Davey backed Dodds before May's Welsh Parliament election, describing her as an "excellent member of the Senedd" who deserved to be re-elected.
Nominations to replace Dodds will open on 23 October and close on 16 November.
"After May's election, I've thought hard about what our party needs," she said.
"Wales needs more than one liberal voice in the Senedd.
"Building that team will take years of hard work in communities across the country, and I believe that work should be led by a new generation.
"Now is the right time to hand it over."
Brecon, Radnor and Cwm Tawe MP Chadwick said Dodds had "given an enormous amount to the Welsh Liberal Democrats and to public life in Wales, and she deserves our sincere thanks for her service as leader".
"There will understandably be questions about what comes next.
"Today should be about Jane and her contribution to our party.
"I will make a statement about my own political future in the coming days."
Welsh Liberal Democrat president Tim Sly said Dodds had "led our party with warmth, determination and integrity through some of the most turbulent years in Welsh and UK politics".
"She leaves the Welsh Liberal Democrats stronger in our communities and ready to build," he said.
Chadwick requires the support of 50 party members to be the only candidate to replace Dodds and take over as leader.
Should that not happen, or he were to decide not to run, all members on the party's approved parliamentary candidates list could then throw their hats into the ring.
description: Dodds said it was time to hand over the leadership to a "new generation" after nearly nine years in the role.

article_title: What’s the future for the Green party? Should it be ecosocialism? | Joe Todd
article_content:
It’s a strange time to be a Green. We have just held our largest conference ever, but it was overshadowed by a controversial motion that was attacked by the media as racist. Then, when we lost a byelection in a Camden seat that is so Labour it has estates named after Blair-era ministers, the headlines called for Zack Polanski to resign.
It does, however, mark the end of phase one for Polanski’s Greens. Polanski burst on to the political scene in 2025 and ate up attention, enjoying an easy monopoly on hope while Labour was sucked into the black hole of Starmerism. Labour has since escaped, with Andy Burnham giving social democracy with Mancunian characteristics a half-hearted go. But Burnham’s honeymoon already seems to be ending. John Healey’s budget of “difficult decisions” and “fiscal responsibility” is likely to disappoint everyone but the financial markets, and a winter energy bill crisis driven by a possible El Niño deep freeze is just one of many problems he’ll soon have to face.
One school of thought says Polanski can carry on as before, focusing on points of difference with Labour. Healey announces a no-change budget; Polanski calls for a tax on wealth to fund public services. Angela Rayner sides with landlords over renters; Polanski proposes an emergency rent brake and explores Berlin’s plan to expropriate the properties of corporate landlords.
These interventions matter, especially in our attention-driven politics. But on their own they are only tactical manoeuvres in response to the politics of Labour. If we act like we’re only a Labour pressure group, that’s what we will become. And in doing so, we will neglect to answer the deeper question: what are society’s fundamental problems and what is our plan to fix them?
In practice, Burnham’s “radical vision” promises only modest regulation of public utilities, limited devolution and reform of the voting system and of social care after the next election. Weighed against the crises we face – climate breakdown, bankrupt public services, rampant inflation, runaway rents, an epidemic of loneliness, a billionaire-owned media, a deranged elite of tech oligarchs who literally want the world to end – his vision reads more like the managed decline of a system in crisis.
If phase two of Polanski’s Green party is about anything, it should be about breaking this spell. Part of this is naming capitalism as the root cause. Naomi Klein made the best-selling case more than a decade ago that the fight of our times is capitalism v the climate – that a livable world and continued resource extraction are fundamentally incompatible.
But Burnham will not go there. He names neoliberalism as the problem and then neglects to fix it, unceremoniously dumping any intention to expand public ownership and shrink the role of the market.
Polanski should go there, rooting his day-to-day interventions in a credible programme to transition away from capitalism – not only imagining the end of capitalism and what might come next, but planning in painstaking detail just how we are going to get there. He must build a credible Green party vision that shows Burnham’s to be meek and hollow.
Don’t get me wrong, the Green party isn’t there yet, nor anywhere close. We have 5 MPs, 10% of the vote and we’re still learning to be a mass of 230,000 members. But if we don’t start taking ourselves seriously, why would anybody else? Trust in political parties is on the floor, and that affects the Greens too. Why should people put their faith in us and dare to hope if we don’t have a programme that is honest, rigorous and credible?
We only need to look to the French leftwing party La France Insoumise to see what this looks like. In 2016 Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s movement published L’Avenir en Commun, which went straight into the bestseller list and has been read by hundreds of thousands of people. It is a visionary, comprehensive programme that would be written into the constitution so that companies can never take more from nature than they give. It’s a plan to provide free water and energy to every household, to redraw France’s regions around river basins, mountain ranges and forests, and to organise ecological planning. It is more extensive and detailed than any manifesto for ecological transition in Europe, and polls suggest Mélenchon could lead the French left into next May’s presidential runoff against Marine Le Pen.
The Green party’s programme must be similarly full of strategy and vision: reckoning honestly with the forces arrayed against us and setting out precisely what we’d do in our first year of government. It should also talk about the good life and what we’re fighting for, in words that resonate with voters, rather than dry policy. Written in a big open process where lots of groups are involved: unions, community groups and thinktanks, farmers watching harvests fail, pensioners battling fuel poverty, renters priced out of homeownership and workers whose jobs are vanishing – it should become a comprehensive point of unity that can provide an answer to those who aren’t voting Green because they doubt our credibility, and fill the void currently occupied by single-issue policy motions.
Polanski is correct when he says that Burnham isn’t serious about socialism. But we have to be honest: right now, neither are we. If Burnham’s vision is meek and hollow, ours is still being formed. And as Labour faces the tests of governing, now is the time to write it.
- 
  Joe Todd is a senior fellow at the Autonomy Institute, the co-host of the Life of the Party podcast and a Green party member

article_title: Burnham risks wrath of Commons Speaker for talking too much at PMQs
article_content:
Burnham risks wrath of Commons Speaker for talking too much at PMQs
- Published
Andy Burnham has only been prime minister for three months, but he is already in trouble with the Commons Speaker for talking too much.
During the first three sessions of Prime Minister's Questions with Burnham at the despatch box, Sir Lindsay Hoyle has made repeated appeals for brevity.
But is he really any more verbose than his predecessors like Sir Keir Starmer, Rishi Sunak, Liz Truss and Boris Johnson?
Armed with a stopwatch for a dive into the archive, I've found that the new prime minister does seem to give fuller, longer answers – by some margin.
The weekly session of PMQs is scheduled to start at midday on Wednesdays when the Commons is sitting, and last for 30 minutes. However it routinely runs for 10, 15, even 20 minutes longer. And that has caused problems.
- Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics 
  - Published2 September
" Can I just say I admire the prime minister?" Sir Lindsay said during Burnham's first PMQs.
"At least he's answering detailed questions. My problem is I'm not going to get through the list, and both of us will be in trouble with the backbenches when we don't make it."
Just last week he complained again: "We really are going to have to try and speed up some of the answers."
Based on an average of his first three times taking PMQs, Burnham has spoken for a total of 22 minutes per session. That's between three and six minutes more than the average for the other PMs I looked at each over three similar autumn sessions.
The number of questions asked each week can differ though, in part because time is running out. So I looked at the average time spent on each answer,
Of those I looked at, Truss was the fastest - averaging just 33 seconds per answer, followed by Johnson on 35 seconds, Sir Keir on 38 seconds and Sunak on 39 seconds.
By contrast Burnham was an outlier, taking on average 51 seconds per answer.
That means he talks for a third more per question than Sir Keir and Sunak, and up to 50% more than Truss.
Obviously the quantity of words is easier to assess than the quality.
Number 10 thinks there is a simple reason why the current PM takes longer than his predecessors. A senior source tells me: "It's because he actually answers the questions."
A spokesman for the speaker said: "The speaker is always keen to get in as many backbenchers as possible for any question session."

article_title: Уиткофф везет Путину новое мирное предложение: Axios узнало, чего США требовали от Зеленского
article_content:
Спецпосланник Белого дома Стив Уиткофф в среду встретится в Санкт-Петербурге с Путиным и представит ему обновленное предложение по прекращению войны в Украине, сообщает Axios со ссылкой на американского чиновника.
Зять и советник президента США Дональда Трампа Джаред Кушнер присоединится к встрече удаленно.
Белый дом надеется, что Путин продемонстрирует большую готовность к компромиссу после того, как Трамп согласился снять санкции на продажу российского дизельного топлива и предпринял другие шаги, которые были положительно восприняты в Москве.
Уиткофф прибудет в Россию после дня переговоров в Осло с президентом Украины Владимиром Зеленским, а также с лидерами Норвегии и Финляндии и представителями Франции, Великобритании, Германии, Польши, ЕС и НАТО.
Зеленский заявил во вторник, что следующим шагом должна стать трехсторонняя встреча между ним, Путиным и Трампом — на что Россия до сих пор не соглашалась.
«Американская сторона надеется, что новое предложение откроет путь к прямым трехсторонним и более широким многосторонним переговорам», — сообщил американский чиновник.
Переговоры в Осло были сосредоточены на разработке единого предложения по «рамочному соглашению» для завершения войны.
Американский чиновник сообщил, что Украина «выдвинула новые идеи и предложения, которые подробно обсудили».
По его словам, стороны достигли «существенного прогресса» и теперь имеют высокий уровень согласованности на рабочем уровне относительно дальнейших шагов.
«Кушнер присоединился к встрече удаленно и вновь настаивал на требовании Трампа, чтобы Украина прекратила удары по российским нефтеперерабатывающим заводам», — сообщил осведомленный источник.
«Джаред был очень прямолинеен», — сказал собеседник.
После встречи Зеленский заявил, что готов прекратить удары по российским НПЗ, если Москва предпримет ответные шаги.
Во вторник Трамп заявил, что, по его мнению, «Россия хотела бы положить этому конец», однако выразил сомнение в том, что Зеленский хочет завершить войну.
«Если он этого не сделает, это будет очень плохо, — добавил Трамп. — Мы хотим, чтобы Зеленский заключил соглашение… Если они не заключат соглашение, для Украины всё станет только хуже».
description: После переговоров с Зеленским США везут Путину новый план.

article_title: Criminals detained in hospital set to lose benefits
article_content:
Criminals detained in hospital set to lose benefits
- Published
Killers and serious sex offenders detained in hospital are among the criminals who will no longer receive benefits under proposals called for by victims' families.
Regulations due to be laid out in Parliament on Tuesday seek to end the "double provision" and prevent serious criminals receiving up to £800 a month in universal credit over several years.
Emma Webber, the mother of Barnaby Webber, who was stabbed to death by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham, before the killer was sentenced to a hospital order, said she would now "demand" ministers reallocate the funds, which she said was a "no-brainer".
The government said closing the loophole would save an estimated tens of millions of pounds a year.
The new regulations are expected to come into force early next year, subject to parliamentary approval.
Currently, serious criminals on hospital orders - where their bed and board is funded by the NHS - continue to receive any benefits they were paid on the outside.
Students Barnaby and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.
Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility, and detained at a high-security hospital.
The parents of Barnaby and Grace met Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden to discuss the change on Monday.
Emma Webber said the move was "long overdue".
Webber told the BBC it was "not an insignificant amount of money - but it is not just the money".
"These criminal patients, who have devastated lives as well as taken lives, [are] not only having their full bed and board and all of their care and rehabilitation provided for them, but also amassing a small fortune while they're inside," she said.
"The rest of us on the outside are desperately trying to survive and find a way forward in our lives."
Webber said she believed the funds should be directed to the victims of serious crime so families "are given the support and the advocacy they need".
She added when her son was killed, her family was allocated a support worker who had 50 other families to look after.
Webber said: "I beg and I plead, and - actually, I demand - ministers now consider the appropriate reuse of those funds."
Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said: "Our campaign has always been about accountability and fairness.
"Offenders with treatment orders already cost the taxpayer an enormous amount.
"On release, every offender gets help with housing and benefits.
"On the principle of fairness alone, we do not see why taxpayers should fund benefits while they are incarcerated."
The mother of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche, who was killed by her partner Gogoa Lois Tape in Hackney, east London, in April 2024, also lobbied for benefits paid to offenders in psychiatric hospitals to stop.
Tape was given a hospital order, detaining him indefinitely after he pleaded guilty to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility.
Kennedi's mother Linda Westcarr said: "For many victims' families, the question of whether serious offenders should continue to receive benefits raises understandable concerns about fairness, accountability and the values we uphold as a society.
"In my view, this is not simply a question of policy, it is also a matter of moral responsibility and ensuring that the impact on victims and their families is properly recognised."
The government said the move followed engagement with victims' families and experts as part of its plan to "put fairness back of the heart of the welfare system".
McFadden said: "We said we'd act to tackle this gross unfairness and we're delivering on that promise.
"For too long these violent criminals have had their living costs paid by the taxpayer twice over, while their victims and families paid the price.
"That ends today, because victims and taxpayers deserve a system that is fair and supports only those who genuinely need it."
Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner paid tribute to the families who had campaigned on the matter.
She added: "I'm aware the secretary of state has met with the families regarding this and was quite frankly astonished that the situation was as it was, and that these people were receiving benefits.
"That's why the secretary of state has taken this action and I welcome it."
She added the reallocation of funds was "something for the chancellor and secretary of state".
Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said: "Killers and rapists should not pocket benefits from a hospital bed.
"Labour has taken all year to stop a loophole it promised to close. And tens of millions saved barely makes a dent in the benefits bill Labour has let spiral out of control.
"The Conservatives would make universal credit a conditional, time-limited benefit, so taxpayers' money goes only to those who genuinely need it."
The proposed regulations apply to individuals subject to a Section 37 order under the Mental Health Act 1983, and a Section 57A order under the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995.
The offences covered include manslaughter, attempted murder, wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, rape, assault by penetration and rape of a child under 13.
Murder is not included, because a hospital order is not an available sentence for the offence.
The change in regulation is expected to affect about 2,500 offenders already in hospital and approximately 200 a year in future, the government said, with the full financial impact of the move due to be published as part of the 2026 Budget on 28 October.

article_title: Reform leader accuses MSP of 'squatting' in seat after resignation
article_content:
Reform leader accuses MSP of 'squatting' in seat after resignation
- Published
The leader of Reform UK in Scotland has accused an MSP of "squatting" in a Holyrood seat won by the party.
Malcolm Offord said Amanda Bland did not have a "personal mandate" to stay in the Scottish Parliament after she resigned from Reform to sit as an independent.
Bland, who was elected as a list MSP for Central Scotland and Lothians West in May's, denied claims she had stood down after being called to a meeting about high turnover among her office staff.
Offord said he was "disappointed" by her decision but Reform "wanted people who could work as a team".
Bland's departure relegates the party to third-largest in the Holyrood chamber, behind the SNP and Labour.
Offord told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast he had not spoken to Bland since she announced her departure from the party.
- Reform MSP quits party to sit as independent 
  - Published1 day ago
- Conservative MSP Graham Simpson defects to Reform 
  - Published27 August 2025
Reform MSP Graham Simpson did not resign when he defected from the Scottish Conservatives in August 2025.
Offord said that situation was different as Simpson only had eight months of his term left before May's election, while Bland is just a few months into her five-year tenure.
"Amanda's got her own reasons and, clearly, I'm disappointed. But she feels she can make more impact standing as an independent," he said.
"She is now proposing to squat in a list place won by Reform for four-and-a-half years."
He added: "It just looks to the voting public like there is a distinction between a constituency, where I would say you have won a personal mandate. If you are a list MSP, you are there just on the vote for the party."
A Reform source told BBC Scotland Bland's departure came amid claims she was "difficult to work with".
She had allegedly been called to a meeting last week to discuss high staff turnover within her parliamentary office, but Bland denied her resignation came as a consequence of that.
In a statement, Bland said her "principles and priorities remain unchanged" and that she believed she could best pursue her goals of "holding the Scottish government to account" as an independent MSP.
Under Holyrood's rules, any list MSP who resigns their seat is replaced by their party's next candidate at the last election.
As Bland is remaining as the Scottish Parliament's sole independent, Reform now have 16 MSPs, one behind Labour's 17.
That means they will not receive joint billing as the main opposition during first minister's questions.
Offord described Reform's slip into third place as "irritating" but said it would not "derail" their objectives.
He said: "We want people who are talented and bright and Amanda is talented and bright, but we also want people who are prepared to work as a team.
"One of the great things we're doing at Reform is building a team."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage was asked about Bland's departure following an event in Plymouth.
He said he "did not know the reasons" behind her decision, but that "parties losing people was always regrettable".
Asked if Bland should stand down as an MSP, he said: "I don't know the circumstances yet, but probably, yes."
Reform MSPs 'surprised by vitriol'
Offord said some in his party had been "surprised" by what he called the "poisonous atmosphere" at the Scottish Parliament.
Prior to their election, only former Conservative MSP Simpson had previous Holyrood experience.
Offord claimed other parties were "resentful" of Reform's presence in the chamber.
The party attracted widespread condemnation for tabling a debate about banning face-coverings, including burkas, from public places.
"We've been taken by surprise frankly, in Holyrood, by the amount of vitriol," he told the programme.
"It's a pretty poisonous atmosphere, quite a difficult atmosphere to be in. The other parties are very resentful of Reform being there.
"For the Reform folk coming in, some of them have been taken by surprise by the amount of unpleasantness around and some of have found it more difficult than others."
description: Malcolm Offord says he is 'disappointed' at Amanda Bland's decision to leave the party and sit as an independent.

article_title: Jobless rate falls but small firms cut back hiring
article_content:
Jobless rate falls but small firms cut back hiring
- Published
The UK's unemployment rate has dropped to its lowest for more than year, but job vacancies have continued to fall as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indicate.
The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, the lowest since July last year.
However, vacancies fell by 21,000 in the three months to September to 691,000, with the ONS saying small firms were citing labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring.
The figures are the last official snapshot of the jobs market before the Budget, and analysts said they indicated the jobs market was showing signs of recovery despite the weakness in hiring.
ONS deputy director of labour market statistics, David Freeman, said the labour market remained "broadly flat", with the latest data showing the employment rate edging up and "a small drop in unemployment".
"The number of workers on payroll remains slightly down over the same period, though data for the most recent month suggests that might be starting to level off," he said.
"The number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, concentrated mainly within smaller businesses, which cite increased labour costs as a key factor."
Energy costs have risen since the Iran war began, and companies have also said that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to employ staff.
The number of job vacancies fell to its lowest level in more than five years, the figures indicated, with the largest decrease in construction jobs.
Average earnings excluding bonuses rose 3.7% in the three months to August, up from 3.5% last month. Taking inflation into account, wages grew 0.8% in real terms.
Pat McFadden, the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, said the figures "show the resilience of our labour market" with the UK's employment rate "now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty".
However, he said that "too many young people still find themselves locked out of employment".
The government is working with industry "to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system", he added.
But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said on X, external that "businesses can't afford to hire".
"This is what happens when you attack employers, tax jobs, and put up red tape," he said.
The latest ONS figures showed the unemployment rate for those aged 16 to 24 was 15.6% in the June to August quarter. While that was down from 16.4% in the March to May period, it was still higher than the rate of 14.6% seen in the June-to-August period last year.
Separate ONS figures have indicated that nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet"
On Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to high levels of youth unemployment.
Ashley Webb, senior UK economist for Capital Economics, said the fall in the unemployment rate was "unexpected", and that it suggests the labour market "continues to recover".
But "with businesses' energy costs likely to fall only slowly, we still think hiring will stay subdued," he said.
Louise Murphy, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said the labour market "has performed poorly in recent years as the number of jobs has fallen and pay growth weakened".
But she added that the UK's "recent bout of economic resilience may finally be creating some green shoots", pointing to "rising employment levels and private sector wage growth stabilising".
The quality of ONS statistics has been criticised in recent years, with a review last year finding "deep seated" issues with the body.
The Labour Force Survey, which it uses to report payroll and employment figures, has suffered from low response rates.
In an update on Tuesday, the ONS said that response levels had improved, but that "some volatility" remained in the statistics.
