article_title: Former Tory election candidate suspended over contract killing claims
article_content:
A former Conservative election candidate has been suspended from the party after he was seemingly filmed discussing the cost of hiring contract killers and offering to “broker” the services of a far-right activist with alleged paramilitary links.
Jack Ross was filmed apparently asking an undercover reporter “What do you want done?” before listing the type of violent options that could be bought.
Ross appeared to tell the Al Jazeera journalist: “They can just kick the fuck out of someone. That’s a certain amount. They can start cutting people’s faces up, that’s another amount. And they can stab someone. They can shoot someone. They can kill someone.”
Police in Scotland say they will be reviewing and assessing the Al Jazeera documentary – Contract Killers and the Far Right – for any criminality.
Ross is the chief executive of Turning Point UK, a spin-off from the campaign group founded by the murdered US Republican commentator Charlie Kirk.
Footage released by TPUK last year showed Ross and others from the group meeting Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, after Kirk’s death.
A profile page for Ross on the website of the Bow Group, a Conservative thinktank that lists him as a research fellow, states he has advised MPs and candidates on political and digital strategy. He has been pictured alongside Boris Johnson and other high-profile figures including James Cleverly, Jacob Rees-Mogg and Liam Fox.
Ross was reported by Al Jazeera to have introduced an undercover reporter to a violent criminal from Glasgow with links to the paramilitary Ulster Volunteer Force, who offers to have people killed for money.
Al Jazeera approached Ross with a fictitious family problem where a deceased uncle’s business was at risk of being taken over by a gang, whose members were supposedly warned they would “get fucked” if anything happened.
Ross replied to this: “Yeah, you have to deliver on that as well. You’ve got to explain to me what’s needed … I can then go and broker from there. But I’ve got to say, even to myself … if there’s lashback I’ve got to keep my name out of it.”
The Scottish paramilitary contact was then filmed at a London hotel offering to arrange different types of killings, ranging from a hit-and-run that could be made to look like drink-driving to a stabbing.
The meeting took place after Ross, apparently acting on behalf of the Zimbabwean government, had reportedly paid thousands of pounds to the Glasgow activist to organise a fake political rally in support of lifting UK sanctions imposed on the African country.
Ross said: “I have had a few things and some of the Zims [Zimbabweans] have said to me they want stuff done. They wanted a fucking shooter.”
He said he had asked them to talk to the paramilitary, adding: “I said I was not putting fucking prints on anything.”
While TPUK was launched as a student movement, it has become increasingly involved in anti-migrant street protests. Its chief operating officer is Nick Tenconi, the leader of the far-right UK Independence party, who visited the Conservative conference in 2022 with Ross.
Ross was filmed in 2022 telling an undercover reporter they should chat to him about what they wanted, adding “keep it simple” and then listing the various violent options that could be bought for cash, including murder.
A Conservative party spokesperson said: “Mr Ross’s membership of the Conservative party has been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation. We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing.”
At another point, Ross expressed concerns that journalists could be recording the sort of things he was saying and could pass them to police.
“The journalist will put it out there and then the police will pick it up and fuck you,” he said. “You’ve got to think that what we were talking about and had someone film it we’d be fucking done for conspiracy.”
Tenconi was filmed alongside Ross as they outlined a plan to use football hooligans to stir up trouble.
Tenconi said: “So let Labour get in. So we build the new right and we have these armies … so, three-pronged. We keep winning MPs over. Then we build the second prong, we build an army, and that’s street demos, protest, just fuck things up, basically.”
A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the documentary. It will be reviewed and assessed for any criminality.”
Al Jazeera reported that Ross had “completely” denied its investigation’s findings, claiming that everything he said to the undercover reporter was not meant seriously.
Ross, who was a local elections candidate for the Conservatives, was approached by the Guardian for comment through TPUK. Tenconi was also approached for comment via his party.

article_title: Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
article_content:
Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills.
These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used.
Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill.
But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock £27 off a typical annual bill.
During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills".
He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity".
No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firm Nesta that they could be moved to the unit rate, external, so people pay for what they use.
This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more.
For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges.
Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers.
Higher cost of electricity standing charges
Average standing charges are 54.8p a day for electricity and 29.7p a day for gas.
When asked why electricity standing charges would not be scrapped as well, the PM's official spokesman said VAT had already been cut on electricity bills.
Standing charges cover costs such as transporting energy to homes via pipes and wires, and the upkeep of that infrastructure.
The standing charges also fund schemes to support low-income households.
Many of these costs will need to be recouped somehow, but Citizens Advice has warned, external about the potential consequences of reform for vulnerable customers.
Vulnerable people who don't have a high income, but have high energy usage, could be penalised.
But Madeleine Gabriel, director of sustainable future at Nesta, said: "Abolishing the gas standing charge and moving those costs onto the unit rate would help those worst hit by rising energy prices."
Pressure remains on the chancellor to offer more fundamental, targeted energy support this winter in his Budget next week, with energy prices forecast to rise by 16% to a four-year high in January.
In addition to standing charges, Burnham said investing in renewables would also bring household bills down "substantially" by breaking the link between gas and electricity prices "in this parliament".
Electricity prices in the UK are mainly set by gas prices, and this is often cited as a reason why electricity prices in the UK are higher than many other countries.

article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy
article_content:
'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy
- Published
A "mindset shift" is needed across the UK's central government to help Number 10 North deliver its objectives, its deputy director has said.
Duncan Parish told a conference in Lincolnshire on Wednesday there were "institutional challenges" within government that needed to be overcome to deliver change.
The Manchester office of Number 10 North - sister to London's Downing Street - was set up by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July.
Burnham's political opponents have called the office a "gimmick" and raised transparency concerns about the costs involved.
Speaking to the Great Exhibition conference of local political and business leaders, Parish said his career in the civil service to date had "not been without its frustrations" and there can be "friction" between different parts of government which have "similar but ever so slightly competing objectives".
Parish, a civil servant in Whitehall before moving to Manchester four years ago, said Number 10 North staff were "delivering outcomes at a national level across a huge range of areas" including health, transport, education and social care.
"But we continually need to work to overcome those institutional challenges," he added.
He said one priority of Number 10 North was to "shift power and accountability" closer to local areas, but acknowledged "that means reforming the civil service as well" - by not viewing national, regional and local government as separate.
Describing Number 10 North's second focus of growth, Parish told local leaders: "We're here to unblock issues that may have become stalled or where boundaries within government end up being a hindrance."
He said that "too often, working within government or departments can be perceived as either difficult or slow".
"But to deliver that change, requires us all to change - and part of that change is a mindset shift within central government," he said.
"We need to focus on the whole country and work across those boundaries, bringing in mayoral strategic authorities like Greater Lincolnshire into discussions that previously they may not have been part of - working bottom-up, rather than top-down."
His comments come as the government continues to face questions about the cost to the taxpayer of the new headquarters.
Few figures released
In September, Conservative shadow minister Mike Wood raised concerns about "little information and so little transparency" surrounding Number 10 North which he described as a "gimmick".
"The minister either doesn't know or won't tell us how much No 10 North will cost, how many people work there or how many of them actually turn up to work - it's almost as though this hasn't been properly thought through," he told a House of Commons debate.
He called for the annual budget, staff levels and office attendance statistics to be published. Current staffing levels have also not yet been clarified.
Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson said last week that the government did not know how much has been spent on hotels for No 10 North staff, ministers and special advisers travelling between London and Manchester since it opened.
The cost is "not centrally collated" but is "being met within existing departmental budgets", Jameson said in response to a parliamentary question.
Number 10 North's latest summit of regional mayors, held in its "situation room", will take place on Thursday. Burnham has previously indicated he will work there at least once a week, and hosted the Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in September.
Parish added in his speech: "How will we know if Number 10 North is working?
"Ultimately, success will be in people in the UK feeling the difference in their communities, with greater opportunities, improved living standards, faster decisions...more joined up services and a stronger voices in the future of their place."

article_title: Inflation and government borrowing highest for a year ahead of next week's Budget
article_content:
Inflation and government borrowing highest for a year ahead of next week's Budget
- Published
UK inflation and government borrowing both hit their highest in a year on Wednesday, adding to the pressure on Chancellor John Healey ahead of his first Budget in a week.
The pace of UK price rises accelerated to 3.5% in the year to September, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices.
The inflation figures came as UK government borrowing jumped to nearly £25bn in September, which means borrowing for the financial year to date is running £6bn above official forecasts.
Healey has promised a Budget which will keep to Labour's commitment not to hike the three main taxes - income tax, National Insurance and VAT - while sticking to the party's fiscal rules.
Inflation, the rate at which prices are rising, jumped from 3.1% in the year to August to 3.5% in the year to September. It is the highest inflation has been since October 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared in recent months as conflicts in the Middle East and Europe continue to squeeze global oil supplies.
The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran after US and Israeli attacks has severely disrupted a major global supply line for crude oil, while oil refining capacity has been hampered globally by Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's infrastructure after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Petrol prices in September were the highest since August 2022, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.
The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p per litre to 169.5p per litre between August and September, while diesel rose to 192.5p per litre.
Motor fuel prices overall rose by 29.8% in the period covered by the figures.
ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said September's "notable" increase meant inflation was at its highest rate in almost a year.
As well as fuel prices, the increase was driven by rising prices for airfares, computer games and live events, Fitzner said.
September's inflation figure is also important because it suggests how benefits will increase next April.
It means the state pension will most likely rise by 3.9%, in line with average wage rises from May to July, due to the triple lock.
The inflation figure for September also dictates how other benefits will rise in April. By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation.
With a week to go until he delivers the Budget, Healey said: "We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide."
He said the International Monetary Fund last week had praised the UK government for its "fiscal discipline", and that the government has just given the go-ahead for getting more gas from the North Sea's Jackdaw field.
The Budget on 28 October will "keep up this momentum", he said, by sticking to the government's self-imposed fiscal rules, and by driving "growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space".
But the inflation figure came as the ONS said the government borrowed £24.5bn in September, £1.8bn higher than a year earlier, as higher inflation helped to push up debt interest costs.
The overshoot means, cumulatively, the government has borrowed £6bn more this year than the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which scores government spending plans, had forecast.
Despite overall debt topping £3tn for the first time, debt as a proportion of the UK's economic output - the measure used by the government to judge whether it is in line with its fiscal rules - fell.
The Conservatives said higher inflation and borrowing showed Labour had "lost control of the economy".
Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith called for Healey to use his Budget to "tackle the deficit, and reduce the red tape and net zero costs that are driving up the cost of living for families".
He added that the Conservatives would cut taxes, the costs of benefits and "wasteful" spending to "make our country prosperous again".
Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the borrowing figures "painted a dismal picture" ahead of Healey's Budget. She said the amount borrowed in September was higher than analyst expectations as well as spending watchdog the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)'s forecast.
"This reinforces our view that the Chancellor will deliver a cautious Budget on 28 October that has little net impact on the economy and leaves the toughest fiscal choices for next year," she said.

article_title: Shabana Mahmood urged to ‘read the room’ on Labour opposition to immigration policy
article_content:
Shabana Mahmood has been urged to “read the room” on Labour opposition to her immigration policy, as No 10 declined to rule out watering down her plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards.
She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residence could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule.
However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”
There is already a cabinet split over the policy, which deepened on Wednesday when Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, repeatedly refused to back the specific plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to claim permanent residency in the UK.
This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”
This year the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, publicly criticised the plans, and dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.
One of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.
“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.
MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, the Home Office has said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.
No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the reforms.
Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.
“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”
In her interview with Sky News on Wednesday, Fahbulleh repeatedly avoided the question on whether she would back an increase in the waiting period for permanent residency to 15 years. She said: “We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution. And so there is a package of reforms. The home secretary has been consulting on this. She’s looking at the range of responses, and she will come out with the measures that we take forward.
“No one can look at our immigration system – and I say this as someone that came to this country as a refugee – and not believe that it’s broken and not believe that we need to fundamentally reform it.
“But our principles has to be a system where we’ve got control, but ultimately a system that when people do come to this country, they are able to integrate, they are able to contribute, and that we both respect but also value that contribution.”
She said she supported “reforms that say that people have to contribute and make a contribution to this country in order to get citizenship”, adding: “I 100% back Shabana Mahmood and everything she is trying to do.”
But she avoided multiple questions on the prospect of a 15-year wait. When it was put to her that she did not back that specific proposal, Fahnbulleh said: “Don’t … put words in my mouth.”
A government source said that “the minister clearly supported the policy and process” in her interviews, “but while subject to review of the consultation, the final policy is not set – so ministers cannot offer opinions on specific parts of it”.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”

article_title: The Guardian view on drilling in Jackdaw: a truly pragmatic approach would focus on Britain’s green transition | Editorial
article_content:
This week a report from the UN Environment Programme concluded that holding global temperatures to a 1.5C warming limit – the centrepiece commitment of the Paris climate agreement – is no longer achievable. If the disastrous consequences of a significant overshoot are to be mitigated, it argued, governments must start delivering the short-term actions to meet long-term targets on reducing fossil fuel consumption.
Disappointingly, Andy Burnham and his energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, took a different view of short-term priorities on Wednesday. Before the November Cop summit, where regaining lost momentum on climate action will be crucial, their decision to approve new drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield sent a dismal signal. The prime minister justified it as a pragmatic move “at a time when people are really struggling”. But the pragmatic arguments don’t stack up.
Going ahead with Jackdaw will have no impact on bills this winter and little in the longer run. It will deliver only a small number of jobs for a very limited period. Tax revenues from new drilling will be substantially negated by the various concessions and breaks enjoyed by the oil and gas industry. Claims that Jackdaw will enhance the UK’s national energy security are hugely overblown, given that it will satisfy a mere 2% of national demand. The country’s heavy reliance on natural gas imports will remain unaltered.
So why? Mr Burnham would doubtless have preferred not to be landed with the judgment call on either Jackdaw or the much larger Rosebank oil and gas field (on which an announcement has yet to be made). Both were already in the licensing system, having been approved by Rishi Sunak as he sought a dividing line with Labour. A successful legal challenge meant the final decision fell in the present prime minister’s lap.
On Jackdaw at least, Mr Burnham appears to have judged that political expediency, particularly in Scotland, was best served by waving it through. A failure by governments to invest gamechanging sums in the green transition has made the politics of net zero more fraught. The recent Tory byelection victory in Aberdeen South followed a campaign focused on reviving oil and gas production in the North Sea. One of the first acts of Scottish Labour’s new leader, Michael Marra, has been to back both the Rosebank and Jackdaw developments.
Mr Burnham inherited this complicated set of circumstances. But rather than rubber-stamping a regressive rearguard action by the fossil fuel industry, he should be using his rhetorical gifts to make the pragmatic case for Britain’s green energy future. As research by the E3G thinktank has laid out, the dubious benefits of drilling for disappearing oil and gas reserves are dwarfed by the potential economic impact of insulating Britain’s homes and investing in heat pumps. The government’s warm homes plan, it estimated, would significantly reduce household energy bills and generate 50,000 new jobs. Yet Ms Fahnbulleh is reportedly under pressure to find cuts so spending can be diverted to defence.
The best way to achieve energy security, back British workers and bring down bills – the three imperatives identified by Mr Burnham in his statement on Wednesday – is to invest ambitiously in the country’s climate goals. Proceeding with Jackdaw does not, in itself, signify a prime ministerial reluctance to do that. But this decision suggests there are grounds for concern about which way the wind is blowing in Downing Street.

article_title: Holocaust school lessons to be improved after 'shocking' antisemitism review
article_content:
Holocaust school lessons to be improved after 'shocking' antisemitism review
- Published
Education Secretary Lucy Powell says the government will "update and strengthen" Holocaust education within schools after a major review highlighted the "shocking scale" of antisemitism in British society.
Schools and colleges in England will be required to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it.
It means anti-Jewish hatred will be treated as a specific safeguarding risk rather than being dealt with through existing measures to stop racism and bullying.
The government has accepted all of the 27 recommendations made in the government-commissioned review including dedicated training for teachers and more consistent recording of incidents.
The review into antisemitism in schools and colleges in England was led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell and presented to Parliament on Wednesday.
Powell told the BBC it marked a "generational moment" to re-educate young people, among whom she said the issue of antisemitism was "particularly prevalent".
She said: "It's definitely a crisis and I think it's actually got worse since Sir David began this review. This has become a real challenge for Jewish people in our country, but also Jewish students and Jewish teachers working in our schools and colleges.
"I do really feel it is a generational moment to educate this generation and the next – that is the job of education – to understand what antisemitism is in the modern world."
Speaking on Holocaust education, the education secretary said new lessons will "challenge" some of the concepts that young people have.
The review also calls for stronger guidance on political impartiality for teachers.
Powell told the House of Commons "teachers should not bring their own political views into the classroom" but they should not avoid discussing important topics.
The review was launched following a series of high-profile incidents including the attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester in October 2025, in which two men were killed.
Separate reviews were also commissioned into antisemitism in healthcare and into public order and hate crime laws.
The BBC revealed in August that the Bell review had found Jewish schoolchildren were experiencing regular harassment and abuse.
It also found that headteachers of some Jewish schools were spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than educational matters.
The review also recommends that the government sets up a type of hotline where school leaders can access immediate advice on tackling antisemitism.
Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations.
He told the BBC: "This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries."
Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism.
Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role.
"When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said.
"We think about it a lot."
In response to the recommendations, the government will also encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory.
The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities.
However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism".
In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability."
Rabbi Charley Baginksy and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leads of the Movement for Progressive Judaism, said that the report "exposes serious failures in how schools recognise and respond to antisemitism".
They said: "Alongside that urgent question of how schools deal with hatred and educate about Jewish persecution, we also need to ensure they teach about Jewish creativity, music, literature, humour and the extraordinary pleasure of belonging to this diverse tradition."
Dan Green, Chief Executive of the Anne Frank Trust UK, said the review "confirms what we see in classrooms every day".
"Antisemitism in our schools is real, it is widespread, and too often it goes unrecognised and unchallenged."
"One-off assemblies are not enough, and neither is sitting pupils in front of a video. Young people need the space to ask difficult questions, challenge their own assumptions and understand that antisemitism did not start or end with the Holocaust."
The National Education Union raised concerns about creating a "hierarchy of racism" and adopting the IHRA definition.
It said the latter risked "blurring the line between antisemitism and legitimate criticism of the Israeli government and the genocide in Gaza".
The union welcomed a "strengthened focus on antisemitism" while underlining that "no form of racism should be minimised".
Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security advice and support to the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools.
It found in the first half of 2026 that antisemitism in schools had reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year.
description: Education Secretary Lucy Powell has stressed the importance of reminding new generations of the horrors of the Holocaust.

article_title: Burnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a pen | Zoe Williams
article_content:
When the news broke that the UK government had approved the Jackdaw gasfield, I was at a Guardian climate event at the Royal Geographical Society. Appropriately, the theme suggested by readers was what can the public actually do in the face of what feels like paralysing climate doom?
There is so much going on that is hopeful: biodiversity tracking, river protection, rewilding. Shruti Suresh, from the independent watchdog Global Witness, told those in attendance that if they wanted to effect change, they should protest against Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project. The message was so well understood that it didn’t need labouring. The mood in the room when the news came in was one of audible dismay. People had just watched the minister for climate transition declare that she could see the challenges ahead and was ready for them. The Jackdaw announcement will face immediate protest and legal challenge, but it sends a very clear signal from the government: we don’t mean what we say about ending emissions.
It turns out you can take all imaginable personal responsibility to arrest the climate crisis, make lifestyle adjustments that even five years ago you wouldn’t have dreamed of, miraculously summon the energy to take collective action from what is often private despair, but it will be insufficient as long as corporations – assisted by the government – are working against you, in effect with impunity. At some point, you need to get the people you elected to do what we all know – and they acknowledge – is necessary.
The Jackdaw decision had been quietly parked during the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when the threat of the Greens seemed greater to Labour than it turned out to be. But while Labour successfully buried the issue during the campaign, the underlying issues surrounding Jackdaw – and Rosebank, which is yet to be decided upon – persist.
Since the 2015 Paris agreement, we have been committed to try to limit temperature rises to 1.5C, and we’ve known for at least five years that means the vast majority of fossil fuels have to stay in the ground. As of 2024, there’s been scientific consensus that the target of 1.5C is “deader than a doornail”, while this week’s emissions-gap report could not be clearer: the threshold will be breached and it will cause unimaginable damage, yet with urgent emissions reduction, there is a way back from the abyss. There is no workable argument that runs: “Everyone has to leave their fossil fuels in the ground, as a matter of the utmost urgency, except for us; everyone has to prioritise the long-term survival of a livable planet over energy bills, except for us; we all need to reach carbon neutrality and worry about high-skilled jobs later, except for us.” The Jackdaw field isn’t huge, will peak in a short time and won’t on its own reduce energy bills, which are determined by global markets. So it’s tempting to shuffle it off as a side-order issue, but it matters: it destroys our moral authority as a nation and it extinguishes hope.
The climate debate operates on two tracks that don’t meet. On the one hand, we talk about non-linear irreversible tipping points whose effects would be so seismic that the question of mitigation is too vast and, frankly, too painful to consider. The only bearable discussion of the collapse of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) – a system of currents within the Atlantic Ocean – is how to avoid it, and the contested matter of whether that is even possible. We talk about heat deaths across 854 European cities over the past summer, and we talk about areas in the UK of environmental deprivation, flood risks and poorly insulated housing. We also talk about food security both in the short term, with potato crops destroyed by the weather, and in the long term, with supply chains subject to the incomprehensible devastation of every country going through its own particular climate crisis simultaneously. We look at the social unrest across Europe – which is the fastest-warming continent – and ask to what extent the deprivation created by an unstable climate is being weaponised by a far right hell-bent on choking off climate action.
Then we gate off all that knowledge, all that anxiety, all that will to action, and turn our attention to the UK’s immediate energy compromises. The arguments here run that since we’re going to import gas from somewhere anyway, because any transition will take time, we may as well get it at home. Even though it’s well known that household energy prices won’t be reduced, the government can use the tax take to reduce VAT. Some categories of emission are lower from UK gas than they would be from energy imported from the Gulf.
We need to bring these conversations together, because what they describe is one shared reality. Alongside the carbon that Jackdaw and Rosebank would release, they’ve “sucked all the oxygen out of the debate around what to do about climate change”, Chris Stark, the former CEO of the Climate Change Committee, has said. A warm homes initiative would create vastly more jobs, research recently found, and by reducing bills would also bring far more prosperity, with the additional advantage of not undermining the climate goals we claim to hold.
Thinking of agriculture alone, the headroom, investment and planning we’re ploughing into carbon extraction could make an immeasurable difference to building resilience for an already uncertain future. The most meaningful way to reduce household bills is to reduce reliance on increasingly turbulent world markets, by separating the renewable price from the fossil fuel price, which would immediately boost the already flourishing wind and solar sectors.
Gas and oil proponents beg us to be pragmatic, while their own arguments are floridly impractical: conducted as though the outside world doesn’t exist; as though carbon emissions are tomorrow’s problem; as though there aren’t better solutions for high prices and insecurity everywhere you look; as though we have time to quickly exhaust all our bad answers before we move on to good ones.
One depressing aspect of the Jackdaw announcement – although by no means the most depressing – is that it’s all about the optics. Even its most trenchant supporters would admit that it’s not a long-term solution to energy security. Rather, it’s a flag to the fossil-fuel industry that the government isn’t an enemy. It’s a toxic smoke signal to the US that the UK might not be with it, but definitely isn’t against it. It’s a feeble attempt at domestic politicking by Labour, trying to deflate the Conservatives’ anti-net zero bubble. It’s a statement of intent to make no trouble, when the trouble is already upon us.

article_title: Скандал між Польщею і Україною через УПА і Шухевича: що буде з військовою допомогою
article_content:
Скандал між Польщею і Україною через УПА і Шухевича: що буде з військовою допомогою
Речник Міністерства національної оборони Польщі Януш Сеймей спростував інформацію про нібито зупинку постачання Україні великого пакета військової допомоги.
Міністерство національної оборони Польщі спростувало повідомлення про призупинення постачання військової допомоги Україні через рішення Львівської облради оголосити 2027 рік роком УПА та Романа Шухевича.
Про це заявив речник польського Міноборони Януш Сеймей в коментарі польському виданню Fakt.
«Ця інформація є неправдивою», — сказав він.
Між Польщею та Україною спалахнув новий історичний скандал — що відомо
20 жовтня Львівська обласна рада оголосила 2027-й роком вшанування Романа Шухевича та УПА, що одразу ж викликало різку реакцію Варшави.
Міністр оборони Польщі Владислав Косіняк-Камиш розкритикував рішення Львівської облради щодо «року Шухевича». «Воно не сприяє побудові взаємної довіри між народами, а навпаки, поглиблює розколи», — написав він у Х.
Згодом МЗС України у своїй заяві не підтримали рішення Львівської облради, але й закликали польську сторону до стриманості.
ЗМІ повідомляли, що Польща вже зупинила надання Україні пакету військової допомоги через рішення Львівської обласної ради щодо вшанування УПА та Романа Шухевича.
Попереднє загострення історичних суперечок між країнами почалось навесні, коли президент надав ім’я Героїв УПА одному із підрозділів ЗСУ.
Тоді скандал набув великого розголосу, і зрештою президент Польщі Кароль Навроцький ініціював позбавлення Володимира Зеленського найвищої нагороди країни — Ордену Білого Орла.

article_title: Tory MP questions government advisor's position after wife's Palestine Action post
article_content:
Tory MP questions government advisor's position after wife's Palestine Action post
- Published
Conservative MP Alicia Kearns has raised concerns over whether Jonathan Powell, the national security adviser, can remain in his post following his wife's references to Palestine Action on social media.
The shadow home affairs minister has written to the PM asking if Powell's position is still tenable, despite the Metropolitan Police concluding no action was necessary over his wife, Sarah Helm's, comments.
A No 10 spokeswoman told the BBC: "These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity."
Posting on X last week, Helm wrote: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action," responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney.
The Normal People writer announced last week that her books will not be supplied to UK booksellers after she announced she would use her royalties to support Palestine Action.
The Met investigation into Helm's post found "it did not meet the criminal threshold" and the matter was dropped on Saturday.
But Kearns has written to Andy Burnham about the handling of sensitive national security information, asking whether the government has investigated the posts and whether he retains full confidence in his adviser.
She told the BBC: "We cannot have the NSA's [national security adviser's] wife tweeting about what decisions her husband has or hasn't made."
On Monday, Helm responded to a question on X about whether her husband had been involved in the decision to ban Palestine Action with the reply "nope".
Palestine Action was proscribed as a terror organisation last year, making it a a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years imprisonment to belong to or support the group.
An appeal against the proscription of Palestine Action is due to be heard by the Supreme Court next month, external, in a battle that has now gone on for more than year.
The Labour Against Antisemitism group also wrote to the prime minister, calling for Powell to either resign or be sacked.
The organisation pointed to Helm's social media posts, including one from 2018 when she wrote: "Palestinians have never had their voice heard in British corridors of power. They have no equivalent of the Jewish lobby here.
"No access to ministers, still less prime ministers."
The letter said Helm discussed her husband's work publicly and cited a 2016 article she wrote for the Guardian, external in which she revealed details of a conversation she had overheard between George Bush and Tony Blair, when her husband had been the No 10 chief of staff.
The group said Helm would have been included in the vetting process when Powell took on the NSA role.
"Either Jonathan Powell lacks full clearance, vetting missed this, or saw it. Each is indefensible," the letter said.
"You promised zero tolerance on antisemitism. Mr Powell's position is untenable and his wife raises security concerns. He must resign or be sacked."
A Downing Street spokesman said: "Jonathan Powell is one of the finest diplomats of our generation. His experience speaks for itself.
"I am not going to get into people's private lives... the spouses of public officials are entitled to hold and express their own views."

article_title: As Miatta ignites the speaker’s gas-fuelled inferno, Reform show up as snowflakes | John Crace
article_content:
When is a licence not a licence? When it’s a new licence that is an old licence. After months of faffing around – there were the small matters of a party conference and a byelection to negotiate first – the government finally gave the go-ahead to drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. What swung it wasn’t so much the irresistible excitement of creating 27 new jobs and securing 2% of the UK’s gas supply for the next 10 years, it was the politics. If other countries were going to carry on drilling then we might as well do so, too.
There would still be the same amount of greenhouse gases created and we wouldn’t have to rely on anyone else for our gas supply. Though we would for the other 98%. Small steps and all that. At a time of global insecurity and rising energy costs, it was time to drill, baby, drill. So the inconvenience of a Labour manifesto that promised no new North Sea licences could be rethought. It was now merely re-allowing a licence that had already been granted and then deemed unlawful by the courts. AKA dancing on the head of the pin.
Donald Trump greeted the decision with wild enthusiasm. Though he appeared to be under the impression Jackdaw would be drilling for oil and would turn the UK into a land of plenty overnight. No one in the UK could quite bring themselves to enlighten him. Fair to say, that not everyone in the UK was quite so thrilled. Not least Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, and Miatta Fahnbulleh, the current one.
Miatta had sought permission to be as far away as possible from Westminster for prime minister’s questions and the subsequent ministerial statement on Jackdaw. So she had taken the trouble to go all the way to Aberdeen to make a television statement that she could have made in her own department. And she is the one worried about her carbon footprint.
Only it turns out that any amount of emissions is a price worth paying for a minister anxious not to have the hypocrisy of her former opposition to Jackdaw replayed to her by many of her own backbench MPs. Life comes at you fast when you’re a politician climbing the greasy ministerial pole. You find yourself in some awkward places, the most awkward being the House of Commons. Hence the – ahem – unfortunate diary clash.
The speaker was less than impressed. Lindsay Hoyle sounded as if he had swallowed a fistful of amphetamines and steroids and was mid-roid rage. He only just stopped short of calling the Labour frontbench a bunch of fucking fucks. Maybe he was just having a bad day.
For decades now, governments of all colours have been going out of their way to make sure that junior ministers take the flak to save their bosses the embarrassment of an hour’s humiliation at the dispatch box. The parliamentary equivalent of droit de seigneur. Lindsay demanded assurances this would never happen again, and the junior energy minister Michael Shanks duly nodded sheepishly. Not that he cared. He mainlines oil for breakfast. Inside, he was just counting down the seconds till the speaker had calmed down a bit. And then carried on as normal. Of course it will happen again. Maybe even next week.
PMQs itself also took on a familiar look, with Kemi Badenoch unable to make any inroads into Andy Burnham. You could even sense her frustration. There were times when she could get under Keir Starmer’s skin, but now both she and the Labour party have seen him off, she is faced with Mr Congeniality.
Against him, Kemi’s attack lines feel half-arsed. Not properly thought through. Everything she tries just bounces off him. He seems almost untouchable. Mostly because he’s a better politician, but also because he has the air of a reasonable grownup. Someone you feel is doing his best and comes across as someone you can trust. Well. As close to honest as you get in Westminster.
By contrast, Kemi feels like a second-rate opportunist. She tried making something of Labour taking years to approve the Jackdaw licence, a charge that rather melted away when Burnham pointed out we could have been drilling ages ago if the Tories had bothered to get the necessary legalities right in the first place. This was about putting pragmatism before ideology, Andy insisted. Fair enough. Though expect him to say precisely the opposite when it comes to the Rosebank oilfield. Then ideology will take precedence over pragmatism. Fahnbulleh had already as good as confirmed that Rosebank was dead in the water.
For the rest of PMQs, it was Kemi who was dead in the water. Seemingly having no other real questions she wanted to ask. It felt like she was sulking. Or underprepared. Her pre-budget attack lines went nowhere. First Andy pointed out that he was the only one with a plan to ditch the triple lock and sort out social care – still more vibes than policy – and ended by making fun of Liz Truss’s forthcoming new book on the mini-budget.
It wasn’t her who had screwed the country, apparently. Liz had been captured by the Blob. But it could have been any number of the current members of the shadow cabinet. Including the shadow chancellor who was part of the Trusster’s team. Incidentally, Liz was due to be interviewed by a robot on Wednesday afternoon at a Lincolnshire fair. But how would we know which was which?
That just left time for Burnham to take one question from a Labour backbencher about the ITV exposé of Reform. Though Nigel Farage had already left the chamber by then, so he couldn’t get all heated and declare that it was all a London plot and that it was perfectly normal for people to be as racist as possible in the comfort of their own homes. It was political correctness gone mad.
As if by telepathy, Zia Yusuf had chosen just that moment to post a video on social media in which he expressed his immense sadness that the media had stooped so low. He would be reporting ITV to the police, he insisted, because they had betrayed the racist code of honour.
How could everyday racists feel comfortable expressing their racism in the workplace if they couldn’t be sure that their colleagues weren’t undercover journalists looking to expose them? The world had gone mad. Who would have guessed that deep down, Zia – the man even the Reform elite have come to hate – was a snowflake at heart.
author: John Crace
description: The energy secretary’s trip north provokes Hoyle’s futile rage, while ITV’s Reform exposé leaves Zia Yusuf immensely sadWhen is a licence not a licence? When it’s a new licence that is an old licence. After months of faffing around – there were the small matters of a party conference and a byelection to negotiate first – the government finally gave the go-ahead to drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. What swung it wasn’t so much the irresistible excitement of creating 27 new jobs and securing 2% of the UK’s gas supply for the next 10 years, it was the politics. If other countries were going to carry on drilling then we might as well do so, too.There would still be the same amount of greenhouse gases created and we wouldn’t have to rely on anyone else for our gas supply. Though we would for the other 98%. Small steps and all that. At a time of global insecurity and rising energy costs, it was time to drill, baby, drill. So the inconvenience of a Labour manifesto that promised no new North Sea licences could be rethought. It was now merely re-allowing a licence that had already been granted and then deemed unlawful by the courts. AKA dancing on the head of the pin. Continue reading...

article_title: Can UK pop cut immigration and stop the boats? I suppose we’ll find out with GB News Music Radio | John Harris
article_content:
If you want a quintessential “It wouldn’t happen now” story, try this. Two months before Margaret Thatcher became prime minister in May 1979, a national Militant Entertainment Tour was organised by Rock Against Racism.
On 20 March 1979, it came to the West Runton Pavilion near Cromer, the (very) small town on the coastal edge of East Anglia. The bill mixed the black and white musicians in three bands then at their artistic peak – the post-punk maestros Gang of Four, the punk-reggae hybridists The Ruts, and Misty in Roots, the renowned reggae collective from Southall in west London – and thereby made a stark symbolic point: that the multiracial nature of large swathes of the UK was not to be decried or attacked, but actively celebrated.
The UK was then – and some of this may sound familiar – in a bitter, polarised state, seemingly locked into deep economic problems, amid rising fear about the neo-fascist National Front. The previous year, Thatcher had said – and this may feel familiar, too – that British people “were really rather afraid that this country might be rather swamped by people with a different culture.” Amid such a grim political atmosphere, RAR and the musicians who supported it felt duty-bound to try pulling their audiences away from such toxicity, and point out that what we now call diversity was something to be celebrated.
Nearly half a century on, the lack of any comparable cultural response to this country’s equally unsettling current state seems quite remarkable. There is, then, a vacant cultural-political space – and look what has now come along to fill it. GB News, that bracingly rightwing TV channel whose regular faces include Nigel Farage, the Reform MP Lee Anderson and the party’s failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin, is about to launch a music radio station.
According to its promotional blurb, it will be “dedicated exclusively to artists from Great Britain and Northern Ireland”, with tagline “all British, all day”. By way of further explanation, one of its presenters, the black GB News host Nana Akua, says that “It’s easy to forget how this country has shaped the global music landscape” – a strange point instantly disproved by a mention of any number of artists (such as those four fairly successful fellas from Liverpool). But here, perhaps, is the strangest thing of all: according to GB Media, every track on the station’s playlist will be an “artist from Great Britain or Northern Ireland, or where the main proportion of the band is British.”
This sparks no end of questions. Does anyone in the ordinary world actually perceive music like this? Will someone frantically be employed to sift through Wikipedia, finding out whether this or that band fits the “main proportion” criterion? What will happen in the case of, say, the Gallagher brothers, who self-identify as Irish – and should, therefore, be excluded for the same reasons as U2, CMAT and Fontaines DC? Should the Jimi Hendrix Experience be ruled in or out, given that the two supporting members of the trio were respectively from Ealing and Folkestone? And to get into the real nitty-gritty, how exactly are the programmers defining “British”?
We all know the jaw-dropping conversations taking place in GB News-adjacent circles about national identity. The Tory-to-Reform defectors Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman see Englishness as an ethnic identity. If this definition wins out, which is quite conceivable, what will happen then? A playlist cull that will leave little apart from the musical equivalent of sliced white bread?
There are more fascinating questions to ask. There has been an on-off debate about whether Britpop was partly responsible for Brexit. As the writer of a book about that cultural wave, I have always clung on to the idea that because its nationalistic(ish) animus was focused on the US, and the demographics of Leave voters do not map on to the Britpop generation, no one had any case to answer. But this latest development brings on a slight pang of unease. In retrospect, the large-scale whiteness of Britpop was, as we say these days, rather problematic. On a musical level, it accounts for its chronically limited range of influences and inputs, which led to it burning out pretty quickly. But it also left it open to what might turn out to be a belated act of appropriation: whatever music the new station plays, I would imagine that Oasis, Blur, Pulp et al will be an integral part of its output. Put another way, the Farage-ist tanks are now surely heading for Britpop’s metaphorical lawn.
Inquiries to a couple of music lawyers established that musicians cannot stop radio stations that possess the relevant licences and pay the required royalties from playing their material. Self-evidently, however, they could quite easily express their displeasure at the prospect of being part of a constant Farage-ist soundtrack. In the excellent new Oasis documentary, Don’t Look Back in Anger, Noel Gallagher rightly says that his band was never “a rightwing thing … All are welcome. It’s we and us.” In the context of GB Music Radio, he should translate that into something slightly more specific. So should the already embattled Ed Sheeran, Adele, what remains of the Rolling Stones, the former members of Dire Straits and everyone else who is – and isn’t – mentioned in the station’s launch statement. The music all of them make, after all, is founded on precisely the kind of cultural mixing that so many voices associated with GB News take against.
Oh, and one last thing. This message needs to be out there in the fabric of people’s lives, not only pouring out of their phones, but arriving in their towns. The West Runton Pavilion was demolished in 1986. But imagine some modern equivalent of Militant Entertainment pitching up on the Essex coast, the old Nottinghamshire coalfield, the seaside towns of Kent, or any number of Reform’s supposed heartlands. Is that really now as inconceivable as it seems?
- 
  John Harris is a Guardian columnist

article_title: Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain
article_content:
Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain
- Published
The decision to grant approval for drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea and the further delay in a decision about the Rosebank oil field, also in the North Sea, are case studies in the slow-motion awkwardness the UK has collectively had, over years, about energy.
At the heart of that awkwardness, these questions: where should our energy come from, and with what costs and consequences, for the customer and for the environment?
Since becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham has talked about a desire to be "pragmatic" about the North Sea as he puts it, which is why this decision about Jackdaw isn't a surprise.
In fact it felt near inevitable after President Trump blurted out – after his first phone call with Burnham in the summer – that the prime minister had told him he would "open up the North Sea".
Burnham acknowledged the two leaders had discussed the issue, arguing: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that."
What we now know is the government is approving drilling of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen.
A decision on Rosebank, an oil field about 80 miles north east of Shetland, is expected to take a bit longer.
The timeline of back and forth about both projects is worth revisiting. Jackdaw was first approved four years ago, Rosebank three years ago.
But after a legal challenge by environmental campaigners, it was ruled that consent had been granted unlawfully and there needed to be a more detailed assessment of the environmental impact.
And then, of course – there is politics, international and domestic, between parties and within parties.
Debate about energy security and spiralling prices, given the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the environmental impact, carbon emissions and the message new drilling sends to the wider world.
But others point to the extra carbon emissions when energy is imported, the tax revenues generated from domestic energy and the social and economic consequences of the British oil and gas sector deindustrialising too quickly and, in particular, the impact on cities such as Aberdeen.
Then, for the government, there are the promises the Labour Party made when it was seeking your support at the general election in 2024.
Page 52 of Labour's manifesto reads like a rhetorical twister – a paragraph of promises seeking to stretch in multiple directions at the same time, trying to keep a breadth of people happy simultaneously, or perhaps not annoy too many people too much.
"Labour will not revoke existing licences and we will partner with business and workers to manage our existing fields for the entirety of their lifespan. Crucially, oil and gas production in the North Sea will be with us for decades to come, and the North Sea will be managed in a way that does not jeopardise jobs," it reads.
"And our offshore workers will lead the world in the industries of the future. We will not issue new licences to explore new fields because they will not take a penny off bills, cannot make us energy secure, and will only accelerate the worsening climate crisis," it adds.
Crucially, the Jackdaw and Rosebank licences had already been issued, leaving political wriggle room on these two outstanding and high profile decisions the Labour government inherited on taking office.
But the multiple trade-offs, of course, remain very real, including for some of the key individuals involved.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who used to be the energy secretary, has long been vocal about what he sees as the need to move away from fossil fuels.
His successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh, who has announced this decision, previously wrote, external that "to have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can't have any new oil or gas fields," adding "it's irresponsible and short sighted to be funding new fossil fuels when we need to get to Net Zero fast."
Fahnbulleh has today told BBC Radio Scotland gas from Jackdaw will be "in our homes and businesses this month" but acknowledged that it "won't lower our energy bills this winter".
Instead, she is grounding her argument for approving this in energy security and saying the tax revenue generated will go into an "Energy Wealth Fund" to pay for "low carbon and renewable projects".
Rosebank, she added, was a "different proposition" as its oil would be exported, but she will "look at it".
Politically, the decision on Jackdaw is considerably easier for the government than the decision on Rosebank.
Broadly speaking, most Labour MPs are comfortable with endorsing Jackdaw. It is also a project backed by the Conservatives and Reform (who argue a decision should have been taken much sooner) and the Scottish National Party and the Liberal Democrats. The Green Party of England and Wales are opposed.
On Rosebank, the argument is much more contentious within the Labour Party. Some, who can see the rationale for Jackdaw cannot see it for Rosebank. Bluntly, it is a much more difficult decision, as Fahnbulleh has acknowledged.
What we can expect in the coming hours and days - as it has started already - is a resumption of all the arguments these projects have already provoked, with some saying approval should have happened ages ago, alongside plenty more.
And others arguing the announcement is utterly irresponsible.

article_title: Putin orders release of jailed American as he meets Trump envoy for Ukraine talks
article_content:
Vladimir Putin ordered the release of an American man from a Russian jail as he met Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday for fresh talks on ending the war in Ukraine, amid increasingly close relations between Moscow and Washington.
Trump had previously asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine.
His release appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine, while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections.
Hubbard was released unilaterally by Russia, rather than as part of a prisoner exchange as has often been the case with previous releases of Americans held in the country.
Writing on social media after the release was announced, Trump said it followed a request he had made “directly” to Putin last week.
He wrote on Truth Social: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
Hubbard’s younger sister told the Associated Press she had spoken to her brother, who said he had thought he was “going to die in prison”.
“He’s out of Russia territory. He is free, praise God,” Patricia Hubbard Fox said, adding that her brother suffered beatings and starvation while he was held captive.
Witkoff, meanwhile, lavished praise on Putin during their meeting at the grand Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, describing the Russian president as a humanitarian.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin. He also conveyed Trump’s thanks for a deal to resume Russian diesel exports to the US.
The Russian president is wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) as a war criminal, in relation to the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia during the war.
More than 17,500 civilians have been confirmed killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the UN, which says the true toll is likely to be significantly higher.
The warmth of Witkoff’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the increasingly hostile rhetoric directed at Volodymyr Zelenskyy by senior US officials, most notably Trump, who has called for the Ukrainian president to resign and portrayed him as the main obstacle to peace.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Oslo, where he had met Zelenskyy and European leaders a day earlier in an attempt to inject momentum into stalled negotiations, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Witkoff told Putin during a televised portion of their meeting: “We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure.”
The visit was Witkoff’s ninth to Russia since Trump tasked him with brokering an end to the war.
Witkoff described his meeting with Putin as “constructive” but said “important work” remained and trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine “at the technical level” would follow.
The Kremlin said it had agreed “in principle” to the talks, which would focus on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended.
The latest rupture in relations between Washington and Kyiv was triggered by Trump’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal with Putin, followed by his call for Zelenskyy to be replaced after Ukraine refused to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv has since complained of disruptions to US intelligence-sharing and restrictions on its access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Washington had resumed providing advance warnings of Russian missile attacks after his meeting with Witkoff in Oslo.
But Ukraine continues to face restrictions on Starshield, although it remains unclear who ordered them. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had personally ordered the slowdown, while Reuters, citing sources, said the directive had come from inside the White House.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Wednesday that the decision to restrict Ukraine’s access came from Musk.
“I’m not aware that we knew about this decision beforehand. But that’s irrelevant,” Rubio told reporters during a trip to India.
“The bottom line is that, that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at.”
During Wednesday’s meeting with Witkoff, Putin thanked Trump and his wife, Melania, for “their attention to efforts to end the war”.
Yet there are few signs of an imminent breakthrough. Despite repeated Ukrainian calls for a ceasefire, including a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow has given little indication that it intends to end its bombardment of Ukraine as winter approaches, apparently confident that continued pressure will help it extract greater concessions from Kyiv.
The Russian leader remains intent on sticking to his maximalist war aims, including his demand for full Russian control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region.
Putin also sought to emphasise the prospects for closer economic ties between Russia and the US once the war ends, suggesting that Moscow could significantly increase its exports of fertilisers to the American market.
Russian officials said the first tanker carrying diesel to the US would depart on Thursday as part of an initial shipment of about 300,000 tonnes.
Energy analysts and traders have questioned whether Trump’s agreement to temporarily resume Russian diesel imports will deliver meaningful relief to US consumers before the midterm elections, arguing that the volumes involved are too small to significantly ease the global supply squeeze.
The talks on Wednesday also touched on a possible meeting in China next month between Putin, Trump and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. The Kremlin said Beijing was already making preparations for what it described as an unprecedented summit between the three leaders.
