article_title: Everyone hates Oxford Street. Will pedestrianisation save it?
article_content:
In February, the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, announced that Britain’s best-known thoroughfare, Oxford Street, would be pedestrianised. To the surprise of every Londoner that I have spoken to in the past few months, it is actually happening. On Monday 26 October, the busiest shopping street in Europe – or, precisely, half of its 1.2-mile stretch – will be closed to traffic, putting an end to several decades of bitter arguments, obstructions and delays. Cars, lorries, vans, taxis, buses, bicycles, ebikes, scooters will be banned. Nothing but pedestrians (and emergency vehicles) will be allowed in.
This change will mark the most remarkable transformation to the streetscape of central London since at least 2003, when Trafalgar Square was turned from a glorified roundabout into one of London’s most recognisable public spaces. It will also form the most visible part of the mayor’s legacy, whether or not Khan runs for a fourth term in 2028. Three years ago, Khan published a memoir and manifesto, Breathe, attributing his asthma to growing up inhaling London’s polluted air. For the mayor, pedestrianising Oxford Street is the culmination of a mission to create a greener city that is oriented around public health, walking and cycling.
Pedestrianisation is one thing; making Oxford Street somewhere anyone actually wants to spend time is another. For weary Londoners and anxious visitors alike, it is a headache in the form of a high street. Its primary associations are crowds, stress, dirt, noise, the tackiest incarnations of consumer capitalism, and crime. At one point during my research I approached a harried police officer in the throng outside Tottenham Court Road tube station and asked if she thought pedestrianisation would be good for Oxford Street, or make her job harder. Both, she said.
This is not to say Oxford Street is an empty, dying high street. At the last count, it receives more than 500,000 visitors every day – equivalent to the population of Edinburgh. It seems reasonable to assume that most of London’s 22 million annual foreign visitors set foot on it at some point. The street generates 5% of the capital’s economic output, and lives in the national imagination the way few others do. “When I was 17, London meant Oxford Street,” sang Everything But the Girl, in their 1988 song of the same name: “It was a little world.” And yet, nobody loves Oxford Street. During the course of writing this article, I haven’t met anyone who will even admit to liking it.
On a Sunday evening in September, I did something I had always carefully avoided doing before and cycled its full length. Even at the end of the weekend, it was overwhelming – with teenagers careening on rented ebikes and gaudy pedicabs parked in the middle of the pavement, blaring music. The pavements were thick with people, in part because the road was still thick with traffic. On another occasion, I watched a late-middle-aged woman perch awkwardly outside Ikea on a narrow black electricity box, in the absence of anywhere else to rest. For most Londoners, Oxford Street is a necessary evil, to be visited with surgical precision before fleeing the scene: a site of crime, grime and perhaps some Christmas shopping. “Who,” wondered the FT’s architecture critic in 2020, “lingers any longer than they have to in London’s worst thoroughfare?”
The grime itself is no joke. In the 1990s, when Oxford Street was known for its huge record shops such as HMV and Virgin Megastore, I remember returning to my south London home on the tube, blowing my nose and seeing a tissue full of jet-black snot. Its narrow streetway and tall buildings on either side create an “urban canyon”, trapping the heavy diesel fumes emanating from its buses and taxis (private car access has been restricted since 1972). In 2014, it was found to have the highest concentration of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the world. In the same year, the crime had become so bad that the United Arab Emirates warned its citizens to avoid the area for their own safety.
Since then it has become better known for its lawbreaking small businesses, where substantial raids have hauled in counterfeit goods and illegal vapes. This decade has seen the rise of mysterious US candy stores and empty souvenir shops that allegedly thrive thanks to tax evasion. Covid and internet shopping hit Oxford Street hard: vacancy levels soared from 4.5% in 2019 to 16.9% by early 2023, and it was often these businesses that filled the gaps. The current Google Street View images of its shopfronts, taken just two years ago, already look like a postcard from the past.
That Oxford Street has been struggling hurts the reputation of London as a whole. This is in tabloid parlance, “the nation’s high street”, home to the flagship branches of iconic department stores alongside global retail brands. Khan’s gamble is that the pedestrianisation can reverse what he conceded in 2024 was a case of “managed decline”, and will flood the street with life again.
In the offices of East, near London Fields, Julian Lewis and Archie Bashford were seated around a 4ft-long cardboard model of Oxford Street and talking animatedly about bollards. Lewis and his team are public realm architects, devoted not to buildings, but the world beyond them: signage, benches, perches, kerbs, paving, lighting, planters, trees and public art. East have carried out nearly 30 high street redesign projects in as many years, but this is the big one.
The first thing Lewis’s team did after being awarded the contract last year was to dive into the archives. The starting point was a little-known 1932 article in Good Housekeeping by Virginia Woolf. For Woolf, Oxford Street appeared as a “great rolling ribbon … the pebbly bed of a river … washed by a bright stream”. She saw it as gaudy, but also sparkling, thrilling and overwhelming, defined by the restless movement of its messy public. (Her essay also shows us how weird the street has long been – in 1932, it was apparently full of hawkers selling live tortoises.) It was these riverine characteristics that became the starting point for the thousands of material, small-scale design decisions that East are making. The “play of light on surfaces, the subtle reflectivity of a bench or a column” can all help bring out those tendencies, Bashford told me.
The pedestrianisation happening next week will cover 0.6 miles, stretching westwards from close to the Oxford Circus crossing to Selfridges. (Sadiq Khan has expressed his commitment to eventually pedestrianise all 1.2 miles of the street.) The most noticeable transformation will be how much greener it is becoming. The architects’ plan is to experiment with introducing young trees in pots, alongside new places to sit. They will use the test phase – which will last from next week until spring 2027 – to learn about how people respond to the trees. Will they become meeting points? Rest stops? Landmarks for wayfinding? Ideally they will provide respite, Lewis said, “a refuge from the flow of people, which is the river analogy again – maybe that’s optimistic, but instilling some relative calm”.
The pedestrianised zone’s edges will be marked by bollards. Lewis has strong opinions on this subject, and speaks about bollards as if they were people. “Bollards are generally horrible things,” he told me. Too often they seem “apologetic”, he said. “A misaligned, plasticky reflective strip [on a bollard] sends the message: ‘Sorry, I didn’t really mean to be here, but I need to let you know there are some vehicles nearby.’ Instead, they should be saying: ‘I’m happy to be here, because I’m doing a job.’”
An abundance of considerations go into designing the right kind of bollard, including security, maintenance, aesthetics, accessibility, climate, foot traffic, crowd flow and civic pride. Oxford Street’s bollards have to be exactly 1.2 metres apart, for reasons of HVM – hostile vehicle mitigation – but they also need to be helpful and use “the existing language of the street”. They will be made of ductile iron, because it is more resilient than cast iron: it’s springy, and doesn’t crack when you hit it. They are also matt, because shiny bollards are too flashy, and detract from the ambience. “They’re very sophisticated,” Lewis said, and he meant it.
One of the project’s primary ambitions is to better integrate Oxford Street with its neighbours. It is surrounded by four areas with strikingly different identities: Soho, Fitzrovia, Mayfair and Marylebone. “There’s this slightly numb connection to Oxford Street itself, like: where the hell is Oxford Street? It might as well not be there, with regard to the relationship with these incredible centres,” Lewis said. “People want to go to Soho. They want to go to Marylebone. People live in Fitzrovia. Oxford Street does not have a place yet, it’s a non-spatial space, which is unbelievable given how famous it is.”
This is where landscape architecture and design comes in. The noun the architects use over and over is “invitation” – how do you encourage people to do the unthinkable, and linger in the newly pedestrianised space, and move freely in and out of it? The built environment has to invite them to do so. One innovation Lewis’s team wants to explore is outdoor public dining – not outdoor tables for restaurants, because there are barely any on Oxford Street, but continental-style tables to sit and eat whatever you want; takeaway food bought in Soho, or a packed lunch you made at home. “The idea of sitting there having sandwiches at a picnic bench, next to a shop in which you can buy a Prada handbag, is a fantastic kind of paradox,” Lewis said with a smile. “And it’s also very London.”
To understand where the idea of pedestrianising Oxford Street came from, you need to acquaint yourself with the work of a Danish urban planner called Jan Gehl. In 2003, when Ken Livingstone was mayor of London, Gehl was asked to spend 18 months researching the flaws in London’s streetscape, and in June 2004 he produced a 120-page report entitled Towards a Fine City for People. Gehl thought there was a huge amount of work to be done. “London comes only after Moscow in the contempt the city planners show for pedestrians,” he said that year. “You never see any children on London streets – what have you done with them all?” The answer is that they have been increasingly shut indoors: driven everywhere in cars or not trusted to play outside – compared both with earlier generations of Londoners, and with most other children across Europe.
Gehl wanted to transform the capital into one of the world’s most walking-friendly cities by 2015. But with the 2004 mayoral election taking place the same month, the radical edges of the final report that was published by Livingstone’s City Hall were sanded down. Gehl’s full recommendations were confined to a “secret document”, distributed to the capital’s decision-makers but never published. Among other things, it recommended the full pedestrianisation of Oxford Street. It has taken 22 years for that dream to be realised. “I see some signs of improvement in London,” Gehl told me recently on a video call from his home in Copenhagen, “but for God’s sake, the tempo and the amount of change have not been impressive.”
Gehl, who is 90, has long sought to turn cities into places that put the people that live there first. His motto is “the city at eye level, and at 5km/hour” – walking pace. Life Between Buildings, his first book, from 1971, was a challenge to the orthodoxy that had shaped postwar urban planning. Rather than judging the city principally by its buildings, its roads or the efficiency of its layout, Gehl asked planners to pay attention to what people actually did in public: where they walked, where they stopped, whether they met, talked or sat down to watch the world go by. These values are now finally at the centre of so much city planning – and it is no coincidence that his organisation Gehl Studio was appointed by City Hall to advise East on Oxford Street’s transformation.
For Gehl, city halls across the world should be looking to Australia. Sydney, Perth, Melbourne and Adelaide have moved dramatically towards pedestrianisation and light rail – they are “more ambitious, daring and faster in making decisions” than their peers in the UK. In Sydney, Gehl said, the rapid transformation of the equivalent of Oxford Street, George Street, is improving the atmosphere in the city around it. With ageing populations, “the end of the shopping era” for cities, and the need to reduce fossil fuel consumption, his once-radical ideas are becoming common sense. “If I am looking back at my professional career, it’s been one big struggle to reclaim public spaces from cars, which in the 1960s filled all of the streets and all the squares – they filled every possible place. We have spent many decades reconquering cities for their citizens.”
What we know as Oxford Street, which has been a street for the best part of two millennia, has always been a stage for the evolving society around it. It was previously called Tyburn Road, and for six centuries formed the processional path to the infamous Tyburn Tree, the gallows at what is now Marble Arch. Thronging crowds would line the route on hanging days, making for a rather different participatory public spectacle than that provided by its window-shopping era.
The evolution of West End neighbourhoods brought stables, barns, abattoirs and breweries, fortifications, countless pubs and coaching inns, and eventually department stores, theatres and music halls. Oxford Street has long been a centre not just of commerce, but culture and social life. Howard Carter gave his first public lecture about the discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb at the New Oxford Theatre in 1923, and the most famous punk gigs in history – featuring the Sex Pistols, the Clash, Buzzcocks and more – took place at the (still running, still pleasingly dingy) 100 Club in 1976. Oxford Street’s long list of fallen pubs – the Hog in the Pound, the Jolly Trooper, the Man Loaded with Mischief – today leaves just one survivor, the Flying Horse. At 6pm on a Tuesday in late September, the atmosphere inside the latter was surprisingly gentle and convivial; the dark wood panelling and Victorian fittings offering a calming refuge from the rush-hour chaos outside.
There have been many experiments in recent decades to bring social life back to Oxford Street: tweaks to crossings, traffic restrictions and pavements, and, largely to accommodate more shopping, from 2005 to 2012, one single traffic-free day in the run-up to Christmas called Very Important Pedestrians Day.
One thing everyone agrees on is that a dramatic transformation is long overdue. By the time Khan replaced Boris Johnson as mayor in 2016, London had fallen behind cities such as Paris, Barcelona and Berlin when it came to infrastructure for cyclists and pedestrians, and measures to curb car numbers. Then, the systemic shocks of the pandemic, and an electorate voting ever more to the left (and more Green), offered Khan the opportunity and the mandate to catch up.
There are two big structural changes sweeping through the great cities of western Europe that have also shaped Khan’s ability to finally get this done. The first is that the motorcar is no longer king in the modern city. The second is that shopping has been displaced. Even though Oxford Street remains a river bobbing with more than 20 flagship stores, maximal spending is no longer the only consideration. In the age of same-day delivery, out-of-town fulfilment centres, and peer-to-peer secondhand marketplaces such as Vinted, what should replace shopping at the heart of the modern city?
This week, I walked down Oxford Street with Nabeel Khan, CEO of the Oxford Street Development Corporation (OSDC). His earliest experience of Oxford Street was going to HMV to buy his first CD: 2Pac’s Me Against the World. Today, he is the man in charge of making pedestrianisation happen.
On our walk, the first signs of change were visible: the concrete bases of the new bollards were in place and the old wooden planters – “really poorly designed”, in Khan’s view – had had their dying shrubs removed. Outside the flagship UK store of the US shoe brand Vans, which styles itself as not merely a skateboarding attire shop, but “a space to express yourself” and a “cultural hub”, Khan spoke with gusto about the so-called experience economy.
In city centres post-Covid, there is “this desire, particularly among young people, for human connection,” he said, gesturing through the open concertina doors of the Vans shop, where a full drum kit, guitar and amps had been set up, facing out on to the street. “When you can buy almost anything you want, what’s the one thing that you can’t buy? That proximity to someone else and having that human experience.”
Given that everyone agrees Oxford Street needs overhauling, why has this taken so long? “The West End doesn’t have a single owner,” Khan said. “There are two local authorities, a transport authority, a strategic authority, five business improvement districts, hundreds of businesses and some major landowners.” The maestro trying to conduct this unruly orchestra is now the OSDC, which was created by the mayor. While reporting this story, I noticed the OSDC sought to keep an iron grip on press coverage. Perhaps this is because the local politics around Oxford Street have been fiercely contested for so long.
In fact, angst over vehicle traffic on Oxford Street is about as old as London’s mayor. In 1971, when Sadiq Khan was a baby, so many pedestrians were spilling from overcrowded pavements into the road and being hit by cars that an Oxford Street Action Committee was formed. During one protest calling for cars to be banned, 22 people were arrested. The Greater London Council introduced the first ban of private cars (between 7am and 7pm) the following year, marking the beginning of 50 years of gradual traffic restrictions.
Full pedestrianisation has faced decades of opposition and obstruction, primarily from the Conservative-run Westminster council – continuing when Labour took it over from 2022 to 2026 – but also from taxi drivers, disabled access groups, local residents, smaller traders and local neighbourhood groups such as the Soho Society and Mayfair Forum. The latter worry that plans to reroute buses, delivery lorries and taxis into quiet conservation areas surrounding the street will “destroy” those areas, as Tim Lord of the Soho Society put it. Accessibility advocates and the Licensed Taxi Drivers’ Association argue that pedestrianisation will create a transport desert for older people and disabled visitors. (In a statement, the OSDC admitted that journeys to Oxford Street will change for some, but said that accessibility has been at the “heart” of the planning process. Bus stops, it said, will be no more than about 200 metres from the pedestrianised area; it added that the street furniture was designed with input from specialist disabled groups.)
Khan’s predecessors tried, and failed, to transform Oxford Street. As mayor, Boris Johnson called pedestrianisation the “Schleswig-Holstein question of London traffic”, referring to the infamously complicated 19th-century German constitutional debate, because “everybody in abstract would love to do [it]” until they look at the “actual economic impact”. But by 2016, the tipping point had been reached – all the major mayoral candidates that year proposed pedestrianising it in principle, and when Khan won, he pledged that it would be completed by 2020. For a brief period, City Hall, Transport for London (TfL) and Westminster council appeared to be pulling in the same direction. Polling in 2018 and 2024 has shown about two-thirds of Londoners support the idea.
But the political fight over Oxford Street has often been less about how it is transformed than who gets to decide. In 2018, local opposition to Khan’s pedestrianisation plan crystallised into the creation of Capo, the Campaign Against Pedestrianisation of Oxford Street, which stood three candidates in 2018’s local elections, winning more than 1,000 votes between them. Spooked by this, Nickie Aiken, the council’s Conservative leader, used the backlash to nix the plan. Khan was furious, calling Westminster’s withdrawal “a betrayal” and claiming that £8m of public money had been wasted by the scheme’s collapse.
A decade and a pandemic later, it is finally happening because the planning authority is now held by the OSDC, which was established by the mayor’s office. The Better Oxford Street campaign, a coalition of local opponents to pedestrianisation, called this transfer of power a display of “jaw-dropping audacity” by the mayor, with the OSDC superseding the council “and its democratically elected representatives”.
As Jan Gehl observed to me, compared with some city halls around the world, London mayors have limited power. They can’t raise taxes (or introduce rent caps, legislate or control health services), which makes urban change that much harder to achieve. One thing that is under the mayor’s remit though is TfL: after he got the latter to agree to reroute their buses around the street, and with the OSDC up and running, Khan was finally in the driving seat.
What happens next week is just the beginning. The first half of Oxford Street will close to traffic on Monday – but the pedestrianisation process that follows will stretch on for well over a year.
The people behind the project are anxious that the initial testing phase is not misunderstood as a permanent project that has been built cheaply, or half heartedly. The testing process will involve a lot of people standing around with clipboards and measuring things, observing the different ways and places that pedestrians dwell. Even the picnic benches they are installing will be engaging in data collection, thanks to a “beacon”, a sensor recessed into the seat, that will measure how many people sit down, for how long, and the ambient temperature at the time.
There are other problems to navigate. On my first “site visit” to Oxford Street with East’s Archie Bashford, he showed me an example of how not to do public-realm architecture. We were on a little side street behind Oxford Circus station. There stood three vast steel plant pots, each hosting a leafless, skeletal young tree. The soil base was crisscrossed with a lattice of slats, the gaps completely stuffed with cigarette butts. The planters had become giant ash trays, which presumably hadn’t done much for the dying trees. At the root of this miserable scene were security concerns, Bashford explained – the designers had wanted to keep the soil out of reach. I was confused. “Some planters,” Lewis later explained, “are quite conducive to hiding things.” Such as knives.
This might sound like Metropolitan police hyperbole. But the knife threat is not just a scare story: weapons hidden by organised crime groups are often found in “soft landscape”, usually soil, for easy extraction and future use, removing the danger of being caught in possession.
There is a delicate balance to be struck between public safety and a more sociable public realm. The social optimist’s view is that you minimise crime in the public realm not by making it so miserable that nobody wants to visit in the first place, but by overwhelming the minority of people behaving badly with people who are behaving well. The architects at East hope that some forms of crime, such as drug dealing, will become harder, for the simple reason that it will be more visible. “Sometimes you do have to mitigate [criminal activity],” Lewis said, “but I think it’s more successful in the long term to provide an infrastructure that supports social activity, and invites it.”
Another concern is that the new Oxford Street becomes something rather more mundane: a successfully pedestrianised but ultimately disappointing place. An open-air shopping mall, a tourist trap, a hyperbranded open-air events venue, or an empty corridor after closing time. Some observers worry it could acquire some of the same problems that Barcelona’s La Rambla is still tackling. In recent decades the Catalan boulevard has been a tawdry sacrifice to tourists, largely abandoned by local residents. In an effort to avoid that outcome, there has been a great deal of communication between Barcelona and London. Barcelona’s city hall is keenly watching Oxford Street, Nabeel Khan told me, and East’s architects have visited Barcelona to procure their data-gathering seating.
What would success look like in two years’ time, I asked Khan, as we lingered outside Selfridges, occasionally apologising as we sidestepped passersby. “Of course there’s an economic side,” he said. “We want to see retail doing well, we want to see the return of flagship stores. We want to see more people spending time and coming back to Oxford Street: not just first-time visitors, but return visitors.” It should also form the first stage of a wider transformation of London’s entire West End, he added. “We want to see Marylebone benefit from this, we want to see Soho benefit from this. We want to show people that this is how the heart of a global city should feel, should look, should be experienced. That will be success.”
Archie Bashford believes the change in atmosphere will be profound: “Even if we were doing nothing else, and they just shut the street, it would feel amazing and transgressive.” In just a few weeks’ time, visitors will be able to look up at Oxford Street’s glittering Christmas lights without worrying about being run over. People don’t tend to look up on Oxford Street, I’ve noticed, because they can’t – they’d be mown down.
But it turns out, if you gaze above shop-window height, that Oxford Street has a rich architectural history, stretching across styles and centuries, from the modernist Barbara Hepworth statue on the side of John Lewis to the imposing 18th-century Pantheon that hosts Marks & Spencer. It is worth your time to linger, even beyond the fundamental human right to sit down, have a sandwich and breathe some clean air.
author: Dan Hancox
description: In a few days the busiest shopping street in Europe will be closed to traffic. The hope is that an unloved and polluted thoroughfare will turn into somewhere that people actually want to spend timeIn February, the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, announced that Britain’s best-known thoroughfare, Oxford Street, would be pedestrianised. To the surprise of every Londoner that I have spoken to in the past few months, it is actually happening. On Monday 26 October, the busiest shopping street in Europe – or, precisely, half of its 1.2-mile stretch – will be closed to traffic, putting an end to several decades of bitter arguments, obstructions and delays. Cars, lorries, vans, taxis, buses, bicycles, ebikes, scooters will be banned. Nothing but pedestrians (and emergency vehicles) will be allowed in.This change will mark the most remarkable transformation to the streetscape of central London since at least 2003, when Trafalgar Square was turned from a glorified roundabout into one of London’s most recognisable public spaces. It will also form the most visible part of the mayor’s legacy, whether or not Khan runs for a fourth term in 2028. Three years ago, Khan published a memoir and manifesto, Breathe, attributing his asthma to growing up inhaling London’s polluted air. For the mayor, pedestrianising Oxford Street is the culmination of a mission to create a greener city that is oriented around public health, walking and cycling. Continue reading...

article_title: No surprise and lasting anger: families of people who died in care homes react to Covid inquiry report
article_content:
“At the time it felt like a devil’s bargain – it was horrible, but it was what [we thought] we had to do to keep people safe,” says Amy of the “devastating” and “terrifying” restrictions that led to her maternal grandparents being locked down in separate care homes during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Eva and Eric had been married for more than 60 years when her dementia and his increased frailty meant they needed separate residential support. When the first lockdown was announced in March 2020, however, it in effect cut them off from each other and their granddaughter, to whom they had been especially close after the early death of Amy’s mother.
“I spoke to Grandad on the phone when it was possible – it often wasn’t possible due to staff not being able to take him a phone – and he was desperately lonely, isolated in his room, unable to talk to anyone because they were worried about [the spread of Covid],” says Amy, 39, who lives in Milton Keynes and works for a large software company. “I consoled myself that they were keeping him safe. That all the isolation was necessary.”
Instead, she says, he was depressed and very afraid until he finally caught the virus in 2022. Amy saw him for the first time on a Covid ward, “when I had to beg and beg and beg the hospital staff to let me visit him”. Eric died shortly afterwards.
Six years after Covid struck, the latest report from the public inquiry into the pandemic, published this week, has convinced Amy that the policy of isolating residents was “cruel and pointless”, she says. “I want to smash something. I can never get that time with them back.
“The impression I had at the time was that [the government] were doing their best in the face of an unstoppable tidal wave, but it sounds like they put out a hand and expected it to stop the ocean.”
The inquiry concluded that the entire care sector had been an “afterthought” to government planners, and that a claim by the then health secretary, Matt Hancock, to have put a “protective ring” around residents was entirely unfounded. Instead, the decision to discharge untested patients from hospitals into care homes led to the virus spreading “like wildfire”, while blanket restrictions on outside contact led to “immense emotional harm” and “profound isolation” for vulnerable residents.
The findings are no surprise to the family members of care home residents, many of whom have told the Guardian of the immense distress their loved ones went through. Roger Dennison’s father, Lucius, was a sprightly 90-year-old care home resident when the first reports of the coronavirus emerged; they watched the news together in Lucius’s room and wondered how quickly it would peter out.
Weeks later, Lucius’s care home had firmly locked down, and the only way Dennison could talk to his dad was through a window that had been opened a few inches at the top. “You’re standing on tiptoe, trying to shout in and then be heard on the other side,” he says. “It was very confusing. It wasn’t very happy as an experience.” They tried it just once but stopped because it was too distressing for Lucius.
After that, Dennison, who had previously visited every other day, was reliant on passing messages through staff, while Lucius was “in his room, largely on his own”. The disease “became a growing apprehension for me once it became clear people were coming into the home and bringing it with them”, says his son. “I think there was a sense of inevitability.” Lucius caught Covid in the first wave and died in hospital in April 2020.
To care workers, too, the situation was terrifying and immensely distressing, says Nick (not his real name), who was a senior worker at a home in West Yorkshire. “The situation from the very start was frightening because we all thought that if you got Covid, you died or were going to be seriously unwell. I remember having to strip naked at the back door of my house because we had a resident return from hospital who had shared a ward with Covid patients. As a care home, we tried to refuse their return based on the risk of infection but were told [by the hospital] that we couldn’t.”
From that point, he says, “all hell broke loose”. “Our first case of Covid was about a week later.” They had already run out of personal protective equipment, he says.
“The mental health impact on all staff was huge. Watching people die at such a high rate in such a small space of time; having to say goodbye to so many people we came to know and love; putting our own health on the line every day and then quite possibly carrying that home to your family. Mentally, we were all spent.”
Like many, Catherine Bennett, a retired teacher from Lewes in East Sussex, says she was not shocked by the inquiry’s findings: “We knew what was happening. I am, however, very angry.” Her father, who had been in a care home since 2018, “felt a terrible sense of abandonment” that no one was able to visit and became paralysingly afraid of catching the virus.
“For a long time he didn’t go down for meals; he stopped doing all his activities so he wouldn’t meet anybody.” After some months, she says, the care home built a room where residents could talk to relatives through a glass panel and speakers. It was, she says, “very distressing for a man of his age to be separated from his loved ones in that way, to be able to see us through the glass but not be able to touch us or have any meaningful contact”. Her father died in the home in 2022.
Diana, a retired social worker from Derby, feels a similar lasting anger about the experience of her sister, Helen, whose mental health needs meant she was living in a care home in Carlisle when the pandemic struck, and who experienced a similar bewilderment at her sudden isolation. The first time Diana was able to sit with her was after a year of lockdown when Helen was very unwell; she died the same day.
“I just think they threw care homes under a bus while they partied in Downing Street, and I do feel rather cross about that,” says Diana. “I think it is a major trauma for this country and I think it should never be forgotten.”

article_title: What is happening to UK prices?
article_content:
What is happening to UK prices?
- Published
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in the year to September, the highest rate in nearly a year and above the Bank of England's 2% target.
The rise was slightly higher than economists had predicted, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.
Inflation is widely expected to rise again in the coming months.
What is inflation?
Inflation is the increase in the price of something over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs £1 but is £1.05 a year later, then annual milk inflation is 5%.
How is the UK's inflation rate measured and what does it mean for UK interest rates?
The prices of hundreds of everyday items, including food and fuel, are tracked by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
This virtual "basket of goods" is regularly updated to reflect shopping trends, with alcohol-free beer, dashboard cameras, and pet grooming equipment among items added in 2026, while premium bottled lager and sheets of wrapping paper were removed.
The ONS uses price changes in the basket of goods over the previous 12 months to calculate inflation.
The main inflation measure is called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), external, and the latest figure is published every month.
The Bank of England looks closely at the inflation figures when deciding whether to increase, lower or hold its base interest rate, which is currently 3.75%.
Putting rates up makes borrowing more expensive, giving people and businesses less money to spend, reducing demand for goods and slowing price rises.
But it is a careful balancing act – increasing borrowing costs also risks harming the economy.
For example, homeowners face higher mortgage repayments, which can outweigh better savings deals.
Businesses also borrow less, making them less likely to create jobs. Some may cut staff and reduce investment.
What is happening to UK inflation?
Although CPI inflation of 3.5% remains above the Bank of England's 2% target, it is well below the 11.1% figure reached in October 2022 as gas and oil prices soared in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
That was the highest rate for 40 years.
While inflation has fallen significantly since then, prices have not. They have just risen less quickly.
The higher figure for September was mostly caused by higher prices for motor fuel, which rose by 29.8% compared to September last year.
Food price inflation remained at 1.3%.
But it can take a year for changes in the cost of food to filter through to the shop floor because of the way supply chains work, so prices could still rise as a result of the widespread disruption caused by the war in Iran.
How do energy prices affect UK inflation?
Inflation soared in 2022 because oil and gas were in greater demand after the Covid pandemic, and energy prices surged again when Russia invaded Ukraine.
Before the war in the Middle East broke out, UK inflation had been expected to be at or around the target level of 2% over the next five years, according to the official forecasts published in March 2026.
But in April, the Bank of England warned that disruption to global energy markets could push UK inflation as high as 6% in the worst-case scenario.
When the latest ceasefire took effect, analysts said it could limit further inflation hikes. Oil prices initially fell sharply after the deal was announced, but have risen again since the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July.
As a result, UK petrol prices are likely to climb back up. This - coupled with the 4% increase in household energy bills from 1 October when the latest Ofgem price cap took effect - is expected to push UK inflation higher.
As part of his pledge to provide "breathing space" for households struggling with the cost of living, Prime Minister Andy Burnham scrapped VAT on household electricity bills in October. It is predicted to have a small downward impact on inflation.
Precisely because food and energy prices can be very volatile, the Bank of England also considers other economic measures such as "core inflation", which excludes these costs.
Core CPI was 2.8% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 2.6% in the 12 months to August.

  - Published2 October

  - Published28 September

  - Published22 July
What is happening to UK interest rates and will they fall again?
The Bank cut interest rates six times between August 2024 and June 2026, which brought rates down to 3.75%, the lowest level since early 2023.
In April, the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee indicated it would act "forcefully" if oil prices did not start to fall, with up to six rate hikes in a worst-case scenario.
At its September meeting, Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.
Are wages keeping up with inflation?
The Bank also looks closely at what is happening to wages and unemployment.
The latest official figures show that regular pay in the UK grew ahead of inflation in the three months to August.
Average annual growth in pay, excluding bonuses, during the three-month period was 3.7%.
After taking inflation into account, it means regular pay grew by 0.8% between June and August.

  - Published21 April
- What needs to change to get more people working? 
  - Published5 November 2025
What is happening to inflation and interest rates in Europe and the US?
The US and eurozone countries have also been trying to limit price increases, but also face challenges with inflation.
The inflation rate for countries using the euro was 3.8% in September, according to EU data, external - up from 3.2% in August.
The European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice in recent months to 2.5%.
US inflation was in 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August, with prices there also affected by higher fuel costs.
The Federal Reserve cited "too high" inflation when it raised interest rates for the first time in three years in September, to a range of 3.75%-4%.
The move came despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.

article_title: Wanted: new No 10 adviser to help citizens deal with rise of AI
article_content:
Andy Burnham is to recruit a number of advisers to plug gaps in No 10, including an expert on how AI will affect society.
The roles advertised by Downing Street give a glimpse into the biggest challenges facing the prime minister – and what he has decided to prioritise.
The new hires will flesh out the threadbare No 10 policy unit – where many of the roles are still vacant after Keir Starmer’s departure. Senior sources have said the prime minister wanted to take time to recruit advisers.
The adviser on AI, who will be expected to have “deep expertise” in the sector, will be expected to lead preparations for the impact of the AI boom on the workforce, amid significant concerns for lower-level professional services jobs, in particular for new graduates.
They will also be expected to be the main adviser to Burnham on frontier AI, the effects and benefits of AI in public service transformation and other major societal impacts.
Several cabinet ministers have openly expressed concerns about the UK’s readiness for the impact of AI on the workforce and economy, as well as the dangers of unregulated systems.
In his Labour conference speech on 28 September, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said there were “daunting” dangers of AI, saying they could not allow technological advances “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”.
Burnham will also hire an adviser to develop policy on greater public control over everyday essentials – with a roving brief across transport, energy, housing, water and the environment.
The adviser will be asked to focus on the cost of living. The job advert specifically demands an individual who can “bring challenge and external perspectives into policy development”.
Burnham is known to be frustrated with the cautious and limited options presented to him by Whitehall on areas where he is seeking greater public control.
The Guardian reported on Tuesday that Burnham had told officials to rip up their plans on how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical choices for what to do with the stricken company, including options that could cost more taxpayer money or carry higher legal risk.
Burnham will also recruit an economic adviser to replace Starmer’s aide, Minouche Shafik. The job, which will examine growth and macroeconomic policy, requires “a strong understanding of the economic, fiscal and political context shaping government decision-making”.
Before he became prime minister, Burnham took advice from Andy Haldane, a former Bank of England chief economist, as well as from Richard Hughes, a former chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, and Jim O’Neill, a cross-bench peer and former Treasury minister.
However, none have agreed to take roles in No 10. Haldane and O’Neill have been critical of Burnham’s economic approach since he entered government, particularly on increased public spending and a lack of growth-oriented policies.
Other roles will include a new adviser on Scotland, an adviser on work and welfare who will report to the new growth director, as well as another post working across immigration, security and justice, looking at cross-border crime, exploitation and illegal migration.

article_title: Aneurin Bevan’s personal security file was ‘remarkably tame’ – National Archives
article_content:
Aneurin “Nye” Bevan, the Welsh Labour firebrand who spearheaded the creation of the NHS, was monitored by security services for more than two decades, though his personal file was “remarkably tame”, according to official files released to the public.
Bevan came to MI5’s attention in the 1930s over concerns about his links with known communists, papers released to the National Archives show. Monitoring continued even after he became a minister in the postwar Labour government that created the NHS.
At one point, his links to a known Russian spy led to the then director general of MI5 approaching prime minister Clement Attlee to warn him.
However, the papers show, some in the security services questioned why Bevan was of interest. Although there is nothing in the files to indicate that MI5 ever tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, one officer wrote in 1943: “I do not think that Bevan’s activities are a matter in which we, the Security Service, should be involved.
“In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently, as any copy of Hansard will show, and it would not therefore be possible to do anything positive.”
Reviewing the file after his death in 1960, another MI5 officer noted: “Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame.”
MI5 first opened a personal file on the backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in South Wales in 1933. He was described in one entry to have “inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the communist cause.”
He was also noted to have been “in close touch” with Harry Pollitt, general secretary of the Communist party of Great Britain, and others in the party who backed his plan to organise “workers’ freedom groups” to defend against “capitalists”.
Bevan fell out with his communist allies who had complained he was not interested in workers’ unity and was intent on building “a movement of his own”. But by 1936 they had reconciled, with Bevan supporting an application by the Communist party to affiliate with the Labour party.
In 1949, MI5 became concerned about Bevan’s friendship with Wilfred Macartney, who had been convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.
Recordings of Macartney’s conversations suggested he was passing on information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt. It led the director general Sir Percy Sillitoe to approach Attlee, who dismissed Macartney’s claims as a “tissue of lies” but agreed to “warn” Bevan about Macartney.
The file was finally closed in 1975, 15 years after Bevan died.
Other newly released papers show MI5 feared communists could attempt to disrupt the coronation of King George VI, with Communist party activists closely watched before the Westminster Abbey ceremony in 1937.
While the party prepared a propaganda drive and printed a million anti-monarchist leaflets to be distributed during coronation week, members were warned to avoid antagonising a largely pro-royalist public.
One MI5 report from April 1937 noted that a “comrade” in Manchester had been “severely censured” for proposing a series of demonstrations as it would be “playing into the hands of the fascists and police”. “It has been pointed out that members will be ‘going against the stream’ in doing this and they must be careful to speak in such a way that they do not make themselves unpopular with their neighbours.”
Sir Michael Tippett, a leading British composer of the 20th century and a famed pacifist, was also monitored by MI5 as a suspected Trotskyist revolutionary, according to the files.
MI5 believed he joined first the Communist party and then the Trotskyists in the 1930s, and remained an active supporter until the end of the second world war.
The files suggest, however, he was unconvincing as a revolutionary. In one intercepted letter to a Communist party organiser in London, he complained of the difficulties of trying to combine his work as a communist with his life as a music teacher living in rural Surrey. His evening commitments meant that it was “quite impossible” for him to attend “cell” meetings in London, he complained.
A report from 1955 noted that Tippett “has not come to notice in connection with communist or Trotskyist affairs”.
However, his radical past meant that as late as 1959 he was blocked from taking up a Foreign Office-sponsored lectureship in Germany, and it was only in the 1960s that MI5 were prepared to give him a clean bill of health. In 1966, he was knighted for services to music. He died in 1998 aged 93.

article_title: Trump praises supporter for allegedly punching protester during rally for Darline Graham in South Carolina – as it happened
article_content:
'I loved that' Trump says after protester was allegedly punched by president's supporter
Tensions flared on Wednesday, as multiple protesters were removed from the Trump rally at South Carolina’s Clemson University.
One demonstrator apparently was socked by a rally attendee, much to Trump’s delight.
“That was great, man. Wow. Man, I loved that,” the president said.
“Who’s the guy that threw the punch?” he continued. “You know, you reminded me of Evander. The real deal Holyfield,” referring to the former heavyweight champion.
“You gotta give them credit. It takes courage to do that.”
We’re wrapping up our live coverage of US politics. Here are some of today’s key developments:
Donald Trump rallied in South Carolina for Republican Senator Darline Graham. The event at Clemson University was marked by tension and aggression toward protesters, which Trump praised. Several demonstrators were removed and in at least two instances Trump supporters allegedly physically attacked them. “That was great, man. Wow. Man, I loved that,” the president said after an attendee punched a protester.
Nancy Pelosi’s office received “a suspicious letter” on Wednesday in what appears to be the latest incident of ill-intentioned mailings targeted at US Congress members before the midterm elections. The offices of more than three dozen members of Congress across the political spectrum recently received envelopes containing white powder. The FBI, the Capitol police and the US Postal Inspection Service are investigating the mailings.
The controversy around Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign ad continued to grow as it emerged that another Republican candidate in Ohio had asked him not to run the spot featuring his Democratic opponent’s estranged mother. JD Vance said he was “disgusted” by Republican outrage over the ad, adding that they should “stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days”. Amy Acton, whose mother was in the ad, told a group of voters her mother was not well and Ramaswamy shouldn’t have “exploited her”.
Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar denied allegations of immigration fraud in a Wednesday appearance on MS Now, her first interview since federal agents raided her residence last week.
Aipac, the most powerful pro-Israel lobby in the US, will cease issuing endorsements and directly contributing to candidates through its political action committee, according to a report from Jewish Insider.
Democrats are suing to stop Donald Trump’s administration from demanding states remove voters, who the federal government alleges are not citizens, from their rolls ahead of the US midterms.
Ilhan Omar gives first interview since federal raid on her home
Uwa Ede-Osifo
Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar denied allegations of immigration fraud in a Wednesday appearance on MS Now, her first interview since federal agents raided her residence last week.
The 12 October raid marked an escalation of a years-long feud between Omar and Trump.
Those in Donald Trump’s orbit – cabinet officials and right wing influencers alike – have promoted baseless theories about the Democratic congresswoman, accusing Omar of being in a sham marriage with her brother and fudging details of her immigration paperwork.
“Obviously, they’d like to see me locked up, deported and all of those things. But I think like the bigger satisfaction for them would be for me to be like ‘I’m tired of all of you and I’m going to leave,” Omar told MS Now host Chris Hayes. “I have a legal right to be a member of Congress.”
Democrats are suing to stop Donald Trump’s administration from demanding states remove voters, who the federal government alleges are not citizens, from their rolls ahead of the US midterms.
Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said “Trump knows he can’t win a fair fight, so he’s resorted to bullying election officials into stripping Americans of their right to vote”.
“It’s illegal, it’s un-American, & we’re taking him to court to stop it. The voters decide who wins elections. Not Trump.”
Trump’s South Carolina rally has continued to see aggression and violence directed toward protesters.
Multiple demonstrators have been removed from the event at Clemson University, including one who was allegedly punched by a Trump supporter, a move the president praised. Footage emerged online of another apparent Trump supporter striking a different protester, who was being escorted out by police, in the back of the head.
While Trump is in South Carolina to stump for Darline Graham, last week the senator was at odds with the US president after he put on hold a new sanctions package targeting Russia.
The legislation had been named for the late South Carolina senator Lindsay Graham, Graham’s brother, who was the primary backer of the package that sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers key to Russian energy. Graham had said she was proud to help get the legislation passed, but that it was up to Trump how he chose to implement it. He ultimately opted to waive the sanctions before they went into effect.
“Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down,” Graham said at a campaign event, according to the New York Times. “Because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia.”
It had been a key accomplishment cited by Darline Graham as she campaigns for the Senate with a brief record after being appointed to serve out the remaining months of her brother’s term.
'I loved that' Trump says after protester was allegedly punched by president's supporter
Tensions flared on Wednesday, as multiple protesters were removed from the Trump rally at South Carolina’s Clemson University.
One demonstrator apparently was socked by a rally attendee, much to Trump’s delight.
“That was great, man. Wow. Man, I loved that,” the president said.
“Who’s the guy that threw the punch?” he continued. “You know, you reminded me of Evander. The real deal Holyfield,” referring to the former heavyweight champion.
“You gotta give them credit. It takes courage to do that.”
Donald Trump digs at Darline Graham's opponent in Senate race, faces protests at SC rally
Donald Trump is back in South Carolina, galvanizing his base to back senator Darline Graham. She is running to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham’s congressional seat.
Her campaign has been dogged by questions about her political inexperience, notably after she struggled to answer a question about Taiwan and US national security.
At the Wednesday evening rally, several protesters heckled Trump, before they were escorted. He dismissed their presence as paid operatives.
As the rally kicked off, Trump repeated a transphobic slur he has used before to deride Graham’s Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews.
Amy Acton responded to the controversy over Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign ad featuring her estranged mother, telling a group of voters her opponent shouldn’t have “exploited her”.
“I haven’t seen my mother since I was 12, and obviously we were removed from her custody. And she’s not well and they shouldn’t have exploited her,” Acton said. She went on to describe it as “another sign of this time, where enough is enough … [This] do anything, say anything just to get ahead. And I think Ohioans are smarter than that.”
In the ad, her mother, Donna Arthur, was critical of Acton and called her a liar. Amy Acton was sexually abused by her mother’s husband when she was 12, her brother Phillip Stearns said. After his arrest, their mother remained married to her husband, even though Acton and Stearns were removed from her care.
Nancy Pelosi's office latest to receive 'suspicious' letter
Nancy Pelosi’s office received “a suspicious letter” on Wednesday in what appears to be the latest incident of ill-intentioned mailings targeted at US Congress members before the midterm elections.
Earlier this week, the Guardian reported that the offices of more than three dozen members of Congress across the political spectrum received envelopes containing white powder. One lawmaker’s office said preliminary tests indicated the powder was not hazardous.
A spokesperson for Pelosi said the letter was “consistent with mailings reported by other congressional offices” and that everyone in the office was safe.
“Speaker Pelosi remains focused on serving the people of San Francisco and is concerned for the members and staff whose offices have experienced similar incidents,” Nicholas Martin, a spokesperson for the speaker emerita, said in a statement.
“She is grateful for the efforts of the US Capitol Police, the San Francisco police department and other law enforcement agencies to thoroughly investigate this series of intimidation across America.”
More than 100 letters thought to contain white powder were reportedly thought to be circulating in the US mail system. Election offices across the US have also reported receiving suspicious mail.
The mailings are under investigation by the FBI, the Capitol police and the US Postal Inspection Service. The FBI declined to confirm “specific instances or letters”, but said in a statement earlier this week: “The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including secretary of state offices and their related election offices, and congressional offices.”
The controversy around Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign ad continues to grow as it emerged that another Republican candidate in Ohio had asked him not to run the spot featuring his Democratic opponent’s estranged mother.
A Republican operative told CNN that a candidate “personally asked” the GOP gubernatorial candidate not to air the ad, and that “Republicans in the state probably couldn’t be more pissed at him”.
In the ad, the mother of Amy Acton, Ramaswamy’s opponent, called her daughter a liar. Amy Acton was sexually abused by her mother’s husband when she was 12, her brother Phillip Stearns said. After his arrest, their mother, Donna Arthur, remained married to her husband, even though Acton and Stearns were removed from her care.
The ad has drawn criticism from some prominent Republicans although others have defended it, including JD Vance, who told Republicans “stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days”.
Meanwhile, footage surfaced on Wednesday of Ramaswamy describing Acton as a candidate who has no vision “other than to complain about what someone else did to her”.
Aipac, the most powerful pro-Israel lobby in the US, will cease issuing endorsements and directly contributing to candidates through its political action committee, according to a report from Jewish Insider.
Since 2022, the group has been directly involved with elections through its Pac and Super Pac and spent hundreds of millions of dollars on US races, though its brand has become increasingly toxic in recent years.
“To win the fight for the future of the country and the US-Israel alliance, we must build a more strategic, consequential, and nimble political operation. We will prioritize increasing direct, organized contributions from individual Americans to candidates – expanding upon our current efforts – and maximizing the emerging political fundraising tools,” Aipac leadership said in a letter, according to Jewish Insider.
“Endorsements, direct PAC contributions, and earmarking will no longer be part of our approach so we can expand individual giving and utilize new tools to help our friends win.”
Historically the group has spent most in Democratic primaries, and donated more to Democrats, rarely backing Republicans in competitive races during general elections. It emerged this week, however, that Aipac made a significant donation to Republican Mike Rogers, who is running against Abdul El-Sayed. The group, which spent tens of millions to defeat El-Sayed in the Democratic primary, plans to donate as much as $9m to support Rogers, the New York Times reported.
JD Vance says Republicans should 'stop whining and go win the race in 13 days' after outrage over Ramaswamy campaign ad
Speaking earlier, JD Vance also chided Republicans for their outrage over the controversial campaign ad from Vivek Ramaswamy,featuring his Democratic opponent’s estranged mother.
Amy Acton was sexually abused by her mother’s husband when she was 12 years old, according to her brother Phillip Stearns. Their mother, Donna Arthur, remained married to her husband after he was arrested, even though Acton and Stearns were removed from her care.
Vance said he wasn’t going to weigh in on whether the spot was “appropriate or not”, instead he said that his “message” for fellow elected Republicans is to “stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days”.
At a campaign stop in Cincinnati, the vice-president added:
I have to admit that I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America.
Musk threatens to 'come for' Democrats who 'pick fights' with him in new Congress
Elon Musk – the tech billionaire, Trump ally, and founder of Tesla and Space X – has threatened to home in on Democrats who pursue him in the next Congress.
“Live by the sword, die by the sword,” Musk wrote on X, the social media platform he bought in 2022. “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets.”
This comes after Politico reported earlier today that Democratic lawmakers were considering how best to investigate Musk, and his businesses, if the party gains control of Congress following the midterm elections.
US envoy Steve Witkoff announced this morning that Russia authorities had freed Stephen Hubbard, the first American known to be convicted of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. Hubbard was arrested when the Russians briefly took over the Ukrainian city of Izium at the start of the ongoing conflict in 2022.
Donald Trump welcomed the news,noting the prisoner release was the result of a direct request he made to Putin in a telephone call last week. Meanwhile, after Witkoff’s discussions with Putin in St Petersburg, he flattered the Russian president by calling him a “humanitarian”. The emissary’s comments drew bipartisan backlash, but Trump defended them: “I guess you could say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life, out,” the US president told reporters in the East Room.
Witkoff also said that his discussions with Putin were “constructive”, and“will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia and Ukraine at the technical level”. This comes after Trump’s reignited feud with Zelenskyy after he urged Kyiv to end its attacks on Russian refineries and waived sweeping sanctions against Moscow.
New polling from the New York Times and Siena University shows thatlikely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans running for office by 11 percentage points. Meanwhile, Trump’s approval rating dropped to a new low for this particular survey – 36%.
At a campaign rally in Cincinnati, Ohio, JD Vance criticized the media and Democrats for focusing on Vivek Ramaswamy’s recent ad for his gubernatorial campaign, which features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent,Amy Acton. The vice-president defended Ramaswamy for having “the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is, and calls Amy Acton a liar”. Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, claimed in the spot that her daughter “lied her entire life” about living in a tent during her childhood. However, Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, said on Tuesday that his sister is estranged from her mother, who had married a man that sexually abused Acton when she was 12 years old. Arthur, he said, remained in the marriage even after her husband was arrested and her children were taken away from her.
The supreme court has refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately deny gender-affirming care for transgender people in federal prisons. The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy while a legal challenge plays out. It was adopted after an executive order from Trump, who’s taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term.
With 13 days until the midterms,Trump will continue his campaign blitz by heading to Clemson, South Carolina, where he’ll rally for Darline Graham – the Republican nominee for US Senate who is hoping to secure a full term for her late brother’s seat. Darline was appointed by the South Carolina governor to carry out the remainder of Lindsey Graham’s time in office after his death in July. However, she now faces a competitive race against Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and the Democratic nominee, in a contest that has become increasingly rancorous in recent months.
Trump defends special envoy Witkoff calling Putin a 'humanitarian'
In the East Room today, Trump defended Steve Witkoff’s comments, noting that the release of Steven Hubbard might warrant praise for Putin.
“I guess you could say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life, out,” Trump told reporters.
Earlier, we noted that Thom Tillis, the outgoing Republican senator from North Carolina, slammed special envoy Steve Witkoff for calling Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian” today – following the release of detained US citizen Steven Hubbard.
Now, more GOP lawmakers are pushing back.
“Vladimir Putin is not our friend, and he is certainly no humanitarian,” said retiring Republican senator Joni Ernst.
She added: “His relentless attacks on innocent civilians in Ukraine show his total disregard for human life. Appeasement won’t end this war. Pressure will.”
With 13 days until the midterms, early voting data is rolling in nationwide. Democrats need to net four Senate seats and hold 218 House seats to reclaim a congressional majority. Here is where the numbers stand so far:
Turnout is surging in key battlegrounds: Over 16 million Americans have already voted in person or by mail. According to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, battleground states -including Michigan, Ohio, Georgia, Texas, Florida and North Carolina – have each passed 700,000 ballots cast as of 21 October. Turnout is being driven in part by widespread voter frustration, reflected in Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings.
Democrats lead in early returns: Registered Democrats account for 47% of early ballots cast, compared with 29% from Republicans (tracking returned ballots, not candidate selection). The party gap is most pronounced in North Carolina, Kansas and Iowa. While Republicans traditionally favor election day voting, strategists worry this widened margin signals a “red undertow” – GOP voters staying home due to frustration over high gas prices, the conflict in Iran and sweeping tariffs.
Early votes are pacing well ahead of 2022: In Georgia, early votes already represent nearly 30% of the total turnout from the 2022 midterms. Florida sits at 18%, with similarly high paces recorded in North Carolina, Michigan and Ohio.
Mail-in voting remains resilient: Over 56m mail-in ballots have been requested or sent nationally – greater than the 52m requested in 2022, according to NBC News (using data from TargetSmart). Despite executive orders from the Trump administration attempting to restrict mail-in voting, which the supreme court struck down in September, voters continue to utilize the process at pre-pandemic rates.
Meta ordered to pay $25bn penalty over deceiving users about data privacy
A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn in penalties, on after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that Cambridge Analytica – a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign – obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent.
The state’s attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm, had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.
“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219bn was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25bn.
In Maine, Susan Collins, the moderate Republican incumbent senator vying for a sixth term in office, joined the growing list of GOP lawmakers to urge the Trump administration to reverse the waiving of Russian sanctions.
“First of all the law is very clear, that we wanted additional sanctions to be imposed on Russia, by cutting the deal on diesel with Russia. [Trump] is not going to increase the supply to the United States in any measurable way. But what he is going to do is to get more funding for Russia to use to attack Ukraine,” Collins told reporters in Lewiston, where she was joined by former independent senator Joe Manchin for a campaign stop.

article_title: ‘Man, I loved that’: Trump cheers South Carolina rally attender who hit protester
article_content:
Multiple protesters were removed from Donald Trump’s rally at South Carolina’s Clemson University on Wednesday, including one who was apparently punched by a rally attender – to the US president’s delight.
“That was great, man. Wow. Man, I loved that. I watched that,” Trump said. “That was incredible. Wow. That was unbelievable. Is everybody OK?
“Who’s the guy that threw that punch?” he continued. “You know, you reminded me of Evander, the real deal, Holyfield,” referring to the former heavyweight champion, who was also in attendance at the rally.
“You gotta give them credit. It takes courage to do that at a Trump rally,” he said. “He got whacked.”
According to a pool report, the president was interrupted at least nine times by hecklers. The crowd chanted “USA” as security guards escorted the protesters out of the arena.
One protester who was removed by security was followed by a rally attendee, who appeared to slap the demonstrator on the head.
Trump was in South Carolina to support Darline Graham, the sister of late senator Lindsey Graham who died suddenly in July from a heart condition. Graham, elected to her brother’s seat in a special election, is facing Democratic challenger Annie Andrews in her bid for a full six-year term.
Protests have frequently erupted at Trump rallies in recent weeks, as the president has ramped up his campaign stops in the final weeks before the 3 November midterm elections. The president often brushes off the demonstrations as being carried out by “paid protesters”.
Trump’s 32-day campaign blitz has largely taken him to Republican-leaning areas that he won comfortably in previous elections, underscoring the challenges facing Republicans as they try to retain control of the US Senate and the House of Representatives.
The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, published on Monday, found that 31% of Americans approve of Trump’s performance in office, a record low for the president.

article_title: Officials confirm flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite found in US wildlife
article_content:
The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) said on Wednesday it had confirmed the first detection of flesh-eating parasite the New World screwworm in US wildlife in an elk in Pecos county, Texas.
The elk was located on a game ranch and was reported after being harvested by a hunter, the USDA said in a statement.
The Texas animal health commission will modify a previously established infested zone, and the USDA and the Texas parks and wildlife department is conducting additional wildlife surveillance in the area, the USDA said.
“We encourage all hunters and landowners to be vigilant for signs of New World screwworm while they are out in the field this season,” Texas wildlife division director Alan Cain said in a statement.
Eradicated from the US decades ago, the pest has surged north from Central America through Mexico, prompting Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports.
The US halted livestock imports from Mexico last year to keep out screwworm, but resumed trade in August at an Arizona port as part of a phased reopening plan.
The halt has tightened US cattle supplies and pushed beef prices to record highs for American consumers.
Despite those efforts, the screwworm was detected in June on a calf in Texas’s Zavala county, located near the US-Mexico border. There have since been dozens of cases detected in the US this year, including on a horse and on a dog.

article_title: Трамп відхрестився від обмежень Starshield для України: хто насправді ухвалив рішення
article_content:
Трамп відхрестився від обмежень Starshield для України: хто насправді ухвалив рішення
Президент США Дональд Трамп заперечив свою причетність до обмеження роботи супутникової системи Starshield для України. Він також заявив, що не вважає Ілона Маска відповідальним за проблеми зі зв'язком.
Президент США Дональд Трамп заявив, що не наказував обмежувати доступ України до військової супутникової системи Starshield, яку використовують українські військові. За його словами, він також не вважає, що відповідне рішення ухвалив власник SpaceX Ілон Маск.
Про це йдеться в заяві американського президента.
Відповідаючи на запитання журналістів про те, хто відповідальний за обмеження супутникового зв'язку для України, Трамп заперечив свою причетність.
«Це був не я. І я не думаю, що це був Ілон. Я навіть не знаю, чи хтось узагалі це зробив. Наскільки я розумію, все залишилося так, як було», — сказав президент США.
Він також заявив, що Сполучені Штати не запроваджували обмежень на використання Україною Starshield.
Що відомо про суперечку між Трампом і Маском
Раніше Ілон Маск стверджував, що рішення щодо обмеження швидкості або використання Starshield належать до компетенції американських військових та зрештою президента США.
Водночас американські ЗМІ оприлюднили суперечливу інформацію про те, хто саме ініціював зміни в роботі супутникової системи.
Зокрема, The Wall Street Journal повідомляло, що Маск особисто ухвалив рішення про обмеження супутникового зв'язку, попередньо провівши переговори з представниками адміністрації Трампа.
За інформацією CBS News, рішення Маска призвело до суттєвого уповільнення роботи системи, яку Україна використовує для військових операцій.
Водночас залишається незрозумілим, чи погоджував ці обмеження Білий дім.
Чому обмеження Starshield небезпечні для України
Проблеми із супутниковим зв'язком виникли на тлі загострення відносин між Києвом і Вашингтоном через українські удари по російських нафтопереробних заводах.
Українська сторона повідомляла про обмеження швидкості зв'язку для безпілотників, які використовують систему Starshield.
Зокрема, йшлося про втрату стабільного з'єднання під час польоту дронів на швидкості понад 160 км/год.
Це створило проблеми для використання окремих типів ударних безпілотників і дронів-перехоплювачів, які застосовують для захисту від російських повітряних атак.
Український фахівець із радіотехнологій Сергій Бескрестнов повідомляв, що Київ веде переговори зі SpaceX та американською владою щодо скасування обмежень.
За його словами, особливе занепокоєння викликають труднощі з перехопленням швидкісних російських безпілотників.
Що заявили в Пентагоні
Міністр оборони США Піт Гегсет також заперечив, що Пентагон наказував обмежувати роботу Starshield для України.
За його словами, американське оборонне відомство не змінювало своєї позиції щодо українських військових і не видавало відповідних розпоряджень.
Гегсет наголосив, що питання використання супутникових сервісів регулюються умовами обслуговування, а рішення щодо них може ухвалювати SpaceX.
Схожу позицію висловив державний секретар США Марко Рубіо. Він заявив, що рішення щодо роботи комерційного Starlink належать компанії та Ілону Маску, а не Білому дому.
Водночас Рубіо підкреслив необхідність розрізняти Starlink і Starshield, оскільки йдеться про дві різні програми супутникового зв'язку.
Попри заяви американських посадовців, остаточної відповіді на запитання, хто санкціонував обмеження зв'язку для України, наразі немає.
Нагадаємо, що раніше Ілон Маск заявив, що обмеження роботи Starshield для України є рішенням американської влади, а не SpaceX.
description: Президент США Дональд Трамп заперечив свою причетність до обмеження роботи супутникової системи Starshield для України. Він також заявив, що не вважає Ілона Маска відповідальним за проблеми зі зв'язком.

article_title: Nancy Pelosi’s office latest recipient of letter containing white powder
article_content:
California representative Nancy Pelosi’s office received “a suspicious letter” on Wednesday in what appears to be the latest incident of ill-intentioned mailings targeted at US Congress members before the midterm elections.
The offices of more than three dozen members of Congress across the political spectrum have received envelopes containing white powder in recent days. One lawmaker’s office said preliminary tests indicated the powder was not hazardous.
A spokesperson for Pelosi said the letter was “consistent with mailings reported by other congressional offices” and that everyone in the office was safe.
“Speaker Pelosi remains focused on serving the people of San Francisco and is concerned for the members and staff whose offices have experienced similar incidents,” Nicholas Martin, a spokesperson for the speaker emerita, said in a statement.
“She is grateful for the efforts of the US Capitol police, the San Francisco police department and other law enforcement agencies to thoroughly investigate this series of intimidation across America.”
More than 100 letters thought to contain white powder were reportedly thought to be circulating in the US mail system. Election offices across the US have also reported receiving suspicious mail.
The mailings are under investigation by the FBI, the Capitol police and the US Postal Inspection Service. The FBI declined to confirm “specific instances or letters”, but said in a statement earlier this week: “The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including secretary of state offices and their related election offices, and congressional offices.”
