article_title: США вигадали новий мирний план: що пропонують Україні, Росії та що буде з Донбасом — The Economist
article_content:
США вигадали новий мирний план: що пропонують Україні, Росії та що буде з Донбасом — The Economist
На Донбасі може бути створена демілітаризована зона, тоді як Росія може розраховувати на відновлення бізнес-домовленостей зі США.
США підготували новий сценарій завершення війни в Україні, який передбачає створення демілітаризованої зони на Донбасі та відмову від НАТО. Журналісти розкрили ключові деталі умови, які пропонуються Києву та Москві.
Про це повідомив журналіст Дмитро Гордон з посиланням на The Economist.
Видання з посиланням на українських посадовців поінформувало про ключові положення можливого мирного плану. Зокрема, на Донбасі може бути створена демілітаризована зона, тоді як Росія може розраховувати на відновлення бізнесових домовленостей зі США, послаблення санкцій та політичну нормалізацію.
Для України передбачають інвестиційний пакет і перспективу членства у Євросоюзі. Водночас Київ має відмовитися від прагнення вступити до НАТО.
«Найновіший „пряник“ для путіна — пропозиція відновити продажі російського газу до Європи, які мали бути повністю припинені до кінця року, і перезапустити трубопровід „північний потік“, — зауважив Гордон.
Нагадаємо, за даними The New York Times, адміністрація президента США Дональда Трампа посилює тиск на президента України Володимира Зеленського, переконуючи погодитися на мирну угоду з Росією та відмовитися від окупованих східних територій в обмін на потенційні економічні вигоди. США паралельно рухаються до нормалізації відносин із Москвою.
До слова, в інтерв’ю Fox News Зеленський назвав вимоги Росії віддати весь Донбас несправедливими та заявив, що 2026 року країна-агресорка не мала успіхів на полі бою. За словами президента, окупанти намагаються примусити Україну відступити за допомогою тиску та масованих атак ракетами й дронами. Зеленський наголосив, що українці тримаються міцно й не покинуть власні домівки.

article_title: UK to draft in military aircraft to fight wildfires, Burnham says
article_content:
UK to draft in military aircraft to fight wildfires, Burnham says
- Published
Military planes and helicopters will be drafted in to tackle wildfires, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to tell the UK's first summit on the issue.
Civilian fire services in all four nations will be able to request the support of the Royal Air Force's Chinook helicopters and A400M planes to fight wildfires on tough terrain such as remote moorland and steep hillsides.
Burnham said the measures were needed because "we cannot put people through another summer like this one".
The government will host its first "wildfire resilience summit" on Friday to discuss how to prevent, respond to and recover from such blazes after a record-breaking summer 2026.
There have been 1,350 wildfires in England and Wales this year, an all-time high and up by more than 300 on last year and more than 1,000 on 2024, according to figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council.
Records for the number of reported wildfires were also broken in 2022 and 2025 - but the UK's Climate Change Committee has warned the risk will rise in the coming decades.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said this was the first time the RAF's Chinooks and the four-engine A400Ms were being equipped to tackle wildfires. Some areas struggled with no air assistance in the summer.
RAF Chinook crews have already helped respond, external to wildfires in Cyprus.
In addition to military aircraft, the government said it would also spend £45m on wildfire-specific personal protective equipment for firefighters on the ground.
It is lighter than current firefighting equipment which is designed for fires in buildings and not meant to be worn for a long time, the government added.
Ministers are also pledging a £25m scheme from April 2027 to April 2029 to restore dried-out peatlands in England so they are natural firebreaks, and financial support for farmers to fireproof their land such as by digging ponds.
"The government will also look at tougher local restrictions or product bans to stop people starting fires when the risk is high," a briefing ahead of the summit said, following a temporary ban on disposable BBQs.
Burnham will meet fire chiefs, local leaders and experts from tech companies at the summit.
"I stood in Stourbridge and watched families lose everything," he said on Thursday, recounting the night of a wildfire that destroyed 19 homes in the West Midlands in August.
"I will never forget it. Our firefighters were heroes that day, but heroes shouldn't have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs."
Earlier this month, MPs on the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee said there were weaknesses in the UK's wildfire preparedness, including access to aerial firefighting resources, securing water supplies during major incidents and coordinating resources at a national level.
MPs said the current system for obtaining aerial firefighting support was "no longer fit for purpose".
At the summit, a "Wildfires AI Unit" will be announced to combine universities, tech firms and officials on the Cobra emergency committee, along with Met Office wildfire forecasts and closer work with devolved governments.
In August, the government convened a Cobra meeting before sending an emergency alert to millions of phones across England and Wales - which sparked a backlash from some.
Summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record, according to the Met Office. In a study on how this summer was impacted by human-induced climate change, it said the heat experienced was made 130 times more likely.
"The wildfires that tore through our countryside this summer showed the urgent need to adapt to our changing climate," Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said ahead of the summit.
"Nature is our greatest ally in preventing wildfires starting in the first place," she added.
Major incidents were declared for wildfires this year in areas such as Dunwich Heath and RSPB Minsmere in Suffolk, the Cairngorms, Hampshire and Holme Fen in Cambridgeshire.

article_title: Every Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advises
article_content:
Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.
The Be Ready campaign is aimed at persuading people to stock up with supplies to last 72 hours, amid growing official concern about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.
Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said that “those who can follow this advice should follow this advice”. It amounted to “simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies” as part of a wider, community-oriented effort “to improve our resilience as a nation”, he said.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, added that Britain also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.
“Terms like ‘hybrid warfare’ and ‘grey zone threats’ do not accurately capture or convey to the general public what I prefer to describe as ‘state-sponsored terrorism’,” he said.
“So in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.
“It’s really important that we ask households and businesses, are they prepared? Are they ready? Do they know how they would respond in the event of everyday challenges that might manifest themselves?”
People are advised to keep a ready supply of blankets and cash at home plus a first aid kit, a torch with batteries and a wind-up FM radio. Three litres of water per person per day should be stored for drinking – and more is needed for cooking and washing, the guidance adds.
The government had indicated in August that UK citizens would be told to stock up on tinned food but the Be Ready campaign from the Cabinet Office is more specific. It will be followed up with an advertising campaign on social media and radio.
Stocking up for three days is considered to be a realistic and practical proposal for households and would bring the UK in line with France, the Republic of Ireland and the Netherlands in advising people how to prepare for serious disruption.
Ministers timed the launch of the campaign to come before the winter storm season after a series of intense storms that have battered the UK in recent years. Tens of thousands of homes were left without power in the Midlands, the south-west and Wales after Storm Goretti hit in January, with winds reaching nearly 100mph.
There is also concern about the potential impact of the “super El-Nino”, a global phenomenon that could lead to 2027 being the hottest year ever recorded and uncertain weather patterns, affecting global food supplies and energy systems.
The guidance emerged as 32 UK government websites were taken offline in a precautionary measure in response to the discovery of a security vulnerability in the PHP programming language used by millions of websites around the world.
Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, in a reminder of the high degree of dependency that modern societies have on the internet and other critical technologies.
Spain and Portugal were suddenly left without power for several hours in April 2025, in a cascading failure triggered by voltage instability in the network. About 55 million people were affected in the incident, the worst blackout in Europe in recent memory.
People also need to consider how to respond to hybrid warfare attacks by Russia or other hostile states, including cyber-attacks that could knock out payment systems used by businesses or cause supply chains to collapse, Streeting said.
The minister was speaking at a new tank gun barrel factory in Telford in the West Midlands. The factory, owned by the German manufacturer Rheinmetall, is part of efforts to accelerate rearmament in the face of Russian military threats, but Streeting also emphasised that the public should be prepared for hybrid warfare, or sabotage actions that stop short of outright war.
Russian spy ships have been tracked by the Royal Navy monitoring undersea pipelines and cables that connect the UK to the continent of Europe and elsewhere, raising concerns they could one day be attacked, though this would represent a major escalation by Moscow.
European states have become increasingly vocal about the threat of sabotage efforts by enemies, particularly Russia, which can cause disruption or even directly threaten safety. These efforts have included an explosives-laden drone found next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport in August, and a series of explosions and fires at defence facilities.
Britain has only rarely embarked on public information campaigns, with governments of both parties reluctant to be accused of scaremongering. A 1980 campaign advising people on how to survive a nuclear war, Protect and Survive, advised people how to build a bomb shelter at home and retain enough food for 14 days.

article_title: В ЕС сохраняются разногласия по поводу "ассоциированного членства" для Канады — Politico
article_content:
Германия, Франция и как минимум шесть других стран ЕС выступают против использования термина “ассоциированное членство” для обозначения более тесных связей между Евросоюзом и Канадой, сообщает Politico со ссылкой на слова дипломатов.
Этот термин является одним из главных камней преткновения в переговорах по совместной декларации, определяющей сферы углубленного сотрудничества между Брюсселем и Оттавой в преддверии саммита ЕС—Канада в Монреале 29–30 октября.
Дипломаты отметили, что возражения касаются именно формулировки “ассоциированное членство”, а не общей цели сближения.
Спустя пять недель после того, как президент Еврокомиссии Урсула фон дер Ляйен впервые предложила Канаде стать “ассоциированным членом” Евросоюза, между странами сохраняются разногласия, свидетельствующие о том, что этот термин остается политическим и коммуникационным препятствием.
“ЕС очень заинтересован в тесном сотрудничестве с Канадой”, — заявил глава комитета по вопросам торговли Европарламента Бернд Ланге.
Однако он также предпочел бы избегать использования термина “ассоциированное членство”, поскольку это создает слишком много путаницы с другими формами партнерства с ЕС, такими как соглашения об ассоциации.
Германия наиболее активно настаивает на исключении этого термина из проекта декларации, тогда как Франция, Италия и Бельгия выразили скептицизм по поводу такой формулировки.
Главная обеспокоенность стран, выступающих против этого термина, заключается в том, что ЕС определяет характер отношений, не договорившись предварительно о том, что это будет означать. Они утверждают, что формулировку необходимо было согласовать еще до начала переговоров с Канадой. Страны, высказывающие возражения, возмущены тем, что фон дер Ляйен предложила этот термин, предварительно не проконсультировавшись с национальными правительствами.
Еврокомиссия будет вести диалог со скептически настроенными странами и работать над приемлемой формулировкой, отметил чиновник ЕС. По его словам, разногласий относительно цели укрепления и без того тесных отношений, в частности в сфере экономического и оборонного сотрудничества, международной деятельности и институциональных связей, нет.
“Важно то, что мы делаем, а не то, как мы это называем”, — заявил чиновник.
По словам одного из дипломатов, этот термин призван охарактеризовать отношения между ЕС и Канадой как более тесные, чем партнерские связи Брюсселя с другими странами, не делая при этом Оттаву членом Евросоюза. Канада не может стать членом ЕС, поскольку учредительные документы Евросоюза ограничивают этот статус географически только Европой.
Такое разграничение имеет значение, поскольку существующие соглашения с европейскими соседями, в частности с Великобританией, Швейцарией и странами Европейской экономической зоны, в значительной степени сосредоточены на доступе к внутреннему рынку ЕС. Канада, расположенная на другом континенте, не стремится к такой же модели.
Идея заключается в том, чтобы сначала определить практические сферы сотрудничества, а затем решить, нужны ли новые договоры или официальные переговоры, отметил дипломат.
Ожидается, что работа над шестью приоритетными направлениями начнётся после саммита в Монреале, а прогресс проанализируют через шесть месяцев. После этого через год на следующем саммите, который состоится в Европе, проведут полноценный итоговый обзор.
В ходе подведения итогов рассмотрят, приблизилась ли Канада к ЕС, став полноправным участником программ “Горизонт Европа” и Erasmus, строит ли она подводные кабели и создает ли запасы критически важных сырьевых ресурсов совместно с Евросоюзом, а также изучает ли она возможности инвестирования пенсионных фондов. Если Канада будет соответствовать этим критериям, она может стать первым ассоциированным членом ЕС, добавил дипломат. Он назвал эту идею экспериментом, отметив, что Канада, возможно, будет единственной страной, которая когда-либо получит ассоциированное членство в ЕС.
Саммит в Монреале призван придать партнерству более четкие политические очертания.
Декларация находится на стадии доработки, и послы стран ЕС планируют вновь обсудить её в понедельник, 26 октября. Один из чиновников ЕС предупредил, что по некоторым частям декларации до сих пор поступают замечания.
Еще один спорный момент касается сотрудничества в энергетической сфере: Австрия выступает против любых упоминаний об углублении сотрудничества в ядерной отрасли, тогда как Франция, Румыния, Словакия и некоторые другие страны поддерживают включение этого пункта в декларацию.
Сближение между Канадой и ЕС отражает изменение подходов с обеих сторон. Канада уже давно в значительной степени зависит от торговли с Соединёнными Штатами, но пошлины и политическое давление со стороны Вашингтона при администрации президента Дональда Трампа усилили обеспокоенность по поводу этой зависимости. Премьер-министр Канады Марк Карни стремится диверсифицировать торговлю и модернизировать инфраструктуру страны. Для ЕС более тесное партнерство с Канадой является частью более широких усилий по налаживанию международных отношений на фоне растущего давления со стороны Соединенных Штатов, Китая и России.
В речи на Всемирном экономическом форуме в начале этого года Карни предупредил, что международный порядок, основанный на правилах, подорван, призвав так называемые средние государства создать новую глобальную архитектуру, чтобы противостоять тактике давления и запугивания со стороны великих держав. Он не называл напрямую имя президента США Дональда Трампа, но призвал к созданию новых альянсов, которые станут линией обороны против стран, навязывающих свою экономическую и военную мощь по собственному усмотрению.
description: Камнем преткновения остается сам термин “ассоциированное членство” в ЕС.

article_title: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns
article_content:
Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns
- Published
Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber-attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, the defence secretary has said.
Wes Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them.
He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies.
Streeting also said that cyber incidents - like the recently discovered critical security flaw in the programming language which powers much of the internet - will happen "more and more".
Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that the UK is facing a greater threat to the country, "than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime".
Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford earlier on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households.
He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and the flooding that is expected this winter.
Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".
The defence secretary referenced the critical security flaw in the PHP programming language which has left organisations around the world scrambling to update their systems.
In the UK, 32 government services were offline while the potential cyber-security issues were addressed.
"It's not just from foreign states engaged in espionage or sabotage; it's also organised criminals," Streeting told Question Time.
"In this world of AI that we live in... it does also present threats if people are innovating and pushing against conventional [cyber] defences."
The government hopes to improve the UK's preparedness for emergencies, such as those caused by increasingly likely severe weather events and cyber-attacks by hostile states.
Incidents could leave the public without access to everyday services such as mains water, sewage, phones and the internet.
The "Be Ready" campaign encourages households to stock up on supplies to survive for three days, including non-perishable food, bottled water, a torch, sleeping bags, and first aid items.
It also suggests having a FM radio for updates during outages, and writing down the frequencies of any national or local radio stations you use for news.
Asked by a Question Time audience member whether the campaign amounted to scaremongering, Streeting said the government want "people to be alert but not alarmed".
He said that there was not a "specific thing we've got in mind" when putting out the advice.
But, he added that the supplies on the list "might help you through some power cuts, or might also help you through if... your local shop's subject to a cyber-attack and your card isn't working at the till".
Security Minister Dan Jarvis MP said the advice will ensure emergency services can prioritise people who need more support during crises, and hopes it will "improve our resilience as a nation".
It follows on from similar campaigns by European countries, like France, Ireland and the Netherlands, where the advice is a "normal part of everyday life", he added.
Last month Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said people should prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean.
She said the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country", and that households should stock up on food to be more resilient.
Her comments came as an National Audit Office (NAO) report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.
The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience, and that UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland and Sweden.
The government launched its national security strategy last year, which warned that the UK must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario".
It said the nation was "in an era in which we face confrontation with those who are threatening security", and referred to Russia's war against Ukraine and "Iranian hostile activity on British soil".
The government said building national resilience meant reducing reliance on others and ensuring UK supply chains and energy security could be maintained "even in times of crisis".

article_title: Minister insists she backs migration policy after joking she couldn’t lie about supporting it
article_content:
The energy secretary has been forced to clarify that she backs Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy, after earlier joking that she had not been able to “lie” about supporting a key element of the changes.
Miatta Fahnbulleh made the original remarks to a journalists’ event in Westminster, referring to an “awkward” Sky News interview in which she repeatedly refused to say she was in favour of plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
She told the event: “I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments, including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge yesterday.”
The implication that she could not bring herself to lie about supporting the changes appears to have gone down badly among colleagues in government, although No 10 refused to be drawn on whether they requested her to issue a clarification.
Fahnbulleh posted a statement on social media on Thursday evening saying: “Today I made what was meant to be a lighthearted, self-deprecating remark. I didn’t get it right and it hasn’t come off as I intended.
“I fully support our home secretary and the government’s position on migration reform. As I said earlier this week, it’s absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship.”
The clarification represents a twist in the cabinet split over the issue of the migration changes, with Fahnbulleh and Angela Rayner among those not keen on elements of the original plan.
Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards.
She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residence could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule.
However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”
This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”
And earlier this year, Rayner, the housing secretary, publicly criticised the plans, while dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.
One of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.
“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.
MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, the Home Office has said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.
No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the planned changes.
Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.
“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”
Earlier this week, a Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”

article_title: Fahnbulleh says she backs home secretary on migration after comments to journalists
article_content:
Fahnbulleh says she backs home secretary on migration after comments to journalists
- Published
The energy minister has insisted she backs Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's immigration reforms after she made what she described as a "light-hearted remark".
Miatta Fahnbulleh was repeatedly asked in an interview on Wednesday whether she supported the government's plans to increase the time it takes for migrants to gain permanent UK residency, but refused to.
Referring to that exchange, she joked to reporters on Thursday that she did not explicitly answer the question because she had told herself she would "never lie".
In a later statement, she said: "Today I made what was meant to be a light-hearted self-deprecating remark. I didn't get it right and it hasn't come off as I intended."
She added: "I fully support our home secretary and the government's position on migration reform."
Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.
The government wants to double the time it takes most migrant workers to qualify for permanent residence from five years to 10 years, while in the case of refugees it could take 20 years.
Mahmood told Labour Party conference in September the government would "come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country".
But a significant number of Labour MPs and trade unions want her to water down the proposed policy.
Downing Street has repeatedly insisted that Mahmood is considering responses to a consultation exercise before finalising the reforms.
On Wednesday, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to make sure we get this right."
Asked earlier on the same day on Sky News, whether she backed the proposed reforms, Fahnbulleh said: "We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution."
She was pressed several more times on the issue, saying the government was consulting on the proposals and would "will come out with the measures that we take forward".
At a lunch with political reporters on Thursday, Fahnbulleh said: "I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge [on Sky] yesterday, but nevermind."
In her later statement, she said this was a joke and suggested it was not intended to show she did not support Mahmood's reforms.
"As I said earlier this week, it's absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship," Fahnbulleh said.
It comes after another Cabinet minister, Angela Rayner, criticised the proposed changes ahead of Labour's conference in Liverpool.
Rayner warned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules.
She later denied there was a split within the heart of government over the issue.

article_title: ‘No indications’ PHP code flaw has led to government systems being hacked, cyber security official says – as it happened
article_content:
Cyber security official says there are 'no indications' PHP code flaw has led to government computer systems being hacked
Ollie Whitehouse, chief technology officer at the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, told Radio 4’s the World at One that incidents like today’s computer system shutdowns because of a coding problem were likely to re-occur. He explained:
[This] highlights to a lot of organisations that technology is not a one-time purchase now, that it needs that continuous investment throughout its operational lifetime.
We’re in an era now of digital dependency, coupled with heightened cyber threat, coupled with increasing capability, which means all organisations are going to likely have to revisit their risk assumptions and work out how they are able to invest in technology to be able to meet the contemporary era.
Whitehouse said there were “no indications” that the PHP flaw now being fixed had been successfully exploited by hackers.
He also said that the problem that had led to 32 government websites being temporarily shut down (see 12.54pm) was originally identified months ago. He said the NCSC had been conducting a “coordinated disclosure process” to warn organisations of the vulnerability, until a leak meant that the process had to be accelerated.
A UK cyber security official has said that there are “no indications” that the PHP computer coding flaw, that has led to 32 government websites being taken down, has been successfully exploited by hackers. (See 4.46pm.)
MPs pay tribute to Diane Abbott as they debate black history month
MPs debated black history month earlier today. Politicians are often fairly unpleasant to their opponents, but there was a surprise moment near the start of the debate when Joy Morrissey, the Tory spokesperson for women and equalities (and not someone known for being particularly woke or leftwing), paid a moving tribute to the veteran Labour MP Diane Abbott. Morrissey said:
In 1987, the very same year black history month began here, a young woman from Paddington walked into the House of Commons as Britain’s first black female MP. Today, she is the mother of the House.
When she arrived, there were only 41 women in the entire Commons. She was told in a hundred ways that she didn’t belong. She stayed anyway.
For nearly four decades, she has represented the people of Hackney, championed black children in London schools, and chaired parliamentary groups on West Indian and sickle cell disease.
She has faced more abuse than almost any politician of her generation, and she has never stopped turning up.
You don’t have to share her political her politics to recognise what her presence meant. For millions of black Britons, especially black girls, she was proof that the doors of power could open and that someone who looked like them could walk through.
Florence Eshalomi, the communities minister, opened the debate, and she also paid tribute to Abbott. She said she remembered when Abbott was elected in 1987, along with Paul Boateng and Bernie Grant. They were the first black MPs. Eshalomi said:
I was just six years old when [Abbott] was elected, and I remember that quiet hope I felt in watching TV and seeing her in parliament to see that, yes, a black woman can have that voice and that we don’t have to stand by when decisions are made to us and not by us. That gave me the confidence to stand for public office as a local councillor in the borough where I grew up, and later for the London assembly.
Voters significantly more likely to back progressive coalition led by Burnham than Tory/Reform UK one, poll suggests
YouGov has published some interesting polling on what voters think about various coalition options. Here are some of the key points.
Voters are significantly more likely to support a progressive coalition than a rightwing coalition. The most popular coalition option polled was a Labour/Lib Dem one, with Andy Burnham as PM. Some 42% of people would support that. Other progressive options, with Burnham as PM, would get the support of more than a third of voters. But only a quarter of voters would back a Conservative/Reform UK coalition, with a Kemi Badenoch-led version only marginally more popular than a Nigel Farage-led one.
Conservative supporters would rather see the party go into coalition with the Liberal Democrats than with Reform UK. In its write-up, YouGov says:
Most current Conservative supporters would support either arrangement, though more are in favour of the party forming a coalition with the Lib Dems (68%) than Reform (60%), and with at least 28% opposed to either coalition. Lib Dem supporters do not return the favour, with 58% of those currently intending to vote for the party opposed to a repeat of the Cameron-Clegg government, although 36% are in favour.
This is interesting because, on immigration, Brexit, and the European convention on human rights, Badenoch has shifted her party to a position where its policies are near identical to Reform UK’s. Recently there have been signs she has started to steer back the other way.
Most Conservative supporters would not be in favour of a coalition with Reform UK, with Nigel Farage as PM, if the two parties combined could form a majority government. In December last year Conservative supporters (defined as people who voted Tory in 2024) were narrowly in favour of this option. They would still favour a Conservative-Reform UK coalition if Badenoch were PM, but by a narrower margin than last year. YouGov says:
Britons have become less inclined towards a Farage-led Reform-Tory coalition, with net support for such a government falling from -27 to -41 since last December. This includes 2024 Conservative voters going from being effectively divided on the question (+5) to being clearly opposed (-13).
Conservative voters have also become less receptive to a Badenoch-led Tory-Reform coalition, with net support falling 15 points since the end of last year to +23, even if those who voted Reform at the last election have become more open to the idea, with net support doubling to +22.
Fahnbulleh says ministers won't 'faff around' in getting rid of gas standing charges, implying decision coming in budget
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, has heightened speculation that a government announcement about getting rid of the standing charges on gas bills will come in the budget on Wednesday next week.
Andy Burnham implied this strongly yesterday when he said he had asked John Healey, the chancellor, and Fahnbulleh to look at this idea and to report back to MPs “at the earliest opportunity”. The “earliest opportunity” is Wednesday next week, because that will be the first time either of those two MPs gets to address the Commons.
Today, speaking to a press gallery lunch, Fahnbulleh confirmed that an announcement is likely very soon. She said Burnham had made it clear the government “can’t faff around”.
She explained:
I love working with him because Andy is very clear … in his mind about the sorts of things that he wants us to do, and he’s really impatient with change.
And so, if you ask the department, ‘Oh, you know, standing charge reform’, they’re like, ‘Oh, we’d have to consult. This is a 10-year proposition’. And Andy’s like, ‘I want you and John to look at it and come back with an answer’. So we’re looking at the options.
Fahnbulleh said getting rid of standing charges would be popular.
The thing I do know is that the public absolutely hates standing charges, and it’s a control question. People just find that really egregious, and their ability to manage their energy bills by deciding how much they want to use on their terms is essentially taken away from them. So, even shifting it into the unit rate gives people that agency.
She said modelling suggested the move could reduce the bills of “a big stack of low-income through to middle-income households”.
She went on:
There are some people that will be impacted negatively because they are essentially low-income, high users, and so you need to think about mitigations. But we’re looking at all the options.
But the thing that he is very clear on is we can’t faff around. We need to get on with this. So watch this space.
According to research by Nesta, a research foundation, 64% of households would benefit if the government got rid of the standing charge and instead loaded those costs onto the unit charge. But households using large amounts of gas would pay more.
Our analysis shows that, on its own, abolishing the gas standing charge would save the typical dual fuel household £27 per year, and that 64% of dual fuel households will be better off under this policy.
Because the distribution of gas consumption is skewed by a small number of (predominantly wealthy) households, the average and median household are quite a way apart. The threshold at which this policy would start to increase bills is around 12,400 kWh, but a majority of homes (64%) use less gas than this. This is why the typical household (using only 9,500 kWh of gas) would expect to save around £27 per year under this policy.
TDCV stands for typical domestic consumption values – a figure for how much gas and electricity an average household is using at any point.
Burnham has flu jab, as NHS encourages those eligible for free injection to get one
Andy Burnham has had his flu jab. He has posted about it on Instagram, and at the same time the Department of Health and Social Care is launching a publicity campaign to encourage people eligible for a free jab to get one.
James Frith, a health minister, said:
Vaccines save lives. It has never been easier to find out if you are eligible and get vaccinated, helping protect yourself and reduce pressure on the NHS during the winter season.
Eligibility is focused on those most vulnerable - from young children to older adults and people with long-term health conditions - so if you are eligible, please come forward this winter.
In England, most children under 17 are eligible for a free flu jab, as well as people over 65, people with some long-term health conditions, pregnant women, carers and people living in a care home, people living with someone with a weakened immune system, homeless people and frontline health and care workers.
The latest edition of the Guardian’s Politics Weekly UK podcast is out. It features Jessica Elgot and Alexandra Topping talking about whether or not the government will allow the Rosebank oilfield development to go ahead, after the less controversial Jackdaw gasfield was approved yesterday.
Starmer granted core participant status in grooming gangs inquiry
Keir Starmer may be summoned to give evidence at the grooming gangs inquiry, the Press Association reports. PA says:
The former prime minister, who ordered the probe last year, has been listed as a core participant for the inquiry’s hearings which are due to begin in December.
This means he is among people, groups and organisations formally granted special status by the chairwoman under public inquiry rules, giving him rights to participate in the investigation.
While this does not automatically mean he will be required to give evidence, many core participants are asked or compelled to do so.
Victims and their families, charities, whistleblowers, police chiefs and government departments are among those also listed as core participants.
The scandal-hit probe is looking at how grooming gangs operated in England and Wales and the actions of police, councils, health and social care services, schools and other public bodies.
An inquiry spokesman said the decision on core participant status “considers whether a person played, or may have played, a direct and significant role in relation to the matters to which the inquiry relates, whether they have a significant interest in an important aspect of the matters to which the inquiry relates, or whether the person may be subject to explicit or significant criticism during the inquiry proceedings or in the report, or in any interim report”, adding: “Nobody is beyond examination or transparency, and that the inquiry is following the evidence, wherever it leads.”
Starmer was prime minister when the grooming gangs inquiry was announced last year. But he was also director of public prosecutions from 2008 to 2013, at a time when the CPS was being accused of being too reluctant to prosecute in many cases of alleged child sexual abuse. As DPP, Starmer set out to change this – ordering prosecutors to be more sympathetic to victims, and less inclined to disbelieve them or to drop cases because victims might not make compelling witnesses.
According to Christopher Hope from GB News, Kemi Badenoch is unhappy about Andy Burnham going on Gogglebox (see 2.35pm) – but only because she wants an invite too! Hope says:
A political row has broken out over Andy Burnham’s decision to go on Channel 4’s programme ‘Gogglebox’. A Tory source tells me that Kemi Badenoch should be invited on to the show. One says: “It’s Channel 4’s job to ensure political balance.”

Ollie Whitehouse, chief technology officer at the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, told Radio 4’s the World at One that incidents like today’s computer system shutdowns because of a coding problem were likely to re-occur. He explained:
[This] highlights to a lot of organisations that technology is not a one-time purchase now, that it needs that continuous investment throughout its operational lifetime.
We’re in an era now of digital dependency, coupled with heightened cyber threat, coupled with increasing capability, which means all organisations are going to likely have to revisit their risk assumptions and work out how they are able to invest in technology to be able to meet the contemporary era.
Whitehouse said there were “no indications” that the PHP flaw now being fixed had been successfully exploited by hackers.
He also said that the problem that had led to 32 government websites being temporarily shut down (see 12.54pm) was originally identified months ago. He said the NCSC had been conducting a “coordinated disclosure process” to warn organisations of the vulnerability, until a leak meant that the process had to be accelerated.
Burnham to appear on Gogglebox with Steve Rotheram
Kemi Badenoch has been routinely complaining about Andy Burnham spending time on supposedly trivial things, like discussing how he makes his tea in a summer Q&A, or doing a social media video about pork scratchings. So God know what she is going to say when she finds out he’s on Gogglebox tomorrow night.
The PM will be appearing on the show tomorrow night for a Gogglebox for Stand Up To Cancer special. He will be on the sofa with his friend Steve Rotheram, the Liverpool city region mayor.
As Max Goldbart writes in an article for Deadline, there is some precedent for his appearance.
Seen as something of an everyman, Burnham will now get the chance to broadcast his thoughts on the week’s TV to millions. An Instagram reel teasing his appearance shows him offering crisps and beer to Rotheram.
Burnham is the first prime minister to appear on Gogglebox. Jeremy Corbyn, who was leader of the opposition at the time, came on the show a decade ago, while former PM Boris Johnson’s father Stanley Johnson appeared two years later.
“Nearly 7,000 miles of road resurfacing – the equivalent of travelling between London and Singapore – will be completed this year,” the Department for Transportis saying. It says councils in England are doing 10% more resurfacing than last year, because they are getting more government funding.
Mahmood condemned by Unison for refusing to let care worker attend private meeting about her 'nasty' proposed ILR changes
Andrea Egan, the Unison general secretary, has criticised Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, for not letting her bring a care worker to a meeting to discuss Mahmood’s plans to tighten the permanent residency rules for foreign workers.
Egan described the proposals as “nasty”, and said Mahmood’s failure to engage with people affected by the rules was “totally unacceptable”.
The Unison leader was commenting in a post on social media that referenced a story by Arj Singh for the i, which said talks between Mahmood and Unison “broke down after the home secretary refused to allow a migrant care worker to attend the meeting”. Singh said:
The meeting was cancelled by Unison after Mahmood refused Egan’s late request to bring a migrant care worker who will be affected by the “earned settlement” changes, The i Paper understands.
Mahmood is under pressure to water down her proposals, particularly those relating to care workers, and Unison, which represents many workers in the care sector, has campaigned particularly forcefully against the plan.
In her social media posts, Egan said:
Shabana Mahmood’s failure to engage properly with the migrant workers whose lives her nasty proposals will devastate is totally unacceptable.
These are brilliant, committed workers who hold our public services together. UNISON won’t tolerate them being attacked and ignored.
I’ve changed UNISON’s political approach to put members first. That includes taking members with me to government meetings.
Engaging directly with workers should be standard for Labour cabinet ministers, not something they run away from.
In his report, Singh says:
The care worker who Egan wanted to bring to the meeting has completed an NVQ level 3 and is set to do further qualifications so that he can develop his career in the sector, and was planning to tell Mahmood about why he and many other Unison members had chosen to work in the sector.
Singh quotes a Home Office source as saying that Egan had been invited to a private meeting with Mahmood and that it was Unison that chose to cancel it. The source also said that it would be wrong for Mahmood to prioritise the views of just one care worker when 200,000 responses to the government’s consultation were being considered.
In a social media post commenting on the same story, the Labour MP John McDonnell said:
The work visa issue is causing totally unnecessary division in the Labour Party at a time when the new leader is settling himself into the job. Listening to numerous workers employed on work visas in the care sector has been essential in gaining an understanding of what they face and the effect on our public services of the proposed rule changes. All Unison wanted was to ensure the home secretary had the opportunity to appreciate fully the concerns of the people who will be affected by her proposals. I urge her to think again on this decision not to meet.
32 UK government services offline while work carried out to sort out PHP programming flaw, minister says
Some 32 government services are offline and four are partially unavailable while work is carried out to address potential cybersecurity issues, a minister has said.
As the Press Association reports, organisations around the world have been scrambling to fix a critical security flaw in the programming language PHP used by the majority of websites.
Downing Street on Thursday said no large UK public-facing critical services have been affected, but some “limited” government websites have gone dark while issues are resolved. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) experts are working with OpenAI, whose technology was used to discover the vulnerabilities, and partners around the globe to address potential problems, a No 10 spokesperson said.
In the House of Lords, Liz Lloyd, the tech minister, said:
The information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable.
Lloyd said that “has largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied”.
The No 10 spokesperson told reporters:
Work has already taken place across government to identify and fix potential exposures to our systems, and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue.
Here is our story about the global impact of the problems identified in the PHP programming language. It’s by Robert Booth and Aisha Down.
Steve Witkoff wrong about Putin being a 'humanitarian', says No 10
Yesterday Steve Witkoff, the property developer appointed by Donald Trump as his lead foreign policy envoy, described Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian”. Andrew Roth has more about that here, in a piece pointing out that this is an extraordinary lie.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish secretary, was giving interviews this morning. Asked if he agreed with Witkoff’s description on LBC, he was reassuringly blunt. He replied:
No, we don’t.
We see him as somebody who illegally invaded Ukraine at the start of this conflict, who has been responsible for conduct by his government that included attempted assassinations on UK soil.
So we simply do not recognise the description of Vladimir Putin as a humanitarian.
In contrast, we are crystal clear that we stand foursquare behind Volodymyr Zelensky and the people of Ukraine in their battle for freedom.
At the No 10 lobby briefing, a No 10 spokesperson also argued that Witkoff had got it wrong. Asked about Witkoff’s comment, the spokesperson said:
We do not recognise that characterisation … Putin has killed thousands of people, Ukrainians and his own. He’s starving children and the elderly of heat and warmth and destroying critical national infrastructure.
Tories claim crime figures 'spiralling out of control' - and why the data doesn't back this up
The Conservative party seems to have missed the bit in the ONS report on the crime figures where it said “crime against individuals and households has generally decreased over the last 10 years”. (See 9.54am.) Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, has issued a statement saying:
Crime is spiralling out of control under Labour. Record numbers of sexual offences, knife crime and shop theft show what happens when criminals know they can get away with it. This is a direct consequence of Labour cutting police numbers by 2,000 and letting thousands of prisoners out of jail early.
The Tories justify this claim by looking at the ONS report and picking out all the worst bits (a technique not unfamiliar in the world of journalism). Their briefing highlights four figures in particular. Here is an extract.
Sexual offences have reached the highest level on record under Labour, with the police now logging around 600 of them every single day. Police in England and Wales recorded 218,994 sexual offences in the year to June 2026, the highest annual total since the series began in 2002-03 …
Police are recording more rapes of women than at any point since records began, at a rate of around 142 every day. There were 51,731 recorded rapes of women aged 16 or over in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2004-05 …
More people are being caught carrying knives and blades than at any point since records began. Police recorded 30,216 offences of possessing an article with a blade or point in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2008-09 …
Thefts and robberies from shops have reached a record high under Labour, with more than 1,500 recorded every single day. Police recorded 519,516 shoplifting offences and 31,089 robberies of business property in the year to June 2026, a combined 550,605 and the highest total since the series began in 2002-03.
But these claims are highly selective – to the point of being misleading.
On sexual offences, and rape, the ONS report points out that much of the increase over time is due to more offences being recorded, and not necessarily more of them taking place. It says “there has been a general increase in police recorded sexual offences over the last decade, largely because of improvements in police recording practices”. And it includes a specific warning about drawing the wrong conclusions from the figures.
Police recorded sexual offences are not a good indicator of trends over time. Improvements in police recording practices, the introduction of new offences, and increased reporting by victims have contributed to the level of offences in recent years.
On knives, while more people may be carrying them, the Tories have ignored the figures suggesting fewer criminals are actually using them. The ONS says:
Knife-enabled crime recorded by the police decreased by 6% in year ending (YE) June 2026 (to 48,615 offences), compared with YE June 2025 (51,567 offences). Levels remained 12% lower than YE March 2020 (55,170 offences).
And, on shoplifting, the Tories are again presenting the data in a misleading way. The ONS says:
Following a period of increases in shoplifting, there has been a 2% decrease (to 519,516 offences) in YE June 2026 when compared with the previous year (530,336 offences).
The Tories have justified their “record high” claim by combining the shoplifing figures with the figures for robberies from business properties. They describe this as “shop crime” – even though many business properties are not shops. And the ONS has a caveat about these figures too.
The number of robbery of personal property offences fell by 7% (to 57,193 offences) compared with the previous year, however, overall robbery increased by 10% (to 88,282 offences) mainly because of improvements to recording practices for robbery of business property.
And the ONS says, with shoplifting, more offences are also now being recorded than in the past.
Recent increases in police recorded shoplifting likely reflect both growth in offences and improved reporting resulting from closer engagement between police and retailers. Reporting rates for shoplifting are known to be very low and police are actively encouraging the reporting of all incidents and the submission of supporting evidence, such as CCTV, to strengthen intelligence, identify offenders, and link related offences.

article_title: Police should not be scared to wade in to stop wrongdoing, says Badenoch
article_content:
Police should not be scared to wade in to stop wrongdoing, says Badenoch
- Published
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised punishments for people who intervene to "do the right thing" in a speech at the Police Federation conference.
Telling delegates she was "not scared to wade in", she called for more support for members of the public as well as police officers who step in to stop wrongdoing.
Badenoch also criticised Labour for failing to send a minister to the conference for two years in a row.
The prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman rejected the claims, stating the police have the government's "full backing" and are benefitting from investment. The BBC has contacted the Home Office for comment on ministerial attendance at the police conference.
In a speech at the conference, Badenoch said: "Too often these days, we fail to recognise sacrifice and service.
"Whether it's hounding brave and elderly veterans through the courts, hounding police officers who try to do the right thing, or even ordinary members of the public who step in to help only to find that they're in trouble themselves.
"It's no wonder the people in this country are becoming too scared to wade in, too scared to do the right thing. Well, I am different. I am not scared to wade in, and I am not scared to back the police."
The Conservative leader listed police officers who have been killed in the line of duty, such as PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough who died in the Cleveland A66 crash, and PC Andrew Harper, killed investigating a quad bike theft.
She also attacked police being investigated following controversial cases, including the case of 24-year-old Chris Kaba, who was shot by Sgt Matthew Blake in 2022 after he tried to ram his way past police cars.
The police officer was put on trial for murder before being cleared, with Badenoch saying his "job was made harder because he didn't get the backing he deserved".
Badenoch also attacked Labour, saying: "I think it is telling that for two years in a row, the Labour Government has not sent anyone to address this conference – not the policing minister, not the Home Secretary.
"You are the ones who enforce the law. You are the ones who ensure there are consequences for bad behaviour. That's why, if we want law and order back in our country, back on our streets, we need to back the police."
Responding, the prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman said: "I would reject those claims.
"The police have the government's full backing and as you will have seen from various reports this morning, we are continuing to invest in our police and we are bringing forward reforms following the Bernard Hogan Howe report in due course."
The Home Office has been contacted for comment about ministerial attendance at the conference and whether the government is still planning to recruit 13,000 police officers.

article_title: Britain’s gas security needs reinforcement. Last-minute deals with Belgium are not a proper fix
article_content:
After the overdue approval of the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, here comes a reminder that Britain still imports almost 60% of its gas and the stuff has to come from somewhere. We’re now doing a deal with Belgium to ensure enough supply can flow through a connecting pipeline this winter should a “low-probability but high-impact stress event”, to quote the regulatory mouthful, occur.
To be fair, the arrangement to maintain capacity from Belgium is a belt-and-braces measure. The imagined events do sound genuinely stressful and may never happen. A critical piece of infrastructure, such as the two import terminals in Milford Haven to bring in liquefied natural gas (LNG) into Britain, would have to be out of action during a prolonged cold snap in which demand is very high.
Equally, though, the “high-impact” bit matters: we’re talking about having enough supplies to run gas-fired power stations at full pelt if necessary to keep the lights on. You don’t take chances.
In short, 10p a month will be added to bills to cover the cost of paying Interconnector Limited, the Belgian owner of the pipeline, to maintain the compressors needed to shove big volumes of gas to Britain in a hurry if required. Without the arrangement, the company had already warned it would cut capacity, in part because the big pipe was not used much in practice last year.
The first conclusion – the comforting one – is that the deal sounds like decent value for money. As insurance policies go, £1.19 a household a year is not much.
The second, however, is that risks to Britain’s gas security are plainly mounting. The Ofgem document describing the Belgian deal says it was “the only currently available intervention identified that both addresses the immediate security of supply position for winter 2026/27 and provides continuing security of supply benefits over the following four years”. It was Belgium, plus any future deal on the Dutch pipeline, or nothing.
Nor is the Belgian shuffle a cure-all. “The agreement does not remove the need for further measures led by government that are likely to be required to support security of supply and wider gas system resilience over the medium and longer term,” says Ofgem.
The government should take that line as a heavy hint to get a move on. Do we need more gas storage, more LNG terminals, or both? And post-Jackdaw, what’s a realistic appraisal of how much will be sourced from the North Sea?
It is now almost a year since an alarming report from the National Energy System Operator (Neso) warned of an “emerging risk to gas supply security” in 2030. The government promised to “do whatever it takes” to avert a crunch but one cannot say it has actually done much. An interim response to the Neso report came in August but no timetable was given for choosing what kit or arrangements were needed and by when. The final response isn’t due until next year.
Read the “winter outlook” report from National Gas, published on Friday, and a few points stand out. Yes, it’s good news that, with the help of the Belgian deal, this winter’s outlook is positive. But the company also says that, even as annual consumption drifts down slightly, the peaks for demand remain as high as ever, driven by the role of gas-fired power generation when renewables output is low.
Like Ofgem, National Gas says “continued progress on government plans to reform security of supply arrangements will be vital to address enduring challenges in the years ahead”. It is becoming a theme.
The obvious answer is more gas storage to address Britain’s skimpy current levels. That could mean Centrica’s Rough facility in North Sea (currently due to close next spring), the Bains development led by dCarbonX off the north-west coast of England (which may happen anyway), more on-shore salt caverns or any combination. Or, perhaps, German-style forward-buying deals on LNG.
But something has to happen soon. None of this infrastructure gets built quickly and that 2030 potential crunch is getting closer. Certainly, the government cannot agonise for as long as it did over Jackdaw. Eleventh-hour deals with Belgium are not a permanent fix for Britain’s gas security headache.

article_title: UK plans emergency powers to protect undersea cables
article_content:
UK plans emergency powers to protect undersea cables
- Published
The government has outlined new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables amid increased fears of Russian interference.
Ministers are set to gain powers to order telecom companies to remove or disable services during national security emergencies, as well as granting officials access to sites including cable landing stations.
The government has also outlined plans for stronger criminal penalties for those convicted of tampering with either undersea internet cables or energy pipelines.
The new powers would be backed up with prison sentences of up to 14 years for intentional conduct, 10 years for reckless conduct and two years for grossly negligent conduct, alongside unlimited fines.
It comes amid growing fears of suspicious activity in UK waters, and concerns that legal powers over the network have not kept pace with its growing importance to national security.
An extensive network of undersea cables and pipelines owned and operated primarily by the private sector are thought to carry almost all the UK's international data traffic and three-quarters of its gas supplies.
The growing importance of undersea infrastructure prompted a parliamentary report last year, external to warn of security vulnerabilities in areas including transport and supply chains, financial services and payment systems.
The UK and its Nato allies are concerned about the risk Russia poses to offshore infrastructure.
In April, the government accused Russian submarines of conducting a covert operation over cables and pipelines in waters north of the UK.
The UK has also accused Russia of mapping undersea infrastructure using spy ships. Last year, it revealed the Royal Navy had tracked one such suspected ship, the Yantar, after it passed near UK waters.
Russia has denied the claims, and accused the UK of stirring up tensions through "anti-Russian alarmism".
In a policy paper on Thursday, the government said it currently lacked emergency powers to deal with incidents affecting undersea infrastructure.
It added there were currently no equivalent powers to measures that allow intervention in the water and air traffic sectors, whilst broader powers for national emergencies could prove too slow to exercise during a crisis.
It is now proposing new powers that would allow it to force telecoms companies to hand over information or modify or disable services in connection with specific threats or incidents.
The changes will require new legislation, to be set out after a consultation with industry closing in January.
Companies that refused to comply with the orders could be fined up to £17m or 10% of global turnover. The orders would typically be published, but could be made secret on national security grounds, it added.
The proposed powers are not intended to apply to companies operating energy infrastructure, although the document added that new powers in this area were being considered separately.
Ministers said they hoped the new powers would apply across the "full extent" of undersea services, including outside the UK's territorial waters, which extend up to 12 nautical miles from the coast.
However, the document concedes this is likely to require co-ordination with other countries, adding that the government was considering how its proposals compare to equivalent regimes internationally.
It was also uncertain that existing laws on undersea infrastructure, dating from the Victorian period and designed for telegraphic cables, could be used for breaches of modern fibre-optic cables, the document added.

article_title: Imagine if, for once, Labour decided to tell the truth about immigration | Gaby Hinsliff
article_content:
My mum’s carer was uncharacteristically late one morning. She didn’t want to say why at first, but it turned out she’d found her previous client – an elderly lady living all alone, with no family to visit – collapsed on the floor, barely alive. It was a lot to cope with for someone only in their early 20s, a reminder of the heavy responsibility this job carries. Watching the carers who helped both my parents in their respective final weeks taught me that while the work itself might seem mundane, the emotional and social skills needed to do it well – to coax some sense out of the confused, to jolly along the lonely, and to soothe the dying, to walk in and out of unfamiliar houses all day long without quite knowing what you might find – are anything but.
Yet like so many jobs predominantly done by women, care has long been relentlessly undervalued. That means lousy pay, little public recognition, and now – at least for the disproportionately large chunk of this workforce who are migrant workers – the disorientating realisation that the government can snap its fingers and all your life plans are upended overnight.
Under the latest attempt by the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, to ratchet immigration numbers ever further down, “low-skilled” foreign workers will now have to wait up to 15 years for the right to become permanent residents. The new rules would be backdated to 2021 to catch what the right dubbed the “Boriswave”, that unexpected surge of workers who came to Britain in the Boris Johnson years – many on health and care visas – and would under the old five-year rule have started qualifying for settlement in 2027. What has unsettled some of Mahmood’s own cabinet colleagues is the sense of the state reneging on what was understood to be the deal when those workers came here. Having to be continuously employed for 15 years instead of five without a break means in practice that some will have to leave, while others will live in mortal fear of losing a job. A growing cabinet revolt against Mahmood’s reforms is now becoming the first real challenge to Andy Burnham’s authority as prime minister, but also more broadly a test of where he really stands on immigration.
This month’s budget throws a problem that governments have been trying to ignore for a decade into sharp relief: kneejerk hostility to foreign workers is costing Britain dear, and not just because public services would fall apart without them. Last month, the Institute for Fiscal Studies warned that falling immigration would inevitably mean falling tax revenues, shrinking John Healey’s headroom at the budget by about £4bn. So much for the rightwing myth that migrants are a drain on their host country: if anything, they’ve been bailing Britain out.
It’s not just taxes, either. Immigrants pay a surcharge on top for the right to use the NHS if needed while they’re here, which is now raising £2.5bn a year, according to new research from the Nuffield Trust. It seems all those pesky liberals who argued that migrants are generally healthier than the average Briton – and therefore less likely to need a GP – were right after all: the trust estimates that migrants are on average paying in 60% more in surcharge per year than they take out in healthcare services, a handy little revenue stream that for some reason we never talk about. But immigration crackdowns threaten that income too. The trust notes that falling immigration can lead to “a sharp drop in income” for the NHS, much as slashing foreign student visas has hurt universities that were reliant on their fees.
As the Office for Budget Responsibility spelled out in 2024 – when it calculated that the surge of immigration under Johnson that so offended Tory voters at the time would help knock more than £7bn off projected government borrowing by 2028-29 – economically speaking, immigration is basically good news. If the country really wants it to fall, then something else – higher taxes, lower spending or more borrowing – is going to have to plug the resulting hole in the finances. Yet for years now, successive governments, fearful of confronting leave voters, have tried manfully to pretend that that choice does not exist.
Mahmood’s plan is essentially yet another attempt to square the same old circle, gearing the system around letting in as few people as possible – in keeping with what a furious public has for the last decade seemed to want – while trying to cherrypick those most likely to make an outsize economic contribution. Under her reforms, the highest paid workers (who are likely to pay lots of tax over their lifetimes) would be fast-tracked to settlement, while those judged more likely to be an economic burden on the state overall would be pushed away. What she doesn’t seem to have bargained for, aside from the fact that the rest of the world is in hot competition for high-skilled migrants, is the sense of deep disquiet that engenders. As the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, has pointed out, endlessly prolonging settlement risks undermining social cohesion. A country that makes very clear its foreign workers are here at best on sufferance, even if they do hold lives in their hands at work every day, does nothing to encourage them to integrate and put down roots.
The logic of Burnham’s announcement that a future Labour government might consider rejoining the EU, meanwhile, leaves Mahmood’s reforms looking strangely like the relics of a bygone era. If rejoining the single market or customs union would inevitably mean accepting freedom of movement again, what’s the point?
The truth is that grimly ratcheting immigration down to next to nothing has come at extraordinary fiscal and social cost, and if the aim was to destroy Reform’s raison d’etre then it hasn’t worked. The mainstream right has switched seamlessly from the pre-Brexit days of complaining that Polish plumbers were taking Britons’ jobs, to a much darker post-Brexit stage of painting migrants as rapists and criminals. The far right, meanwhile, has simply moved on from cheerleading for deportations to insisting that even people who were born here aren’t English unless they’re white.
Legal migrant numbers are at a historic low and small boat crossings have halved, yet that didn’t stop anger at asylum seekers spilling on to the streets again this summer. There is no level of migration low enough to satisfy some people. There is, however, very much a level of migration low enough to make us all even poorer, and the angry somehow even angrier. And right now, we’re living with it.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

article_title: Tank barrel production returns to UK after 20 years
article_content:
Tank barrel production returns to UK after 20 years
- Published
The production of gun barrels to be used on tanks has returned to the UK for the first time in 20 years with the opening of a new manufacturing facility.
The UK Gun Hall in Telford, run by German defence firm Rheinmetall, has supported 100 jobs and will make barrels and breaches for large calibre weapons.
Defence secretary, Wes Streeting, attended the opening ceremony on Thursday and said Britain was "back in the business of making weapons" for its armed forces.
"From an empty site to full production in eight months, this is rapid reindustrialisation in action," he said.
"One hundred skilled jobs in world class manufacturing and the return of large calibre weapon production to UK soil for the first time in 20 years - this is what defence as an engine for growth looks like," Streeting added.
The barrels and breaches will be made for both 120m and 155mm weapon systems, including for the RCH 155 and future artillery platforms, according to Rheinmetall.
The firm is already involved in the UK's Boxer combat vehicle programme and is upgrading the country's Challenger tanks.
Specialist workers from Telford have been recruited and the firm said it would expand its workforce as production ramped up.
Ahead of the factory's opening, staff spent time at a Rheinmetall facility in Germany where they were trained in precision manufacturing, quality assurance and specialist weapon production.
Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall, said the gun hall was an "important milestone" that would strengthen the country's industrial base "for decades to come".
"We are committed to investing in the UK for the long term, expanding our industrial footprint and working together to deliver the capabilities needed for the future," he added.
'Statement of intent'
Papperger told BBC Radio Shropshire it was a significant investment in Telford, adding that the firm only had one similar production line in Germany.
"At the moment, we have a lot of orders and we need the capacity. Telford has very well-educated people, highly-motivated people," he added.
Papperger said the company currently had 1,300 employees in the UK but was looking to build up that number.
During his speech at the event, Streeting described Telford as being "synonymous with engineering and manufacturing".
"Today is a vote of confidence in our country," he continued, "a statement of intent on our mission to reindustrialise Britain and create good, well-paid jobs across our country."

article_title: The Guardian view on AI safety: the push for global regulation must advance | Editorial
article_content:
Organisations around the world scrambled on Thursday to fix critical flaws in PHP, the software that powers much of the web. The vulnerabilities could allow attackers to take control of affected servers. Some websites were taken offline as a precaution while fixes were installed. The paradox is that while AI helped researchers uncover the flaw, it also threatens to accelerate the ability to exploit it. Amazon said that it had detected an attempt before the public disclosure of the PHP flaws.
What the episode highlights is AI’s central role in security – and not always for the right reasons. OpenAI’s models have also been responsible for two alarming hacks this year – a security breach of an Australian health department website and a raid by a swarm of AI bots on Hugging Face, an AI services platform. Citing those incidents, the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, warned that a similar cyber-attack on the UK is “likely, if not inevitable”.
Britain is not uniquely vulnerable. In some respects it is more advanced than many countries in grasping the scale of the challenge. The London-based AI Security Institute is internationally recognised as an authority in a rapidly evolving field. A cybersecurity bill to protect critical digital infrastructure is going through parliament.
As Mr Narayan concedes, national governments face limits in protecting their citizens from a global threat. Having Donald Trump in the White House makes the international challenge harder. The US president has rejected calls for international negotiations on AI regulation. He is even dismissive when the bosses of US technology companies recognise the need for external monitoring and ask for statutory guardrails on their own activities.
Mr Trump takes the view that America’s lead at the most advanced frontier of AI is a national strategic asset that would be compromised if other nations, and China in particular, were allowed to set the pace of advancement. In the president’s eyes it is a race for global supremacy and only losers urge caution. “Whoever wins AI, wins,” he has said. That is a disturbingly reckless approach to technology that, in some of the more apocalyptic prognoses, has the potential to destroy humankind. Even in more circumspect scenarios, the risk of some catastrophic incident or severe economic shock caused by the malicious or accidental use of AI is growing at a rate that more responsible leaders than Mr Trump cannot afford to ignore.
Andy Burnham has said that he intends to put AI at the top of the agenda when the UK holds the G20 presidency for the first half of next year. In his speech at the Labour party conference earlier this month, the prime minister compared his role to the global leadership position that Gordon Brown took on as the chair of the G20 in early 2009, coordinating a response to the financial crisis.
But the world looks very different in 2026. Mr Burnham’s convening power will not move a US administration that treats historic allies and multilateral institutions with contempt. That is not a reason to abandon the ambition. The drive to build some global regulatory architecture has to advance. If Mr Trump cannot be moved by care for humanity, this week’s PHP emergency should remind him that America’s technological lead offers no protection from disruption. Shielding US citizens and businesses from such turmoil requires international cooperation that a race for AI supremacy puts at risk.
