article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family
article_content:
Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family
- Published
Tougher punishments for offenders who refuse to attend their sentencings will "rebalance the power" in the justice system, the aunt of murder victim Zara Aleena has said.
From next year, prisoners could be blocked from prison visits and confined to their cells for weeks on end if they do not follow orders to go to court.
This builds on an existing law that orders criminals to attend sentencing or face being fined or jailed for another two years.
"A year or two added to a life sentence wouldn't make any difference to an offender. But taking away these privileges would," Farah Naz said.
Naz said the refusal of the man who murdered her niece to go to his sentencing "left a sense that justice was not quite complete".
Aleena, an aspiring lawyer, was murdered by Jordan McSweeney as she walked home from an east London bar in June 2022.
McSweeney remained in his cell when he was sentenced to life in prison at the Old Bailey later that year.
He was jailed for at least 38 years, which was later reduced to 33 years after he won a Court of Appeal challenge.
Naz said Zara's Aleena's family had hoped that by reading their victim impact statement in front of her murderer, he would see "the consequence of his actions, of what he'd done, the devastation that he had caused".
She added that the new measures would "bring accountability and rebalance the power in the justice system from offender to victim."
Offenders who refuse to attend sentencing can already face a fine or up to two years additional imprisonment for contempt of court.
But the Ministry of Justice has acknowledged that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter those already behind bars.
The new measures mean offenders could be confined to cells for up to three weeks, while social visits could be banned for 27 days and other prison privileges revoked for longer.
Judges will also be able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for a period of almost three months.
For criminals aged 18-20, similar restrictions could be handed down, but for shorter periods of time, the Ministry of Justice said.
However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions.
"Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice," Prisons Minister Catherine McKinnell said.
"Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences," she added.
But Pia Sinha, the CEO of Prison Reform Trust, has called for evidence that sanctions will increase attendance and warned the measures will punish relatives of prisoners who "have committed no offence themselves".
The families of murdered primary school teacher Sabina Nessa and mother-of-three Jan Mustafa joined Zara Aleena's family in campaigning for changes to the laws.
All of their loved ones' killers did not attend their sentencing hearings.
Thomas Cashman, the gunman who murdered nine-year-old Olivia Pratt-Korbel, and triple crossbow and knife killer Kyle Clifford, also refused to face their punishment in court.
Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman, said the announcement followed "tireless efforts of victims' families" not accepting offenders simply "opting out of facing justice".
She said it was "essential" the powers were used "consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve".

article_title: The Guardian view on England's north-south divide: Burnham must deliver more than devolution | Editorial
article_content:
Andy Burnham’s call to abandon “40 years of neoliberalism” rests partly on the damage that he says it has done to northern England. A new study – published in the Lancet this week – adds weight to his argument. It found that for adults aged 25 to 49, death rates in the north were 13% higher than in the south in 1981. By 2024, that gap had more than tripled to 42%. What happened in the four decades that left younger adults in northern England with so much worse chances of survival?
The answer lies in the lives and jobs that people have, and the homes they can afford, as well as the state of the public services, like the NHS, that they rely on. Deindustrialisation stripped secure employment from many communities in the north of England – as it did in Scotland and Wales. Austerity then weakened support systems. These reasons also underscore Mr Burnham’s analysis that Britain’s economic model and concentration of power in London have failed its regions.
The question for the budget is what will it do about these inequalities. The north has substantial levels of deprivation, lower rates of pay and fewer healthy years of life for its people. Among people under 75, the Lancet study found that mortality in northern England was 26% higher than in the south. To close these gaps means helping poorer households with the rising cost of essentials and sending more resources to deprived areas. Investment in, say, early years education and council budgets would help to deal with the social conditions underlying ill health.
Reducing regional inequalities requires redistribution – not just devolution alone. Giving a poorer area more control over an inadequate budget does not increase the cash it can spend. Mr Burnham’s idea to let mayors retain locally raised taxes may help. But without a way to ensure each region gets enough resources to meet their needs, such a policy might simply preserve existing disparities. Researchers at Manchester and Liverpool universities and Health Equity North divided England into two roughly equal populations along a line from the Wash to the Severn Estuary. Closing the north’s health gap, they claim, could add £18bn a year to its economy.
Regional policy plays a complementary role to redistribution by aiming to change where wealth is produced. However, in a recent paper, Steve Fothergill of the Industrial Communities Alliance warned that “the UK has moved away from a long‑established framework that explicitly sought to promote jobs and growth in its less prosperous places … the UK now deploys a weaker set of tools for regional economic development than at any point since the mid-twentieth century”. Mr Burnham needs to reverse this trend.
The chancellor, John Healey, says that he wants a budget for “bloody-minded entrepreneurs”. But a richer northern England would not necessarily be a healthy or more equal one. During the 19th century, when Manchester became known as “Cottonopolis”, Friedrich Engels – bemoaning the city’s “disgraceful unhealthy slums” – was shocked to be told by a local businessman: “And yet there is a great deal of money to be made here.” Bringing investment and good jobs to economically weaker regions matters. But whether the resulting prosperity translates into secure incomes, decent homes, good public services and longer lives is just as important. Mr Burnham’s ambition needs to meet twin challenges: where wealth is created and what life it lets people enjoy.

article_title: Four London councils challenge funding reforms
article_content:
Four London councils challenge funding reforms
- Published
Four London council leaders have formally submitted a challenge to government reforms that are set to see their central funding slashed by up to 58%.
The leaders of Wandsworth, Richmond, Westminster and Kensington and Chelsea councils delivered revised funding proposals to the Treasury on Thursday urging the government to rethink its overhaul of local authority funding rules.
Among those councils, the leaders said the reforms would result in funding cuts ranging from 40% to 58% by 2029.
The government said the "outdated" local authority funding model was being reformed to ensure "money goes where it is most needed".
'Every route available'
The changes, known as the Fair Funding Review 2.0, aim to shift more cash towards areas with higher deprivation.
Wandsworth's Conservative administration said the reforms would cut funding by 40% and force it to slash services and raise council tax.
The authority is proposing to raise council tax by 94% from April, in addition to making sweeping cuts – including shutting its cost-of-living reserve with £6.2m of unspent funds, replacing Labour's Access for All with a much smaller concessionary scheme, cancelling its Borough of Sanctuary status and suspending voluntary sector grants for four years.
Kensington and Chelsea is set to lose £108m, or more than 40% of its central funding over the next four years under the reforms, while Westminster is due to see these resources drop by around £100m (46%). Richmond is set to be stripped of £26m (58%) of its core funding.
The councils have now formally submitted their revised funding proposals, under the Sustainable Communities Act, asking the government to reconsider its decision.
Wandsworth Council leader Robert Morritt, who heads a Conservative minority administration, said: "Residents should not have to pick up the bill for changes imposed by Whitehall. This proposal takes our case directly to government.
"We are using every route available to fight for a fairer deal and protect Wandsworth taxpayers."

Lib Dem Richmond council leader Gareth Roberts said the cuts risked "pushing this council towards a financial cliff edge".
He said: "We will not stand by while Whitehall forces our residents to pay the price for a deeply flawed formula."
Tory Kensington and Chelsea council leader Elizabeth Campbell said: "I will use every tool at my disposal to fight these cuts, stand up for our residents and secure the fair deal our borough deserves."
A Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government spokesperson previously said: "We have consulted extensively on reforming the outdated council funding system to ensure money goes where it is most needed, following on from a longstanding consensus.
"We're also protecting councils through transitional arrangements so no area faces a cliff edge."

article_title: Council vows support for Toxic Town public inquiry
article_content:
Council vows support for Toxic Town public inquiry
- Published
A council leader says he will support a public inquiry into contaminated land in a town, following a report published last week that revealed it could pose a risk to human health.
The charity Earthwatch Europe says trained citizen scientists have found potentially harmful levels of metal or metalloid at 52 freshwater sites across Corby.
Children in Corby have been born with birth defects, believed to have been caused when steelworks were demolished in the 1980s.
As first reported in the NN Journal, Martin Griffiths, Reform UK leader of North Northamptonshire Council said: "We have nothing to hide."
He added: "We would welcome a genuinely independent examination of the historic events and the questions that remain unanswered, and we would cooperate fully with any inquiry established by the government."
Griffiths challenged the Labour MP for Corby and East Northamptonshire, Lee Barron, to take his longstanding calls for a public inquiry directly to the Labour government.
In response, Barron said it was "baffling" the council would ask for a public inquiry.
He said the authority needed to immediately publish a plan to investigate and clean up any contaminated land.
Barron said: "It is important that North Northamptonshire Council investigates the [Earthwatch] report.
"People deserve answers and it is the role of the council to provide them."
Earlier this week, Barron wrote to both the leader of North Northamptonshire Council and the Health Secretary Yvette Cooper.
In his letters, seen by the BBC, he said the findings from the environmental charity "need to be investigated as a matter of urgency".
He has also called on the health secretary to "ensure North Northamptonshire Council take immediate action to clean up any contaminated land".
Earlier this year, a number of families gathered outside North Northamptonshire's Corby headquarters calling for a public inquiry to clarify the situation.
Des Collins, the solicitor who represented families affected by the town's toxic waste scandal, said: "We welcome the leader's announcement, which finally admits what we have been telling his council for the past year - our clients need, and deserve, a public inquiry as it is the only feasible way of getting to the truth behind the disposal of toxic waste around Corby."
He urged Barron and the council to push for an inquiry with the Cabinet Office.
"Quite literally, local lives depend on it," said Collins.
A spokesperson from the Department of Health and Social Care said: "The government is aware of this issue, and the relevant agencies are monitoring the situation closely to keep the public safe.
"The UK Health Security Agency will continue to provide the necessary support to local authorities, and the Environment Agency will keep the situation under review and will determine whether further action is required."

article_title: We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the plan | Andy Burnham
article_content:
On Wednesday, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, gave the go-ahead for gas production to begin at the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. This has been the subject of fierce debate for many years, with strong views on both sides. I want to explain what the decision means and how it fits with Britain’s climate commitments.
At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home. Gas from this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter. In the longer term, it will significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK’s energy supply for more than a decade. Wednesday’s decision will also protect hundreds of jobs in Scotland and add almost £3bn to the UK economy over the lifetime of the project.
There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering. The simple truth is that even as we pursue our ambitious target of net zero by 2050, we will need oil and gas for years to come as a bridge to that clean-energy future. And imported gas has a higher carbon footprint than gas produced at home. The transition to net zero is a process, not a moment. I want Britain to make that transition on our terms: reducing our dependence on foreign fossil fuels, supporting good jobs and growing our economy so we can help people with the cost of living.
I know this news will be warmly welcomed in Aberdeen and by oil and gas workers across Scotland. Their jobs support families, businesses and entire communities. Yet, like many others, their industry has suffered from deindustrialisation, with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives. Our oil and gas workers have powered our nation for decades, and they will continue to play a key role for decades to come. Last week, I promised the Scottish people that we would reindustrialise their nation. I believe the transition to clean energy represents the best chance we will ever get of making that happen. I am determined to ensure that the next generation of energy jobs is created across Scotland and all nations of the UK.
That is why, alongside the decision on Jackdaw, we are establishing an energy wealth fund – something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago. It will begin with an initial £2bn and allow us to convert future North Sea oil and gas tax revenues into clean-energy programmes across the country. This investment in renewable energy will enable us to substantially delink gas and electricity prices by the end of this parliament and bring down bills in the long term.
This government is taking a pragmatic approach that supports our oil and gas industry today, while driving the growth of the clean-energy industries of tomorrow. We are also making a sustained effort to bring energy costs down over the next decade and in line with those of our European neighbours. I know, however, that people need breathing space right now. I will do everything I can to ease the pressure on household budgets in the short term. One of my first acts as prime minister was to remove VAT from electricity bills, and households have seen that reduction in their bills this month. I have now asked the chancellor and the energy secretary to look at removing standing charges from gas bills at the earliest opportunity.
I will ensure the government continues to take action to reduce both gas bills and electricity bills as part of our fundamental changes to the energy system.
The manifesto on which Labour was elected committed us to issuing no new oil or gas licences to explore new fields in the North Sea and to reaching net zero by 2050. I stand by both promises. Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus drivers working in intolerable conditions and families losing everything to wildfires. More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations.
There are two ways we can transition to clean energy. One way, the traditional Whitehall way, is to make people carry the burden of change while others take the rewards. The other is to make the transition work for people by creating good jobs, backing British industry, keeping bills as low as possible, strengthening our energy security and giving communities a greater say over their future. This government chooses the second path.
I want Britain to believe in itself again. We can have secure energy, strong industries and a cleaner future. And we can make net zero mean jobs, opportunity and prosperity. That is how we bring back hope.
- 
  Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

article_title: Ten councillors quit after leader's fraud conviction
article_content:
Ten councillors quit after leader's fraud conviction
- Published
Ten Ashfield Independent councillors have quit the party this week following the former leader's fraud conviction.
Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion last month
He resigned as leader of Ashfield District Council the following day, but was later given a seat on the authority's planning committee.
As of Thursday, 13 councillors are sitting as non-aligned independents, while 18 Ashfield Independents remain, meaning the party is one councillor away from losing its majority.
Zadrozny was accused of setting up a fake heritage group to defraud Nottinghamshire County Council out of thousands of pounds.
Prosecutors also alleged that he had failed to pay tax on four rental properties.
The 46-year-old, who served as an Ashfield Independents councillor on the county council, was told by the judge he would be sentenced on 27 November, and was "at risk of an immediate custodial sentence".
Councillors Warren Nuttall and Kier Barsby had quit the Ashfield Independents group prior to this week.
One of the 10 members to quit this week is John Wilmott, a cabinet member who is also a Nottinghamshire county councillor for Hucknall North.
Another is the chairman of the council, Dale Grounds.
Councillor Matt Relf, executive lead member for growth, regeneration and local planning, said quitting the party was an "enormously upsetting" decision.
"The understandable controversy around Jason's conviction and the choices he made that led to that have upset and surprised a lot of people in the group," he said.
"With the election of a new leader we hoped that would put everything behind us, but unfortunately the decision to appoint Jason back on to the planning committee was just a step too far.
"That decision was made with no consultation with the broader group.
"To stay true to our principles of integrity and democratic accountability I was left with no option but to leave, and I think others have reached the same conclusion."
Hucknall Central councillor Lee Waters, who was another one of the councillors to quit this week, said his decision "follows a period of reflection, and I believe the time is right to move on".
"Throughout my time as a councillor, my priority has been to listen to residents, address their concerns and work hard on the issues that matter to our community. That remains unchanged," he added.
"I will continue carrying out my council responsibilities and dealing with ongoing casework with the same commitment and dedication as always."
Lee Anderson, the MP for Ashfield, posted on Facebook to warn that former Ashfield Independent councillors would not be accepted into Reform UK.
He said there would be "no deals" between the parties.
Samantha Deakin has taken over as leader of the council, but has so far declined the BBC's request for an interview.
A demonstration was held outside the council house on Thursday in protest at Zadrozny being able to remain as a council.
Protesters told the BBC they had been "let down" by the authority.
John Green, of the Ashfield Community Action Group, said: "We are disgusted that the Ashfield Independents have voted a convicted fraudster onto the planning a committee."
Tim Curtis, who also attended the demonstration, said: "There's no mechanism to get him out. He should stand down from the council and not be anywhere near making any decisions."
Fiona Fillingham, a local business owner, added: "If I got done for fraud I am sure I wouldn't get my job back.
"It seems backhanded, shoddy, unfair and unrealistic. They can't keep getting away with it."

article_title: MI5 spied on NHS founder Nye Bevan for more than 20 years, newly released files show
article_content:
MI5 spied on NHS founder Nye Bevan for more than 20 years, newly released files show
- Published
NHS founder Aneurin "Nye" Bevan was spied on by MI5 for more than 20 years, according to newly released files.
Papers given to the National Archives show he first came to the attention of the Security Service in the 1930s when he was considered a firebrand left-winger linked to prominent communists.
Monitoring continued after Bevan, from Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent, became a minister in the post-war Labour government when he drove through the creation of the NHS in the face of opposition from doctors.
At one stage the-then MI5 director general became so concerned about his links to a Russian spy that he went to see Prime Minister Clement Attlee in No 10 to warn him.
But some in the service questioned why it was taking an interest in him, given everything he did was in the open.
After his death in 1960, one MI5 officer called the content of the file "remarkably tame".
The papers show MI5 first opened a file on Bevan when he was backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in 1933.
One of the first reports included an account of an anti-Nazi rally in Montreal, Canada, which Bevan addressed in 1934.
"Bevan has inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the Communist cause," it said.
In 1943, Roger Hollis, future director general, summarised what they knew of Bevan's activities.
In 1933 he said the MP had been "in close touch" with Communist Party of Great Britain general secretary Harry Pollitt and party members who backed his plan to organise "workers' freedom groups" to defend against "capitalists".
Although there was nothing in the files to indicate MI5 tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, some wondered why they were watching him at all.
"I do not think that Bevan's activities are a matter in which we, the security service, should be involved," one officer wrote in 1943.
"In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently."
The reporting continued after the war when Bevan was made health minister in Attlee's government.
In 1949 MI5 became increasingly concerned about Bevan's friendship with Wilfred Macartney, "an unsavoury, unscrupulous character" convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.
Recordings of conversations suggested he was passing information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt.
That May the Security Service's chief Sir Percy Sillitoe took evidence to Attlee, who dismissed Macartney's claims as a "tissue of lies" but agreed to warn Bevan about him.
One of the final reports dates from 1954 when Bevan, now back in opposition, was invited to meet the Soviet ambassador, Yakov Malik, at London's Polish embassy.
The event "went off very badly", partly because the Russian had difficulty in understanding Bevan's accent, which led to misunderstanding.
"The party broke up in a none too friendly atmosphere," the report said.
The file was not closed until 1975 - 15 years after Bevan died.

article_title: Youth mobility scheme may be delayed to ensure success of UK-EU summit
article_content:
A deadline for a youth mobility scheme between the EU and the UK could be deferred by six months in a bid to ensure Andy Burnham has a successful “reset” summit on 20 November, diplomats have said.
EU ambassadors in Brussels on Wednesday heard that the UK was still insisting on international tuition fees, quotas and an NHS surcharge for EU students. This has fuelled fears the summit could fail, just as the prime minister is promising to unveil a new vision for Britain’s long-term relationship with the EU.
Sources say the UK also continues to push for a cap of about 50,000 a year on the numbers of EU citizens allowed in the country for work, travel or study under the mooted youth experience scheme (YES) visas. Some EU member states want the cap much higher, at up to 500,000. Others want no cap at all.
The UK is also insisting that any YES visa holders pay the £1,035 NHS surcharge to cover potential doctor or hospital visits, although it is understood that a 25% discount has been suggested.
Negotiations on two other issues – a food and drink trade deal and the emissions trading system – are almost complete but views on the youth mobility scheme remain divided.
Sources say there is near-agreement on demands from the National Farmers’ Union that crops grown using fungicides yet to be approved in the EU could be sold in the bloc under a transition arrangement in the sanitary and phyto-sanitary agreement.
“A lot of member states were in favour of keeping the trio of issues together and not breaking the agenda up, but there are others that think it is acceptable to decouple them and there is no agreement yet on which approach to take,” said one diplomat.
But the reciprocal youth experience scheme designed to allow under-30s from both sides to work, travel or study in each other’s countries remains deadlocked.
Talks on a fourth issue, in relation to the reintegration of the UK into the EU’s energy market, will also, as expected, continue after 20 November. More time is needed to resolve significant barriers that have emerged, such as state aid and oversight frameworks, including a role for the European court of justice.
Tuition fees remains the thorniest problem, with UK universities putting pressure on the Labour government to maintain full international student fees for EU citizens – which can run to £69,190 a year at Oxford.
One diplomat said there was an “emerging consensus” at the meeting in Brussels around a European Commission proposal to take tuition fees out of the package altogether, with wording in a joint statement on 20 November committing both sides to negotiating a solution by May 2027.
It was thought that the landing zone was somewhere between home fees of £9,790 and the average international fees, but universities outside the elite 24-strong Russell Group have told the UK government they cannot afford to drop fees for EU citizens.
According to several diplomats, the bloc is still divided on whether to remove tuition fees from the table. There are also divisions over how a cap on numbers would work amid fears in the UK that voters – particularly in “red wall” constituencies – would see it as opening the gates to workers coming from economically less wealthy countries such as Bulgaria.
A proposal to cap the figures per country has been suggested, although how that would work in practice has not been detailed.
Some countries such as France are still arguing for an “all or nothing” approach, with all three topics on the table, arguing if the UK cannot agree tuition fees now, 17 months since the last EU-UK summit, “why would they do so in six months?”.
Others say with pressure to move on from three “significant but modest” issues to the bigger issues of deeper economic, security and defence ties, they cannot risk a failure on 20 November.
“YES is politically, emotionally and diplomatically very important. But if we can get an agreement at the summit by removing one element from the agenda it is a price worth paying,” said one diplomat.

article_title: Revealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regime
article_content:
Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic.
Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer and donated £50,000 to Farage to cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum.
He has said he is moving his tax residency from Switzerland to the UK in order to make “regular payments” of more than “one or two million” to the party.
The 61-year-old Iranian-born British businessman, who says he runs a $10bn (£7bn) fund called HP Trust, has declined to give details about how his family made its money beyond saying the fund owns assets in Europe and North America.
Now, a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardian sheds some light on Ghandehari’s past dealings with Iranian state-linked entities between 2013 and 2016.
It also reveals Ghandehari’s further Iranian business links to another Reform UK donor, John Richard Simpson, an administration professional and church warden from Potters Bar, north of London. Simpson’s design firm, Interior Architecture Landscape, counts the Ghandehari family as a client and gave £200,000 to Reform UK last year.
Farage has been highly critical of Iran over the past year, and in March accused it of being a bigger danger to the UK than Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.
The French judgment reveals that Ghandehari was the major investor behind a deal to supply and build a fibre-optic cable to carry telecoms traffic across Iran in a joint venture with a state-linked Iranian partner.
The businessman’s HP Trust was the ultimate owner of Ori Group, which took a 49% stake in the venture, called Omran Razavi International Co, in 2015.
The other 51% of the venture was owned by Astan Quds Razavi (AQR), a multibillion pound religious foundation in Iran’s second city of Mashhad.
AQR’s leader at the time was ayatollah Abbas Vaez Tabasi, who was appointed custodian of the foundation by the first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and served from the 1979 revolution until his death in 2016. Vaez Tabasi had been an ally of some reformers but remained close to the next supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and, according to the BBC, was reported by state media in 2009 to have said of opposition protest movements that those behind “sedition” in the country were “enemies of god” who deserved to be executed under sharia law.
The joint venture ended in about 2016, with the Ghandehari-backed entities being pushed out of the deal as a hardliner was appointed to replace Vaez Tabasi.
The US imposed sanctions on AQR in 2021, saying it controlled “large swaths of the Iranian economy, including assets expropriated from political dissidents and religious minorities, to the benefit of supreme leader Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian government officials”. It describes it as a bonyad, one of the “opaque, quasi-official organisations generally controlled by current and former government officials and clerics that report directly to the supreme leader”.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said it would be misleading to characterise him as “working with Iran” without the context that, after 2016, he was targeted by Iran’s supreme national security council with the false allegation that he was working with hostile western powers. They also said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information, which he believed was why the US and French authorities authorised the project.
Tom Keatinge, the director of the Centre for Finance and Security at Rusi, the foreign affairs thinktank, said dealing with Iran “has always been a risky business as a financial institution because of this blurring between kind of state and the private sector. The private sector is not free to operate. It’s just very hard to operate in that country without touching a live rail.”
He said there was clearly a range of positions among ayatollahs but it would be “pretty difficult to operate in an industry like telecoms” without the acceptance of the core leadership.
The judgment also revealed that, until 2016, Ghandehari’s HP Trust was the owner of Orico General Trading LLC, which was contracted to supply telecoms equipment from France’s Alcatel-Lucent and transport it from Dubai to Iran. After 2016, this company was transferred to Simpson, the administration professional, who was responsible for winding down Orico’s operations and taking hundreds of staff out of the region.
Simpson told the Guardian he acquired the company after Iranian extremists took over AQR, when the project’s assets were seized and those involved faced political persecution on national security grounds, including accusations of working for hostile western governments. He said his plan was to wind down the business, adding that he carried out detailed checks before acquiring Orico.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said AQR was independent and respected, and therefore the only viable choice for a joint venture in Iran. They said Ghandehari had never met Vaez Tabasi and that he did not regard him as an advocate for freedom or human rights but had believed him to be the only force in the Iranian hierarchy capable of holding back the hardliners in order for the project to go ahead.
The original contract for the deal was awarded to the Omran consortium in 2012 by the Iranian state-owned Telecommunication Infrastructure Company of Iran.
According to Iranian corporate filings, Omran Razavi International Co also owned stakes in two majority state-owned banks, Bank Mellat and Bank Tejerat, in 2013. Both were subject to sanctions over involvement in Iran’s nuclear programme at that point.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said Omran Razavi disposed of the small stakes in the banks before HP Trust’s Ori Group signed its agreement for a 49% stake in the venture in December 2014. They added that the deal was fully approved by authorities in France and the US.
In 2016, AQR took over the whole of the joint venture. Around the same time, the project’s chair, Mohammed Reza Noory, ended up in Iran’s infamous Evin prison, serving an 18-year sentence.
Ghandehari and Noory are both named on leaked judicial papers published by the hacktivist group Edaalat Ali as having being under investigation in Iran after the deal collapsed. Ghandehari’s lawyers say he first became aware of the “bogus allegations” during French court proceedings and that the intelligence services had not given him any further details. Ghandehari’s representatives said fabricating financial and social cases against its targets to discredit them was part of the Iranian regime’s playbook and had been widely documented and recognised by western governments, human rights organisations and independent journalists.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said he had not been to Iran for 30 years and his wealth had no connection to the country, since his ancestral property and assets were confiscated in 2016.
Farage has been highly critical of Iran’s government this year, supporting Donald Trump’s war against it, and attending a protest outside the Iranian embassy with pro-democracy activists in the spring. Last week he warned about Iranian agents entering the UK via small boats across the Channel.
In a joint interview with Farage and Ghandehari in July, the Telegraph described Ghandehari’s business deal in Iran without mentioning its connections to Iranian regime-linked companies. It described it as a project to bring access to high-speed internet to Iran that would help drive reform, but that it later went wrong and resulted in Ghandehari’s assets being confiscated.
It is still not clear how Ghandehari and his family have built up their extraordinary wealth. His fortune is said to have gone from an estimated $2bn, when his late mother bought a property on London’s “billionaire’s row” in 2008, to a reported $10bn now.
In a recent court case over a Picasso painting, Ghandehari was asked to provide proof that he could afford £1.5m in legal costs. His lawyers pointed only to a brochure from his Davos trip with Farage, with a description that he controls a trust with a “collective investment value in excess of $10bn”.
At one point, he offered a letter from a “partner in a leading accountancy firm” confirming he was the principal beneficiary of HP Trust, and drawing an annual income from it. However, this was later withdrawn, as Ghandehari decided he did not want its contents to enter the public domain.

article_title: MoD seeks out-of-court resolution over compensation battle with gay veterans
article_content:
Wes Streeting is pursuing an out-of-court resolution to a legal battle over compensation for gay veterans who were forced to resign from the armed forces because of their sexuality.
The defence secretary told the Guardian the Ministry of Defence was holding talks this week in the midst of a high court challenge over rules that blocked some veterans receiving £50,000 payments despite being forced out of military service.
Next week a high court judge will decide whether two former personnel, Steven Stewart, 55, and Mark Shephard, 49, can proceed with a judicial review of the government’s LGBT financial recognition scheme that was established in 2024 under Keir Starmer’s premiership.
The case has raised questions over whether the Labour government is prolonging an injustice against people who were persecuted by the armed forces, with veterans who resigned under pressure potentially receiving thousands of pounds less than those who were formally dismissed.
The defence minister said he would be “careful” what he said because the case “might be subject to judicial review”.
When asked if he would review the rules to make sure those who were not formally discharged could also be eligible for the dismissal payment, Streeting told the Guardian: “We do want to get this right so we’ll keep the conversation going and see if there’s a way forward that doesn’t require legal action.”
Streeting stopped short of promising to change the rules or confirming that any sort of settlement was being considered. Stewart, a former Royal Military Police corporal, and Shephard, who served in the Royal Air Force, brought the challenge forward because they say they were targeted owing to their sexuality, which forced them to leave.
Neither qualified for the scheme’s £50,000 dismissed or discharged payment because their departures were recorded as resignations, rather than formal dismissals. Instead, Stewart received £7,000 and Shephard £5,000 under a separate payment recognising the impact of the ban on LGBT personnel.
Gay men and lesbian women were banned from serving in the British military until 2000. Proper records have not been held but about 200-250 personnel were thrown out each year because of their sexuality.
Streeting said the government had tried to balance cases where formal dismissal records existed with the experiences of veterans who had left without records. “It’s tricky,” he said. “The balance the review tried to get was making sure that where we’ve got records of dismissal, we’re able to act. But also recognising there’ll be lots of people who left for whom there were no formal records, and making sure they’re still eligible to apply for support, which they are.
“I’d say to people, if you are one of those veterans who haven’t yet applied please do, the money is there, we’ve got £75m allocated to this. Over £60m has already gone, but I’m sure there are still more people who could benefit so we want to make sure we get people the compensation that they’re owed.”
Streeting, Britain’s first out gay defence secretary, said some veterans had already died without receiving justice. “For me, a lot of these veterans, they’re getting older and some of them sadly have not lived to see justice,” he said. But he added: “What [the payment] can’t do is erase the pain and the indignity of asking people who serviced their country faithfully to leave a career, to leave a service they loved because of who they are.”
The looming high court hearing means the government could soon face a judicial examination of whether the rules intended to address historical discrimination have left some of its victims facing another injustice.
“I have a personnel responsibility to make sure that we don’t see a repeat of those indignities and those injustices for our trans service personnel,” Streeting said. “Talent is everywhere. Opportunity isn’t.”
Asked whether he had been involved in approving new MoD guidance on the use of single-sex spaces and whether he would consider it, Streeting said: “We’re still finding our way on this … we’re not inundated with huge numbers of trans people serving. It does mean we can get this right on a case by case basis. I want every member of our armed forces to know I’ve got their backs. I want every trans person serving in our armed forces to know I’m proud of them and their service.”
He acknowledged some trans people had questioned whether the Labour government respected them because of decisions he had made as health secretary under Starmer’s premiership. “Some of the decisions I took as health secretary around children’s medication … which I stand by … they led trans people to think well … does this government respect us? And I hope the message is getting through day by day.”

article_title: Финская компания Nokia поможет Украине развивать спутниковую связь для нужд обороны
article_content:
22 октября президент Владимир Зеленский провел в Киеве встречу с премьер-министром Финляндии Петтери Орпо.
Зеленский сообщил, что стороны подписали семь документов, а общий объем договоренностей составляет около 300 млн евро.
«Сегодня есть новый пакет поддержки для Украины от Финляндии, и есть соглашения, которые открывают перед нами новые возможности для сотрудничества. Было подписано семь документов. И общий объем сегодняшних договоренностей — около 300 миллионов евро», — отметил президент.
Кроме того, обсуждалось расширение использования спутниковых возможностей для нужд обороны в сотрудничестве с финскими компаниями Nokia и ICEYE. Министерство обороны Украины подписало с компаниями письмо о намерениях по сотрудничеству в космической сфере, в частности о создании украинской системы спутниковой связи для оборонных нужд.
Ранее в Кабмине сообщили, что Финляндия передаст Украине 10 локомотивов. В настоящее время финская железнодорожная компания VR выводит их из эксплуатации и готовит к передаче Украине.
Отметим, что, по данным газеты The Wall Street Journal, основатель SpaceX Илон Маск лично распорядился ограничить скорость работы военной версии Starlink, которую использует Украина. Это сделало некоторые ударные дроны и дроны-перехватчики практически непригодными к использованию. После того как президент США Дональд Трамп позвонил Маску, система начала работать в режиме, более близком к нормальному.

article_title: Трамп заявив про відновлення Starshield для України, але є нюанс: що з'ясувало AP
article_content:
Трамп заявив про відновлення Starshield для України, але є нюанс: що з'ясувало AP
Президент США Дональд Трамп стверджує, що обмеження супутникового зв'язку для українських військових уже скасували. Однак європейський посадовець запевняє, що швидкісні обмеження залишаються чинними.
Адміністрація президента США Дональда Трампа надає суперечливі пояснення щодо обмежень роботи супутникового зв'язку Starshield для України. Американський лідер заявив про відновлення повноцінної роботи системи, однак джерела, обізнані із ситуацією на місцях, стверджують, що обмеження досі діють.
Про це повідомляє Associated Press.
За інформацією агентства, запроваджені минулого тижня обмеження Starshield — військової версії супутникового інтернету Starlink від компанії SpaceX — серйозно вплинули на роботу українських безпілотників.
Військові повідомляли про втрату дронів і зрив бойових завдань через проблеми зі зв'язком.
Трамп заявив, що обмеження Starshield скасували
У четвер, 22 жовтня, Дональд Трамп запевнив журналістів, що система супутникового зв'язку для України знову працює на повній швидкості.
Раніше The Wall Street Journal повідомило, що Ілон Маск погодився скасувати обмеження.
Водночас американський президент ухилився від прямої відповіді на запитання, чи особисто просив власника SpaceX відновити роботу системи.
«Не має значення, чи телефонував я, чи хтось інший. Головне, що він усе повернув», — заявив Трамп.
Однак високопоставлений європейський посадовець, обізнаний із ситуацією в Україні, повідомив AP, що станом на четвер нічого не змінилося.
За його словами, обмеження швидкості залишалося на рівні приблизно 160 км/год.
Українська сторона також не отримала чіткого офіційного пояснення, хто наказав запровадити обмеження та з якої причини.
Хто наказав обмежити Starshield для України
За інформацією Associated Press, представники американської адміністрації висловлюють суперечливі позиції щодо відповідальності за рішення.
Дональд Трамп неодноразово заявляв, що особисто не наказував обмежувати роботу супутникового зв'язку. Він також висловлював сумніви щодо причетності Ілона Маска.
Водночас віцепрезидент США Джей Ді Венс фактично допустив координацію дій між компанією SpaceX та американською владою.
«Я думаю, цілком зрозуміло, що він не хоче втручатися у війну між двома державами без того, щоб уряд США фактично визначав, що йому робити», — сказав Венс, коментуючи позицію Маска.
Віцепрезидент також наголосив, що головне питання полягає не в діях власника SpaceX, а в тому, якою має бути політика США щодо України та Росії.
Натомість державний секретар Марко Рубіо категорично заперечив причетність американської адміністрації до обмежень.
За його словами, ні Трамп, ні інші представники уряду США не вимагали змінювати роботу супутникових систем.
Міністр оборони Піт Гегсет також заявив, що Пентагон нічого не обмежував.
Водночас він зауважив, що користувачі мають дотримуватися умов обслуговування, а компанія SpaceX може самостійно ухвалювати відповідні рішення.
Маск перекладає відповідальність на Пентагон
Сам Ілон Маск раніше заявив, що системи Starshield належать уряду США та перебувають під його контролем.
За словами бізнесмена, будь-які обмеження швидкості або використання Starshield визначають американські військові, а остаточне рішення залежить від президента США.
Водночас Маск наголосив, що комерційний Starlink належить компанії SpaceX і має інші правила використання.
Зокрема, він стверджував, що комерційний сервіс не призначений для наступальних військових операцій.
Таким чином, представники Білого дому, Пентагону та SpaceX фактично перекладають відповідальність один на одного, не пояснюючи, хто саме ухвалив рішення, яке вплинуло на українські військові операції.
Що говорить Зеленський про обмеження зв'язку
Президент України Володимир Зеленський раніше заявляв, що швидкісні обмеження супутникового зв'язку стосуються саме України.
За його словами, аналогічних обмежень у країнах Європейського Союзу немає.
«Іншими словами, це спланована операція», — наголосив український президент.
Під час спілкування з американськими законодавцями Зеленський також повідомив, що українські військові продовжують стикатися з обмеженнями Starlink і Starshield на різних ділянках фронту.
Він зазначив, що Київ досі не отримав зрозумілих пояснень причин таких рішень.
В інтерв'ю Fox & Friends 21 жовтня Зеленський заявив, що Марко Рубіо пообіцяв допомогти розв'язати проблему.
У Сенаті США вимагають розслідування
На тлі суперечливих заяв американських посадовців сенатор-демократ Річард Блументаль ініціював розслідування обставин обмеження супутникових технологій для України.
Він вимагає пояснень щодо того, хто ухвалив рішення, яке вплинуло на українські оборонні можливості під час російських атак.
За інформацією AP, ситуація викликала серйозне занепокоєння серед американських законодавців, які підтримують Україну.
Наразі питання про відповідальність за запровадження обмежень залишається відкритим, а заяви Трампа про повне відновлення роботи системи суперечать інформації джерел агентства.
Варто зауважити, що збої в роботі супутникових систем Starlink і Starshield, за повідомленнями військових, призвели до втрати українських дронів на понад $1 млн та зупинення більшості бойових вильотів на три доби.

article_title: Andy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approval
article_content:
Andy Burnham has said he will not “abandon the responsibility” of fighting the climate crisis after the government approved the Jackdaw gasfield, pledging to block new North Sea licences and keep Britain on track for net zero by 2050.
The comments are the prime minister’s most forthright yet on net zero, after many MPs have privately cast doubt on the authenticity of his commitment to tackling the climate crisis.
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted that she alone would make a decision on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield – a decision sources say she is minded to block.
Burnham has been under pressure from industry and political opponents, as well as some Labour MPs, to water down Labour’s manifesto promises on new oil and gas licences and the net zero targets.
“There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering,” the prime minister said in an article for the Guardian.
He said he was conscious of the “acute global instability” affecting energy security and wanted to treat oil and gas workers with more dignity.
Burnham said that would not stop the government from abiding by its climate targets, saying he was “personally committed to confronting” the challenges of the climate crisis.
“Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus drivers working in intolerable conditions and families losing everything to wildfires,” he wrote.
“More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations.”
Meanwhile, Fahnbulleh doubled down on her insistence that she would not be influenced by other departments on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield, setting up a potential standoff with the Treasury.
The chancellor, John Healey, has said he expects “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, but Fanhbulleh said “only I can make that decision”, insisting that she bore the legal responsibility to ensure the UK did not violate its climate commitments.
Dismissing speculation that Burnham, or his chancellor, would make the final call, she said: “[It] sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because, in the end, only I can make it. And if it is overturned by other colleagues, all that means is we’re going to be overturned in the courts. So we will do the process and we will do it properly.”
Fahnbulleh said she was “really concerned” and “quite sad” about the breakdown in consensus about the climate crisis. She said: “I think it’s a sad place where Reform has gone and got to. But I’m even sadder about the Tories because they know better, and they’ve had a long tradition, including Boris Johnson, of working cross-party on climate action.
“It has been really painful and tragic to watch that consensus burn at a time when we’re seeing the impact of climate change this summer.”
The climate crisis was having a real impact on communities, she added. “It’s people’s livelihoods, it’s their jobs, their communities. Even if you don’t care about climate – care about that, you’ve got to take action.”
Reflecting on the decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield, Burnham said he wanted to make the transition to a greener future “on our terms”, saying that meant giving oil and gas workers a path to new jobs and using homegrown rather than imported gas.
“At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home. Gas from this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter.”
He said he had been moved by the plight of oil and gas workers in Aberdeen, adding that it was an industry that had suffered from deindustrialisation “with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives.”
Fahnbulleh echoed the prime minister’s words, saying the private sector had invested £100bn in clean energy in the last two years. “It’s a huge opportunity for parts of our countries that have been left behind,” she said. But that investment had to have a real-world impact, she added. “When you say jobs are going to be created, don’t say it. People need to see it.”
Burnham said the energy wealth fund that was being created to convert North Sea oil and gas tax revenues to clean energy programmes was long overdue – “something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago”.
It comes as Burnham announced that military planes and helicopters would fight wildfires for the first time, ahead of a major wildfire summit with fire chiefs, local leaders and experts.
The RAF’s chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft will fight fires and help crews across the UK tackle blazes on remote moorland, steep hillsides and other hard-to-reach terrain.
“Heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs,” said the prime minister.

article_title: Trump tells Iowa rally crowd he encouraged Ramaswamy to keep running widely criticized campaign ad – as it happened
article_content:
'You’ve got to ride with it'. Trump says he encouraged Ramaswamy to keep running ad featuring Acton's estranged mother
Speaking in Iowa on Thursday, Donald Trump told supporters that he had personally encouraged Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for Ohio governor, to keep running an attack ad featuring the mother of his Democratic rival, Dr Amy Acton, who had lost custody of her daughter at age 12 because her husband was charged with raping the young girl.
“They did an ad of the mother saying the daughter is incompetent, a liar and disgusting unreliable person,” Trump said, adding some claims that were not, in fact, in the ad.
“My mom would not say that about me - even if she believed it,” the president added, making light of the testimony of a woman who sided with the man charged with raping her own 12-year-old daughter.
“When I first saw it, I said, ‘Wow, that means Vivek easily will win the race’. And then I got a call from Vivek,” Trump said. “He said, ‘What would you recommend? Because I’m getting killed in the press.’ Why? He said, ‘Because they think I should immediately take the ad off.’”
“The mother said horrible things about your opponent,” Trump said. “I said, ‘You’ve got to ride with it’”.
The president made no mention of the fact that the Republican Senate candidate he was there to support, Ashley Hinson, denounced the ad earlier on Thursday. “I think it’s absolutely terrible, and I think they should take the ad down,” Hinson told ABC News ahead of Trump’s appearance.

… or at least the stage, exiting to the live-blogger’s favorite tune, YMCA. The president just wrapped up 90 minutes of remarks, saying very little that he has not said before, but he did devote an extended portion of the speech to defending the attack ad his ally, Vivek Ramaswamy, is running in Ohio, to the dismay of many Republicans, including Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson – the person Trump was there to promote.
'I am, really, on the ballot', Trump says, without offering to resign if Republicans lose the midterms
“I’m asking you to pretend that I’m running… pretend I’m on the ballot,” Donald Trump told supporters in Iowa on Thursday, as he has at each stop on his “midterm blitz”.
“Remember, I’m on the ballot,” he said later in the speech. “Because I am on the ballot. Really, it’s our stuff, it’s going to be taken away. If we if we don’t win, it’s going to be taken away. So I am, really, on the ballot.”
Of course, if the president really wanted to make the midterms a referendum on himself, he could take a page from the leaders of parliamentary democracies and pledge to resign from office should Republicans lose the House and Senate, something he has not done.

Describing cognitive test, Trump recites math problem he claims he solved, but does not provide the answer
As he frequently does at campaign rallies, Donald Trump boasted to supporters in Iowa on Thursday that he “aced” what he called “an aptitude test” that is, in fact, a screening for mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer’s disease.
While the test does include a short test of basic mathematical ability, in which patients are asked to perform serial subtraction by 7 starting at 60, Trump claimed on Thursday that the mathematical test was much more complicated.
“The first question easy. The second question is easy. And by the time you get up to number 30, there are many people that can answer those questions. I’ll tell you,” the president said.
“They’ll say like: ‘Take a number, any number’. Say, 49, ‘triple it’, and they go pretty much in this speed, ‘triple it and divide by four; add 2,019; subtract 87; divide by three; multiply by nine. What is the number?’”
As supporters shouted out numbers, Trump just asserted that he solved the problem without saying what the answer is. “Not a lot of people are going to be able to do that,” Trump said. “Not a lot. I did it. I did it three times,” the president said.
The president has given similarly detailed descriptions of mathematical problems he says were on the test, and claims to have solved, in previous speeches, but never once provided an answer.
“These are tough questions, you know,” Trump told elderly supporters at The Villages in Florida in May. “They say, ‘Take a number, any number.’ Okay, I’ll take 99. ‘Multiply times nine.’ Okay. ‘Divide it by three.’ Good. ‘Add 4,293.’ That’s good. ‘Divide by two; subtract 93; divide by nine. What is your answer?’ Now they go a little slower than that, but not much. I don’t want to waste a lot of time, but there aren’t a lot of people that get it right. I got it right.”
Trump tosses conspiracy theories about Ilhan Omar to Iowa crowd, prompting chants of 'Lock her up!'
Despite the fact that he is in Iowa, ostensibly to support Republican candidates, Donald Trump quickly turned to attacks on two candidates running in other states, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, repeating false claims he has made before about two prominent Muslim Americans.
Making no effort to conceal the anti-Muslim racism and fear-mongering he has put at the center of his pitch to Republican voters, Trump claimed that El-Sayed is “a jihadist”.
He then recited multiple falsehoods about Omar, including the false claims that she married her brother and that she told an interviewer this week that she did not, “as far as I know”, which she did not.
Trump begins Iowa rally in support of Republican candidates with heaps of praise for himself
Donald Trump started speaking, about 40 minutes late, to supporters in Sioux City, Iowa on Thursday by boasting about how well he had done in the state in his own three runs for office.
Unusually, the president acknowledged that his term in office is drawing (slowly) to a close. “You know, we only have a little more than two years left. Can you believe it?” Trump said, before adding: “But I’m going to have a lot of power when I leave.”
He then turned to reciting a litany of lies about Josh Turek, the Democrat running against Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, casting him as a supporter of “taxpayer-funded transgender brutalization surgeries and in favor of men in girls bathrooms.”
Lebron James mimed a golf swing and took an imaginary jump shot, as the national anthem was performed during Tuesday’s Philadelphia 76ers and New York Knicks match-up. His gestures provoked the ire of Donald Trump, who berated him as “no good” and a “TOTAL DISGRACE” on social media.
“LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!” Trump wrote in a Wednesday Truth Social post.
The NBA star and Trump have been at odds for several years.
In 2017, Trump rescinded a White House invitation to the Golden State Warriors, after Stephen Curry indicated he would not want to go. James famously called Trump a “bum,” saying his presidency took away from the customary honor.
The feud appeared to rekindle this summer, when in July, Trump suggested James was a “racist,” without much further explanation, after being asked to compare his career to that of Michael Jordan’s.
As Trump travels to Iowa, Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson denounced Ohio ad he supports
Donald Trump is expected to speak soon at a rally in Sioux City, Iowa in support of Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, who broke with the president on Thursday by denouncing an attack ad he has supported in the Ohio governor race.
As Trump defended the ad, from Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, in which the estranged mother of the Democratic candidate, Dr Amy Acton, calls her daughter “a liar”, Hinson joined the bipartisan backlash against the ad triggered by the fact that Acton was removed from her mother’s custody at age 12, after her stepfather was charged with raping her.
In an interview ahead of today’s rally, Hinson was asked by Jonathan Karl of ABC News about the ad from Ramaswamy’s campaign. “It’s terrible,” Hinson said. “I think about it as a mom, and you think about kid surviving childhood sexual abuse and having to relive that trauma on TV again. I think it’s absolutely terrible, and I think they should take the ad down.”
Hinson also called the comment from vice-president JD Vance, that he was disgusted by Republican criticism of the ad, “ridiculous”.
“Again, I think it’s wrong and should come down.”
Hinson, who currently represents Iowa in the House, is campaigning to replace Republican senator Joni Ernst, who revealed in 2019 that she was a survivor of sexual assault who had been raped in college.
Hinson spoke at the rally on Thursday about 90 minutes before Trump’s schedule arrival time.
Student IDs will not be accepted at New Hampshire polls, Supreme Court rules
Uwa Ede-Osifo
The US supreme court ruled on Thursday that New Hampshire students cannot use their school-issued ID cards as proof of identity to vote, handing a victory to the state’s Republicans.
The high court cited a previous ruling, “lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election,” in its decision to keep intact an April state law that struck high school and college IDs from a list of acceptable voter documents. House Bill 323, signed by New Hampshire’s Republican governor, Kelly Ayotte, requires government-issued IDs, such as a passport or driver license.
The Coalition for Open Democracy, a New Hampshire-based nonprofit, had sued to block the legislation, arguing that it raised unconstitutional barriers for the state’s young voting bloc.
Republican legislators nationwide have embraced stricter voter ID laws, framing them as a safeguard against alleged voter fraud. Voting rights groups have argued that the narrow range of acceptable forms of identification disenfranchises millions of voters.
According to the Brennan Center, “more than 49 million American adults don’t possess an unexpired driver’s license with their current name and address. Seniors, people of color, people with disabilities, low-income voters, and students are especially likely to lack such documents.”

article_title: Flu cases rise on west coast earlier than usual as US health experts encourage vaccine
article_content:
Flu cases on the west coast are on the rise months earlier than normal, prompting US health experts to stress the importance of the annual vaccine.
Flu activity typically ramps up in December, hitting its peak in February. But this season has kicked into action earlier this year, with higher positive cases than normal recorded.
Several experts have credited the early seasonal start to a new mutation of the influenza A strain H1N1, which was behind the 2009 swine flu pandemic.
This strain has accounted for 242 of 300 influenza viruses reported by public health laboratories to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to date (CDC).
In California, during the past two flu seasons, influenza test positivity hovered slightly above 1% in early October. As of 10 October, that rate is 9.65%, according to data from the state’s department of health.
As of 11 October, Utah has recorded 242 influenza A cases, up from 10 cases this time last year, according to Germ Watch, an Intermountain Health database.
Parts of central Oregon have also seen an influenza A surge.
Influenza vaccines can reduce severe illness and hospitalization, according to the American Medical Association, which recommends flu shots for all people 6 months and older.
The 2026-27 flu vaccines, approved by the FDA in August, target H1N1, H3N2 – the dominant strain last flu season – and one influenza B virus.
Scott Hensley, a microbiologist at the University of Pennsylvania, said two of the three components of this year’s vaccine appear to be very well matched to circulating flu strains.
However, the H1N1 mutation might affect antibodies in younger people, and with flu season picking up steam, “it is probably a good idea to get vaccinated early”, Hensley said via email.
Promotion of flu shots has been reduced under US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has engineered an overhaul of long-standing childhood vaccine schedules.

article_title: Department of Justice opens criminal investigation into Corey Lewandowski
article_content:
Corey Lewandowski, a former political adviser to Donald Trump and top aide at the Department of Homeland Security, is under criminal investigation over allegations he profited off his role in the US government, three US officials and a fourth person familiar with the matter told Reuters on Thursday.
The investigation began with a criminal referral to the justice department from the internal watchdog at DHS, according to the four people. The DHS inspector general’s office has been investigating Lewandowski’s involvement in the handling of certain government contracts, according to one of the people, a DHS official.
A lawyer for Lewandowski, Adam Trigg, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The investigation was first reported in the Wall Street Journal, which quoted Lewandowski’s lawyer as saying that his client denies all allegations of wrongdoing.
The DoJ has not yet issued subpoenas or other legal demands in the criminal investigation, according to one of the people. All four of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The justice department under Trump has investigated several prominent critics of the president, including the former FBI director James Comey and the New York attorney general Letitia James, but investigations of people close to Trump have been rare. The department has also moved to dismiss several existing cases involving Trump allies, including supporters charged in connection with the 6 January 2021 attack on the US Capitol.
Asked about media reports on the investigation, Trump told reporters that he did not know the specifics of the investigation, but said: “I want my people to be honest.”
“And if they’re not honest, I’ll have my DoJ go and do whatever they have to do,” Trump added.
Lewandowski served as a top aide to the former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem during her tenure leading DHS. Trump fired Noem in March after months of controversy, including the fatal shootings of two US citizens by federal officers in Minneapolis and lawmakers’ questions over a $220m advertising contract promoting Noem that was awarded without a standard bidding process.
Lewandowski had signed some DHS contracts despite having questionable legal authority as a special government employee, according to the DHS official. Certain grants and contracts, including those involving the Federal Emergency Management Agency, were put on hold at Lewandowski’s direction, according to two of the people, both of whom are DHS officials.
Lewandowski previously served as a campaign manager during Trump’s first presidential run in 2016 and advised his 2024 campaign.

article_title: Мир із Росією неможливий, поки Путін при владі: у США пояснили, що має зробити Захід
article_content:
Мир із Росією неможливий, поки Путін при владі: у США пояснили, що має зробити Захід
Президент американського Гудзонівського інституту Джон Волтерс заявив, що Володимир Путін зазнає стратегічної поразки у війні проти України, але залишається небезпечним для Заходу. На його думку, справжній мир можливий лише після зміни влади в Росії.
Сполучені Штати та їхні союзники повинні відмовитися від уявлення, що російський диктатор Володимир Путін є незамінним учасником мирного процесу. Його політика вже послабила Росію, а подальше перебування при владі лише збільшує загрозу для України та Європи.
Таку думку висловив президент і генеральний директор американського Гудзонівського інституту (Hudson Institute) Джон Волтерс у своїй аналітичній статті.
На переконання експерта, головна помилка американської політики щодо Росії полягає в тому, що здатність Путіна завдавати руйнувань помилково сприймають як ознаку стратегічної сили.
Насправді повномасштабне вторгнення в Україну призвело до результатів, протилежних тим, яких прагнув Кремль.
Чому Путін зазнає стратегічної поразки
Як зазначає Волтерс, російський президент розраховував підкорити Україну, послабити НАТО та розколоти європейські країни.
Натомість війна зміцнила українську національну ідентичність, сприяла вступу Фінляндії та Швеції до Північноатлантичного альянсу й прискорила переозброєння Європи.
Важливу роль відіграли також стійкість українського суспільства, військові інновації, застосування безпілотників та далекобійного озброєння.
За оцінкою Волтерса, навіть нові територіальні захоплення або посилення російських атак не змусять Україну капітулювати.
Він також вважає, що можлива зміна президента Володимира Зеленського не означатиме відмови Києва від опору.
Серед потенційних наступників експерт згадує колишнього головнокомандувача ЗСУ Валерія Залужного, наголошуючи, що українське військо та політичне керівництво не погодяться на капітуляцію лише через зміну президента.
Чому Путін може посилити атаки, попри невдачі
Водночас Волтерс застерігає, що стратегічні невдачі Росії не роблять її менш небезпечною.
Навпаки, на його думку, Путін може вдатися до подальшої ескалації проти України та європейських держав.
Експерт звертає увагу на диверсії, кібератаки, кампанії дезінформації, залякування та ймовірні політичні вбивства, які пов'язують із Росією.
Він розглядає такі дії як систематичне посягання на суверенітет і безпеку західних держав.
Додаткову загрозу створюють регулярні ядерні погрози Кремля.
За словами Волтерса, Захід має усвідомити, що зіткнувся не зі зростанням російської могутності, а з небезпечною ескалацією держави, яка не досягла своїх стратегічних цілей.
Чому мирні переговори з Путіним можуть не завершити війну
Окрему увагу президент Гудзонівського інституту приділив перспективам переговорів щодо завершення російсько-української війни.
Він переконаний, що Путін не здатний погодитися на умови, які означатимуть визнання його поразки.
На думку Волтерса, збереження влади російського президента значною мірою залежить від продовження війни.
Саме тому експерт сумнівається, що Кремль погодиться припинити агресію, повернути всіх викрадених українських дітей, вивести війська під міжнародним контролем і прийняти надійні гарантії безпеки для України.
Волтерс робить висновок, що досягнення справжнього переговорного миру за нинішнього російського керівництва неможливе.
Водночас це є оцінкою автора аналітичної статті, а не офіційною позицією адміністрації США.
Що США та Європа мають зробити для України
Волтерс закликає Вашингтон і європейських союзників рішуче посилити військову, економічну та дипломатичну підтримку України.
На його думку, допомога має бути достатньою, щоб переконливо продемонструвати Кремлю безперспективність подальшої агресії.
Експерт також пропонує зміцнити ядерне стримування, зокрема шляхом передислокації сил, здатних нести ядерне озброєння.
Окрім цього, Захід повинен підтримувати контакти з представниками російського суспільства та еліт, які потенційно можуть сприяти політичним змінам у країні.
Йдеться, зокрема, про налагодження комунікації між західними політиками, військовими, розвідниками, бізнесменами та російськими представниками, зацікавленими в майбутньому без Путіна.
Як Росія стає залежною від Китаю
Ще однією стратегічною проблемою Кремля Волтерс називає дедалі більшу залежність Росії від Китаю.
На його думку, така співпраця загрожує перетворити Москву на молодшого партнера Пекіна.
Експерт вважає, що збереження путінського режиму посилює міжнародні позиції китайського лідера Сі Цзіньпіна та створює додаткові ризики для американських інтересів.
Він також наголошує на довгострокових проблемах російської економіки: великих військових втратах, дефіциті робочої сили, інфляції, технологічній ізоляції та виїзді кваліфікованих спеціалістів.
Попри здатність економіки РФ пристосовуватися до санкцій, витрати на війну скорочують ресурси, які країна могла б спрямувати на розвиток.
На завершення Волтерс наголошує, що Сполучені Штати повинні вибудовувати стратегію, розраховану не лише на стримування нинішнього російського керівництва, а й на майбутнє після Путіна.
Що відомо про переговори України, США та Росії
Нагадаємо, Кремль продовжує відкидати змістовні пропозиції щодо припинення вогню, зокрема не погоджується на енергетичне перемир'я.
Водночас білоруський політичний аналітик Ігор Тишкевич припустив, що Володимир Путін погодився продовжити тристоронні переговори не через готовність до поступок, а щоб зберегти американське посередництво. На його думку, Москва прагне впливати на порядок денний і правила переговорного процесу, навіть попри відхилення пропозицій спецпосланця США Стіва Віткоффа.
Зауважимо, що слідом за РФ американський президент Дональд Трамп заявив, мовляв, Володимир Зеленський нібито не зацікавлений у домовленостях щодо завершення війни. Натомість він кинув улесливі заяви на адресу російського «фюрера».
Сам Зеленський раніше повідомляв, що наступний раунд тристоронніх переговорів між Україною, США та Росією може відбутися не пізніше початку листопада. За його словами, Київ підтримує якнайшвидше відновлення діалогу та готовий розглядати будь-які ініціативи щодо припинення вогню.
Тим часом, за інформацією Axios, перед зустріччю Віткоффа з Путіним Вашингтон вимагав від президента Володимира Зеленського припинити українські удари по російських нафтопереробних заводах.

article_title: «Таке відбувається часто»: Трамп відреагував байдужою фразою на ракетний терор Путіна
article_content:
«Таке відбувається часто»: Трамп відреагував байдужою фразою на ракетний терор Путіна
Трамп проігнорував масовані удари РФ і сухо прокоментував слова Зеленського про небажання Путіна зупиняти війну.
Президент США Дональд Трамп прокоментував заяву українського лідера Володимира Зеленського про те, що нові російські удари по Україні свідчать про небажання Володимира Путіна завершувати війну.
Про це глава Білого дому сказав у розмові з журналістами у четвер, 22 жовтня 2026 року, у Вашингтоні.
«Побачимо, як усе складеться. Таке відбувається вже досить часто», — лаконічно сказав Трамп.
Раніше Володимир Зеленський заявив, що послаблення тиску на Росію з боку окремих міжнародних партнерів заохочує Путіна продовжувати війну. Глава держави наголосив, що характер російських атак не свідчить про реальне прагнення Кремля припинити війну.
