article_title: Трамп підігрує Кремлю і відвертається від України: що насправді задумав президент США
article_content:
Трамп підігрує Кремлю і відвертається від України: що насправді задумав президент США
Останнім часом Трамп зближується з Путіним і тисне на Зеленського, але, наголошують експерти, зміна риторики президента США має конкретну мету.
Останніми тижнями президент США Дональд Трамп вдався до кроків, які не лише посилюють позиції Росії у війні з Україною, а й можуть допомогти відновити зіпсовану репутацію «фюрера» Володимира Путіна на міжнародній арені. Втім, дії очільника Білого дому мають конкретну мету.
Втім, чи спрацює така стратегія, залишається відкритим питанням, йдеться у матеріалі NBCNews.
Автори статті наголошують, що знову сівши у президентське крісло, Трамп пообіцяв швидко завершити війну. Торік він заявляв, що не стає на жоден бік у протистоянні, а підтримує лише «бік людства». Однак така нейтральна позиція поступово відійшла на другий план. Тепер американський лідер з усіх сил намагається налагодити відносини з Путіним.
Водночас, експерти зауважують, що за діями Трампа і його команди стоїть конкретна стратегічна мета — Вашингтон намагається схилити російського диктатора до переговорів, щоб покласти край війні, яка триває вже п’ятий рік.
Вихваляння Путіна і критика Зеленського
Організація Freedom House, що займається захистом свободи і розвитком демократії, характеризує РФ як авторитарну державу, де влада «зосереджена в руках Володимира Путіна». Втім, Дональд Трамп схильний розглядати дипломатію крізь призму особистих стосунків і ніколи не приховував свого прихильного ставлення до «фюрера» Кремля.
Торік, йдеться у статті, американський президент приймав президента-диктатора країни-аргресора на Алясці. Тоді Путіна зустріли з червоною доріжкою, а в Білому домі, у Пальмовій залі, висить фотографія, на якій лідери двох країн стоять поруч.
Натомість Трамп посилив свою непослідовну критику президента України Володимира Зеленського. Зокрема, він звинуватив його у нібито небажанні завершити війну та навіть заявив, мовляв, переговори від Києва має вести «хтось інший».
Ексрадник Трампа з національної безпеки Роберт О’Браєн вважає, що лестощі та демонстративна приязність — інструменти, за допомогою яких президент намагається схилити Путіна до укладення угоди, бо інші методи не дали бажаного результату.
«Ми думали, що зможемо врегулювати війну ще два роки тому, але Путін виявив непоступливість і відмовлявся сідати за стіл переговорів. Президент Трамп використовує доброзичливість, щоб спонукати Путіна до переговорів», — висловився експерт.
З його слів, господар Кремля навряд чи погодився б на переговори за посередництва США, якби вважав, що Трамп у цьому конфлікті на 100% підтримує Україну.
Своєю чергою, експерт із зовнішньої політики аналітичного центру Brookings Institution Майкл Кіммедж вважає: Білий дім розраховує досягти результату за столом переговорів, дистанціювавшись від Києва і демонструючи прихильність до Москви.
Однак експерт О’Браєн сумнівається, що така стратегія спрацює, бо прогрес важко уявити «за відсутності дуже серйозних форм впливу на Росію».
Як Трамп підігрує Путіну
«Поки Трамп працює над укладенням мирної угоди, одним із його нещодавніх жестів щодо Путіна є ставлення до нього як до державного діяча, а не як до глобального ізгоя», — пише NBCNews.
Так, президент США подякував «фюреру» після того, як вони досягли дизельної угоди. Крім того, він запросив Путіна взяти участь у міжнародному саміті G20 у своєму гольф-курорті Doral у Маямі в грудні і заявив про готовність до зустрічі, до якої може долучитися лідер Китаю Сі Цзіньпін.
Зустріч на вищому рівні разом з лідерами двох найбільших економік світу була б благом для Путіна, якого Захід ігнорує від моменту вторгнення Росії до Криму 2014-го. Зокрема, після цього світові лідери виключили “фюрера” з елітної міжнародної організації під назвою G8.
Директором з питань глобальної взаємодії в Білому домі за часів Барака Обами Бретт Бруен вважає, що «Трамп намагається реінтегрувати Путіна у вишукане суспільство».
Водночас голова комітету із закордонних справ парламенту Естонії Марко Міхкельсон застерігає: «винагороджуючи агресорів» і даючи їм зрозуміти, що вони можуть досягати своїх цілей силою, міжнародна спільнота лише «заохочує їх до подальшої агресії».
Заява Віткоффа про «гуманіста» Путіна — що відомо
Не лише Трамп сипле дифірамби на адресу російського «фюрера». Вихваляють воєнного злочинця і члени його команди. Так, під час переговорів 21 жовтня у Костянтинівському палаці в Петербурзі посланець США Стів Віткофф приголомшив компліментом Путіну, улесливо назвавши його «гуманістом»: «Ви так багато говорите про те, що президент Трамп — гуманіст. Ви теж гуманіст, пане. Я це високо ціную. Я висловлюю вам свою повагу».
Водночас цій заяві обурилися навіть однопартійці Трампа. Сенатор-республіканець Том Тілліс жорстко відповів Віткоффу: «Що за чортівня, Стіве?». Він наголосив до подібні висловлювання є неприпустимими.
Втім, віцепрезидент США Джей Ді Венс став на захист спецпосланця. Мовляв, «можна сказати щось хороше людині», яка звільнила 74-річного американця Стівена Габбарда, який перебував в ув’язнері в Росії понад чотири роки.

article_title: Сі Цзіньпін хоче грати у власну гру: Китай має причини зірвати саміт із Трампом і Путіним
article_content:
Сі Цзіньпін хоче грати у власну гру: Китай має причини зірвати саміт із Трампом і Путіним
Саміт трьох лідерів під питанням, адже Сі Цзіньпін може не підтримати плани Трампа і Путіна.
Президент США Дональд Трамп і «фюрер» РФ Володимир Путін поставили лідера Китаю Сі Цзіньпіна в незручне становище, висловивши зацікавленість у тристоронньому саміті. Зустріч може відбутися в середині листопада під час саміту Азійсько-Тихоокеанського економічного співробітництва у місті Шеньчжен. Пекін не підтвердив свою готовність, але Москва і Вашингтон активно обговорюють таку можливість.
Про це йдеться у статті аналітичного журналу The Diplomat.
Автори матеріалу зауважують, що обережна позиція Сі Цзіньпіна може зіграти на користь Європи та України, адже дає шанс уникнути сценарію, за якого великі держави вирішуватимуть долю регіону без їхньої участі.
Ідею тристоронньої зустрічі запропонувала Москва, яка прагне домовленостей щодо України «за зразком Ялтинської конференції 1945-го», коли США, Велика Британія та СРСР обговорювали повоєнний устрій Європи.
Втім, навіть значно скромніший результат такого саміту став би для Кремля успіхом. Адже лише сама участь у переговорах на одному рівні зі США і КНР допомогла б Росії відновити міжнародний статус і послабити дипломатичну ізоляцію. Водночас зустріч потенційно могла б поглибити розбіжності між Америкою і Європою, а аткож дати Москві додаткову трибуну для просування наративу про нібито загрози з боку Заходу.
Економічна вигода для США
«Тристороння зустріч зіграла б на руку самовдоволенню Трампа як укладача угод та миротворця — і, цілком можливо, його прагненню до економічної вигоди», — йдеться у статті.
США нещодавно послабили санкції щодо експорту дизельного пального з РФ. За повідомленнями, перша партія обсягом 40 тисяч тонн уже прямує до Штатів. Крім того, Москва запропонувала збільшити постачання добрив на тлі дефіциту, спричиненого кризою на Близькому Сході.
Однак у Трампа можуть бути й ширші стратегічні мотиви для тристоронньої зустрічі з Путіним і Сі. Американський президент заявляв, що головною темою переговорів має стати ядерне роззброєння, а не Україна.
Сі уникає тристороннього саміту
Водночас проведення тристороннього саміту у Китаї могло б стати символічною перемогою для Сі Цзіньпіна. Він отримав би можливість постати перед світом як лідер, здатний зібрати за одним столом керівників двох найбільших ядерних держав. Втім, зустріч потенційно могла б поглибити розбіжності між США та Європою.
Втім, Пекін має вагомі причини уникати такого формату переговорів, бо виграє від окремих контактів із Вашингтоном і Москвою, а раніше наполягав, що до будь-якого мирного процесу мають бути залучені і Київ, і Москва. Саме тому саміт США-Китай-Росія, на якому обговорюватимуть майбутнє України без участі її представників, суперечив би цій позиції китайської влади.
Окрім того, тристоронній саміт може затьмарити основні заходи АТЕС, які Пекін прагне використати для демонстрації свого економічного лідерства та просування принципів відкритості, інновацій і співпраці. Також широко розрекламована зустріч лідерів трьох великих держав погано узгоджувалася б із постійними закликами Китаю до інклюзивної багатосторонньої співпраці. Особливо з огляду на те, що форум АТЕС покликаний сприяти економічному партнерству в Азійсько-Тихоокеанському регіоні.
«Успішна тристороння зустріч може зробити ризик виправданим. Але такий результат невизначений — не в останню чергу через непередбачуваність Трампа та Путіна», — йдеться у статті.
Зрештою, попри значні стратегічні мотиви для зустрічі, які мають Трамп і Путін, Сі має причини уникати її. Наполягання очільника Білого дому на тому, щоб головною темою переговорів стало скорочення ядерних арсеналів, створює для Китаю складну ситуацію. Адже його ядерка значно менша, ніж у США і РФ.
Китайська влада наполягає: перш ніж залучати КНР до таких переговорів, Вашингтон і Москва мають суттєво скоротити власні арсенали. Втім, наголошують у статті, відмова від цієї позиції загрожувала б тим, що Пекін буде змушений дотримуватися тих самих обмежень, що й дві ядерні наддержави, попри значну різницю в їхніх можливостях.
Відкинути ідею зустрічі Сі не може
«Водночас Сі Цзіньпін розуміє, що повністю відкидати ідею зустрічі не варто. За повідомленнями, китайські дипломати не виключають проведення тристоронніх переговорів. Якщо Пекіну не вдасться запобігти саміту, він може спробувати вплинути на його формат і порядок денний», — наголошує видання.
Замість офіційного саміту, присвяченого Україні чи ядерці, КНР могла б організувати менш формальну зустріч із нечітко визначеним порядком денним. Це дозволило б не створювати завищених очікувань у суспільства. Водночас Сі Цзіньпін навіть міг би позиціонувати себе не як учасника тристоронніх переговорів, а як господаря зустрічі Трампа і Путіна.
Такий дипломатичний маневр не захистив би Європу й Україну від обговорення їхнього майбутнього за зачиненими дверима. Проте європейські уряди могли б представити зустріч лише як обмін думками. Натомість офіційний саміт, присвячений Україні, створив би небезпечний прецедент: він міг би продемонструвати світові, що троє лідерів вважають себе вправі ухвалювати стратегічні рішення щодо Європи без участі самих європейців.
«До саміту АТЕС у листопаді ще багато чого може змінитися. Зокрема, обговорюється новий раунд переговорів між Києвом і Москвою за посередництва США в Абу-Дабі. Водночас позиція Трампа щодо України і президента Володимира Зеленського продовжує змінюватися», — йдеться у статті.
Однак, зауважують автори матеріалу, незалежно від того, у якому форматі відбудуться переговори в Шеньчжені, європейські уряди мають наполягати на участі України в будь-яких обговореннях її майбутнього.
«Окрім закликів до Вашингтона враховувати позицію Києва, Україна та європейські столиці можуть апелювати й до застережень самого Сі Цзіньпіна, адже тристоронній саміт несе ризики також для Китаю», — підсумували у статті.
Нагадаємо, Дональд Трамп заявив, що готовий докласти всіх зусиль для досягнення миру, незалежно від складу учасників переговорів. Він не виключив зустрічі з Путіним і Сі Цзіньпіном для обговорення шляхів завершення війни в Україні. Водночас американський президент припустив, що переговори можуть відбутися без участі президента Володимира Зеленського.
Аналітики ISW припускають, що Кремль розробив новий план щодо України, тому наполягає на тристоронній зустрічі Володимира Путіна, Дональда Трампа та Сі Цзіньпіна. Москва, ймовірно, прагне відновити образ Росії як впливового дипломатичного гравця та посилити альтернативні міжнародні об’єднання, які конкурують із організаціями під проводом Заходу.

article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
article_content:
UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
- Published
The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.
As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.
The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.
"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.
"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.
"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."
The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.
But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.
"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.
"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."
The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.
- What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it? 
  - Published14 September
- Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says 
  - Published1 day ago
The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).
Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.
The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.
It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.
It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.
Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.
There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.
But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

article_title: Reform UK braces for Farage standards verdict over undeclared £5m gift
article_content:
Nigel Farage’s Reform is braced for a negative report from the standards commissioner over his failure to declare a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne and plans to appeal against any adverse findings.
The party is on tenterhooks over the report, with multiple Reform insiders saying they are readying for a fightback through the appeals process and fully expect the initial verdict to find against their leader.
Any attempt by Farage to oppose a negative verdict could mean the process drags on for months, as an MP under investigation has the right to present further evidence to the standards committee as well as to appeal through the independent expert panel.
After any appeals process, and if parliament agrees with a penalty of more than 10 days of suspension from the House of Commons, Farage could end up facing a second byelection in his Clacton constituency. This would require a recall petition, triggered by signatures from 10% of voters in the MP’s constituency over six weeks.
Farage was interviewed by the standards commissioner, Daniel Greenberg, last month and the party expects to be notified of the verdict at any time.
While it awaits the findings, Reform has been overhauling its HQ operations, having been destabilised by undercover investigations by Channel 4 and ITV in recent weeks and fallen in the polls.
The Channel 4 reporting with the investigative group Verbatim has led to a police inquiry into alleged attempts to orchestrate illegal overseas donations, as well as the suspension of James Orr as head of policy and Dan Jukes as Farage’s communications chief. They deny wrongdoing and an internal party report has cleared them, but the matter remains under police investigation.
The ITV reporting uncovered racist councillors and election candidates for the party caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.
One Reform insider said the ITV documentary in particular was extremely bad and showed the party’s vetting had not been up to scratch, despite its claims to have professionalised.
But they said the party was well on its way to bringing in changes in its organisation. Harvey Griffiths, Reform’s new treasurer, has been taking a central role in handling day-to-day party business, while Tom Waterhouse, its general secretary, has taken on the role of getting to grips with vetting.
There have also been departures. Aaron Lobo, its former head of operations, has moved to a new role running a Reform-focused TV channel, which is hiring dozens of “journalists” to increase communications directly to voters.
Amar Johal, a former government lawyer who had been working for the party as head of policy, has taken on the role of acting head of people operations and is said to be a rising force within the party.
Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s polling guru and former campaign lead, has been asked to return to play a role as an informal sounding board on strategy for the party. Raheem Kassam, a former communications chief for Farage now based in the US, has been playing an unofficial role as an attack dog mostly aimed at the Tories, including calling Kemi Badenoch a “Nigerian scammer”, which has been condemned by the Conservative chair, Kevin Hollinrake.
While Jukes, who was a longtime aide to Farage, was considered a loss, the party’s communications are now being handled by Ed Sumner, its communications director, and Miles Goslett, a former journalist.
The mood at Reform is said to be down but less bad than expected given its polling slide, partly because of the £72m gift from two donors, Harborne and Ben Delo. The Guardian reported undercover footage from Verbatim this week in which Orr suggested Harborne could be caught by the forthcoming overseas donor cap, given he has only been a registered domestic voter in the UK since June. However, Reform has insisted the money will not have to be handed back.
The party has begun a hiring spree since the windfall and is planning to take on 400 campaign managers in target seats. It has also sent a mailshot directly to voters – a move that may be repeated in the coming weeks.
Farage has been under investigation over the £5m gift from Harborne just before the last election in 2024 since shortly after the Guardian revealed it in May.
The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not a political one, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.

article_title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?
article_content:
Why should I stockpile and what will I need?
- Published
Do you have three days' worth of food and water in your home?
That is what the government has told all of us to have on hand to get through a national emergency, as well as some other basic items.
Its "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need to get through a rocky few days.
On Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unexpected events "seem to becoming more common" and everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".
As one expert warns the UK is "light years" behind our neighbours when it comes to preparing for major disruption, we've drilled down into what you need and why.
What is on the 'Be Ready' checklist?
The government recommends having enough supplies in the kitchen to last three days, including bottled water and non-perishable foods.
Wet wipes, a torch and cash are also recommended - you can scroll through below to see the full list.
Disaster planning expert Professor Lucy Easthope said the goal of asking household to prepare is to make it easier for emergency service to cope in the event of a national emergency.
For example, the government says people who need medication should have an extra supply just in case. Prof Easthope says: "If people have got their heart pills for an extra 48 hours, it stops [response crews] from having to immediately find an emergency pharmacist."
While the latest government campaign only launched on Thursday, some people are well ahead of the game.
Speaking to Radio 5 Live, Bridgette Clamp, who lives in near Penzance in Cornwall, said she has stocked up on "lots of tinned goods" as well as "flour, yeast and everything to bake bread".
"We're rocking and rolling," she says.
One woman, who spoke to 5 Live anonymously, said she bought "loads and loads" of emergency food - but ended up eating it before it was strictly necessary.
Like others, she wondered if the government was "scaremongering", adding: "I don't know but I've certainly bought into it."
Rob, who lives off-grid in north Wales, told the programme he has stocked up on so many supplies he "wouldn't even notice" if a disaster struck.
But he said he still felt there was "a bit of scaremongering" going on and wondered if he would ever need it all.
Why is the government telling people to stockpile now?
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the advice - which is similar to guidance issued by the previous government - was not triggered by any "particular piece of intelligence", but rather about improving "national resilience" more generally.
The government's announcement focused on extreme weather events, which are becoming more frequent because of man-made climate change - but Streeting also referred to the threat of "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, and supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".
Prof Easthope said she has been lobbying the government to launch this sort of campaign for "about 16 years".
She said successive governments have been hesitant of "putting out information that might cause tension" - and speculated that this advice may have been "rushed" out ahead of Storm Austen hitting the UK.
While many of us will already have a stash of tinned food in the cupboards, fewer homes are likely to have a store of bottled water.
Paul from Torquay, Devon, said to Radio 5 Live: "Who on earth carries three day supply of water?"
He added: "I think they've made it our responsibility, rather than their responsibility."
Do other countries have similar emergency advice?
Prof Easthope described the UK as "light years" behind neighbouring countries when it comes to preparedness.
"Countries like Scandinavia, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, they've been good at this for years," she said.
France advises people to store 72-hours' worth of food, while the German government says homes should have enough supplies to last for a 10-day period.
"This is one area where I'm very comfortable saying we are playing massive catch-up," added Easthope.
Awareness campaigns such as "think 72 hours" make a big difference in the US, Australia and "all around Europe", she said.
However, in the UK, she said disaster messaging often gets parodied, or governments are accused of "panic-mongering".
"We have seen the pendulum shift" in recent years, she adds, saying that "we are now seeing people recognise this" as an issue that needs tackling.

article_title: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
article_content:
Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
- Published
The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.
With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common".
The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.
Burnham added: "It's not about panicking... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."
At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner joked that her emergency box, external would include a bottle of wine.
She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while."
Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work.
"But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup.
"I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those."
Last month, the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.
The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".
Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.
"Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.
"It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience."
- Why should I stockpile and what will I need? 
  - Published16 hours ago
- Military aircraft to help get UK 'on front foot' to fight wildfires, Burnham says 
  - Published17 hours ago
A checklist drawn up by the government recommends having nine litres of water per person – enough for three days – along with non-perishable food such as tinned meat and vegetables or dried fruit.
The government suggests having an FM radio, either battery or wind-up. During a national crisis, the BBC would prioritise broadcasting news, as well as health and safety information. In the event of a severe power cut, FM radio will be the best way to receive these updates.
The list also suggests hand sanitiser, wet wipes and toiletries, food for any pets, supplies for any babies, a torch, blankets, a charged power bank for devices, cash in case payment systems collapse, a first aid kit and copies of important documents.
Earlier, Treasury minister James Murray told BBC Breakfast he has not yet followed the government's guidance on stockpiling supplies to prepare for a crisis.
He said he had a stockpile of coffee, but pointed out that neighbouring countries including Ireland, France and the Netherlands had given the same guidance "for quite a long time".
He added: "I'm not going to pretend I've followed all that advice myself yet."
Speaking on the same programme, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she was "stocked up for the week at any time".
She said the previous Conservative government had issued similar advice on preparing for emergencies, but added: "What I'm more concerned about is that it doesn't look like [the government] are explaining what the risks we are under are, and what they are doing about the big things.
"Families can stock up but what's going on with defence, the cyber attacks, the hybrid warfare? The money to look after the country has not been forthcoming."

article_title: Rubio tells Cubans ‘now is the time’ to act to see political change
article_content:
Marco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change in their country to act, saying “now is the time” moments after Donald Trump told a Friday rally for candidates in south Florida that US warships could intervene in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.
The US secretary of state, in his social media post addressed “to those who seek to create positive change”, urged Cubans to capitalize on Trump’s plans. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said.
The top US diplomat, whose parents left Cuba for the United States before the socialist revolution there, seemed to mistakenly use the word “discrete”, meaning separate, rather than “discreet”, meaning private or secret.
Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days before midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the US war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.
“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”
Havana on Friday mocked the “desperation” of the US following the comments made by Rubio and Trump.
“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban deputy foreign minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.
“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”
Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would “be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.
In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of US military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it”.
Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba had been a national security threat for years because of its ties to US adversaries and that Trump was intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wanted to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the US could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.
Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a 29 September interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.
“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.
“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing. We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”
Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the US side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.
During his address to the United Nations general assembly last month, Trump said Rubio – son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership – was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”, saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep”.
Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal”, adding: “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”
Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.
Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk , and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have immigrated, many to the United States.

article_title: Free Speech Union hit by internal allegations of racism and sexually inappropriate remarks
article_content:
The Free Speech Union (FSU) is reeling from internal grievances involving allegations of racism, workplace discrimination and sexually inappropriate remarks by senior members of staff, the Guardian can reveal.
A key figure in the campaign group, the chief operating officer, Sigrun Olafsdottir, departed late last week after employees alleged that she told a junior member of staff she would “never hire a black person” as a part of a one-on-one meeting late last year.
The organisation’s legislative affairs director, Sam Armstrong – who is also head of communications for the Reform MP Robert Jenrick – has meanwhile been accused of making staff members uncomfortable by discussing the American actor Sydney Sweeney’s “assets” in a meeting with more than a dozen staff.
The claims cap a difficult period for the FSU, which was founded by the Conservative life peer Toby Young, and which critics see as a partisan rallying point for anti-woke grievance.
And they may complicate how the organisation seeks to publicly present itself, as a nonpartisan group that seeks to defend “free speech” from the overreach of censorious authorities – one which often raises money from its 50,000 members to do so.
In July, the Guardian reported that the US state department had allocated $5m to the international umbrella organisation that oversees the FSU, part of a larger effort by the Trump administration to promote rightwing causes in Europe. The state department appeared to withdraw this grant after the Guardian reported on the allocation.
In August, the Guardian reported on questions about the organisation’s practices around charity crowdfunding, centred on an instance in which the FSU appeared to raise £60,000 for a legal case that was ultimately fought pro-bono. Much of the FSU’s work consists of raising money for people who it argues have faced inappropriate consequences for exercising their right to free speech.
Lord Young told the Guardian that that case was “not handled on an exclusively pro bono basis”, saying there was another lawyer involved and the person whose case it was had separate legal costs.
These revelations have come alongside a period of internal turmoil. Eight members of the FSU’s small staff have departed within the past year. The Guardian understands that a crucial part of this disquiet has been the allegation of racism against Olafsdottir. The Guardian has spoken to multiple sources about these allegations and viewed documentation related to parts of the claims.
Employees complained that Olafsdottir was frequently “hostile” towards younger members of staff. This alleged hostility was said to occur during the FSU’s in-person gatherings.
The staff of the FSU work remotely but meet regularly for in-person events. These often take place at pubs and hotels, with some personnel said to drink heavily late into the night. Employees of the FSU described blurred boundaries and instances of aggression and discriminatory behaviour on the part of some senior staff during these sessions.
Olafsdottir and Armstrong declined to comment. Young told the Guardian he could not comment on “internal employment matters”. On the incident in which Sydney Sweeney was discussed, he said it related to an FSU member’s case, adding: “There was therefore nothing untoward or unprofessional about the conversation.”
Sources who spoke to the Guardian described Olafsdottir as a prominent presence in an organisation that employs slightly more than two dozen people across the UK and Scotland, and close to Young.
She was not the only senior leader alleged to have made staff members uncomfortable. Several FSU staff members described discomfort at Armstrong’s behaviour. They described an all-staff video meeting during which Armstrong discussed Sweeney’s physique, shortly after Sweeney had appeared in the controversial American Eagle “good jeans” ad. More than a dozen staff were present, and more than half were women. Armstrong joked that Sweeney was the “biggest” story in free speech that week.
“He [went] on to talk about her ‘assets’ at length. It was this continuous joke about her ‘assets,’” said a staff member who was on the call. “It was really stupid and really weird.”
The Guardian has seen FSU text messages referring to the Sweeney episode. In one of them, the FSU’s engagement director ribbed Armstrong and others as “a bunch of chaps so alpha in appreciation of Sydney Sweeney’s assets”.
Armstrong, whose webpage describes him as a political consultant and journalist, attended one high-profile meeting between Young and Sarah B Rogers, a US state department official who has aggressively mocked the UK in public appearances.
The group remains active in raising funds from its 50,000 members, and this week representatives visited 10 Downing Street to deliver a petition on saving jury trials.
Staff who have left the organisation – many of them early in their careers – expressed a sense of betrayal to the Guardian over the workplace climate in the FSU. One suggested the prospect of funds from the state department, and blurred lines around crowdfunders, had eroded internal checks further.
The FSU was “getting a bit cowboy” with “too much money sloshing around”, they said.

article_title: Trump says Burnham 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
article_content:
Trump says Burnham 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
- Published
US President Donald Trump has praised Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the UK government's decision to approve production from the North Sea's Jackdaw gas field.
He said he had spoken with Burnham, telling reporters on Friday that the decision would "make the UK a very rich country".
Trump said: "The other prime minister, the previous man, Starmer. He's a very nice man, but he never got it done, and this one is getting it."
The decision had been subject to intense debate around its environment and economic impact and came after years of legal challenges.
Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week.
Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.
Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.
Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas.
He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years."
Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country."
In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw.
The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read.
It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power".
Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK.
Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world".
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed.
However, Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision by not giving any regard to climate obligations - things he said "have to be considered in the round".
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month, but that it would not lower energy bills this winter.
She said the decision was "compatible" with legally binding climate commitments, adding: "We remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050."
Environmental groups have criticised the Jackdaw approval. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said it was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Meanwhile, Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments".
During their Friday talks, Trump and Burnham spoke about the Falkland Islands and the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between British and Israeli companies.
In September, the Argentinian government threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands, and earlier this month, it began legal action to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields.
Burnham raised the "economic consequences of Argentina's coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the Islanders' right to develop their natural resources", Downing Street said.
The two leaders also discussed Ukraine, with the prime minister underlining the importance for Ukraine "to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion", according to Number 10.
Starlink technology is a satellite system owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company which Ukraine has relied upon during the war.
In recent days, Ukraine has been recording issues with the network, according to sources within the defence ministry. This has affected the country's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations.
The Downing Street statement added: "The Prime Minister recognised the work of President Trump to bring Putin to the negotiation table and the leaders agreed to work together, alongside international partners to bring an end to the bloodshed."

article_title: UK politics: Andy Burnham warns of ‘winter of greater flooding’ – as it happened
article_content:
Burnham: 'Winter of great flooding' could be on its way
As south west England deals with the aftermath of Storm Austen, Andy Burnham said the United Kingdom could face “a winter of greater flooding”.
The prime minister was asked if the Government was playing catch-up with civil preparedness as he attended a summit organised to learn from the summer’s record wildfires.
A second storm, Storm Boelo will bring disruption across the UK on Saturday.
Burnham told reporters on Friday: “No, we are having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.
“Obviously weather events – and we’re in a situation today where the UK is facing storms, and obviously we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now – it is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments.
“So we are having that conversation about resilience. That’s why we’re holding this summit today, it’s why we’re putting the guidance out to the public.
“We potentially are facing a winter of greater flooding, so it’s about recognising all of those risks and taking action.”
The government has continued to tell people that they should prepare 72 hours worth of supplies at home, including a torch and radio.
The prime minister did not follow Angela Rayner’s lead, who said her emergency supplies would include mascara and wine, but said his crisis staples were beans, soup and twiglets.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the government should focus on “looking after us” rather than urging people to stockpile.
Burnham will appear on Channel 4 this evening on Gogglebox as part of the Stand Up To Cancer fundraiser.
As the government continues to talk about the importance of building up supplies at home in case of an emergency, Andy Burnham has told BBC Radio 5 Live what would be in his essentials.
According to the prime minister it’s baked beans, soup and twiglets making up his crisis store. In fact Burnham said he “can’t get by for too long” the marmite-flavour rod-shaped crisps.
Asked on BBC Radio 5 whether, like Angela Rayner, he would make sure his emergency supplies included a bottle of sauvignon blanc, Burnham said: “I’m not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you’re in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you’ve done the hard work.
“I’ll stick to the basics, I think. I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard and soup. I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have as well as well as Twiglets. I’m not sure I can get by for too long without those.”
He and Healey rated their favourite crisps from a selection provided, with the PM deciding McCoy’s Salt and Vinegar beat the pub staples pork scratchings and scampi fries to take his top spot. Twiglets were not an option.
The Scottish Greens remain open to joining the SNP in government again, the party’s co-leader has said.
Speaking in Inverness ahead of his party’s conference, Ross Greer, asked if the Greens would join an SNP government again, told PA: “The short answer to that is yes. The Greens believe that the public expect politicians to cooperate together to actually get stuff done where that’s possible. Where we disagree, we’re going to do it really, really robustly.”
Andy Burnham has rather light-heartedly defended the length of his answers at PMQs when presented with statistics suggesting he takes much longer the predecessors to make his points.
PA reports that after being told by BBC Radio 5 Live’s Matt Chorley that his answers were “up to 50%” longer than those of his near predecessors in the role, the prime minister said:
People can be the judge, can’t they? I try and answer people’s questions and I give them a proper answer rather than dismissing what they say. If that makes me a little longer than others, well, so be it. Don’t people want politicians to answer the question?
I feel they do but I’m only – what is it, four or five PMQs in? – I will always take all kinds of feedback but I’m not going to change the approach that I’ve taken so far which is to answer people’s questions, focus on problem solving rather than point scoring. I was praising the Leader of the opposition at PMQs last week, maybe that made my answer longer.
Political correspondent Lexy Topping has taken a step back to look at Andy Burnham’s approach to governing since entering No 10. The key, it seems, is ‘everyday fixes’ to win public support.
Before that, as part of the focus on “everyday fixes”, the prime minister announced a plan to remove VAT from electricity bills, a £2 cap on single bus fares across England and take action on “auto-renew” subscriptions. There’s also promises to crack down on pricey branded school uniforms, ban specious discounts, limit vape and betting shops and stop airlines charging families to sit together on planes. At this rate all minor annoyances in the UK will be eradicated by Christmas.
The idea is simple, says one policy adviser. “People expect the government to be able to do something about things which are unfair – big or small,” they said. “It sends a message that the government is on people’s side, its ready to act, and it can genuinely make a difference.”
Ahead of next week’s budget the Guardian is giving you the chance to step into John Healey’s shoes and see what measures you would put into his red box next week.
Our ‘You be the Chancellor’ game allows you to make a series of decisions, and see how it would affect the government’s fiscal headroom on Wednesday. Meanwhile the markets and polls will react to your policies.
As the former king of the BBC’s election swingometer Peter Snow used to say, just a bit of fun.
Kemi Badenoch has waded into the preparedness debate and said ministers should “look after us” rather than just giving advice.
She told the Press Association during a visit to Cheshire constabulary headquarters that many people in rural areas already take precautions because they have no shops nearby.
Badenoch said: “We have power cuts on occasion, and if you’re in the middle of nowhere, it’s dark and cold. You do need to look after yourself.
“What I want to see is the government doing what it needs to do to look after us.
“The Defence Secretary is talking about stockpiling, but he won’t tell us if he’s found the money to pay for our defence.
“We need him to be looking after this country, manning the borders, ensuring the soldiers have all the equipment that they need.”
She later added: “I don’t mind them giving advice. I worry that between the prime minister being on Gogglebox and then talking about stockpiling canned goods, they’re not actually doing the really difficult stuff that will protect the country.”
In a comment piece, Polly Toynbee has said London Assembly member Andrew Boff, who resigned from the Conservative party this week, is a sign of where the party’s future should be.
The chair of the London Assembly, Andrew Boff, resigned this week from the Conservative party after 53 years of membership. He quit after being blocked from entering the race to be Tory candidate for London mayor because he supports the European convention on human rights (ECHR), putting him at odds with Kemi Badenoch’s hardline position.
Messages of support for one of the capital’s longest-serving Conservative politicians quickly poured in from fellow Tories. Gavin Barwell, Theresa May’s Downing Street chief of staff, has backed Boff, warning Badenoch that others would follow him over the ECHR edict. But the rest sent messages privately, not daring to reveal themselves under a leadership that doesn’t tolerate dissent. In an interview last year, Badenoch decreed that rebels “should not and cannot stand as a Conservative candidate” if they do not agree with leaving the ECHR. She also bars anyone supporting net zero.
When Boff applied, for the seventh time, to be considered as Conservative candidate for London mayor, he didn’t really expect to be selected – but nor did he expect to be summoned to be told he was barred from entering the race. In a statement he pointed to the fact that Winston Churchill helped found the ECHR after the second world war, arguing “it was never a leftwing project” but a “safeguard against arbitrary government”. What’s more, he points out to me,the “convention doesn’t even mention asylum seekers”, Badenoch’s main justification for leaving the treaty.
Andy Burnham has said the final decision on the Rosebank oil field will be “done properly” when asked about the potential for an approval to be overturned by the courts.
It comes after ministers gave the go-ahead to the Jackdaw gasfield, 150 miles east of Aberdeen in Scotland, after years of uncertainty and a court case.
The decision drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland in Scotland’s north.
Asked about the possibility of courts overturning a Rosebank approval, Burnham said on Friday: “Well, that’s a decision that will be taken in due course.
“What we have done this week is taken great care over the decision about Jackdaw because it wasn’t done properly in the past, and that led to the decision being struck down.
“What people can be certain about is things will be done properly going forward.
“And in relation to Jackdaw, people will question: Was that the right decision? It is going to be a bridge to a renewable future?
“The funds that it will release will be able to go into building out that clean energy system that the country needs, which is a further part of our national resilience going forward.”
A DUP minister has said he is confident MP Carla Lockhart will stay in the party despite leaving its main decision-making body amid a row with party leadership over the future of Stormont.
Lockhart is at odds with DUP leader, fellow MP Gavin Robinson, over whether the party should withdraw deputy first minister Emma Little-Pengelly from the power-sharing executive.
Lockhart has argued that the party should pull Little-Pengelly from her post as it would automatically remove Sinn Féin first minister Michelle O’Neill from her position in the joint office they lead together.
Such a step would effectively collapse the devolved administration in Belfast. However other individual departmental ministers would remain in post and the Northern Ireland assembly would continue to sit for a further six months.
Lockhart believes the party should no longer serve alongside O’Neill after the Sinn Féin vice-president took part in an allegedly unlawful protest on the Garvaghy Road in Portadown last month.
Education minister Paul Given told BBC Radio Ulster: “Carla bleeds DUP just like I do, and of course it’s disappointing that she felt not able to remain as a party officer.
“But I very much welcome her remaining within the DUP because she is a valued member of our party, and I know that she’ll continue to make an important contribution to the party and in leading people in Upper Bann.”
According to the Press Association, when asked about his views on the Celebrity Traitors so far, the prime minister said: “Well, obviously, I would say that politicians have got a lot to offer to those who are looking for tactics in relation to The Traitors.”
Burnham, who seized power from Sir Keir Starmer after plotting to be prime minister for more than a year, added: “I think we can spot faithfuls and traitors a mile off.
“Our profession teaches us to do that, but it’s a great programme.
“It’s a great example of how strong British broadcasting is, and of course the BBC.”
Meanwhile he responded to housing secretary Angela Rayner’s suggestion wine and mascara would be in her emergency supplies kit, after the government recommended people to prepare, Burnham said: “I’m not sure that that’s the top of the list in terms of the advice that we’re giving to the to the public.
“You need to have a clear head when it comes to a challenging situation.
“So yeah, some tins of food, some bottled water. But I’m sure people are allowed a glass or two as well to get them through a difficult situation.”
Burnham: 'Winter of great flooding' could be on its way
As south west England deals with the aftermath of Storm Austen, Andy Burnham said the United Kingdom could face “a winter of greater flooding”.
The prime minister was asked if the Government was playing catch-up with civil preparedness as he attended a summit organised to learn from the summer’s record wildfires.
A second storm, Storm Boelo will bring disruption across the UK on Saturday.
Burnham told reporters on Friday: “No, we are having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.
“Obviously weather events – and we’re in a situation today where the UK is facing storms, and obviously we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now – it is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments.
“So we are having that conversation about resilience. That’s why we’re holding this summit today, it’s why we’re putting the guidance out to the public.
“We potentially are facing a winter of greater flooding, so it’s about recognising all of those risks and taking action.”
Andy Burnham is addressing the wildfire summit in north west England after a summer which saw homes destroyed by fires during the record-breaking heat.
He said Britain needs to be on the “front foot” and that the country had been playing “catch up” for too long.
The prime minister said he expected similar summers going forward.
He told the summit: “I think too often in the past we’ve been playing catch up, and today is trying about trying to get on the front foot and recognise that the summer we’ve just had is likely to be a more regular situation going forward. So make ourselves that bit stronger when it comes to the summer of 2027, and then indeed summers beyond.”
He earlier told journalists: “We lived through a summer that we’ve never seen before, with so many wildfires across the country. Fire and rescue services were stretched, firefighters working extremely difficult conditions, and it was right in that moment to commit to this summit, and today we’re making good on that, but also making some initial steps to improve our response because we will have to plan for summers like this going forward.
“So firstly: better equipment for our firefighters, particularly the PPE, more appropriate to working in very hot summer conditions because it’s very punishing work what they did this summer.
“Secondly, aerial support: so we may see on holiday other countries where there are planes putting water from above on the fires. We believe we need that capability. The Ministry of Defence will be equipping aircraft with that capability, so we’ll be better prepared for summers to come.
“Then thirdly: just better management of the land, so that fire doesn’t get the ability to spread. Those are the early commitments, but the summit will give us more as we go through it today, and people can be sure that we will be even better prepared next summer.”
Andy Burnham has said he believes indefinite leave to remain needs to be “earned through contribution”, but stopped short of committing to all of home secretary Shabana Mahmood’s immigration and citizenship reforms.
There has been speculation that Mahmood’s plans to double the amount of time care workers will need to live in Britain before claiming indefinite leave to remain will be watered down under pressure from Labour MPs.
Currently the wait is five years, but Mahmood said it should be raised to ten.
Burnham said: “We’re in a position where we’ve been consulting on those reforms, and we will come forward with our decisions soon.
“But I strongly support the Home Secretary when she says that settlement is a right to be earned through contribution, and that will be the principle that guides our reforms.”
Foreign secretary Ed Miliband is in Turkey today as he is set to join talks on the strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia.
Ministers from Britain, France and Germany as well as Italy, will meet in Turkey to discuss issues in the Middle East and the war in Ukraine.
Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt will also attend.
The UK said this week it would extend its military support for the Saudis, providing British fighter jets to shoot down Houthi drones and missiles fired into the kingdom.
Miliband will use the talks to point to Iranian tactics being replicated, including with Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia putting pressure on the maritime choke points of Bab El-Mandeb and the Suez canal.
Andy Burnham is “determined” to introduce the tourist tax across the country and could overrule councils and elected mayors, the Times has reported.
Burnham told an online meeting of mayors he wanted to counter the “negative” atmosphere around the overnight visitor levy. It has received some opposition from the hospitality sector and some mayors.
According to the Times, the prime minister told the National Economic Council: “If the mayor’s name is linked to a tax, it shouldn’t be the case that they’re not able then to pursue what is a mayoral ambition.
“So I think the rewiring of the state needs to clean out this a bit more as we go forward … We’ve got to get the brakes off growth basically and that’s something I’m determined to do.”
As Wes Streeting and James Murray have been recommending in the last 24 hours, the Government is advising people to stockpile supplies for three days.
Have you been persuaded to follow this advice? The Guardian would like to speak to you about what you have in your cupboard, and what other items you have in case of emergency.
Andy Burnham has been meeting armed forces veterans and Royal British Legion Poppy Appeal collectors to mark the start of the year’s campaign.
Burnham welcomed them to Number 10 North’s office in central Manchester, contrary to the usual convention of making a donation to the cause on the steps of Number 10 in Downing Street.
Good morning from London, where we’re less than a week from Andy Burnham and John Healey’s first budget, and the Government has been telling people to build up 72 hours of supplies in case of a disaster. We’ll be bringing you updates throughout the day. I’m Harry Taylor.
The Government has said that will not be putting together a “shopping list” for the public to buy in anticipation of a disaster, despite launching a campaign on Thursday which told people to stock up on supplies.
However Murray told Times Radio this morning: “This is not about the Government sending out a shopping list to everyone in the country.
“This is about putting the right information there on the government website, having an information campaign so that people are aware about it and then people taking the right choices for themselves about what they need to make sure they have supplies of at home.”
Meanwhile it’s five days until Healey’s budget, and Murray was asked on BBC Radio 4 whether he would be reducing red tape for business.
He said cutting “pointless bureaucracy” was “at the heart of what the Chancellor is going to be thinking about”.
Healey said the Treasury would aim to cut £800m of red tape for businesses at the budget, including reduced reporting requirements.

article_title: «Я не настолько гуманист, как Путин»: Зеленский объяснил, почему иногда вынужден отвечать жестко
article_content:
Президент Украины Владимир Зеленский заявил, что старается быть максимально прямым и честным в отношениях с президентом США Дональдом Трампом и, в отличие от российского диктатора Владимира Путина, «не играет с ним в игры». В то же время Зеленский признал, что нынешнюю политику Вашингтона в отношении Украины не всегда воспринимает как поддержку, а отношения Трампа с Путиным назвал «довольно хорошими». Об этом он сказал в интервью ABC News.
Журналист спросил Зеленского, чувствует ли он себя преданным Соединенными Штатами.
Президент ответил отрицательно, но добавил:
«Я чувствую то, что чувствую. Это не поддержка».
На вопрос, что пошло не так в его отношениях с Трампом, Зеленский ответил, что это личное решение американского президента: дружить с российским тираном или нет.
По его словам, Трамп действительно дружит с Путиным.
«Думаю, да. У них довольно хорошие отношения», — ответил президент Украины.
«Я не играю с Трампом в игры»
В то же время Зеленский подчеркнул, что стремится строить отношения с американским президентом максимально прямо. По его словам, между союзниками должна быть такая же честность, как между друзьями или членами семьи.
«Я не играю с Трампом в игры. В этом разница между мной и Путиным. Я не играю с ним ни в какие игры. Я прямой и честный», — заявил Зеленский.
Он также заверил, что Украина не пытается устраивать «политический театр» в отношениях с США.
По словам президента, Вашингтон должен знать истинную позицию Киева, так же как Украина должна уважать позицию американской стороны, даже когда между союзниками возникают разногласия.
Во время интервью Зеленский также прокомментировал неоднократные обвинения в том, что он якобы недостаточно благодарен Соединенным Штатам за помощь.
Президент признал, что иногда может быть «не очень вежливым», но объяснил это ситуацией, в которой находится страна.
«Сегодня, если Украина хочет выжить, ей нужны сильная армия, сильный президент, сильный народ. При всем уважении ко всем. Вот и всё. Именно поэтому моя реакция сильная. И именно поэтому на любое давление на меня я, конечно, буду отвечать. Конечно. Потому что иначе они нас съедят. Я имею в виду россиян. Конечно, им проще, потому что мы меньше, как они говорят. Но с нами, с народом Украины, не все так просто», — сказал он.
На вопрос журналиста, не обижают ли его обвинения в неблагодарности, Зеленский ответил отрицательно.
«Всё нормально. Я обычный человек. Я просто человек. Возможно, не такой большой гуманист, как Путин, конечно. Мы разные. Но в любом случае я действительно делаю всё, что могу», — сказал он.
Зеленский подчеркнул, что остается благодарным американцам и партнерам за помощь. Однако, по его словам, он не считает, что должен демонстрировать благодарность «каждую секунду».
«Между нами говоря, когда кто-то благодарит меня несколько раз, я чувствую, что с этим человеком что-то не так. Он хочет казаться лучше, чем есть на самом деле. Поэтому достаточно поблагодарить один раз, два раза, три раза — этого достаточно», — пояснил президент, добавив, что считает честные отношения лучше показной вежливости.
Зеленский иронично заметил, что лучше иметь партнера, который искренне благодарит тогда, когда испытывает благодарность, чем вести себя «как Путин»: демонстрировать благодарность, а потом «втыкать нож в спину».
description: Президент Украины ответил на обвинения в неблагодарности.

article_title: Tory activist in 'contract killing broker' claim had worked for party HQ
article_content:
Tory activist in 'contract killing broker' claim had worked for party HQ
- Published
A former Tory activist who appeared to offer to "broker" the hiring of contract killers in an undercover film report previously worked for Conservative headquarters.
Jack Ross was contracted to do social media work for the party until earlier this year, the BBC has been told.
It comes after Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch referred to them as "shocking allegations", adding that she did not "believe that person is a member anymore".
A Conservative spokesman said Ross's party membership had "been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation". It has reported that Ross said his words were not meant to be taken seriously.
Ross was paid to provide social media advice to the party for a brief period, the BBC has been told. He was never an employee or Conservative Campaign Headquarters pass holder.
However, he met Badenoch on several occasions as part of his role as chief executive of Turning Point UK, an offshoot of a right-wing American organisation.
Ross has also met several other right-wing politicians including the former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.
In undercover filming broadcast this week by Al Jazeera, Ross appears to offer to "broker" the services of contract killers.
The Al Jazeera report said its undercover journalist approached Ross in 2022 with a fictitious situation of a family business at risk of being taken over by a criminal gang.
Ross is alleged to have asked the undercover reporter what was needed from him, and listed violent options that could be bought including stabbing, shooting and killing.
Al Jazeera said Ross denied the finding "completely" and claimed everything he said to the reporter was not meant seriously.
Turning Point UK has been approached for comment.
description: Jack Ross was contracted to do social media work for the party until earlier this year, the BBC has been told.

article_title: UK government to make unprecedented intervention in setting of water bills
article_content:
Ministers will make an unprecedented intervention in water bills and how companies prioritise investment, directing bosses to bring down costs and stop leaks and sewage overflows.
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has told suppliers in England and Wales she plans to intervene in the next price review – conducted by the water regulator, Ofwat.
Sources at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Andy Burnham’s 10-year plan, which will follow next week’s budget, would hand the government more robust powers to keep bills affordable and direct local investment. But sources close to Eagle said there also needed to be immediate action as companies began to make decisions before the next price-setting process, expected to conclude in 2029.
There has never been government intervention in the five-year review process. It is run by Ofwat, which analyses companies’ business plans and determines how much can be charged to customers in their bills to fund investment and running costs.
Eagle has written to regulators and water company chief executives, saying that the process must meet specific government priorities, including offering bill payers much better value for money – though stopping short of demanding bill cuts.
The letter to companies and regulators says they must be focused on investment in new technology to save money, and early intervention on leaks and sewage. It also called for far better communication and decision-making power handed to local communities and leaders.
The first priority must be affordable bills, the letter says, adding: “Affordability means a laser focus on value for money for customers.”
The letter says the public is clear about what the objectives for the industry should be. “They want clean rivers. They want reliable water services. They want to know that their money is being spent wisely, and that bills are kept affordable. And they want confidence that the system is working in their interests.”
The letter warns company bosses that it will “not be a business-as-usual price review … it is the beginning of a long-term transition to a different model for the water sector”.
Defra sources said Eagle intended it to be the first in a series of changes that will be announced in the coming months on the water industry, calling it “one of the clearest symbols of public frustration with Britain’s infrastructure”.
A Defra source said the intervention by Eagle was a down payment on bigger changes that would come in the 10-year plan. The source said: “Angela will take a much more bullish approach to telling water companies and regulators what is expected from them. This is the start of a journey to a very different water system and one that delivers for the public.
“There are also things we want regulators and companies to be doing now and so Angela is using the levers she’s got to influence their investment decisions at an early stage and make sure they’ve got no excuses. As well as looking at ownership structures, there are other ways we can go further than what came before.”
The new intervention from Eagle comes as the government continues to explore more radical options for the stricken company Thames Water. The Guardian reported earlier this week that Burnham had told officials to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that meant spending taxpayer money and going to court.
Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames Water – which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn – but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.
The outcome of the last price review process in 2024 led to highly controversial bill rises, after Ofwat authorised a £104bn modernisation programme, funded in large part through progressive annual rate increases that will see average water bills surge by 36% over the second half of the decade. The biggest increase was allowed for Southern Water, whose customers will pay 53% more by 2030, at an average of £642 per year.
Over the summer, several major suppliers requested permission to charge billions more to cover mounting capital costs and debt obligations, sparking fury from campaigners and from politicians, including Burnham.
The prime minister criticised the decision, warning that bill payers must no longer be treated as a “blank cheque” or a “bottomless source of funding for other people’s failures”, saying ordinary households were being forced to plug massive corporate balance-sheet deficits.
However, campaigners for public ownership have warned the move will do little in practice to reduce bills or the environmental impact of sewage or leaks. Sophie Conquest, the lead campaigner at We Own It, said: “These proposals are yet more reshuffling of the deckchairs on the Titanic, and fall far short of Burnham’s promise to end 40 years of neoliberalism.
“This government should be intervening on behalf of households to stop bill hikes. If water companies can’t function without siphoning more and more money out of our pockets, then this government should let them go bust.
“From there, we can bring water affordably into public hands. Under public ownership, we can put people and the environment ahead of the interests of faraway shareholders and hedge funds.”
