article_title: Green councillors face Labour deadline to disown Zionism policy
article_content:
Green councillors face Labour deadline to disown Zionism policy
- Published
Labour is set to decide whether to end power-sharing with Green councillors after demanding they disown their party's policy that Zionism is a form of racism.
The BBC has been told Green groups have been given until Sunday to respond to the demand, after which Labour's ruling National Executive Committee (NEC) will decide whether the party will continue with local deals to share power.
Green groups in some areas have publicly stated they do not agree with the policy or have distanced themselves from it, reducing the likelihood the pacts will end.
But in other areas Green councillors are yet to specify where they stand on the issue, meaning local alliances appear more vulnerable to collapse.
The issue is the most acute in nine local authorities where Greens are key partners in power-sharing arrangements, such as making up majorities that enable budgets to be passed and policy decisions to be made.
These include Sheffield City Council, Warwick District Council and Lewes District Council, three authorities where Labour and the Greens are in direct coalition.
The other areas where the Greens play a key role are: West Oxfordshire District Council, Stafford Borough Council, Havant Borough Council, Broadland District Council, Derbyshire Dales District Council and Wealden District Council.
In other areas, Green councillors are not central to local alliances continuing to function. These include Runnymede Borough Council, where Green councillors have left the local ruling alliance folllowing Labour's ultimatum.
In some areas, such as Lewes, Wealden, Broadland, West Sussex and North Somerset, local Green groups have distanced themselves from their party's Zionism policy, or said they do not agree with it.
But other Green groups are yet to publicly respond to Labour's demands, meaning there is greater uncertainty over the future of their co-operation with the party.
In Stafford, the power-sharing arrangement means the Greens have one cabinet member on the authority, councillor Tony Pearce, who holds the climate change portfolio.
Councillor Pearce has been contacted for comment but has not yet responded.
The leader of the Stafford Green group, Doug Rouxel told the BBC they were "formulating a response" to Labour's letter which they would like to put to party members first.
Labour confirmed the if the Greens refused to reject the Zionism policy, a process would then be triggered to remove Pearce from his cabinet position in Stafford.
Elsewhere, the leader of the Labour group on the Green-led Lewes District Council has resigned from the party, following his own party's ultimatum.
Chris Collier, who has been contacted for comment, will now sit as an independent cabinet member on the Labour-Green alliance that was formed to run the council in May 2023.
The BBC has been told Collier did not agree with the tone of Labour's ultimatum to the Green Party over the Zionism policy.
Conference motion
The "Zionism is racism" motion was passed by members of the Green Party of England and Wales at its annual conference in Brighton last month.
The policy motion adopted by members said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.
It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
It has led to a backlash from Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including four of its five MPs.
Green leader Zack Polanski, who skipped the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, has said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.
Labour councillors require the approval of the party's NEC before entering into local tie-ups.
According to the party's rulebook, local groups must also "stand down" from power-sharing arrangements when asked to do so by their regional office.
By contrast, the Green Party of England and Wales allows local groups to make the final decision on where and whether to share power locally.
A Green Party spokesperson said: "For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong.
"Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic."
Additional reporting by Victoria Walton, Jennie Aitken, Hannah Miller, Vikki Irwin, Emily Hudson, Lucinda Adam.

article_title: Andy Burnham says he has emergency stockpile of beans, soup and Twiglets
article_content:
Andy Burnham has said he has stockpiles of beans, soup and Twiglets in case of a civil emergency, as he said a new government campaign was not a reason for panic buying.
The prime minister was questioned on his domestic supply situation after the Be Ready campaign advised households to have enough bottled water and long-life food to keep going in case of an emergency, such as one caused by a weather event or a cyber-attack.
Asked on BBC Radio 5 Live whether, like Angela Rayner, he would make sure his emergency supplies included a bottle of sauvignon blanc, Burnham said: “I’m not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you’re in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you’ve done the hard work.
“I’ll stick to the basics, I think. I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup. I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets. I’m not sure I can get by for too long without those.”
The campaign says people should ensure they have at least three days of supplies, including water, in case of an emergency, which is similar to advice given to citizens in some other European countries.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the nation also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.
The advice was general and longer-term, Burnham told 5 Live, rather than urgent. “It’s not about panicking, is it? It’s just about being prepared and having a sensible amount of supplies in the home … These events, sadly, in the world that we’re in are becoming more likely, and therefore it’s just sensible to be prepared.”
Asked about a message from a listener who was worried about supplies running low as people tried to stock up, Burnham said: “It’s not about panic buying. I understand what your listener is saying there, but it’s about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation.”
Speaking earlier to the BBC, the Treasury minister James Murray admitted to being less prepared. He said: “I’ve got quite a lot of coffee in my house … it’s for individual people to take choices. I’m not going to say: ‘Here’s a government shopping list.’” He added: “I’m not going to pretend I’ve followed all that advice myself yet.”
He said the advice was in part a matter of bringing the UK into line with other countries. He told BBC Breakfast: “If you look at, say, Ireland or other countries in Europe like France and Netherlands, they’ve had this system for quite a long time, the idea of having a bit of stuff at home to protect yourselves in case something goes wrong.
“So it’s quite normal in other countries. I think it’s a bit more interesting here because we haven’t really talked about it as a country in recent years.”

article_title: Earnings limit of up to £140K for first-time buyers loan scheme
article_content:
Earnings limit of up to £140K for first-time buyers loan scheme
- Published
Households will need to earn less than £110,000 to qualify for the government's new loan scheme for first-time buyers, or £140,000 for homes bought in London.
As first reported by The Times, external, the earnings limits are expected to be confirmed at the Budget next week.
The Your First Home scheme will offer government-backed equity loans worth 20% of new-build properties in England bought from participating developers.
The loans, which will also be subject to an initial interest-free period, are designed to help people buy a home with deposits as low as 2.5%.
Previous schemes to help first-time buyers did not restrict eligibility by income but faced criticism for stoking house prices by allowing relatively wealthy households to borrow more.
Unveiling the Your First Home Scheme at last month's Labour conference, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it would focus on those who "really need support".
The Times reported that ministers had initially decided to set the earnings limits at £90,000 for homes outside outside London and £110,000 in the capital, before concluding this would deny access to too many middle-earning couples, such as teachers and nurses.
The government has also argued that the scheme will help to boost housebuilding, after ministers conceded they are set to miss a target to build 1.5 million homes in England by the next election.
Help to Buy
Labour has said the scheme will be funded by within existing government budgets, but is yet to provide details of which other areas will see their spending cut.
Developers taking part in the scheme will also be asked to contribute towards running costs.
The Home Builders Federation, which represents developers, has welcomed the plans and urged the government to move quickly to set up the scheme.
The Conservatives have however branded the proposals a "colossal admission of failure" of Labour's housebuilding record, and expressed concerns that the new developer levy could push up the price of new homes.
Like the Help to Buy scheme launched under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, the scheme will use equity loans, which are linked to changes in the value of properties they are used to purchase.
That scheme, which initially ran between 2013 and 2021, enabled all home purchasers to put down a 5% deposit on a newly built home worth up to £600,000.
Up to 20% of the cost of the home was funded by a shared equity loan, which was interest-free for the first five years.
A second version of that scheme, which ran from 2021 to 2023, restricted access to first-time buyers and applied regional-level price caps to the properties could be bought under the programme.

article_title: Briton facing forced separation from baby son after Sweden orders his deportation
article_content:
A British photographer is facing deportation from Sweden and forced separation from his 16-month-old son after authorities ruled in favour of the country’s immigration interests.
Simon Montgomery’s application to remain after the birth of his son last year was rejected on several grounds by Sweden’s migration agency, a decision that was then upheld by the migration court.
He is appealing to the higher migration court, arguing that he has EU freedom of movement rights as his son is a German citizen through his mother. “I am not here because I want to be in Sweden, I am only in Sweden to be with my son,” he said.
The couple separated shortly after the child was born but Montgomery, who grew up without his father in his life, said he was determined to stick around and be there for his newborn.
The pair have legally recognised joint custody, with a parenting agreement that meant his time with his son increased as he got older and no longer needed night-time breastfeeding.
He said he saw his son three days a week and took an active part in his care and daily routine with a “stable parenting plan” agreed via discussions with the municipal family law service.
He moved to Sweden after Brexit so was not entitled to any withdrawal agreement residency rights, but applied to stay on the basis he was the father of an EU citizen.
Montgomery said it was shocking that Sweden was prepared to separate a son from his father, even though the child had rights under EU law as well as international conventions. “Everything in Sweden is about the children’s right to both parents,” Montgomery said.
“But this seems to be ignoring all of that, when it comes around to immigration. Sometimes I feel like people don’t know what happens here. That’s why it’s so important to have these stories told.
“Everyone’s so friendly here; society works and things are nice. And when you tell them what’s happened, they just look shocked. They think you must have done something wrong, and when I explain I have done nothing wrong they just don’t understand.”
Montgomery said he was unable to leave Sweden to see elderly relatives in the UK for fear he would be blocked from returning to be with his son.
“It’s almost like torture in some ways, like having to make these decisions between staying to fulfil your parenting roles and not being able to visit my 98-year-old grandmother back in the UK and say my goodbyes,” he said.
His residency application, made when his son was six months old, was rejected last December by the migration agency on the grounds there was no evidence he had “actual care” for the child, who at that point still stayed overnight with his mother.
It also said he was free to maintain a relationship with his son from afar as he could enter the country visa-free and “still have the opportunity to visit the child in Sweden”.
He appealed against the decision but the court this month sided with the authorities, which assessed, according to the ruling, that the “state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs your interest in the protection of your private and family life in a proportionality assessment”.
Montgomery said he was taken aback by the court’s suggestion he did not need to be in Sweden full-time because he could visit his son by entering the country as a visitor. “Because I can come here visa-free, [they say] it shouldn’t interrupt my parenting ability. That’s crazy because I look after my son three days a week now … and overnights are about to start very soon.”
According to court papers, the decision to reject an application for residency and a simultaneous decision that he should be deported was made “primarily on the grounds that he had not demonstrated that he met the conditions for the right of residence as a family member of an EEA citizen”.
His lawyer argued that if he were “forced to leave Sweden, this would undermine the process and create instability for his son”. They added: “His son is an infant and is in a critical attachment phase where it is in his best interest to have both parents physically present and actively involved.”
They argued that the boy’s father’s presence was “particularly important” because his former German partner did not have a family network to rely on if she was sick or at appointments.
“Deportation would constitute a disproportionate interference in their family life,” they said, arguing that the lower migration court had interpreted “actual care” – evidence of a child’s relationship with a parent – “too narrowly on the grounds that the son primarily lives with his mother”.
They alleged forcibly separating a son from his father would violate article 8 of the European convention of human rights.
Montgomery is appealing against the case to the higher court but said he wanted to share the story so people understood how immigration law was being implemented.
Sweden’s migration agency has been approached for comment. The German government said it could not comment on the case.
author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent

article_title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets
article_content:
Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets
- Published
The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have received suspended prison sentences after they admitted to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election.
Anthony Lee used "inside information" emerging from a private meeting called by then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak to bet on the general election date months before it took place, Southwark Crown Court heard.
Lee and his wife Laura stood to win more than £23,000 had their cheating not been uncovered, the court heard.
Lee was sentenced to 10 months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, while his wife was sentenced to four months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for a year.
Amy Hind, a former Tory party employee who was working as an NHS business support manager, was also sentenced to six months' imprisonment, suspended for a year, after previously pleading guilty to cheating on the date of the election.
Judge Tony Baumgartner, sentencing the three of them, said their conduct "risked undermining" the confidence the public has in the Conservative Party "as an institution", "undermining trust in the democratic process" and the "integrity of the gambling system".
The trio were among several people charged with betting offences by the Gambling Commission.
The trials of other defendants will take place next year and in 2028.
Former Conservative MP Craig Williams, who was Sunak's closest parliamentary aide at the time, pleaded guilty in June and will be sentenced at a later date.
'Profit for themselves'
Sunak's decision to call a general election for July 2024 was a surprise to many, including several Conservative MPs, who were expecting an autumn date.
The court heard that Sunak held a private Downing Street meeting on 10 March of that year to discuss possible dates.
Neither Lee nor his wife attended the meeting, but the couple began betting online on the election being held in July or between July and September, the court heard.
Prosecutor Zoe Johnson said: "Although not at Number 10, the overwhelming inference is that Anthony Lee was receiving inside information as the meeting went on and was acting upon it."
She added: "Together they were using it to make a profit for themselves."
Lee placed or tried to place 71 bets during the period, while his wife placed eight and attempted a ninth, the court heard.
Baumgartner described Anthony Lee as a "central figure" in the preparation of the general election, who sat at a group of desks within Tory HQ known as the "God Pod".
Representing Lee, barrister Richard Pratt said his client did not concretely know the working date of the election, saying it "still represented a gamble from his point of view".
The barrister told the court: "It was always possible the prime minister could change his mind."
Pratt said there "wasn't any direct manipulation" by the defendant.
Laura Lee worked for the Tories as their "head of international" and had been selected as the party candidate for Bristol North West for the election.
Baumgartner said she had no involvement in the election planning and her access to information "came predominantly" from her husband.
The court heard Hind's husband Anthony worked as a deputy digital director for the Conservatives but did not place any bets himself.
Baumgartner said Hind's husband "was party to emails relating to the forthcoming general election and was one potential source of your inside information".
The judge later said "someone else who worked within the heart of CCHQ" could have given her the "highly confidential" information.
The court heard Hind placed four bets and made three further unsuccessful attempts to place bets. The unsuccessful attempts were for £767, £700 and £750.
The judge described Hind's bets as a "clear departure from your previous betting history", noting: "Before the present offending, your largest stake had been £10.50, and only seven of your 3,399 recorded selections involved a stake of that amount."
'Justice has been served'
Neither of the defendants have previous convictions and they are all of good previous character, the court heard.
Baumgartner described them all as having expressed remorse for their actions.
The trio are now subject to a 12-month prohibited activity requirement, banning them from accessing or using online gambling websites or applications.
Anthony Lee was ordered to complete 100 hours of unpaid work and pay more than £6,600 in compensation to a betting company, while Laura Lee must carry out 40 hours of unpaid work and pay £4,265.
Hind was ordered to complete 50 hours of unpaid work.
Katharine Diamond, General Counsel of regulators the Gambling Commission, reacted to the sentencing of the trio by saying "justice has been served".
She described the case as "a first of its kind" and said it demonstrated the commission's "commitment to protecting the integrity of betting markets".
description: Anthony Lee passed confidential information to his wife Laura Lee about when the 2024 general election would be held.

article_title: EU leaders to press Burnham to pay more towards Ukraine’s defence
article_content:
EU leaders will press Andy Burnham at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort in 2027.
EU officials argue that the UK, Canada and Japan should do more to support Ukraine, but entreaties to these G7 countries for extra financial aid at recent international meetings have not been answered, Brussels says.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, will call on the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, to contribute to Ukraine’s looming financial shortfall at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next week.
A similar request to the British prime minister will be made when he meets von der Leyen and the European Council president, António Costa, for a long-awaited EU-UK summit on 20 November in Brussels. It comes as the UK chancellor, John Healey, prepares for his first budget next week, weighing numerous calls for more spending against the rising cost of government borrowing and a darkening economic outlook.
Healey said earlier this month he was “working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine – military, diplomatic and economic”.
Ukraine says it faces a €70bn (£58bn) funding shortfall in 2027 to pay for its defence and civilian needs.
The EU and its member states are paying for 80% of Ukraine’s financial needs, according to the commission, which considers a “fair” EU share to be two-thirds, with the remaining third covered by other allies. “We will continue to lead, but we urgently need other partners to step up,” von der Leyen told reporters last week, without naming countries.
The EU last year agreed a €90bn loan for Ukraine, intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s funding in 2026 and 2027. But as Russia escalates its attacks, dragging the war into its fifth winter, Ukraine’s costs continue to spiral.
EU officials have prioritised non-EU G7 countries, above all the UK, Canada and Japan. But they are now casting the net wider and may look to Switzerland, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand to promise additional aid to Ukraine.
The British government says it has committed £25bn to Ukraine, including £16bn in military aid.
The UK is Ukraine’s fourth largest donor, behind the US, Germany and France, according to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine Support Tracker. But the picture changes when the UK’s share is weighted to GDP. The UK was assessed by the Kiel researchers as spending 0.86% of national income to support Ukraine, compared with 1.1% from France and 1.5% from Germany. These three large European economies spent significantly less than the Nordics and Baltics, such as Denmark (4.2%) and Estonia (3.8%). The UK is more in line with France and Germany when their contribution to EU programmes is stripped out.
The UK government has been contacted for comment.
The European Commission declined to comment on specific countries, but referred to a recent statement: “We always said that we cannot walk this alone … therefore our partners in general must step up.”
Ukraine will be one of several issues on the agenda at the EU-UK summit, where leaders are expected to conclude three agreements: a food and animal health (SPS) deal to reduce Brexit paperwork; the linkage of the EU and UK emissions trading schemes (ETS) to protect British industry from European carbon taxes; and a youth mobility scheme to enable 18- to 30-year-olds to live, work, travel and study across both sides of the Channel.
In a positive sign for British negotiators, the European Commission proposed deferring the question of university tuition fees, one of the last big sticking points. The UK would like to charge EU students at British universities the international rate, about four times higher than the domestic fee. The EU, where many officials are alumni of British universities, wants to return to the pre-Brexit status quo, when EU students paid home rates.
Commission officials have proposed resolving this thorny question in technical talks within six months of the 20 November summit, rather than risk derailing the high-profile leaders’ meeting. But senior EU sources are confident they still have leverage on the issue, as the SPS and ETS deals will not come into force until there is a youth mobility agreement acceptable to the European side, including on tuition fees.
“The three elements are a sort of gift to the UK, but not a massive gift,” an EU diplomat said, adding that the EU would still have clout in the negotiations over the fees. “The leverage is that the UK needs this [the other agreements].” UK hopes to strike economic security agreements with the EU, to avoid British industry becoming collateral damage of Europe’s defensive measures against China, are seen as another source of leverage.
But a second diplomat said there was no consensus among the EU’s 27 member states on postponing the tuition fees question until after the summit: “There is no clear majority saying ‘let’s drop it now for six months’,” they said.
author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels

article_title: PM defends Gogglebox appearance after Badenoch criticism
article_content:
PM defends Gogglebox appearance after Badenoch criticism
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has defended his decision to appear on a celebrity episode of Channel 4 hit show Gogglebox after opposition leader Kemi Badenoch said she was "amazed" he had time to do it.
Badenoch told BBC Breakfast that "even as a junior minister or as a secretary of state, I never had time to go on Gogglebox" and it "takes hours to do".
"I'm proud to support Stand Up To Cancer. I make no apology for trying to lead with a bit of lightness and at times a bit of humour, that's the way I go at things," Burnham said.
The former Greater Manchester mayor will appear on the programme alongside friend Steve Rotheram, the Labour mayor of the Liverpool City Region.
Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Burnham continued: "It is always a moment in the annual calendar where we support Stand Up To Cancer through Gogglebox," Burnham said of the recurring charity special.
"Steve and I are proud to do it.
"I'm trying to give the country a lift - trying to give the county some hope.
"That's always my approach and it's what I'm trying to do.
"It may not appeal to everybody when it comes to Gogglebox.
"It's Stand Up To Cancer night and I've always been somebody who puts my shoulder behind the fight against cancer."
However, Badenoch said appearing on the programme was "not my thing".
"What I'm amazed at is that Andy Burnham has got time to go on Gogglebox," she said.
"When you get a new job in politics it's so difficult.
"There's so much to do and it's like drinking from a fire hose.
"Even as a junior minister or as a secretary of state I never had time to go on Gogglebox - I just don't know how he's got the time.
"Gogglebox takes hours to do."
Describing Burnham as "on social media all day", she said she could do the same but "I wouldn't actually be able to do my job as leader of the opposition".
"My job is to hold him to account and I've seen a lot of prime ministers up close and I've never seen a prime minister have the time to do this much Goggleboxing, social media and Lad Bible," she added.
The special Gogglebox edition airs on Channel 4 at 21:05 BST.

article_title: Andy Bloke appears vaguely normal on Gogglebox – but Kemi dodged a bullet
article_content:
On nights like this a man can feel like he’s slipped through the looking-glass. I’m sitting on the sofa watching the TV, poised to make some gags about the prime minister and the mayor of Liverpool, who are themselves sitting on a sofa at No 10, poised to make some gags about what they are watching on TV.
Life doesn’t get more meta. The saving grace is that this episode of Gogglebox is a charity special for Stand Up to Cancer. Andy Burnham has requested that any journalist writing about the programme makes a donation to SU2C. I’m happy to oblige. Cancer is costing me a great deal more than money.
Meet Andy Bloke and his best mate, Steve Bloke. Two career politicians who still manage to look and sound vaguely normal. Not totally normal, mind. In real life, Steve Bloke would have said to Andy Bloke: “This is a total shithole you’re living in.” And Andy Bloke would have replied: “I know. It’s been a complete tip since Boris was here. You can’t get rid of the stains.”
You can’t deny that Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke are naturals at this. Not so bland that you want to turn off, a genuine connection with one another and a sense of fun that can’t be faked. Kemi Badenoch is reportedly annoyed she wasn’t invited on the programme.
The reality is that she’s dodged a bullet. Kemi just doesn’t have the woman of the people shtick. It’s something you’ve either got or you haven’t and she really doesn’t. If you let her on Gogglebox the only laugh you would get from her would be if she was livestreaming an execution from the US.
Mind you, it’s a slow burn. At first Andy and Steve look like they are feeling their way into the programme. But then so do the other celebs, Joe Lycett and his aunties, Stanley Tucci and his wife, Felicity, and Paul Whitehouse and Lenny Rush. The bantz feels a bit contrived and Andy Bloke – a Cambridge English grad – fails to recognise a photo of Margaret Atwood.
If Steve Bloke had been more on the ball, he’d have taken the piss mercilessly. But Andy and Steve are nothing if not a team. They’ve got each other’s backs and bond over filling in the blanks on members of the royal household in Only Connect.
“The king will be pleased with me at our next weekly meeting,” says Andy Bloke. He probably will be. I suspect Camilla will have made Charles watch this. The Man of the People meets the King of the People.
Halfway through, we get a reminder that this isn’t all about the laughs. There is the story of Callum who died at the age of 16 from brain cancer. Then the story of a woman whose mother died of pancreatic cancer when she was 11, was diagnosed with cervical cancer shortly after her child was born and whose husband died of bowel cancer a week after diagnosis. Sometimes shit really does happen to good people. All the celebs were fighting back tears. Andy was no exception.
“I’d like to see Match of the Day,” says Paul Whitehouse. “Why? To hear how crap Spurs are?” Lenny joked. Careful, Lenny, careful. We might be past the watershed but it’s still way too early for gags about Spurs.
But some football would have been nice. Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke would have been in their element. You could have made an entire programme of the pair of them pissing themselves laughing as Manchester United were beaten 4-1 by Como in the Champions League. It might even have earned a Bafta nomination.
For some reason, Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke were excluded from watching an X-rated natural history about some young birds that haven’t yet learned to fly and are so dim that they literally just stand there as tortoises eat them alive. Well, not all. One bird managed to hop on top of a tortoise shell. Though not before the tortoise had taken a chunk out of a wing. A happy ending of sorts. The celebs couldn’t quite believe they were being forced to watch such ultra-violence.
Normal service was resumed with a mercifully brief excerpt from Strictly Come Dancing. Brief because none of the real celebs had any idea who the celebrity contestants were. Andy Bloke admitted he still had PTSD from watching Ed Balls crashing around the dancefloor. Steve Bloke wisely helped himself to another beer. Maybe this was the way they used to do business when Andy Bloke was also a mayor.
We ended on an upbeat note. The Celebrity Traitors. Steve Bloke had no idea what was going on so Andy Bloke tried to fill him in as they cracked up over some crisps, pork scratchings and Skips. Me neither. I guess that was one were you had to be in the room.
“You should be quite good at this,” Andy Bloke said, encouragingly. “You can generally spot the wrong ’un in the room.” I guess that depends on how often you’ve been in the same room as Michael Gove.
Claudia Winkleman was announcing that the murder would be done in plain sight by boring a Faithful to death. Steve Bloke had the solution. Just make them watch the proceedings in the House of Commons. Boom boom.
Neither Steve nor Andy Bloke had much to say about Ross Kemp’s worrying levels of paranoia or Jerry Hall’s complete charisma bypass. How do you bore someone who is already boring? That could have been a question for Only Connect. Maybe we had come full circle. Or perhaps their gags about Rupert Murdoch got cut in the editing suite.

article_title: Police yet to receive £2m after A66 crash, says commissioner
article_content:
Police yet to receive £2m after A66 crash, says commissioner
- Published
A police force has still not received the £2m it was promised by the government in the wake of a car crash that led to the deaths of seven people, including two police officers, the local police and crime commissioner (PCC) says.
Cleveland PCC Matt Storey said Cleveland Police was still waiting for the extra funding promised by the home secretary in August.
Shabana Mahmood pledged the cash in light of challenges faced by the force following the deaths, which followed a pursuit on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August. Five young men were also killed.
The Home Office said the force would receive the £2m it had been promised by the end of November.
During the fatal crash, a Volkswagen Passat in which the five young men were travelling hit an oncoming marked Cleveland Police vehicle on the dual carriageway near Middlesbrough at about 03:39 BST.
Officers PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died at the scene.
The occupants of the VW Passat, which was travelling the wrong way down the A66 at South Bank - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy - were also killed.
On the morning of the crash, Cleveland Police said it received several reports of two vehicles being driven dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 had been seen ramming properties.
Further arrests were subsequently made in connection with organised crime, including the following weekend after another vehicle ramming.
Storey called for the immediate release of the £2m but also said policing costs linked to the crash, which had led to the arrests of 50 people so far, were now forecast to exceed £5m.
"These are exceptional and unavoidable costs arising from utterly tragic and devastating circumstances," he said.
"They are not costs that should be borne locally or met from existing policing budgets."
The PCC also criticised the lack of a "substantive" communication from the government about Cleveland Police's long-term funding.
Storey said the current police funding model, which Mahmood had previously committed to reviewing, disadvantaged the Teesside force.
He said the upcoming Budget was a chance to "align resources more fairly with demand" and "place Cleveland on a sustainable footing".
The 50 arrests have come as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following the crash.
Fifteen people have been charged - 13 men and two women ranging in age from 19-45.

article_title: This man has quit Badenoch’s increasingly hard-right Tory party – others should be brave enough to do the same | Polly Toynbee
article_content:
The chair of the London Assembly, Andrew Boff, resigned this week from the Conservative party after 53 years of membership. He quit after being blocked from entering the race to be Tory candidate for London mayor because he supports the European convention on human rights (ECHR), putting him at odds with Kemi Badenoch’s hardline position.
Messages of support for one of the capital’s longest-serving Conservative politicians quickly poured in from fellow Tories. Gavin Barwell, Theresa May’s Downing Street chief of staff, has backed Boff, warning Badenoch that others would follow him over the ECHR edict. But the rest sent messages privately, not daring to reveal themselves under a leadership that doesn’t tolerate dissent. In an interview last year, Badenoch decreed that rebels “should not and cannot stand as a Conservative candidate” if they do not agree with leaving the ECHR. She also bars anyone supporting net zero.
When Boff applied, for the seventh time, to be considered as Conservative candidate for London mayor, he didn’t really expect to be selected – but nor did he expect to be summoned to be told he was barred from entering the race. In a statement he pointed to the fact that Winston Churchill helped found the ECHR after the second world war, arguing “it was never a leftwing project” but a “safeguard against arbitrary government”. What’s more, he points out to me, the “convention doesn’t even mention asylum seekers”, Badenoch’s main justification for leaving the treaty.
The time may come, he warned, when extremists win an election on an even smaller vote share than Labour’s 34% in 2024 – and overturn all human rights legislation without the protections the ECHR affords. “That’s what authoritarian governments do,” Boff said. But he insisted that the committee, which vets Conservative candidates, didn’t listen. “They just repeated the same tropes, that activist judges are using the ECHR against parliament.”
Now he is free of the party straitjacket, Boff is planning to stand for London mayor as an independent, allowing him to say what he thinks about Badenoch.
He complains to me that the energy and resources that should promote the party “all go to promoting Kemi, Kemi, Kemi”. Thinking well of her in 2015, he says he had encouraged her to stand for the London assembly, where she served until 2017 before being elected to parliament. He says he found her “lazy and combative”.
Few will be surprised by Boff’s departure. But many will be wondering what took him so long. He was ejected from the Tory conference in 2023 for quietly heckling the then home secretary Suella Braverman’s speech, accusing her of homophobia and transphobia. “It is a signal to people who don’t like people who are LGBT+,” Boff, who is gay, said at the time as he condemned her speech as “trash”. Boff said that Braverman “was basically vilifying gay people and trans people by this attack on LGBT ideology”.
He was not alone in voicing criticism over the party’s direction. The former Tory MP Robert Buckland, fellow one-nationer and director of the Tory Reform Group, hurried out to defend Boff after his ejection from the conference, saying heckling was “part of the democratic debate” and that his treatment by security staff was “heavy-handed”.
Buckland was among the many one-nationers who lost their seat at the 2024 general election. But that traditional strand of Conservatism has not vanished – nor have those who used to vote for the Tories but now turn to the Liberal Democrats or simply boycott the ballot box.
Boff’s views represent a growing centre-right moderate strand that has been expelled or silenced under Badenoch’s leadership. Facing this hostile climate, one nation Tories have gone to ground in parliament; but outside the Commons, Prosper UK, a centrist Tory grouping led by the former mayor of the West Midlands, Andy Street, and the former Scottish Tory leader Ruth Davidson quietly gains strength.
Its mission statement is to win back moderate voters who snubbed the Conservatives at the last general election, and this message seems to have struck a chord, with the group attracting nearly 30,000 supporters since its launch in January.
It is worth examining Boff’s views, as many Conservatives who have signed up to Prosper UK are likely to share them. He calls himself a Thatcherite, strongly opposing Labour’s renationalisation plans, backing low taxes and a small state. He voted for Brexit, believing the words of the likes of Daniel Hannan, who claimed “absolutely nobody is talking about threatening our place in the single market”. But instead the Tories delivered a hard Brexit after what he calls an “atrocious” campaign.
Times have changed; as the political analyst Peter Kellner pointed out this week, Britain’s pro-Brexit majority has literally died out. Any so-called betrayal of the referendum is only betraying the dreadful legacy of the departed.
If the Conservative party has any future as a government, it won’t be under its present leader. A small bounce for improved performance in parliament will never overcome Badenoch’s growing distance from voters, including those who should be natural Tories.
Boff may be a throwback to an irretrievable, more moderate Conservative brand, like that of the Macmillan era – a voice from the good old days when traditional party allegiances were clearly defined. Or possibly he and Prosper UK are the vanguard of a reconstituted centre-right able to attract new voters as well as those who have deserted the Tories.
That won’t be easy: already there are gloating Spectator-aligned Tories who say that the party is better off without the likes of Boff, or any real concession to centrism. But we should have a care. The success of a respectable right matters to all in the left bloc of progressive parties, too. A centre right is needed to fight off the dark forces of the hard right and worse, here and across Europe. That Overton window framing politics needs a firm shunt towards a more rational debate on our future in Europe – and on saving the planet.

article_title: ‘Realistic and reassuring’: UK public ‘responding calmly’ to Be Ready campaign
article_content:
When the UK government launched its “Protect and Survive” public information campaign in 1980 on how to stay alive after a nuclear attack, it was met with a combination of scepticism, disbelief and derision.
The advice included how to build a “fallout room” at home, how to whitewash windows to protect from a blast, and how to store a dead body for up to five days.
You might expect this would have prompted widespread panic, but in fact it led to a political backlash, and was later lampooned on TV and in music.
It shows the risks governments take when launching such campaigns, and the fine balance that must be struck between hammering home a practical message without causing panic – or other unintended reactions.
The government’s new Be Ready campaign is advising the public to stock up on three day’s worth of supplies for use during severe weather or cyber-attacks, so help can be directed to the most vulnerable first.
In a concise, two-page document, it suggests people stock bottled water and non-perishable food for three days, a torch with spare batteries, a wind-up FM radio, a first aid kit and a copy of their passport. To stave off panic buying, it advises people to check their cupboards first and build up items gradually on regular shopping trips.
While there is no evidence the advice has triggered mass panic, the public is clearly responding. Jack Brown, who co-owns Sgt Prepper Shop, which stocks emergency food and survival tools, said he received a month’s worth of orders in the first 24 hours of the Be Ready campaign.
“I thought my phone was glitching or being hacked with the number of orders coming in,” he said.
Brown said the advice seemed sensible and proportionate. Three days was the “sweet spot”, he said, with most everyday emergencies like power cuts, a burst water main or flooding sorted within that timeframe.
It is also “realistic, affordable and fits in a cupboard”, he said, adding that asking people to stock up on a month’s worth of supplies would feel overwhelming and most people would do nothing at all.
A wind-up radio was also a sensible suggestion, and ones with a built-in torch and phone-charging USB port make them “one of the most useful bits of kit you can own”, he said.
Dr Sarita Robinson, associate dean for the school of psychology and humanities at the University of Lancashire, said there was little evidence to suggest these kinds of messaging campaigns cause panic.
“There’s this perception that if we tell people the truth we’re somehow going to panic them and it isn’t the case,” she said.
“When we use accurate messaging about emergency situations, the public will engage with that proactively. It’s when we start to hide information and there’s a void of information, that’s when things can go wrong for government.”
She said Be Ready was “realistic, quite low level, and should be reassuring because it’s basically treating the public like the grownups they are”.
Dan Goss, who runs Start Prepping UK, said traffic to his website was up 700% since news of the campaign emerged in August. He said he was glad to see the subject finally being taken seriously and spoken about in “plain language” by the government, and felt the risk of panic was low.
“The level of uptake required for that would be huge – you would need to have an enormous number of people all take the government’s advice very seriously and all jump on it as a priority,” he said.
“We’re definitely in a phase now where we’re seeing lots of more disruption to people’s lives – not necessarily apocalyptic disasters, but things that have a big impact on small areas, so this advice is very much needed.”
Robinson said the campaign showed how the perception of “prepping” has shifted, especially since the Covid-19 pandemic when most people will remember seeing empty supermarket shelves.
“We did a study during Covid that showed people who did mild levels of prepping, such as having food, masks and hand gel in the house a few weeks before the pandemic, had lower anxiety and depression, and less stress,” she said.
“The government really needs to portray that this is just normal, everyday, very common in other countries, and isn’t wearing a tinfoil hat and building a nuclear bunker in your back garden.”

article_title: Падіння російського дрона: сусідня країна вперше відреагувала рішучими діями
article_content:
Падіння російського дрона: сусідня країна вперше відреагувала рішучими діями
Молдова оголосила жорстку відповідь Росії через падіння дрона на території країни.
Міністерство закордонних справ Молдови засудило порушення повітряного простору країни та поклало відповідальність за інцидент на Росію. У зв’язку з цим Кишинів оголосив працівника російського посольства персоною нон ґрата.
Про це повідомляє МЗС країни.
Приводом для реакції став безпілотник, який упав у селі Кіштельниця Теленештського району за 100 метрів від житлового будинку.
За попередніми даними поліції, ніхто не постраждав, а територію навколо місця падіння одразу оточили.
У МЗС Молдови назвали цей випадок грубим порушенням суверенітету та прямою загрозою для безпеки громадян. У відомстві наголосили, що подібні інциденти неприпустимі, вони вкотре демонструють ризики через агресивну війну Росії проти України.
З цього приводу висловилася й президентка Молдови Мая Санду. Вона різко засудила інцидент і наголосила, що війна Росії створює пряму загрозу для молдавських громадян.
Що передувало
23 жовтня поліція Молдови заявила, що у селі Кіштелніца Теленештського району безпілотник впав на землю на відстані близько 100 метрів від житлового будинку.
Точну дату, коли було виявлено дрон, поліція Молдови не назвала, зазначивши лише, що до правоохоронців «нещодавно» звернувся місцевий житель.
Президентка Молдови Мая Санду згодом повідомила, російський дрон впав поблизу енергооб’єкта.
21 жовтня очільниця МВС Молдови Даніела Місаїл-Нікітін повідомила, що наразі розглядається можливість перенесення українських контрольно-пропускних пунктів на територію Молдови — щоб зменшити ризики, спричинені війною Росії проти України та російськими атаками поблизу державного кордону.

article_title: Wales plans to ban steel pylons as government launches consultation
article_content:
Wales plans to ban steel pylons as government launches consultation
- Published
The Welsh government has announced plans to ban the use of traditional steel pylons to support electricity lines over which it has control.
Plaid Cymru ministers favour burying cables underground instead.
Plans for a network of pylons in the Towy Valley have faced a fierce local backlash with local Plaid politicians speaking out against the proposals.
The company behind the plans, Green Gen Cymru, said it welcomed the consultation and that it supported using "the right infrastructure in the right place".
Prohibiting the use of large steel lattice pylons for new lines up to 132 kilovolts was a Plaid Cymru manifesto pledge before May's Senedd election.
Launching a consultation on its policy on Friday, the Welsh government said undergrounding electricity circuits could "reduce the visual impact of electricity infrastructure, helping to protect landscapes and local amenity".
It also said that burying cables could make them less vulnerable to severe weather and could reduce the potential impact on birds and other wildlife.
However, the consultation document also acknowledges that undergrounding was "generally considered more expensive to install and maintain and could create construction impacts during installation".
The government's policy would allow for wooden poles or "equivalent, less intrusive infrastructure" to be used to support overhead cables where undergrounding isn't feasible.
Green Gen has plans to build three major power line routes connecting onshore wind farms planned by its sister company Bute Energy with the wider grid network.
It has previously said it would invest nearly £1bn by 2030, with proposals affecting parts of Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion, Powys and Shropshire.
But it has faced considerable opposition in certain communities, with groups representing hundreds of landowners taking the company to court in 2025.
In a bid to address concerns, Green Gen recently unveiled a "slim and compact" 22 metre (72ft) pylon, designed "with the Welsh landscape in mind".
The company has consistently said that undergrounding its cables would cost on average 4.5 times more, external than running them overhead.
That would mean an extra cost of £500m for the Towy Usk project between Carmarthenshire and Powys, according to Green Gen.
Welsh Energy Minister Adam Price said: "We know the necessary changes in the way energy is generated and used in Wales will require new grid infrastructure, however, we also know that new infrastructure can impact on the communities and the environment that hosts it.
"We want to see infrastructure that is sensitively designed to minimise impacts on the environment and the communities that host them, while offering the maximum benefits for Wales."
Andrew Hardcastle, executive director at Green Gen Cymru, said: "We welcome the Welsh government's consultation and its recognition of the importance of delivering the electricity infrastructure Wales needs in a way that is sensitive to our landscapes, environment and communities.
"Like all grid companies across the UK, we believe there is no one-size-fits-all solution to developing new electricity networks.
"Our approach is to use the right infrastructure in the right place, drawing on a range of technologies including underground cables, wooden poles and our recently announced lower-profile monopoles."
The company said it was "pleased that the consultation recognises the potential role of less visually intrusive overhead infrastructure, including monopoles, and invites evidence on their use".
Reform's Senedd spokesperson for rural affairs, Laura Anne Jones, said: "As part of our energy policy, we will continue to push for new power lines to be placed underground wherever possible, protecting our landscapes and rural communities.
"Reform will always stand up for our countryside and fight against its industrialisation."
The Welsh Conservatives welcomed the policy consultation.
The party's environment spokesperson, Andrew RT Davies said: "We recognise that Wales needs a modern electricity network to support economic growth, but communities should not have to accept eyesores across our beautiful natural landscapes, which must be conserved."
The consultation, external will run until 15 January 2027.
Eirian Edwards, a campaigner in the Llandovery Pylon Group, said: "We welcome that they are seriously looking at undergrounding as the preferred option - to protect landscapes and people's livelihoods.
"If infrastructure has to be planned, then we're not against that process at all. We realise that we need to strengthen our local grid, but certain projects that are planned do not fulfil that at all."
Dyfan Walters, a farmer in Llandovery who is also a member of Llandovery Pylon Group, called it "a positive day for us".
"We're fully supportive and understand that the infrastructure is required.
"Putting that underground means that there's less impact on agriculture, less impact on tourism.
"In a world where there's an ever-changing climate, having that resilience - having infrastructure placed underground - is a sensible way forward."

article_title: Potholes, bus fares and headphone dodgers: will Burnham’s strategy of ‘everyday fixes’ succeed?
article_content:
In the first episode of Armando Iannucci’s political satire The Thick of It, the hapless minister Hugh Abbot is in the back of a taxi, frantically brainstorming for an on-the-hoof policy he can announce to the assembled national press.
“So you want something sexy and eye-catching, and that is free and universally popular and instantly applicable. No one can possibly object to it,” says the addled junior adviser Ollie Reeder. “Well, really, you should have said something before then, because I’ve got a file about that fucking thick of that back in the office.”
After a three-month micro-policy blitz from Downing Street, the question now being asked is: did Reeder pass said file on to the government’s battalion of special advisers? In the past week Andy Burnham has vowed to clamp down on social pariahs blaring out TikTok videos on public transport, outlaw “rip-off” private car park fines and – on Thursday – fill in potholes in 7,000 miles of England’s roads.
Before that, as part of the focus on “everyday fixes”, the prime minister announced a plan to remove VAT from electricity bills, a £2 cap on single bus fares across England and take action on “auto-renew” subscriptions. There’s also promises to crack down on pricey branded school uniforms, ban specious discounts, limit vape and betting shops and stop airlines charging families to sit together on planes. At this rate all minor annoyances in the UK will be eradicated by Christmas.
The idea is simple, says one policy adviser. “People expect the government to be able to do something about things which are unfair – big or small,” they said. “It sends a message that the government is on people’s side, its ready to act, and it can genuinely make a difference.”
Government insiders say the policies are not the product of standing around in a circle, throwing a stress ball and shouting out ideas. “There isn’t someone with a whiteboard brainstorming new bicycles for special constables,” says one, furthering the Thick of It comparison. Instead, the everyday fixes were a central policy strategy from Burnham’s first day in office. “We did this sort of thing under Keir too,” said another source. “But under Andy it’s a whole different thing; he’s put rocket boosters under it.”
In the first days of his premiership, Burnham gave his close ally Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, the job of establishing taskforces for three core areas – cost of living, public control and regeneration. One government source said: “There is a very intentional drumbeat of those because they do make a difference, but also it’s constantly showing people that we understand where those frustrations and low-level pressures are.”
Ideas are “kicked around” between the cost of living taskforce in the Cabinet Office and the policy unit in No 10, with all departments encouraged to feed in. “There’s a sort of filtering up process,” the source said. “It’s quite a sprawling sort of cross-government approach.”
Another said that while some departments were better placed to find “not hugely spendy” fixes, every minister was encouraged to contribute. “I think a lot of people had sort of resigned any hope that the government can actually get things done – and this is showing them that, yes, actually, we can,” another source said.
The small policy announcements have been, one delighted adviser said, a roaring success. Another source said: “Some people are very snotty about it, but in a world where it’s really hard for a government to cut through, this is working. You put some ideas through the grid and you often don’t know if they’re going to fly. But when you see one go gangbusters, it’s kind of like Christmas morning.”
One single fact policy idea dominated the news cycle for an entire day. Another generated tens of thousands of posts on X. Burnham’s faintly hokey video on antisocial phone use garnered 2m views. “It helps that he’s just really good at it,” the source said.
The small-fix policies have not been appreciated by everyone. Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick said the UK was “going down the pan and our prime minister is faffing around tweaking parking tickets” – despite trying to implement the policy himself when he was a Conservative minister. The former Olympian Sharron Davies said: “As Paris burns our prime minister has stopped people playing loud music on buses & trains,” leading some to question whether she expected Burnham to invade the French capital.
Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, has been dismissive, saying in a speech this week that cracking down on loud music on public transport was a “job for ticket inspectors, not the prime minister”. Reprising the theme at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, the leader of the opposition implicitly accused Burnham of fiddling while Rome burns. “We are spending more on interest payments than we do on schools, the army and the police combined,” she said. “Meanwhile, the prime minister is worrying about loud music on trains. This is not serious.”
Across the dispatch box, Burnham hid his delight at her response behind a disappointed look. “I’m not going to apologise for doing the small things that help people have better lives,” he said sombrely, while his advisers likely high-fived in private.
Regardless of the reaction of Burnham’s opponents, the focus on minor grievances is a canny strategy that appears to be working, said the pollster Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common. In recent polling, when people were asked whether Burnham understood the pressure of high energy bills on ordinary people, 45% said he did. When the same question was asked about Starmer, that figure was 23%. “I think the Tories and Reform have got it dead wrong on this,” Tryl said. “People bring this sort of stuff up in focus groups all the time. It cuts across left- and rightwing voters. People care about immigration, about the NHS – but they also care about everyday frictions.”
But behind the scenes there is an acknowledgment that a focus on ticking off small things from the PM’s to-do list will be significantly more challenging in moments of crisis. There has to be a “twin-track” approach, said one insider. “It’s combining a big picture, long term, dismantling 40 years of neoliberalism and addressing questions about ownership and control, but at the same time tackling more immediate daily bugbears,” they said. “What you’ve seen so far is these smaller level interventions, but the bigger structural, longer term piece will be in the 10-year plan.”
While the everyday fixes may be popular, the sugar-high they produce could be short-lived, said Ed Shackle, the head of qualitative research at the policy consultants Public First Global. “The government should be under no illusion that as soon as any real substantive event rears its head, any small popularity boost will be instantly blown away,” he said. “Quick fixes are popular, but they are a poor substitute for fixing the big issues the public care about.”

article_title: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
article_content:
How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
- Published
Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.
The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.
But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.
Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.
And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.
Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.
But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries?
One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate.
The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.
On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries.
And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes.
If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.
- Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care 
  - Published29 September
- State pension likely to top £13,000 a year 
  - Published15 September
- What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it? 
  - Published29 September
But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows.
However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.
So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK?
Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund.
But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.
But there are two issues to consider.
Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.
And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes).
Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing.
As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.
So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap.
The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.
It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men.
But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.
Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.
So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere.
But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action.
The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.
That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.

article_title: Трамп після Ірану пригрозив ще одній країні: що задумав президент США
article_content:
Трамп після Ірану пригрозив ще одній країні: що задумав президент США
Трамп прагне домогтися зміни комуністичного режиму на Кубі, який Вашингтон вважає противником США.
Президент США Дональд Трамп заявив, що Вашингтон візьметься за Кубу після завершення операції проти Ірану. До розв’язання цього питання залучать державного секретаря США Марко Рубіо.
Про це американський лідер сказав під час мітингу у Флориді, повідомляє Reuters.
«Ми розберемося з Кубою на зворотному шляху з Ірану, а потім відправимо Марко Рубіо, щоб завершити цю справу», — заявив президент.
Зауважимо, ще у вересні Трамп висловлював упевненість, що США та Куба зможуть домовитися. Тоді він також наголошував, що для цього, на його думку, не знадобиться військова сила.
Своєю чергою, держсеркретар Марко Рубіо звернувся до тих, хто незадоволений кубинською владою, із закликом скористатися нагодою для змін. Він запропонував прихильникам реформ налагодити конфіденційну співпрацю з Центральним розвідувальним управлінням США, не розкриваючи деталей.
«Тим, хто прагне позитивних змін на Кубі, — зараз саме час», — наголосив Рубіо.
Стосунки США і Куби — що відомо
Нагадаємо, після початку операції в Ірані та подій у Венесуелі Трамп не одноразово погрожував країні через її комуністичний режимЮ який Вашингтон вважає противником Америки. Він натякав на на швидке падіння режиму в країні та мріяв про «честь взяти Кубу», посилював тиск на Гавану через санкції й обмеження постачання нафти.
Вже не перший місяць з’являється інформація, що США готуються до вторгнення на Кубу. Зокрема, у вересні CBS News написало про те, що потенційна військова операція може розпочатися вже найближчими місяцями. Про це, пише видання, свідчить внутрішній документ американської армії, який потрапив у розпорядження.
Водночас Трамп прогнозував, що США та Куба досягнуть угоди. Мовляв, на його думку, військові дії для цього не знадобляться. Адміністрація Білого дому заявляла, що її метою є зміна комуністичного уряду країни.

article_title: Democrat James Talarico targets Elon Musk at rally: ‘Texas is not for sale’
article_content:
James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has taken aim at Elon Musk, warning that the tech mogul is trying to buy political influence and declaring: “Texas is not for sale.”
Talarico held a campaign rally on Friday at the University of Texas at Austin, packing an auditorium at his alma mater with hundreds of students and other supporters, who cheered, whooped and waved campaign signs.
The Presbyterian seminarian’s insurgent run against Texas attorney general Ken Paxton – a staunch ally of Donald Trump – has become one of the most closely watched races in next month’s midterm elections to decide control of Congress. Democrats are seeking their first statewide win since 1994.
Talarico, 37, struck his usual upbeat message on Friday but also pulled no punches in denouncing Paxton – who was impeached by his own party over corruption accusations and had a very public divorce – as the most corrupt politician in the state’s history.
“I have a legislative record; Ken Paxton has a criminal record,” said Talarico, a state representative, wearing a dark blue jacket, white open collar shirt and blue jeans. “This election is about whether you want a senator who puts money in your pocket or who puts money in their own. This election is about whether you want a senator who is for Texas or for himself. This election is about whether you want senator who serves you or serves their billionaire mega donors.”
Paxton, he continued, has the ultimate mega donor. “Elon Musk is trying to buy the Senate seat. We just found out that the richest man in the world is almost single-handedly bankrolling this effort to install Ken Paxton in the US Senate and stop the movement that we are building in our state.
“In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your screens, that was Elon. If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you received a text message saying scary things about me with scary black and white photos, that was Elon too.”
Speaking against the backdrop of a giant Texan state flag and 40 young supporters holding “Talarico” signs, the Democrat said that, where his movement is funded by 1.3 million individuals, Paxton is funded by “one dude”.
In a state where data centres have become an incendiary issue, Talarico said: “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas. But on November 3rd, we are going to deliver a crystal clear message to the world’s first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale.”
Musk, who lives in Texas and has relocated SpaceX, Tesla, X and other businesses there, has contributed $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund, which in turn transferred the same amount to Texas PAC, a Republican super PAC supporting Paxton, according to federal filings.
Talarico has offset the outside-spending disadvantage with grassroots fundraising. His campaign says it raised $64m from July through September, more than triple Paxton’s total, with 97% of donations under $100 each.
Talarico told the crowd that super PACs and “billionaire mega-donors” are spending $200m in the most expensive Senate race in US history to defeat his grassroots campaign. “Big money is powerful, but it is nothing compared to people power,” he insisted, invoking biblical imagery comparing his supporters to “the slingshot” that David used to defeat Goliath
Talarico’s rally capped a turbulent month in what has emerged as America’s biggest battleground state. Talarico fell ill with the flu at the end of September and was not seen in public for nine days.
At a rally in San Antonio, Texas, Donald Trump claimed without evidence that “Tala-freako”, as he nicknames the Democrat, is vegan and had fallen ill because he tried eating meat for political purposes. That quickly metastasised into an online rumour that Talarico had checked into a mental health facility in Ohio. It was comprehensively debunked.
Meanwhile the Wall Street Journal published a video showing Paxton celebrating New Year’s Eve in Dubai with two US fugitives, Anosh Ahmed and Sameer Suhail, who were indicted in Illinois on healthcare-fraud charges. Ahmed donated $190,000 to Paxton, including $25,000 after his indictment.
Back on the campaign trail, Talarico set out on a “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts” tour of the state. He held a CNN town hall with sceptical Republicans and independent voters.
Paxton, meanwhile, launched an 18-day bus tour of Texas. His message was aimed at conservative voters with the slogan “Come and Take It”, an attack on what he called the far left. Republicans sought to tie Talarico with positions on transgender issues that have proved potent in conservative campaigning.
The campaign entered its final stretch with the Democrat holding a narrow polling advantage. The RealClearPolitics average for polls conducted from 6 to 19 October put Talarico ahead by 1.8 percentage points. An Emerson College Polling/ Nexstar Media survey released on Thursday found that 48% of voters support Talarico while 46% favour Paxton.
Early voting began on 19 October, giving both campaigns an immediate test of their ability to mobilise supporters. Talarico voted earlier on Friday.
Supporters at Friday’s rally expressed growing frustration with incumbent Republican officials such as Paxton along with optimism that Talarico’s message could signal a new political era for the Lone Star State.
Alina Anil, a 19-year-old student at the University of Texas, who had already cast her ballot, said she attended the event to see Talarico in person and demonstrate her support.
“We’ve been red for a long time and nothing has really come out of it,” Anil said. “As a student, I don’t think there’s been a lot of changes in Texas. We need some change and James Talarico seems promising. He was a teacher before, so I have faith in that and I have faith in him.”
Dakota Walker, 31, a pediatric physical therapist, arrived wearing a custom T-shirt reading “Talafrico: Talarico refreshing for Texas”, in the style of the Topo-Chico brand of sparkling mineral water.
“What’s not to like about him, what’s not to love about him, honestly?” Walker said. “He has morals, he has values, he’s an overall good human being and I think we need a drastic change.
“I have to spend so much of my time fighting for my kids, making sure that they get what they need when a family with a child with a disability or different abilities shouldn’t have to do that. I know we need healthcare reform and he is very big on that.”
Texas Democrats have had their hopes dashed before, notably when former congressman Beto O’Rourke lost a race to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz in 2018 by less than 3 percentage points.
Asked what a Democratic statewide victory would mean, Walker replied: “Oh man, I’ll probably cry, honestly. We need a lot of change and I feel like it’s time for a new era.”
Patrick Pearson, 46, an assistive technology professional, said he wanted to back Talarico because of his commitment to policy change. “From everything I’ve read about him and heard, I think he sounds really awesome,” Pearson said. “He’s actually trying to make a change and has a very positive message.”
