article_title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
article_content:
Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.
A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.
During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.
Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.
A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

article_title: Shabana Mahmood launches review into murder of student Henry Nowak
article_content:
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has launched a review to examine whether opportunities were missed to prevent the murder of the student Henry Nowak.
It follows claims that there were several warning signs that the perpetrator, Vickrum Digwa, had a history of threatening behaviour and an obsession with weapons.
Nowak, 18, died in December after being fatally stabbed as he walked home from a night out in Southampton. He was handcuffed by police officers while bleeding to death after Digwa falsely accused Nowak of racial abuse.
In police body-worn camera footage which prompted a public outcry, Nowak was heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replied: “Don’t think you have, mate.”
Nowak’s death sparked widespread protests, allegations of “two-tier policing” and a spike in racist attacks against the UK’s Sikh community. Digwa, a Sikh, was carrying two knives, including a kirpan, on the night of the killing. Carrying the blade is permitted in the UK for religious purposes.
Digwa, 23, has subsequently been accused by young local Sikhs of using threatening behaviour in a Southampton gurdwara, or temple, in the months leading up to the fatal attack on Nowak.
The Sun reported that Digwa was seen brandishing an airgun in his back garden in October 2022. A neighbour who recorded him firing shots said she reported this to the police, but Hampshire constabulary was unable to find a record of the incident.
Speaking in the Commons, Mahmood said the review would be led by the former Conservative lord chancellor Alex Chalk KC and would report its initial findings within five months.
“Last December, Henry Nowak’s life was cut short in a horrific and senseless act of violence. My thoughts today are with Henry’s family and his friends, who have shown extraordinary courage and dignity,” she said.
“It [the review] will investigate what was known about the perpetrator, including any missed opportunities to intervene.
“It will look at the Nowak family’s experience of the criminal justice system and whether they were supported in the manner they should have been.
“Once the Independent Office for Police Conduct [IOPC] has concluded its investigation into the police response, this review will also consider the actions of the IOPC and, if necessary, the police.”
Two officers, who were the first to arrive on the scene, are being investigated by the IOPC for potential gross misconduct.
The investigation is looking at why they did not recognise that Nowak needed urgent medical attention and at the decision to arrest him rather than provide first aid.
Nowak’s family welcomed the review as a “significant moment” in their fight for justice.
“Since Henry was murdered, we’ve fought tirelessly for answers to questions no family should ever have to ask. The emotional toll of that fight, on top of the unimaginable grief of losing Henry, has been immense,” the family said.
“We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for.
“Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have.”
Digwa was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years. He has been given permission to challenge the length of that sentence at the court of appeal on 5 November.
Kiran Kaur, Digwa’s mother, was also jailed for three years for assisting an offender after she removed the knife used by her son. The knife was found by police at their family home along with more than 20 other weapons.

article_title: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
article_content:
No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
- Published
Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement.
Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no".
But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public.
Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options.
He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".
Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.
Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.
After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option."
"He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said.
"What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow."
She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough."
Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.
The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.
- Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement 
  - Published20 hours ago
- Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham 
  - Published30 September
In an interview with the Sunday Times, external, Burnham said he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and the EU.
The PM argued that the type of migration had changed since Brexit, with more foreigners moving permanently.
In contrast, he suggested that when the UK was a member of the EU, migration was "generally younger people", who would spend a few years in the country before returning home.
However, Burnham added: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."
The Schengen Agreement, which the UK was not part of when it was in the EU, allows passport-free travel across member countries.
The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.
Burnham has argued that since Brexit, the UK has lost immigration control the country previously had.
"For instance, the small boats crisis has arisen in the last 10 years because we lost that returns agreement when people came here that we could work with other countries to return them," he told broadcasters.
The Conservatives and Reform UK both oppose a return to free movement with the EU.
However, the Liberal Democrats have argued that allowing freedom of movement would help economic growth.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued most people who voted for Brexit did so because they did not want free movement, while Reform leader Nigel Farage has said such a move would be "a total betrayal of Brexit Britain".
Farage told broadcasters he was "up for the fight again" on the EU and an "election is coming" to decide that.
"Crucially, [Burnham] goes to Brussels on 20 November for a key summit - he must not sign up to anything there without at least putting those minor changes to a general election," he said.

article_title: No 10 plays down UK joining EU single market after Burnham suggests referendum would be needed – as it happened
article_content:
Andy Burnham has claimed that a debate on the UK’s future relationship with the EU could “bring people together who voted in different ways” in 2016. Brexit had not “played out” like it was promised to the public, he said in an interview on ITV’s Good Morning Britain. But he subsequently caused some confusion by seeming to imply that he would only take the country back into the EU single market after a referendum. (See 2pm.) Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey discuss this more in the latest episode of our Politics Weekly UK podcast.
Capita’s attempt to improve its performance over the running of the Civil Service pension scheme has been labelled as “abysmal” by a Cabinet Office minister. Speaking in the Commons, Sally Jameson said the outsourcing giant had failed to improve after thousands of civil servants had been left waiting for payments and retirement quotes. As the Press Association reports, Jameson said she would not rule out in-sourcing the pension scheme’s management after calls from MPs and unions. She said:
Since taking up this role I have met with the CEO and his senior team twice, and on two occasions I have expressed in no uncertain terms my outrage at their performance throughout this contract.
We were promised, and I quote, ‘the most AI-enabled pensions service’, and it’s fair to say that Capita have comprehensively failed to deliver on that commitment.
This progress overall has been abysmal. Complex issues remain unresolved for too long, 1,800 cases for over a year and while some individuals have more than one case, there is too many members and family left waiting in limbo.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has pledged to provide answers to Henry Nowak’s family, as she announced an independent review into the student’s murder. (See 4.07pm.)
For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.
Badenoch claims Labour 'all over the place on defence spending' in light of Burnham interview
Kemi Badenoch posted this on social media about Andy Burnham’s comments about defence spending in his Good Morning Britain interview this morning. (See 10.32am.)
The government are all over the place on defence spending. I don’t think Andy Burnham realises he commits to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 in this interview...his Defence Secretary won’t even make that commitment!
When the government are saying Britain needs to be ready for war in 1000 days, hitting a defence spending target in 2035 is too late. Getting to 3% by 2030 means spending the money to be ready NOW, not in 9 years time.
That makes two comments in TV interviews today where Burnham seemed to go beyond what he intended in an answer. The other was what he said about a referendum on joining the single market. (See 2pm.)
During his press conference, Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s Treasury spokesperson claimed that his party’s plan to bring back imperial measures might be good for growth because it could help exports to the US. (See 2.52pm.)
Jernick is right to say that some of the words used in the US are the same. But, as a reader has pointed out, in the US customary system, although the terminology may be identifcal, the units of volume are actually different. A British imperial pint is not the same as a US pint. Jenrick’s policy won’t help exporters who think otherwise.
Mahmood announces review into murder of Henry Nowak, to be carried out by former Tory justice secretary Alex Chalk
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has pledged to provide answers to Henry Nowak’s family, as she announced an independent review into the student’s murder, the Press Association reports. PA says:
The review will be led by former lord chancellor Alex Chalk and will look at “any missed opportunities to intervene”, Mahmood told the Commons.
The 18-year-old died after being fatally stabbed by Vickrum Digwa in Southampton on 3 December 2025. Nowak was handcuffed as he lay dying, after Digwa, a Sikh, falsely accused him of racial abuse. In police body-worn camera footage Nowak can be heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replies: “Don’t think you have, mate.”
At Home Office questions in the Commons, Mahmood said: “I can announce an independent review led by a former lord chancellor, the right honourable Alex Chalk KC. It will investigate what was known about the perpetrator, including any missed opportunities to intervene. It will look at the Nowak family’s experience of the criminal justice system and whether they were supported in the manner they should have been.
“Once the Independent Office for Police Conduct has concluded its investigation into the police response, this review will also consider the actions of the IOPC and, if necessary, the police.
“The full terms of reference have been published today, and an initial report will be submitted to me within five months.
“We must get to the truth of what happened before, during, and after that awful night, and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate.
“We owe that to Henry and to all who loved him. They deserve answers, and this review will provide them.”
Digwa was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years on 1 June this year, for Mr Nowak’s murder.
As Paul Brand from ITV reports, Nowak’s family have welcomed the review, saying they hoped it would “finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought too hard for”.
Q: Is Reform UK still committed to its Britannia Card policy, which would allow non-doms to avoid UK taxes in return for paying £250,000?
Jenrick said current government policy was chasing away wealthy and talented people. He went on:
Reform set out a policy a year ago. Could we do better than that? I think we actually could do, because I believe that if we enacted these policies (see 12.46pm and 2.42m), if we got a sense of excitement back into the British economy, then we might even be able to charge more than £250,000. And so we’ll be saying more about that in the near future.
Farage defends Reform UK's plan to cut capital gains tax for cryptocurrency assets
Q; Are you still committed to cutting capital gains tax on cryptocurrency assets from 24% to 10%? (Reform UK’s two biggest donors are both crypto billionaires.)
Farage defended the proposals. He said:
You’ve got the choice on crypto. You can leave it to the Wild West. You can leave it completely unregulated. You can leave it where the scammers could operate freely, where people get ripped off, and where the Inland Revenue or HMRC earned virtually nothing. Or you can bring it under regulatory control.
And this is the irony of crypto. I’m the one arguing for regulation and protection for consumers on crypto.
Farage said between 5 million and 7 million people in Britain had cryptocurrency assets. That was more than the number of people owning shares in companies, he said. He went on
So I want it brought under a protective umbrella. And I want a tax rate that makes people declare what their income is. Hence the incentive to do that, bring crypto in from the outside.
Q: What do you think about banking taxes going up in the budget?
Farage said he did not love the banks. He was debanked by one back, and another 10 refused to have him as a customer, he said.
But he claimed bank taxes were already higher than in any other comparable nation. He said it might be possible to squeeze “a bit more” out of the sector. He went on:
Loathsome as I think some of their practices are … I do not want a tax rate that makes the banks leave London, because that will make all of us poorer.
Farage said he think the staying out campaign would win a referendum on rejoining the EU “very comfortably indeed”.
He went on:
People may be frustrated that their hopes were not delivered. I’m one of those.
But a referendum on rejoining? £41bn a year rough estimate of contribution? Commitment to free movement of people? Commitment ultimately to joining the euro?
I can’t see any situation in which the British people vote for that.
Q: This morning Andy Burnham implied free movement could be part of any future deal with the EU, and then No 10 rowed back. What do you think is going on?
Farage said:
He’s all over the place on this and we’re beginning to learn we can’t trust him.
Referring to the forthcoming UK-EU summit, he said:
What I’m saying is [Burnham] must not agree to anything at that summit without putting to the people in a general election. And if he does that and wins a general election, then he has some mandate to proceed with moving on to closer links with Europe. But I do not believe that anybody could rejoin the European Union without putting it back to the British people.
He also he would be happy to fight an election with rejoining the EU a campaign issue.
Farage defends close ally calling Badenoch 'Nigerian scammer'
Q: [From the Daily Telegraph] Do you think Raheem Kassam was being racist when he called Kemi Badenoch a Nigerian scammer? (Kassam used to work as Nigel Farage’s chief of staff in Ukip, and he is still a close ally and supporter.)
In response, Farage turned on the questioner.
Britain’s going broke and you’re asking about what somebody who’s an adjunct of the party says on social media. It shows frankly, the level that we sink to with these debates.
I thought the use of the word scammer was very accurate because she says things often that simply are not true. It’s almost their instinctive response to things. It’s to say things that simply aren’t true.
Farage says he would bury hatchet with Tories and campaign with them in referendum on joining EU
Q: If there is a second referendum on Brexit, will you form a coalition with the Tories to campaign against rejoining?
Farage said the first referendum showe there were “different constituency audiences” and the leave campaign succeeded because it appealed to different groups, like Labour leavers, Tory leavers and Ukip leavers. He goes on:
It was actually the fact that it was a grand coalition that made it succeed. So I don’t think there’ll be any question, in an issue like that, of burying hatchets.
Farage also said they would stress they were fighting for “independence”. He said he would like to use that description more often.
Farage sarcastically describes parliamentary commissioner for standards as 'utterly unimpeachable'
Q: Are you preparing for a second byelection in Claction (in the event of the parliamentary investigation leading to a recall election)?
Farage replied:
If I comment on that, I’ll be in breach of rules. And, as we all know, our standards, procedure, and our wonderful standards commissioner, are utterly unimpeachable people in absolutely every single way. Thank you so much. What a complete and utter farce the whole thing is.
Q: What would you say to Tory claims that many of the plans in your document are policies that they have already announced? Like cracking down on bogus degrees.
Farage points out that, even if they are promoting these ideas now, the Tories did not do these things when they were in power.
Q: Do you think voters want a bit more positivity?
Farage says Andy Burnham is positive. He explains:
Has [Burnham] got a positive spin? Yes. Is he more engaging than Keir Starmer? Yes. Does he appear a bit more normal than Keir Starmer? Yes.
But what does he actually stand for? And if he wants to unite the country, the one way not to do it is to rerun all the arguments from the referendum ten years ago. And what happened to what he said to the people of Makerfield just a few months ago?
So I begin to genuinely doubt his sincerity. I really, really do.
Farage describes parliamentary investigation into claims he broke Commons rules as a 'farce'
Q: What do you say to Andy Burnham claiming that dealing with illegal migration has become harder since Brexit?
Farage says what Burnham is saying is not true. Under the Dublin convention, which applied to the UK when the UK was in the EU, Britain had to take back more asylum seekers from other countries than it was able to send back, he claims.
Q: Have you any update on the investigation into you by the parliamentary commissioner for standards?
Farage says this topic is “a gem”. He says journalists are allowed to ask about this, but, under the parliamentary rules, Farage is in breach if he even menions publicly that an investigation is taking place.
He goes on:
There are some who think that standards are now being used as a political tool. You may very well think that; I couldn’t possibly comment.
Farage says the process is a “farce”. He adds sarcastically:
He’ll judge at some point, but I’ve no doubt he’ll be fiercely independent.
Q: [From Serena Barker-Singh from Sky News] How to you respond to Andy Burnham implying people like you lied about the benefits of Brexit?
Farage claims Adam Boulton, the former Sky News political editor, used to say Farage was the only leading person on the leave side who never lied about the potential benefits of Brexit.
I would say to the prime minister the opportunities of Brexit have not been delivered. This was the chance of a great escape from a failing European single market, which in terms of foreign direct investment growth and every other metric you could look at was failing …
We’ve not had anything like the potential that Brexit could have delivered. Was it the right thing to do? Undoubtedly. And what would rejoining be? Utterly moronic.

article_title: ‘Local services are vital’: Former rough sleepers on what helped them off the streets
article_content:
Martin Fletcher had been homeless for more than 20 years after being made redundant before he finally got accommodation in Sunderland in 2024.
What was the one thing that finally ended his rough sleeping and sofa surfing? “My mindset, mainly,” the 61-year-old said. “The realisation that I was getting old and I couldn’t live like this for ever. And also help from a charity who didn’t judge, who didn’t bombard me with forms – they made me a cup of tea and built up a picture of what I needed and helped me get back on track.”
That charity was Basis Sunderland’s drop-in service for housing support, which closed its doors in July for lack of funding.
Fletcher found this devastating: “How are they going to end rough sleeping when services like this are closing? You’ve got to remember, unless people want to come in off the streets, it won’t happen. They said they did it during Covid but they didn’t – I was still on the streets. And not all homelessness is visible. So these local services are vital.”
Andy Burnham, who had announced plans in July to end rough sleeping and offer everyone in need a bed by Christmas, hosted a summit on the issue on Monday.
The prime minister told the Downing Street event this commitment would be backed by a further £432m to sustain the support into next year. A number of charities had raised concerns that people would simply end up back on the streets after Christmas. Burnham said he was “bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts”.
Those who work in the homelessness sector have warned there is no easy solution. The Guardian has spoken to several formerly homeless people to find out what helped them back into housing, sometimes after decades of sleeping on the streets.
Amy Bell, 37, was street homeless and struggling with heroin addiction for seven years between 2013 and 2020. She said she hit “rock bottom” when her council said it could offer her only a voucher for a two-man tent, which she “cried herself to sleep in at night”.
The next morning, workers employed by the same council put her tent and all her belongings in the bin because it was classed as litter. Borrowing a phone from a Citizens Advice centre, she secured a place at a hostel for a few weeks, which enabled her to reconnect with a local drug treatment service, get a phone with a sim card and start to rebuild.
She said being offered a bed in a hostel, even though she was still taking drugs, was the key to getting her off the streets. “The hostel system is broken. You are basically set up to fail,” she added.
“They don’t accommodate people with addiction problems, and that’s who it should be for. Eventually you will do something that shows you are still using and they ban you. It doesn’t take long to get kicked out of all of them. And then you’re left with nothing.”
Bell said for Burnham to succeed in abolishing rough sleeping he must get rid of the “ridiculous bureaucracy” that stops people from accessing support.
“Everything is done by app now. When you’re homeless, you don’t have that – believe me, if you get a decent phone, you sell it,” she said. “The days of being able to walk into the Citizens Advice bureau or the jobcentre don’t exist any more. Homeless people need a real-life person to help them.”
Others the Guardian spoke to said they moved from England to Scotland because it was easier to get help there after it abolished the priority needs test in 2012. According to Crisis, Scotland has some of the most progressive homelessness rights in the world.
Tony* became homeless after being released from prison in 2024. He told his probation officer he had nowhere to go but was simply advised to contact a council homelessness team the day of his release.
No housing was available and he ended up sleeping in a tent in the woods. “I was a prison leaver, I hadn’t made myself intentionally homeless, but there was nothing. The support was nonexistent,” he said. “I was telling my probation officer where I’m sleeping at our weekly meetings but they didn’t help.”
A chance meeting led him to the Salvation Army, where he has been living in supported accommodation for the past two years. With evidence suggesting the amount of people being released from prison into homelessness is on the rise, Tony said the government must deal with this issue if it wanted to end rough sleeping.
“I was in for three years, and they only started talking to me about accommodation 10 days before I was released,” he said. “If I’d been set up with a bedsit or something like that, the government would have paid less in the long run. I would have begrudgingly gone to a hostel but that wasn’t even offered. Something has to change.”
* Some names have been changed to protect anonymity

article_title: Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of 10 Downing Street
article_content:
Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of 10 Downing Street
- Published
Sir Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of Downing Street because of concerns about its suitability as a workplace, senior figures from his administration have said.
Ministers and officials from successive governments have privately complained that Number 10's rabbit warren-like layout can lead to a lack of collaboration among those working there.
James Lyons, who served as Sir Keir's director of communications, said over the weekend that "moving out was something that was discussed" during his time in post.
Two other senior figures confirmed that discussions were had about moving staff into an open plan space in another government department.
One source said a space inside the Foreign Office building, a short distance from Downing Street, had been identified.
Both stressed that discussions did not go beyond an early phase and it's not known whether Sir Keir himself was consulted.
There's no suggestion that the prime minister would have stopped living in Downing Street if the plan had gone forward.
10 Downing Street is more than 300 years old and is an amalgamation of three houses, which comprises more than 100 rooms.
The building was given to Robert Walpole, widely regarded as the UK's first prime minister, by King George II in 1732.
Lord Walker, the boss of supermarket Iceland and a former adviser to Sir Keir, told the Financial Times on Friday that Number 10 was no longer "fit for purpose".
He said: "I think we should turn it into residences, or a museum. It's a national treasure. It's amazing. But it's ridiculous.
"It's just a Stuart-era building, not fit for purpose. It has tiny, tiny meeting rooms, all on different levels. There are hazards."
Lyons, who led Sir Keir's communications operation from October 2024 to September 2025, posted on LinkedIn that "Lord Walker is 100% right".
He added that staff were "deeply envious" of other departments and described Number 10 as a "gloomy, mice-infested, bomb-curtained rabbit warren".
Lyons added: "Moving out was something that was discussed when I was in 10 Downing Street."
One source said "there were chats at senior staff level about moving to an open plan office in FCDO" (Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office).
They said they didn't believe the idea went far, but said "the reason for discussion was serious" and added that the alternative plan was "about staff being open plan and able to collaborate".
Sir Keir became increasingly frustrated at Whitehall's ability to deliver change during his time as prime minister.
He was accused of picking a fight with civil servants when he said "too many people in Whitehall are comfortable in the tepid bath of managed decline".
Darren Jones, who served as Sir Keir's chief secretary, told MPs last week that he "tried to abolish the Cabinet Office three times but failed".
He proposed replacing it with a new department that would "abolish those barriers and walls and make them just one integrated team, focusing on the same things and really supporting each other to move it forward".
In his first days after succeeding Sir Keir, Andy Burnham created the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.
The move was seen as an attempt to ensure that things happen when metaphorical levers of power are pulled.
It comprises Number 10, Number 10 North and other key parts of the Cabinet Office and is led by the UK's most senior civil servant, Dame Antonia Romeo.
The government says the new office will "ensure the centre of government is focused on our top strategic priorities".
Those around Burnham say he is yet to form a view about the adequacy of Number 10 as a workplace.

article_title: If the PM reboots the UK for working-class people, unions will be with him. But the time for talking is over | Andrea Egan
article_content:
After Keir Starmer, things could only get better inside Labour. But Andy Burnham’s arrival as party leader and prime minister didn’t just clear that low bar. It was a cause for hope, especially for those of us in the trade union movement. That’s less because Burnham is streets ahead of his predecessor as a politician – although he is – and more about just how radically the new prime minister has framed his project for the country.
I’ve been active in the labour movement for almost four decades. In that time, I cannot count how many times I’ve heard talk of reversing the devastation wreaked by Margaret Thatcher. For socialists and grassroots trade union activists, this kind of political thinking is bread and butter. But not so much for a Labour prime minister.
Tony Blair, between torching the Middle East and taking a hammer to our civil liberties, infamously came to build upon Thatcher’s legacy rather than bury it. Gordon Brown and Starmer were more set against the Thatcherite fracturing of our society than Blair. But they both continued to inhabit the political cage she built: the idea that there is no alternative.
Before now, the only major party leader ideologically opposed to neoliberalism in a remotely serious way was Jeremy Corbyn, who drew up a programme that would have started to undo the rule of the market. But it wasn’t to be. So in beginning his premiership by insisting that there is, in fact, an alternative way of organising our economy and society to the neoliberal one, Burnham marked a historic shift.
This kind of talk isn’t cheap. How the prime minister has articulated his vision really matters, both because it has challenged the assumptions that have shaped our politics for decades and because the analysis is fundamentally correct. Virtually every aspect of this country’s malaise, as Burnham powerfully explained to Kemi Badenoch, can be traced back to the “wrong turns” taken in the 1980s.
But the flip side for Burnham is that his diagnosis doesn’t leave any doubt about what Labour must do in government. To measure up to his own ambitions, the party will have to implement changes to the structure of our economy unseen since the immediate postwar period. At a minimum, that means bringing sectors into public ownership and investing on a huge scale to rebuild a social fabric – our public services, infrastructure and collective life – that has been shredded.
Many of the Burnham government’s measures so far have been welcome. Banking quick wins that don’t require wrangling with the Treasury but signal you are on the side of the people was a sensible approach for the early days. Labour’s steady improvement in the polls reflects that. But four decades of neoliberalism won’t be ended through Google Maps updates of petrol prices, or even with measures to provide breathing room in the face of the cost of living crisis.
Following up a bold, historical diagnosis with piecemeal measures just isn’t politically sustainable. From US wars to the climate crisis, the factors making essentials ever more unaffordable are out of control. Without the radical action the prime minister has called for, then, the lives of our people and communities are going to keep getting worse, rapidly. And the stakes remain high: it’s the far right that will benefit if this project fails.
So the budget must be the moment that the prime minister’s programme starts to match his rhetoric. Unison is clear about that, and so are my colleagues across the trade union movement. We’re not expecting neoliberalism to have melted away by the time John Healey finishes reading out his statement. But we are demanding serious measures that actually begin to improve workers’ lives.
We expect a big, multiyear funding plan to restore investment and wages in our public services – alongside kicking profiteering vultures out of the public sector through bringing services back in-house. These measures should be funded by finally making the wealthy few pay their fair share of tax. It’s imperative that the prime minister and chancellor defy pressure from the business lobby and the rightwing media to reject changes such as equalising income and capital gains tax.
The decades-long political settlement the prime minister has rightly defined himself against might have impoverished the vast majority, but there were some winners. And those who have profited handsomely from neoliberalism will fight tooth and nail against any attempt to actually break with it.
So, if the prime minister sticks with his historic ambition to remake Britain in the interests of the working class, it won’t be easy. But the trade union movement will be by his side. There’s no dodging a battle with the vested interests committed to keeping things as they are – and the budget is the place to begin.
- 
  Andrea Egan is the general secretary of Unison

article_title: We’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music too | Sadiq Khan
article_content:
At around 8pm on Sunday evening the last car made its way down Oxford Street, marking the start of a momentous new era for our nation’s high street. Today, after decades of discussions and deliberations, the action we’ve taken means almost one kilometre of Oxford Street is now officially traffic-free – just in time for Christmas. But this is only the start of a much bigger transformation, and the first step towards a bright new future for this historic thoroughfare.
Walk down Oxford Street, and you’re passing through hundreds of years of British history and culture. In 1864, an ambitious young draper called John Lewis opened his first shop on the street. Forty-five years later, the American entrepreneur Harry Gordon Selfridge arrived with a radical idea: to transform shopping from a mundane necessity into an unforgettable experience. He filled his store with dazzling window displays, world-class entertainment, restaurants and lounges. He even installed women’s toilets – a rarity in Edwardian England – giving women a newfound freedom to make the most of the city. As he opened the doors to his first customers, he told them “everyone is welcome”.
That spirit has been at the heart of Oxford Street’s success ever since. We love it because it feels as if it belongs to all of us. It’s where teenagers come for their first shopping trip with friends. Where families marvel at the magic of festive lights and decorations. And where generations of Londoners and visitors have come to discover the latest music, fashion and trends. It’s also the beating heart of British retail – pumping billions into our national economy, with the surrounding area accounting for an incredible 1% of the UK’s total economic output in 2022.
But in recent years this iconic street has started to lose some of its sparkle. Changing consumer habits and the legacy of the pandemic have taken their toll. Footfall has fallen. Some of our best-loved stores have closed their doors, only to be replaced by vape shops and candy stores. And, too often, the experience of visiting a chaotic, congested Oxford Street has felt more like an ordeal to survive than a day out to enjoy.
If we’re to restore this beloved street to its former glory, we must rediscover the pioneering spirit of Harry Gordon Selfridge and create a space for everyone to enjoy, breathing new life into the high street and bringing back big brands. And that’s what our bold plans – backed by the overwhelming majority of Londoners and businesses – are all about. And with household names like Ikea, Puma and Clarks investing in new stores, there’s already excitement for what Oxford Street can become.
People need a reason beyond simply buying something to visit their high street. And in an age when almost anything can be delivered right to our door, that principle matters more than ever. Coming to Oxford Street should feel like a positive experience. Somewhere you want to spend time, as well as your hard-earned money. A place where you’re not choked by tailpipe fumes or deafened by the noise of passing motorists. And that starts with reclaiming it for pedestrians, not traffic – rebalancing the relationship between cars and people in the centre of our city.
That’s why I’m so delighted that, thanks to our efforts, the road stretching between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street is now officially traffic-free. But removing cars is just the beginning. Imagine an Oxford Street where you can stroll at your own pace, take a break from shopping with a coffee under the trees, or stumble across some live music, a fashion show, a sports exhibition or a cultural event. We’re determined to put Oxford Street not just on par with top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla, but make it even better.
And while it’s a process – we’re deliberately keeping disruption to a minimum over the busy Christmas period – by next spring, visitors can expect to see new trees, new seats and new public plazas, alongside improved lighting and signage. This ambitious project has been far from straightforward or easy. As usual, we’ve had to overcome opposition from a vocal minority, and 14 years of a previous government that didn’t back the plans. But with seven in 10 Londoners expressing support for our vision, after extensive consultation, I knew we owed it to our city and to our businesses to deliver these improvements, which will help to boost jobs, growth and investment as we build a fairer, safer, greener and more prosperous London for everyone.
Of course, we’ll continue to listen to Londoners. Many of the initial changes are temporary, and we’ll use real-time feedback to help refine the final designs in a test and review period throughout 2027. But for centuries, Oxford Street has reinvented itself, adapting to changing times and helping shape British culture along the way. And now it’s in need of its next great transformation. One that honours its extraordinary past while creating new possibilities for the future. A future where new memories are made, new businesses flourish and new chapters of British history are written.
Today marks the beginning of that journey – and I encourage everyone to come to explore this newly transformed street, as we work together to ensure its best days are still to come. In the words of Harry Gordon Selfridge – everyone is welcome.
- 
  Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London

article_title: Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget
article_content:
Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget
- Published
Pensioners on low incomes will be shielded from income tax by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget on Wednesday.
The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to increase by 3.9% to £13,036.40 a year from April. This would take the payment above the £12,570 personal tax allowance and therefore be liable for income tax if no changes are made.
The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension. Healey will explain this pledge will be met by plans for a new tax allowance for low-income pensioners.
Healey's plans come as the Conservatives and Reform UK unveil their alternative Budget proposals, including deep cuts to the welfare bill.
- What is the Budget and what could be in it? 
  - Published1 day ago
- An insider's guide to Budget Day: 'Don't fall off the kerb' 
  - Published23 hours ago
- How does the UK state pension compare with other countries? 
  - Published3 days ago
The chancellor's allies argue his plans for pensioners will mean they do not need to face an administrative burden just to pay a small amount of tax.
More specific details, including how many pensioners this will affect, have yet to be confirmed by the Treasury.
The Budget is due to be printed this evening, with Healey's speech likely to be fine-tuned right up until it is delivered on Wednesday lunchtime.
Treasury sources concede it will not involve the scale of tax and spending announcements seen from Labour and Conservative governments in recent years.
The Tories are calling on the chancellor to cut green taxes, red tape and benefits to bring down energy bills.
Reform is recommending the chancellor adopts 60 policies which they claim will create jobs - including approving the controversial Rosebank oil field - a project Healey is understood to back.
Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper has called on the government to agree a new growth and defence partnership with the EU, including joining the single market. She argued this would help "ease the huge tax burden weighing people down".
The Green Party has urged Healey to use his first Budget to "make the UK affordable", including by funding energy bill support by ending a tax relief for data centres.
Senior Green politicians, including leader Zack Polanski, MPs and peers, made clear their suggestions in a letter to Healey.

article_title: Трамп может невольно превратить Европу в сверхдержаву — The Times
article_content:
Попытки администрации Дональда Трампа использовать военную и технологическую зависимость Европы от США в качестве рычага давления могут привести к обратному результату — ускорить стратегическую автономию континента и превратить его в гораздо более мощную самостоятельную силу.
Об этом говорится в материале The Times, авторы которого называют ситуацию «горьким парадоксом»: Вашингтон всё активнее использует зависимость Украины и Европы от американских систем ПВО, спутниковой связи и разведки, но именно это заставляет европейцев срочно создавать собственные альтернативы.
«Положительная сторона заключается в том, что попытки Вашингтона оказывать давление формируют ту европейскую автономию, которая, как считалось, никогда не появится», — отмечают авторы.
По их оценке, если европейские государства выдержат российское давление в течение следующих 18 месяцев и не поддадутся политической дестабилизации, континент может выйти из нынешнего кризиса «гораздо более грозной силой».
Европа уже осознала цену зависимости от США
Сегодня Европа уже способна заменить большую часть американской финансовой помощи Украине и значительную часть вооружений. Однако есть несколько критических сфер, в которых зависимость от США пока остается чрезвычайно высокой: ракеты-перехватчики класса Patriot, спутниковые системы раннего предупреждения о запуске баллистических ракет и система связи масштаба Starlink.
Авторы называют эту уязвимость следствием примерно трёх десятилетий чрезмерной зависимости Европы от американского военного превосходства.
Теперь ситуация меняется. Европейские страны ускоряют создание собственной противоракетной обороны: заказывают новые системы SAMP/T NG, реализуют многонациональную программу FREYJA и ищут дополнительные источники ракет-перехватчиков, в частности в Японии.
Каждый евро, который Европа вкладывает в собственные системы вооружений, — это деньги, которые больше не получат американские оборонные компании, и ещё один вид оружия, поставку которого президент США не сможет задержать.
Европа создает альтернативу американским спутниковым системам
Европейские радиолокационные и оптические спутники потенциально могут в течение относительно короткого времени заменить значительную часть американских разведывательных возможностей.
OneWeb и европейская система GovSatcom уже могут частично обеспечить защиту Европы и Украины на случай проблем со Starlink. В то же время полноценная европейская система, способная самостоятельно обнаруживать запуски баллистических ракет, по оценке авторов, вряд ли появится раньше 2030-х годов. Именно эти технологические «узкие места» в настоящее время оставляют Вашингтону наибольшие рычаги влияния.
Пока заменить американские технологии мгновенно невозможно, Европа может использовать собственную экономическую и финансовую мощь.
Кредит ЕС Украине на 90 млрд евро, а также около 202 млрд евро замороженных российских активов могут стать одним из главных ресурсов для дальнейшей поддержки Киева.
Среди других возможных инструментов авторы материала называют полный запрет на использование европейских услуг для транспортировки российской нефти и дальнейшее усиление борьбы с российским «теневым флотом».
Эти меры способны сильнее ударить по возможностям Москвы финансировать войну без значительных дополнительных затрат для европейских налогоплательщиков.
Украина становится частью новой европейской оборонной промышленности
Еще одним элементом будущей независимости Европы от США может стать украинская оборонная промышленность. Производство беспилотников в Украине в этом году выросло на 370%.
Украинские крылатые ракеты Flamingo стоят менее 600 тысяч долларов — против примерно 3,5 млн долларов за американский Tomahawk.
При этом Дания уже предоставила государственную гарантию по кредиту производителю Flamingo.
Авторы называют модель «европейский капитал плюс украинские технологии и производство оружия» одним из возможных рецептов выживания в условиях непредсказуемой политики Вашингтона.
Вашингтон постепенно исчерпывает собственные рычаги влияния
Политическое давление работает лишь до тех пор, пока сторона, на которую давят, не создала альтернативу. Администрация Трампа уже продемонстрировала Украине и Европе, насколько ненадежной может стать американская гарантия после смены политического курса в Вашингтоне.
Это и задержки с американскими системами ПВО, проблемы со Starshield и решение Белого дома смягчить экономическое давление на Москву. Именно такие шаги подталкивают Киев и европейские столицы к созданию систем, которые больше не будут зависеть от решения американского президента.
В итоге попытка Вашингтона использовать своё военное и технологическое превосходство в качестве средства принуждения может постепенно снижать саму ценность этого рычага.
«Со времён Карла Великого у Европы не было лучшего объединителя, чем Дональд Трамп», — говорится в статье.
Европа, Украина и другие американские партнеры уже увидели, во что может обойтись гарантия США, когда Вашингтон меняет свою позицию.
Теперь Соединённым Штатам придётся увидеть другую сторону этого процесса: политическое влияние, как и запас ракет-перехватчиков, не безгранично — каждое его применение постепенно его истощает.
description: Европа может стать значительно сильнее благодаря политике США.

article_title: Путін готує пастку для НАТО: Кремль може розіграти карту «мир в обмін на Україну»
article_content:
Путін готує пастку для НАТО: Кремль може розіграти карту «мир в обмін на Україну»
Росія може вимагати повернення Альянсу до меж станом на 1997 рік — до вступу до нього країн колишнього соціалістичного блоку.
Під час нового раунду переговорів щодо завершення війни Москва може порушити питання військової присутності НАТО в Європі.
Таку переговорну стратегію припускає доктор філософських наук, професор Університету Короля Данила Віталій Надурак, про що він розповів в етері Еспресо.
«Ми тепер розуміємо, що в цей пакет перемовин по Україні вони хочуть включити також вимогу щодо НАТО у всій Європі», — зазначив професор.
За його словами, російські вимоги можуть стосуватися не лише України, а й інших європейських держав, зокрема Польщі, Фінляндії та країн Балтії.
Надурак також звернув увагу на те, що Москва просуває ідею створення нової архітектури безпеки в Європі. На його думку, це свідчить про прагнення Росії розширити порядок денний переговорів і включити до нього питання військової присутності НАТО на континенті.
Професор вважає, що вимога вивести війська Альянсу з країн, які приєдналися до нього після 1997 року, є нереалістичною. Якщо Москва наполягатиме на її виконанні, це може унеможливити досягнення домовленостей про завершення війни.
«Я думаю, насправді це, можливо, і є стратегія Путіна — висунути реально невиконувані вимоги», — пояснив Надурак.
За його словами, таким чином Кремль може намагатися перекласти відповідальність за провал переговорів на західних партнерів.
«Бачите, ви не хочете йти на поступки, і тому не буде ніякої угоди по Україні», — так професор описав можливий аргумент Москви.
Водночас експерт припускає, що Росія може застосувати іншу тактику: спочатку висунути максималістські вимоги, а згодом погодитися на менш масштабні поступки, створюючи враження готовності до компромісу.
За такого сценарію Москва може заявити про відмову від вимоги вивести війська НАТО з країн, які вступили до Альянсу після 1997 року. Натомість Росія намагатиметься домогтися припинення подальшого розширення блоку та закриття перспективи членства України.
«Можливо, оце останнє якраз є реальною позицією Росії. А максималістські вимоги вона заявляє для того, щоб потім нібито піти на поступки», — наголосив Надурак.
На думку професора, за такого розвитку подій європейські держави можуть сприйняти відмову Москви від найрадикальніших вимог як компроміс. Однак фактично йтиметься про поступки Росії в питанні майбутнього розширення НАТО та євроатлантичної інтеграції України.
Окремо Надурак наголосив на важливості участі європейських держав у переговорах про безпеку континенту. За його словами, спроби вирішувати долю Європи без представників європейських країн створюють небезпечний прецедент, адже саме вони безпосередньо зазнають наслідків російської війни проти України.
Раніше повідомлялося, що Україна намагається домогтися перенесення наступного раунду тристоронніх переговорів зі США та Росією щонайменше на тиждень раніше.
Ми раніше інформували, що прессекретар президента Росії Дмитро Пєсков заявив, що відновлення тристоронніх переговорів про закінчення війни в Україні не означає припинення бойових дій.

article_title: No 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movement
article_content:
Downing Street has been forced to clarify Andy Burnham’s stance on whether the UK would return to having freedom of movement with the EU after the prime minister said an “honest discussion” was needed on the issue.
Burnham fuelled speculation about a return to freedom of movement in an interview at the weekend, prompting questions about how close the UK could become to Brussels.
Confusion deepened after further interviews were interpreted as leaving the door open to an eventual return to freedom of movement and another referendum on the issue.
It forced a Downing Street spokesperson to say the prime minister was not proposing a return to freedom of movement, or any particular option.
“He is saying that it’s time for us to discuss what kind of long-term relationship with Europe is best for Britain and he is referring to the types of areas that that agreement and long-term future could cover,” she said.
“He is crucially not leaning either way, and that will be for the British public to decide. And his focus for now is on next month’s summit and the practical arrangements that we hope to make there, which will add billions to the economy.”
She said the government was not yet at the stage of confirming whether the public would decide on proposals for the UK to move closer to the EU.
Asked whether Burnham accepted that returning to freedom of movement would mean Britain lost control over legal migration, the spokesperson said: “He’s not setting out a concrete position either way. What he’s saying is that he wants to have a conversation with the British public about what our long-term future with the European Union looks like.”
In an interview with the Sunday Times, Burnham indicated that staying out of free movement would no longer be a red line in discussions about how the UK can move closer to the EU.
On Monday, Burnham ruled out the possibility of rejoining the EU within this parliament and indicated he could fight the next general election on a promise to take the UK back into the EU. He said: “I’m not going to move away from the red lines that were in the Labour manifesto.”
Hours later, Burnham told journalists “no” when asked if he would allow the UK to join the EU freedom of movement scheme without a referendum.
When asked whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, he said: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.”
Challenged on how his constituents in Makerfield would feel about his discussions about the EU, given 65% of them voted to leave, Burnham added: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’m doing.
“The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation to Brexit.”
Burnham even ruled out an early general election on a manifesto change on this issue. He told GMB: “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.” However, he left the door open to a future fight on a promise to fully rejoin the EU.
Burnham will be in Brussels for the UK-EU summit on 20 November, as he seeks to strike a better deal with the bloc. He believes the Brexit deal has “weakened our economy [and] weakened our control of immigration” and is not good enough for the country.
author: Aletha Adu Political correspondent

article_title: Портников пояснив, чому зустріч Трампа, Сі Цзіньпіна та Путіна не наблизить мир в Україні
article_content:
Портников пояснив, чому зустріч Трампа, Сі Цзіньпіна та Путіна не наблизить мир в Україні
Кожен із потенційних учасників прагне розв’язати власні геополітичні завдання, а українське питання може стати лише приводом для переговорів.
Можлива тристороння зустріч лідерів США, Китаю та Росії навряд чи допоможе наблизити завершення війни в Україні.
Про це журналіст Віталій Портников розповів в етері Еспресо.
За словами журналіста, обговорення умов завершення російсько-української війни без участі України та європейських держав не матиме належного сенсу. Європа відіграє важливу роль у підтримці Києва та санкційному тиску на Москву. Водночас залишається незрозумілим, навіщо Китаю брати на себе відповідальність за майбутню мирну угоду та гарантії безпеки.
Портников припускає, що тема війни може бути лише формальним приводом для організації зустрічі, тоді як справжні інтереси її учасників лежатимуть в інших площинах.
«Тобто фактично кожен під час цієї зустрічі хоче говорити про своє і використовує цю розмову виключно як привід показати, що лідери Сполучених Штатів Америки, Російської Федерації і Китаю можуть зібратися втрьох — G3», — зазначив журналіст.
На думку Портникова, для президента США Дональда Трампа тристоронній формат є можливістю продемонструвати власне бачення світового порядку, у якому ключові рішення ухвалюють три держави з найбільшими ядерними арсеналами.
Крім того, американський лідер може спробувати використати взаємодію з Росією як додатковий важіль впливу на Китай у питанні ядерного роззброєння.
Однак Пекін, як зауважив журналіст, неодноразово давав зрозуміти, що готовий долучатися до таких переговорів лише за умови співмірності ядерних потенціалів Китаю, США та Росії. За нинішнього співвідношення сил китайська сторона не зацікавлена в домовленостях, які не враховуватимуть її позиції.
Водночас Путін, за оцінкою Портникова, прагне використати війну проти України, щоб закріпити за Росією статус держави, яка бере участь у визначенні глобального порядку денного.
При цьому журналіст сумнівається, що російський президент зможе досягти конкретних домовленостей із Трампом і лідером Китаю Сі Цзіньпіном.
Портников звернув увагу на результати нещодавньої зустрічі американського та китайського лідерів. Тоді сторони не підписали спільних документів і не оприлюднили спільного комюніке, а їхні заяви про перебіг переговорів відрізнялися.
На думку журналіста, це ставить під сумнів перспективи результативних домовленостей у форматі за участю ще й російського президента.
Портников вважає, що зустріч трьох лідерів може мати радше символічне значення, ніж привести до конкретних рішень щодо завершення війни.
«У спільну фотографію я вірю. Більше ні в що не вірю. Ніяких серйозних розмов про російсько-українську війну взагалі не може бути у такому форматі», — підсумував журналіст.
Раніше повідомлялося, що Україна намагається домогтися перенесення наступного раунду тристоронніх переговорів зі США та Росією щонайменше на тиждень раніше.
Ми раніше інформували, що прессекретар президента Росії Дмитро Пєсков заявив, що відновлення тристоронніх переговорів про закінчення війни в Україні не означає припинення бойових дій.

article_title: «Це не зупинить Путіна»: сенатор-республіканець звинуватив Трампа в небезпечній наївності
article_content:
«Це не зупинить Путіна»: сенатор-республіканець звинуватив Трампа в небезпечній наївності
Політика Трампа може послабити позиції Заходу й допомогти російським військам досягти успіхів на фронті.
Сенатор-республіканець США Мітч Макконнелл розкритикував спроби президента Дональда Трампа домовитися з Росією шляхом поступок Москві та обмеження підтримки України.
Про це повідомляє The Hill.
Макконнелл, який очолює підкомітет Сенату з питань оборони, зокрема, розкритикував заяви Трампа про те, що Росія належним чином дотримується домовленостей щодо припинення ударів по енергетичній інфраструктурі.
На думку сенатора, послаблення санкцій проти Москви не змусить Кремль припинити агресію, а натомість може переконати російське керівництво в слабкості Заходу.
«Це фактично неправильно, стратегічно наївно та морально бездарно. Його підлеслива угода Росії, винагороджуючи агресора послабленням санкцій, не переконає пана Путіна зупинитися», — заявив Макконнелл.
Він також наголосив, що історичний досвід свідчить про протилежний ефект таких кроків.
«Історія показує, що така поведінка підбадьорює російського автократа, який розглядає її як слабкість», — зазначив сенатор.
Окремо Макконнелл застеріг адміністрацію Трампа від обмеження військової допомоги Україні, обміну розвідувальними даними та доступу до супутникового зв’язку. За його словами, такі рішення можуть дати Росії змогу просунутися на фронті.
«Погрози припинити надання допомоги у сфері безпеки та розвідки або доступу до важливих систем супутникового зв’язку суттєво не послаблять бажання України захищатися, але можуть дозволити пану Путіну досягти прогресу на полі бою, який досі був недосяжним», — наголосив сенатор.
Він додав, що обмеження підтримки України може мати наслідки, протилежні тим, на які розраховує американська адміністрація.
«Це може продовжити війну, а не скоротити її», — підсумував Макконнелл.
Крім того, сенатор розкритикував домовленості щодо імпорту російського дизельного пального до США. Він звернув увагу, що середня ціна дизеля в країні все ще перевищує 6 доларів за галон.
«Коли обмежені постачання дизельного палива в Росії перейдуть до інших рук, це мало що зробить для зниження цін на заправках», — зазначив Макконнелл.
Він також відкинув характеристику Путіна як гуманітарного діяча, яку озвучив спеціальний посланник Трампа Стів Віткофф.
«Якщо президент серйозно ставиться до того, що говорить про припинення конфлікту, йому слід звернутися до мудрості американського народу, а не до наївних бізнесменів, які, здається, вважають, що дипломатія передбачає підлабузництво перед супротивниками», — заявив сенатор.
Макконнелл окремо наголосив: «Пан Путін багато чого вміє, але він не гуманіст».
За словами сенатора, Путін є союзником Китаю та й надалі використовуватиме можливості для послаблення США і Європи.
Водночас Макконнелл закликав американську адміністрацію уважно вивчати досвід України у веденні сучасної війни, зокрема інновації у застосуванні безпілотників. Він застеріг від ігнорування уроків, які українські військові засвоюють безпосередньо на полі бою.
Раніше повідомлялося, що демократи, які наступного року можуть отримати ключові посади в Конгресі США, вимагають від великих банків і портів зберегти всі документи, пов’язані з можливим імпортом російського дизельного пального та іншими угодами з Росією.
Ми раніше інформували, що Путін та Трамп мають спільні комерційні інтереси та розглядають Європу як противника.

article_title: ‘Digital hostile environment’: AI secretly being embedded across Home Office, report claims
article_content:
AI has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration, according to research.
Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to a report by Open Rights Group (ORG).
It is also being used to conduct surveillance of borders, through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites; to summarise asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence in those interviews; and to prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (Ipic) tool.
Information for the report has been gathered from a mix of limited information published by the Home Office, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs. The report has cross-party support from Labour’s Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party’s Pete Wishart and the Green party’s Siân Berry.
The report, titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment, raises concerns about the use of AI in immigration, saying it is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination within society, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policies and rhetoric.
It says AI is being trialled and tested in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall freedom of information requests and redact disclosures. Successive governments are criticised for pushing an ideology that reduces complex human cases to a technical problem that can be fixed.
The report raises concerns about “reducing people to data points” and replicating the hostile environment first envisaged by Theresa May as home secretary in 2012. “Relying on AI to decide who gets to stay here and who gets thrown back into danger is a deeply alarming move,” it states.
Open Rights Group is calling on the government to regulate AI and ban uses that are undemocratic and risk human rights violations, such as the use of ChatGPT tools in asylum applications.
It also wants more transparency and stronger freedom of information laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools.
Ribeiro-Addy said: “In spite of questions and requests, the Home Office has been reluctant to publish the documents that would explain how AI is used in asylum processing, what the problems are and how they are being addressed. The department has not explained how it will ensure there is accountability when they fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks.”
Sara Alsherif, a programme manager at Open Rights Group, said: “Migration is a human phenomenon and experience, not a technical problem that can be fixed by artificial intelligence. We urgently need transparency, accountability and strict regulation to restrict how AI is used and to prevent its wider rollout.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “Use of artificial intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.
“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims.
“We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their rollout.”
author: Diane Taylor
