article_title: Labour faces accusations of breaking manifesto pledge over minimum wage for young people – as it happened
article_content:
Labour faces accusations of breaking manifesto pledge over minimum wage for young people – as it happened
Greens say Labour has ‘no respect for young people’ amid reports chancellor will pause equalisation of minimum wage for under-21s with that paid to older workers
Greens accuse Labour of breaking manifesto pledge, after minister signals minimum wage age equalisation being paused
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has not contested reports saying that, in the budget tomorrow, John Healey, the chancellor, will pause the process of equalising the lower national minimum wage paid to people under the age of 21 with the more generous national living wage that applies to older workers.
In an interview on the BBC this morning, Reynolds was asked to respond to a story suggesting the equalisation process has been put on hold because of concerns about youth unemployment.
John Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for young people after warnings that they are being priced out of jobs.
The Times has been told that the national living wage, which applies to those aged 21 and over, is expected to rise from £12.71 to around £13.20 – an increase of 3.9%.
However, Healey has decided not to repeat the big rises of the past two budgets in the national minimum wage, which applies to those aged 18 to 21. It will rise broadly in line with the rate for older workers – from £10.85 to around £11.27, an increase of 3.9%.
In its manifesto, Labour said it would raise the level of the national minimum wage to the level of the national living wage to “so all adults are entitled to the same minimum wage, delivering a pay rise to hundreds of thousands of workers across the UK”. The manifesto implied this would happen during this parliament, but in May Torsten Bell, the pensions minister, said implementation of this commitment could be delayed until after the general election – implying the government is worried equalisation now could increase youth unemployment.
Asked about the Times story on the Today programme, Reynolds insisted the new national living wage and national minimum wage rates would be announced tomorrow.
But he went on:
The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies, but it was always clear it would happen over time and we would take into account, as the minimum wage uprating each year always does, the relative strength of the labour market and other pressures …
Of course, you want not just good wages, but good work. And the way this has always been done – it is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account. That is the approach you will see confirmed [in the budget].
The Green party has accused Labour of breaking a manifesto promise. Responding to the Times’ story, and Reynolds’ comments in effect confirming it, Mothin Ali, the Greens’ co-deputy leader, said:
Anyone doing a day’s work, needs to be paid the same rate for the same job. A young person’s rent and food bill is no less because they are young, so they need to receive the same wage.
Healey and Burnham are now breaking a manifesto pledge to young people that even Starmer managed to keep. Labour have no respect for young people, who appear to just be there for cheap labour for the wealthy and their corporate donors.
Ali said the Greens would introduce a £15 minimum wage for workers of all ages.
Labour has been accused of breaking a manifesto pledge to raise the minimum wage for younger people up to the level that applies to workers over the age of 21 after a minister signalled that the process of equalising the two different rates will be paused in the budget. (See 12.52pm.)
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, has said Nigel Farage is “completely unfit for public office” after the Reform UK leader in interviews this morning said he would not block a candidate for liking Tommy Robinson (see 12.13pm) and refused to condemn a former aide who called Kemi Badenoch a Nigerian scammer. In response, Phillipson said:
Nigel Farage is desperately trying to drag politics further and further into the gutter. It seems there is no low he won’t stoop to – he is completely unfit for public office.
Failing to call out blatant racism against the leader of His Majesty’s Opposition despite being given at least ten opportunities to do so and then giving his activists the green light to support Tommy Robinson shows just who he really is.

A National School of Government and Public Services has opened, the Cabinet Officehas announced. Mark Ferguson, a Cabinet Office minister, formally opened it today. The government says:
Regional hubs will be developed across the country, with the first opened in York this week, alongside digital access routes to give civil servants access to modern learning facilities close to where they live and work.
It will provide civil servants and public sector leaders with the world-class learning and development they need to meet the challenges of the future.
The school will build a curriculum around the skills all servants need, including training on devolution, national security, leadership and innovation. Training will also be offered in AI, covering the full range of skills needed now and in the future, from implementing practical solutions at the frontline to cut clerical workloads to cloud engineering courses to develop and deploy the latest technology across government, the School will equip Civil Servants with the tools to build a world-class Civil Service.
Security minister says Britons far less ready for emergencies than other Europeans as he defends Be Ready campaign
Last week the government launched a Be Ready campaign to publicise advice saying people should stockpile water, food and other supplies in the event of an emergency. The announcement attracted a lot of attention, although many Britons probably sided with Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, who signalled that she was not going to get too alarmed by it all by joking about how she would include a bottle of sauvignon blanc and mascara alongside her government-mandated survival supplies.
Dan Jarvis, the security minister, gave a statement about the advice to MPs this afternoon. In his opening comments, he did not pass judgment on the usefulness or otherwise of a bottle of wine, but he did have some points to add.
Jarvis dismissed claims that the advice was an “overreaction”. Anyone who did think that should have been with him when he met victims of Storm Goretti earlier this year, he said. He said 50,000 homes, schools and businesses were left without power, communities were cut off because of blocked roads and families experienced having “the basic necessities of everyday life”, like power, water and the internet, taken away from them.
He said government research shows only 13% of people in the UK feel they are prepared for an emergency, like having power cut off after a storm. He went on:
This figure is far lower than our European neighbours. The very same research showed that 84% of people in the UK want the government to share more information about the steps they can take to increase their preparedness.
He said the last government launched a website giving preparedness guidance, but there was no proper publicity campaign and “not enough people noticed [the advice], and those who did found the guidance hard to follow”.
He said the publicity campaign was not being launched in response to a specific threat.
He said there were two main things people are being asked to do.
The two main actions are ensuring that you have three days of water and non-perishable food, and signing up to the Priority Services Register if you or someone in your household is eligible for extra support in a utility outage.
He said the government would be encouraging communities to get involved in emergency planning.
He joked about how, before he was in the Parachute regiment, he was a Boy Scout where the motto was “Be Prepared”.
UK government to give £15m to anti-misogyny fund amid ‘manosphere’ concerns
John Healey, the chancellor, will give £15m to a dedicated fund to tackle misogyny in workplaces, schools and public places amid concerns in government about the rise of “manosphere” influencers, Jessica Elgot reports.
Burnham says he wants to be PM who ends 'decade of division', as he stresses support for British Muslims
Andy Burnham has said that he wants to be a prime minister who brings to an end “a decade of division”.
He made the remark at a meeting with Muslim leaders in Downing Street this morning, where he said British Muslims were particularly likely to be victims of hate.
Without giving examples, he also said some of the language used by opposition parties about Muslims was “completely unacceptable”.
Speaking at the opening of the meeting, Burnham said
Where I want to start is just to talk a little bit about the style I’m trying to bring into my role.
I’m really clear in saying that we cannot have another decade of division like the one we’ve lived through.
It’s easier said than done, of course. But I did try on the steps outside Downing Street to talk very directly about that, drawing a line on it and building a more positive, hopeful feeling within the country. I’m going to stick to that path and try and move the country beyond some of what we’ve all lived through in the last 10 years.
And I know Muslim communities across different parts of the country have really in many ways lived through some of the worst examples of division and the hatred that people experience.
Burnham said that he wanted to be a PM “alongside the [Muslim] community, visibly so, very much sending that message, particularly to younger Muslims across Britain, that this is their country, this country is behind them, working to support them.”
As the Press Association reports, attendees included crossbench peer Lady Gohir, who leads the Muslim Women’s Network; Shabir Randeree and Akeela Ahmed, chair and chief executive of the British Muslim Trust; Bibi Khan of the London Islamic Cultural Centre; and Javed Khan, managing director of the Equi thinktank.
Shabana Mahmood urged to grant visa to former Weather Underground activist
Human rights activists and celebrities including the lawyer Helena Kennedy, the actor Harriet Walter and the theatre director Phyllida Lloyd have urged the Home Office to overturn its decision to refuse a visa to a former member of the radical US group the Weather Underground, saying her decades of rehabilitation should count in her favour. Nadia Khomami has the story.
SNP claims Burnham's 'minuscule announcements' are 'insulting' to voters
The SNP is also making a last-minute budget submission to the chancellor. It is calling for VAT on petrol and diesel to be removed.
Kirsty Blackman, the SNP’s economy spokesperson at Westminster, said:
In the face of a cost-of-living emergency, Andy Burnham has broken his promise to cut bills and is insulting voters with minuscule announcements that won’t scratch the surface. [See 9.07am.]
The fact is every major household bill has risen under Burnham.
He is treating voters like fools by pretending he is delivering ‘breathing space’ when energy bills will soon be £1,000 higher than the Labour party promised, mortgage rates are up at 6%, and the price of petrol, diesel, food and shopping has gone through the roof on his watch.
At the UK budget on Wednesday, the chancellor must finally deliver meaningful help for the majority of households by cutting energy bills by at least £300 and by removing VAT from petrol and diesel for the remainder of the fuel price crisis.
It could save households in Scotland £500 as prices soar under the Labour government.
(Describing statements like this, and the Lib Dems’ (see 2.20pm), as budget ‘submissions’ is journalistic fiction in some respects, because the budget has already been written. But opposition parties feel it is important to set out their views.)
UK rejoining EU's Erasmus student exchange scheme in January, with applications open next month, minister tells MPs
The government has confirmed that the UK will rejoin the Erasmus+ student exchange scheme from the start of January, the Press Association reports. PA says:
Foreign Office minister Hamish Falconer said applications would open next month for young people who will be able to study, train or get work experience in the European Union.
Speaking during Foreign Office questions, Falconer emphasised to MPs that the opportunities would be open to “educational institutions of all kinds”.
Work on the UK joining the Erasmus programme was announced as part of Keir Starmer’s post-Brexit reset deal with Brussels in 2025.
The UK left the scheme under Boris Johnson’s Brexit deal in 2020, with the then-prime minister arguing it did not offer value for money.
It was replaced by the Turing Scheme, which was ended when the government announced the new deal over Erasmus plus.
The government has previously said it expects more than 100,000 people to be able to benefit, and that disadvantaged students tend to benefit highly from taking part in the scheme.
Lib Dems call for business rates to be scrapped as they highlight their budget proposals
Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, and Daisy Cooper, his deputy, visited an MOT garage today – for the sole purpose, it seems, of providing a picture to illustrate his pre-budget soundbite.
In a statement, he said:
Labour has put the handbrake on the economy. Growth is in the slow lane and hardworking business owners like Bob are facing higher costs, a jobs tax, and a broken business rates system.
The economy desperately needs a tune-up. The Liberal Democrats would scrap business rates, replace them with a fairer system, and negotiate a proper growth and defence deal with Europe, so we can turbocharge our economy by joining the EU single market and customs union.
In a briefing on their own budget proposals, the Liberal Democrats said they would:
• Turbocharge economic growth and spur investment and job creation across the UK, through a new growth and defence partnership with Europe, including joining the EU Single Market and a customs union.
• Scrap business rates and replace them with a fairer system. The Liberal Democrats would replace business rates with a commercial landowner levy. Firms would no longer be taxed on the value of the building or machinery they use, which penalises investment and hits independent businesses hardest.
• Boost skills and tackle the Neet crisis. The party would guarantee every young person 100 hours of work experience and professional enrichment before they turn 18 to tackle the Neets pipeline before young people fall out of education and work. This would also help tackle the growing number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets), by making it cheaper for small employers to offer first jobs. According to latest ONS figures, there were an estimated 981,000 young people aged 16 to 24 years in the UK who were Neet in April to June 2026.
Streeting signs defence agreement with Poland, describing it as 'one of UK's closest allies'
Britain and Poland have agreed to work together to build a new generation of air defence missiles, as the west gears up its defence efforts against Russia, the Press Association reports. PA says:
A new agreement, the Warsaw Defence Plan, will also see the two nations work together to build new drones and anti-drone measures, as well as collaborate closely on more traditional land, sea and air defence.
Defence secretary Wes Streeting signed the pact in Warsaw today, where he met his Polish counterpart Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.
Streeting said: “Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies – from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century.
“The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger Nato.
“From collaborating on Nato exercises that deter our adversaries to working together to support Ukraine in its fight for freedom, we are committed to standing together for European security whilst boosting our economies with stronger defence industries.”
Under the pact, the two nations will share their experiences of developing new warships. Britain’s Type 31 frigate and Poland’s Miecznik are based on a common design.
The allies have also agreed to increase shared patrols in the Baltic Sea, to protect vital communications cables on the seabed.
The agreement comes ahead of a major coalition of the willing exercise next month, which will see British, French and German forces join Warsaw’s soldiers in Poland for training to prepare for a peacekeeping mission in Ukraine once the war is over.
No 10 says Burnham to set out 'next steps' for long-term relations with EU around time of 20 November summit
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said this morning that British government officials would be talking to their EU counterparts about possible changes to the UK-EU relationship. Possible options include the UK joining the single market, and so free movement would be part of that discussion.
The government seems to be nervous about suggestions it is already in talks about the UK signing up for free movement rules and, at the Downing Street lobby briefing this morning, a No 10 spokesperson insisted free movement was not part of the current talks with the EU.
Those talks are “focused solely on next month’s summit, and the practical agreements that we hope to make there that will add billions to the economy and cut the red tape that holds back British business,” the spokesperson said.
She added:
Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements, on what is realistic for both sides, and, crucially, on what the British public supports. And the prime minister will set out the next steps when it comes to our longer term relationship around the time of the summit.
The summit will take place in Brussels on Friday 20 November.

article_title: Trump shows off tanker with ‘1m barrels of oil’ and floats Venezuela as 51st state
article_content:
Donald Trump suggested Venezuela would become the 51st state of the United States on Tuesday as the president showed off a tanker he claimed had “one million barrels of oil on it” from the country, nine months after deposing its president.
At a campaign rally in Corpus Christ, Texas, Trump touted a US oil deal with Venezuela, which the US attacked in January, capturing its long-serving leader Nicolás Maduro.
Trump claims the agreement – struck with the South American country’s interim government, which is backed by Trump’s administration – will cover “billions” of barrels of oil.
Venezuela “will become a prosperous country, and who knows? Maybe some day soon it’ll become a prosperous 51st state,” Trump said at the podium on Tuesday. “That’s possible.”
Venezuela is on a growing list of countries and territories Trump has spoken of acquiring, including Greenland, Canada and Mexico.
With tens of millions of Americans set to vote in next week’s midterm elections, Trump’s aggressive foreign policy – including his controversial war on Iran, and tariffs on goods from much of the world – have challenged his popularity, according to opinion polls, with his approval ratings falling to record lows.
But on Tuesday, the president sought to point to the Venezuela operation as an example of his success. US fuel prices, which surged after the start of the Iran war, piling pressure on Americans’ cost of living, “will soon come plummeting down”, he claimed in a social media post.
“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” he said at the rally, pointing out the ship off the Texan coast. “The oil provided is being provided to the United States at zero cost to the American taxpayer.”
Moments before Trump took the stage in Texas, he claimed on his Truth Social platform: “By unleashing Energy Dominance from Alaska, all the way down to Venezuela, I have made the Western Hemisphere the Energy Capital of the World.”
The deal has also drawn skepticism as critics complained that the Trump administration has not pushed a transition to democracy in Venezuela, where elections have not been held since Maduro was detained by US forces and taken to New York to face criminal charges after a raid on his Caracas residence.
The urgency of the oil agreement stems from Trump’s opting into the war with Iran in February. Gas prices have shot up nationwide after Iran closed the strait of Hormuz, a passageway for 20% of the world’s oil supplies.

article_title: Homes across UK to get low- or no-interest loans to fund solar panels and heat pumps
article_content:
Households across the UK can now cut their energy bills by hundreds of pounds a year at no upfront cost by applying for interest-free or “low-interest” loans to fund upgrades such as heat pumps, batteries and solar panels.
The government-backed Warm Home Loans scheme, which launched on Tuesday, could mean thousands more households are able to access low-carbon energy alternative technologies, thanks to loans ranging from £7,500 to up £35,000.
Energy suppliers including British Gas and E.On have partnered with lenders from Tandem Bank and Homeserve respectively to offer the loans directly to customers at a discounted rate compared with those offered by high street lenders.
People interested in swapping their gas boiler for an air-source or ground-source heat pump could secure loans of up to £10,000 or £35,000 respectively, while also drawing on the government’s existing scheme which offers grants of up to £9,000 a year for households installing the replacements for fossil fuel heating.
Installing a heat pump, battery and solar panels could save households up to £550 a year on their energy bills, rising by a further £300 a year with a time-of-use tariff, according to the government.
Soaring energy costs have led to record demand for low-carbon home energy upgrades over the last year, and the government believes the loan scheme means “thousands more households” will be able to cut their energy bills by fitting clean energy technology and spreading repayments over many years.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said: “Energy is an everyday essential that must be affordable for everyone. These government-supported loans will help families across the UK upgrade their homes with no upfront costs to make them warmer and cheaper to run.”
Chris Norbury, the chief executive of E.On UK, said that a recent trial showed that fuel-poor customers in Coventry were able to save more than £250 a year on average by combining a home battery with a time of use tariff that charges lower rates for using energy outside peak demand hours.
He said the Warm Homes Loan scheme was “an opportunity to take that further” by “removing barriers to low-carbon technologies”.
The government set out the terms of the new scheme a day before the chancellor, John Healey, delivers his first budget on Wednesday, which reportedly will include plans to scale back heat pump grants made through its boiler upgrade scheme.
The scheme is not expected to be scrapped altogether, but sources say hundreds of millions of pounds will be cut from its £2.7bn five-year budget because Treasury officials consider it a subsidy used mainly by middle-class households.
It has typically provided grants of up to £7,500 to help meet the £13,600 cost of installing a heat pump, meaning households have still required a significant outlay to make up the difference.
The Guardian understands that grants of up to £9,000 a year are likely to remain available to households that are not connected to the gas grid and are forced to rely on high-cost heating oil. These grants could be used alongside the low-interest loans to cover the full cost of a heat pump.
Other lenders taking part in the Warm Home Loans scheme include HTG Finance, Propensio, Secure Trust Bank, Selina Finance, South Manchester Credit Union, Sunsave, The Money Co-op and This Bank.
author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent

article_title: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
article_content:
UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
- Published
British and European officials will discuss the future options for the UK's relationship with the EU, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has told the BBC.
Officials on both sides are expected to begin discussions about a range of options, including free movement, before the EU summit on 20 November.
However, Downing Street has insisted the government's current focus is on achieving new deals in areas such as food and youth mobility at the summit.
Reynolds said no "assumptions" had been made about what the UK's future relationship with Brussels could look like.
Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.
But the prime minister has been clear any major changes to the UK-EU relationship would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.
He has vowed to stick by the red lines in Labour's 2024 manifesto, with no return to freedom of movement, the EU single market or customs union, for the duration of this parliamentary session, which will end by 2029.
Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.
The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.
- Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days 
  - Published1 day ago
- Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement 
  - Published1 day ago
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.
He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us.
"We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit.
"He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."
Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be.
"But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."
A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement.
"We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.
Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.
Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.
But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.
Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election.
"I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.
Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."
Speaking to BBC Wales, Labour MP Ruth Jones said: "We need to be very careful here. We must respect the Brexit referendum result."
Asked if a referendum on freedom of movement was something she would support, the MP for Newport West and Islwyn said: "We're a long way from that. Andy Burnham is floating the idea, and it's great to float ideas, but let's talk it through and see what does it mean, because another referendum at this particular time would be divisive."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.
On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.
The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.
But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his own when he told the Sunday Times, external that he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.
The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.

article_title: Landline switchover could cut people off in emergency, minister warned
article_content:
Landline switchover could cut people off in emergency, minister warned
- Published
Plans to switch off the UK's traditional landline phone network could leave people in remote areas unable to contact help in an emergency, MPs have warned.
Landline operators aim to complete the switch to an internet-based network instead of copper-wire cables by the end of January next year.
The government and operators say the move to digital landlines will offer a more reliable service.
But MPs representing remote areas of the UK urged security minister Dan Jarvis to ensure that scrapping the copper-wire network did not make their communities more vulnerable in a storm or other emergency.
Unlike digital services, the traditional landline network does not rely on mains electricity and continues to work in a power cut.
Labour MP Torcuil Crichton, who represents the Western Isles constituency of Na h-Eileanan an Iar, said: "Resilience is inbuilt in the islands but we have major problems with connectivity because of this move from analogue to digital phone lines."
He said that "when the power goes out people don't have the phone, they don't have the internet and often they don't have a mobile signal either".
Retail service providers have been giving back-up battery packs to vulnerable customers, which can keep landline phones operating for an hour or more.
But Crichton said this was "simply not adequate" and that mobile phone providers "simply don't have the means to maintain or keep their signal going during storms".
He urged the minister to get telecoms firms to "up their digital game" to protect places "on the edge where people are vulnerable, isolated from their neighbours, where the ambulance is an hour away and the storm is 70 miles an hour".
Similar concerns were raised by MPs from the West Country and the Lake District.
Markus Campbell-Savours, Labour MP for Penrith and Solway, said: "I ask the minister to imagine an elderly constituent living alone in an isolated Lake District valley where copper phone lines have been replaced by fibre.
"A storm takes out the power to their router in the night and by the time they wake, the modest battery back up has failed, as has the mobile mast, does the minister share my concerns that they would have no way to raise an alarm in an emergency and agree that we need a new technological solution to protect the elderly?"
- 'We won't be able to use our phones if we have a power cut' 
  - Published22 December 2025
- Switchover must protect most vulnerable - MPs 
  - Published24 March 2025
Conservative MP Julian Lewis also raised concerns about the lack of a "back-up system" if digital phone services go down in the event of a cyber attack or other emergency.
He told Jarvis the copper-wire network "could have given us useful levels of resilience in an emergency".
Jarvis, who is spearheading the government's Be Ready campaign, which is advising people to stock up on supplies to be prepared for emergencies, said he would "look very closely" at the Tory MP's point.
He also assured West Country MPs that their concerns would be addressed at a government resilience summit, which was due to take place in Cornwall next month, and promised to raise concerns about telecoms firms with the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.
"Our telephone networks are a vital part of our critical national infrastructure and our emergency response in weather-related crisis supports the functioning of essential services and keeping people connected when they need it most," he told MPs.
The government says the switch to digital phone services is needed because the traditional analogue network is becoming increasingly unreliable.
The government's Be Ready campaign advises people, external who have not yet "migrated to a modern digital network" to contact their landline provider.
"If you are a vulnerable customer, for example if you are a telecare user, your communication provider must provide a free back‑up battery unit," it adds.
More information is available on the government's digital switchover site, external.
description: Plans to switch to digital landlines by January could leave remote areas of the UK vulnerable, MPs say.

article_title: Oriel College urged to cancel student group’s event with Jason Arday accuser
article_content:
The University of Oxford’s Oriel College has been urged to cancel an event featuring Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas that has been organised by student supporters of Reform UK.
Arday, 41, was found dead in August after resigning from his University of Cambridge professorship. He had faced intense media scrutiny after Cofnas made unproven accusations of plagiarism against him and said there were “serious questions” about his biographical claims.
Cofnas, a blogger and academic who has been accused of promoting pseudoscientific ideas of racial difference in his online writings, is expected to appear at an event called “An evening with Nathan Cofnas: Is DEI undermining higher education?” at Oriel’s Harris lecture theatre on 17 November.
The event has been organised by Oxon Universities’ Reform Society (OURS), a student group set up this year to support Reform UK.
Oxford campaign groups, British academics, members of the public and Oxford alumni have signed an open letter urging Oriel to “withdraw its facilities from the event”.
The signatories say the event “risks creating a hostile and exclusionary environment for students, particularly those of ethnic minorities” and “risks undermining Oriel’s role as a world-class educational institution” in 2026, the year of the 700th anniversary of its royal charter.
The letter accuses Cofnas of using his platform to assert discriminatory beliefs, and claims his blogging played a significant role in the coverage Arday faced.
Days before Arday’s death, Kehinde Andrews, the author and the UK’s first professor of Black studies, told the Guardian Arday was facing a “dedicated, coordinated smear campaign from the right, based on the premise that Black people should not be at Cambridge”.
Responding to news of the Oriel event, Andrews said in a post online that it was “despicable and disgusting”.
Oriel College said in a statement: “Oriel College is committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so. This includes the freedom to express views that many find deeply offensive. We are also committed to promoting inclusion and maintaining an environment that is free from all forms of discrimination and harassment, including racial discrimination.
“The college considers events booked by students who are committee members of registered societies according to our code of practice on freedom of speech. When an event is permitted, this does not imply endorsement by the college of the views of its speakers.
“When considering booking requests, the college takes seriously the security implications of events and the safety of its members.”
In a post on X, OURS claimed: “Nathan Cofnas and the event organisers have been subjected to a disturbing torrent of online hostility.”
In a statement, OURS said that since it was a registered student society at the University of Oxford, constituent colleges “are under a legal obligation to host events like ours”.
It added: “The Reform Society is committed to hosting Nathan Cofnas, and allowing attendees at the event to engage in respectful dialogue with the same.
“We find it strange that the University of Oxford or any of its constituent colleges should receive reputational damage in respect of this event. The decision to host Nathan Cofnas was made solely by the committee of the Reform Society, and responsibility for the event rests exclusively with the same.”
Cofnas was approached for comment.

article_title: Healey to promise £15m to tackle misogyny in Budget
article_content:
Healey to promise £15m to tackle misogyny in Budget
- Published
Chancellor John Healey has pledged to give £15m to a fund established to tackle misogyny in schools, at work and in communities.
The government said the money will be provided over three years to schemes such as mentoring for young people, workplace training and communications campaigns designed to improve women and girls' safety.
Speaking on the eve of his first Budget, Healey said: "Every woman and girl deserves to feel safe, respected and able to pursue their ambitions - at school, at work and in their communities."
But Conservative shadow women and equalities minister Joy Morrissey said "not a single woman and girl is going to feel safer with this total waste of public money".
- Swinney to introduce misogyny education in every school in Scotland 
  - Published30 September
- Women to advise mayor how to make London safer 
  - Published4 September
- Students face sexism and misogyny at weekend jobs 
  - Published21 July
The "misogyny prevention fund" is expected to be confirmed in the Budget and is intended to support the work of a national taskforce established last month, external and chaired by Women and Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson.
Healey said the money will support "practical action to tackle misogyny head-on" and he hopes it will attract additional funding from businesses and philanthropists to increase its reach.
Phillipson said daily incidents of misogyny, including sexist slurs and workplace discrimination, have "no place in modern Britain".
She said: "This funding is a critical step as we work to confine misogyny to the history books, where it belongs."
Phillipson added that "everyone, from big business to members of the public, can do their bit to stamp out misogyny and improve the lives of women and girls everywhere".
When launching the taskforce chaired by Phillipson, the government said last month that it would aim to ensure government policy is "shaped by those most affected by misogyny".
It added its first meeting would focus on young people and later look at "workplaces, digital spaces and social cohesion".
Statistics published by the Office for National Statistics this month showed an estimated 12.8% of females aged 16 and over in England and Wales - around 3.2m - experienced at least one of domestic abuse, sexual victimisation or stalking in the year to March 2026.
The figure was an estimated 8.9% for males - around 2.1m.
For the Conservatives, Morrissey cited the estimates for women and girls as she criticised the announcement.
She said: "Labour simply aren't serious about tackling the crisis of violence against women and girls.
"This week it seems they will get the hard-pressed British taxpayer to fork out £15m to fund projects to tackle the 'manosphere'."

article_title: US military says strike on alleged drug vessel in eastern Pacific kills five people
article_content:
The US military said on Tuesday it killed five people after an airstrike on a suspected drug-trafficking vessel in the eastern Pacific.
Tuesday’s strike was among more than 70 such attacks since the beginning of Donald Trump’s second presidency, according to media tallies. Collectively, they have killed more than 240 people.
The Trump administration has maintained the people and boats were involved in trafficking. Trump has said the US is locked in armed conflict with Latin American cartels while justifying strikes as necessary to stem the flow of drugs into the US.
But the Trump administration has not provided definitive evidence to back up its contentions of drug trafficking and has prompted debate about the legality of the strikes.
Legal experts and rights groups argue the strikes could amount to extrajudicial killings because they have apparently targeted civilians who do not pose an immediate threat to the US.

article_title: UK government to give £15m to anti-misogyny fund amid ‘manosphere’ concerns
article_content:
The chancellor will give £15m to a dedicated fund to tackle misogyny in workplaces, schools and public places amid concerns in government about the rise of “manosphere” influencers.
The women and equalities minister, Bridget Phillipson, will helm the UK-wide fund, announced last month, marking the first time there has been specific national cash to address misogyny.
The government said organisations could bid for money from the misogyny prevention fund to provide services including mentoring for young people, workplace training and awareness campaigns to improve safety for women and girls. Ministers will also seek match funding from corporate partners and philanthropists to grow the amount of cash available.
Campaigns that have drawn praise in the past – which could be funded nationwide – are Transport for London’s poster campaigns and adverts that encouraged other men to intervene when they saw abusive behaviour taking place, including the “Have a Word” and “Say Maaate to a Mate” campaigns to challenge misogyny.
The campaigns won advertising awards but some critics argued they had done relatively little to address the major threats of violence against women and girls.
Phillipson, who announced her misogyny prevention taskforce last month, said the fund’s aim was to educate and prevent everyday sexism.
“Day to day misogyny – from sexist slurs and harassment to workplace discrimination – quite simply has no place in modern Britain,” she said, announcing the funding.
“The time for talk has long passed, which is why this government is putting its money where its mouth is when it comes to supporting women and girls. This funding is a critical step as we work to confine misogyny to the history books, where it belongs.
“Government is leading from the front, but we all have a role to play. Everyone – from big business to members of the public – can do their bit to stamp out misogyny and improve the lives of women and girls everywhere.”
The chancellor, John Healey, who is expected to confirm the £15m in the budget on Wednesday, said: “Every woman and girl deserves to feel safe, respected and able to pursue their ambitions – at school, at work and in their communities.
“This investment will back practical action to tackle misogyny head-on, while bringing businesses and philanthropists on board so we can go even further – giving women and girls more opportunity to succeed and hope for the future.”
The government has previously announced a separate fund to tackle misogynistic influences in schools, as part of the violence against women and girls strategy. That £20m package is intended to provide new funding and materials for schools to address relationship issues, online misogyny and misinformation.

article_title: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
article_content:
Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
- Published
Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.
The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.
The rise in sales came after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event.
Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.
The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month.
"Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin.
"These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."
On 22 October, Streeting said that people should ensure they have three litres of water per person per day; tinned goods in the cupboard; baby food; battery powered torches and mobile phone charging packs.
Many of the items cited by Streeting appeared in the list of goods gathered by Newsnight whose sales have shot up.
In response to the increase in retail sales of certain items, the defence secretary told Newsnight: "It's encouraging that people are taking practical steps to be ready. Having a few everyday essentials at home, from tinned food to torches, helps households prepare for disruption, whether that's flooding, power cuts or burst pipes. We can all play our part in making Britain more resilient."
An Iceland spokesperson told the BBC programme: "It's clear consumers have listened to the government's message as we have seen a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend and strong sales of bottled water too. Our supplies of these products remain healthy."
Newsnight also spoke to independent retailers who reported a spike in sales of goods highlighted by the defence secretary.
Josh Pringle, from Sgt Prepper's online store, said his sales had increased tenfold: "We were a small outfit on Wednesday. And then the government launched the Be Ready campaign and we couldn't believe what we were seeing – order after order after order. Most of them were for a wind-up radio."
Lincoln Miles, founder of Preppers Shop UK, told Newsnight of a 650% increase in sales after the government announcement. "Everything about off grid seems to be the key of what people are buying for the minute."

article_title: The Guardian view on supporting carers: the DWP’s problem is deeper than IT | Editorial
article_content:
The reform of carer’s allowance – a benefit paid to people who spend 35 or more hours a week caring for a disabled relative – is overdue and welcome. The cliff-edge design that forces claimants in England and Wales to forfeit their entire payment if they breach an earnings limit of £204 a week by as little as a penny is wrong in principle and made much worse by the appalling way in which rules have been applied.
A Guardian investigation revealed that the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) failed to warn thousands of people who it knew were being overpaid. This resulted in debts and hardship, and hundreds of criminal convictions for fraud. Carers in already difficult personal circumstances described feeling driven to desperation and illness by what one called a “catch-out culture”. Most claimants are women on low incomes; the allowance is £86.45 a week.
The plan to replace this outdated, blunt tool with a taper is a good one. The disincentive to employment built into the existing system is perverse. Adults with caring responsibilities should be encouraged to do paid work in addition to their roles at home if they can. As with child benefit, the promised taper will mean that earnings over the threshold lead to a diminution rather than a loss of the allowance. Demands for repayment should be drastically reduced. Thousands of low-income households with disabled members will gain more freedom as a result.
Details of the policy’s implementation have yet to be set out. But after years of delay and inaction, the main concern is timing. A DWP whistleblower first raised the overpayment issue a decade ago, only for their complaint to be shut down. Successive Conservative governments did nothing despite a detailed 2020 report from the work and pensions committee. Finally, last November, Liz Sayce’s independent review led to the recruitment of extra staff and a new approach. Ministers committed to correcting past errors, including the way that claimants had been unlawfully blocked from averaging their earnings. But progress has been slow, and with the taper expected to be rolled out in 2030-31, the injustice of the current situation looks set to continue for several more years.
The benefit system is complicated, and it is better to make changes properly than to rush through a botched job. But the overhaul of carer’s allowance should not be mistaken for an IT problem. The deeper issue is the ongoing failure to get to grips with the fundamental challenge of care in our society, and to take on board the extent to which millions of people’s lives are shaped by the needs of dependent adult relatives.
Louise Casey has made it clear that her social care commission will deliver recommendations about what it is reasonable to expect of families, as well as the state. There are grounds to hope that her forthright style and years of experience, combined with Andy Burnham’s strong commitment to reform, will finally lead to a breakthrough. In the meantime, the DWP must do all it can to put right the wrongs done to carer’s allowance claimants. There has still been no satisfactory explanation about how such a punitive culture developed. But the new commitment to tapered support is an encouraging indication that the government is now moving in a more compassionate direction.

article_title: The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny | Nils Pratley
article_content:
Two winners in the budget are known already. They are the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, state-funded investment bodies that have rapidly become central to the government’s growth strategy.
The former chancellor Rachel Reeves handed extra slugs of capital to both and now John Healey is going further. The NWF will get another £15.4bn over the next half decade, on top of its existing £27.8bn, and there’ll be another £5bn for the BBB, which already has £25.6bn.
Expect a fanfare about “over 100,000 jobs across the country to be created” via the extra capital for these so-called PuFins. The term means public financial institutions. They invest in private sector assets, either directly or through third-party funds, with the aim of making a profit for the taxpayer – or, at least, earning a return that matches or beats the government’s cost of borrowing.
Cue, also, another round of debate about whether Healey is engaged in fancy financial footwork to get around the constraints of his fiscal rules. Reeves rewrote those rules in her first budget in 2024 to allow the value of financial assets – such the NWF and BBB’s loans and stakes in companies – to be netted off against the public debt.
To fans, the principle makes sense. As long as the PuFins’ assets maintain their value and cover the interest on the government’s extra borrowing (a critical condition), it’s a way to boost investment. More critical projects can be built sooner, and possibly more cheaply; more companies may prosper to the eventual benefit of the public purse.
Critics, such as the right-leaning Centre for Policy Studies in a report last week, see a “financial wheeze” that disguises the true level of government borrowing and stores up trouble, as the Blair-era private finance initiative did. The thinktank called for the wings of the PuFins to be clipped.
Healey, it is safe to assume, will ignore that advice. The PuFins fall squarely within his theory for growth – the idea of “crowding in” private investment and spreading money around the regions.
In Healey’s support, one can say state-backed co-investment vehicles are not new. Governments of all hues have used them. George Osborne even launched a Green Investment Bank. And the NWF, despite its misleading name (it’s not a Norway-style wealth fund), to some degree merely replaces infrastructure lending that might have been done by the European Investment Bank in pre-Brexit days. As for the BBB, its focus on “scale-up” capital for young, fast-growing companies is designed to address a gap that has been a source of grumbles for decades. Both institutions are useful.
There are questions, however, about potential overuse. Are the NWF and BBB sticking in all cases to their core role of “additionality”, the idea that PuFins should bring something extra to the party? They are not meant to be substitutes for private capital. They must crowd in rather than crowd out.
The line can appear blurry at times. This column has questioned the £25m that BBB invested in Kraken Technologies, the software firm being spun out of Octopus Energy. How was that a case of “helping smaller businesses get the finance they need”? Kraken was valued at a thumping £6.45bn, so wasn’t a small firm; and £25m was a rounding error within a wider $1bn fundraising.
Similarly, the Centre for Policy Studies surely has a point when it wonders why the NWF lent to Scottish Power, “an investment-grade company with an investment-grade Spanish parent” on projects to upgrade to the electricity grid. The NWF’s ability to make long-dated loans probably helped the financing, but regulated utilities are supposed to be big enough to stand on their own feet. Weren’t there better targets for the NWF’s loans?
To be fair, the websites of both the NWF and BBB are stuffed with case studies that fit the government’s priorities uncontroversially. For example, the latter’s follow-on £100m investment in Oxford Quantum Circuits, a quantum computing firm, was big and on-message.
And, so far at least, the promise of gilt-like returns is intact, or not disproved. The BBB cites a “3.9% five-year adjusted return” but says the number would be higher if one was counting only its commercial activities. In the case of NWF, it’s too soon to tell: last year’s return on equity was -2.6% but a gilt-like number was only ever promised in 2030-31. The requirement to co-invest with hard-nosed private investors is probably helpful.
But there’s still the issue of being additional. “Assessing additionality is not a precise science, but rather an exercise in judgment,” concedes the NWF in its impact framework. An Office for Budget Responsibility-style body to scrutinise those judgments is starting to look essential. As the allocations from the Treasury increase, there is a risk that the definition of “additional” gets stretched. At the moment, the PuFins are only ultimately answerable to their sole shareholder, the Treasury.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies, in its pre-budget assessment, said: “If the government follows the spirit of the guidelines, and aims to construct a portfolio of investments that align with government priorities and generate a profit, the cases where investment can occur through PuFins may turn out to be relatively limited.”
That sounds like good advice. For the time being, there’s a fair argument there is room for more. The Resolution Foundation argues that, notwithstanding the extra £5.8bn from Reeves, the NWF’s capacity has “barely kept pace with inflation”. But policing the PuFins, and ensuring they stick to their “additionality” brief, is surely equally important. There will be problems if they behave like gannets.

article_title: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
article_content:
Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
- Published
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.
The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years.
Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust.
The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC.
"We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday.
Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support.
In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts.
Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said.
It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder. Chalk told Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that would include looking at whether any reports had been made but people or organisations had held back due to a "misplaced sense of cultural sensitivity".
Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene.
It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added.
The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries.
The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment.
The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice."
"We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement.
"Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have."
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review.
"There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said.
The review is due to report in five months.
Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year accountancy and finance student at the University of Southampton when he was murdered.
On the night of Nowak's muder, it was Digwa's brother who called 999, claiming Vickrum had been attacked "racially".
Bodycam footage released by Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary, with the permission of Nowak's family, showed officers speaking to Digwa and others while Nowak lay on the ground.
Nowak could be heard repeatedly saying that he had been stabbed and could not breathe.
Violent disorder broke out in Southampton in the days following the release of the footage.
After Digwa's sentencing, Nowak's father Mark called for a "full, fearless and transparent" investigation into the police response.
But he also urged people not to use his son's death to "create further division, hatred or tension".

article_title: Schrödinger’s racism, Nige’s latest wheeze to dodge his associates’ bigotry | John Crace
article_content:
Back to the future. Some of us can remember the days when the key to surviving a nuclear war was to kneel down under the kitchen table and keep your eyes closed till you were incinerated or died of radiation poisoning. Now the government wants you to hoard some baked beans and a few litres of water in the hope of getting through the next three days.
But when the apocalypse does come, you can bank on there being one survivor. The politician with seemingly limitless powers of regeneration. As one party of his dies, so another rises from the ashes. Fuelled not by water and tinned food, but by alcohol and grievance. Somehow, Nigel Farage is always the victim in his own story. The man who is forever misunderstood.
Nige must be the unluckiest politician alive. The man who has only ever wanted the best for everybody – deporting immigrants is clearly in their own best interests, even if it involves death or torture – keeps getting mired in scandal. There’s the money. Of course there is. Plenty of it from – how shall we put this? – unorthodox sources. But there’s also the racism. Why is it that so many who are close to Farage and his organisation turn out to be bigots? How can his message of love and peace to all men be so tainted? It’s happened so often now that you could forgive Nige for being a little grumpy.
Last week one of his closest friends was at it again. Raheem Kassam, touted as Reform’s next chief of staff, called Kemi Badenoch a “Nigerian scammer”. You and I know exactly what he meant. The leader of the opposition was like a West African phonejacker who rang you up and tried to scam your bank accounts. It was a fairly obvious racist slur. One designed to denigrate.
Only it wasn’t quite so obviously racist to Reform MPs themselves. Robert Jenrick called it a bit of forensic journalism. At least that’s what he implied by describing Kassam as a journalist. Danny Kruger was even more confused. There again, he often is. He’s meant to be the intellectual and moral compass of Reform, but just appears dim-witted and spinning helplessly in space. He thought “Nigerian scammer” couldn’t be racist because he couldn’t conceive of any of Nigel’s friends being racist. Try a little harder, Danny.
It was third time unlucky – that word again – as Nige took on his first proper morning media round in months. It didn’t end well for him. Car-crash TV. On BBC Breakfast, the presenter Sally Nugent quickly cut to the chase and it soon became clear that Nige doesn’t take it well when an intelligent woman asks him tricky questions. He likes to think of himself very much as a man’s man. Somehow being interviewed by a woman is a sign of disrespect. Or maybe he’s still tetchy about having given a press conference to a near-empty hall the day before.
First Nige tried to claim Kassam had not been a former chief of staff – he had in one of Farage’s previous lives – and was on the point of saying he wasn’t even a friend. But then he had a brainwave. “He’s Indian,” he said. “He’s of Indian heritage.” As if that somehow precluded all Indians – all black and brown people, for that matter – from being racist. A suggestion, dare one say it, that is racist in itself. Nige clearly believes in a hierarchy of racism. If he believes in racism at all. Maybe we’re just all stuck in a doom loop of cultural relativism. We just need to chill out a bit.
Next Farage tried to play the word dissociation game. Just because Kassam had used the words “Nigerian scammer” in conjunction with one another, it didn’t necessarily mean the words were in any way connected to form a single image. All he had done was to state two truths. Kemi was of Nigerian descent, though for the purposes of this conversation he was prepared to concede that she might also be part British. And she was a scammer, because she had said things that were demonstrably untrue. Much the same could be said of Nige, mind. Maybe in his own mind he also longs to be outed as a scammer.
Back in the BBC studio, Nugent wasn’t having any of this and kept at him. Did he think it was racist? “No, I don’t,” said Nige. Perhaps a bit over the top, but definitely not intentionally racist. Farage had spoken, Schrödinger’s racism. Something could be racist and not racist at the same time. In any case, he couldn’t be held responsible for any of the social media posts his friends and supporters made. It was his curse that so many in Reform expressed themselves in racist language. He had no idea why he had become the last refuge for so many bigots.
Things took on a more surreal turn later that morning when Kassam emailed a Guardian journalist to give an update on the situation. In it, he said that Nige had given him a ticking off for a tweet that was neither “clever nor funny”. Just a shame Farage couldn’t have used his position as the leader of Reform to make that same point on the BBC hours earlier. Kassam went on to say that, in hindsight, his tweet could have been better phrased and timed. He also claimed Kemi was a con artist for turning the Tories into a version of the Lib Dems. That will come as news to both the Tories and the Lib Dems. The Tories have been shadowing Reform to the right for the last two years.
The real sorry-not-sorry moment came when Kassam suggested he had spent too much time in the US recently. Over there, out-and-out racism was an acceptable rite of political discourse. People could say what they want. The trouble is that we Brits had lost our sense of humour. It was now a thought crime even to make a racist joke. Time we all lightened up. What was needed was more politicians who called Kemi a “Nigerian scammer” not fewer.
This isn’t quite the end of it. Because Kassam’s new found contrition may not be all it seems. On Tuesday morning he was again posting about “Kemi Scammenoch” on X. A post that has been subsequently deleted. As has his pinned “Nigerian scammer” tweet. If this is remorse, it’s still in its early days. Maybe one should treat Kassam and Farage as one and the same. When they show you what they are, believe them.

article_title: Why won't MPs tax the rich? We asked them – and their answers gave us hope | Faiza Shaheen
article_content:
In John Healey’s first budget this week, we will finally get a sense of the economic policies that will deliver Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism. Or will we? Capital gains tax equalised with income tax? Ruled out. A genuine wealth tax on those sitting on over £10m? Off the table. Even the briefed increase in the banking surcharge only takes us back to where it was until the Conservatives cut it in 2023. We can cross our fingers for trailed policies on supporting high streets, financial devolution and longer-term investment, but there is still more than a whiff of trickle-down economics in the air.
Poll after poll shows that the British public overwhelmingly supports wealth taxes on the super-rich – including three in five Reform-leaning voters. We know that wealth inequality – with the richest 50 families in the UK possessing more wealth than half of the UK population – is weakening our economy, eroding our social fabric and undermining our democracy. Just last year, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, explicitly acknowledged that we have “overtaxed labour and undertaxed wealth”. So what on earth is going on?
To solve this paradox, our team at Tax Justice UK joined forces with researchers at the University of Strathclyde to go straight to the source. We interviewed 30 politicians across Westminster, Holyrood and the Senedd between February and July 2026, while Keir Starmer was prime minister. We made sure, in particular, that we spoke to every faction of the Labour party in Westminster – as the party in government and the party we would expect to be predisposed to higher taxes on the super-rich, its opinions inevitably garner more interest. The findings offer a rare glimpse into the hidden machinery of British politics. They suggest that the barrier to taxing extreme wealth is a deeply entrenched pattern of political fear, economic uncertainty, institutional capture and parliamentary self-preservation. And while these interviews took place under the former leadership, our conversations with MPs since suggest that, unless Burnham commits to higher taxes on wealth, the same barriers do hold.
The problem doesn’t start in parliament. Far from the green benches, a hostile climate is carefully cultivated to make taxing wealth seem undesirable. A billionaire-owned media apparatus relentlessly pushes scare stories, successfully tricking ordinary homeowners into thinking a “wealth tax” targets their modest family homes rather than offshore holdings and multimillion-pound assets. Outlets constantly tell us that billionaires are leaving the UK because of new taxes – even those who actually left a decade ago – and quote “millionaire flight” figures from a seriously flawed report. It doesn’t matter if they are not true – these narratives successfully penetrate the hearts and minds of parliamentarians.
Whether MPs are dismissing the prospect because they assume that the public would never go for it, not wanting to face the press backlash, or wanting stronger empirical proof covering every micro-detail of policy design and its potential impacts, this media backdrop directly undermines politicians’ confidence in fighting for higher taxes on wealth. Demands for evidence are reasonable, of course – yet we rarely see this scrutiny applied to spending on defence or AI.
Then there is the direct influence of elite money. There is a perception that when you are rich enough, you don’t need to shout from the public gallery: you have elite access. As one Labour politician told us: “If the City doesn’t like it then sometimes it can change views here in a way that’s not helpful.”
Inside parliament, this structural pressure transforms into personal paralysis. Even backbenchers who privately champion wealth taxes often won’t stick their necks out ahead of party leaders. One Labour MP confessed to keeping quiet for fear of losing local funding, admitting: “I’m trying not to be an out-and-out rebel, because I want another Pride in Place award for a really deprived part of my constituency.”
When constituency improvements are held hostage to party-line conformity, acting on principle becomes complicated. Yet this dynamic also reveals an opportunity: our interviews revealed that if the party leadership took a decisive stand on taxing wealth, most Labour MPs would fall in line behind it. Furthermore, given that Burnham has been far warmer towards higher taxes on wealth than Starmer – who notoriously referred to wealth tax campaigners as “snake oil merchants” – there is potentially more space and opportunity for MPs to speak up.
For the PM himself, this may or may not be an issue he is willing to be brave on. The danger, of course, is that the view looks very different from the inside. The retreat we are seeing suggests that Burnham and his team are already succumbing to the very same Westminster pressures our research laid bare.
One might assume that underlying some of this political resistance is an ideological dogma that taxing extreme fortunes somehow “punishes success”. But while we encountered this view among interviewees on the political right, we found little evidence of it elsewhere. Which perhaps is some cause for celebration: if many of the barriers are not ideological, there are practical things we can do.
First, we would do well to remember that winning the argument on wealth taxation isn’t just a policy battle – it’s a narrative one. As several interviewed politicians noted, the movement for economic justice must stop focusing too heavily on “who pays”, and start relentlessly highlighting “what the money buys”. People are far less interested in taxing billionaires than they are in fixing their local NHS hospitals, repairing crumbling schools and investing in green infrastructure. Taxing wealth must be framed positively as a seed investment in collective prosperity. Positive, gain-focused messaging strips away the weaponised narrative that tax is inherently bad.
Ultimately, our research reminds us that civil society cannot sit back and wait for a progressive frontbench to deliver change from above. The structural incentives inside parliament are designed to manufacture caution, not courage.
Until we make it more dangerous for politicians to ignore the public than to challenge the super-rich, we will continue to get budgets that fail to correct a fundamental unfairness at the heart of our tax system. The polls show the country is already with us. Now we must translate that quiet consent into unshakeable public pressure to push on the door left ajar by Burnham’s previously stated positions. Just like wealth, true reform has never trickled down from the top – it is built from the ground up.
- 
  Faiza Shaheen is executive director of Tax Justice UK

article_title: My advice for Burnham’s first budget? Hit the banks – and hit them hard | Polly Toynbee
article_content:
Vibes matter. We live by how we feel – an idea that orthodox economics gets wrong and Andy Burnham’s first budget looks set to get right.
This walking good-vibes maestro is spreading a confetti of small good deeds. These may not shift the dial yet on 40 years of neoliberal economics, but they show the way he’s heading. Eyecatching everyday things – from capping bus fares to that small but resonant sum of £45 VAT on average off electricity bills – get people talking, alongside bigger plans for a national care service, electoral reform and a possible journey back to the EU.
Though his first budget is billed as unradical, one tax rise stands out for its Burnham vibes. After years of no penalties, no apologies, no payback for their bailout from the crash they caused, banks face a tax rise. The Tories’ cuts to the bank levy and bank profits surcharge were left in place by Rachel Reeves. No longer.
UK profits from the country’s four biggest banks were reportedly £13bn for the first half of this year, 16% up on last year.
Don’t undervalue the toughness it takes to ignore bankers’ intimidation, as the boss of their pressure group UK Finance writes to the chancellor saying a tax rise will encourage banks to move to competitor countries. The group’s claim that London has the highest bank taxes is a fabrication: only Ireland has a lower rate among western European countries. Paris’s is far higher, according to the authoritative Tax Policy Associates.
Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said that any move against bank profits could cause him to scrap plans for a £3bn London headquarters, a tower in Canary Wharf to house more than half of the bank’s 23,000 UK staff. He threatened Reeves likewise, and announced the tower go-ahead only after she left banks in peace in her 2025 budget.
Pause here to examine Dimon, the essence of the business power that Labour governments are always up against. Forbes lists his net worth as $3.1bn, and he took home $43m last year. In 2009, when the then chancellor, Alistair Darling, imposed a 50% levy on bankers’ bonuses over £25,000, Dimon called him to protest. In his memoir, Back from the Brink, Darling recalled that a “very, very angry” Dimon had threatened that JP Morgan might reconsider its UK investments. “He said that his bank bought a lot of UK debt and he wondered if that was now such a good idea.” And, yes, again Dimon reportedly warned that he might not build a new London office.
This year, documents released in the Epstein files revealed how the then business secretary, Peter Mandelson, had urged Dimon to “mildly threaten” Darling over the tax. That’s their milieu and how they operate. But Darling didn’t back down, though he was besieged by bankers with identical scripts. He stood firm, and JP Morgan built its London office and didn’t stop buying UK government debt. The BBC’s Faisal Islam recounts that episode as told him by Darling as “an incredible live example of the relative power of government and financial markets, of the actual dynamics of the ‘bond vigilantes’”.
The bank payroll tax raised an estimated £2.3bn in four months. But it was dropped. Are you surprised to learn that what was billed as a bonus levy was paid by the banks, never by the bankers? Or by their lack of shame or collective responsibility as they bargained squalidly over bonuses even in the aftermath of a crash they caused?
Officially the bank bailout cost the public £23bn, after some asset sales. But that’s trivial compared with the colossal lasting damage right across the economy. Official estimates cite a loss of up to 7.5% of GDP; others suggest double that amount.
Bankers hiss at any hint of plucking a few feathers off them, but we wait to know how much John Healey dares take. Dimon visited No 10 last month to warn them off a tax raise, but Burnham only “dropped into the meeting briefly”.
So, how much? Returning the corporation tax surcharge on banks to its original 8%, from the 3% to which the Tories cut it, would yield £2bn. It’s a puny sum, and the banks owe the country much more. But nonetheless, Burnham resisting their bullying would send a self-confident message.
TUC polling finds strong support for a bank windfall tax, as it does for higher gambling and wealth taxes. Raising capital gains tax is popular, too. In the air, more long-term, is a money-raising idea backed by the Institute for Fiscal Studies and Resolution Foundation, to merge national insurance and income tax and no longer exempt pensions, rent and share income from NI.
Burnham knows the trick to raising tax is linking it to good spending, such as ending the triple lock to invest in social care. So banks, shedding jobs by the thousand, could be funding Alan Milburn’s upfront costs to get Neets (young people not in education, employment or training) into work.
Good vibes greet this budget. Though inflation is up, so is employment, growth, business investment and average pay. Earnings inequality jumped up for the first time in a decade, but from Friday, trade union reps get the right to recruit in every workplace, a gamechanger in anti-union companies. Union membership is the surest way to raise pay, by a reported 4-5%, so ignore Tories raging about the “red tape” of workers’ rights.
A budget signals a government’s way forward. Willingness to defy bank bullying, even a bit, is a good early sign. Watch out for more Burnham emblems.
- 
  Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist
