article_title: «Росія стає нецікавою»: Портников пояснив, чому Китай не готовий утримувати Кремль
article_content:
«Росія стає нецікавою»: Портников пояснив, чому Китай не готовий утримувати Кремль
Китай, попри інтерес до російських енергоресурсів, значно більше залежить від американського ринку.
Президент США Дональд Трамп може бути зацікавлений у домовленостях із Путіним, однак не сприймає себе як молодшого партнера російського диктатора.
Про це політичний оглядач Віталій Портников розповів у етері Еспресо, аналізуючи можливі відносини між Дональдом Трампом, Путіним і лідером Китаю Сі Цзіньпіном.
За словами журналіста, інтереси Росії та Китаю частково збігаються в контексті протистояння зі Сполученими Штатами. Проте економічні інтереси Пекіна значно ширші, ніж співпраця з Москвою.
Китай зацікавлений у постачанні дешевих російських нафти й газу, але водночас залежить від доступу до американського та європейського ринків.
«Якщо немає дешевого газу, Росія стає нецікавою», — зазначив Портников.
Він звернув увагу на те, що Москва та Пекін досі не узгодили остаточних умов постачання газу газопроводом «Сила Сибіру». Китай прагне отримувати російський газ за вигідними для себе цінами й не готовий платити за нього за міжнародними тарифами.
Портников також пояснив, що американський президент не сприйматиме себе як підлеглого партнера російського диктатора. На думку оглядача, Трамп переконаний у власному лідерстві, зокрема з огляду на економічний і військовий потенціал США.
«Трамп може сприяти Путіну, але він не бачить себе молодшим партнером. Він вважає, що він головний у цій трійці», — пояснив журналіст.
Окремо політичний оглядач звернув увагу на ставлення спецпосланця президента США Стіва Віткоффа до Путіна.
На думку Портникова, Віткофф може розглядати Росію передусім як джерело потенційного прибутку. Журналіст припустив, що фінансові інтереси можуть пояснювати прихильне ставлення американського представника до російського керівника.
«Віткофф бачить у Путіні мішок із грошима», — заявив Портников.
Портников також наголосив на відмінностях між політичними системами Росії та західних країн. За його словами, російське керівництво не розуміє принципу незалежності судової влади, коли рішення судів не залежать від політичної волі керівництва держави.
«Вони вважають, що весь світ влаштований так само, як Росія, що просто люди граються. А насправді все це декорація. Вони щиро в цьому впевнені», — підсумував журналіст.
Раніше повідомлялося, що президент США Дональд Трамп і диктатор Путін поставили лідера Китаю Сі Цзіньпіна в незручне становище, висловивши зацікавленість у тристоронньому саміті.
Ми раніше інформували, що президент України Володимир Зеленський заявив, що Китай має достатньо важелів впливу на Росію, щоб спонукати Кремль припинити війну проти України.

article_title: Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellor
article_content:
John Healey will deliver his first budget on Wednesday as UK households and businesses come under pressure from the unfolding economic shock caused by the war in the Middle East.
Against a febrile backdrop in global markets, the chancellor is facing a delicate balancing act to provide “breathing space” measures to ease the cost of living crisis while increasing growth and sticking to the fiscal rules.
Healey will also flesh out Andy Burnham’s pledge to deliver “good growth in every postcode”, with measures to hand local leaders more money and power.
Here are six charts that will underpin the chancellor’s decisions.
Sticking to the fiscal rules
At the spring statement, Healey’s immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, left herself £23.6bn of “headroom” against the fiscal rules, which require day-to-day spending to be matched by receipts by the end of this parliament.
 
 
 However, the buffer is widely expected to have been slashed by a surge in debt interest costs, as the war in the Middle East causes a global inflation shock that is rattling the bond markets.
The Resolution Foundation estimates headroom has been halved to about £12bn. Much will depend on the judgment of the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the independent Treasury watchdog, which will take into account the hit from rising debt costs, but also other positive and negative developments for the public finances – including inflation, pay growth, employment and productivity.
Healey is thought to be willing to allow the buffer to take a hit. However, jittery bond investors will be looking for him to retain some headroom to guard against further negative shocks, with at least £14bn thought to be needed to avoid provoking a bond market reaction.
‘Breathing space’ measures
The chancellor has pledged “breathing space” measures for households and businesses grappling with the cost of living crisis, as the energy price shock fuelled by the Iran conflict hits consumers.
Petrol and diesel prices have surged close to record highs and energy bills are forecast to increase to £2,000 a year from January for the typical household. Since 2021, consumers have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills.
Healey is thought to have earmarked more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which will go on increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits. He has also vowed to help businesses, and has been urged to extend a cut in fuel duty.
Alongside energy support, Andy Burnham has already promised Labour will cut living costs through other measures – including a new mortgage scheme for first-time buyers, and a pledge to build more social homes.
Rewiring the state
Burnham has made “growth in every postcode” his top political slogan since becoming prime minister. With devolution likely to be a central theme of the budget, a raft of measures are expected to add some substance to the rhetoric.
Central to the devolution package will be plans to allow local leaders in England to retain a share of income tax, alongside a new £1.5bn borrowing facility for directly elected mayors.
Britain is the most centralised G7 country for tax and spending policy, and is among the most economically unequal, according to the Centre for Cities thinktank. The aim of redrawing the political map – including establishing a new hub for No 10 in the north, based in Manchester – is to increase regional economic growth, and with it the performance of the UK economy at large.
Burnham has also signalled that a strengthened industrial strategy will be key to his agenda, as well as measures to support high streets and towns.
Tackling the youth jobs crisis
The prime minister has said Britain is facing an “economic catastrophe and a moral failure” after a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost 1 million.
Tackling the youth jobs crisis will be a key budget theme. Business leaders have pressed Healey for tax cuts and help with labour costs to encourage youth recruitment, while ministers have explored options for overhauling the benefits system and making changes to apprenticeships.
Healey has indicated that welfare reform will be critical. There could though be costs attached – as any savings from changes to the system could be offset by higher spending on employment support. The government is handling the process carefully to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion faced by Keir Starmer, and is still awaiting recommendations from two key reviews – by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn and the Department for Work and Pensions minister Stephen Timms.
The government is understood to favour handing local leaders more power and money to support young people as part of the solution. Analysis from the Youth Futures Foundation, a charity, shows the risk of a young person becoming Neet is geographically uneven: rates are significantly higher in Blackpool, Birmingham, and Bradford than in Bath, Harrogate or Guildford.
Increasing defence spending
Having resigned as Starmer’s defence secretary over funding, Healey is widely tipped to use his budget to find more cash for the military. Burnham has also spoken of the importance of the defence sector for his reindustrialisation plans.
First, the chancellor will need to find an additional £1bn a year to fund Labour’s defence investment plan. Announced by Starmer in his final weeks in office, that put defence spending on track to reach 2.7% of gross domestic product by 2029.
However, Healey has expressed an ambition to spend 3% by 2030. The Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates an extra £11bn would be needed in that year. Longer term, the government is targeting spending of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035. This is equivalent to a £25bn increase in today’s terms.
Repairing the economic damage of Brexit
Burnham reopened the debate over Brexit in his speech to Labour conference in Liverpool, arguing that leaving the EU had damaged the UK economy and failed to bring the benefits promised.
This week’s budget is expected to underscore the economic hit, including from a drop in net migration.
Net migration to the UK has fallen sharply from a record peak of almost a million in 2023. Earlier this year, the Office for National Statistics downgraded its estimate for the long-run figure to settle at about 230,000 annually, down from a previous assumption of 340,000.
On average, immigrants are net contributors to the exchequer, and so how the OBR accounts for this drop in its forecasts will be critical. Should it adopt a similar approach to the ONS, the Resolution Foundation thinktank estimates this could lead to a drop in tax receipts of £4.7bn by 2029-30 relative to previous forecasts.

article_title: США и Россия обсуждают нефтяные соглашения в рамках переговоров о мире в Украине — FT
article_content:
США и Россия обсуждают возможное возвращение американских нефтяных компаний на российский рынок в рамках переговоров о прекращении войны против Украины. В случае достижения договоренности компании из США могут возобновить совместные проекты у побережья Сахалина и присоединиться к поставкам российской нефти в Европу. Об этом сообщило издание Financial Times.
Белый дом и Кремль рассматривают возможность возобновления после войны совместного предприятия с участием крупнейших американских и российских нефтяных компаний. Речь идет о проекте у побережья Сахалина — острова на Дальнем Востоке России. Еще одно предложение предусматривает привлечение американских компаний к возобновлению поставок российской нефти в Европу по нефтепроводу «Дружба».
Эти идеи являются частью более широких усилий Вашингтона по прекращению войны России против Украины. Администрация президента США Дональда Трампа предлагает экономические стимулы, надеясь привлечь российского диктатора Владимира Путина к переговорам. Американские чиновники неоднократно подчеркивали, что реализация таких проектов возможна только после окончания войны.
Спецпосланник Трампа Стив Виткофф обсуждал потенциальные бизнес-сделки с Путиным на встрече в Санкт-Петербурге в начале сентября, рассказали собеседники. Во время последующего визита в Москву на прошлой неделе в его записной книжке заметили слова «Бизнес-сделки». Надпись наряду с другими заметками попала на фотографии, обнародованные кремлевским пресс-пулом.
Американский чиновник подтвердил, что представители Трампа обсуждали экономические предложения также и с Украиной: речь идет о послевоенной экономической основе для долгосрочного роста и инвестиций. С Россией рассматриваются возможности экономического сотрудничества после завершения боевых действий. По словам чиновника, соответствующие соглашения должны стать частью всеобъемлющего мирного соглашения и будут зависеть от него. Он подчеркнул, что ничего еще окончательно не согласовано.
Москва, однако, рассматривает бизнес-предложения как стимул для Трампа нормализовать отношения ещё до завершения войны, заявили двое собеседников. Кремль открыто демонстрирует готовность возобновлять экономическое сотрудничество с США, продолжая боевые действия против Украины. В то же время перспективы многих проектов остаются неопределёнными из-за неуступчивости Путина в вопросе завершения войны и осторожности американских компаний в отношении возвращения в Россию.
ExxonMobil была единственной американской компанией, участвовавшей в масштабном проекте «Сахалин-1». В прошлом году она сообщала о переговорах с Россией о компенсации за изъятую 30-процентную долю, но заявляла, что не планирует возобновлять деятельность в стране.
Другие предложения касаются авиации и поставок сырья. Одно из них — восстановить доступ американских авиакомпаний к российскому воздушному пространству для транзитных полётов и пролётов над страной. Это могло бы существенно сократить расходы на топливо.
Также обсуждается возобновление сотрудничества американских компаний с Россией в сфере производства и поставок титана, важного для гражданского авиастроения. Ранее у Boeing было совместное предприятие по производству титана в России, но компания приостановила сотрудничество после вторжения в Украину. С тех пор компания диверсифицировала источники поставок этого металла.
Эти и другие бизнес-предложения представители США и России обсуждают без непосредственного участия Украины или Европы. Их реализация означала бы резкое изменение отношений Москвы с Западом после многих лет изоляции. Вашингтон при этом заявляет, что полноценное восстановление экономических связей возможно только после того, как Россия и Украина договорятся о прекращении войны.
Нынешние обсуждения опираются на предложения, которые рассматривались в ходе переговоров о мирном плане для Украины в конце прошлого года. Тогда Виткофф и зять Трампа Джаред Кушнер обсуждали их с экономическим спецпредставителем Путина Кириллом Дмитриевым.
В феврале Дмитриев оценивал потенциальную стоимость проектов в 14 миллиардов долларов. Вскоре эта инициатива застопорилась, поскольку Украина отвергла российские требования территориальных уступок в качестве предварительного условия для переговоров. План Дмитриева изначально предполагал ожидание замораживания войны. Однако теперь эти проекты решили продвигать уже сейчас.
Среди других обсуждаемых проектов — возможная продажа международных активов «Лукойла» инвесторам, связанным с Белым домом. Также речь идет о проекте по сжиженному природному газу на Аляске с участием российской компании «Новатек». Еще одно предложение — возобновить поставки газа в Европу по уцелевшей нити «Северного потока». Остальные нити были разрушены взрывами 2022 года.
Белый дом и Кремль также обсуждали более широкую договоренность об ослаблении санкций в отношении калийных удобрений и их экспорта через балтийские порты. Для этого Европейский Союз должен был бы отменить соответствующие ограничения. Другая потенциальная идея предусматривает передачу управления Запорожской АЭС на оккупированной Россией территории Украины американской структуре. Она должна была бы распределять произведенную электроэнергию между Украиной и Россией.
Бывший чиновник администрации Трампа отметил, что предыдущие американские попытки склонить Москву к мирному соглашению практически не повлияли на Путина. По его словам, переговорщики подготовили реальные предложения, которые давали России возможность завершить войну. Однако они не смогли преодолеть паранойю Путина, из-за чего ни одна из этих идей не имела шансов на реализацию, считает собеседник.
Напомним, что администрация Трампа рассматривает возможность отмены санкций против Российского фонда прямых инвестиций. Учреждение во главе с Кириллом Дмитриевым помогает организовывать поставки российского дизельного топлива в США. Минфин США считает, что фонд уже имеет необходимые разрешения для операций с топливом.
Кроме того, сенатор-республиканец от Кентукки Митч Макконнелл раскритиковал уступки Трампа в адрес России. Он заявил, что отмена санкций и сокращение помощи Украине не заставят российского диктатора Владимира Путина завершить войну. По мнению сенатора, ограничение военной и разведывательной поддержки Киева может помочь Москве на фронте и затянуть боевые действия.
description: Европейские дипломаты выступают против экономических уступок Кремлю до окончания боевых действий.

article_title: How has Andy Burnham used his first 100 days in power?
article_content: Burnham promised a more open approach to managing Labour, with greater consultation and less reliance on party discipline to suppress debate. Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenBurnham promised a more open approach to managing Labour, with greater consultation and less reliance on party discipline to suppress debate. Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyHow has Andy Burnham used his first 100 days in power?From ‘everyday fixes’, party management and communications to long-term plans for care and pensions, the PM’s six key acts so farAndy Burnham arrived in Downing Street promising to transform the way Britain works, restore hope and bring an end to years of political division. One hundred days later, the prime minister has announced a series of measures aimed at making everyday life easier, he’s reopened the debate over Britain’s relationship with the EU and set out plans to overhaul public services. He has also managed to maintain an unusually visible public profile, appearing regularly on social media and even taking part in a charity edition of Channel 4’s Gogglebox. Burnham has said he’s been surprised by the public’s appetite for change, insisting his first budget on Wednesday would offer some breathing space for households and businesses.But the early weeks of his premiership have also exposed tensions between immediate political wins and the structural changes he has promised. Here is how his first 100 days have unfolded in six key ways.Quick policy winsBurnham made a series of what Downing Street calls “everyday fixes” central to his premiership, targeting everything from electricity bills and bus fares to misleading discounts, subscription traps and antisocial behaviour on public transport. One of his first announcements, the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills across Britain, took effect on 1 October. The government estimates an annualised saving of £45 for a typical household, although the temporary measure is funded only until March. Other announcements have yet to take effect. A £2 cap on participating bus services in England outside London and new rules making subscriptions easier to cancel are due to start in January.The bus measure also involves trade-offs. It is partly funded by switching international climate finance from grants to loans, a decision criticised by development charities. The strategy is intended to demonstrate that the government understands ordinary frustrations and can respond quickly. Yet questions remain about whether a collection of relatively modest interventions can significantly improve living standards. The VAT cut on electricity bills is not likely to help struggling households, who are more likely to be reliant on gas than electricity.Rough sleeping and social careEnding rough sleeping was among Burnham’s earliest commitments, drawing on his experience as the mayor of Greater Manchester. The government initially allocated £442m to tackle the problem, and announced a further £432m on Sunday, bringing its commitment to £874m over different funding periods.View image in fullscreenBurnham speaks on a visit to St Martin‑in‑the‑Fields, a homelessness charity in central London. Photograph: Ian Vogler/ReutersBurnham wants everyone sleeping rough in England to be offered a route off the streets or appropriate support before Christmas. But the success of the initiative will depend on whether people can access suitable accommodation and the services needed to help them remain housed. And it remains unclear how exactly the prime minister hopes to keep people from going back on to the streets and not staying permanently in temporary accommodation. A big proposal is Burnham’s plan for a national care service in England, which he intends to help finance by reforming the state pension triple lock from 2030. The government plans to legislate during this parliament, while maintaining the existing guarantee until then. But the savings from changing pension uprating are uncertain and depend heavily on future economic conditions. Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, welcomed Burnham’s proposed changes of the triple lock but said “it will not be the answer to funding universal social care”. Party managementBurnham promised a more open approach to managing Labour, with greater consultation and less reliance on party discipline to suppress debate. His appointments have included members of the Socialist Campaign Group, bringing MPs from Labour’s left into government roles. But he has disappointed a lot of soft-left MPs who campaigned for him after the Labour conference in 2025, when he made a number of media appearances attempting to prove he could replace Keir Starmer. His failure to include many of those from Mainstream, Open Labour and larger soft-left factions has been noted from MPs in the new intake, and those who have been in the parliamentary Labour party for a long time.Disagreements have emerged, particularly over immigration. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, faces opposition from Labour MPs and some cabinet colleagues over proposals that could require some migrant workers to wait 15 years before securing permanent residence. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, declined to endorse the specific proposal before being forced to clarify her support for the government’s broader approach. Burnham backed the principle of earned settlement but stopped short of committing to every detail of Mahmood’s proposals.A government source believes Burnham has avoided public rows so far because he is “taking his time to get policy right”, but they added, “isn’t it strange that a sitting cabinet minister had to apologise for making a joke … clearly we’re not one big happy family”. Difficult decisionsBeyond the everyday fixes, Burnham has begun confronting choices that divide opinion within his own party. He has reopened discussion of Britain’s relationship with the EU, arguing that Brexit has damaged economic growth and weakened immigration control. On Monday, he revealed his personal desire to see Britain rejoin the EU during his lifetime, while ruling out abandoning Labour’s manifesto red lines during this parliament. View image in fullscreenActivists from Fossil Free London stage a protest against the Rosebank oilfield and the Jackdaw gasfield outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockEnergy policy has presented another dilemma. Last week, the government approved the Jackdaw North Sea gasfield, arguing that domestic production would support energy security and employment. The development is expected to create only 27 new direct jobs and safeguard 273 existing positions. Environmental groups argue that further fossil fuel production undermines Britain’s climate commitments, while domestic gas does not automatically reduce household bills.CommunicationBurnham has drastically changed the way Downing Street presents itself. The prime minister’s social media updates, which are pretty much daily, his collaborations with public figures including Mo Farah and online creators, and his appearance alongside Steve Rotheram on Gogglebox have taken his message beyond the traditional Westminster audience or those who avidly follow politics. His approach has attracted substantial online attention and made short, accessible explanations of government announcements a recognisable feature of his premiership. Andrew Chadwick, professor of political communication at Loughborough University, has described Burnham’s collaborations with influencers as generating a “constructed sense of authenticity”. But there is a big difference between attracting audiences, of all ages and backgrounds, and explaining policy and persuading voters that measures will actually help them. What do the public think?UK poll averages graphLabour has recovered ground in the polls, although the measures of how satisfied the public are seem slightly more complicated. As soon as Burnham entered No 10, the party’s ratings rose to 23% then reached 26%, overtaking Reform UK on 24%.After the Labour conference, an Ipsos survey conducted between 15 and 22 October put the party on 32%, eight points ahead of the Conservatives, with Reform UK on 20%. But 66% of those surveyed expressed dissatisfaction with the government’s performance, against 23% who were satisfied.Meanwhile, YouGov polling conducted earlier this month revealed 46% viewed Burnham favourably and 42% unfavourably. His net favourability rating had fallen from 13 points in August to four points.Despite this, Opinium pollsters declared: “Burnham remains the only party leader with a positive net approval rating and holds a commanding lead over both Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage on who would make the better prime minister.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourSocial carePensionsBudgetUK cost of living crisisState pensionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

article_title: П’ять червоних ліній України на переговорах: дипломат назвав, чим не можна поступатися
article_content:
П’ять червоних ліній України на переговорах: дипломат назвав, чим не можна поступатися
Наразі складно оцінити, навколо яких саме питань тривають так звані мирні переговори між США, Україною та РФ.
Україна має відстоювати власний суверенітет, територіальну цілісність і право самостійно визначати курс на вступ до ЄС і НАТО під час мирних переговорів.
Про це заявив дипломат Костянтин Єлісєєв, який також назвав необхідні умови для укладення мирної угоди, інформує NV.
За словами дипломата, наразі складно оцінити, навколо яких саме питань тривають так звані мирні переговори. Водночас, на його думку, Україна має наполягати на дотриманні принципових умов.
Єлісєєв сформулював три основні принципи, яких, як він сподівається, дотримуватимуться українські переговорники.
Перший — «нічого про Україну без України». Другий — усі питання, що стосуються Європи та її безпеки, мають вирішуватися за участі європейських партнерів.
«Нічого не погоджено, поки все не погоджено», — заявив дипломат.
За його словами, доки не узгоджено цілісний документ із мирним планом, не можна вважати погодженими всі його окремі положення.
Єлісєєв наголосив, що про реальний початок мирних переговорів можна говорити лише після повного та безумовного припинення вогню.
Він також назвав дві важливі складові майбутньої мирної угоди — гарантії безпеки для України та механізми економічного відновлення держави.
Окремо Єлісєєв окреслив п’ять принципових питань, щодо яких, на його думку, Україна не повинна йти на поступки.
«Ні обмеженню суверенітету України. Ні юридичній зміні міжнародно визнаних кордонів України. Ні будь-якому обмеженню Збройних сил, Сил оборони України», — наголосив дипломат.
Він також виступив проти будь-яких обмежень української національної ідентичності та рішень щодо членства або нечленства України в ЄС і НАТО, які ухвалювалися б без згоди самої держави.
За словами Єлісєєва, саме ці п’ять аспектів мають стати основою будь-якого мирного плану.
Раніше повідомлялося, що прем’єр Польщі Дональд Туск заявив, що переговори України, США та РФ в Абу-Дабі попередньо відбудуться 4 листопада.
Ми раніше інформували, що Україна прагне закінчити війну з Росією та готова розглядати як часткове припинення вогню, так і повне припинення бойових дій.

article_title: UK officials discussing options including free movement with EU ahead of summit
article_content:
British officials have begun discussions with the EU about a long-term relationship that could include a return to free movement, the business secretary has said while promising the British people “are the boss” when it comes to what the UK will accept.
Jonathan Reynolds said the focus for British negotiations was the EU summit in November to seal an agreement to ease some trading restrictions and a youth mobility deal. But he said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, had made it clear he wanted to see a long-term and stable relationship with the bloc.
“They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be. But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we’re going to make,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.
He said the changes announced at the EU summit, including a food and drink deal and on emissions trading, would make a significant difference. But he added: “What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us, and we need to get as little uncertainty as possible.
“We need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be, and he is going to set that out after the summit. And he is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are.”
Reynolds said there had been “no assumptions made about the next stage after that. It’s the prime minister quite rightly saying he wants to set out to the British people what the options are to resolve some of the tensions that exist.”
He said no decision would be made without voters being given a say, without specifying whether this would be through a general election or a referendum. “No assumptions have been made on this. The British people are the people who will decide this. They’re the boss on this,” he said.
A number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU.
The Labour MP for Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes, Melanie Onn, was among those urging caution. “I am still not over the kind of very divisive debate that we had when we were leaving the EU post the referendum, and I don’t think that the scars have healed for many people around the country,” she told Today. “So I do think that this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time.”
The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the programme it would be “very, very poor indeed” to begin discussing freedom of movement. “Five months ago, Andy Burnham says to leave-voting Makerfield: ‘I’m not going to reopen these arguments.’ Two and a half years ago, a Labour government got a massive majority in parliament saying we will not be re-entering the single market, the customs union, or opening up the debate on the free movement of people,” he said.
“What I am saying is this: this prime minister has no mandate, and to hear that his officials are negotiating in Brussels already is really very, very poor indeed.”
Burnham made his plea for an “honest discussion” about freedom of movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.
Burnham also shared his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in its manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.
The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].
“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

article_title: What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India
article_content:
When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.
The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.
Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.
As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.
Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.
I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.
Trump the deal-maker
Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.
But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.
The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.
While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.
“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.
But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.
“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.
In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.
As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.
The way forward
Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.
“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.
His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”
If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”
Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.
What else we’re reading about
Student protests | Bikaner House, one of Delhi’s premier arts venues, asked visual artist Raihan Vadra to remove from his show more than 70 photographs that featured recent student protests. Vadra, the son of the Congress leader, Priyanka Gandhi, defended his work and also refused a request to remove images featuring the national flag. In a press statement, the venue said certain photos were “inconsistent” with its policy.
Fashion | Designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee, celebrated for his maximalist aesthetic, hosted a Diwali party at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. In September, he unveiled a high-jewellery collection inspired by the Byzantine, in collaboration with the museum.
Air pollution | Emergency measures, including a ban on coal-fired tandoors in restaurants and restrictions on diesel generators, have come into effect in Delhi, as air quality dropped to the poor category at the onset of the annual pollution season.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Film-maker Ritu Sarin, director of the annual Dharamshala international film festival, which runs from 29 October to 1 November, suggests a film from this year’s lineup:
“Shot over three years on real locations, Anmol Sidhu’s sophomore feature, Flowers of Acacia, follows wedding orchestra dancers in rural Punjab with a gaze that allows all the large brutalities and smaller intimacies to shine through. Sidhu’s confident, consummate grasp of the medium is on full display in terrifying scenes that stretch to the edge of what is palatable. The camera refuses to look away.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
7,633
That’s the number of trees Mumbai’s municipal authorities authorised to be felled over five months this year, to make way for development works, according to the Indian Express. Of these, about 3,500 will be permanently removed, while the rest will be replanted elsewhere.
Vibe check
Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.
“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.

article_title: Chancellor targets cost of living crisis in budget for a ‘difficult moment’
article_content:
John Healey has acknowledged the UK faces a “difficult moment” but insisted he would put the country on a better path as he delivers his first budget on Wednesday against a turbulent global economic backdrop.
But despite the international uncertainty, the chancellor will signal “fresh hope for the future” as he attempts to sound a more optimistic note, by providing households with breathing space from rising cost of living pressures.
The budget, which will be interpreted as a signal of Andy Burnham’s intent, is nevertheless expected to be a relatively modest affair as Healey grapples with stark fiscal realities, putting off important decisions on tax and spending until next year.
“The world’s a highly uncertain place,” the chancellor said, in a video released before the budget. “Conflicts abroad are pushing up energy prices, and the cost of living here at home – piling pressure on the families, on businesses and on our public finances.”
Healey insisted the government would move to ease the cost of living “responsibly” by sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, as he attempts to reassure the markets that his plans for longer-term reform will make Britain “more resilient” from global shocks.
The chancellor has limited scope for big giveaways because of the stretched public finances, made worse by international market turmoil caused by the Iran conflict, but changes aimed at easing the cost of living are set to feature heavily.
In his pre-budget address, he added: “This budget is about getting through this difficult moment. But it’s also about putting Britain on a future path, a better future path.”
Healey is expected to offer temporary support for poorer families before a steep rise in typical energy bills in January; while pledging energy market reforms aimed at bringing down bills for all households in the longer term.
Andy Burnham recently told MPs he was keen to see the gas standing charge – a fixed daily levy on all users – abolished. The move would bring down bills for consumers who use less energy, and the cost would be picked up by those who use more.
Industry experts fear further investment in hydrogen and carbon capture is likely to bear the brunt of efforts to rein in extra spending, in a blow to the UK’s net zero targets.
As part of a series of “everyday fixes”, the chancellor is expected to end the carers’ allowance cliff edge, which has penalised unpaid carers for going over their earnings limit, even by as little as a few pence a week. Healey is also expected to cancel January’s planned increase in fuel duty.
The government has been under pressure to use the budget to set out a clear path for defence spending to hit 3% of national income by 2030 – a target Healey claimed to be committed to when he resigned as defence secretary earlier this year.
But while he is expected to confirm more investment in defence industries – described as a “downpayment” on hitting the target – Healey is expected to wait until next year’s spending review to confirm the timetable.
The budget will also set out a “roadmap” to devolving more tax revenues to local leaders in a significant shift towards moving spending power away from Whitehall to the regions and nations of the UK.
But the detail of Burnham’s devolution agenda in areas such as skills and employment support is not expected until the government publishes a white paper in the weeks ahead.
Cutting energy prices has the added benefit of bringing down inflation, helping to ease pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates. Markets are now expecting the Bank to hike rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months.
Healey is also expected to take action to offset part of the hit to the public finances from higher interest rates on government borrowing – the result of rising inflation and turmoil in global bond markets.
The government had to pay the highest yield, or interest rate, on new five-year bonds since 2008 on Tuesday, above 5%.
City analysts say bond market investors will be watching the budget closely – though the upward move in UK yields, or interest rates, have echoed those seen in other major economies.
The UK’s economy has proved more resilient than expected in the face of the Iran conflict but recent data has pointed to a deteriorating outlook.
At a cabinet meeting last week, Healey told ministers that rising inflation caused by the conflict, which hit an in-year high of 3.5% last month, was the political backdrop to the budget.
Consumer confidence has fallen at the fastest rate since Brexit; while the number of businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, according to data published by consultancy BTG on Thursday, with hospitality and construction hardest hit.
Healey struck an optimistic note, however, saying: “Britain’s economy is showing real signs of resilience: investment’s up, productivity is growing and we had the joint fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of this year.”
Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for younger people under the age of 21 after warnings that they are being priced out of jobs but prompting accusations that Labour had broken a manifesto pledge.
He is also expected to protect pensioners and those saving for their retirement by shielding nearly one million people from paying income tax and is preparing to make the government’s revived Help to Buy scheme more generous, in a boost to middle-earners.
To help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, Healey is poised to raise taxes for Britain’s banks, potentially reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt, which would raise upwards of £2bn a year. Online retailers will be responsible for collecting tax owed by firms selling on their platforms.
The Tories said the chancellor was set to “shy away” from the difficult decisions, including bringing down the welfare bill, which the prime minister has said he does not want to do through “crude cuts”.
The shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, Richard Fuller, said: “Britain’s public finances are on a cliff edge. A ‘do-nothing’ budget will not solve the problems staring us in the face: a spiralling welfare bill, a crippling tax burden, mounting debt and rising global threats.”
The Lib Dems warned against a “steady as she goes” budget. Their deputy leader, Daisy Cooper, said: “Families are being squeezed from all sides, businesses face mounting costs and for many it feels like even the basic joys in life have become unaffordable.”

article_title: Зеленский отметил операции «Велес» и «Вивальди»: что известно об успехах ВСУ
article_content:
Президент Владимир Зеленский заслушал доклады об успешных операциях ВСУ на фронте. Среди них он отметил операцию «Велес», которую назвал «продуманной и технологичной».
По словам президента, россияне пытались использовать подземные газовые трубы, чтобы продвигаться мимо позиций ВСУ, однако потерпели поражение. Украинские военные использовали эти подземные коммуникации против самих оккупантов.
«Операция “Велес” от “Хартии” укрепляет наши позиции и демонстрирует россиянам, что и под Купянском у них нет того результата, который им определило их политическое руководство», — отметил Зеленский.
Он также отметил успехи операции ДШВ, в ходе которой было освобождено 800 квадратных километров территории. В ходе операции «Вивальди» освободили ещё более 200 квадратных километров — именно в тех районах, где россияне проводили наибольшее количество штурмов.
Зеленский добавил, что с 2022 года позиции Украины на фронте остаются самыми сильными.
В то же время президент сообщил о нехватке ракет для защиты от российской баллистики и задержках с поставками пакетов противовоздушной обороны. Это происходит на фоне того, что только с 14 октября оккупанты запустили по Киеву и области более 100 баллистических ракет.
«В эти дни мы стараемся сделать всё возможное, чтобы появились новые пакеты поддержки. Также продолжается координация с партнёрами, чтобы велась дипломатия, чтобы состоялись встречи, причём как можно скорее. В ноябре мы ожидаем трехсторонний формат: украинские, американские и российские представители. Важно, чтобы Европа также участвовала во всех дипломатических инициативах. Украина всегда настаивает на том, что Европа должна присутствовать, должна участвовать в принятии решений. Причем это касается всех в Европе. И чтобы никто не остался в стороне от этих процессов», — подытожил Зеленский.
Ранее ZN.UA сообщало, что во время ночной атаки 22 октября Россия применила против Киева 21 баллистическую ракету. В результате ударов были повреждены жилые дома, энергетические объекты и транспортная инфраструктура, в частности метро и Южный мост.
description: Президент рассказал об использовании подземных газопроводов против российских войск и освобождении территорий на фронте.

article_title: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban
article_content:
AI bots flooded a government consultation with tens of thousands of fake responses in a failed attempt to stop the UK’s ban on disposable vapes.
Three-quarters of all the responses to the 2023 consultation on the tobacco and vapes bill were machine-generated, in what is thought to be the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.
The attempt to manipulate the outcome of the consultation was disclosed on Tuesday in research published in the journal Tobacco Control by the health policy experts Dr Nason Maani, from the University of Edinburgh, and Prof Anna Gilmore, of the University of Bath.
The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) used bot-detection methods to identify that 90,835 of the 118,756 responses it received, 76%, were submitted by bots.
All but two of those 90,835 automated responses answered the same question in the “smoke free generation” consultation, in which they opposed Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government’s plan to ban disposable vapes. The submissions were “often duplicated many times and sent at high frequency from a small number of IP addresses”, the DHSC said.
The bombardment “appears to be the first documented instance of large-scale automated interference in a formal public health policy consultation”, the researchers said.
Maani added that while this attempt was identified, “the threat is that future campaigns become harder to catch, and what we can’t catch, we don’t know about. Such campaigns are a threat because they raise the possibility of a handful of powerful interests looking like a mass movement.”
The DHSC excluded the 90,835 automated responses from its decision-making. Keir Starmer’s Labour government inherited the tobacco and vapes bill in 2024 and passed it into law, including the ban on businesses selling or supplying disposable vapes.
Caroline Cerny, the deputy chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said: “Evidence that AI bots have been used to swamp a Department of Health consultation is deeply concerning.
“Given the tobacco industry’s history of seeking to undermine public health regulation, we need to be alert to the risk that technological advances can be used to further commercial interests around health policy and put safeguards in place.
“Decisions that affect public health must be based on sound evidence and expertise, not manipulated response numbers.”
Azzurra Moores, the associate director for information ecosystems at the thinktank Demos, described the attempt to derail the ban as “pretty alarming”.
“Public consultations are one of the main ways government opens up its decision-making, so any interference with them is a serious concern,” she said. “These findings are pretty alarming: if a consultation can be swamped like this, it stops telling policymakers what the public actually thinks and undermines trust in the process.
“This is a problem without easy answers. Every barrier that keeps bots out also makes it harder for real people to take part, and AI makes fake responses far harder to spot. Interference can adapt faster than departments can update their checks. Better screening and more transparency will help, but there’s no single fix.”
The DHSC said its “robust controls” identified the attempt to influence the consultation.
A spokesperson said: “We always have robust controls in place to prevent the manipulation of our public consultations, and those controls worked effectively in this case.
“As a result, the fake responses were removed, and the consultation helped inform the landmark action we are taking to create a smoke-free generation.
“We will remain alert to interference of this kind in future consultation processes, and we will not be deterred from doing what is necessary to promote healthier living.”

article_title: Trump tells Texas campaign rally crowd he’s rolling back environmental rules to curb methane pollution – as it happened
article_content:
Speaking in Lubbock, Texas on Tuesday, Donald Trump announced a rollback of federal rules issued by the Biden administration in 2023 to force oil and gas companies to cut their emissions of methane, a “super pollutant” gas that traps heat in the atmosphere.
“Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, lifting what he called “crippling regulations on methane that caused prices to skyrocket” for small oil and gas operators.
In a press release, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator, Lee Zeldin, priased what he called Trump’s move “to end the war on oil and natural gas” by revising oil and natural gas regulations under the Clean Air Act.
According to the EPA, the proposal is expected to save $45bn in costs to consumers and businesses, including small businesses operating marginal wells, and produce an estimated 210m additional barrels of oil and 1.41tn cubic feet of natural gas.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
Faced with widespread voter discontent over the spike in oil prices since he attacked Iran, Donald Trump staged his rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on Tuesday alongside a vast oil tanker, the Angerona, which, the president said, had just arrived from Venezuela bearing a personal gift for him: a million barrels of oil.
A senior State Department official told the Associated Press that the US will “will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States.”
In his remarks to supporters in Lubbock, Texas Trump attacked James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate, for having shown compassion for transgender children who demonstrated for their rights at the Texas state capitol in 2023.
Trump lied that “our gasoline prices are lower than when Barack Hussein Obama- our oil prices, gasoline, lower than they were with Obama”.
Democratic congressman demands to know if Trump administration helped Flávio Bolsonaro flee justice in Brazil
As we await confirmation of a BBC report that Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right Brazilian senator who lost a presidential election on Sunday, has arrived in Florida, fleeing corruption investigations in Brazil, one Democratic lawmaker has rejected the idea of giving him asylum.
“Losing an election is not grounds for asylum,” congressman Joaquin Castro, a Texas Democrat posted. “Yet the Trump Administration is giving Flávio Bolsonaro safe haven in the United States. In Brazil, he is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and currency evasion, and was ordered to surrender his passports. The Trump Administration owes Congress answers on its role helping Bolsonaro flee Brazil in contravention of Brazilian law.”
As the Brazilian journalist Octavio Guedesobserved on Brazilian television on Tuesday, Bolsonaro “is not fleeing a dictatorship.”
“Flávio Bolsonaro is fleeing a country in which he ran for office freely—a country where his brother is a senator, another brother is a federal deputy, his party holds a majority in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, and his stepmother is a senator,” Guedes said.
“He is fleeing a country where 59 million people went to the polls and freely cast their votes for him. In short, he is fleeing a democracy. He is fleeing a reckoning with the justice system.”
Speaking in Lubbock, Texas on Tuesday, Donald Trump announced a rollback of federal rules issued by the Biden administration in 2023 to force oil and gas companies to cut their emissions of methane, a “super pollutant” gas that traps heat in the atmosphere.
“Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, lifting what he called “crippling regulations on methane that caused prices to skyrocket” for small oil and gas operators.
In a press release, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator, Lee Zeldin, priased what he called Trump’s move “to end the war on oil and natural gas” by revising oil and natural gas regulations under the Clean Air Act.
According to the EPA, the proposal is expected to save $45bn in costs to consumers and businesses, including small businesses operating marginal wells, and produce an estimated 210m additional barrels of oil and 1.41tn cubic feet of natural gas.
Trump lies that gasoline prices are lower now than when Obama was president
Speaking in defense of his record as president in Lubbock, Texas on Tuesday, Donald Trump once again claimed that his war on Iran was necessary to stop Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, despite a US intelligence finding that Iran stopped pursuing nuclear weapons in 2003.
The president then told a more blatant lie. “With all of this that we’re doing, our gasoline prices are lower than when Barack Hussein Obama- our oil prices, gasoline, lower than they were with Obama, and a guy named Crooked Joe Biden.”
In fact, the current national average for a gallon of regular gasoline in the US is now $4.27, up from $3.05 a year ago, before Trump started the war with Iran that has spiked fuel prices globally. A gallon of gasoline never rose above $4.17 during the Obama administration, and was under $2.50 for a quarter of his time in office, including his the last three years of his second term.
As Reuters reports, the price has now averaged $3.472 since Trump took office in January 2025, passing the $3.471-per-gallon average for Biden’s term, according to data from the AAA.
In Lubbock, Texas, Trump attacks Talarico for showing compassion for transgender children
In his remarks to supporters in Lubbock, Texas on Tuesday, Donald Trump attacked James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate, for having shown compassion for transgender children who demonstrated for their rights at the Texas state capitol in 2023.
The president began by repeating a string of false claims about Talarico and then insisted, falsely, that the Democrat, who is Presbyterian seminarian, said that “God is transgender”.
In fact, as a selection of statements from Talarico that Trump played for his rally crowd showed, what the state lawmaker actually said, during an October 2021 debate on a Texas bill barring trans children from competing on school sports teams, was that “God is nonbinary”.
“The first two lines of the Bible, the first two lines in Genesis use two different Hebrew words to describe God – one is the masculine Hebrew noun for divinity, the second is the feminine Hebrew noun for spirit. God is both masculine and feminine and everything in between. God is non-binary,” Talarico said.
In Genesis 1:26 and 1:27, Talarico added, “God speaks of God’s self in the plural, saying ‘Let us make human beings in our image, to be like us’. That’s the infinite multitude of God, the masculine, the feminine and everything in between. Trans children are God’s children, made in God’s own image, there’s nothing wrong with them nothing at all.”
Trump’s summary of those remarks was to claim this: “He actually said that if Jesus Christ himself came and visited the Texas legislature, Jesus would be promoting sex changes for little children.”
Trump also attacked Talarico for saying, “that he loves transgender children”.
This is a highly misleading reference to comments Talarico made on a podcast in 2023, when he told the host about how impressed he had been by a group of young trans activists and their parents who had come to the Texas legislature to protest a bill that would deny trans children life-saving health care. After they were removed from the gallery, Talarico said, “there was video of one of the law enforcement officers violently throwing down one of those trans activists outside the House chamber”.
At the end of the podcast, during a lightening round, when the host asked Talarico to name one thing he hates, he said: “I hate people who are not willing to change their mind”.
Asked then to name one thing that he loves, Talarico paused a moment and said: “Um, I love… and I just say this because it’s on my mind, the trans children who showed up yesterday at the state capitol to advocate for their humanity; they shouldn’t have to but it was an inspiration to watch.”
This is the statement that JD Vance, Trump’s vice-president, has used to suggest, mockingly, that Talarico’s internet search history must be obscene.
Apparently unaware of its origin, Trump once again uses the phrase ‘to the victor belong the spoils’ to claim Venezuela's oil
Faced with widespread voter discontent over the spike in oil prices since he attacked Iran, Donald Trump staged his rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on Tuesday alongside a vast oil tanker, the Angerona, which, the president said, had just arrived from Venezuela bearing a personal gift for him: a million barrels of oil.
The president told reporters before the event that he intends to re-gift the oil, giving it to the people of the United States of America.
During his remarks, Trump pointed to the tanker, which can hold an estimated 800,000 barrels of oil, and said: “See that little ship out there? It’s got one million barrels of oil on it from Venezuela.”
“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” Trump continued. “‘To the victor belong to spoils’, right?” he added, referring to a phrase he has used in the past to suggest the US has a rightful claim to Venezuela’s oil since US forces kidnapped its leader.
Trump first used the phrase in public during an April 2011 appearance on Fox News, when he told the host Bill O’Reilly that, if elected president, he would not withdraw US troops from Iraq but redeploy them to secure its oil fields.
“In the old days, when you had wars, you win, right? You win. ‘To the victor belong the spoils’. So when we go to Iraq, we spend $1.4 trillion so far and thousands of lives are lost … and we’re going to leave,” Trump said. “I like the old system better: You won a war, you stay there, and you keep the oil. And you know, then those people will not have died in vain.”
“You stay and protect the oil, and you take the oil and you take whatever is necessary for them and you take what’s necessary for us and we pay our self back $1.5 trillion or more,” Trump added.
Since the US military operation seized Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro, Trump has repeatedly used the same phrase to lay claim to the country’s oil, but the president appears to be unaware of its original meaning.
The phrase was first used in 1832 by New York senator William L. Marcy during a speech in defense of president Andrew Jackson’s right to reward his supporters with appointments to public office, arguing that “to the victor belong the spoils of the enemy.”
The phrase gave rise to describing the system of political patronage as “the spoils system”.
US will grant visas to defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro - report
A senior State Department official told the Associated Press on Tuesday that the US will “will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States.”
Bolsonaro, a rightwing Brazilian senator who lost a presidential election on Sunday to Brazil’s incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula.
As our colleagues Tiago Rogero and Tom Phillips report from Brazil:
A report by the news website Metrópoles, citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.
Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.
Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that he was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.
“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.
The younger Bolsonaro, who had Donald Trump’s tacit support, had been under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in Brazil and had been ordered to surrender his passport.
Bolsonaro’s brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election.
Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.
Standing before a birthday cake on the day he turned 81, Lula called it “shameful” that his rival had fled the country.
‘This is what the Bolsonaro family is like,” the president said. “Brazil is their second country, the US is their first.”
US Federal Election Commission’s website targeted by hackers - report
Reuters reports that the US Federal Election Commission’s website has been targeted by a hacker or hackers, disrupting the agency’s electronic filings system to disclose campaign spending a week before the midterm elections.
In a statement to the news agency, the FEC said, “at this time, the FEC’s electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service.” The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said users could still search the website for past reports. It declined further comment on the outage.
The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters’ ability to cast ballots, although it will keep information on how much political groups are spending on specific races from the public as they cast ballots.
“We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we’ve had to temporarily shut down our web facing services,” an FEC electronic filings officer said in an email seen by Reuters.
In Texas, Trump repeats a stream of false claims and screens misleading edit of CNN polling data segment
Near the end of his speech to a Republican campaign rally in Corpus Christi, Texas, Donald Trump just screened two short clips, edited from longer CNN segments first broadcast in August and September, highlighting polling data that flatters him.
As we have reported previously, screening these brief clips has become a routine part of Trump’s argument as he tries to convince supporters, and perhaps himself, that he is far more popular than other polling suggests.
The clips, however, were created by editing out negative information the president does not want his supporters to hear.
The first clip is 43 seconds of CNN’s chief data analyst, Harry Enten, showing viewers in September that Trump remains very popular with self-described “Maga Republicans,” which is to say people who describe themselves as loyal to his Make America Great Again movement.
“Maga GOP on Trump. In the 2024 election versus Kamala Harris, he got 99% of the Maga GOP vote—perhaps surprisingly, I might have thought it’d be 100%, but it was 99% percent,” Enten said in the first part of the clip. “Compare that to his approval rating now with the Maga GOP. It’s 98%; that is, there’s been no real decline in Maga support.”
“Look, now in terms of the congressional vote, 98% of them say they’re going to be voting for House Republican candidates,” Enten added. “So, that support is actually really holding up strong. It’s really, really strong when it comes to Maga GOP and Republicans holding on to that vote.”
However, a look at the full 14-minute segment broadcast in late September shows that what the White House edited out was Enten carefully explaining that Trump’s approval rating among Republicans who do not describe themselves as Maga loyalists had suffered a sharp drop, plunging from +56 points in the 2024 election to just +7 points in September 2026.
“You know, when it comes to non-Maga, this is where we’ve absolutely seen Donald Trump’s numbers plummet into the ocean,” Enten said, in a part of the report Trump did not screen at the rally.
The president also screened for his supporters a portion of a prior CNN segment, from August of this year, in which Enten showed viewers that according to polling conducted in May, Trump was, at that time, called the president Republicans most admire by 53% of Republicans, ahead of Ronald Reagan at 18% and Abraham Lincoln at 8%.
Trump is so fond of these two cherry-picked pieces of data, from months ago, that he included both in his 1,300-word social-media tirade against the comedian Bill Maher on Sunday.
Trump cited the data as supposed proof that Maher was wrong to say that the president is unpopular. “I have High Ratings and, more importantly, he said that I’m losing the support and approval of the Republican Party when, in fact, CNN just came out with a Poll showing that I’m at 98 and 99% support within the Republican Party, an All Time Record High,” Trump wrote.
Given that the president has repeatedly screened the clip of Enten clearly saying these were his ratings with Maga Republicans, not the party as a whole, this is not the evidence that he seems to think it is.
Addressing the crowd in Corpus Christi, Trump said that he was expecting the price of oil to spike even higher than it has when he launched the war in Iran – and he was still willing to go ahead with it.
“I knew that oil would go up,” Trump told the crowd in Corpus Christi. “I actually thought it would go up two or three time higher, and I was still willing to do it.”
The stark rise in gas and diesel prices, a product of Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the war’s opening days, has been a major source of grievance against Republicans going into the 2024 midterms.
During his address, Trump stated, as he has before, that gas prices were set to drop imminently, and that he views the temporary economic strain facing Americans as a worthwhile sacrifice to dismantle Iran’s military and prevent it from obtaining a nuclear weapons. A lasting deal to end the war and realize either of those goals long-term has, so far, remained elusive through months of fighting.
Trump flaunts Venezuelan oil shipments at campaign event in Corpus Christi, talks of making Venezuela '51st state'
Trump has taken the stage in Corpus Christi, Texas, the first of two campaign events in the state he’ll be speaking at today.
He started off by gesturing to an oil tanker docked just outside the campaign event, filled, he said, with Venezuelan crude – a product of the deal his administration inked with Venezuela’s new, US-pliant leadership.
“The oil in the ships outside is being provided to the United States at zero cost to the American taxpayer,” Trump said.
US forces launched a surprise incursion into Venezuela to seize its former leader, Nicólas Maduro, in January, dragging him to the US to face criminal charges. Since his ouster, his former Vice President, Delcy Rodriguez, ruling with the Trump administration’s blessing, has agreed to deals that would funnel vast shares of the nation’s oil wealth to US coffers.
Trump spoke of his relationship with Venezuela in unsparing terms, as a conqueror extracting resources from a defeated nation.
He described the oil as being the byproduct of “our big victory in our recent war with Venezuela,” and repeated a phrase he used while addressing the United Nations last month about his toppling of Maduro: “To the victor belong the spoils.”
Trump continued: “We’re bringing out a lot of oil for ourselves, a lot.”
He went on to say, repeatedly, that the US should make Venezuela the 51st US state.
“It will become a prosperous country, and who knows, maybe someday soon it will become a prosperous 51st state. That’s possible. Let’s make it the 51st state, and instead of a president, we’ll have an election for a governor.”
Trump’s remarks about Venezuela’s oil shipments come against the backdrop of surging oil prices downstream of the war in Iran. At several point in his remarks, Trump has vowed that gas prices are set to drop precipitously any day now.
Trump is campaigning in Texas alongside Marco Rubio and a tanker of Venezuelan oil. The President is making two stops in Texas, one in Corpus Christi and another in Lubbock, to try and rally voters behind Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton. Paxton is fending off a stiff challenge from Democrat James Talarico, which risks putting one of the state’s Senate seats back in Democrat hands for the first time in decades.
Vance attacked Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign rally in Michigan. While Trump was in Texas, his vice president returned to Michigan to stump for Republican Mike Rogers, and to bash his opponent, Abdul El-Sayed. Vance, who has traded words for months with El-Sayed online and at campaign rallies, connected the progressive candidate to recent mass protests in Paris, accusing El-Sayed of endorsing similar unrest in the United States.
US Senator Chris Murphy condemned Republican attacks on Muslim Americans. Murphy, responding to a clip of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. dismissing Arab contributions to art and science, said that remarks like those served to “delegimatize Muslim Americans - not just as citizens but as humans.” He continued: “these increasingly hysterical attacks are a prelude to Republicans bringing us to a very, very dark place after the election.”
Trump said he would accept the midterm election results “if they’re honest.” The remark, given to reporters en route to Texas, seemed to allude to the possibility Trump might deem results of the midterms fraudulent if they aren’t in his favor. But he also said he saw a path to working with a Democratic majority in Congress, if Republicans were to lose control of the legislative branch in November.
Voters in Israel are turning out for an election that will decide whether Benjamin Netanyahu will remain in charge of the country. Netanyahu is facing his first serious election test since the October 7 attacks and the start of the wars in Gaza and Iran. The results of that election will shape who, exactly, the Trump administration will be working with as it seeks to settle those conflicts.
