article_title: Союзник Путіна на чолі ООН: навіщо Трамп просуває Орбана на ключову посаду
article_content:
Союзник Путіна на чолі ООН: навіщо Трамп просуває Орбана на ключову посаду
Адміністрація президента США просуває кандидатуру колишнього прем’єр-міністра Угорщини Віктора Орбана на посаду генерального секретаря Організації Об’єднаних Націй.
Білий дім запропонував кандидатуру колишнього прем’єр-міністра Угорщини Віктора Орбана на заміну Антоніу Гутеррешу на посаді генерального секретаря ООН, а також розглядає його у ролі посередника у переговорах щодо України. Ініціатива Вашингтона викликала негативну реакцію в Європі.
Про це повідомляють іспанське видання ABC та італійське Il Sole 24 Ore.
За даними медіа, в адміністрації президента США Дональда Трампа активно просувають кандидатуру Орбана на посаду. У своїй кампанії вони описують угорського експрем’єра як генерала в армії ООН, яка, на їхню думку, складається переважно з бюрократів.
Прихильники руху Make America Great Again називають Орбана «кандидатом мрії». У Білому домі роблять акцент на його позиції щодо захисту західної цивілізації, зокрема у питаннях імміграції, свободи слова, незалежності судової системи та цінностей ліберальної демократії.
Водночас сама ідея просування Орбана на одну з ключових міжнародних посад викликала обурення в Європі. За оцінками джерел у Брюсселі, його кандидатура може натрапити на серйозний опір з боку європейських держав.
Реакція на кандидатуру Орбана
Зазначається, що наразі невідомо, наскільки серйозними є наміри Вашингтона просувати Орбана. У Штатах припускають, що Росія та Китай також можуть підтримати політика. У такому разі угорський експрем’єр потенційно міг би стати спільним кандидатом цих трьох країн.
«Якби Орбан з’явився, маючи за спиною підтримку трьох великих держав, то, насамперед, європейські країни, зокрема Франція та Велика Британія, мали б можливість виступити проти цього та прийняти рішення щодо застосування права вето, яке вони мають як постійні члени», — пише Sole 24 Ore.
Втім, ця ідея вже викликала негативну реакцію в Європі. Зокрема, прем’єр-міністр Польщі Дональд Туск назвав її «комічною».
Український міністр закордонних справ Андрій Сибіга саркастично розкритикував кандидатуру угорського прем’єра, натякнувши на його «витончену майстерність» використовувати право вето та шантаж для блокування важливих рішень ЄС. Зокрема тих, що стосуються підтримки України у протидії російській агресії.
Водночас у Москві таку перспективу зустріли прихильно. Заступник міністра закордонних справ Олександр Алімов привітав можливе висунення Орбана і навіть закликав його якнайшвидше подати кандидатуру. За словами російського дипломата, жодних обмежень щодо кандидатів немає і можуть з’явитися інші претенденти.
Ставка Вашингтона на Орбана
Не виключено, що цей крок Вашингтона стане ще одним прикладом хаотичної зовнішньої політики Дональда Трампа та його спроб послабити міжнародні й багатосторонні організації, які він звинувачує в антиамериканській позиції.
Відкрите захоплення Трампом, тісні особисті зв’язки з «фюером» Володимиром Путіним і постійні суперечки з європейськими інституціями стали основою міжнародної стратегії Віктора Орбана за 16 років його перебування на посаді прем’єр-міністра Угорщини. Водночас він назвав Україну «ворогом номер один для Угорщини».
Попри це, представники Білого дому вже перейшли до конкретних кроків: вони безпосередньо з’ясували, чи готовий Орбан долучитися до цієї ініціативи. Угорський прем’єр, за даними видання, висловив готовність за умови, що успіх буде гарантовано.
У Вашингтоні також заявили, що можуть заручитися підтримкою щонайменше восьми, а можливо, й десяти з 15 членів Ради Безпеки ООН. Для офіційної рекомендації кандидата необхідно отримати щонайменше дев’ять голосів і не зіткнутися з вето постійних членів Ради. Американська сторона, як стверджується, розраховує на підтримку Росії, а також Китаю, з яким Орбан налагодив тісні відносини.
Розслідування проти Орбана і його оточення
Після усунення Орбана від влади навесні цього року перелік відкритих розслідувань щомісяця зростає. Так, у березні угорська влада перехопила автомобілі, які перевозили гроші та золото, що належали українській банківській операції. Документи, на які посилається угорське видання Telex, свідчать, що Орбан міг бути причетним до рішення зупинити колону та привласнити її вміст.
Під підозрою також опинилися можливі фінансові втрати та зловживання, пов’язані з управлінням коштами колишнього голови центрального банку Дьєрдя Матолчи. Йдеться про суму близько 1,38 млрд євро.
Після перемоги Петера Мадяра на виборах у квітні 2026-го нова влада розпочала розслідування можливих зловживань і фінансових схем, пов’язаних із попередньою адміністрацією. Зокрема, перевіряли ймовірне розкрадання коштів, виділених на культурні проєкти, а також можливі хабарі під час укладання державних контрактів. Окрему увагу становлять майнові операції, пов’язані із підприємцями, наближеними до колишньої влади.
Посада в ООН — як уникнення суду
Стаття 19 Конвенції про привілеї та імунітети Організації Об’єднаних Націй надає генеральному секретарю привілеї та імунітети, передбачені міжнародним правом для дипломатичних представників. Це потенційно могло б допомогти Орбану уникнути можливих судових переслідувань.
Для цього йому довелося б очолити організацію, яку він неодноразово зневажливо критикував, а згодом використати її для просування моделі, яку сам називає «неліберальною демократією».
Цей термін відображає його неприйняття ідеї, що демократія обов’язково має ґрунтуватися на ліберальних цінностях, зокрема захисті індивідуальних прав, політичному плюралізмі та системі стримувань і противаг, яка обмежує повноваження виконавчої влади.
Як Трамп просуває Орбана — деталі WSJ
The Wall Street Journal із посиланням на джерела у трьох країнах повідомило, що адміністрація президента США Дональда Трампа просуває кандидатуру колишнього прем’єра Угорщини Віктора Орбана на посаду генерального секретаря Організації Об’єднаних Націй.
За даними видання, американські посадовці вже запропонували Орбану розглянути цю можливість. Угорський політик зацікавився пропозицією, однак остаточного рішення поки не ухвалив.
Водночас 28 жовтня в Раді Безпеки ООН має відбутися неформальне голосування, яке допоможе оцінити рівень підтримки кандидатів. Однак, як зазначає WSJ, наразі невідомо, чи буде кандидатуру Орбана включено до цього голосування.
description: Адміністрація президента США просуває кандидатуру колишнього прем’єр-міністра Угорщини Віктора Орбана на посаду генерального секретаря Організації Об’єднаних Націй.

article_title: Після років російських ударів: ООН визнала атаки РФ на енергетику злочинами проти людяності
article_content:
Після років російських ударів: ООН визнала атаки РФ на енергетику злочинами проти людяності
Російські удари по енергетиці України, через які мільйони людей залишалися без тепла, світла та води, в ООН кваліфікували як злочини проти людяності. У новій доповіді Комісія також розкрила подробиці вербування іноземців до армії РФ.
Незалежна міжнародна комісія ООН з розслідування щодо України встановила, що Росія вчинила воєнні злочини та злочини проти людяності, систематично атакуючи українську енергетичну інфраструктуру. Крім того, розслідувачі виявили докази торгівлі людьми з 29 країн, яких обманом і примусом залучали до російської армії для участі у війні проти України.
Про це повідомляється у пресрелізі Управління Верховного комісара ООН з прав людини за результатами нової доповіді Незалежної міжнародної комісії з розслідування щодо України, поданої Генеральній Асамблеї ООН.
Російські удари по енергетиці України: що встановила ООН
Під час розслідування Комісія вивчила наслідки масштабних атак російських військ на енергетичну інфраструктуру України, зокрема взимку 2025–2026 років. Також експерти проаналізували вплив ударів, яких Росія завдає від осені 2022 року.
За висновками розслідувачів, протягом цих років російські атаки ставали дедалі частішими та інтенсивнішими, а їхня географія розширювалася. Війська РФ одночасно застосовували сотні ракет і безпілотників, завдаючи значних руйнувань українській енергосистемі.
Особливо тяжкими наслідки обстрілів були минулої зими, коли температура повітря опускалася до мінус 21 градуса. Через пошкодження енергетичних об’єктів мільйони українців тривалий час залишалися без світла, тепла, водопостачання та газу.
Голова Комісії Ерік Мьозе наголосив, що з наближенням нового холодного сезону російські атаки знову посилилися. За його словами, це створює серйозні загрози для життя та здоров’я цивільного населення.
Українці розповіли ООН про життя без тепла та електрики
Для підготовки доповіді Комісія зібрала свідчення 255 людей, які пережили енергетичну кризу в Києві, а також у Дніпропетровській, Київській, Харківській, Херсонській, Миколаївській, Одеській, Полтавській, Запорізькій та Житомирській областях.
Зокрема, 53-річний житель Києва розповів, що під час сильних морозів боявся засинати, оскільки не був упевнений, що прокинеться.
«Найстрашніше було заснути і не прокинутися; боятися померти від холоду було схоже на тортури», — поділився чоловік.
Особливо вразливими виявилися люди похилого віку та особи з обмеженою мобільністю. Через постійні відключення електроенергії вони ризикували застрягти в ліфтах, тому часто не могли спуститися до укриттів під час повітряних тривог.
Деякі люди були змушені залишатися у холодних квартирах без води, електрики, необхідних ліків і доступу до медичного обладнання.
«Я лежала холодна та голодна, без ліків, без нічого», — розповіла 74-річна мешканка столиці.
Складною ситуація була й для родин із дітьми. Через енергетичну кризу школи тривалий час не працювали, що перешкоджало навчанню. Водночас відсутність опалення у помешканнях призводила до захворювань серед дітей.
У Комісії наголосили, що постійне перебування в холоді, відсутність основних комунальних послуг та необхідність щодня шукати способи виживання негативно впливали як на фізичне, так і на психічне здоров’я українців.
Атаки РФ на енергетику визнали злочинами проти людяності
За оцінкою Комісії ООН, російське військове командування усвідомлювало, що об’єкти теплопостачання, які ставали цілями ударів у великих населених пунктах, є життєво необхідними для цивільного населення, особливо в зимовий період.
Розслідувачі також звернули увагу на офіційні заяви представників російської влади, які повідомляли про подальші атаки та посилалися на плани їх здійснення.
Зібрані докази, за висновками Комісії, свідчать, що удари по українській енергетиці були навмисними та здійснювалися відповідно до державної політики РФ.
Їхньою метою, як встановили розслідувачі, було позбавлення цивільного населення електроенергії та інших життєво важливих послуг, залежних від енергопостачання, а також заподіяння людям страждань.
На підставі цих висновків Комісія кваліфікувала навмисні удари по цивільних об’єктах як воєнні злочини, а систематичні атаки на енергетичну інфраструктуру — як злочини проти людяності у формі інших нелюдських діянь.
«Комісія також розглянула напади українських збройних сил на енергетичну інфраструктуру в Російській Федерації та на окупованих територіях України. Однак вона не змогла додатково розслідувати наслідки таких нападів, оскільки Російська Федерація не надала доступу до інформації або не відповіла на запити Комісії», — зазначено в пресрелізі.
Росія вербувала іноземців для війни проти України
Ще одним напрямком розслідування стало залучення громадян інших держав до російської армії.
Комісія ООН заявила про наявність переконливих доказів того, що російська влада здійснювала торгівлю людьми з 29 країн, використовуючи обман і примус.
За даними розслідування, вербування відбувалося через посередників та агентства, які працювали в різних країнах світу. Вони представлялися законними компаніями, діяльність яких нібито схвалена державою, та організовували оформлення віз і проїзних документів.
У деяких випадках представники агентств навіть супроводжували завербованих чоловіків під час поїздки до Росії.
Проте після прибуття іноземців змушували підписувати контракти з Міністерством оборони РФ, складені російською мовою.
Дружина одного із завербованих чоловіків із Карибського басейну розповіла Комісії, що в її чоловіка відібрали паспорт і під тиском змусили підписати документи.
«Вони забрали його паспорт і просто сказали йому підписати контракт тут, тут і тут. Він був лише російською мовою», — розповіла 35-річна жінка.
Після цього чоловіків відправляли на передову в Україні, де доручали виконувати небезпечні бойові завдання.
За даними Комісії, багато завербованих іноземців загинули або зникли безвісти. Інші здалися в полон чи були захоплені українськими військовими та отримали статус військовополонених.
Розслідувачі також встановили високий рівень координації між агентами, які діяли в різних частинах світу, та представниками російської влади.
За результатами розслідування Комісія дійшла висновку, що такі дії порушують міжнародне право у сфері прав людини.
У підсумку Комісія ООН закликала Росію припинити атаки на цивільне населення та цивільні об’єкти, а також звільнити з лав російської армії всіх людей, які стали жертвами торгівлі людьми.
Нагадаємо, раніше в ООН повідомляли, що за перші вісім місяців 2026 року кількість загиблих і поранених цивільних в Україні перевищила показник за весь 2025 рік. Зазначається, що за січень–серпень 2026 року ООН підтвердила 15 280 цивільних жертв війни в Україні — 2 222 людини загинули, ще 13 058 були поранені.
description: Російські удари по енергетиці України, через які мільйони людей залишалися без тепла, світла та води, в ООН кваліфікували як злочини проти людяності. У новій доповіді Комісія також розкрила подробиці вербування іноземців до армії РФ.

article_title: Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
article_content:
Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
- Published
Millions of households will get £100 to help with soaring energy bills to be paid for by a tax on bank profits, John Healey has announced in his first Budget.
The chancellor said he wanted to give hard-pressed families "breathing space now" and "hope for the future" as the UK economy is battered by "global economic storms".
He also unveiled tax breaks to boost high street businesses - but confirmed that many big decisions, including on defence spending and welfare, will not be made until next year.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Healey's plans were "not bold enough" and the government was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".
In an hour-long speech to a packed House of Commons, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other frontbench colleagues cheering him on, the chancellor unveiled a string of measures aimed at cutting the cost of living.
These include:
- One-off £100 energy payment for people living in council tax bands A to D in England, with Wales saying it will match the payment and the Scottish government planning to "replicate" it
- Gas standing charges in England, Scotland and Wales, to be scrapped during 2027 "or as soon as possible after". These fixed daily fees will be shifted onto the price of each unit of energy, meaning heavy gas users will face higher bills
- Extending the 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel to July
- Increasing minimum wage rates by 3.9% in April, although there will be no progress on narrowing the gap between rates for older and younger workers
Healey increased the tax on the profits of big banks from 3% to 6%, which will last from January next year to April 2028, and increased taxes on high-stakes gambling machines.
- Budget 2026: Key points at a glance 
  - Published13 hours ago
- Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you 
  - Published13 hours ago
- Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite its range of small measures 
  - Published13 hours ago
As part of a package to help business, Healey increased the point at which High Street shops in England start paying business rates from £12,000 to £18,000, with vape shops and adult gaming centres excluded from the relief.
But he had little scope for big giveaways as the public finances remain stretched, with the UK set to spend £14bn more on debt interest payments this year.
Income tax thresholds will remain frozen and the tax on income from savings and property rental will rise to 24% for basic rate taxpayers from April 2027, after it had been scheduled to go up to 22%.
But a cut to the cash ISA allowance from £20,000 a year to £12,000, announced last year by Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves, will be axed.
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded its growth forecast for next year to 1%, with slightly higher increases predicted for subsequent years.
In its latest assessment, the OBR said British households were set to be little better off than before the Covid pandemic even a decade after Covid-19 hit, a situation the watchdog's boss David Miles described as "pretty grim".
In his Budget speech, Healey repeatedly stressed that the UK economy was being battered by "global uncertainties" and soaring oil prices caused by conflict in the Middle East.
"Those are the storms we face. We can't wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them," he told MPs.
Healey also used his speech to announce plans to allow regional mayors to keep 20% of business rates and a share of income tax to spend on local priorities.
The aim was to allow mayors to retain 100% of business rates raised in their areas by the end of the decade, he added, in "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".
And he sought to address opposition claims the Labour government is unwilling to cut benefits, insisting that both he and Burnham were committed to bringing down the welfare bill in a "Labour way".
But he said no decisions would be taken until reviews by Alan Milburn, into young people not in work or training, and Stephen Timms, on Personal Independence Payments, had been published, with legislation to follow next year.
The £4.7bn black hole in the defence investment plan will be funded, the chancellor revealed, in part through taking money from capital budgets across Whitehall.
Healey said he will set out how the government plans to meet its commitment to spend 3% of the national income on defence by 2030, and 3.5% by 2035, at next year's spending review.
But Badenoch said he "should have set out a plan for 3% today," highlighting his claim when he resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June that UK forces were at risk due to a lack of cash.
"So now he is the man who is increasing risk to personnel on operations, he is the man who is making our country less safe, he has failed his own test," the Conservative leader said.
"This is on him and no-one will ever forget. If he had any decency he would resign again today."
The Tory leader said that with the UK heading for a record tax burden and "spending more on debt interest than on the army and schools combined", Healey's Budget was "not good enough, not strong enough, not bold enough".
Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the Budget "has a raft of fiddly measures but very little that will move the dial on growth".
Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said that until the government has "the courage" to fix the UK's trading relationship with the EU any Budget will just be "tinkering around the edges" and will not provide the growth the country needs.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the Budget was full of "little giveaways" but "doesn't overall do very much" and did not offer "anything of any value on defence whatsoever".
Healey also faced criticism from the left, with the general secretary of the Unite union, Sharon Graham describing the cost of living measures in the Budget as "baby steps".
"Scrapping standing charges on gas and a £100 energy payment for households in council tax bands, A to D, whilst welcome, will not touch the sides, when many forecasts show bills set to jump over £400 in January," she added.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was a Budget "that betrays the future for young people and the planet they inherit".
He added: "The chancellor didn't mention climate once but praised bankers repeatedly."

article_title: Nigel Farage skips budget in Commons over seating ‘altercation’ concerns
article_content:
Nigel Farage skipped the chancellor’s first budget because he was worried he would get in a “physical altercation” with another MP in a row over seating arrangements.
The Reform UK leader was not present in the House of Commons but gave a press conference afterwards in which he said he was “shocked” by the £10bn going to support Ukraine and doubled down on his party’s policies on cutting tax for crypto investors.
In a joint event with Robert Jenrick, his party’s Treasury spokesperson, Farage said he had decided to give parliament a “wide berth” as he was concerned he would get into a fight because another MP had removed a green paper slip saving him a seat. He said this situation had turned physical on a previous occasion.
“At the state opening of parliament, I got involved in, I didn’t want to, but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber,” he said.
“I didn’t make a fuss about it. I didn’t complain. But I could see, given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation, and just sometimes, it’s better to avoid conflict, is one reason. Second reason is, actually, I sat going through the budget with the economists in the office line by line.”
It later emerged that the seat reservation was removed for not being properly stamped with the date.
A House of Commons spokesperson said: “There are clear and long-established arrangements for members to reserve their own seats in the chamber using prayer cards displaying a valid date stamp. Today, a prayer card placed on a seat did not display a valid date stamp and was removed in line with the usual chamber protocol.”
In his response to the budget, Farage said John Healey’s small giveaways suggested there would be a general election in May next year and added that Reform would be ready for one as early as December.
Farage criticised the extra taxation announced on gambling shops through higher machine-games duty, saying it would be bad for the horse-racing industry and drive gambling offshore and through crypto.
Asked whether Reform still had a policy of cutting capital gains tax on cryptocurrency, which could benefit its big donors, Farage said his plans still stood and would not benefit his backers overall.
He said his policy was trying to “bring crypto in from the cold … A 10% tax rate on crypto gains is a way of incentivising people to come into the system, to go straight in a new regulated industry.”
On Ukraine, Farage said he was “surprised by the amount” of promised economic and military aid but that he did not “mind the amount, provided I can be absolutely assured it’s not going to get swallowed up in corruption and making Ukrainian officials richer than they already are”.
He claimed to be more worried about Vladimir Putin’s “rationality” than at any point before in the conflict, but said he was “shocked by the size of [the aid package]” and was “really concerned the money’s going to get used properly and spent well”.
Farage has previously expressed admiration for the Russian president and in 2024 suggested the west “provoked” Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, although he has supported the UK’s position in the war and declined to repeat Donald Trump’s harsher criticisms of Kyiv.
Asked whether he preferred Healey’s budget or the disastrous one given under Liz Truss in 2022, which he previously praised but led to Truss’s demise as prime minister, Farage said he had liked the top lines of the Truss budget but “what I hadn’t understood was they didn’t cut spending”.
He added: “That was their mistake … If they cut spending radically, they could have cut taxes, and that was the big lesson that came from it.”
The Reform leader also gave his response to Tommy Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists, saying the far-right agitator’s behaviour had obviously been “very wrong”. But he repeated suggestions that his party’s members would not be penalised for admiring Robinson, saying just because they liked a social media message “doesn’t make them full-blown marchers in support of their cause”.

article_title: Budget briefing: the key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa Crerar
article_content: The Guardian’s political editor, Pippa Crerar, and economics editor, Heather Stewart, examine John Healey’s first budget and how it will be received by voters. Photograph: Jill Mead, Andy Hall/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Guardian’s political editor, Pippa Crerar, and economics editor, Heather Stewart, examine John Healey’s first budget and how it will be received by voters. Photograph: Jill Mead, Andy Hall/The GuardianExplainerBudget briefing: the key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa CrerarOur economics and political editors dissect John Healey’s maiden budgetThe Guardian’s economics editor, Heather Stewart, and political editor, Pippa Crerar, assess the chancellor’s budget: what he said, why – and what he left out.Did the chancellor’s budget panic the financial markets?Not at all. Reassuring febrile financial markets appeared to be one of Andy Burnham’s motivations in putting Healey in No 11, and this ‘steady-as-she-goes’ budget seems to have met that brief, for now.The chancellor promised to keep Labour’s deficit-reduction plans on track, albeit at a slower pace in the early years of the forecast – raising taxes modestly to do so.The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) now expects him to meet his crucial first fiscal rule – to balance day-to-day spending with revenues – with a margin of £15bn to spare. That’s a slimmer cushion than the £24bn Rachel Reeves had at the spring statement, but investors appear to have taken it in their stride, with barely a flutter in the bond markets. Healey stressed that he plans to rebuild his headroom back to £22bn by 2030-31. “That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can,” he said.However, the OBR’s forecasts underlined the significant hit to Britain’s public finances from higher borrowing costs – which it said had cost the government an additional £14bn in interest costs alone. Partly as a result, borrowing is set to be £8bn higher than expected this year, before heading back to target over time. And Healey has delayed a series of knotty decisions on tax and spend for a critical spending review next year.Has Healey done enough to reassure restive Labour MPs and the public?Government insiders had briefed that the budget would be “low key”, with tough decisions over public spending – including on defence and welfare – put off to the spending review. But that didn’t stop Labour MPs asking “Is that it?” when Healey sat down from the dispatch box.While they welcomed support for energy bills – the only rabbit in the budget – and other cost of living measures, they are impatient for Burnham to deliver the radical change he has argued the country needs. “That won’t end 40 years of neoliberalism, will it?” one MP remarked to the Guardian.Healey’s decision to increase taxes on banks is likely to land well with the public – it is an industry which has made massive profits and does not elicit much sympathy from voters – but some Labour MPs are already questioning why he did not go much further to give himself more room for manoeuvre this winter.For now, though, MPs aren’t kicking up a fuss. The polls – some of which put Labour eight points ahead – suggest the public is on board, and Burnham’s approval ratings remain high. He has won them a second hearing. Whether the public expected more than a signal of intent will become clear in the coming days. But questions over the timing of the next general election have not gone away. After the budget, Burnham ruled out calling one in the next 12 months (he’d previously said there wouldn’t be one soon). Labour’s prospects at the ballot box remain very much on the mind of its MPs. And if there are suggestions the public is getting impatient, the pressure on Burnham will grow.Has the budget really given consumers a “breathing space” amid the cost of living crisis?Higher energy prices as a result of Donald Trump’s war in Iran have made the UK – an energy importer – poorer, as well as raising the cost of government borrowing. Healey’s key challenge was to decide who should have to bear the pain.He announced a more generous package than expected to contain energy costs this winter, costing the Treasury about £4bn in total. That included sending £100 to every householder in council tax banks A to D; cancelling Rachel Reeves’s planned fuel duty rises; and extending the VAT cut on electricity bills until next summer.But households will still be hit by a sharp rise in the energy price cap in January – which EDF predicts could be as much as 27%.And because the cost of energy feeds into the cost of making almost everything, higher oil prices will push up economy-wide inflation, which the OBR now reckons will be 3.5% next year, instead of the 2% it expected in March. The Bank of England is expected to respond by pushing up interest rates, perhaps as soon as its meeting next week, causing fresh pain for mortgage-borrowers.Despite the government’s interventions, the OBR reckons higher energy costs will make the outlook for living standards even worse than it previously feared. On its preferred measure, real household disposable income, living standards are expected to fall slightly this year as the impact of the war takes its toll – and then to climb gradually, to just 2% above pre-Covid levels by 2030.What does it tell us about the relationship between Healey and Burnham?John Healey and Andy Burnham have had regular Sunday night curries in the No 11 flat in advance of the budget. While they are both of the soft left and agree the north is in need of investment, they haven’t fought in the political trenches together or shared a joint project, like Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.Healey wasn’t even Burnham’s number one choice for the role. However, he was seen as capable and trustworthy and – crucially – more likely to sign up to the Burnham project than other figures touted for the role. Even so, there were early concerns that the chancellor could be “captured” by the Treasury, which still wields great power despite Burnham’s attempts to rebalance the government machine. But the budget – a low key, defensive one which was small in scale and ambition – suggests the prime minister has had to accept the fiscal constraints to his ambition for more radical change. For now. Healey did, however, lay the groundwork for more significant reform in his boss’s priority areas: devolution and housing.For his own part, he still has plenty to prove on defence spending – having quit Keir Starmer’s government over the failure to commit to 3% of GDP on defence by 2030. Healey signalled he will hit the target – but can’t say how until next autumn’s spending review. His own political reputation relies on it.What big decisions have been postponed by the breathing space budget?Higher inflation will make it more expensive to deliver public services. Many Whitehall departments were already facing a tight spending squeeze towards the end of this parliament, on the plans Healey inherited from Reeves. The darker global backdrop is only likely to make that worse.In its pre-budget analysis, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) suggested that, alongside the £11bn he would need to find to hit the 3% of GDP defence spending target by 2030, these additional pressures amounted to £35bn a year.Healey gave little indication of how he intends to respond – though he did suggest that more digitisation of service delivery, and a significantly slimmed-down civil service at the centre as additional powers are devolved, would help to cut the government’s costs, and expressed the hope that better-than-expected economic growth might help.“I believe Britain can beat the forecasts again,” he said. If not, next year’s spending review looks formidably challenging.Will people accept that the economic pressures aren’t the government’s fault?Healey’s speech was littered with references to the difficult international picture, with Donald Trump continuing to wreak havoc on the global economy with his war in Iran. “Analysts like to speak of economic headwinds, but what we face today are global economic storms,” the chancellor told MPs.The main risk identified by the OBR to its fiscal forecast is the evolution of the Middle East conflict and its implications for energy prices, interest rates and inflation. The US midterms are a key moment – and the big unknown is what the US president does next, which Downing Street is watching anxiously.For now, however, the public appears willing to accept that the government is not to blame for resulting cost of living pressures. No 10 sources say their own research shows that most people still see the global context as a justifiable reason for their current plight, rather than an excuse. But government insiders are concerned this might change this winter, as soaring bills and costs really start to bite.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyLabourEconomicsEconomic policyexplainersShareReuse this content

article_title: Budget 2026: £100 energy payment for millions and rise in bank tax as watchdog warns on stalling living standards – as it happened
article_content:
OBR: living standards forecast to rise by just 1% over whole post-Covid decade
The OBR report says RHDI (real household disposable income – one measure of living standards) is rising at a record slow rate – less than 0.1% per decade. That means, by the end of the decade, it will be just 1% higher than its pre-Covid level, it says.
Our central forecast represents a continuation of the historically weak growth in RHDI per person since the global financial crisis. Chart 2.7 shows the rolling 10-year average annual growth in RHDI per person. This slowed significantly in the aftermath of the financial crisis, due to lower growth in productivity and real wages. Growth reached a historic low over the 10 years to 2025-26, averaging just ¼ per cent a year, and we expect it to fall further in the near term. By 2029-30, our central forecast sees growth over the prior 10 years averaging less than 0.1 per cent a year. As a result, 10 years on from the onset of the pandemic, RHDI per person would be just 1 per cent higher than its pre-pandemic level.
Here are comments on the budget from a Guardian panel, comprising Polly Toynbee, Hettie O’Brien, Rohan Sathyamoorthy, Kevin Cashman, Nik, and John McDonnell.
And here is Polly’s conclusion.
Is this the “growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” Andy Burnham promises? No, not yet, not yet … Wait for his 10-year plan, spending review and an election with a new manifesto. And hope.
Jim O’Neill, the former Goldman Sachs chief economist and a Treasury minister under David Cameron, told the PM programme that he thought it was sensible for John Healey not to “rock the boat” with this budget. He said his old City friends were pleasantly surprised by what was in it.
My friends in my old world of business and investing, from the ones that have contacted me, every single one of them has been slightly positively surprised by what was announced today.
Treasury minister Torsten Bell rejects charge budget lacks 'ending 40 years of neoliberalism' ambition
Torsten Bell, the Treasury minister, has just finished an interview on Radio 4’s PM programme. Asked about claims (like this one, assuming the MP is being sarcastic, or ours at 8.50am) that the budget did not live up to Andy Burnham’s ambitions to end 40 years of neoliberalism, Bell said he did not accept that. In many areas, the government was taking a very different approach, he argued. He said Margaret Thatcher hollowed out local government, while today’s fiscal devolution roadmap will reverse that. He also said the proposals to change the way energy pricing works (see 12.50pm) would transformative.
Here is a chart from the fiscal devolution roadmap document setting out what rules will change, and when.
MSAs are mayoral strategic authorities, and FSA are foundation strategic authorities, equivalent bodies which do not have a mayor to lead them.
Minister dismisses as 'garbage' Tory and Lib Dem claims that defence spending actually being cut
A Treasury minister has dismissed as “garbage” opposition claims that the small print in the budget book shows that John Healey is actually cutting defence spending.
The budget red book says that, while £42.6bn had been set aside for MoD spending in 2027-28, that has now been revised down to £41.1bn.
The Treasury says this is because less money than expected is needed for pensions. But James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, said that not allocating the unused money for other areas of defence spending was “a complete dereliction of duty from the chancellor”.
And James MacClearly, the Lib Dem defence spokesperson, made the same argument. He said:
It is disgraceful that after pitching Labour as serious on defence, Healey and [Wes] Streeting are cutting the military’s resource budget by nearly £1bn next year. This will leave our troops worse off and undermine our security.
In response, Torsten Bell, a Treasury minister, posted this on social media.
Absolute garbage - this is a technical change that happens when public sector pension contributions change. There’s no impact on defence spending power & the Tories used the same mechanism in govt. What does matter for defence spending? The chancellor, who has increased it
Today’s ‘picky bits’ budget has pushed tough decisions into next year, says Tim Sarson, head of tax policy at KPMG UK:
“When it comes to tax rises, as expected with his options limited by the 2024 manifesto, the chancellor was left with a pick and mix or ‘picky bits’ approach.
Overall the announcements today will raise £7bn per year by 2031-32 with some winners and losers including a widely trailed bank surcharge, which came in lower than expected at 3% and further taxes on the gambling sector
James Smith, ING’s developed markets economist in the UK, says the budget has left more questions than answers.
Those questions include:
How will the government account for higher inflation in departmental budgets? How will it fund defence? Both questions were left unanswered today. The government’s overall spending pot for government departments was left largely unchanged later this decade, despite a higher path for inflation and the chancellor’s reaffirmed commitment to 3% Nato spending by 2030. Implicitly, that pledge is being funded by squeezing other areas of government; the OBR’s numbers imply real-terms cuts of 2.6% a year for unprotected departments later this decade.
That almost certainly won’t happen – and this is before you take social care or any of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s other bold policies into account.
These thorny issues have been punted into 2027, potentially in the autumn, when the government will have to unveil its long-awaited spending review.
The NewEconomicsFoundation says the budget is a missed opportunity to bring down inflation, through more ambitious cost of living measures.
They say:
The chancellor has missed an opportunity to bring down inflation rates, according to analysis from the New Economics Foundation (NEF). The research suggests a more ambitious package of cost-of-living policies would take inflation from the OBR’s projected 3.64% to 2.88% by June 2027.
But CapitalEconomics say the chancellor has done enough to keep the markets on side.
Today’s UK budget announcement has proven the non-event that newly-minted Chancellor Healey had signalled in advance. While his first budget is hardly inspiring, it contrasts favourably with the initial efforts of some of his recent predecessors.
By sticking to a gradual fiscal tightening path, and to the expectations set over the past couple of months for a muddle-through budget, Healey has probably done enough to keep the Gilt market on side for now.
We think that Gilt yields will fall over the coming year as the UK’s fiscal risk premium remains contained and the Bank of England policy takes a less hawkish path than money markets discount.
Ministerial direction needed for £6.5bn loan for Ukraine after export finance agency warns of 'exceptionally high' risk of default
The government needed to issue a ministerial direction to get UK Export Finance to approve a £3bn increase in lending for Ukraine, it emerged today. This is a procedure that happens when a civil servant judges that a decision is not justified under normal responsible public spending rules, and insists that it can only go ahead if a minister explicitly overrules the objections.
In his letter explaining the need for a ministerial direction, Tim Reid, UKEF’s chief executive, argued that this was not a core obligation for the agency (which is there to help British exporters, not to fight Russia) and that the risk of the £6.5bn not being paid back was too high.
Reid said:
UKEF has played a significant role in delivering the government’s support to Ukraine by staying on cover with £3.5bn of capacity to provide export finance, supporting strategically important transactions including the supply of nuclear fuel, reconstruction of critical infrastructure and air-defence missiles. These have supported Ukraine’s resilience at a critical time while also creating jobs and industrial capacity across the UK.
However, the financial risks associated with UKEF providing support in Ukraine remain far beyond those that we would normally be willing to accept. The probability of default and expected loss is exceptionally high …
UKEF is close to capacity against its existing £3.5bn limit. You have now asked me to consider a £3bn increase in UKEF’s cover limit, taking UKEF’s Ukraine country risk limit to £6.5bn.
In response, Jonathan Reynolds, the business secetary, said he was issuing a ministerial direction because “the United Kingdom has been steadfast in its support for Ukraine’s defence, economic resilience and long-term recovery, and I consider UKEF’s support to be an important component of that wider effort.”
OBR: Employment Rights Act will have negative impact on economy
Labour’s Employment Rights Act is likely to have a negative impact on the economy, the OBR says today.
This is the first time that the OBR has assessed the potential economic impacts of the ERA, which received royal assent at the end of last year.
And the fiscal watchdog has concluded the ERA will probably have a negative impact on potential output, though it isn’t making an explicit assessment today.
The OBR says:
Our analysis suggests that the ERA will likely have a negative economic impact from negative impacts on businesses, particularly through increased uncertainty, lost flexibility and higher labour related costs, which will more than offset any potential positive impact on worker productivity.
That fits with the government’s own analysis, which said the reforms could cost businesses up to £5bn a year.
How budget includes £10bn in extra support for Ukraine
Earlier John Healey got an endorsement for what he said about defence spending from Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general. (See 2.15pm.)
George Robertson, the former Nato secretary general and the lead author of the strategic defence review, has also welcomed Healey’s defence announcements. (See 1.30pm.) He said:
John Healey is acting in the national interest – and has done exactly what he said was needed for defence in his resignation letter, by setting a headmark for 3% in 2030.”
I am strongly in favour of innovative ways of financing defence – and this is a credible route to get more into UK defence. Today’s annoucements strengthens UK leadership in Nato once again.
In his speech Healey announced an extra £10bn in economic support for Ukraine. This Treasury news release explains where that money is going. It says:
The £10bn package includes £7bn of economic support being made available over three years, including up to £5.5bn of World Bank guarantees and a £500m grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association’s crisis facility, mobilising £1.5bn of support for Ukraine.
Alongside this, there will be a £3bn increase in UK Export Finance (UKEF) capacity for Ukraine, prioritised for military support. It will bring the total UKEF support to £6.5bn.
What business organisations are saying about budget
Business groups have given the budget a mixed reaction.
Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the CBI, welcomed some measures, but argued John Healey should have done more for growth. She said
On the face of it, this budget lacks the bold moves that would have made it easier for firms to invest, hire and grow.
At a time of exceptional geopolitical pressures, using some fiscal headroom to absorb genuine short-term shocks is preferable to loading additional permanent costs onto business and weakening investment.
Slowing the convergence of youth rates with the national living wage is a sensible move in face of the Neets crisis and current labour market pressures. But the chancellor could have gone further. Reducing the cost of hiring by increasing the employer NICs threshold would have given firms more space to create entry-level jobs and boost employment.
Jonathan Geldart, director general at the Institute of Directors, said his members were relieved.
Business leaders will be relieved that the chancellor’s budget included no nasty surprises, having been conditioned in previous budgets to expect the worst. We very much welcome the numerous measures intended to support British start-ups and scale-ups, such as the new Founders’ Relief, Young Entrepreneurs Allowance and EMI2 [enterprise management incentive] share incentives (as well as support for small brewers).
What might at first blush be a case of small beer today could start adding up to something promising in the future.
But Tina McKenzie, national chair of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), said the budget was a disappointment.
This budget should have been the moment to help small businesses with the soaring costs holding them back, and the taxes restricting job creation. Instead, they got nothing to ease sky-high energy bills and nothing to make hiring someone more affordable, while the increase in business rates relief excludes too many.
A JP Morgan spokesperson has criticised the decision to hike the UK’s bank tax today, arguing that targeting one of the UK’s most lucrative sectors “lacks principle”:
“We are committed to the country, and we recognise the cost of living challenges there and the global economic headwinds that it faces, but to single out this industry for additional taxes again, one of the UK’s biggest generators of growth and jobs, lacks principle.
“It also overlooks that the banking industry operates in a highly competitive global marketplace.”
But despite the bank’s disappointment, JP Morgan is due to charge ahead with its £3bn new UK HQ, according to a source familiar with the matter.
What opposition parties are saying about the budget
Kemi Badenoch’s reaction to the budget on behalf of the Conservative party was covered earlier, at 2.11pm. Here is some reaction from other oppostion parties.
The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, told MPs that John Healey should have done more to address the problems with Brexit. He said:
I do think this budget will be more defined by Labour’s red lines on Europe and the Conservatives’ Brexit red tape, rather than faster growth.
And at the root of so much of what’s gone wrong in our country – the cost of living crisis, higher taxes, broken public services, empty high streets, the lack of jobs and opportunity – at the root of all of that is the lack of economic growth.
Our economy is being held back. British business is being held back, and it’s been held back above all by the terrible damage of the Conservative Brexit deal.
Ellie Chowns, the Green party Treasury spokesperson, said the budget was lacking in ambition.
You’d have thought that, after going to the trouble of ousting the last PM, taking his job, and installing a brand-new chancellor, Andy Burnham would be keen to ensure Labour displayed a bit more ambition at today’s budget than it did under his predecessor.
Unfortunately, what Britain actually saw today was a business-as-usual budget which failed to engage with the real issues facing our country – choosing to tinker round the edges, rather than properly taxing extreme wealth and profits, making essentials genuinely and permanently affordable, or investing in our long-term climate resilience.
There was no discussion of the climate crisis in Healey’s speech today, nor any new investment in renewables and climate adaptation, despite the devastating impact of this summer’s deadly heatwaves and wildfires on our communities, public services, and economy.
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, said Britain was broke. In a post on social media, he said:
These are the stats John Healey doesn’t want you to read.
Unemployment will rise to 5% in 2027.
The tax burden is going up AGAIN to the highest since WW2.
By 2031 we’ll be spending £160bn/year on debt interest alone – up £36bn/year …
We are on a fiscal knife-edge. Britain is Broke. Britain needs Reform.
Kirsty Blackman, the SNP’s economy spokesperson at Westminster, said this was not a budget for Scotland. She said:
The UK Budget shows the Labour government doesn’t get Scotland – and isn’t doing anywhere near enough to protect people from the looming cost of living emergency this winter.
This isn’t a budget that a Scottish chancellor would have delivered. Instead of providing meaningful help, it has abandoned families in the face of soaring bills and has imposed another betrayal on Scotland’s energy – with the decision to scrap Scottish carbon capture funding.
Andy Burnham promised to cut the cost of living but every major household bill has increased on his watch – and the UK budget completely fails to address the scale of the challenge families are now facing.
Ben Lake, Plaid Cymru’s economic spokeperson at Westminster, said Wales was just an afterthought in the budget.
Today’s budget was UK Labour’s opportunity to prove that Wales is more than an afterthought in Treasury decisions. Instead, it appears to have delivered the worst funding settlement for Wales in years.
After months of promises about a new relationship with Wales and a new approach from the Treasury, the question many people will be asking is – where is the ambition
The chancellor chose not to announce what Wales would receive in consequentials from this budget. Buried in the documents is around £450 million of additional funding spread over three years. That falls well short of keeping pace with inflation and risks forcing the kind of spending reductions Wales experienced during the worst years of Tory cuts.
UK gambling firms' value jumps after chancellor resisted large duty hike
Rob Davies
Machine games duty (MGD) is the tax levied on slot machines found in bookmakers, casinos, bingo halls and adult gaming centres (AGCs). The chancellor faced calls to double the rate of MGD from 20% to 40%, a policy backed by one of his predecessors, Gordon Brown.
Amid fierce lobbying from gambling firms, which issued dire warnings of thousands of job cuts, Healey opted for a more modest rise to 25% today. This, he said, would bring in nearly £150m a year, “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.
Investors responded with relief, adding £240m to the combined stock market value of Entain (Ladbrokes/Coral), Evoke (William Hill), RankGroup (Mecca Bingo/Grosvenor Casinos) and Playtech (designer of slot machine games). Entain said the MGC hike will cost it £25m, which it expects to be able to mitigate, including by shop closures. Betfred boss Fred Done, whose family took a £30m dividend from their betting empire earlier this year, also warned that closures and job losses would follow.
The chancellor singled out AGCs, sometimes known as “slot farms” for particular attention. As well as the duty rise, they will also be excluded - along with vape shops - from business rates relief available to retail and hospitality businesses.
Burnham rules out general election in the next year
Andy Burnham has ruled out calling a snap general election in the next year amid ongoing speculation (including among economists and investors) that he could seek to consolidate his position.
He said he was thinking “about people” and not “my own party and its prospects”, Press Association reports.
The prime minister was asked if he would call an election in the next year as he visited a community centre in central London after the Budget.
He said:
“I don’t know how many times I’ve done this now, but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months.
“I have said repeatedly since coming into this job, I’m not thinking about myself. I’m not thinking about my own party and its prospects.
“I am thinking about people, and I’m thinking about what I can do to help them to have that care for people, which I spoke about on my first day in Downing Street.”
He added that he was “leading from the front” and “putting Britain on a different path”.
He said:
“We’ve got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage.”
Several City economists are suggesting that today’s budget may be teeing up an early general election.
AndrewWishart, senior UK economist at Berenberg, suggests there is a 40% chance of a general election before the end of 2027.
He points out that this would allow Labour to discard its previous manifesto commitments not to raise taxes on working people.
Wishart says:
The big questions, about how to fund a national social care service and a £15bn increase in defence spending by 2030 remain unanswered. The government will hope that the combination of a decline in gilt yields a reduction in transfer payments to those with disabilities and efficiency savings enable them to fund their priorities without a major increase in taxes. It’s just about possible, but pretty unlikely and requires tax hikes pencilled in for the back end of the parliament to come in, potentially just before the next general election.
More ambition would require a new mandate without the manifesto constraint on tax, achieved by via a general election. We put the chances of one before the end of next year at about 40%.”
Eoin O’Callaghan, macro strategist at Wellington Management, says there is a “significant question mark” over the credibility of the projections, including the biig squeeze on departmental spending in a few year’s time.
Like last autumn’s budget they incorporate an unrealistic real term freeze in departmental spending in 2029-30, after the next election. And they now incorporate an even more challenging 3% real terms cut to next year’s departmental spending too to help offset rising interest rate and unfunded public sector pensions costs. The forecasts are also predicated on nominal growth staying relatively elevated close to 4% throughout the forecast.
“That may not concern the market for now. But it highlights how challenging the UK public finances are. How difficult the fiscal decisions ahead of this government are. And why there is a risk of early elections given the tough spending decisions ahead.”
BenjaminJones, Invesco’s Global Head of Research, predicts speculation about an early election will continue to build:
“After two blockbuster, tax-hiking budgets, investors will welcome this more ‘steady as she goes’ package from the new Labour Chancellor. Against a backdrop of rising gilt yields and geopolitical uncertainty, Healey’s decision to limit spending increases and tax rises shows sensible caution.
His opening comments were clearly aimed to ease bond market fears. However, many of the difficult fiscal choices - such as delivering welfare savings and boosting Defence spending - have been postponed until the Spending Review next year, which will continue to fuel speculation of an early election.
John Healey announced a first-time buyer ISA in his speech. This is what the Treasury says about how it will work.
The government will introduce a new FTB ISA from April 2029. The product will replace the Lifetime ISA (LISA) for new savers and provide a 25% government bonus, paid on withdrawal, towards the purchase of a first home worth up to £450,000. The maximum value of the bonus will be capped at £20,000. Existing LISA holders will be able to continue contributing to and using their accounts under the current rules. In addition, the government will reduce the withdrawal charge for existing LISA holders who use their savings to purchase a first home above the £450,000 property price cap.

article_title: Healey tells departments to make 1% cuts to fund defence
article_content:
Healey tells departments to make 1% cuts to fund defence
- Published
Chancellor John Healey has told every government department to find 1% cuts in their capital budgets to fill a £4.7bn hole in the funding of the Defence Investment Plan.
The reductions come on top of the 1% cuts departments were asked to make earlier this year in order to pay for the initial £10.3bn of the plan's overall £15bn price tag.
The plan boosted defence spending; however the chancellor continues to come under pressure to explain how he will meet a further target of spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the chancellor of only offering "a plan to have a plan" adding: "I bet [Vladimir] Putin's really scared now."
Setting out his Budget, Healey hinted that meeting that goal would require further cuts, telling MPs it would involve "looking hard at public spending".
He said he would set out how the UK would reach the 3% target by 2030, as well as 3.5% of GDP by 2035, at next year's spending review.
Government departments have yet to decide what will be cut from their capital budgets.
Capital budgets are focused on long-term investments, rather than day-to-day spending. For example, earlier this year, when departments had to make capital budget cuts to fund the initial defence spending rise, a number of major road improvement schemes were scrapped.
Badenoch criticised Healey for not using his Budget to explain how he would boost defence funding to 3%.
"He is the man who is making our country less safe. He has failed his own test. This is on him, and no one will ever forget," she said.
The Conservatives have previously urged the government to pay for defence by making cuts to the welfare budget.
Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said the UK was on "a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all Nato Allies in The Hague - to ensure we're all investing what's needed to remain ready & able to deter aggression and defend our freedom and security".
Chair of the Commons defence committee - and Labour MP - Tan Dhesi said "some of the key decisions on defence spending have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review".
He added: "There is a cost to inaction. Investment in our nation's defence and security cannot be kicked into the long grass."
Former Nato secretary general Lord Robertson told the BBC the Budget was "pretty good news for defence generally" but warned there would be "battles ahead with the spending departments" to reach the 3% target.
Earlier this year, Healey resigned as defence secretary, accusing the then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer of not providing enough money to keep the UK safe.
In a scathing resignation letter, he specifically emphasised his belief in the importance of reaching a 3% target by 2030.
Now chancellor, Healey told the House of Commons on Wednesday: "At the spending review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our Nato commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030.
"And today, I am getting work under way to get there in a fiscally sustainable way."
In addition to looking at public spending, Healey said he also wanted to use "more innovative financing alongside the private sector and our international allies".
The chancellor said this would include:
- starting treaty negotiations with Finland, Poland and Netherlands to set up a "multilateral defence mechanism" which would allow allies to share resources
- increasing the amount of private investment in defence through public-private partnerships
- directing the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to put £5bn into "defence, dual-use technology and sovereign capability"
The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that the UK government's target to increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 will cost £35bn.
Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Increasing investment in defence companies may contribute to the target but it is unclear how much this will lead to an increase in UK defence capabilities.
"There is much further to go to get to 3% of GDP on defence and it is hard to believe that this government will want to get there without topping up spending totals."
- Burnham treads carefully with Zelensky visit, balancing Trump and Ukraine 
  - Published14 October
In his Budget speech, Healey also announced £10bn of economic and military support for Ukraine, in the form of loans and export guarantees.
The funding includes £5.5bn of loans through World Bank guarantees and a grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association's crisis facility.
A further £3bn will be made available to Ukraine through loans facilitated by UK Export Finance, a government export credit agency.
Healey told the House of Commons that the week had started with Russia launching a "brutal ballistic missile attack" and that the extra money would send "a clear message to Moscow".
He said that when he told the Ukrainian leader about the additional support in a phone call, President Volodymyr Zelensky had said: "You've made my day."
Later on social media, Zelensky welcomed the money, saying: "Every step to strengthen Ukraine brings Russia closer to realising that it must end this war of its own making."
The money comes on top of the UK's pledge to provide Ukraine with £3bn of military support until at least 2030-31.

article_title: US ambassador suggests Trump could blame Canada if midterms don’t go his way
article_content:
The US ambassador has suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans perform poorly in next week’s midterm elections, the latest intervention from a controversial figure who has been accused of inflaming a bitter dispute that has angered and baffled residents of both countries.
On Wednesday, CTV news reported that Pete Hoekstra told business leaders at a closed door meeting that if a number of swing races – including Maine and Michigan – go to the Democrats, it could make things harder for Canada because Donald Trump might try to blame the loss on it.
“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” the prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters when asked about the allegations.
For months, Canada and the US have been locked in a bitter tariff war, with Ottawa retaliating against illegal US tariffs and targeting goods in states that rely heavily on trade with Canada.
Carney said that Canada “will pursue” such a deal if it presents itself, but that Ottawa’s trade negotiators are “not in that position right now”.
Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particular for his response to Trump’s rhetoric about making Canada the 51st US state. Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the threats as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”. He had previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election as “anti-American”.
This year a House of Commons petition signed by more than 225,000 Canadians called for his expulsion, suggesting his statements violated diplomatic protocols, including the prohibition on diplomats interfering in the internal affairs of a host country.
More recently, Hoekstra has accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections, pointing to Canadian politicians who have criticized the tariffs in US media, and the province of Ontario’s anti-tariff advertisement that ran on US television.
“We see all of that. We are monitoring it. We are evaluating it. And if some of it becomes election interference, America will respond to it,” Hoekstra, who comes from Michigan, recently told a Canadian podcast, adding that Canadians should “keep your nose out of American politics”.
Canada’s industry minister, Mélanie Joly, who was a target of Hoekstra’s comments, told reporters in Ottawa that her country “would never do that” and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada”.
Carney, while in Turkey, told reporters there was “no merit” to the claims of interference and that he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.
Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the remarks were an “extraordinary thing” for a US ambassador to say about his host country and looked like an effort to “manufacture a pretext for the Trump administration’s own political difficulties”.
“The job of an ambassador is to represent the interests of his country, but it’s also to maintain channels of communication and build relationships and manage disagreements,” he said.
“His comments have repeatedly aggravated tensions instead of helping to manage them. I don’t think that he’s serving American interests very well. I’m not even sure that he’s serving the interests of his president.”
Paris points to polling in the US that shows voters have increasingly linked tariffs, the war and cost of living. There is also widespread confusion over why the White House has chosen to treat Canada as a trade adversary.
“It’s certainly not working in Canada. It’s on the contrary. It seems that every time Mr Hoekstra opens his mouth, the Canadians are more determined than before to stand up to the bullying of the Trump administration,” he said. “That’s not serving American interests.”
The US embassy denied Hoekstra said Canada would face blame for a poor Republican showing, suggesting the remarks were “grossly taken out of context” from a broader discussion.
“The ambassador has consistently said that the Canadian media is attempting to overstate the relevance of Canadian issues in American elections. As we have previously stated, Americans will decide American elections based on issues that are important to them,” the embassy said in a statement.
At a Canadian American Business event last year, Hoekstra delivered what witnesses say was an expletive-laden tirade at Ontario’s trade representative after the province ran a series of anti-tariff ads in the US that featured Ronald Reagan. Ontario’s premier called the outburst “absolutely unacceptable” and “unbecoming of an ambassador”.
Last week, Barack Obama noted the unusual choice to attack a longtime ally while speaking at a Democratic campaign rally in Detroit, mocking Trump’s fixation on Canada and jokingly referring to his northern neighbor as a “well-known evil empire”.
“That historical adversary of ours: Canada,” the former US president said. “It’s your neighbor! It’s a few minutes drive over the bridge. These are the people who gave us Martin Short … and maple syrup. They are the nicest people. And somehow we’ve gotten them so mad.”
author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto

article_title: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
article_content:
Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
- Published
Andy Burnham has insisted there is "no confusion" over his position on the European Union, as he criticised the UK's current deal with the bloc.
The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the deal, which was ratified in 2020, at a summit in Brussels next month.
He denied he had shifted his stance since the Makerfield by-election when he promised not to "re-run" the Brexit debate. Earlier this week, he suggested he could call a referendum on the UK returning to EU freedom of movement, before No10 appeared to backtrack.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday of failing to "respect" the 2016 Brexit vote.
Badenoch said Burnham had created confusion and asked if he wanted a referendum on rejoining the EU.
"There is no confusion at all," Burnham told MPs.
"The government has a collectively agreed position, which I have set out today.
"It is entirely consistent with everything that I've said, including in the by-election.
"The red lines in our manifesto, including on freedom of movement, will stay in place firmly for the whole of this Parliament."
Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
Freedom of movement allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country.
It is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market, which enables goods, services and people to move freely between EU member states.
Badenoch accused Burnham of having "opened his mouth without engaging his brain" over freedom of movement during "the chancellor's big week" as the Budget is unveiled.
- No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion 
  - Published2 days ago
- Burnham pledges not to 're-run' Brexit arguments 
  - Published18 May
- Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days 
  - Published2 days ago
Recalling the mood in Parliament and the country in 2017 when the current Brexit deal was being fought over, Badenoch said: "We do not want to go through that again - the country was paralysed.
"It was miserable, regardless of which side of the debate you were on."
Burnham said Badenoch was "speaking the truth" here and the country had suffered from low growth and insufficient control on migration as a result of a "harder Brexit than what was promised" in the 2016 referendum.
"Where I am focused is getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility, and I will lead from this despatch box over the next few weeks," Burnham said.
At a summit in Brussels on 20 November, Burnham will push options for a reset of relations with the bloc on issues such as youth mobility, food, drink, energy and cooperation on illegal immigration.
Burnham's comments at Prime Minister's Questions came as a letter emerged addressed to his Cabinet ministers, asking them to be "aligned and disciplined" around the summit.
"It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process," he wrote in a letter on Wednesday.
He said he hoped the summit led to "some important, concrete steps" and he would set out the next steps "to consider the UK's long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan".
"Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote," he said.
"Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality."
Any "fundamental change" to this relationship "would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next Parliament," he added.

article_title: The Guardian view on Labour’s budget: bold ambitions and welcome first steps | Editorial
article_content:
John Healey’s first budget was a Rorschach test. Supporters saw dozens of measures offering “breathing space” to a public worn down by rising prices. Critics admitted to a slew of announcements but countered that each was modest in value. Underlying both views is that the budget was more ambitious on how a state can do more to protect the public than on how much it spends. The chancellor has taken a small step in the right direction – a tricky feat in a turbulent world. But an economy marked by entrenched inequality and more than a decade of stagnation will need a bigger stride.
The Office for Budget Responsibility’s “pretty grim picture” of living standards exposes the budget’s central weakness: its relief is temporary, while the squeeze on households persists. As the government deficit shrinks and company profits recover, households are expected to move from saving roughly £50bn in 2026 to borrowing roughly the same amount in 2031. By then, mortgage repayments are expected to reach 4.25% of household disposable income – the highest level since 2009. The OBR expects growth to recover from 1% in 2027 to 1.8% in 2029, while weak worker “bargaining power” allows firms to rebuild profit margins. That sits uneasily with Mr Healey’s promises to working people.
Admittedly, the budget’s ambitions – shaping energy markets, ending rough sleeping, devolving tax and spend decisions – go beyond its winter relief package. Mr Healey is also right to ask banks, gambling companies and landlords to contribute more. Preventing hardship is better than repeatedly paying for its consequences. In ringfencing homelessness prevention in local government spending, even though the savings are experienced in the NHS, he is making both moral and financial sense.
The problem, however, is not that Mr Healey’s budget lacks ambition, but that it lacks firepower. The bank tax raises just £1.5bn over 15 months, against the projected £11bn that a Thatcher-style levy on interest-free deposits could have yielded. The Resolution Foundation has a point when it says that 80% of homes get a £100 energy payment, while 1.4 million poor families miss out. Relying on revenues from the giant Rosebank oilfield before its approval is settled would be reckless. So would treating the export of its oil as an answer to the climate damage caused by burning it.
The choices that Mr Healey makes all too often reflect the fiscal constraints he opted to retain. Is it really “credible” to claim that there will be £11bn of cuts to “unprotected” budgets (those that aren’t defence, the NHS, schools or international aid) in 2031-32? Many experts think not. Should the defence budget be funded by “reprioritising” other departments’ capital spend? Mr Healey thinks so. The prime minister called the 2009 Marmot review his bible on reducing inequalities – it advocates for widescale economic rebalancing. But devolving tax revenues without adequate redistribution risks giving the wealthiest places the most to spend, rather than giving the poorest the help they need. Mr Healey has yet to explain how he will prevent that.
Global events could make Mr Healey’s life much tougher. Prolonged disruption in the strait of Hormuz would further squeeze real incomes. But the chancellor has in his budget sketched the outline of a social-democratic active state: taxing rentiers, protecting vulnerable people and investing in prevention. The question is whether those commitments have enough resources to succeed.
