article_title: Will John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ budget deliver what Britain needs? Our panel responds | Panel
article_content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFP/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFP/REX/ShutterstockWill John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ budget deliver what Britain needs? Our panel respondsPolly Toynbee, Hettie O'Brien, Rohan Sathyamoorthy, Kevin Cashman, Nik and John McDonnellAmid global economic storms, the new chancellor has promised to steer the course – with promises of more help to come. Will it be enough?‘Growth in every postcode’? Not yet, but hope at lastPolly ToynbeeGuardian columnistFirst, he did no harm. Then he scattered sprinkles of feel-goods. He told the truth about the state we’re in, deep in an extra £14bn of expensive debt, and, though he put it politely, at the mercy of the monster in the White House’s whims on Iran and tariffs.The losers were popular targets: the banks and gambling companies. But plainly bank threats to decamp partly paid off. Their shares leapt up on the news that their surcharge would rise to only 6%, not its original 8% before Tory reductions. They expected to pay more, and indeed they should. Gambling company shares jumped up too, with Rank up more than 10% on the day when the companies were only hit with five percentage points more tax on high-stakes machines, a missed chance, but better than nothing. The Treasury makes £4bn from gambling. Time to ban their advertising next.The chancellor gave a gracious nod to his predecessor. He should be grateful, as she took the pain and he takes the gain for her £66.6bn in tax rises, in NI for employers and frozen income tax thresholds that slide by unseen, but yield mightily until 2031.The public expected more personal taxes, according to Ipsos. It didn’t happen. Labour can take comfort that they think the Conservatives and Reform would both raise tax and cut public services. Instead, help comes for their energy costs, one of the greatest causes of household debt, with bills set to rise brutally in January. Homes in council tax bands A-D get £100 and the VAT reduction has been extended until July, while abolished standing charges leave 60% of homes better off. But the rumbling discontent that has upended our politics since Brexit is easily explained by the unprecedented long fall in median household income, only in the last year rising back to levels six years ago.Yet people’s priorities remain perverse: immigration stays top of their concerns, above inflation and the economy. Spending more on tougher border controls is second only to the NHS as the most popular expenditure. What do you do? Give in and let Shabana Mahmood be her harshest – or start telling people about the trade-off? Visas for work for another 200,000 migrants would bring the Treasury £18bn, says the Office for Budget Responsibility. Think what people could have for that.Is this the “growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” Andy Burnham promises? No, not yet, not yet … Wait for his 10-year plan, spending review and an election with a new manifesto. And hope.Voters might have been hoping for something bolder than thisHettie O'BrienWriter on the Guardian’s morning newsletter First Edition, the Guardian Long Read, and the author of The Asset ClassWhile Keir Starmer promised to tread more “lightly” on voters’ lives, interpreting political disaffection as a sign that people wanted to hear less from their politicians, Andy Burnham has interpreted this loss of faith as a demand for more political action. But there was always a risk that without a theory of power, his premiership would come to resemble the Downing Street equivalent of the TV show Rip-Off Britain, giving voters “everyday fixes”, starter ISAs and cheaper gherkins while failing to change the economy or society as a whole. The charitable reading of John Healey’s budget is that it was better than it could have been (and better than the Treasury, which briefed this as a “low-key” event, wanted us to expect). His energy package, including a £100 cut to bills for houses in council tax brackets A-D, will help ease the cost of living and should lower inflation. He also proposed a series of changes that should help to bring down energy bills in future. But there was no help for low-income renters, nor any plans for funding public services that are facing real-terms cuts. Bankers, meanwhile, will be breathing a sigh of relief after Healey imposed a temporary 6% tax on bank profits, below the pre-crisis level of 8%.For a government that has promised to turn back 40 years of neoliberalism, you might have been hoping for something much more radical than this. Small, short-term fixes and making it easier to cancel your Netflix subscription don’t equate to a political philosophy, let alone a programme capable of convincing voters that difficult trade-offs – whether on defence spending or the costs of an ageing society – will be worth it. Governing, as Mark McVitie wrote recently, requires political imagination and a sense of where you want to end up. Let’s hope that Andy Burnham has more to offer than this. Budget cuts to fund military spending will lead to job losses and lower growthKevin CashmanResearcher at Transition Security Project, a centre founded by Common Wealth and Climate and Community InstituteJust last month, the prime minister made the significant promise to “break with the direction of the past 40 years” and “build a new economy and a new politics”. John Healey’s budget, unfortunately, doesn’t do enough of either.Department budgets were already slashed this summer to help finance the Ministry of Defence’s demand for an extra £15bn. Now, this budget adds £3bn more in cuts.In July, Transition Security Project estimated that the defence investment plan, funded partly through £6.8bn in cuts, would result in more than 10,000 net job losses. With a further £3bn in cuts, those losses are now likely to exceed 15,000.The reason is simply that military spending is a weaker driver of growth than the investment being sacrificed to fund it. Too much of the money leaves the country – flowing, especially, to the United States. These cuts also undermine programmes that would help bring down the cost of living. The budget confirms a £1bn cut to Warm Homes, which supports heat pump grants. The additional help with household energy bills is welcome. But directing up to £5bn from the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank towards defence reinforces the same misplaced priorities when these resources could have been invested in areas that help with living standards. Burnham does not have to accept these constraints. Healey has left the detailed funding route to the Nato spending targets until next year’s spending review. These targets – pushed by the US – imply a colossal transfer of wealth from the public to the military sector. Burnham should abandon these targets he inherited, which will steal more investment from every other department. Healey was right that wars are driving up our energy bills and making Britain less safe. But let’s be honest about the role the government is playing. The US used British bases in its unprovoked attack on Iran, and our government is now backing Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen. Diplomacy and de-escalation are part of a serious cost of living strategy – not bombing.Welcome news on apprenticeships, but otherwise little cheer for young people Rohan SathyamoorthyWriter from south-west LondonLook hard enough at this budget, and there are some signs that the chancellor is serious about bridging the age divide: an increase in tax for Britain’s banks, increased investment in apprenticeships and a new scheme for first-time buyers will be a welcome relief for many young and working people who are tired of bearing a disproportionate share of Britain’s economic burden. However, the limitations of even these mild reforms are already apparent: bank stocks rose conspicuously this morning on news that the rise would be temporary and only a mere three percentage points. And although the first-time buyer ISA will help young savers in the immediate term, in the long run it is only continuing to subsidise the housing crisis at the expense of the taxpayer, rather than intervening directly in the market to bring prices back down to an affordable level.Furthermore, while pensioners, businesses, workers, women, carers, families and even nightclubs all received explicit support from Healey, outrageously absent was any real help for young people, nor any mention of the student loan crisis. The only mention of young people not in employment, education or training was made in the context of reforming welfare. Instead of addressing the problems facing young people and making clear that he would tackle intergenerational fairness, Healey made his priority clear, with “the biggest increase in defence spending since the end of the cold war”.Ultimately, it will be impossible to fully judge this budget until we see the one that succeeds it. This “breathing space” budget will be beneficial only if it really is just that – buying time for the government to solve the painful, unignorable issues still crippling Britain’s young people: jobs, student loans, soaring rents. If the mixed rhetoric today is anything to go by, I won’t be holding my breath.I wish more had been done to help us pay our rent and fill our fridgesNikParticipant in the Changing Realities projectThe chancellor said “hope starts with a home”, but for me, it’s the cost of my home that keeps me in poverty. I work multiple jobs just to pay my rent, and nothing in today’s budget will make that situation better. Where is the “breathing space” for families like mine, or hope for the future?Families struggling through the storms of living on a low income deserve more than modest, micro-policies and everyday fixes to protect them from the incessant headwinds.Extending the removal of VAT from electricity bills to next summer is being presented as help for households, but for rural families like mine, it offers little (or no) meaningful relief. I have no access to mains gas and can’t afford heating oil, so I depend on electricity to heat my home. Yet this measure does nothing to address the reality of living rurally without affordable alternatives. A record number of people now live in very deep poverty, with incomes that don’t cover the basics of food, housing or energy. We need meaningful, targeted support, not policies that offer some households a small saving while leaving others struggling to keep warm. In Cornwall, many homes rely on heating oil, and removing the kerosene tariff may help, but any savings depend on supplies holding up and suppliers passing them on.The chancellor promised a distinctly Labour approach to welfare but I know many will feel incredibly fearful about the white papers to come later this year, after Alan Milburn and Stephen Timms deliver their reports on youth unemployment and disability benefits.What we know from this budget is that families will be able to save about 40p on the weekly shop, assuming toffees and caramels are a part of your weekly essentials. Food poverty directly impacts health, productivity and social inclusion. I wish more had been done to help fill our fridges.This budget buys time to go bigger and bolder in next year’s spending reviewJohn McDonnellLabour MP for Hayes and Harlington. He was shadow chancellor for Labour from 2015 to 2020The chancellor has called his budget a “breathing space” budget and that’s exactly what it is. It’s less a break with Keir Starmer, but hopefully the start of a step away.The range of small-scale cost of living assistance offered on energy and food costs are all welcome elements of relief, but the harsh reality is that they provide an extremely limited breathing space.The government has to be extremely careful that the goodwill that Andy Burnham’s arrival has generated does not degenerate into disappointment and disillusionment. Reform UK may have dipped in the polls but the rise of the far right in Germany, France and Italy demonstrates all too clearly where that disappointment can lead to. This budget indicates to people that the government appreciates their concerns and is on their side, but it is absolutely critical that the time this budget may buy is used to demonstrate that it also has the plan needed to tackle the financial pressures people are under.Next year’s spending review provides that opportunity.The government has committed to the large-scale capital investment programme in council housing, home insulation and alternative energy that can stimulate the growth promised in every postcode.But there has to be demand in the economy too. That means putting money to spend in people’s pockets by modernising our taxation system to redistribute wealth and tackle the underinvestment in our public services, low pay and poverty that have held our economy back.Nobody doubts the pressure John Healey has been under as a result of the crass geopolitical nightmares caused by Donald Trump’s attacks on Iran. Both Benjamin Netanyahu and Vladimir Putin have played Trump like a fiddle to their own advantage, and we are all now paying the economic price. With the potential change in the midterms, perhaps it’s also time for leaders to start talking less about defence spending and more about peace making.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026The panelTax and spendingJohn HealeyHousingMilitarycommentShareReuse this content

article_title: Burnham rules out early general election in next 12 months
article_content:
Burnham rules out early general election in next 12 months
- Published
Andy Burnham has ruled out an early general election in the next 12 months, after opposition parties suggested one would be called.
The next UK general election must be held by August 2029, and there has been speculation that the prime minister is preparing for an earlier poll.
Asked directly if he would call a snap election within the next year, the prime minister told broadcasters: "I don't know how many times I've done this now but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months."
He said he was focusing on people over the Labour Party, adding: "I'm not thinking about myself. I'm not thinking about my own party and its prospects."
Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch suggested Burnham may go to the country early.
She said the Conservative Party was "coming back" after it slumped in popularity at the end of 14 years in government, telling BBC South East: "This is an era of political volatility and multi-party politics."
She added: "I do think Andy Burnham is going to call an election sooner than he is saying... all the policies he announced are for after an election."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said in September he believed there would be an election "next spring".
"I believe there must be a general election because Andy Burnham has no mandate - the messiah without a mandate, we deserve a general election on who continues to govern this country."
Burnham was elected MP in June after the Makerfield by-election, before securing the Labour Party leadership and becoming prime minister after Sir Keir Starmer lost the support of Labour MPs and quit Downing Street.
He has since outlined a number of ambitions, which has led some to question whether he will try to secure a fresh mandate before 2029.
One of these issues is Brexit, where Burnham has said he wants an "honest conversation" about the UK's future relationship with the EU.
On Wednesday, he promised to stick to the red lines in his party's 2024 manifesto on EU freedom of movement, the single market and customs union "for the whole of this Parliament".
The current Parliamentary term runs until the next general election.
Burnham has repeatedly denied he is seeking a snap poll. He told broadcasters on Wednesday: "We've got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage."

article_title: He promised fresh hope and delivered doom, but Dr Death’s budget succeeds in doing no harm | John Crace
article_content:
It was as if John Healey was taking the Hippocratic oath. First do no harm. For your first budget, this may be no bad thing: we can all think of plenty of chancellors who have done untold damage. Take a bow George Osborne. It might just have been better if the doctor that Healey had chosen to impersonate was not Dr Death.
John can’t help looking like the last man you would want to stop by your hospital bed. Not everyone can have a naturally sunny disposition. His face seems to be carved out of despair. But it would be a big help if, when called upon to make his most important speech of the year, he didn’t reinforce the impression when he opened his mouth. A one-way journey to the slough of despond.
“I’m very sorry to let you know, Mr Crace,” he would say with Voldemort delight. “But your cancer is now terminal. You have months to live.” And just when you are trying to process what he’s said and are preparing to say your goodbyes, he would let you know he had made a mistake. You only had weeks to live after all. He would then smile wanly, pat you on the shoulder before moving on to kill off his next patient. You wouldn’t be seeing him again.
Healey began with a few cheery words. Cheery by his standards, that is. This was a budget for working people. People often talked about global headwinds. John was here to let us know that these headwinds were more like a storm. Make that a hurricane. One we’d all be lucky to come out of alive. The wars in Iran and Ukraine, the rising cost of energy. The whole world was basically screwed. He knew the government had suggested we all stockpile food and water ahead of the apocalypse, but frankly we might as well not bother. Why prolong the agony?
“Fresh hope for Britain’s future,” he said. The word hope died on his lips. Only Healey can send you into a vortex of existential futility with an attempt at optimism. Even the normally upbeat Andy Burnham who was sitting next to him looked lost in his own sense of pointlessness. Not even a glimmer of a smile. The main reason he had appointed Healey was because he could be relied on to do his bidding. To deliver the kind of budget Andy had in mind. Ed Miliband was far too much his own man. But Burnham hadn’t factored in the aura of gloom.
The one consolation was that even John couldn’t be as depressing as Rachel Reeves. But Healey was working on it. Give him time. Most budget statements try to tell a story. To create a coherent narrative of the state of the economy, the government’s plans to stimulate growth and fix the problems they inherited. Even when the problems the chancellor is inheriting are the ones they created. But Healey was going to try a different approach. Just a series of unstructured, random spending announcements. Dr Death’s Seven Last Words on the Cross.
Most budget speeches also contain the odd joke. Or what passes for a gag in the minds of MPs. None of them are going to get gigs at the Edinburgh fringe. But on the few occasions that the mirror cracked and Healey’s mouth tried to form a rictus grin, his words fell flat. Turns out that not everyone finds telling people they have nothing to live for quite as funny as John. Worse still, he is a man with no sense of timing. He makes Ed Balls sound like a comedy giant.
There was the obligatory reference to Liz Truss’s mini-budget, and the hand that the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, played in it. That should have been fertile comic ground as it has the benefit of being true. Four years on, we are all still suffering PTSD. Everyone apart from the Trusster, who believes the real problem was that she was forced to reverse £70bn of unfunded tax cuts. But Healey couldn’t land the punchline. Labour backbenchers were willing him to succeed, but they still couldn’t bring themselves to laugh.
The only really funny moment was completely unintentional, when Healey said that the energy secretary had opposed Jackdaw. That was supposed to be kept an open secret, not broadcast to the world. The Tory benches couldn’t contain themselves with forced laughter. The chancellor tried to redeem the situation by ad-libbing that at least the opposition was still awake. Which was more than could be said for many Labour backbenchers.
Fresh hope and breathing space, Healey said again. It had become his only leitmotif. And, yet again, it felt like another nail in the coffin. The world was in turmoil, the country bouncing from crisis to crisis and the chancellor was doing not very much. Or rather he was doing a lot – he announced 98 different measures – but none of them amounted to a lot. Not that anyone was going to complain about getting £100 off their council tax or not having to queue up at the post office for your Amazon returns. These things do make a difference.
It was just that we were waiting for the big reveal. The major surprise. But time passed. And passed. And none came. There was a promise to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, but no details of how. It was the miserabilist’s dream. Growth baked in at less than 2%, living standards predicted to fall.
A sense of drift. But maybe it was all deliberate. A country put on palliative care because it wouldn’t survive extreme surgery. Healey had said he had called an early budget because it was time to inject some urgency into the public finances. But many of the really big decisions had been kicked into the long grass. He had said the budget was to give the country some breathing space. It felt as if the government were the ones who needed the breathing space.
Kemi Badenoch’s response was similarly underwhelming. Then she had rather shot herself in the foot by admitting that the country had been paralysed and miserable under the Tories. She even found herself agreeing with some of Healey’s measures but her overall assessment – Was that it? – was echoed by many Labour MPs. Not that Kemi had any answers herself. None to be taken seriously, at least. At his own press conference, a disinhibited Nigel Farage had just sounded mad. There is no appetite for the Tories or Reform. So a breathing space it is.

article_title: Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget | Aditya Chakrabortty
article_content:
Was this Andy Burnham’s budget – the bold vision of a new prime minister who burns with a passion to topple “40 years of neoliberalism”? Fat chance. Was it John Healey’s budget – the repair job of a cautious chancellor fretting about record-high taxes, £3tn of public debt and an economy stuck in first gear? Little sign of that.
This budget was cast in the image of a man who isn’t in Burnham’s government or even a Labour politician – but who appears almost every day on TV, on podcasts and is probably better known than 649 of the MPs at Westminster. Today’s budget was the Martin Lewis budget.
Lewis is the MoneySavingExpert, whose weekly Money Tips email advises 10 million British subscribers on cheap mortgages, Black Friday deals and how to score two pizzas for £10. Tips and tricks to stave off rising prices and make the most of the money you have. Given that the Bayeux tapestry is French, and the Koh-i-noor is Indian, Lewis may be the closest thing Britain has to a genuine national treasure.
Over the past four years, since Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine and sent energy prices soaring, Lewis has become more political and wielded greater influence in Westminster. His fingerprints were all over this “red book”. This morning, before the cabinet had even had its traditional pre-budget pep talk, Lewis had gone to Downing Street for a personal briefing from the chancellor on its key measures. On Radio 4’s Today programme, he was the big budget interview, rather than any politician or BBC editor.
No wonder, because the most eye-catching of the budget’s measures had been written by the money saving expert. Scrapping standing charges on gas bills, shielding more pensioners from income tax and fixing energy bill credit against council tax bands – all of these came from Lewis’s wishlist. Beyond policies, he has also informed Burnham’s politics. At last year’s Labour conference, Lewis advised any new prime minister to “pick a hundred things that piss people off and fix them at one a day for the first hundred days”. Et voilà! The King of the North has vowed to end loudcasting on public transport, crack down on unfair parking fines and introduce more drop boxes for the post … and more and more.
For Labour ministers, government by MoneySavingExpert may seem a no-brainer. After a wretched couple of years under Keir Starmer, they can pose as the people’s champion, for ever on your side. Best of all, all these micro-policies cost micro-money. Today’s budget had 98 measures – more than any I can remember in decades of covering fiscal events, yet they all cost trifling sums.
Which brings us to the killer problem: Lewis is one of the most trusted people in Britain. But he’s not a politician. He’s never claimed to be. He speaks the language of terms and conditions, not financialisation – and he knows his limits. To quote a New Statesman essay last week on the new MoneySavingPolitics: “As governments have embraced retail policies and suggestion-box-style politics in his image, Lewis has been raising the alarm that there are too many people who can no longer help themselves and it is time for structural change.”
The difference was clear today. In her first budget, Rachel Reeves announced extra spending worth £74bn by the end of the period. By comparison, Healey announced a grand total of £380m. For all Burnham’s grand ambition and soaring rhetoric, his first budget was only 0.5% of Starmer’s first budget.
This is obviously not how the King of the North wants you to see him. Listen to Burnham speak, and you hear a changemaker, an ideas man, a leader with a 10-year plan. But does he put his money where his mouth is? Does he heck. The anxiety I have heard for months from so many of his advisers and MPs was borne out in this budget: he’s big talk and small stick.
The best line of the day came from Kemi Badenoch. “The prime minister came to power promising to end 40 years of neoliberalism, and instead we got 4p off gherkins,” the Tory leader said, while Burnham and Healey frowned like men caught bang to rights. What’s the point of cut-price marmalade when a few months ago you promised to nationalise Thames Water?
Why, for that matter, chuck out the old boss when the new one is less ambitious? Whacking banks with a tax in order to cut energy costs is good politics, but this new government should have been much more ambitious. A hundred pounds is a token saving when the typical household’s fuel bill is about to top £2,000. Given how harsh this El Niño winter is likely to be, I imagine the government will have to cobble together another intervention before the new year.
Ministers are now caught in a pincer movement between Badenoch to their right, who can argue they aren’t tackling the really big problems and, to their left, the Greens and Plaid, as well as the Scottish nationalists, who will keep on saying they aren’t doing enough for their own voters. In a day of grim economic forecasts, perhaps the worst was from the Office for Budget Responsibility, which said that in the face of high inflation, earnings will not rise at all next year – while 2030 would see households with take-home pay just 2% above where it was before Covid struck in 2020. Put those two figures together and – despite all the Westminster chat – you can forget about a snap election that delivers Labour a new majority.
If ministers can’t offer any protection against an economic outlook that bleak, they will face an angry and mutinous public. If the Labour party wants to be re-elected, it needs to give people a reason to go out and vote for it. Pointing to bond markets isn’t a defence, because markets aren’t in open rebellion. Yes, government borrowing is a lot more expensive than it was in the post-crash years of cheap money and the interest bill on the nation’s debt is high. But no one thinks Britain is France. Gilt traders today looked at a government running down its financial buffer and were completely unruffled. Had Healey borrowed much more to invest in social and cheap housing, he could have argued that such spending would soon enough bring down benefit bills – and markets would have believed him.
I write this as someone who wants Burnham to do well – and certainly to do better than today’s tiny raft of tweaks. Unlike many Labour politicians, he can talk sincerely about where disastrous rightwing politics have led this country. When he promises a new economic and political model, I – and many others – am up for it. In contrast to Starmer he doesn’t act as if he hates 80% of his own party members. Unlike Starmer’s advisers, his team doesn’t subsist on a diet of received wisdom and petty vindictiveness. But at some point, the grand rhetoric and the romantic notions need to cash out into a programme of change. Otherwise, voters will draw the conclusion that this summer’s coup against a recently elected prime minister had no grand motivation apart from saving the skins of Labour MPs and fanning a few egos.
A Martin Lewis budget is fine, but Labour chose Andy Burnham as its leader and the public were promised a Burnham budget. They’re still waiting.
- 
  Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist and the Guardian’s senior economics commentator

article_title: Dharshini David: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions still unanswered
article_content:
Dharshini David: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions still unanswered
- Published
John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.
It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.
While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.
The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.
Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.
But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.
Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%
However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.
The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.
As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.
And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.
So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.
The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.
- Budget 2026: Key points at a glance 
  - Published13 hours ago
- Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you 
  - Published13 hours ago
So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.
Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.
There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.
And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.
The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.
Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.
Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out.
And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.
Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.
So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.
With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.
The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.
So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.
For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.
A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.
description: The chancellor talked of charting a new course for Britain, but the impact of Iran war has limited his options.

article_title: Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you
article_content:
Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you
- Published
Families facing cost-of-living pressures are being offered some help, or "breathing space" as Chancellor John Healey is calling it.
The help comes as prices are rising faster than expected with annual energy bills in particular likely to increase by hundreds of pounds in January.
Here's how the key announcements in the Budget affect you and your money.
Energy bills
If you are living in a home in council tax bands A to D in England, you will receive a one-off £100 "Household Energy Payment" from January, funded by extra tax on banks.
It will be paid directly into your bank account.
Council tax bands are listed below - you can check which one you are in by looking at your annual bill or checking the government's website, external, although that was struggling to cope with traffic after the announcement.
Administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive the equivalent funding, and they will decide whether to introduce the same payment.
This is designed to help with soaring energy bills, with some forecasts suggesting a typical annual bill could rise by £400 or so to £2,100 in January the saving will be only a portion of that. Although it's designated for energy bills, you can spend the money on anything you wish.
The VAT cut on electricity bills, which was introduced in October, will also be extended to July. It was due to end in April.
- Budget 2026: Key points at a glance 
  - Published13 hours ago
Gas standing charges
The fee for connecting to your gas supply so called standing charges will be scrapped in England, Scotland and Wales, next year "or as soon as possible after", the chancellor said.
These fixed daily charges will then be shifted onto the price you pay for each unit of energy.
The Treasury calculates that 60% of households will save an average of £45 a year, with lower users gaining the most. But the saving will come after the projected big rise in bills in January.
Higher users - in the biggest houses but also large, low-income families - will pay more than they currently do.
The government wants to extend reforms to electricity standing charges later.
Fuel duty
The 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel, introduced by Rishi Sunak in 2022, will be extended to July. It was scheduled to be phased out from January.
It means drivers will still pay the levy at 52.95p per litre.
Motor fuel prices have risen sharply owing to the continued impact of the Iran war on drivers, with diesel having recently hit new records when it moved above £2 per litre.
The cost of filling a typical family car with diesel has gone up by around £30 since late February. A tankful of petrol costs about £23 more.
Changes to cash Isa scrapped
The chancellor has scrapped his predecessor's plans to reduce the annual amount people can save tax-free in cash in Individual Savings Accounts (Isas).
Rachel Reeves had wanted the policy to encourage personal investment in stocks and shares.
It meant, from April 2027, if you're under 65, you would only be able to save £12,000 a year in cash in an Isa, rather than £20,000.
But that plan has now been ditched.
Instead, the government plans to create a new "Starter Isa" for first-time investors.
More tax for some savers and landlords
If you have a large amount in savings, or if you fail to use the tax-free Isa allowance, then you will pay more tax from April.
You do not pay tax on all savings. There is the annual £20,000 Isa allowance, and an annual savings income allowance (in other words, the interest received on a savings pot) of £1,000 for basic rate taxpayers and £500 for higher-rate taxpayers.
But beyond that savings tax rates will rise by four percentage points to 24% and 44% respectively from April.
Landlords could also pay more in tax. In analysis published on Wednesday, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said these steps along with measures over the past decade that have reduced private landlord returns "collectively risk leading to a steady rise in rents".
Minimum wage rise but you'll pay more tax
Minimum wage rates will rise by 3.9% in April. It means:
- Eligible workers aged 21 and over on the National Living Wage will receive £13.21 an hour, up from £12.71
- If you are aged 18, 19 or 20, the National Minimum Wage will increase to £11.27 an hour, up from £10.85
- For those aged 16 or 17, the minimum wage will rise to £8.31 an hour, up from £8
- The separate apprentice rate which applies to eligible people under 19 - or those over 19 in the first year of an apprenticeship – will also increase to £8.31 an hour, from £8
However, these figures mean, this time around, there's no progress on Labour's manifesto promise to narrow the gap in minimum wages between older and younger workers.
For all workers, the ongoing freeze in the income bands, or thresholds, at which income tax is paid went unmentioned in the Budget.
But it means any kind of pay rise could drag you into a higher tax bracket, or see a greater proportion of your income taxed than would otherwise be expected. Scotland has its own income tax bands.
- How much is the minimum wage going up by? 
  - Published15 hours ago
State pension changes
The triple lock policy means that the state pension will go up in line with average wage increases, at 3.9%.
It means:
- the flat-rate state pension for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 will be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year, up £488 on now
- the old basic state pension for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 will be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, up £374.40 on now
The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension.
The chancellor said this would be the case until at least 2030, as there will be a new Pension Tax Allowance, so pensioners with an income up to the value of the full new state pension will not pay income tax.
First-time buyers
The First Time Buyer Isa has been in the planning stages with the government for a while.
Healey has confirmed that it is intended to replace the often-criticised Lifetime Isa.
The penalty for withdrawing savings from a Lifetime Isa if you are buying a home above the £450,000 threshold will be scrapped.
Separately, he confirmed the Your First Home equity scheme to allow first-time buyers in England to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.
Student loans
The government has made no changes to student loan rates - saying only that it is being "kept under review".
There has been some backlash after the previous chancellor froze the repayment threshold for Plan 2 student loans, which were given out for just over a decade in England from 2012.
It means the salary at which borrowers start paying back their loans is due to stay at £29,385 in April and remain there for three years – so graduates start repaying sooner and repay more each month than they would otherwise have done.
What else will affect your money?
Some announcements affecting your finances have already been made by the government.
They include:
- Tariffs removed from 100 food items such as baked beans and garlic, which the government calculates could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June
- Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead. However, this will not come in until 2030
- Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period
- Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that
- The prime minister's plan to reinstate the £2 cap on bus fares in England from January to be in effect throughout 2027. Some cities already have caps, and funding is being given to the devolved nations
description: Changes announced by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget will affect your finances directly. Here's how.

article_title: Will the budget deliver ‘growth in every postcode’?
article_content:
In just two years, there could be dozens of mayors preparing to spend billions of pounds as part of Andy Burnham’s mission to devolve greater powers across England.
Fresh devolution deals could also be in place following negotiations with leaders in Scotland, Wales and possibly Northern Ireland, allowing the prime minister to say at the next election that he has fulfilled a promise to rewire Britain’s political landscape with a view to giving more local control.
This was the message from John Healey’s first budget, which outlined the direction of travel and put in some milestones, including a 2028 commitment to devolve some income tax receipts to mayors of strategic authorities (MSAs). He added the commitment that next year, 20% of business rates revenues will go to mayors.
He told MPs that he was offering mayors 100% of their business rates income by the end of the decade and the ability to tax visitors who stay in hotels and B&Bs in their aream, via a new overnight visitors levy.
It would mean, Healey said: “New powers to the people who know their areas best, not sentimentality but supply-side economics. The biggest wave of devolution in a generation, driving good growth in every postcode delivered to the British people by this Labour government.”
However, Burnham’s signature phrase that he will bring “good growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” will face scrutiny once it becomes clear large parts of the country are excluded.
Manchester, the West Midlands and Liverpool City region head a list of 14 areas already governed by a mayor.
Healey said the 14 were on course to get enhanced deals, while ministers were in the final stages of signing 10 more agreements, creating MSAs for Devon, Plymouth and Torbay; Hertfordshire; Lancashire; Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland; Stoke and Staffordshire; Surrey; Thames Valley (Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Swindon); and Wessex.
Last month, Essex county council leaders agreed to adopt an MSA to secure about £1.2bn of funding over 10 years. Cornwall’s leaders, who secured a special devo deal under the previous Tory government, were at No 10 North last week – the hub of devolution discussions – hammering out an enhanced set of powers matched by extra money.
Yet there is concern that while these areas might come on board before next year, many others will be left out.
Jonathan Carr-West, chief executive of the Local Government Information Unit, a thinktank, said: “A rewired state needs every tier of government to play its part, and it needs every tier of government to be financially resilient.”
In his view, those areas without a mayor, or without a special devo deal like Cornwall, will begin to fall behind the rest, exacerbating regional inequality.
Next month, No 10 is due to publish the much-anticipated Rewiring the State delivery plan, which Burnham has said will contain the thrust of what he wants to achieve as prime minister.
Carr-West said the holes in Healey’s speech will need to be filled in by Burnham if there is to be some clarity about the way forward. “Today’s budget statement puts more, rather than less, pressure on that document,” he said.
One of the major barriers to progress is likely to be the stalled reorganisation of local government in England, which was due to convert county and district councils into a web of unitary authorities. Angela Rayner, the secretary of state for housing, local government and communities, suspended the plan in September.
Unitary authorities will carry out all the roles previously divided between counties and districts, from providing social services and education to overseeing parking and local business licences.
Several county councils have used judicial reviews to challenge the plans, forcing Rayner to rethink.
Kent is an example of an authority that is a long way from having an MSA, after the Reform UK-run county council objected to a government plan for a split into four unitaries. It has gone to court saying Kent should remain as a single entity, much like Cornwall.
Vince Maple, head of Medway council in Kent, accepts the dispute is a barrier to a deal at the moment, but says it was clear from Healey’s speech that local government reorganisation (LGR) will go ahead in some form and devo deals will follow.
“Government has made itself clear that LGR is going ahead. Most people accept it will happen,” he said.
Maple also heads the Key Cities Group of second-tier urban areas, which includes Gloucester, Sunderland and Salford. He said the expansion of MSAs to include a further 10 areas meant the government was getting closer to its “every postcode” target.
“Our members will be part of the conversation now in a way that they weren’t 24 hours ago,” he said.
There is also scepticism that the economic growth Burnham hopes to achieve from devolution may be slow to materialise.
In a judgment on the budget, the consultancy Oxford Economics, said: “A combination of limited detail, unaddressed challenges, and the length of time for any upside to show means that the devolution announcements will not lead us to revising our regional forecasts.”
Burnham will hope that rearranging the structure of local government will be enough at the next election to convince voters that change is beneficial, even if he cannot show a boost to economic growth.

article_title: Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay
article_content:
Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay
- Published
Income tax thresholds, which have been frozen under successive chancellors, will stay at current levels until April 2031 as planned. But after that they are expected to start to rise again with inflation.
John Healey may not have mentioned the end of this policy in his Budget speech - after all, it is still some way off - but according to the documents released by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) the freeze, which has been shaving additional tax off people's take-home pay for the past five years, is scheduled to end.
The proportion of your income that is taken in tax will continue to go up over the next four years in line with decisions made in previous Budgets.
But then the personal allowance - the point at which you start to pay tax - and other thresholds, where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax, will rise again with inflation, meaning you keep more of what you earn.
Freezing thresholds is often dubbed a stealth tax because, unlike raising the headline rates, it is not as obvious on your payslip.
It has been a useful way for chancellors from Rishi Sunak onwards to raise more money to help pay for things like defence, the NHS, schools and support for the sick, disabled and the elderly.
The amount of extra money brought in by freezing tax thresholds has risen steadily every year, and is due to reach £58bn by 2030-31, more than the UK government spends on transport and not far off current defence spending.
Who is affected by frozen thresholds?
They hit you hardest if your income is close to one of the tax thresholds, but anyone who gets a pay rise is affected, as long as you earn enough to pay tax. Only people earning under £12,570 - the personal allowance threshold - pay no income tax.
By 2031 an extra 6.8 million people will be paying tax who wouldn't have if the personal allowance had not been frozen, the OBR calculates.
The state pension is currently just below the personal allowance threshold, and pensioners looked set to be drawn into paying tax from next April, when the basic state pension rises to £13,036.
However, the chancellor is putting in place a new separate Pension Tax Allowance, which will ensure that low-income pensioners, with income up to the value of the full new state pension, will not pay income tax.
The personal allowance threshold is set for the whole UK, so people in Scotland will also be affected, although other tax bands there vary, external.
National Insurance Contributions (Nics) are levied according to the same thresholds.
- Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you 
  - Published13 hours ago
- Budget 2026: Key points at a glance 
  - Published13 hours ago
How does it work?
Wages usually go up year-on-year to cover the rising cost of living. Normally tax thresholds would also be raised in line with rising prices. Currently that isn't happening - the thresholds have been "frozen" at 2021 levels.
So, as your pay rises, a bigger proportion of it ends up above the threshold where you start to pay tax.
If the personal allowance had risen with inflation over the last five years, you would now be able to take home the first £16,070 of your salary without paying any income tax. Instead you pay 20% on anything you earn above £12,570.
Will I pay the higher rate?
As incomes rise, frozen thresholds also mean more and more people are dragged into the higher, 40%, tax bracket.
An extra 5.4 million will be higher rate taxpayers by 2031, thanks to the freeze, according to the OBR.
If thresholds had risen with inflation you would have had to be earning £64,470 this year before you tipped into the higher tax bracket.
As it is, with thresholds frozen at 2021 levels, you pay the higher rate on anything you earn over £50,271.
If you were already earning more than the threshold and you get a pay rise, a bigger proportion of your earnings will be taxed at the higher rate.
Almost one in four taxpayers will pay some of their tax at the higher rate by 2031, according to the government's official forecaster.
The same principle - that rising income can push you into a new tax bracket - applies to the additional, 45%, rate that is charged on a person's income over £125,140.
Will I be better off after 2031?
Wages have risen sharply to keep up with inflation in recent years, making the impact of the first five years of this policy quite noticeable, and that is set to continue.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) says if Healey had unfrozen the personal allowance this week, instead of keeping it in place until 2031, basic rate taxpayers would have saved up to £198 in tax a year.
Higher rate taxpayers would save £395 a year.
However, for people in the middle of the earnings range, a cut to Nics introduced in 2024 has offset the higher income tax bill.
How much of a difference "unfreezing" thresholds will make in four years' time depends on how fast wages are going up at that point.
There is no fundamental principle at stake, no point that is the "right" level for tax thresholds. Before the financial crisis the personal allowance was much smaller than today, and it was allowed to grow until the pandemic hit. Even in 2031 you'll be able to take home a bigger proportion of your earnings before income tax than you could back in 2008.
description: The point at which you start to pay tax, and the point where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax have been frozen for three more years.

article_title: ‘There has to be a bolder shift’: retail and hospitality businesses assess relief in budget
article_content:
“It is like letting the tyres down and then handing you a pump,” says James Nye, assessing the relief handed to businesses in John Healey’s first budget as chancellor.
The managing director of Norfolk’s Anglian Country Inns argues that the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but added more labour costs for already burdened companies.
Nye, who employs 500 people at the height of the season at its 10 venues across Norfolk and Hertfordshire, was among those business owners watching Healey carefully on Wednesday, after two previous Labour budgets under Rachel Reeves had loaded extra costs on to businesses.
Healey aimed to help high street operators by removing the business rates burden from more small businesses and limiting the rise in the minimum wage for younger workers.
The chancellor put a lid on increases to business rates, so they will only rise in line with inflation for two years, and clamped down on VAT dodging by online sellers, among other measures intended to help high streets. However, some businesses argued Andy Burnham’s chancellor could have gone further.
Pets Corner, family-owned retailer
Dean Richmond, the owner of the Pets Corner chain, says the chancellor has not fixed the “fundamental problem” that its costs are rising faster than it can increase sales.
The family-owned business, founded by Richmond’s parents in 1968, now employs 1,200 people and has 159 stores. He does not expect to get much benefit from the increase in the threshold at which business rates begin to be paid.
“It’s a bit ‘moving the deckchairs on the Titanic’ on rates. There has to be a bolder shift if the government is going to help offline retail,” Richmond says.
He welcomed the move to ensure that online marketplaces such as Amazon collect VAT from more sellers, but was disappointed that Healey did not bring forward the end of tax breaks for online sellers, such as Shein and Temu, importing cheaper items from overseas.
“It feels like the world’s against us. When offline retailers all but disappear the world will miss us,” he says.
While he says Reeves’s budgets had been “really damaging, this is safe but isn’t going to change anything”.
“It is not a good news budget with the minimum wage going up,” he says, on top of the previous changes to employers’ national insurance contributions (NICs) and big increases in the minimum wage for employers.
Richmond says the business, based in Crawley in Sussex, had been forced to make “pretty drastic cuts” to the number of people it employed and to reduce bonus incentives, and had shifted to hiring older, more experienced people as there was less incentive to hire new starters.
Herdy, independent retailer and brand
Spencer Hannah is the co-founder and owner of Herdy, which has five shops in Cumbria and sells its cartoon sheep-branded homewares and clothing online and to other retailers in the UK and overseas.
“The chancellor’s key narrative was that he wanted to support British businesses doing business with Britain and we applaud and support that,” says Hannah, whose business employs 28 people directly.
But Hannah says the budget lacked the “seismic difference” to help UK retailers and their local suppliers. He welcomed relief on business rates for smaller shops but says that was “not counterbalancing what’s happened in the last two years”.
“Like everybody else running small and medium-sized enterprises, life has got slowly harder over the last two budgets and some poor choices have been made by the [last] leadership in government.”
He says increases in national insurance contributions, the minimum wage and other costs such as rent and energy have weighed on the business directly, but the “most frustrating thing” has been the impact of the higher costs for his domestic suppliers. He has been forced to ditch some of them, such as its mug manufacturer in Stoke, and look abroad.
Anglian Country Inns, pub and hotel operator
Nye says the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but against a very tough backdrop.
He welcomes help on business rates for smaller venues but says this is unlikely to assist Anglian directly. He was disappointed that the chancellor had yet again put up the legal minimum wage from April, which will more than offset the rates change for most.
A failure to cut VAT for hospitality businesses or cut national insurance contributions for younger workers were further disappointments.
Nye hopes that Healey’s support for household energy bills “might help consumer confidence”, but added: “We were expecting a little bit more to offset the massive tax increases hospitality has faced.”
“We are being crippled by taxes as a sector and the cumulative tax burden is horrific. We pay 83% as a percentage of our profits in tax,” Nye says.
“I don’t mind paying people more, but we’re then being taxed on it because the NICs threshold hasn’t changed, and the rate of NICs has gone up, so every time that the national minimum wage goes up, we’re paying more and more in tax.
“The cost of going out is getting more and more expensive. My biggest fear is that hospitality starts becoming a luxury rather than a convenience.”

article_title: Путин хотел, чтобы Мелания Трамп выступила посредником в переговорах о перемирии в Олешках — The Kyiv Independent
article_content:
Российский диктатор Владимир Путин «очень хотел», чтобы первая леди США Мелания Трамп выступила посредницей в перемирии в Олешках, заявил её старший советник Марк Бекман. По его словам, Путин направил официальное письмо о признании её эксклюзивным посредником от России. Об этом сообщило издание The Kyiv Independent.
По словам Бекмана, Путин стремился к участию Мелании Трамп в переговорах и письменно согласился признать её эксклюзивным посредником от Москвы. Ранее советник также рассказывал о письменных полномочиях, которые она получила от руководства обеих стран.
Он заявил, что российские военные якобы предложили начать перемирие на два дня раньше и распространить его за пределы Олешок на другие части Херсонской области. Это должно было облегчить доставку гуманитарной помощи и подготовку к эвакуации. Украина согласилась на это предложение. Бекман назвал эти изменения проявлением доброй воли.
«Их действия в конечном счете говорят сами за себя. То, что мы видели до сих пор, — это огромное сотрудничество с обеих сторон», — сказал он.
Бывший военный атташе Великобритании в Киеве и Москве Джон Форман высказал иную оценку мотивов России. По его мнению, Москва действует расчетливо. Позволяя Мелании Трамп получить заслугу за перемирие, Россия укрепляет свой образ миротворца среди сторонников движения MAGA перед промежуточными выборами в США.
До полномасштабной войны в Олешках проживало около 24 тысяч человек. Город расположен на противоположном от Херсона берегу Днепра и оккупирован российскими войсками с начала вторжения. Российские силы фактически блокировали его и препятствовали поступлению гуманитарной помощи.
Белый дом объявил о достижении договоренности при посредничестве Мелании Трамп 23 октября. Вскоре её подтвердили Украина и Россия. По состоянию на 28 октября перемирие продолжалось второй день. Ожидается, что оно будет действовать до начала ноября, пока в город будут доставлять помощь, разминировать ключевые дороги и проводить эвакуацию.
Договоренности предшествовало международное внимание к положению гражданского населения в оккупированном городе. В октябре Папа Римский Лев XIV позвонил Путину и попросил согласиться на прекращение огня. В ответ Путин возложил ответственность за ситуацию на Украину. По словам Бекмана, сторонам не удалось привлечь к посредничеству Ватикан, ООН и Красный Крест.
Украинские власти предупредили, что Россия может использовать эвакуацию в пропагандистских целях. Президент Владимир Зеленский 25 октября выразил опасения, что российская сторона будет пытаться разминировать дороги так, чтобы люди уехали в Россию и остались там. Министр иностранных дел Андрей Сибига предупредил о подготовке десятков постановочных видео.
«Ключевые российские медиадеятели уже начинают распространять нарратив о том, что Россия «спасает» жителей, которых она терроризировала», — обратил внимание на пропагандистские риски исполнительный редактор The Reckoning Project Питер Померанцев.
Бекман сообщил 28 октября, что ожидает прибытия уполномоченного Верховной Рады Украины по правам человека Дмитрия Лубинца в Олешки в течение следующих 36 часов. По его словам, омбудсман должен возглавить работу украинской стороны на месте.
Советник рассказал, что представители Украины и России лично встретились в Беларуси для подписания соглашения о прекращении огня. Обе стороны независимо друг от друга попросили его не разглашать часть договоренностей из-за конфиденциальности информации. Бекман отказался раскрывать эти подробности, сославшись на их просьбу о конфиденциальности.
Напомним, что Украина и Россия поддержали гуманитарную инициативу Мелании Трамп о временном прекращении боевых действий в Олешках в Херсонской области. Договоренностям предшествовали закрытые консультации первой леди США с представителями обеих стран, занимающимися гражданскими вопросами. Стороны также выразили готовность возобновить мирные переговоры при посредничестве Вашингтона.
Кроме того, уполномоченный Верховной Рады Украины по правам человека Дмитрий Лубинец сообщил о разминировании маршрутов для гуманитарной миссии в Олешках. Их готовят для безопасной доставки помощи и дальнейшего выезда гражданских лиц, желающих покинуть город. Подготовку миссии он продолжает совместно с российским уполномоченным по правам человека Яной Лантратовой. Работа ведется при посредничестве и координации первой леди США Мелании Трамп.

article_title: New book makes fiery claims about Jared Kushner’s finances in Trump’s first term
article_content:
A new book containing incendiary claims about Jared Kushner’s financial dealings during Donald Trump’s first term has ignited a political and media firestorm.
The book by author Matthew Cole is called Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East and was released in the US this week. An excerpt was published by Vanity Fair last Thursday, and immediately drew a furious response from Kushner, who called its claims “completely insane”. The book contains numerous allegations about Kushner, whose father-in-law is Trump and who has served as one of his top diplomatic envoys in the Middle East – the most explosive of which are claims linking him to huge bank accounts allegedly funded by Gulf states.
Kusher denounced the book on his site last week, and writing on X: “We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them.” He has demanded that Vanity Fair retract the excerpt and has threatened legal action against the book’s publisher, Simon & Schuster.
He added: “During the period in question, I was one of the most scrutinized people in the world, subjected to intense media coverage, multiple congressional investigations, and a special counsel investigation. I voluntarily cooperated with these investigations, providing over 30 hours of testimony. None of these allegations ever surfaced, because none of these events ever happened.”
The Guardian contacted Kushner’s legal counsel from Clare Locke as well as Chad Mizelle for comment and received no response.
Cole’s sources are predominantly anonymous and he does not print images of emails or other documentation to support his reporting. Extensive footnotes indicate sources of information, including confidential interviews.
In the book, the top intelligence official in the United Arab Emirates, Ali Al Shamsi, is reported to have called Kushner “the most expensive employee we’ve ever had”. The book details alleged payments into two “slush fund” bank accounts allegedly set up for Kushner by Emirati prince Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) and Saudi Arabian prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) during Trump’s first term. The Guardian contacted the Saudi Arabian and Emirati embassies for comment and did not receive a response.
In the book, Cole claims the accounts were partially managed by Kushner on an iPhone hacked by Russian and Dutch intelligence.
But despite the Emirati spymaster’s opinion of Kushner, Cole alleges that the New Jersey real estate scion was not entirely trusted. Cole describes a dangerous world in which blackmail is as common a tool of statecraft as torture and murder, as in the cases of the Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, killed on the orders of MBS in Turkey in 2018, and the Emirati journalist and poet Habib Al Sayegh, whose killing by agents of MBZ in 2019 is described by Cole.
Kushner continues to steer US foreign policy despite having no official role, with questions about his business interests accompanying him as he travels the world with New York real estate magnate Steve Witkoff, this week seeking peace in Ukraine, if on terms favorable to Russia.
In response, an attorney “who has represented President Trump in multiple defamation lawsuits”, Alejandro Brito, told Cole that, “during his time working for President Trump, Kushner ‘always represented and sought the interests of the United States and the President of the United States and did not make any agreements or arrangements with leaders or officials in foreign countries that were not agreed by the President of the United States and in the best interests of the United States.’” He further said that “[a]ny allegation that Kushner knew of, had access to, had authorization for or engaged in or directed any conduct related to any government-funded or government-linked bank account is totally false and defamatory”.
Brito told Cole that “‘there are no accounts and never were.’” Cole writes that the Dutch government refused to comment in response to his questions about the alleged hacking of Kushner’s phone.
According to Cole, MBZ and MBS wanted Kushner to help achieve their “vision of a new Middle East, one in which Israel would become an integral part of the region, recognized diplomatically by Gulf Arabs today and eventually by the rest of the Arab world; the Palestinians would end their conflict with Israel and accept a peace built on prosperity; Islamic extremism would be defeated; and Iran’s expansionism and militancy would retreat, either by persuasion or force.”
Nearly 10 years later, the US and Israel are planning new strikes in their eight-month war with Iran; Saudi Arabia is at war with Houthi rebels in Yemen, and Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023.
Kushner entered Trump’s first administration with his wife, Ivanka Trump, as close presidential advisers. MBZ and MBS, Cole claims, saw a chance to secure the best access money could buy. Cole alleges that in early 2017 the two princes “proposed to give Kushner a fund, a bank account, which the two leaders, working with Jared, would use to identify and pay for projects and foreign policy goals to advance for President Trump’s benefit”.
According to Cole, an idea to fund Trump’s proposed wall on the US border with Mexico apparently did not work out but the author claims that “MBZ and MBS initially, and then MBZ alone, put at least $2bn into at least two banks for Kushner.” Classifying the accounts as “Alpha” and “Beta”, Cole claims the Alpha account was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest in UAE, and contained “roughly $750m” to be “used as a foreign policy fund” overseen by Kushner and MBZ and meant to help end the Israel-Palestine conflict.
Cole quotes a source who says he knew of the UAE’s alleged deal with Kushner as saying: “‘Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy.’” Cole writes: “This person held discussions with both senior UAE and Israeli officials about the secret financial arrangement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia. ‘Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off,’” the source alleged.
The same source claimed that “a slush fund – a shared pool of money for off-the-books diplomatic objectives – was a common form of Gulf Arab government corruption … ‘The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.’”
Citing “a person briefed on the Beta account”, Cole claims it contained “roughly $1bn” and at the suggestion of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was moved by MBZ to the Israeli Central Bank via Azerbaijan, a favored conduit for laundering money.
“It is … unclear how Kushner used the money the UAE deposited into the Beta account for him,” Cole alleges, “but according to the person with knowledge of the money, its allocation was for Kushner’s personal benefit.”
Kushner’s attorney, Brito, told Cole his client “had no financial relationships with any foreign countries or leaders”, adding that his “complete financial disclosures are publicly available in his OGE [office of government ethics] form 278e filings during this period.”
Cole alleges that the “Alpha” account established for Kushner in Trump’s first term was drained by failed schemes and Kushner’s access was cut off. “It is unclear if the Israeli government allowed Kushner access to the Beta bank account” after the end of Trump’s first term, Cole writes.
Cole also examines the widely reported story about how Kushner ultimately secured Qatari investment in 666 Fifth Avenue, a marquee Manhattan property, thereby profiting from interests on both sides of a bitterly divided Middle East, given Saudi Arabia and UAE’s rivalry with Qatar. (Kushner has denied engaging in any conflicts of interest.)
In Trump’s second term, Kushner’s diplomatic work has been dogged by questions about another massive financial asset: a $2bn investment by the Saudi sovereign wealth fund in Kushner’s Affinity Partners private equity firm, made after Trump left power in 2021. Cole quotes an unnamed Arab official and Affinity investor who claimed: “We don’t pay Jared because he’s a savvy investor. We pay him to keep him happy. That keeps his father-in-law happy.”
Cole writes: “Deep relationships with MBZ, MBS, Emir Al Thani [of Qatar], and Bibi Netanyahu were useful as [Kushner] shuttled between capitals, trying to find a way to end the daily slaughter in Gaza. But as it had been when he was a government employee, there was little record of what his investors were negotiating with him.”
In his epilogue, Cole writes that Kushner “declined multiple requests for an on-the-record interview for the book”, adding that he “first contacted him with a list of questions in May 2026 and followed up via email twice more, asking additional questions.”
Through his lawyers, Kushner denounced all of Cole’s reporting. Also on X, Chad Mizelle, a Trump administration lawyer who identified himself as “Jared’s attorney”, said: “The central allegation in this book is categorically false. These are not questions of interpretation or competing recollections: there are no bank accounts. They don’t exist. These are egregious and defamatory claims without a shred of evidence to substantiate them.”
