article_title: Lib Dems and Reform UK in war of words over alleged shove
article_content:
Lib Dems and Reform UK in war of words over alleged shove
- Published
A war of words has broken out between Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage over an alleged physical altercation in the House of Commons.
The row was triggered when Farage, explaining why he had not attended Wednesday's Budget, said he had been involved in a "physical altercation" with another MP at the State Opening of Parliament in May and had wanted to avoid a similar incident.
Voaden revealed herself to be the MP Farage had been referring to, writing on social media that she had been left "shocked and bloody angry" by the confrontation.
The Lib Dems have claimed that Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accused the party of "lying".
The Reform insider added: "The Lib Dems were claiming Nigel shoved her and that she was shaken, the video disproves that clearly."
Footage, first unearthed by the Daily Telegraph, shows the pair leaving the chamber together at the state opening of Parliament but there is no visible evidence of a major altercation.
However, Voaden has said the incident between herself and Farage was not shown in the clip originally posted by the Telegraph, external.
The incident does not appear to have been captured on the official feed of the state opening provided by Parliament.
Voaden said Farage had been ordered to apologise to her after she complained to Commons authorities. The House of Commons would not comment on this.
In a statement, Voaden said: "The truth is that on the day of the King's Speech, Farage missed his chance to process with the other party leaders to the Lords, and rather than queue with the rest of us, he shoved me out of the way to barge past.
"Such behaviour is unacceptable in any workplace, and it has no place in the House of Commons.
"Shoving a colleague out of the way on a staircase just shows the complete disdain he has for Parliament and for other MPs."
Asked about the incident on Sky News, Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "My understanding - I didn't see it, I wasn't there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that."
Reform MP Robert Jenrick told Sky: "I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates."
The issue has only now emerged, nearly six months after the alleged incident, because Farage was pressed on why he had not been in the House of Commons chamber for the Budget on Wednesday.
In response he said: "At the State Opening of Parliament, I got involved… I didn't want to… but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber.
"I didn't make a fuss about it, I didn't complain, but I could see given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation.
A spokesperson for the House of Commons said that a prayer card for Farage - the way in which MPs reserve seats in the Commons - did not "display a valid date stamp" and therefore "was removed in line with the usual Chamber protocol".

article_title: Cuts like a knife: Canadian rocker Bryan Adams trolls Trump with new song
article_content:
Lake Ontario, the vast body of water that straddles the US-Canada border, has gone by many names over the centuries: Lac Saint-Louis, Lacus Ontarius, Skaniadorio, Cataraqui Lake. But one thing it will never be called, says the Canadian rock star Bryan Adams, is Lake America.
In his new song Lake Ontario, Adams takes aim at the US president, Donald Trump, accusing him of “breaking the peace” between the people who live on the lake’s shores.
Trump signed an executive order in August directing US federal agencies to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”, echoing his earlier, widely mocked decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico “the Gulf of America”.
The move further escalated a feud with Canada that has strained the longstanding alliance between the two countries. Trump’s decision has largely been met with derision in Canada, with some pointing out that the province of Ontario is named after the lake, not the other way around. Adams’s lyrics emphasise the roots of the name:
 The ‘lake of shining waters’ is what the Iroquois called her
It’s a First Nations name – not an executive order.
Adams’s lyrics also suggest that Trump’s naming stunt was intended to deflect from the president’s other political problems, including the war in Iran and renewed scrutiny of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
 But things weren’t going his way in Iran
So like a baby tossing the toys from the pram
But it feels like another distraction
While the Epstein files were getting traction
The song is part of what Adams described in a recent interview as a broader “love letter” to Canada: a songwriting project that began with an invitation from a film company to write about the Maritimes provinces of Canada and has since morphed into the upcoming album How’s It Goin’.
“After finishing the first song, I moved on to that one, and then moved on to another one, and then started thinking maybe I should just carry on with my theme,” he said.
As well as homages to Canadian heroes, the album also includes 51st State, released on 1 July – Canada Day – as another repudiation of Trump, in this case his efforts to annex Canada.
 You can push us to the brink
But where the open road divides
You’ll find a wall of maple
With us on the other side.
The first time he played the song in public was in the US.
“We weren’t sure how people were going to respond to it,” he said. “But we got a standing ovation every night for it. It made me think: perhaps, finally, the tide’s turning.”

article_title: UK politics: Burnham denies preventing ministers from speaking about plans for closer relationship with EU – as it happened
article_content:
Burnham insists letter telling ministers not to argue for specific UK-EU renegotiation outcomes doesn't mean they're gagged
Andy Burnham has rejected claims that he has stopped ministers speaking out about his plans for a closer relationship with Europe.
As mentioned earlier (see 12.14pm), Burnham wrote to ministers yesterday saying he does not want them to “advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process” as he opens a debate on forming a closer relationship with the EU. At GB News, this has been written up under the headline: “Andy Burnham gags Cabinet on rejoin EU plot”.
Asked if he was preventing ministers from speaking out in his pooled interview with broadcasters today, Burnham replied:
Not in the slightest. I have been working with the cabinet on the approach that we’re taking to Europe, and we have a clear approach now as we go into the next UK-EU summit, which is three weeks away.
For the record, this is what Burnham said in the letter sent to cabinet ministers yesterday.
I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain. It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration.
It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum.
Burnham said that at the UK-EU summit on 20 November he wanted to lock in deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. But he said he would also set out the next steps for considering the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU. He went on:
Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality.
I am also clear that any fundamental change to the direction of the relationship would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament.
Burnham said there was an “agreed mandate” in government for the summit. He went on:
In the period beyond the summit, government policy will be to explore options for the long-term relationship with the EU for consideration in the next parliament.
At the end of this process, we will set out to the country the respective merits and drawbacks of the various options.
It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period.
It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.
Streeting says Labour committee chair's criticism of defence spending in budget 'completely unfounded'
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has criticised the senior Labour MP Tan Dhesi for saying the government is not raising military spending quickly enough.
Dhesi is chair of the Commons defence committee and yesterday, in his capacity as committee chair, he issued a statement about the budget saying:
The defence committee is pleased that the defence investment plan has been fully funded in the budget, but we had hoped to see the chancellor set out a precise pathway to spending 3% - and eventually 3.5% - of GDP on defence. Instead, some of the key decisions on defence spending have lamentably been delayed until next year’s spending review.
There is a cost to inaction. Investment in our nation’s defence and security cannot be kicked into the long grass. Our adversaries are not bound by fiscal years and spending cycles. We need to urgently rebuild our capabilities now, or we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict.
Speaking in the Commons during the budget, Streeting referred to this statement saying:
I think that is completely unfounded criticism … It would be fair criticism if this government had not already made decisions that is leading to the fastest increase in defence spending since the end of the Cold War. Not in future years, already, on the basis of our first two years.
But Streeting also insisted Dhesi was “a good friend”.
Healey (66) says he does not expect UK to rejoin EU in his lifetime
Last year Andy Burnham told a Guardian podcast that he hopes to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime. He is currently 56, and he has recently said that he stands by this comment – although he has also stressed that this does not necessarily mean that he expects his proposed debate on a closer relationship with the EU to result in a proposal to rejoin after the election.
In his interview on Channel 4 News, John Healey, the chancellor, was also asked if he wanted Britain to rejoin in his lifetime. He replied:
I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that …
I expect, and my job is to try and make the most of Britain’s position now.
Healey confirms government not committed to bring down welfare bill before next election
John Healey, the chancellor, has now personally clarified that the government is not committed to bringing down the welfare bill before the next election. He did so in an interview with Channel 4 News, revising a message he gave out with an ambiguous answer in an interview with the Today programme. (See 9.23am.)
Asked if he was committed to reducing the welfare bill this parliament, he replied:
We’re certainly committed to bringing the cost of the welfare bill down. I’ve said that, the prime minister’s said that. It is not correct to say that we set any schedule or time limit for that.
Asked if that meant it would not come down this parliament, he replied:
It’s not correct to say that we’re going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.
Channel 4 News sent out a press release with the transcript headlined: “John Healey tells Krishnan Guru-Murthy Labour will not bring welfare bill down in this Parliament”. Healey’s not having much luck with media today because this does not seem 100% accurate either. He is saying the government has not committed to bringing the welfare bill down this parliament. But that is not the same as saying the government has committed to not bringing it down. In practice, given the circumstances and what Healey and Andy Burnham are saying, it seems very unlikely that welfare spending will fall this parliament. The press release headline is a bit misleading because it implies Healey has actually ruled that out as an option.
Councils complain they've been left 'frustrated' as latest local government reorganisation update leaves many still in limbo
Patrick Butler
Patrick Butler is the Guardian’s social policy editor.
One of the government’s arguably most unloved policies – the biggest reform of local government for 50 years – continues to stumble on, with few signs that the rancour and confusion surrounding the project is dissipating.
The process started nearly two years ago, with proposals to abolish the current two-tier system of districts and counties in favour of a smaller number of unitary authorities – or “mega-councils” – covering large areas.
Plans juddered to a temporary halt in September amid legal challenges from several councils, including Reform-led Kent, Essex, and Lancashire. Ministers said a short internal review was needed to reassess merger decisions.
The outcome of that review was announced today. (See 3.20pm.) Local government minister Jim McMahon said merger decisions already made in 13 areas would be withdrawn and “reconsidered” – plunging the project into another period of uncertainty. There are another two areas were decisions are still being awaited.
The frustration across local government, which has never shown huge appetite for what it sees as a costly and time-intensive reorganisation agenda, was palpable.
Jonathan Carr West of the Local Government Information Unit said:
Councils in all of those 15 areas have put serious time, money and goodwill into this process, at government’s urging. All that effort feels in jeopardy … That is a fragile basis for a national reform programme.
Ministers insist that withdrawing those decisions does not mean the process has been abandoned. It says fresh decisions will have been made by early next year in all areas, and the new councils will be up and running by 2029.
But many councils remain unconvinced. Richard Wright, chair of the Local Councils Network, said:
Unfortunately, with some councils threatening legal challenges, even final decisions from government may not be the end of the process, so uncertainty is likely to continue for a while.
And Eamonn O’Brien, chair of the Local Government Association, said:
While today’s announcement provides some certainty for some areas, many councils remain frustrated by the situation they have been placed in. All councils affected need urgent clarity on next steps and how costs already incurred will be met.
Shadow communities secretary Katie Lam branded the government’s approach to local reorganisation “nothing short of a farce” and “a complete joke”.
Areas where plans will be reconsidered are: Derbyshire and Derby; Devon, Plymouth and Torbay; Hertfordshire; Kent and Medway; Lancashire, Blackburn with Darwen and Blackpool; Leicestershire, Leicester, and Rutland; Lincolnshire, North Lincolnshire and North East Lincolnshire; Nottinghamshire and Nottingham; Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent; Essex, Southend on Sea and Thurrock; Hampshire, Isle of Wight, Portsmouth and Southampton; Norfolk; Suffolk.
Areas where reorganisation is going ahead: Surrey; East Sussex and Brighton and Hove; GLoucestershire; Oxfordshire; Warwickshire; Worcestershire.
Decisions are awaited in: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough; West Sussex.
NI's first minister says she's been blocked from summit with PM after Drumcree row provokes DUP into using veto
Andy Burnham is chairing a national economic council in Glasgow tomorrow. Ministers from the Scottish and Welsh governments will be there, but the Northern Ireland executive will not be represented because of an increasingly acrimonious dispute between Sinn Féin and the DUP.
Emma Little-Pengelly, the DUP deputy first minister, has in effect blocked Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minster, from attending. Under the power-sharing arrangements that apply at Stormont, designed to ensure unionists and nationalists have to govern together, the FM and deputy FM have equal status and Little-Pengelly has exercised her veto over their attendance at the meeting in Glasgow.
In response, O’Neill posted this on social media, accusing Little-Pengelly of a “reactive stunt”.
But Little-Pengelly defended her action, which relates to unionists being furious with O’Neill for supporting the Garvaghy Road residents who blocked an Orange Order parade at Drumcree that had been allowed by the Parades Commission. O’Neill was siding with nationalists objecting to a parade they find intimidating, but unionists argue that she should not have backed an unlawful protest.
The situation surrounding the first minister’s recent conduct remains extremely serious. There is significant anger, hurt and legitimate public discontent arising from her actions. These concerns cannot simply be dismissed or minimised. This is an exceptionally serious matter, particularly given the responsibilities of the office she holds and the importance of public confidence in the rule of law.
Of further concern is the first minister’s continuing refusal to recognise or meaningfully acknowledge the depth and legitimacy of the discontent caused by her behaviour. Her approach has contributed to a significant deterioration in confidence and in the working relationship necessary to discharge the responsibilities of our joint office.
At a news conference today, Gavin Robinson, the DUP leader, backed Little-Pengelly. He said her move showed O’Neill that “law breaking must have consequences”.
Relations between Sinn Féin and the DUP were already extremely strained before Drumcree – seven months into the financial year, the executive still has not passed a budget – and this latest development shows how they are getting ever closer to collapsing entirely.
Nigel Farage accused of shoving female Lib Dem MP in parliament
Nigel Farage has been accused of having shoved a female Liberal Democrat MP earlier this year, after he spoke about missing this week’s budget because of a previous altercation about seating. Rowena Mason has the story.
Tories dismiss Labour's local government reorganisation as 'nothing short of farce' as 15 areas remain subject to review
The Conservatives have branded the Labour’s local government reorganisation programme “nothing short of a farce”. Speaking in the Commons in response to Jim McMahon’s statement saying some reorganisation projects are going ahead, while 15 are still being reviewed (see 3.20pm), Katie Lam, the shadow communities secretary, said:
It gives me no pleasure whatsoever to say that from start to finish, this government’s approach to local government reorganisation has been nothing short of a farce …
The vast majority of councils are none the wiser after what we have heard today … People across the country are left without any sense of which council will be providing services in the year and years to come, while councillors and council officials have spent millions of pounds of taxpayers’ money planning and preparing for new authorities, which may never materialise.
The money spent on this farcical reorganisation process should have been spent instead on resurfacing roads, collecting bins, and maintaining parks, local government functions that people actually care about.
For all the prime minister’s talk about local government, this whole approach to devolution has shown nothing but contempt for local democracy.
Five counties have had local government reorganisation plans confirmed, MPs told, as others still subject to review
Five counties have had their local government reorganisation plans confirmed, as officials said all regions in England would have final decisions by next year, the Press Assocation reports. PA says:
In a Commons statement, local government minister Jim McMahon said ministers had found the original criteria for the reorganisations was “robust”, after they were reviewed when Andy Burnham became PM.
The changes are part of the government’s flagship local government policy announced by Keir Starmer’s government.
It aims to replace existing two-tier systems of councils with one unitary body that will look after all local services, to streamline decision-making.
The previous proposals were announced by former communities secretary Steve Reed earlier this year, but reviewed by Labour in September.
Eamonn O’Brien, chair of the Local Government Association, said councils were “frustrated” by the process and needed “urgently clarity”.
The five areas where the government is minded to proceed are:
-In East Sussex and Brighton and Hove, the two unitary proposal including boundary changes requested by Brighton and Hove City Council, except for the parish of Falmer.
-The one unitary proposal in Gloucestershire;
-The three unitary proposal in Oxfordshire, including boundary changes.
-The two unitary proposal in Warwickshire;
-The two unitary proposal in Worcestershire.
In another 15 areas, plans are still being reviewed.
Healey says he does not accept joining EU single market would automatically be good for growth
John Healey did not just sound sceptical about rejoining the single market, or the EU proper, in his GB News interview. (See 12.14pm.) In an interview with LBC, he said that he did not accept the growth would automatically be better if the UK were in the single market.
Asked by the presenter, Nick Ferrari, if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU, or the single market, Healey replied:
Well, I don’t actually accept that.
Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union.
The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient. It’s confounded the forecasters.
When it was put to him that being in the single market could boost GDP by 4-5%, Healey said:
Well, that’s part of a bigger conversation that the prime minister wants the country to have because he recognises - and everybody, many other people do – that our Brexit deal was not a good one. It’s not been good for Britain over the last decade.
But my job now is to make sure, when you’re talking about growth, is to try and reinforce that resilience in the British economy.
Most economists believe being in the single market would boost UK growth significantly. But it would also involve aligning with EU regulations and allowing free movement, which Brexiters view as politically unacceptable.
Burnham insists letter telling ministers not to argue for specific UK-EU renegotiation outcomes doesn't mean they're gagged
Andy Burnham has rejected claims that he has stopped ministers speaking out about his plans for a closer relationship with Europe.
As mentioned earlier (see 12.14pm), Burnham wrote to ministers yesterday saying he does not want them to “advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process” as he opens a debate on forming a closer relationship with the EU. At GB News, this has been written up under the headline: “Andy Burnham gags Cabinet on rejoin EU plot”.
Asked if he was preventing ministers from speaking out in his pooled interview with broadcasters today, Burnham replied:
Not in the slightest. I have been working with the cabinet on the approach that we’re taking to Europe, and we have a clear approach now as we go into the next UK-EU summit, which is three weeks away.
For the record, this is what Burnham said in the letter sent to cabinet ministers yesterday.
I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain. It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration.
It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum.
Burnham said that at the UK-EU summit on 20 November he wanted to lock in deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. But he said he would also set out the next steps for considering the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU. He went on:
Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality.
I am also clear that any fundamental change to the direction of the relationship would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament.
Burnham said there was an “agreed mandate” in government for the summit. He went on:
In the period beyond the summit, government policy will be to explore options for the long-term relationship with the EU for consideration in the next parliament.
At the end of this process, we will set out to the country the respective merits and drawbacks of the various options.
It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period.
It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.
Burnham says he's confident economy will go 'from strength to strength'
Andy Burnham has claimed that the British economy is going “from strength to strength”.
Economists have argued that the documents published alongside the budget suggest this parliament will be dire for living standards. (See 10.21am.) But, asked about the country’s economic prospects when speaking to reporters on a visit in Derby, Burnham said:
The British economy is defying the expectations of forecasters, so this year we will grow more strongly. The growth forecast has been upgraded.
The IMF [International Monetary Fund] said last week we’re the standout nation for deficit reduction, so it remains difficult because the world is difficult and the situation in the Middle East has an impact.
But I think people should look at what the chancellor said yesterday, see a country that has got a platform of stability in the economy. We’re beginning to defy those expectations, and I’m confident that we will go from strength to strength from here.
Burnham claims government working 'flat out' to cut welfare spending
Andy Burnham has said the government is working ‘‘flat out” to cut welfare spending.
Speaking to reporters at a Rolls-Royce factory in Derby, when asked if he could confirm what John Healey was reported to have said about planning to cut welfare spending by the next election, Burnham replied:
We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we’re working flat out to that end. Now that we are through the budget, the big next priority in front of us is the publication of the [Alan Milburn report on youth unemployment], long awaited, but it’s coming soon.
We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There’s no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible.
Burnham also argued that “crude cuts” on their own would just leave people “in crisis”, requiring more public spending down the line.
At the Downing Street lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson was also asked if John Healey’s comments about the EU in a GB interview this morning (see 12.14pm) were out of line with Andy Burnham’s. No, was the answer. The spokesperson said:
The position of the government, and the prime minister and the chancellor, is that a stronger relationship with our closest neighbours is in our national interest.
Healey did not say anything that contradicted Burnham’s views on Brexit. But if Burnham had been asked the GB News questions, he would have stressed the problems with the current EU relationship. Healey, instead, said “we’ve got a Brexit decision” and stressed the importance of making the best of the current arrangements.
No 10 confirms government not setting timetable for when it will cut welfare spending
Downing Street has said John Healey was not committing to cutting welfare spending before the general election in his Today programme interview this morning. (See 9.23am.)
Although one answer he gave to a question could be interpreted as saying that, the PM’s spokesperson said that was not Healey’s message. The spokesperson said:
We’ve never set an arbitrary target or timetable [for when the welfare bill starts to fall]. But both the prime minister and the chancellor have been crystal clear that the welfare bill needs to come down, and that we need to do that in a progressive and sustainable way and not through crude cuts which push people into hardship and puts pressure on the system elsewhere.
Asked if Healey mis-spoke in his interview, the spokesperson said:
The chancellor is completely in line with what the PM has said over the last few months that the welfare bill needs to come down and, as I say, we are not setting an arbitrary target or timetable on that.
The spokesperson said the government would be publishing Alan Milburn’s report on youth unemployment and Stephen Timms’ report on the personal independence payment (Pip), and that these would be followed by a white paper on welfare reform published next year. That will be followed by legislation.
Badenoch claims it's 'astounding' Healey won't commit to cutting welfare bill before general election
Kemi Badenoch has described the Treasury clarification that John Healey is not promising to cut the welfare bill before the general election (see 9.23am) as “astounding”. In a response on social media, she said:
This is astounding. The government’s own figures show working-age welfare will go up by £60 BILLION by 2030, yet the Treasury has to rush out and correct the Chancellor to say there is no timetable for cutting the benefits bill. Looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading.
John Healey couldn’t even find £10 billion to get defence spending to 3% of GDP - the thing he quit over.
Don’t let anyone tell you this was a ‘do no harm budget’. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they’ve harmed our national security.

article_title: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
article_content:
'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
- Published
People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.
Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.
Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.
The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.
In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a £100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.
But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said.
"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.
"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.
However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.
- Treasury will not commit to reducing welfare bill before next election 
  - Published19 hours ago
- What we now know about the UK economy in four charts 
  - Published1 day ago
- Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you 
  - Published14 hours ago
In response to this "painful" situation the government had provided a "scattergun" Budget that did not do enough to address the challenges facing the country, Curtice said.
Over the course of this parliament, incomes for non-pensioner households, after taxes, benefits, and housing costs are taken into account, will have risen by "a paltry" £600, the Resolution Foundation said, with the gains "already behind us".
Even after the extra support provided by the government, households will be left paying higher energy bills than during the last energy crisis in 2022, according to its analysis.
The Resolution Foundation said the support should have been more targeted at the poorest households.
Lost decade
Alongside the Budget the OBR issued its economic forecast indicating a slowdown in GDP growth from 1.2% in 2026 to 1% in 2027.
The forecast for next year is sharply lower than what was predicted at their last assessment in March.
The OBR also put its forecast for inflation for 2027 up from 2% to 3.4%.
Frozen tax thresholds are also eating into people's take-home pay.
However, the OBR also emphasised the difficulties in economic forecasting, highlighting uncertainty over the future path of inflation, in particular, which could turn out to be either significantly higher or lower than their predictions.
While the Resolution Foundation focused its forecast for living standards on working age households, the OBR looks at all households, including pensioners and reflects a 10-year rolling average growth to take into account short-term fluctuations.
The OBR found that by the end of the decade living standards for all households would have barely grown, by less than 0.1% per year.
Helen Miller, director of the influential think tank, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the outlook was "depressing".
"This decade looks set to be the worst decade for growth in household incomes on record," she said.
"No amount of temporary cost of living packages will fix that. We need a stronger economy."
'Fragile' finances
There would also be growing pressure on the government's spending plans over the parliament, Miller added.
"Spending plans look extremely tight. They don't look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver," she said.
"Whether or not they are delivered matters because the spending plans underpin the plan to bring down borrowing," she added.
Miller said she was left with the impression that Healey was hoping the economy would improve to take the pressure off those spending decisions.
Healey, speaking on the BBC's Today Programme, said "economic storms", including the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, were affecting countries around the world and the government was seeking to help where it could.
He said energy bill help would create "breathing space" for most households.
Around 20 million households are set to receive the £100 payment based on which council tax band they are in.
But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Budget had left the public finances "more fragile" as Healey had reduced the "headroom" or the buffer that the country has between what it takes in revenues and what it spends.
Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said the £100 energy payment would be identified as the best item in the Budget for many people, but said that it was "not good enough" when you considered the "stealth tax rises" that were taking money out of people's pay packets.

article_title: Eight of England’s nine water companies still failing on environment, report finds
article_content:
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has summoned water industry bosses to Whitehall after a report found that the environmental performance of the big companies has worsened despite investment.
“People are sick of excuses,” Dame Angela said, after the Environment Agency joined the Drinking Water Inspectorate, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat for a joint report that rated eight of the nine water companies in England as “poor” or “requiring improvement”.
There were 74 serious pollution incidents, the category that causes significant harm to the environment, the report said. That was just one fewer than the previous year, despite billions of pounds of investment, bans on bosses’ bonuses and a public outcry. The watchdog’s environmental performance assessment ratings of water companies added up to 16 “stars” out of a possible 36, a fall from 19 the previous year, and the lowest score since the process began.
Changes could be imposed on the industry, Eagle warned: “Water companies have let the public down time and time again, and today’s report is further proof that root-and-branch reform cannot wait.”
The UK is one of only two countries in the world where the provision of water is fully privatised. The other is Chile, where water privatisation was imposed in the 1980s by a military dictatorship.
Overall, there were 2,666 pollution incidents in England in 2025 – a 40% increase on 2016, the EA said. Thames Water had the most, followed by Anglian Water, United Utilities, Yorkshire Water and Southern Water.
The Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Eagle was preparing to take “further action”, with “tougher consequences” for executives at failing companies.
Defra said it would “set out a clear set of improvement actions”, such as “tackling leakage”, “reductions in pollution incidents” and “improving customer satisfaction”. Rules that took effect last year would block bonuses for executives at companies receiving a one-star rating.
Environmental campaigners called for stronger action. “This is a system that rewards shareholders and creditors while our rivers, wildlife and bill payers lose out,” said James Wallace, the chief executive of River Action.
Thames Water, the worst offender, ought to go into special administration immediately, he said. “Ministers must end the failed privatisation experiment, review alternative models including public ownership, and give regulators the power to make polluters pay not the public.”
The four agencies have pooled their data in a joint report for the first time – a step towards combining currently fragmented regulatory responsibilities under a single watchdog. But Richard Benwell, the chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said a new regulator “must be more than a merger of existing institutions”.
“It needs a clear legal duty to restore nature, strong environmental targets and the powers and resources to enforce the law across the water industry, industrial agriculture, and chemical companies,” he said.
Water UK, the industry trade body, said: “Today’s report shows the lowest level of leakage in history, as well as other areas of good performance. However, the fact remains that the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough.
“While more than half of all pollution incidents last year were caused by blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies, there is clearly more work to do.
“It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth and end sewage entering rivers and seas.”

article_title: HMRC puts 200 billionaires on UK tax crackdown hitlist
article_content:
The UK’s tax authority is assigning dedicated “customer compliance managers” to more than 200 billionaires as part of a crackdown meant to raise £500m for the public purse.
HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) said it had for the first time compiled a list of billionaires who are required to pay tax in the UK, regardless of whether they formally live in the country, to tackle a “wealthy tax gap” caused by those who do not pay what they ought.
In an announcement after Wednesday’s budget, the authority said it was allocating a customer compliance manager (CCM) to each billionaire with a UK tax footprint, whose complex tax affairs are often hard for HMRC to manage.
“Billionaires can present a particular example of this, with affairs often spanning multiple taxes, entities and jurisdictions and a greater need for early and coordinated engagement,” HMRC said.
It said the managers would offer voluntary discussions to each billionaire before they filed their taxes, to “help build a shared understanding of the customers’ UK tax affairs and make subsequent engagement more focused and proportionate”.
The authority also plans to start deploying new tech to monitor wealthy individuals – defined as those with income of more than £200,000 or assets over £2m in any of the last three years – involving “advanced analytics, automated triggers and artificial intelligence (AI) to identify emerging risks earlier and target compliance activity where it will have greatest impact”.
It is part of wider efforts to tackle the wealthy tax gap, whereby rich people are failing to pay what they should if all of their assets were disclosed to the tax authority. The wealthy tax gap for 2024-25 was estimated to be worth £3.6bn, equivalent to 6% of the total tax gap across the UK’s entire tax-paying population.
The tax authority said its actions would contribute at least £500m towards a larger commitment to raise £10bn of additional tax revenues by 2030.
HMRC was grilled in July last year by MPs on the parliamentary public accounts committee over its lack of understanding of tax compliance by about 1.3 million wealthy taxpayers.
 
 
 Adam Craggs, the head of tax, investigations and financial crime at the law firm RPC, said anyone with more than £200,000 of annual income, or net assets above £2m, should now “reflect on how clearly they understand and can evidence their UK tax position and their interaction with HMRC”.

article_title: Further delays for major council overhaul in nine of 14 proposed areas
article_content:
Further delays for major council overhaul in nine of 14 proposed areas
- Published
The government has announced further delays to nine of 14 major council mergers, with only five now going ahead.
Proposals for 14 regions to undergo mergers of smaller councils to form larger unitary authorities was put on hold by Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner last month, following concerns around legal challenges.
Local Government Minister Jim McMahon has told MPs the review had found the government's decision-making to be "robust", but nine areas have now been withdrawn for further review.
Only five of the original 14 regions will be taken forward, after three more weeks of consultation. Shadow local government secretary Katie Lam condemned the latest news as "a farce".
Mergers will continue to progress in East Sussex, Gloucestershire, Oxfordshire, Warwickshire and Worcestershire.
But the government is seeking "legal clarity" in the remaining nine areas, which are: Derbyshire, Devon, Hertfordshire, Kent, Lancashire, Leicestershire, Lincolnshire, Nottinghamshire, and Staffordshire.
In a Commons statement, McMahon said the government was "withdrawing the decisions announced in July" for those nine areas.
"I want to be absolutely clear that this is not a reflection of the work underpinning those proposals," he added.
The review will now focus on the nine areas where current plans have been withdrawn for further review, as well as four areas where plans were withdrawn in September, in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.
Two further areas, Cambridgeshire and West Sussex, are still waiting for merger plans to be agreed, totalling 15 regions where local government reorganisation plans remain undecided.
McMahon said: "We will move faster where we can, and some of the remaining areas may receive an outcome decision before others.
"I commit to coming back to the House with updates for another set of areas by Christmas, and every area will have an outcome by early next year."
Reconfirming local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries, he announced plans for elections to shadow councils, set to run for a year before taking over from old authorities, will now be held in May 2028.
Responding, Lam set out how the reorganisation had been beset by delays over the past two-and-a-half years.
"From start to finish this government's approach to local government reorganisation has been nothing short of a farce," she told MPs.
She added: "Naturally the taxpayer was left to pick up the tab for all of these delays - a bill which runs into the tens of millions of pounds."
Local Government Association chair Eamonn O'Brien called for a re-set of relations between the government and local councils across the country.
He said: "While today's announcement provides some certainty for some areas, many councils remain frustrated by the situation they have been placed in.
"All councils affected need urgent clarity on next steps and how costs already incurred will be met.
"There needs to be a reset in the relationship between government and councils on local government reorganisation, with local government fully engaged in shaping decisions from the outset."

article_title: Reform UK launches its own ‘newspaper’ with Farage on front page
article_content:
Reform UK has launched what it is calling a newspaper, featuring large pictures of Nigel Farage, which the party hopes will replace mainstream media for its supporters.
Though the party is hiring qualified journalists to write its newspapers, the only “reporter” credited with writing articles is Farage, the party leader.
Political parties often put out pamphlets made to look like newspapers in local areas during elections, but it is unusual for a party to put out a paper nationally, year-round. The party has said it wishes to build a “significant national publishing operation” as well as its TV channel hosted on YouTube.
In his first column for the publication, Farage writes: “We have had enough of what we say and do being distorted by the media. So instead, we want to talk to you directly, and make sure that you get our message straight from the Reformer.”
Its front-page story features a photograph of Farage smiling and posing with a labrador, with the headline “Nigel Farage: we will fix broken Britain”.
Other stories include “Clacton result: Farage 22,239, Establishment 0.” This refers to the byelection called by Farage after he resigned his Essex seat following revelations about an undeclared £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. The gift was revealed by the Guardian earlier this summer. The other main parties declined to stand in the ensuing byelection, with the result that Farage’s main opponent was Count Binface.
One piece advertises Reform’s plan to use the Royal Navy to send back migrants who travel across the Channel in small boats. It says: “A Reform UK government will launch Operation Fortress. Prime Minister Nigel Farage will order the Royal Navy to stop the boats and return the illegal immigrants to France. Not one will make it to Britain.” Military experts have criticised this plan, saying the navy should not be used as a ferry service.
Other articles include a short tribute to Ann Widdecombe, the Reform politician who was killed in her home in July, featuring a quote from Farage, and another piece by Farage in which he vows to declare a national emergency should he become prime minister. Other features include updates on local Reform politicians’ progress on filling in potholes and picking up litter.
Reform insiders said the first edition was “rushed” and to expect more news and features in subsequent editions, coming monthly.
Roles at the publication are still open, with 12 journalist jobs including executive editor, website editor and multimedia reporters/producers advertised online.
Reform sources said they thought the newspapers, being delivered to homes across Britain and available in the lobby of the party’s Westminster office, would drive up membership rates. Those who join the party using the cut-out form included in the newspaper are offered a free mug and badge.
Rather than being kept on the news stands in the lobby of Millbank Tower, where Reform has its headquarters, the Reformer is kept behind the desk at reception and available on request. The party says the paper has been sent to 15 million people across the country.
Readers of the publication are also urged to sign up as Reform candidates in the May 2027 local elections.
A report by Printweek revealed that the paper has been printed by Walstead Group, which has contracts with several of the UK’s leading newspapers including the Sunday Times and Sun on Sunday.
The paper is reportedly being led by Mick Hume, the founder and former editor of the online libertarian-right politics magazine Spiked, and is part of Reform’s drive to build a “national publishing operation” with a digital newsroom and expanded video content.
Though the first edition of the free paper does not appear to contain any exclusive news stories, budding reporters hoping to join the Reformer need to be able to produce scoops.
A job advert states: “Reform UK is building a seven-day digital newsroom at its Westminster headquarters and is looking for hard-working, NCTJ-qualified multimedia reporter/producers who can report, write and publish high-quality content at speed. The role sits at the heart of the party’s ambition to build the Reform UK website into a significant national publishing operation.”

article_title: Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
article_content:
Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
- Published
Bereaved families will no longer be hit by an unexpected tax bill because of severe delays paying out civil service pensions, following a change in Wednesday's Budget.
Under previous HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments had to be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.
Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.
The government has now changed the rules so payments will no longer become taxable solely because more than two years has passed.
The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.
Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.
Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.
Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.
According to the latest figures up to 30 September, external, 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.
The Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, previously said only a small number of these cases were approaching the two-year threshold.
However the PCS union, which represents civil servants, had warned there were "serious questions" over how long cases would remain unresolved.
- Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says 
  - Published12 February
- Emergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensions 
  - Published29 January
- Retired civil servants left in pension limbo 
  - Published23 January
Rob Wassell, 58, had to wait more than two years following the death of his brother until he finally received the lump sum from his civil service pension on Tuesday.
After his case was highlighted by the BBC last week, Rob says he got a call from the pension scheme's complaints department who told him the payment was on its way.
However, because it was made after two years it was taxed at 45%, amounting to thousands of pounds.
If the payment was made after the rule change, it would not have been subject to tax.
Rob told the BBC he was pleased the government had addressed the issue in the Budget as this would mean others in his situation would not face a tax bill.
While he said he was happy to finally get his payment it was "a bitter pill to swallow" as he is now waiting for the outcome of a complaint review to find out if the tax will be reimbursed.
Rob said he was hopeful he would get the money back, adding: "I don't want to have to fight it anymore, it's been an ordeal already."
Pensions minister Torsten Bell confirmed the rule change in a letter to the chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, external, Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who had raised concerns about the issue after it was highlighted by BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live programme.
Bell said the move would "make the position fairer for all grieving families and friends where there are delays in the payment of death benefits, whether in the Civil Service or any other pensions scheme".
He added: "Removing the tax deadline does not remove [a pension scheme's] wider duties to administer schemes prudently and without avoidable delay."
Under the previous rules, if someone died before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit was only tax-free if it was paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value was below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.
However, the government has now removed the two-year deadline so payments will no longer become taxable solely because they were made more than two years after a pension scheme was notified of the death.
The change applies to payments made from 28 October.
In his letter, the pensions minister said people who had already been impacted by avoidable delays and been taxed as a result could seek compensation through the pension scheme's complaints process and the Pensions Ombudsman.
Sir Geoffrey welcomed the announcement but said it does not "absolve Capita from processing and making payments to members of this scheme in a timely manner".
Fran Heathcote, general secretary of the PCS union, also welcomed the change but said "this situation should never have arisen in the first place".
She added: "Bereaved families must not pay the price for failures in the pension system.
"Capita is not off the hook, it continues to fail members and their families, which is why the scheme must be brought back in-house."
Capita has previously apologised for the impact of delays on pension scheme members and their families.
The company has said it is working to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with a particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging circumstances.

article_title: The Guardian view on a changing Brexit debate: Kemi Badenoch is trapped in denial | Editorial
article_content:
British politics is still polarised around Brexit, although 10 years on from the referendum, the terms of debate are very different. Or they should be. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has moved discussions of European solidarity from the realm of abstraction to a matter of urgent defence partnership. Donald Trump’s presidency in the US, marked by scorn for European democracies and indulgence of Vladimir Putin, has undermined confidence that Britain can rely on any “special relationship” with Washington.
Under these circumstances, it would be absurd to deny that a reappraisal of Brexit is in order. The prime minister acknowledged this in his speech at the Labour party conference last month, calling for a national conversation about the future relationship with every option, including rejoining, on the table. The Eurosceptic opposition are having none of it. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, accuses the government of stirring division by raising the European question. She told MPs this week that Labour should thank the Tories for the Brexit deal they negotiated.
The Tories and Reform UK like to remind Andy Burnham of comments he made when campaigning in Makerfield earlier this year for the seat that became his launchpad to reach No 10. Mr Burnham said that rerunning the old Brexit arguments was “the last thing we should do right now”. That can be made consistent with his current position in the sense that an exact rerun of the 2016 debate would indeed be pointless, which is why something different, more future-facing, is being proposed instead. Mr Burnham’s critics see that as sleight of hand to conceal a flagrant change of line. But the distinction between relitigating outdated arguments and engaging with present realities is a vital one.
The Tory position, shared with Reform, contains no audit of Britain’s foreign and economic policy interests. It is based on ideology and fear of confronting the facts that such an evaluation reveals. Brexit has made Britain poorer and diminished its influence on the world stage. The public know this all too well, as evidenced by opinion polls indicating majority support for a closer EU relationship.
Mrs Badenoch’s position is also disingenuous, given her commitment to pull Britain out of the European convention on human rights. That would pointlessly reopen some of the most fissile Brexit arguments because of the ECHR’s codification in the Good Friday agreement for Northern Ireland.
A phenomenon that Mrs Badenoch and Mr Burnham have observed, but respond to differently, is that voters have no desire for a return to the poisonous political atmosphere of the immediate post-referendum period. The Tory leader uses that aversion to justify her lack of a strategic concept for Britain’s future relationship with its continental neighbours. The prime minister’s approach is to sound ecumenical, saying that he aspires to national consensus on the best way forward, while sounding vague about his personal preferences.
That ambiguity has given the opposition cause to accuse the prime minister of conspiring to undo Brexit, but it has also dissolved some of the taboo around discussion of much closer models of reintegration with the EU, which is a necessary condition for a healthier fact-based debate. That isn’t a conversation the Conservatives want to have, but for the prime minister to share in their denial would be, as he has said, a dereliction of duty.

article_title: MP apologises over bullying and harassment
article_content:
MP apologises over bullying and harassment
- Published
A Labour MP has said sorry in the House of Commons following complaints over his behaviour towards a female member of staff.
It comes as the Independent Expert Panel published a report, external requiring Tony Vaughan to apologise for breaching Parliament's bullying and harassment policy.
The MP for Folkestone and Hythe was found by the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards to have committed the breach after a constituency staff member complained he "behaved towards [her] in an overbearing and belittling manner".
Vaughan said on Thursday he accepted the findings in full.
"As a result of these behaviours, my former colleague was upset and humiliated," he said.
"My behaviour had a real and continuing impact on her and her family, and I am truly sorry for this."
The Labour Party said it "expects the highest standards of conduct from all our members and elected representatives.
"We have robust processes in place to ensure those high standards are upheld.
"It is right that Tony Vaughan has apologised following this independent process," a spokesperson added.
'Abuse of power'
Vaughan, who has represented his Kent constituency since 2024, was found to have hugged the complainant without consent at an office event.
He also took her personal mobile phone from her hand to join an online meeting without asking permission and failed to explain why phone calls between them had ended abruptly.
Vaughan appealed the Commissioner's findings, though the Independent Expert Panel confirmed the majority of them, according to Parliament.
The sub-panel stressed that "oppressive and bullying behaviour towards [MPs'] staff members is wholly unacceptable".
It added that Vaughan's actions were breaches of "basic boundaries and courtesy" - rather than failures in management - and an "abuse of his power".
The politician told MPs on Thursday that he was not "sufficiently alert" to the power imbalances between him and his employee.
He added he recognised his behaviour could well impact on "someone who is vulnerable whether or not that is known".
"I made mistakes," Vaughan continued.
The 36-page report said it took account of the impact of what happened on the complainant, who has a right to anonymity.
She said she was left feeling stressed, exhausted and offended, it adds.
The report also stated that Vaughan had "expressed genuine and thoughtful remorse".
He should be required to make an "unreserved apology" to the complainant and the House by way of a personal statement in the House of Commons Chamber, it continued.
"We consider that this achieves the appropriate balance and clear messaging required regarding the behaviour expected of MPs," the report said.
Vaughan added he had undertaken further training as a result of the incident.

article_title: The Guardian view on online harms: Ofcom is failing at its job | Editorial
article_content:
One thing is clear following last week’s report from the media regulator, Ofcom: the mammoth task of protecting children from online harms has barely begun. Campaigners said that they were dismayed but not surprised that the proportion of children viewing harmful content has stayed the same despite a raft of measures in the Online Safety Act designed to protect them. Research showed that high-priority material including pornography and self-harm, as well as a broader category covering bullying, abuse and the promotion of violence, continued to be encountered regularly in the nine months after new safety duties came into force.
The regulator found that personalised feeds were the main way that such content was presented, and noted that such feeds show different material to boys and girls. Suicide and self-harm content were more commonly seen by girls and children with special educational needs or disabilities. In a grim irony, Ofcom’s report appeared one day after a coroner in Norfolk ruled that suicide imagery viewed on TikTok “may have played a significant part” in the decision by a 14-year-old girl to take her own life in May.
This is a deeply concerning situation. Significant resources went into the UK’s online safety bill on the understanding that, after two decades during which tech companies had been granted extraordinary freedom over the terms of their engagement with citizens, democratic control was being reasserted. Silicon Valley’s reckless disregard of children’s safety and wellbeing convinced the public, and then parliament, that action was needed. Yet three years after the bill passed, Meta, TikTok and X are all engaged in legal challenges against Ofcom and appear to believe that their interests should trump the law.
Andy Burnham’s government needs a step change in how it treats big tech, which currently differs little from its predecessor. Lisa Nandy held on to her job as secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport; a ban on social media accounts for under-16s is due to come into force in spring 2027. Ministers want the UK to take a tougher approach than Australia, a pioneer in preventing online harm, and are looking at proposals requiring photo ID for teens to access sites.
But the new age limit and other safety rules can only work if the regulator is capable of enforcing them. And the Ofcom report was not encouraging. In evidence to MPs about the lack of a “safety culture” at social media companies, Ofcom’s chief executive, Melanie Dawes, sounded far too tentative. Whistleblowers have been making similar points more forcefully for years.
The Online Safety Act was never meant to be a once-and-for-all law. The pace of technological change – above all, the rise of AI – made further legislation inevitable. But searching questions must be asked about a situation in which a new law has led to no benefits at all for the user group – children – that it was designed to protect. As the Guardian has argued previously, ministers should have imposed a duty of care and made businesses accountable for improvements, rather than simply obliging them to follow a code.
Accountability remains too easily evaded at the top of tech. Executives should face a greater risk of criminal penalties for serious failings. Expressions of disappointment are no substitute for action. Regulators and ministers have the powers to secure change. They need to demonstrate an appetite for using them.

article_title: Treasury will not commit to reducing welfare bill before next election
article_content:
Treasury will not commit to reducing welfare bill before next election
- Published
The Treasury is disputing that Chancellor John Healey suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next general election.
When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."
But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election, with one suggesting Healey was explicitly attempting to avoid that impression being left.
This suggests, instead, that ministers are not committed to cutting the benefits bill by the next election.
The chancellor told Today: "I have said clearly and the prime minister has said as well, we have to bring the benefits bill down. You don't do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures."
He said two "big reports" next month would help the government "map out the way that we need to change the system for the long run" and the government has "been reducing the rate of increase in the welfare bill".
Healey said the current system was "unsustainable" and the government had a "moral duty" to help the almost one million young people out of work, education or training.
He said young people would be expected to take up offers of work or training "and that's the way we can take welfare bills down in the long term".
- Budget 2026: Key points at a glance 
  - Published1 day ago
- What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out 
  - Published1 day ago
Asked whether would be cuts in welfare before the next election, the chancellor said: "There will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way and we'll do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progressive to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.
"And I feel a moral duty to deal with these youngsters that have been written off by previous governments."
A review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn will be published in November.
The government is then expected to respond by the end of the year and publish a policy document setting out proposals, and legislation next year.
The Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare", while Reform UK said the Budget did not address the "ballooning" benefits bill. Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year by £19bn to £353bn.
Watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said this figure is expected to rise to £431bn in 2031/32, driven primarily by health-related and pensioner benefit spending.
Of the figure forecast for 2031/32, £209.8bn is on pensioners, including the state pension and winter fuel payments, while £110.7bn is on universal credit and legacy equivalents and £69.6bn is on disability benefits such as personal independence payments.
The government has already pledged to reform the existing state pension triple lock from 2030, and more proposals and changes to the welfare system are expected to emerge in the coming months.
'Out-of-control welfare system'
The chancellor's remarks came after Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch responded to the Budget by saying the benefits bill was "going up by tens of billions of pounds because this government has put welfare first".
She said the country was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed, and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system", adding that the Budget was "not bold enough".
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said welfare reform "needs to be done right", adding this should involve "cutting the bill by helping people into work and giving people the care and support they need so that they can work".
Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, noted the government still has "many difficult decisions" to take after not fleshing out several big issues, including disability benefits and support for young people.

article_title: Hold your nose: a £1.25bn subsidy for rich Rolls-Royce’s new engine had to happen
article_content:
It wasn’t a “nothing” budget for engine-maker Rolls-Royce. The company was handed £1.25bn from public coffers to part-fund the development of a next-generation engine for single-aisle commercial planes.
The chancellor buried this giveaway in two short sentences in the stodgy middle of his speech, presumably because it would look too much like a case of corporate welfare just after he had grumbled about the £14bn extra we’ll be paying in debt interest this year.
And it’s not as if Rolls is on its uppers. The pride of Derby is the UK’s most radically improved major company of the past few years. It sits in fifth spot in the FTSE 100 index, sporting a market value of £105bn, and has enough spare cash to spend up to £9bn on share buy-backs this year.
But there had been an air of inevitability about this subsidy ever since the company’s chief executive, Tufan Erginbilgiç, talked earlier this year about how he would “appreciate” financial support from the government in developing the UltraFan engine. Appreciate? What he meant is that other governments would cough up if the UK didn’t.
That, unfortunately, is how life works in the global aerospace business. Subsidies are a down payment on the jobs and factories that can follow. Germany, reeling from the woes of its carmakers, would love to have a bigger slice of the hi-tech UltraFan action (and has a role in the gearboxes anyway). The US aerospace industry is a study in how generous defence contracts subsidise civil operations. Healey couldn’t ignore those facts of aerospace life.
What’s more, one can see how the possible long-term return on the £1.25bn could turn out very well. “The single biggest opportunity in aerospace over the next 50 years is to secure a UK engine position on next generation narrow body programmes,” said the government’s strategy document for advanced manufacturing. Aircraft engines are high-value products. About 80% would be exported, doing wonders for the national balance of payments. Projections of “tens of thousands of highly skilled jobs” eventually are credible.
The big “if” is that Rolls hasn’t yet got a slot on a narrow-body programme. The company exited that market a couple of decades ago; its civil aircraft side currently only supplies engines to the smaller wide-body long-haul market. Rolls needs to get on to either the Airbus or Boeing narrow-body programmes, and success or failure won’t be known until some time around 2030.
Thus the government is only contributing to a joint 10-year £2.5bn research and development programme, including a “demonstrator” engine to show off the gas turbine tech. There will be spillover benefits for defence capability but, ultimately, UltraFan needs to be on a civil project. It is a big bet – and Rolls, even if it wins, will need a corporate partner at a later stage.
The point, though, is that the UK government had to get behind the UK runner in this race. One trusts the guarantees on UK jobs and investment, beyond the 3,300 roles supported initially, will be written in triplicate in the final agreement. That must be a fundamental condition of support on this scale.
But this is an occasion to hold your nose. Rolls is plainly not a corporate pauper but, yes, it is justifiable to shove £1.25bn its way. Andy Burnham’s “reindustrialisation” talk would otherwise ring very hollow.

article_title: The ‘breathing space budget’ – breathing space for the government, that is | John Crace
article_content:
Maybe it had been one of the greatest acts of political genius after all. The day after the budget is usually the moment when things start to fall apart. When clued-up journalists and economists have had a chance to go through all the fine points the chancellor would rather everyone had missed. The forecasts that suggest everything is predicated on a wing and a prayer. The hidden unfunded tax cuts. The greater-than-expected spending commitments.
But on Thursday morning Andy Burnham and John Healey could afford themselves a sigh of relief. All had gone about as well as they could have hoped. It turns out that when you don’t make any massive tax or spending commitments, there isn’t a great deal to unravel. All there had been was a raft of small-scale interventions designed to help people with their personal finances. Call it the Martin Lewis budget. In fact, Healey and Lewis now seem unable to get through the day without spending some time with each other. They certainly can’t stop talking about one another. It’s becoming unhealthily co-dependent. The gods of small things.
It had been billed as the “breathing space” budget. A budget to help get everyone through the coming year more or less alive. No hiding under tables or breaking open the emergency supplies of baked beans. Apocalypse averted. But the breathing space might just as well have been for the government. Difficult decisions delayed. Hope that we all wake up in 52 weeks’ time and the world looks like a less frightening place. And even if it doesn’t, it will always have had a year’s grace. A chance for the Tories and Reform to implode. You can always hope.
Come the traditional morning-after interview with the chancellor on the Today programme, the presenter Nick Robinson seemed uncharacteristically subdued. Normally he’s a terrier on occasions like these. There’s never been a budget that Nick wouldn’t have been able to do far better himself. But this one? This one was something you might find on the consumer affairs programme, You and Yours. And the BBC was in the process of axing that.
So the 20 minutes passed with little fuss. More a softball back and forth. Healey started with his usual infectious brand of pessimism. He was born to be the bearer of bad news. The poster boy for assisted dying. Everything was absolutely terrible. He wasn’t quite sure why anyone was still bothering with anything. If it had been up to him he would have ended the interview before it had started. There was nothing to say. Other than that, given the chance, he wouldn’t have started from here. Brexit, the pandemic, Ukraine, Iran, energy prices. The world was screwed. Britain was screwed. Lie back and prepare for the worst 10 years of your already miserable life.
Nick tried to find a reason to believe. Couldn’t the chancellor have made just a little more effort? Having a plan to have a plan wasn’t the usual budget fare. Healey, AKA Dr Death, shrugged. It was one up on having a plan to not have a plan. By now Robbo was audibly struggling. How could he put it politely? In the third year of a government with a 160-seat majority, surely Healey could have been a little more ambitious. This wasn’t exactly the big transformation that had been promised.
Could he even say if he would bring down the benefits bill? Apparently he could. “There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Dr Death. Cue panic stations in the Treasury. Within seconds of Healey opening his mouth, dozens of government spinners were on the phones to every journalist to tell them they hadn’t heard what they had just heard. There had been collective false consciousness. When Healey had said that he would be bringing down a benefits bill that everyone agreed was too high and that the country could not afford, what he had really meant to say was that he would not be bringing down the benefits bill that he had no idea how to pay for. Fag packets gratefully received. That was about as close to news as we got.
Maybe it was just that while Healey was having one of his better days, Robinson was having one of his worse ones. Because he had also sounded uninterested in his interview with Andrew Griffith an hour earlier. An exercise in box-ticking rather than revelation because the shadow chancellor never has anything useful to add on the day after. Sure enough, Griffith insisted that he would have done everything differently while never going into the details of how. At which point, Robbo opened half an eye and observed that if it was really that easy, how come the Tories hadn’t fixed it when in office?
Indeed, Nick continued, it could be argued that Labour had been left to clear up the mess the Tories created. “I’ve never shied away from saying that the Tories have a chequered record,” Griffith said defensively. Er, I’m not sure that’s entirely true, Andrew. Your usual line is that history started in 2024 and that everything is the Labour government’s fault.
That just left time for Robinson to remind the shadow chancellor that he had been part of the Treasury team that had defended the Liz Truss mini-budget even as it was being shredded. “I will never publish plans without saying where the money is coming from,” said Griffith, before announcing £30bn of planned tax cuts without specifying which benefits he would cut to pay for them. Fair to say, he’s not a man who seems to learn from experience. Once in the Truss image, always in the Truss image.
The final piece of the Thursday jigsaw was the verdict from the Institute for Fiscal Studies. In the past this has been enough to completely destroy the reputation of some chancellors. I could never look at George Osborne in quite the same way after the IFS had rubbished one of his budgets. It’s one thing to be thought of as an economic quarter-wit. What’s really devastating is to have it proved.
Helen Miller, the IFS director, looked a bit knackered. She and her team had been up most of the night, going through both the budget and the OBR figures line by line, searching for the fatal flaw. And she was gutted to announce that there actually wasn’t one. There was as little in the budget as had first appeared. She announced that she was grumpy about some measures. Disappointed in others. Another was cack-handed. The tax system had been made more complicated, not less. Yet, all in all, these were minor gripes.
“This chancellor is hoping that things get better without actually needing to do anything,” Miller said in conclusion. I don’t think that’s right. Healey never travels in hope. Like the rest of us, he’s pretty confident everything is going to be worse in a year’s time. But he had got himself some breathing space.
