article_title: Andreas Malm condemns UK travel ban as ‘drift into authoritarianism’
article_content:
The Swedish climate academic Andreas Malm has condemned a travel ban imposed on him by the UK government as a “drift into authoritarianism” amid criticism of the move.
Malm, the author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline, said he had been “kept in the dark” by the UK’s immigration authorities over the reasons for his electronic travel authorisation (ETA) being revoked.
He said he had only been told that his presence in the UK was “not considered to be conducive to the public good”, as the Guardian revealed.
Speaking to Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday, he speculated that the only plausible rationale for the ban was his advertised appearance at a conference next Wednesday alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the proscribed group Palestine Action.
He said: “I cannot see any other explanation than the scheduled appearance of me on stage for a panel on Wednesday evening in London, together with Huda Ammori. That … makes me somehow a terrorist or associated with terrorism, and therefore barred from travelling to the UK. That’s pretty scandalous.”
He added: “What I am going through here is just a very small part of a major trend: this drift into authoritarianism that is targeting the Palestine movement, the climate movement, and others who oppose the destructive forces that are in control of this world. And that’s a very sad thing.”
Malm confirmed to the Guardian that he would speak via video link at the event organised by Tribune magazine.
In his BBC interview, he denied supporting or helping to finance Palestine Action. But Malm, who has long campaigned for Palestinian rights, added: “You might be able to guess my opinions and sympathies.”
The Home Office said it could not discuss individual cases. However, a source said: “Decisions to refuse or cancel an ETA on the grounds that presence in the UK may not be conducive to public good are based solely on an assessment of the potential risk an individual may pose to UK society.”
Malm said: “I don’t have any concrete evidence for what this is all about. I’m left in the dark. I have asked for clarification, explanation. I haven’t received any.”
Malm was challenged on Today over whether his description of the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023 as an “act of liberation” could be the reason for the ban.
He replied: “It could be. But my views about what happened on 7 October and in Palestine have been in the public realm for a long time. I was most recently in the UK in May.”
Malm added: “I’ve done nothing in public that is associated with Palestine Action. I have not publicly supported them or promoted them in any way.”
Malm said he was invited to speak alongside Ammori to discuss the war in Iran.
“So, what they’re preventing here is for us to have a discussion about the drivers of the imperial aggression in the Middle East,” he said.
“The only link to Palestine Action is her [Ammori] as a person. If you continue with these guilt-by-association links, then presumably if I am a threat to the public good in the UK by dint of talking to her, then someone who talks to me presumably is also a threat to the public good. Where does that end?”
The travel ban has been widely criticised. The author Sally Rooney said it was a “sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm”.
In a post on X, the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said: “This all feels very much Starmer’s Labour government 2.0. An extraordinary attack on free speech from Andy Burnham.”
The Labour MP Clive Lewis, who last year offered to stand down from his Norwich South seat to allow Andy Burnham the chance to return to parliament, said: “When any government starts barring academics for their political views, alarm bells should be ringing.
“If ministers have evidence Andreas Malm is dangerous, produce it. Otherwise, this looks like political censorship dressed up as public safety. That’s a dangerous road for any democracy.”
Ammori said in a post on X: “Banning academic and author Andreas Malm from entering Britain to stop him from speaking alongside myself, a Palestine Action co-founder, is another disgusting attack on free speech as a result of the draconian ban. The ban must be overturned.”
Neal Lawson, the director of the thinktank Compass, tweeted: “This makes me ashamed to be British and ashamed of an @UKLabour government that enacts illiberal attempts to stifle legitimate voices.”
The former shadow chancellor John McDonnell wrote: “You would have thought there was someone in government to appreciate the irony of effectively censoring someone who wanted to come here to discuss censorship. Home Office policy-making has degenerated into dangerous farce.”
How to Blow Up a Pipeline, which inspired a film of the same name, argues that sabotage and destroying property are morally and strategically justified forms of activism.

article_title: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
article_content:
'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
- Published
The prime minister has said the UK's four nations must "move together" to devolve more power to regions and cities, following a meeting with the Scottish and Welsh first ministers in Glasgow.
Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind" after the sit-down, which also included representatives from Northern Ireland.
SNP leader John Swinney said he welcomed recognition that "Westminster is not working for Scotland" and pledged to work "constructively and collaboratively" with Burnham, while Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iowerth said the meeting was "positive".
Both first ministers have called for a wider conversation about independence but Burnham has ruled out referendums.
- Scotland 'not like Manchester', Swinney says in dig at PM Burnham 
  - Published17 October
- Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution' 
  - Published16 October
- First minister says Budget not serious about Wales ahead of meeting with PM 
  - Published13 hours ago
Speaking after the first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow, Burnham highlighted plans for devolution at the regional level, saying he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind".
"It's really important we all move at the same pace together, and I won't allow anything to delay that," the prime minister said.
"Growth can't wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK."
Northern Ireland was represented by officials at the meeting amid the political fallout from the Drumcree parade dispute.
Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation.
"It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said.
He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution".
In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding.
Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.
The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".
Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.
He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth.
The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities.
'Welcome start'
John Swinney said while he and Burnham disagree on independence, the meeting was "a welcome start" on further devolution.
"When the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will about," Scotland's first minister said.
"To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with the prime minister to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland - as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living."
A Downing Street spokesperson said the UK government would review issues raised by the first minister but this would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland.
Rhun ap Iowerth said: "I was pleased to meet with the prime minister in Glasgow today where I once again pressed the need for Wales and the Welsh government to have the necessary tools to better serve our communities.
"I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd."
He added he welcomed the prime minister's "step forward" on the Welsh government's fiscal and borrowing powers and gave his "full support" in pushing for a stronger relationship with the EU.
The prime minister had "positive discussions" with the Welsh leader, Downing Street said.
A spokesperson added: "The first minister of Wales agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."
description: The meeting involved representatives from the UK's four nations to discuss devolving more powers to regions and cities.

article_title: Public sector an ‘afterthought’ to North Sea oil jobs, says Unison leader
article_content:
The leader of the UK’s biggest trade union has called for the same political focus to be given to NHS, education and care sector workers as there has been on those employed in North Sea oil and gas.
Andrea Egan, the general secretary of Unison, said too often public sector workers were treated as an “afterthought” by the government compared with the “massive political focus” on protecting jobs in the North Sea.
“There’s no question it is vital for oil and gas workers to be guaranteed secure, well-paid jobs in the industries of the future,” Egan said. “But public service workers, in contrast, often seem like an afterthought for ministers. What about the thousands of jobs cut in recent years across local government, the NHS and education? Care workers, nurses, teaching assistants.”
North Sea oil and gas has been in the headlines again in recent weeks after the government gave the go ahead to the Jackdaw gasfield following huge pressure from the fossil fuel industry and rightwing politicians – in the UK and abroad.
The decision caused anger among climate campaigners and scientists, as well as many Labour supporters, who argue that extracting more fossil fuels will further escalate the crisis and do nothing to reduce bills, significantly improve energy security or halt the long-term decline in jobs in the sector. A final government decision on the more controversial Rosebank oilfield is expected before the end of the year.
After Wednesday’s budget, which factored in the project’s approval in its forecast, the Guardian revealed some Labour MPs were lobbying Andy Burnham and John Healey not to overrule the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, if she decided to block Rosebank.
Egan said approving Jackdaw was “a serious misstep from the government” and sent the wrong signal about the UK’s climate commitments. She said ministers should instead focus on creating secure, well-paid jobs in the renewable sector for oil and gas workers and give similar support to the millions of employees in the public sector, which has also been hit by severe cuts in recent years.
“It’s time for the government to get its priorities straight: invest in clean energy, invest in the public services that communities rely on – to the benefit of us all.”
There is a split among the UK’s main trade unions on allowing fossil fuel companies to drill in the North Sea. Unite and GMB, which represent many oil and gas workers, back more licences, while Unison and the National Education Union oppose more drilling as part of a wider drive to create long term sustainable jobs and tackle the climate crisis.
One concern among unions is that jobs in the rapidly growing renewables sector are often not unionised and therefore not as secure or well paid as in those in the oil and gas sector.
However, last week Unison announced a new recognition deal with the UK’s largest energy company, Octopus Energy, known as a progressive organisation with a focus on renewable energy.
The GMB union had been attempting to gain recognition at Octopus but the company said Unison “stood out for its commitment to the energy transition”.
Egan said it was an important step to securing good, secure jobs in the renewable sector. “Unison is proud to be leading the way as the clean energy union. We urgently need more well-paid, unionised jobs and to transition away from fossil fuels at pace. This agreement is a step in the right direction on both counts.”

article_title: Очільник МЗС Британії жорстко звернувся до Лаврова на G20: просто в обличчя нагадав про вбитих українців
article_content:
Очільник МЗС Британії жорстко звернувся до Лаврова на G20: просто в обличчя нагадав про вбитих українців
Британський міністр поставив Лаврова перед фактом: згадав убитих у Дніпрі та звернувся до Путіна.
Очільник МЗС Великої Британії Ед Мілібенд жорстко розніс російського колегу Сергія Лаврова: нагадав про вбитих українців і прямо назвав Росію агресором.
Про це він заявив під час зустрічі міністрів закордонних справ G20, повідомляє Sky News.
Мілібенд нагадав про загибель мирних жителів в Україні та наголосив, що Росія не перемагає у війні завдяки мужності українців і підтримці союзників.
«Давайте поговоримо про те, що сталося вчора на залізниці у Дніпрі. Лише вчора ваші дрони атакували та вбили 15 людей», — звернувся британський міністр до Лаврова.
Він додав, що це лише один із прикладів убивств мирних жителів за майже п’ять років повномасштабного вторгнення. Британський політик закликав тиснути на Москву і позбавляти диктатора Володимира Путіна доходів, які дають змогу продовжувати «цю варварську війну».
«Путін тоді думав, що легко переможе у цій війні. Але ви не перемагаєте. Завдяки мужності українського народу та солідарності країн за цим столом ви не перемагаєте», — заявив Мілібенд.
Він також закликав Лаврова набратися сміливості та сказати правду російському диктаторові.
«Якби у вас вистачило сміливості говорити правду і чинити правильно, ви сказали б Путіну, що він не перемагає у цій війні й не переможе», — наголосив очільник британського МЗС.
Окремо Мілібенд Ця заява пролунала на тлі нещодавнього блокування Дональдом Трампом санкцій проти Кремля.
Звинувачення Каллас
Водночас висока представниця ЄС із закордонних справ Кая Каллас звинуватила Лаврова у поширенні брехні про війну і охарактеризував поведінку російського міністра на засіданні як «доволі провокативну».
«Звісно, він навів чимало брехні та перекрутив факти, які ми згодом змогли спростувати», — заявила Каллас, повідомило видання Der Stern.
За її словами, Лавров під час зустрічі не продемонстрував жодних ознак готовності Москви до мирних переговорів. Зокрема, свідченням цього є смертельні атаки РФ по Україні.
Каллас також закликала посилити тиск на Крнмля, зокрема задля досягнення припинення вогню в Чорному морі.
«Для нас цілком очевидно: щоб покласти край цій війні, тиск потрібно чинити на агресора», — підсумувала вона.
Скандал із Лавровим на саміті G20
Перед початком саміту організатори скасували заплановану спільну фотосесію. Причиною стала відмова Мілібенда і інших європейських лідерів фотографуватися поруч із Лавровим.
Сам Лавров згодом іронічно прокоментував цей епізод,
«Якщо для них найважливіше — як вони виглядають на спільному фото і хто стоїть поруч, то це саме за себе говорить», — заявив російський міністр, назвавши епізод «дипломатією сімейного фото».
Зауважимо, що Лавров летів до Атланти у США понад 20 годин через обхід так званих «недружніх країн», які закрили свій повітряний простір для російських бортів. Візит очільника МЗС РФ відбувається попри спротив частини американських законодавців, які закликали не впускати політика країни-агресора до Штатів.

article_title: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
article_content:
Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
- Published
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has denied "kicking the can down the road" over how much the UK spends on defence.
The government has faced criticism for not setting out a pathway at Wednesday's Budget to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
Streeting is at odds with MPs on the Commons defence committee over the issue.
It comes as Chancellor John Healey and Streeting announce that foreign firms which are awarded defence contracts of more than £50m will need to invest an equal value back into the UK.
Under the new investment rules, described as an "offset strategy", these companies will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.
The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said. Healey and Streeting will unveil the policy on a visit to UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow later.
Countries including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the government said.
While ministers hope the rules increase investment in Britain's defence industry, they appear designed to do so in a politically palatable way rather than committing to spending cuts.
Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the cross-party Commons defence committee, said on Wednesday that decisions had been "kicked into the long grass" to next year's government spending review, rather than announced in the Budget.
He warned that without building capabilities now, "we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict".
Streeting hit back at these comments as "unfair" and "unfounded".
Speaking on Thursday, Dhesi said the committee stands by its criticism.
"We had hoped to see that the chancellor would set out a precise pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030," Dhesi told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
"But instead some of those key decisions on defence have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review."
He praised the government for plugging a £4.7bn hole in the Defence Investment Plan in the Budget, through asking government departments to cut their capital budgets by 1%.
Responding on Thursday, Streeting told Today: "I like Tan very much, he's a friend and I respect him, but I strongly disagree with him.
"And I don't think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we're funding right now."
Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules, aiming to create "bang for the British buck", would help achieve this target given increasing defence spending "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".
He said waiting for the spending review, which does not have a fixed date and could come in the second half of 2027, was "the right thing to do" so ministers can look at "spending in the round".
He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be".
"There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.
Defence analysts have questioned the government's ability to deliver on its 2030 target and the Nato-wide target of 3.5% by 2035. UK defence spending is at an estimated 2.6% of GDP this year.
Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional £10bn annually to reach its targets.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%".
Healey resigned as then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June over not spending enough on defence.
In the Budget, Healey said the UK was negotiating with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to set up an international bank - the Multilateral Defence Mechanism - to boost defence investment and joint procurement.
But Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said this amounted to "turning to borrowing at a time when the national debt is over £3 trillion".
"The answer is not more borrowing – it's to cut welfare to fund defence," he said.

article_title: Healey’s budget cuts mean Britain is likely to miss green heating targets
article_content:
Britain is unlikely to hit its targets on green heating after the cuts announced by John Healey this week, experts have warned, as critics of Ed Miliband claim the former energy secretary’s green agenda is being dismantled.
The chancellor unveiled more than £3bn worth of cuts to the energy department’s budget this week, much of which will pay for higher defence spending.
One casualty of the cuts is the government’s scheme to subsidise heat pumps, leading to warnings that clean heating ambitions are being undermined.
Some believe the cuts are evidence of a broader shift away from the pro-renewables agenda pushed by Miliband and his successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh. However, energy department sources insisted the government’s longer-term changes will incentivise people to move towards cleaner power sources and benefit the overall green agenda.
Andrew Sissons, a director at the research charity Nesta, said: “After the cuts announced on Wednesday, it is very difficult to see how we can hit our clean heating targets. It is even possible that a Labour government will be the first to miss the targets it has signed up to in the current carbon budget.”
Healey announced on Wednesday that the government would fund the defence investment plan in part through cuts to other departments.
Much of that will come from the energy department, including £741m from the boiler upgrade scheme, the government’s plan to incentivise people to replace their gas boilers with electric heat pumps.
Under the scheme, a typical household can claim £7,500 towards a heat pump, with about 60,000 a year being fitted in existing homes. The government has a target to raise that to 250,000 a year by 2030, and was planning to increase the scheme’s funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30.
The plan forms a key part of the UK’s programme to clean up its heating networks and hit its overall emissions reduction targets. However, ministers said on Wednesday the scheme’s funding would rise only in line with inflation, meaning the number of installations is likely to stagnate or rise much more slowly than previously planned.
“It’s disappointing – so frustrating,” said Ed Matthew, the director of the UK programme at the thinktank E3G. “We are behind a lot of other countries in rolling out heat pumps and we need a sea change in take-up to change that.”
The cuts to heat pump subsidies came alongside about £250m of other cuts to the warm homes plan, £500m worth of cuts to hydrogen schemes, and £200m to funding for carbon capture and storage technology – all projects once championed by Miliband.
Healey also announced that renewable projects would only be approved in future if they could be shown to bring costs down and were ready to be connected with the grid. Officials insist the government remains committed to its target of having clean power by 2030, though many experts believe that will be impossible under the new system.
One government source said: “This is probably the most significant shift we have seen in energy policy since we came to office. The emphasis now is on cost, not just building to make sure there is enough capacity to hit our green targets.”
Paul Ovenden, a former adviser to Keir Starmer, said: “It is fascinating to see the energy capital budgets being raided to fund defence – this is the bones of Ed Miliband’s project being picked clean.
“This was something that has been discussed in government before – but Miliband always won that argument. Now he’s not in that department any more, it’s happened.”
Ovenden added: “Had he not helped to oust Starmer and Reeves, he’d probably be in post still and it wouldn’t have been possible.”
But allies of Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government’s green agenda remained as strong as ever. They pointed out that Healey also announced a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and on to taxpayers – something the two energy secretaries have both championed.
They also said the government’s intention to change energy markets so electricity prices are no longer so attached to gas prices would help encourage consumers to move away from fossil fuels.
One source said: “Ed and Miatta have both made affordability their focus. It would be wrong to suggest that prioritising cost is in any way a shift away from the green agenda.”
A spokesperson for the energy department said: “Over the last two years, we have made considerable progress, thanks to the momentum of clean power 2030, seeing £110bn of private-sector investment announced and securing enough clean power for over 20m homes.
“We are committed to making the most of clean, homegrown power and meeting our heat pump target to protect consumers from volatile fossil fuel prices.”

article_title: Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree
article_content:
Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree
- Published
Andy Burnham's Number 10 North has gone on a multi-million pound hiring spree with dozens of new jobs being advertised.
The office in Manchester, set up by the prime minister in July, has launched 50 external job adverts, including a "rewiring the state deputy director".
It is the latest sign of how pivotal the government outpost - designed as a sister office to London's Downing Street - may prove to Burnham's aim to devolve power across the country.
Government sources say the roles will be paid for out of existing budgets.
The new recruits "will work with mayors and councils to identify barriers holding places back", but the Conservatives have described the office as a "gimmick".
There will be no redundancies elsewehere in the civil service as a result of the hiring spree, the BBC has been told, with some jobs expected to be relocated and other vacant roles closed.
The new roles, all based in Manchester, cover areas including strategy, communications, engagement, private office and policy.
BBC News has calculated they total up to £2.8m for basic salaries alone, excluding employer pension contributions in the civil service of 28.97%.
No10 North now has 120 members of staff, nearly half of the 280 staff who work in No10 London.
Among the highest paid of the roles are a "rewiring the state deputy director", with a salary band of £86,000 to £117,000, who will "lead the Rewiring the State Unit... shaping the government's approach to devolution across departments".
The government said it was launching a recruitment campaign for staff who would "bring fresh perspectives and knowledge of the places they serve, moving decisions closer to the people they affect".
No10 North "is driving the most significant transfer of power out of Westminster in a generation," the government added in a statement.
Some apprenticeships and secondments are also being advertised.
It comes as the government confirmed on Friday that No10 North would move from its current temporary home in Heron House, on Manchester's Albert Square, to a new government office on First Street in spring 2027.
No10 North will share the city centre building with other government departments spanning business, education, local government and the Cabinet Office.
Burnham made opening No10 North one of his first acts as prime minister, describing it as "the nerve-centre of a rewired Britain" that would help bring growth to more areas of Britain.
No10 North's deputy director Duncan Parish said in a speech last week that officials faced "institutional challenges" with delivering on these aims and called for a "mindset shift" across the UK's central government.
Conservative Party deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "He [Burnham] promised to streamline the civil service, but now he is hiring extra staff and, once again, won't say where the money is coming from.
"Manchesterism is just more bureaucracy at taxpayers' expense."
Meanwhile, Tory shadow cabinet minister Mike Wood has said there is "so little transparency" around No10 North after ministers told him they could not reveal figures on headcounts and office attendance.
According to the new job adverts, the Office for the Prime Minister - with exceptions for certain roles - expects No10 staff to be in the office a minimum of 60% of the time.
Since opening, No10 North has hosted summits of regional mayors, at least two of which have been partly held as video calls on Microsoft Teams. At one of these meetings, ministers unveiled controversial powers for mayors in England to charge new fees on visitors' overnight stays.
It has also hosted an education summit of school leaders and Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin met Burnham for the first time as PM at No10 North in September.

article_title: Andy Burnham admits he would have liked more radical first budget
article_content:
Andy Burnham has admitted his first budget as prime minister was not as radical as he would have liked because of the economic uncertainty facing the country.
He said he would have liked to have gone further with this week’s announcement – including with higher energy support payments – but felt hemmed in by external events such as the war in Iran, which has pushed up borrowing costs.
Burnham’s chancellor, John Healey, announced a range of relatively inexpensive measures on Wednesday, including a £100 payment for most households to help with energy bills this winter.
He has faced criticism for not doing enough on a range of issues including defence spending, welfare cuts and support for the cost of living.
Burnham told ITV: “The room for manoeuvre wasn’t what I would have hoped it to be. I guess then the question is, you know, radical within what we were able to do.
“It was quite a big call to ask the banks to repay the help they had off people 20 or so years ago. And a payment – OK, you’d like it to be more – but a payment to 20 million households is quite a significant step.”
Asked whether this was the budget he had wanted to deliver, he added: “I don’t think any prime minister and chancellor would say that, because a budget is by definition a very difficult thing.
“In the times that we’re currently in, I feel that the volatility of things means you just can’t necessarily deliver the budget that in an ideal world you would want to deliver.”
He said he wanted major changes to the benefits system that would prevent most young people having to claim benefits at all.
Burnham will spell out his plans for welfare reform in the coming months after two major reports on the system, one by the former minister Alan Milburn and one by the current minister Stephen Timms.
He told ITV on Friday the changes would not involve “brutal cuts” that would leave people in “absolute crisis”.
But he added: “I don’t actually want to see anyone in their 20s on benefits. I just don’t think that’s a good place to be, unless people can’t be in work for reasons due to disability or whatever else it might be.”
Burnham came to office this year promising an end to “40 years of neoliberalism” and a plan for sweeping change of the economy, including higher taxes on wealth and nationalisation of major utilities.
So far, however, he has made a series of smaller announcements that he and Healey say are meant to give voters “breathing space” while the government works on more radical plans for the future.
They have included tax cuts on energy bills, lower bus fares and fines for people playing music out loud on their phones on public transport.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said on Wednesday: “Most people in the country, listening to that budget, will be thinking to themselves ‘is that it?’.”
Burnham told ITV he was limited not only by geopolitical crises but also by Labour’s 2024 manifesto, which helped propel the party to a landslide victory but ruled out major policy options such as raising income tax, national insurance or VAT.
“Obviously, when the time comes, I would seek my own mandate,” he said. “If you’re asking me a very direct question, if I had held the pen on the current Labour manifesto, would I have written it exactly like it is? Well, no is the answer to that question.”
Burnham is also under pressure to spend more on defence, with the Labour chair of the defence select committee, Tan Dhesi, accusing the government this week of inaction.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, hit back at that criticism on Friday, saying the government was investing in defence immediately and would announce more at the spending review.
“I like Tan very much,” he told BBC Breakfast. “He’s a friend, and I respect him. But I strongly disagree with him, and I don’t think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we’re funding right now.”
Streeting hinted there could be further departmental cuts next year to pay for another increase. “As the budget showed yesterday, there are choices and trade-offs,” he told Sky News. “I recognise that other government departments, as well as taxpayers, are doing some heavy lifting to make sure we prioritise defence. That’s the right thing to do.”

article_title: Mayors will be free to use share of tax to give residents grants
article_content:
Mayors will be free to use share of tax to give residents grants
- Published
English regional mayors due to be handed a share of tax revenues by central government will be free to use it to give cash grants to individual residents and businesses, it has emerged.
In his Budget, Chancellor John Healey unveiled plans to allow mayors to keep some cash from income tax and business rates collected locally, describing it as "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants local leaders to be given more control over how money is spent in their areas to boost economic growth and services.
But Conservative Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen says he has been given assurances that he will be able to give grants to local residents instead.
Lord Houchen told the BBC he is working on a voluntary scheme that would give local residents the opportunity to apply for a share of the tax distributed to his region.
He said Treasury officials had told him this would be acceptable within the government's rules around the devolution of funding.
"It's a technical point around spending decisions," Lord Houchen told the BBC.
He said devolution of funding was a "good thing" and "means mayors are able to decide spending commitments, which includes rebates".
The BBC has been told mayors could choose to use the tax revenues they received from the government to offer grants to individual residents or businesses.
But any mayor who decided to use the money in this way would have less for other local priorities, such as housing and transport.
Lord Houchen has described his proposal as a "tax rebate scheme".
The Treasury would regard these payments as grants, because His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC) is the only government authority in the UK that can issue income tax rebates.
Most of England's 14 strategic authorities are led by Labour mayors who have welcomed the move to give them a portion of income tax receipts.
Sources close to Reform UK's Greater Lincolnshire Mayor Andrea Jenkyns, and her counterpart in Hull and East Yorkshire, Luke Campbell, say they are waiting for more details to fully understand how they could use these tax revenues to benefit their regions.
The government published its broad approach, external to reforming funding for local and regional government in England after Wednesday's Budget.
As it stands, mayors of English strategic authorities receive most of their funding from ring-fenced grants, allocated by central government to be spent on specific policy areas.
From April 2028, all mayors of strategic authorities in England will be assigned a share of basic-rate income tax generated in their areas.
Each mayor will receive a bespoke funding allocation that takes into account regional inequalities in tax bases, with the exact amounts to be set at the government's spending review next year.
"The government is not devolving the power to set income tax rates or thresholds to mayors but will be granting significantly more flexibility as to how assigned revenues are spent locally," the government's plan says.
"Mayors will be able to choose where to target funding, for example whether to maintain funding for local transport or prioritise other interventions."
From next year, mayors will also receive a 20% share of locally retained business rates.
This will be the first step towards allowing local and mayoral authorities to retain 100% of their business rates income before the end of the decade.
From 2028, strategic authorities led by mayors will also be given the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy, often dubbed a "tourist tax".
This charge will be an uncapped levy as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.
Labour mayors in 10 city regions said they would voluntarily limit the charge to 5%, but others - such as Lord Houchen - said they would not introduce the levy.
Burnham - who used to be a mayor himself in Greater Manchester - argues that funding and decision-making powers are too centralised in the UK.
The share of national taxes collected at a local level in the UK is 5.8%, the lowest in the G7, according to the OECD, external, a global policy forum.
That share is far below that of other countries with large economies such as France (20.4%), Japan (36%) and the US (45.7%).
But critics of fiscal devolution raise concerns about local capability, and inequalities between areas.
The Centre for Cities think tank says some areas may not have the expertise to manage developed powers effectively, risking deeper economic inequalities between areas.
The think tank supports fiscal devolution and believes it can offer significant benefits, if the challenges are managed effectively.
The Tees Valley Combined Authority (TVCA) led by Lord Houchen is facing a government inspection into its finances, after Local Government Minister Jim McMahon said he had concerns about its "long-term financial sustainability".
The authority said it welcomed the scrutiny and would continue to make improvements where needed.

article_title: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
article_content:
The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.
European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.
During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.
A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”
The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.
But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

article_title: British people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated history | Andy Burnham
article_content:
On 28 October 1787, Thomas Clarkson pushed through the crowds to reach the pulpit of Manchester Cathedral. A campaigner for abolishing slavery, he spoke urgently about the horrors of the slave trade and the humanity of enslaved people. “He drinks the cup of sorrow,” Clarkson said. “And he drinks it at our hands.”
During Black History Month, these are the stories it is important to remember. They show us the complicated truth of our history. Thousands of people in Manchester signed a petition against slavery after Clarkson’s sermon. And yet Manchester’s cotton industry was built on the labour of enslaved people. There are similar stories up and down the nation. We are a country where brave people led the way in abolishing slavery, but we are also a country that participated in the trade in human lives.
The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity. They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today.
Our history is intertwined with countries that are now our allies, particularly in the Commonwealth. Next week, I will attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm). In an increasingly divided and dangerous world, our family of nations in the Commonwealth is vital to our interests: a beacon of stability, strength and security. Together we can face down shared challenges. We can seize opportunities for trade and economic collaboration. We can strengthen our respective countries and share our values to build a safer world for us all.
But facing a changing world together requires us to stand on firm foundations. To meet those challenges of the future, we need to face up to the past. For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function.
Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do. Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.
So we are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.
Some have called for financial reparations for the slave trade. I do not believe that is the right answer. I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.
My focus is on building a future where people at home and abroad live in greater peace and prosperity.
So we will bring to the Chogm our determination to tackle the issues that affect people across our Commonwealth family and beyond.
Today, debt-servicing costs in the poorest and most vulnerable countries are at their highest in more than 25 years. More than 40% of these countries spend more on interest repayments than on health. I want to launch a new drive on debt, working with our global partners to help those countries repay over a longer time period and with better rates. That is why the chancellor, foreign secretary and I have asked Gordon Brown, who will join us at the Chogm, to help with this work.
We will also support the energy transition in the face of the climate crisis. And we will build on the incredible work being done to educate women and girls, give smaller countries a louder voice on the world stage, and end global poverty and inequality.
I want us to build stronger relationships with each other and renew the relevance of the Commonwealth in a new era. We do that by facing our past together and focusing on a future where every person living within it has equality, security and hope.
We stand on the shoulders of those such as Thomas Clarkson and the many ordinary people who spoke out for justice and humanity.
In 1862, at the height of the American civil war, Manchester was the cotton capital of the world. In a vote at the Free Trade Hall, the humble cotton workers resolved that they would no longer handle slave-picked cotton. Their actions helped end the civil war, prompting Abraham Lincoln to write to them praising their “sublime Christian heroism”.
It is so often the case in British history that huge injustices ignored by the powers-that-be are eventually overturned by ordinary people. Those Manchester cotton workers represent that proud British tradition, and I will take inspiration from them as we go forward into our new dialogue.

article_title: Mayor defects from Greens after Zionism motion
article_content:
Mayor defects from Greens after Zionism motion
- Published
The leader of the Green Party on Cornwall Council has defected following the party's recent "Zionism is racism" motion.
Drew Creek joined the Labour and Co-operatives on Thursday after the policy motion was passed at the Green Party's conference earlier this month.
Creek, who is Mayor of Newquay and serves as a councillor for Trenance ward, said he had "huge respect" for Greens across Cornwall but the motion "crossed a line".
The Cornwall Green Party said it was "deeply saddened" by Creek's decision to join Labour and said it does not "try to impose uniformity of belief" among its members and elected representatives.
The motion backed by Green members at its party conference said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".
It has been criticised by Jewish groups, as well as some Green MPs and opposition political parties.
Creek said he hoped the Green Party would step back from the stance – but said instead, "Zack Polanski and the leadership has doubled down".
"I can't stand behind that, and I won't pretend otherwise," the councillor said.
He added: "People in Newquay don't want politicians driving division. They want someone who'll fix the roads, protect our coast, fight for local services and bring people together.
"That's the kind of politics I believe in and the kind of politics Andy Burnham has shown.
"Newquay is my home and where I am raising my family. I came into politics for one reason, to stand up for this town and the people in it. Labour is where I believe I can do that best, and I'm looking forward to getting on with the job."
Councillor Kate Ewert, Labour and Co-operative Group Leader on Cornwall Council said Creek's decision "highlights the serious questions about Zack Polanski's leadership".
Noah Law, MP for St Austell and Newquay, added: "In this period of polarised politics, it takes great courage to stand up for what you believe in.
"Having worked with Drew since my election, I have always found him to be steadfast in his beliefs, easy to work with, and a good advocate for Newquay."
'Disagreements'
A spokesperson for the Cornwall Green Party said Creek had "done excellent work as a Green councillor" and they understood there were "different views within the Green Party on the 'Zionism is Racism' motion".
They said: "Disagreements over the wording of this one motion should not distract from the fact that the Green Party is united in its condemnation of the racist genocide and ethnic cleansing that Israel is perpetrating in Gaza and the occupied territories, and united in its demand for much tougher sanctions on Israel.
"Labour, by contrast, refuses even to recognise that what we are seeing is genocide, and continues to allow arms exports to and intelligence-sharing with the government that is committing it.
"It's hard to see how anyone who is serious about action on climate, action to end extreme inequality, and action to prevent an ongoing genocide could switch their support to a party that is not serious about any of these."

article_title: The Guardian view on Labour’s fiscal devolution: the future of Burnhamism will play out in municipal England | Editorial
article_content:
Following Wednesday’s budget, the Treasury minister, Torsten Bell, was challenged by the BBC’s Evan Davis on whether its modest series of “breathing space” measures could truly be said to have ended “40 years of neoliberalism”. This line of questioning is becoming a familiar one. Andy Burnham’s ringing declaration of long-term intent is now being regularly deployed by commentators to suggest an emerging gulf between rhetoric and action.
Mr Bell’s response was a good one. Recalling how “Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s hugely hollowed out local government [and] tried to emasculate our big cities”, he called the fiscal devolution roadmap unveiled in the budget a step change and a really big deal.From 2028, mayoral strategic authorities will for the first time receive a share of income tax receipts, and from next year they will be allocated 20% of business rates revenue. That figure will potentially rise to 100% by the end of the decade, while a new overnight visitors levy will add another local income stream.
These are structural changes that will transform the relationship between local government and a notoriously overly centralised state. They have so far failed to generate anything like the coverage that accompanied the Conservatives’ levelling-up programme, which degenerated into a tawdry pork barrel exercise for “red wall” Tory MPs. But it is on this municipal terrain that Mr Burnham’s aspiration to rebalance the country, reduce regional inequality and “roll back” the 80s will be played out.
Replacing government grants with guaranteed income streams will give strategic authorities more certainty over future revenue – against which they will be able to borrow – and the ability to plan flexibly according to locally set priorities. The devil will be in details to be announced in next year’s spending review, in particular regarding mechanisms to ensure poorer areas with a smaller tax base do not lose out. But the roadmap is a first move towards restoring proper agency to local authorities struggling to cope with the disastrous twin legacy of deindustrialisation and austerity.
Further steps will need to be taken if, as the prime minister intends, local government is to drive “good growth” that improves general living standards and prospects throughout communities. As the Local Government Association pointed out, cash-strapped councils on the frontline face a £7bn funding gap by 2028-29, and are in a perennial struggle merely to meet their statutory obligations on social care. Strategic authorities need to be given the capacity to gradually reassume control of priorities in sectors such as care, housing and the utilities. That will take time and investment at scale in forms of community provision that can offer an alternative to a model in which services have been outsourced and profits offshored.
Devolution will not of itself reduce inequalities or restore a degraded public realm. But this week’s budget measures began the necessary process of rewiring British politics. Mr Burnham’s core conviction is that radical devolution can redistribute power to those who know their own community best, and allow councils to rebalance the relationship between the public and the private sector. After decades in which the latter has profited hugely from calling nearly all the shots, that is very much the right direction of travel. The starting gun has been fired in a process that can lead to a genuine renaissance of municipal England.

article_title: В Турции ожидают визита Зеленского 31 октября
article_content:
31 октября в Стамбуле состоятся переговоры президента Украины Владимира Зеленского с его турецким коллегой Реджепом Тайипом Эрдоганом. Как сообщил глава Управления по коммуникациям администрации президента Турции Бурханеттин Дуран, основными темами встречи станут российско-украинская война, безопасность в Черном море и дальнейшее развитие двустороннего сотрудничества, передает Anadolu.
По его словам, особое внимание в ходе переговоров будет уделено российско-украинской войне и ситуации с безопасностью в Черноморском регионе. Эти вопросы имеют стратегическое значение для обоих государств, в частности с точки зрения безопасности судоходства и международной торговли.
В начале октября Эрдоган уже обсуждал ситуацию в Черном море во время телефонного разговора с президентом России Владимиром Путиным.
В то же время Верховный представитель Европейского Союза по иностранным делам Кая Каллас призвала международное сообщество содействовать восстановлению полноценного торгового маршрута через Чёрное море.
В вечернем видеообращении накануне поездки в Турцию президент Зеленский отметил, что переговоры будут «очень важными». Также он выразил надежду, что в ноябре удастся перейти к новым форматам переговоров, которые ранее лишь обсуждались.
description: Президент Украины встретится с Эрдоганом в Стамбуле.

article_title: Treasury accepts role in staff member's death
article_content:
Treasury accepts role in staff member's death
- Published
The Treasury has accepted it contributed to the death of a personal assistant and said "immediate steps" have been taken to tackle outstanding risks.
Chloe Moffat, 26, took her own life in May 2025, the day after managers told her of allegations that she had shared sensitive confidential information, which she denied.
A coroner found a practice within HM Treasury of "informal fact-finding" meetings with employees accused of misconduct had no basis in the ministry's policy and posed a risk of future death.
Responding, the Treasury and the Cabinet Office wrote that they "accept the concerns identified" and "take them extremely seriously".
The Cabinet Office said it would also undertake a wider review of workplace conflict and resolution across Whitehall within a year.
At Moffat's inquest in August, the Treasury was found to have "materially contributed" to her death by not telling her that the likely penalty if allegations against her were proven would be a written warning and not dismissal.
In a response to the coroner's report, external, the Treasury "accepted the findings in the report in full" and said it had taken immediate action to mitigate the concerns raised.

Strengthened "wellbeing safeguards" had been introduced and the use of informal fact-finding meetings had been stopped while a full policy review was conducted, the department said.
Employees facing misconduct allegations would be informed of the possible outcomes before being asked to respond and a suicide prevention framework was being developed, it added.
"HM Treasury has considered these concerns carefully and has taken immediate steps to mitigate the identified risks," according to the department's response.
"While this work introduces some enhancements, much of it is intended to strengthen, clarify and build on the procedures and support already in place."
A Treasury spokesperson added: "The Treasury's deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe's friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague.
"An independent review found staff acted in good faith and with a duty of care throughout."

article_title: How do you bounce back from Liz Truss-level public failure? Don’t be shameless; do show remorse | Gaby Hinsliff
article_content:
Gabriel Weston made a mistake at work this summer. It doesn’t define her – she was and is a well-regarded NHS surgeon and author – but it was serious enough, as she explained in an extraordinarily candid series of Instagram and Substack posts this month, to prompt an investigation that left her feeling “ashamed and alone and really quite nervous”. Whatever went wrong in the operating theatre was bad enough to be classed a “never event” (something that should never be able to happen if the process is working properly) and triggered a nagging anxiety that she might somehow do it again, unless she figured out where she had unexpectedly gone wrong.
It’s a fascinating insight into a process that most people never have the courage to talk about openly. But it also highlights why it’s so hard in practice for doctors and other professionals to acknowledge and learn from mistakes – as every public inquiry into every public scandal ends up recommending, only to repeat it all over again after the next one – rather than close ranks and cover up. Weston says she only spoke up out of frustration with what she saw as her employers’ failure to support her (she had asked to reduce what she considered an overloaded operating list to take some pressure off, which she says has now happened, leaving her full of praise for the hospital’s ultimate response). Judging by the responses to her posts, she’s not alone.
I thought of Weston this week when Liz Truss published Bank Job, the second book she has written in two years circling the drain of her career. This one seems if anything even less self-aware, blaming the Bank of England, not herself, for the spectacular failure of her mini-budget (even her old cheerleaders at the Telegraph called it deranged). But it’s also oddly sad. There’s something near-pathological about the inability to engage with an excruciatingly public failure, as if the truth would shatter her. She can’t seem to leave the whole episode alone – can’t withdraw, as Keir Starmer has, into stony silence about his own prematurely curtailed time in Downing Street – yet can’t really face it head-on either.
How does anyone learn from cataclysmic failure? I don’t mean the frothy, early-career kind that seemed the end of the world at the time, but which you can laugh about now from the security of knowing that eventually everything turned out fine. Those aren’t the kind of failures the state really cares about avoiding. Nor do I mean the kind whose authors somehow manage to fail upwards anyway – or at least onwards, like Truss, into some strange reincarnation on YouTube. The failures that most haunt their authors, but which often hold the most useful lessons for preventing such a thing ever happening again, are often of the “there but for the grace of God go you and I” kind, involving formerly blameless and conscientious people who make one inexplicably dumb mistake, often under pressure or when exhausted.
Richard Jackson was a high-flying civil servant working on counter-terrorism, who one night accidentally scooped up two classified documents that should never have left the building along with some routine papers he was taking home. Realising his error that night, he fatally compounded it by deciding to sneak the files back before their absence was noticed, only to accidentally leave them on the train – where they were found and handed into a BBC reporter, resulting in a security scandal that cost Jackson his job and left him close to suicide. The advice on coping he shared in a recent episode of BBC Radio 4’s Life Changing series – get dark thoughts out of your head by writing them down or telling someone; keep a note of all the nice things people have ever said to you; don’t let your life be defined by one mistake – seems useful for individuals in the eye of the storm. But so perhaps is what Weston calls a degree of professional “care and acceptance” for good people who have failed, and want help working out why.
Shamelessness has a deservedly terrible reputation in public life, and for some mistakes forgiveness can be too much to ask.
But it’s shame that prevents thoughtful people learning from failure; shame that drives the cover-up; shame that ruins, and sometimes even ends, lives. People willing to honestly examine their own mistakes for others’ benefit deserve some grace in return. The true shame lies with those refusing to offer it.

article_title: First minister says Welsh spending powers takes step forward after Andy Burnham meeting
article_content:
First minister says Welsh spending powers takes step forward after Andy Burnham meeting
- Published
Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth says there has been a "significant step forward" with regards to his country's spending and borrowing powers after meeting the prime minister.
Andy Burnham held a meeting of his National Economic Council with the first ministers of Wales and Scotland on Friday, after which ap Iorwerth said it was a matter of "how and when" a loosening of financial restrictions will take place.
At the summit in Glasgow, Burnham lobbied the government leaders to devolve "deeper" to the regions of Wales and Scotland.
The prime minister said the two first ministers had agreed to work with him on "regional empowerment".
No timescales were announced for changes to Wales' finances.
Friday's meeting followed rows between the Welsh and UK government over the chancellor's Budget on Wednesday, which ap Iorwerth had said was "not serious about Wales".
His party Plaid Cymru said the budget left the Welsh government with a real-terms cut in funding, which the UK government denied.
Ap Iorwerth had set out a range of demands to the prime minister in a letter sent at the start of October.
As well as calling for powers over policing and justice, and for more funding for rail projects, he called for an end to restrictions on access to the Wales reserve - spare funding that the Welsh government can store in one year to use in another.
It is capped at £385m, and the Welsh government can only draw down £137.5m and £55m for resource and capital spend respectively per year.
The Welsh government can also borrow up to £1.1bn for infrastructure, with a limit of £165m a year.
Ap Iorwerth said: "There were some real positives here.
"On fiscal flexibility, the ability for us to use our funding better in Wales, use our reserves better in Wales - and on borrowing powers, I was told clearly that its now was a matter of how and when. That is a significant step forward."
He said there was "clearly an interest" for the prime minister to "really understand that sheer injustice of underfunding of rail in Wales that we have seen for many years".
"That is a particular issue we will be taking forward now between my office and his," he said.
On policing, the first minister said "I think instinctively the prime minister wants to go there and there's still work to do".
At a speech this month the first minister called for "practical agreement" on how the two governments could work together on the economy, calling for Westminster to avoid duplication in areas that are devolved already to the Welsh government.
Burnham said Friday's meeting was "positive", and that both first ministers had agreed to "work together jointly on regional empowerment in Scotland and Wales as well".
"We now have a process where we have detailed work by officials on both sides to see if we can come to a set of arrangements that are right for Scotland and right for Wales," Burnham said.
"We had a good discussion today on two fronts, one around re-industrialisation and the offer of more devolution of innovation funding to the regional level."
He said it was for Scotland and Wales to decide how that looks.
Burnham also said the UK government will now look at arrangements for further devolution of employment support.
Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock fiscal flexibilities and borrowing was on the agenda for future Welsh government discussions with No 10 North.
"It is going to take some conversations on how that would work in practice.
"I can't give you a specific time frame as things stand," he said.
Following Wednesday's Budget, which saw an extra £450m announced for Wales over the next three years as well as funding for individual projects, the Welsh government claimed the extra money would represent a real-terms cut to its own finances.
A £30m funding pledge for a new railway station in Cardiff was also described as "an insult" by Wales' transport minister.
On Radio Wales Breakfast on Friday before the summit, ap Iorwerth said there were "paltry sums of money coming on rail, when they've said there's £14bn on the way" and a "real terms cut in the money we have to spend on public services".
"The Budget was not serious about Wales," he said.
He said in another interview he could "only assume that the prime minister is holding something back".
After the meeting, Downing Street said ap Iorwerth had "agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode".
"This would be a policy sprint led by No 10 North, involving officials from each government, to take this agenda forward," they said.
Ap Iorwerth said in a statement: "There was an encouraging consensus that the fiscal and borrowing powers which have for so long put Wales at a disadvantage compared with other UK nations must be revised as a matter of urgency.
"I welcome the prime minister's comments that this is now a matter of how and when."
Welsh ministers had called for changes to their borrowing rules and assurances that child poverty payments it wants to introduce would leave recipients' tax and benefits allowances unaffected.
None of that was addressed in the Budget, although Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock has said "positive" talks were continuing regarding the child poverty payments.
Friday's meeting of the National Economic Council - a summit to help boost the UK economy - was due to be attended by the prime minister and all the devolved leaders.
However, it emerged on Thursday that Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill would not be there after her attendance was blocked by her Democratic Unionist Party (DUP).
Since he became prime minister, Burnham has consistently spoken in favour of devolution.
He has said he is "open" to transferring powers over policing and justice to Wales and, during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, he said he was "ready to make an offer" on the devolution of employment support.
description: Rhun ap Iorwerth says new powers for more cash matter of how and when, after meeting.

article_title: Digested week: The Traitors suddenly feels tired – time for a politicians version? | John Crace
article_content:
Monday
You would have thought someone would have made an intervention by now. To save Liz Truss from the worst excesses and delusions of herself. Most former prime ministers – and there are enough of them by now – make the transition into civilian life with little fuss. More or less. John Major found himself elevated from national joke to statesman after 20 years; Tony Blair took the grandiose step of establishing his very own institute; Boris Johnson took his grumblings to the Daily Mail where he is now more or less ignored; Theresa May opted for obscurity; we have yet to find out Keir Starmer’s next move. Yet Liz Truss seems permanently scarred by her 49 days in office and its abrupt ending. Constantly feeling the need to pick away at the wound that will never heal.
She has been abandoned by a Tory party for whom she is nothing but an embarrassment and now finds herself posting conversations on YouTube with people as deranged as herself for just a handful of viewers. And now she has written a 95-page book that is essentially a distillation of her previous book. Just even worse and a bit more desperate. Having read the book for a Digested Read, I would suggest you give it a miss. It reads as one extended cry for help. Still insisting that her budget was derailed by the Bank selling gilts the day before – something she had personally signed off – and that the establishment had been out to get her. She is like a broken record. Time for her family and friends to step in.
Tuesday
There are some footballers who will be for ever Tottenham. At least for me. There was Jimmy Greaves. He may have played for Chelsea, AC Milan and West Ham too but it is White Hart Lane for which he is most remembered. Likewise Gareth Bale. He won all sorts with Real Madrid but for Spurs fans he will always be one of us. Even if, in retirement, he seems at his happiest when he is playing golf. Then there is Harry Kane. Arguably the greatest of the three. The footballer who seemed to have less raw talent than Greaves and Bale but forged himself into the world’s best striker by sheer will and hard work.
I was lucky to see almost all of the home games – and many of the away ones – during Kane’s 11-year stay at the club. It would be nice to be able to say I spotted his ability from the off. But I didn’t. I assumed that, like many academy players who were being sent out on loan, he would eventually be shipped out to a lower league club. But when he did get his first-team chance, he scored goals. And kept on scoring them for a decade. A proper team player. As happy making goals for the team as he was knocking them in. Well, almost. A striker measures their seasons in goals. And he acknowledged the fans. When the team had played badly and lost, most of the rest of the players couldn’t wait to leave the pitch. Harry always made sure to thank the fans for their support.
Nor was I that sad when he joined Bayern Munich. I thought he had earned the move. He had given us more than enough and deserved the chance to play for a club that regularly won something. This week he won the Ballon d’Or and I couldn’t have been happier. Some may have thought it a reward for all the goals he scored for Bayern and England in the last year. I liked to think of it as the culmination of a journey. Come on you Spurs.
Wednesday
Budget day comes with its own set of rituals. First the photos of the chancellor holding up the red box outside No 11. In the Commons, the budget speech is always preceded by prime minister’s questions. Normally, PMQs are the high spot of the Commons week, but on budget day both the prime minister and the leader of the opposition know that no one is really listening and so they rather just go through the motions. No point in wasting your best lines if no one is going to write them up.
If the budget statement is a tough gig for reporters trying to make an instant assessment of its economic impact, it’s a nightmare for the leader of the opposition. She has to make an instant reply with only what’s already been leaked to back it up. So what you normally get is 20 minutes of “it’s all terrible” and “we wouldn’t have done any of it”. It’s only a day later, when economists and politicians have had a chance to go through the numbers line by line, that a proper assessment can be made.
John Healey isn’t everyone’s go-to guy as the standard bearer for Andy Burnham’s new brand of optimism. His is the voice of despair, a harbinger of the apocalypse. So it was hard going listening to him rattle off 98 not very big measures designed to help with the cost of living through what is forecast to be the toughest decade for the country on record. Healey said he was trying to give everyone some “breathing space”. Very Gen Z. Everyone wants some breathing space these days. But it sounded most that it was the government that needed the breathing space, with the tricky decisions on defence and the welfare bill parked until the next budget. Or the election. Whichever comes sooner.
One person who wasn’t in the Commons to hear the budget was Nigel Farage. He claimed someone had moved his prayer card. This sounded about as plausible as Burnham claiming he couldn’t make it to PMQs because Lucy Powell had taken his seat. If a party leader needs a seat, one can always be found. At the very least, a junior MP is told to make way. If Nige wasn’t in the Commons, it was because he couldn’t be bothered to turn up.
Thursday
It’s amazing how quickly the unbearable becomes bearable. When we first started to go to the Marsden in Sutton for Jill’s chemo, it all seemed overwhelming and terrifying. Today, as we went back for the latest round, it feels if not comfortable then reassuringly familiar. Jill sometimes sleeps, sometimes reads a book on her Kindle, during the infusions. I sit beside her and watch the proceedings in parliament and write the sketch and diary. Like now. The wifi is better than at home. The Oak Centre, where the treatment takes place, is modern and state-of-the-art. More like what I imagine the BA business class lounge at Heathrow to be. A friend whose husband has Alzheimer’s couldn’t believe just how welcoming the centre was. There’s so much more money being invested in cancer than there is in dementia. The best time for a chemo slot is first thing in the morning. That way you can be sure to get a parking slot – free if you are having treatment – and you can also get a window bay in the centre.
For the staff, nothing is ever too much trouble: you never feel as if you are being rushed and they are happy to talk through your fears. Every patient facing their worst nightmare and being held and understood. Made safe. You can always tell where the other patients are in their cycle. There was the Indian woman with the most beautiful hair, hoping the cold cap would do its job. It probably wouldn’t. Then there was the middle-aged bloke who arrived, said hello to the nurses and was asleep in minutes. You could hear the snores from the other end of the room. Best of all is the trolley offering free drinks and sandwiches. It’s staffed by volunteers. My favourite is Sandra who joined the team having been a patient first. Another friend, whose wife died of cancer a few years ago, still volunteers at the hospice where she had palliative care. He makes cocktails for everyone once a week. I call that style.
Friday
My bad. Having previously raved about Celebrity Traitors, I feel somewhat embarrassed to say I have changed my mind. Halfway through last Friday’s episode, I realised not just that I was no longer enjoying myself but also that the celebs were actively irritating me. The whole format suddenly felt tired. As if the show had come to the end of its shelf life mid-run. I no longer cared what happened during the missions, murders and banishments. I just wanted someone – anyone – to go as soon as possible. I didn’t want to hear one more celeb saying “I really love you. We’re going to be best friends for life” when the only time they are likely to meet in the future is on a panel show.
James Acaster’s round table admission of guilt was an epic failure of self-awareness. The claim that he had been playing the game as “faithful” traitor was comically absurd. He had lasted that long precisely because he had played a traitor’s game so well. Mind you, I am planning to watch to the end, out of sheer “I’ve started so I will finish” bloody-mindedness. But the producers do need to think of ways of refreshing the look for next year’s version or it won’t be just me who is bored. I still think there is potential for a politicians version. If you’re near Worcester on 26 November, come to my show at Huntingdon Hall. We can try to make it happen.
