article_title: MP Carla Lockhart quits DUP in Drumcree row
article_content:
MP Carla Lockhart quits DUP in Drumcree row
- Published
Carla Lockhart has quit the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) in a row over its response to the Drumcree parading dispute.
The MP for Upper Bann had been calling for the party to withdraw Stormont's deputy first minister to force First Minister Michelle O'Neill from their joint office.
Lockhart said she was leaving the DUP on a "point of principle" and would continue in the House of Commons as an independent unionist.
The fall-out comes after unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests on Garvaghy Road, which blocked a contentious Orange Order parade from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh.
O'Neill and several other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating the demonstrations, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.
Last week the DUP, which shares power with Sinn Féin in Northern Ireland's devolved government, announced it would block official engagements involving O'Neill in response to the fall-out.
The Sinn Féin vice-president has defended her involvement in the protests, saying it was the "right thing to do".
DUP leader Gavin Robinson stopped short of Lockhart's call to force O'Neill from office.
In an open letter to colleagues last week, Lockhart said it was the "only one credible option" and any kind of "graduated response" would be "insulting to those who have trusted us".
In a statement posted on her Facebook page on Monday, the MP said: "My first responsibility remains to the people of Upper Bann.
"You placed your trust in me, and I will continue to work every bit as hard for you, your family and our community."
Lockhart said it was a "sad day and a deeply personal decision" but her departure from the DUP was "on a point of principle".
"I cannot stand idly by whilst Sinn Féin wilfully ignores the rule of law and the promised profound consequences fail to materialise," she added.
Lockhart concluded that she would "look forward to working with all shades of unionism, elected or not, to advance the cause we love".
In a statement, the DUP said: "We regret Carla Lockhart's decision to resign from the Democratic Unionist Party. We thank her for her service to the party and recognise her work on behalf of the people of Upper Bann.
"The only winner out of further divisions within unionism is Sinn Féin."
It added: "We share the anger felt across unionism at Michelle O'Neill's actions. Our disagreement is over the course of action that will secure accountability and best serve Northern Ireland."
In a statement, Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister congratulated Lockhart on her decision.
"Having myself resigned from the DUP almost 20 years ago, I know this was not an easy decision. But for honest politicians principle matters more than position.
"The DUP's preference for 'O'Neill Must Stay' caused them to choose Michelle O'Neill over Carla Lockhart. Little wonder their electoral base is deserting them."
"Allister added that he looks forward "to working closely with Carla" and said it is "a hopeful day for unionism".
Analysis: Lockhart has been on a collision course for weeks
BBC News NI political editor Enda McClafferty
Cutting links with a party she first joined as a teenager was a big call for Carla Lockhart.
Her family ties to the DUP run deep prompting one colleague to say, "Carla bleeds the DUP".
But not anymore.
She has been on a collision course with the DUP leadership for weeks and now the "profound consequences" are being felt by the party.
Though she had some support within the DUP, she became a lone voice in her battle with the leadership.
She had the backing of Portadown Orangemen and many unionists, but Gavin Robinson crucially had the full support of the DUP officer and assembly teams.
He was able to face down the demands from his Upper Bann MP safe in the knowledge he had the numbers on his side.
Collapsing the executive without a budget agreed and running the risk of his party being blamed for a nurse's pay dispute strike was not a gamble he was willing to take.
But it has come at a cost for Robinson as he has now lost an MP from the DUP benches leaving just four for a party which once boasted ten members of parliament.
It has been a bruising time and one he needs to recover from quickly with just seven months until the assembly election.
The party has lost seats in the last two elections and now its losing seats in between elections.

article_title: Labour to end cooperation with Greens in 11 councils over ‘Zionism is racism’ policy
article_content:
Labour is to stop cooperating with the Green party in 11 councils across England following an ultimatum for Greens in local government to disown a new policy stating that “Zionism is racism”.
A statement from Labour said coalitions or other deals with Greens would stop in all local authorities where they had refused to condemn the policy motion passed at their party conference last month, which also called for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel.
Cooperation would cease on Arun, Derbyshire Dales, Havant, Lewes, Sheffield, Stafford, Warwick, Wealden, West Devon and West Suffolk councils, Labour said, and had already stopped in Runnymede because of the motion.
According to Labour, six Green council groups have condemned the motion, meaning deals will remain in place in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire, West Sussex. The same, it said, had happened with the West of England mayoralty, where the mayor is from Labour and the deputy mayor is a Green.
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, said the party had been clear that the motion, which has been met with unease by some Greens and has faced significant outside condemnation, “crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government”.
The Greens said they were “hugely disappointed” at the move, saying it would result in worse outcomes for residents in affected areas.
Phillipson said just over a fortnight ago that any Labour groups working with Green party politicians should review their agreements and end them unless they reject the motion, which Andy Burnham called “antisemitic”.
Some Greens, including the party’s former co-leader Adrian Ramsay, had called on local parties to renounce the policy, a stance that put him at odds with Zack Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales. The party’s official response was that the Greens would “not take lectures” from a Labour government that supplies arms to Israel.
The policy equates Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism. It also rejects a two-state solution and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”.
The Equality and Human Rights Commission has written to the Greens to seek more information about the motion “and assess its practical implications and potential impact”.
Phillipson said: “Any local power-sharing arrangement cannot come at the expense of upholding the moral obligation we have to stand up for everyone in our communities and the values we share.
“We are pleased that some local Green parties have rightly opted to disavow this policy and have called on their party’s leadership to do the same. It is disappointing that some local Green parties have not met the conditions Labour has set out. Labour continues to oppose this divisive policy and calls on the Green party to do the right thing and rescind it.”
She added: “The Labour party fought hard to root out antisemitism within our own party and ensure it had no place in our politics.”
In a joint statement, the Greens and the Local Government Association Green group said they were “hugely disappointed in moves designed by national parties to force local council leaders into jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents”.
They added: “Across the country, Green, Labour, independent and Liberal Democrat councillors have worked together to provide stable local government, protect services and deliver positive change. Leaders across these parties are rightly proud of what those partnerships have achieved.
“Those who issued ultimatums that destabilised power-sharing agreements have often ignored the judgments of their own local leaders, failed to respect the choices made by local voters, and are disrupting successful partnerships.”
Under the party’s direct democracy rules, policy is decided by party members. The Zionism motion won just over 1,000 votes, equating to approximately 0.4% of the total membership. It has been criticised by four of the Greens’ five MPs, as well as the former MP and party leader Caroline Lucas.
On Sunday, Ramsay said the Greens must fix their internal democracy to avoid a takeover by the hard left, saying some new members “might be more at home” in Your Party or the Socialist Workers party.

article_title: No10 defends flight to Manchester to collect Andy Burnham
article_content:
No10 defends flight to Manchester to collect Andy Burnham
- Published
Downing Street has defended sending the official UK government plane to Manchester to pick up Andy Burnham, rather than the prime minister travelling to London in advance of the flight.
The Airbus A321neo departed London Stansted Airport for Saint John's, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, at about 06:00 on Monday without the prime minister on board.
Half an hour later it landed in Manchester to collect Burnham, before taking off again to cross the Atlantic for the Commonwealth heads of government summit (Chogm).
The trip sparked a backlash on social media with some questioning the value for money, but Number 10 said security, cost and "operational requirements" were all factored in.
The official UK government plane, carrying the registration G-GBNI, is often used by British prime ministers and royals for overseas trips.
Flight tracking data shows the jet made a 35 minute flight on Monday morning to Manchester, where it spent an hour and a half on the tarmac, before taking off at 08:00 to head to St John's.
In response, Tory MP and shadow cabinet minister Neil O'Brien accused Labour of managing to "waste taxpayers' money and jet fuel so they can posture".
"You have to pay through the nose for energy and fuel to pursue their Net Zero obsession... But when it's them, the rules are different," he added.
Asked why Burnham had not travelled to London instead, his official spokesperson told reporters: "The prime minister's travel arrangements reflect where he was carrying out official government business at the end of last week.
"As you know, he spent the day in Scotland on Friday; returned to Manchester to work from Number 10 North on Friday evening."
Burnham will meet Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday, coming at the end of the King's Caribbean tour, with the prime minister saying he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery.
It is unclear how much the London to Manchester trip cost, or whether there is a precedent for it, as the Cabinet Office's transparency data for the plane only lists overseas trips.
None of Burnham's trips are listed yet, as the data is published quarterly.
The latest data for April to June 2026 shows then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer made four round trips on the jet, including a £121,000 trip to Armenia with 21 officials for the European Political Community Summit.
A trip from the UK to Paris in April cost £39,000.
The precise cost of each flight can depend on how many officials were with the prime minister, fuel costs and other factors such as landing fees.
It is also unclear whether transporting the prime minister, his security detail and officials by train or road transport from Manchester to Stansted would have been much cheaper.
A previous version of the UK government official plane, an RAF Voyager, was given a £900,000 repaint job in 2020 before being replaced with a different plane.

article_title: Half-witted at best, a people-pleaser at worst: step forward, Chris Philp | John Crace
article_content:
Better late than never. It had seemed as if some apologies from the prime minister were more sincere than others. The one that he has planned to deliver for Britain’s role in the slave trade at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua fell on the right side of genuine. There had been no need to make one at that time. Indeed Kemi Badenoch saw it as a sign of weakness. There again, she would refuse to apologise for running someone over on a pedestrian crossing. Somehow it would have turned out to be the victim’s fault.
Andy Burnham’s apology for not being able to turn up in the Commons to lend support to his home secretary might rather fall into the “sorry, not sorry” category. Making life more difficult for migrants was more one for Keir Starmer’s legacy than part of the new government’s agenda. Andy couldn’t have been more thrilled to be on a plane as Shabana Mahmood stood up to make her statement on “earned settlement”. It was almost as if the statement had been timed for when Burnham was away. At the very least, it was the perfect coincidence. If not divine intervention.
Even on Monday lunchtime, the prime minister’s spokesperson was refusing to give Burnham’s wholehearted support for Shabana’s proposed changes to indefinite leave to remain (ILR). Even after he and other cabinet colleagues had managed to water them down a little. The best that Andy would say was that “It was a good thing that immigration had fallen”.
Nothing about the home secretary’s role in this. Nothing that hinted at an endorsement. It felt as if Mahmood had been rather hung out to dry. Even more so when Angela Rayner, another of the home secretary’s critics, pointedly left the chamber by the far door so she wouldn’t have to look the home secretary in the eye after housing and communities departmental questions. No need for an awkward “That cup of tea isn’t going to drink itself”.
But at the very last minute – as if by magic – a short, unequivocal message of support from Burnham was released. “People want to see an immigration system based on control, contribution, and which rewards those who play by the rules,” he said. Shabana was not being abandoned, after all. Not that she wouldn’t have coped if she had. Even if she had not come to the house with Lou Haigh and Lucy Powell as her outriders, Mahmood is more than capable of looking after herself. She is a woman who knows her mind.
The statement was all much as we had expected. A reaffirmation of previous proposals with a few important concessions to Burnham, Rayner and backbenchers from the left of the Labour party. There would be a five-year route to settlement for care workers who had arrived prior to March 2025: a 10-year process for those who had arrived afterwards. Otherwise all was as it had been, plus or minus a couple of tweaks. New safe routes for refugees and a 30-year wait for those who had arrived in the country illegally. All with the usual caveats of speaking English, national insurance contributions and no criminal record.
We haven’t seen much of the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, in recent months. A relief to us all. Partly because even he had begun to have a sense of his own ridiculousness, partly because immigration had ceased to be such a hot topic for the country. There was more than a sense that the government was legislating for a problem that no longer really existed. Legal immigration has fallen to the tens of thousands a year from its high point of one million during Boris Johnson’s time in office. And the small boat crossings have more than halved. But Shabana doesn’t believe in taking chances. Happy to double-lock the doors to the country.
But this was The Philpster’s time to shine. To remind us all that he is at best half witted; at his worst, a people-pleaser par excellence. The ultimate nose in search of a bum. And so we got Philp at his most absurd. A joy to behold. A performance to make the whole statement worthwhile. A chance to give the entire Commons its Proustian madeleine moment. The Unbearable Lightness of Chris. Just when you think you’ve seen it all, The Philpster searches for the futility inside himself.
It had taken a whole year for Mahmood to establish her credibility, Philp declared. And she had destroyed it all in the space of her 12-minute statement. There will come a time when Chris compiles a show reel of all his political lowlights. A chance for him and his therapist to try to make sense of his career. How can someone of so little ability have come so far? Would Kemi really be daft enough to make him her home secretary if she won an election? Luckily she will never have to answer that one.
But know one thing. The Philpster’s reply will feature heavily in any lowlights reel. Above all else for his lack of self-awareness. The government should be ashamed of itself. This was virtually an open-doors policy. There would be foreigners everywhere if we weren’t careful. You could not be more detached from reality if you tried. It had been the Tory government that had presided over the mass wave of immigration. A Tory government that had failed to secure the country’s borders. And who had been a Home Office minister while this was going on? Step forward, Chris.
Mahmood scarcely bothered to grace The Philpster’s delusions with a reply. She would have been doing him a favour to offer him a prescription of some anti-psychotic drugs. Nor was it just Labour who put the boot in. The Tory father of the house, Edward Leigh, is becoming increasingly disinhibited in opposition. Determined to make up for a decade or more of supporting a failing government by telling inconvenient truths.
The former Tory government should be holding its head in shame, Leigh said. And anyone who had been in the Home Office should wear sackcloth and ashes. It was a complete evisceration of The Philpster and his empty words. Enough to almost make you feel sorry for Chris. Almost. Philp gestured half-heartedly towards Robert Jenrick, another former Home Office minister. Anything to try and mitigate the shame.
For the rest of the statement, various Labour backbenchers protested about the lack of fairness to immigrants; the retrospective nature of some proposals. Shabana really wasn’t bothered. She had given away as much as she was going to. The Labour party would just have to live with it. Elsewhere, Nigel Farage and Zia Yusuf were holding a press conference on ILR. The government had been weak, they claimed. The only answer was to deport every immigrant. It would have been nice if, to show he meant what he was saying, if Zia had promised to deport himself. Not for being brown or Muslim. But for being thoroughly unpleasant.

article_title: Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked
article_content:
Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked
- Published
The Reform UK leader of Leicestershire County Council has announced he is standing down after comments he made about staff redundancies were leaked online.
Dan Harrison announced on Monday that he would be stepping down from the role he has held since May 2025.
He said he had made the decision after taking advice from senior Reform colleagues, and added deputy council leader Kevin Crook had taken over as acting leader.
It comes after Harrison had apologised after being recorded saying 76 council solicitors would be made redundant, branding them "incompetent", before saying "what I want to look at now is the women", in remarks which were then released on social media.
In a statement, Harrison said it had been the "honour of his life" to lead the county council's first Reform administration.
Harrison has said he will remain as a councillor, representing the Ashby-de-la-Zouch division.
The Conservative opposition at County Hall had called for Harrison to resign after his comments about staff were leaked.
In the recording, Harrison said: "There's 76 solicitors will be made redundant.
"We'll buy in the service, because [they are] incompetent. They're not doing a good job.
"What I want to look at now is the women so it is ongoing, I would like it to be at great pace but I can tell you now if we suddenly drove massive redundancies the liberals would walk away."
Earlier on Monday, Harrison had told the BBC he would not be stepping down - but he later said he made his decision after talking to Crook and group whip Andrew Hamilton-Gray.
He had apologised over the remarks, which were made on Tuesday during a Reform party meeting.
Despite his apology, Harrison had insisted his remarks had been taken out of context.
Harrison said: "I would like to apologise unreservedly to the staff and officers of the county council for any hurt, distress or offence caused by the publication of these comments, which were made during a heated meeting with the expectation of privacy and confidentiality.
"However, I would like to stress that these discussions were just that, and I have not given any instruction or direction to officers in these matters and that there has not been any discussion nor agreement on these issues with officers."
He added: "I unequivocally reject any suggestion that staffing decisions are being taken based on gender.
"The comments made in that meeting were taken completely out of context."
Position 'untenable'
Before Harrison's resignation, the council's 15 Tory councillors had called for an emergency vote to try to remove him from the leader's role.
Group leader of the Conservative group, Deborah Taylor, said: "That was not a decision we took lightly.
"The serious concerns raised over recent days, particularly around the treatment of council employees and the comments contained in leaked recordings, left us feeling that his position had become untenable.
"His resignation brings an end to his leadership, but it does not mean those concerns should simply be forgotten.
"There are still questions that deserve answers, and it is important that the council learns from what has happened."
The Reform group remains the largest party on the authority, and runs it as a minority administration.
In a statement, Jeevun Sandher and Amanda Hack - Labour MPs for Loughborough and North West Leicestershire respectively - said: "Since taking office in 2025, the Reform UK administration has become increasingly embroiled in controversy and scandal, rather than focusing on delivering for the residents of Leicestershire.
"This is far from an isolated incident. Just last week, councillor [Joseph] Boam was found to have breached the council's own code of conduct through his actions against the former monitoring officer, while other Reform councillors have also been forced to apologise to residents over their behaviour. All of this in less than two years.
"Leicestershire residents deserve better."

article_title: A decade of magical thinking since Brexit has taught me that it’s always OK to hope for better | Zoe Williams
article_content:
However sunny your disposition, it wears you down, 10 straight years of being asked to accept facts about Brexit that aren’t true: 52% as an “overwhelming majority”; a flaky, half-baked referendum as the endpoint of purest democracy; the severance of a complicated trading and geopolitical relationship that took decades to build as the dawn of a new prosperity. All such nonsense, all delivered with such conviction, by such a wide variety of sources, many of them self-describing as impartial, that in the end you just surrender to it. None of it magically becomes true, don’t be silly. It’s more that you come to accept that everyone else talks nonsense now.
Nobody get too excited – just because Andy Burnham has reopened a debate that upside-down world said couldn’t be reopened, it doesn’t mean the UK is on the brink of coming to its senses. I have no idea what’s going to happen; all I can say for certain is that times have changed more than I realised. The pro-Brexit crew have updated their arguments. They no longer say leaving the EU will bring untold riches, and they never even namecheck all the control we were meant to have taken back. They rarely mention any immigration benefits because that unwieldy issue now has a life of its own – or, to put that more simply, it turns out that in or out of the European Union, we can still fight about our borders like rats in a sack.
Instead, they have a new narrative, and these are its contours. Remain sympathisers are apparently very divided. Some of us want freedom of movement, especially for young people, while others of us just want our trading relationships rebuilt with our nearest gigantic market. Different remainers again wish for greater collaboration on security and defence with nations who share our values. Those who can be trusted, for example, to oppose Vladimir Putin and his war of aggression, rather than opposing him on a Tuesday and calling him a great guy by Thursday. Some of us just miss the days when we made coherent, continent-wide decisions about the climate emergency. Given that degrees of global heating observe no nationality and pick no favourites, given that people who believe in scientific evidence tend to get on quite well together, however stark that evidence is, it would be quite relaxing to club together, no?
All these different interest groups, I’ve heard it said by those who defend the status quo, can cooperate from a distance, but sooner or later, the remain coalition will fall apart. Here, I rediscover the certainty I thought I’d lost for ever in the post-2016 melee: there is absolutely no way will we fall apart. We are a match made in heaven. I have a fair idea which of those issues I care about the most, between climate, young people, defence and trade, but seriously, this is like choosing my favourite song on Surfer Rosa (the Pixies album), or adjudicating my favourite guest at the wedding of, say, my sister. In the joy of the moment, my preferences could take a backseat. I’d really just want everyone to have a good time.
There’s one other new rhetorical strain: Brexit supporters point to Europe and say, that place is on fire. It’s not a blip caused by arson-happy French protesters, nor the housing-impoverished Spanish, it’s not a peculiarity of new German political movements, nor rage at the policing tactics of the Portuguese. Everyone, everywhere, is absolutely furious. Would this not be a good time to keep our distance? This might be the weakest argument of all, since all it underscores is that the cost of living crisis affects us all; the wars in Ukraine and Iran have hit everyone; the long tail of the financial crash and subsequent austerity has left no one unscathed; the disfigurement of the housing market was only temporarily a London thing, a Madrid thing – sooner or later, it would be an everywhere thing, and later’s where we are. There is no isolationist course that protects you from civic unrest, unless you can miraculously protect yourself from the conditions driving it. And those conditions were not made in Strasbourg.
Again, if a decade of magical thinking has taught me anything, it’s that predictions are futile, and however absurd an argument looks, you can’t bank on toppling it. But these fresh lines are so weak it’s almost endearing.

article_title: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
article_content:
What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
- Published
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has set out plans to overhaul immigration rules.
Proposals to change the requirements to qualify for permanent settlement in the UK were first outlined in detail in November 2025, when Mahmood was home secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government.
Following a consultation, external, Mahmood has now announced her final decision on what changes should be taken forward.
- Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes 
  - Published8 hours ago
- Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers 
  - Published1 hour ago
What is settlement and indefinite leave to remain?
Indefinite leave to remain (ILR) – also known as settlement – gives someone the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like.
Under the current system, people with ILR can also apply for benefits if they are eligible.
People who have lived in the UK for 12 months after being given ILR can apply for British citizenship, if they also meet other requirements, external.
How will the new rules affect migrants?
Under the government's plans, the standard length of time migrants will have to live in the UK to qualify for permanent settlement will double from five to 10 years.
Under this 10-year pathway, applicants must have earned at least £12,571 for five of the seven years immediately before being granted settlement.
However, there will be a shorter qualifying period of five years for certain groups, including:
- People who earned at least £50,271 for three of five years immediately before applying for settlement
- Care workers who earned at least £25,000 a year while meeting their visa conditions and arrived in the UK before May 2025
- "Skilled" public service workers, such as doctors, nurses and teachers
- Other health and education public service workers who fall below this skill level, for example nursing auxiliaries and teaching assistants, if they arrived in the UK before May 2025
- People from Hong Kong who hold British National (Overseas) status
People earning over £125,141 a year, as well as "highly skilled" migrants such as those on Global Talent or Innovator Founder visas, will qualify after three years.
Migrants who have claimed certain benefits or breached immigration rules will only be able to settle after at least 20 years.
To qualify for settlement, migrants will also have to meet other conditions including:
- Have no criminal record
- Speak English to a high standard
- Owe no debt to the taxpayer
- Earn at least £12,571 a year for at least three years, aligned with the threshold for paying income tax
What about refugees?
There will be a different set of rules for refugees – people who have been granted asylum in the UK because they are unable to return to their own country as they fear persecution.
Refugees who arrived in the UK through an official government scheme will qualify for settlement after five years.
However, other refugees will need to wait 10 years and either work or study.
Those who do not work or study will need to wait 20 years.
Refugees who arrived in the UK by small boat or another illegal route will have to wait 20 years if they work or study, and 30 years if they don't.
Will migrants already in the UK be affected?
The changes will apply to migrants who are already in the UK but not those who have already been granted settlement.
What about family members?
A partner who arrives with someone who then applies for ILR will be able to settle at the same time, as long as they meet the relevant requirements.
However, a partner who joins later will need to complete the same qualifying residence period before they are eligible for settlement.
Eligible couples will be able to combine their earnings to meet the minimum income requirement.
The household income threshold will be £25,142 – twice the individual minimum income requirement.
Children under 18 will continue to be able to settle with their parents.
They will be exempt from the income, government debt, English language and Life in the UK test requirements, but will remain subject to the relevant suitability and criminality requirements.
Young adults aged 18 to 24, who remain dependant on their family, will also continue to be able to settle alongside them.
They will be expected to meet all the adult mandatory requirements but not the individual income requirement.
Someone who is aged 25 or over when their family becomes eligible for settlement will be expected to qualify independently.
Eligible partners, parents and children of British citizens will continue to qualify for settlement after five years.

article_title: Rachel Reeves and the Starmerites are back – and they’re pointing out how little has changed | Gaby Hinsliff
article_content:
Rachel Reeves wants you to know she thinks Britain’s future belongs in Europe. She would also like to mention that she “absolutely” got all the big calls right as chancellor, even if there were a few things she would have done differently, and that John Healey’s budget last week would have been far harder for him if she hadn’t put in so much of the groundwork.
The gist of her argument in last weekend’s Sunday papers – previewing a lecture at Harvard University today, reflecting on her time in power – was essentially that if anyone imagines Andy Burnham somehow invented pro-Europeanism and putting more money in people’s pockets, they can think again.
Reeves was clearly devastated by losing a job she loved, and her return to the fray after a summer of quietly licking her wounds has inevitably sparked speculation over whether she now seeks a comeback. But her timing is acute enough to suggest that this goes a little deeper, coming as it does days after a deliberately low-key budget that left some Labour MPs wondering what happened to the much-hyped end of neoliberalism.
How much of the Burnham agenda is really new, and how much is essentially the old Starmer one, repackaged with rather more warmth, charm and political skill?
Inside what’s left of the old inner circle, loyalists point out that Reeves and Starmer were both fervent remainers at heart and of course they would have loved to be back inside the EU one day; it’s just that the time wasn’t yet right to talk about it when they ran for office.
Similarly, the package of sanctions on Israeli settlers that the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced in September, alongside an apology for what he considered Starmer had got wrong on Gaza, wasn’t a dramatic break with the past but essentially the measures his predecessor, Yvette Cooper (now health secretary), had spent her last weeks at the Foreign Office working up, which couldn’t be published until a new prime minister was formally in place.
Starmer’s former close lieutenant Darren Jones, meanwhile, is openly arguing that this administration’s answer to a looming crisis in defence spending – basically shunting the hard questions about funding it into next year’s spending review – is “what Keir and Rachel were going to do”, if only they hadn’t been forced out by the very same John Healey resigning as defence secretary in protest at something remarkably like the strategy he’s now pursuing. Starmer himself, who has kept his counsel over the summer, made a rare public intervention in Dublin last week to warn pointedly that the US withdrawal from European defence will outlast the Trump era, and Europe cannot afford to be left exposed.
If the Starmerites are understandably smarting at what some see as history being rewritten by the winners, some are also failing to recognise their part in their own downfall. Starmer was ultimately ousted by his own MPs because they wereexasperated by his failure to lead and sensed the country had turned inexorably against him.
Burnham has shown not only that he can take decisions – across Whitehall there seems to be more clarity now about what Downing Street wants – but that he can build the emotional bond with the public his predecessor couldn’t, without which even the boldest moves wouldn’t have worked. He might only have moved the needle fractionally on issues such as Palestine or Europe, where the manifesto red lines effectively mean nothing significant can change that wouldn’t have under Starmer, at least this side of a general election. But each time he has done just enough to achieve the political impact that Starmer was seemingly chasing but couldn’t pull off. Where his predecessor could never quite get the dosage right, Burnham seems to instinctively know how far to go: it’s the difference between a novice cook clinging fixedly to a recipe that isn’t quite right, and an experienced one who tastes and adjusts the seasoning as they go. And judging by the polling, it’s working.
Yet still some MPs are anxious to hear a bigger vision of where Burnham wants the country to go than fixing social care and banning people listening to loud music on the bus. Since there wasn’t one in the budget, all eyes are on the 10-year plan, now expected some time in December.
Burnham has made much of promising to give Britain some breathing space after years of rolling crises and financial struggle. But the small, popular changes he has offered so far – £100 off your energy bills, a No 10 North office in Manchester – have also been in part about buying some breathing space for himself while he gets to grips with bigger and potentially more controversial challenges, from welfare reforms to defusing a Labour revolt over Shabana Mahmood’s plan to make migrants wait longer for the right to settlement.
A confident and relaxed debut has masked the fact that transitioning from mayor to prime minister was always going to be a steep learning curve, and that he didn’t get the long summer of planning that his team had wanted to prepare for power. But now that period of grace is coming to an end, along with a period of silence from those he ousted, some of whom are keen to defend their legacies. By Christmas we should know whether Burnham is offering genuine new thinking in British politics, or something more like the old kind, regifted.

article_title: Chris Mason: Home secretary to face scrutiny over changes to rules for legal migrants
article_content:
Chris Mason: Home secretary to face scrutiny over changes to rules for legal migrants
- Published
At the heart of the debate around legal migration are contested notions of fairness.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has talked of her parents coming to the UK from rural Kashmir. Now, this daughter of immigrants is responsible for reshaping the very system that brought them here decades ago – and doing so in a way that both her party and the country regard as fair.
"Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did. And fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young," is how Mahmood put it in her speech to the Labour Party conference in September.
The debate has come at a time of huge legal immigration in recent years and during a period in which Reform UK have been particularly prominent in the national political conversation.
Both of these things are factors in Labour wanting to be seen to be taking people's concerns about the scale of arrivals seriously.
But her political opponents smell what they see as weakness and retreat, with parts of her original plan now being revised, as the BBC's Iain Watson reported over the weekend.
It is worth examining this policy throughout the last year or so, as it is instructive in how we have arrived at today's announcement.
- Mahmood to set out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants 
  - Published1 hour ago
In November last year, Mahmood set out a plan called "a fairer pathway to settlement".
The idea was opinions on her instincts would be sought in a consultation. And boy, were there plenty of opinions offered.
Around 200,000 people contributed to the consultation, of which 140,000 responses came from visa holders themselves I'm told.
"It's been a colossal exercise and a genuine one," is how one Whitehall source put it to me, claiming: "We have taken the time to get this right."
Or is the real truth that they have buckled under political pressure from their own side – and a change of prime minister?
Mahmood said last year that she felt compelled to act because "between 2021 and 2024, we have seen net migration of an additional 2.6 million people. Around one in every 30 people in this country today arrived in these four years." It is what critics have labelled "the Boriswave", named for the changes made under former Prime Minister Boris Johnson.
And, Mahmood argued, it was important to act with urgency, as very soon significant numbers of those recent arrivals would start qualifying for indefinite leave to remain, or ILR.
"Migrants on lower wages who bring non-working dependants and children are likely to present significant fiscal costs to the UK.
"It is therefore right that we apply more stringent controls for this group before they qualify for settled status," she said, adding: "Under our current rules, they will usually qualify for benefits payments and council housing five years after arrival.
"As the majority of this group began arriving from 2022 onwards, this is currently set to begin in 2027. We consult here on a separate baseline qualifying period, of 15 years, for this group."
But plenty within the Labour Party and beyond were uncomfortable – and yes, they cited fairness, or the perceived lack of it, in mounting their criticisms.
As the now Housing Secretary Angela Rayner put it in March, before she returned to government, the ideas were "un-British" because they involved "moving the goalposts" - migrants who had arrived in good faith under one set of rules would have their future in the UK determined by the new ones.
Associated costs
Just a few weeks before Rayner's intervention, Mahmood had doubled down on her plans. Addressing the centre left IPPR think tank, she said "in just four years, this country experienced levels of migration it had previously seen across four decades.
"It was not just the scale, but also the nature of that change that was so destabilising."
There was more, and with a big number attached.
"We have never, in the history of this country, had so much low-skilled migration in so little time.
"We estimate, based on findings from the Migration Advisory Committee, that the lifetime cost to the taxpayer will be £10bn. That figure would be paid for by working people in this country."
She added: "It is an affront to the idea of fairness within our migration system."
Incidentally, the £10bn figure is contested by some – or at least placed in a wider context.
The aforementioned IPPR argue that the original plans were "never in reality going to create a £10bn long-term saving, given they were meant to delay care workers' eligibility for ILR rather than prevent them from settling altogether.
"Delaying ILR would save money on welfare, whereas the £10bn figure includes much broader long run costs once care workers enter retirement, claim the state pension, and make greater use of health and social care."
Nonetheless, Mahmood's message in March left senior Conservatives privately agreeing with her – and struck by her willingness to be unflinching in her approach to the subject.
But around 100 of her Labour colleagues were not happy – and making their views known publicly.
By the time I found myself in the dusty car park of a sports club near Wigan in May, waiting to talk to an ambitious by-election candidate by the name of Andy Burnham, it was clear changes were highly likely.
He told me it was important to "work hard to get the balance right" but that the "broad thrust" of what the home secretary was doing "is right".
"Broad thrust" will be the words that account for the gap between what Mahmood used to say and what she is saying today.
The Conservatives and others will seize upon the change. The Tories will argue it amounts to an "excruciating U-turn" as one senior figure described it to me, claiming it would be "deeply personally embarrassing" for the home secretary.
They also ponder how the government will choose to make the changes, as they believe if primary legislation isn't used to do it – such as via an amendment to the Immigration and Asylum Bill currently before parliament – the plans could be successfully challenged in court.
Mahmood will argue she has tried to finally arrive at a policy the widest range of people may see as fair.
We will see and hear the range of reaction she provokes in the coming hours and days.

article_title: US reportedly strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island as Vance voices optimism about a deal
article_content:
The US launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday, according to reports in US media, hours after US vice-president JD Vance said he was optimistic diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction.
The strikes were reported as being “defensive”, and not thought to be a signal of a return to full hostilities, but came on the eve of crucial midterm elections in which Donald Trump’s Republican party is expected to be punished by voters for the cascading effect the war has had on the US cost of living.
When asked earlier on Monday whether he had considered resuming strikes on Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump replied “no”.
Several explosions were heard on Qeshm Island on Monday evening, according to Iranian state media, with local outlets describing their cause as unclear. The strikes – first reported by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) – targeted surface to air missiles being used against US assets, according to Reuters and the Associated Press.
US Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Reuters news agency, and the WSJ described the attacks as part of a series of strikes carried out against the country in recent weeks that have not been made public.
The paper said that sources suggested the recent strikes have been carried out on a smaller scale and purposefully kept secret by the Trump administration so as not to signal any intent of resuming the military campaign against Iran.
The US has targeted Qeshm Island on multiple occasions throughout the war. Positioned in the mouth of the strait of Hormuz, the island has been used in the past to launch attacks on shipping in the waterway.
Despite attacks having ceased in recent weeks, Iran has continued to enforce its closure of the strait by targeting oil tankers, shipping containers and other vessels attempting to transit the waterway.
If confirmed, the attack would mark the first publicly known strike by the US on Iran in weeks. On Monday Vance said that he and Trump were optimistic about securing a deal with Iran, after Tehran revealed indirect negotiations with Washington.
“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance told reporters. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”
Speaking to Fox News hours before the polls opened in the US on Tuesday, Trump continued to play down the significance of the conflict and its effects on the US economy.
“There’s no war raging. It could happen if they don’t make a deal, but they want to make a deal very badly and there’s a very good chance we make a deal.”
Speaking from Washington in his closing message of the midterms campaign, Trump hailed a sharp drop in oil prices that came as his administration touted a renewed diplomatic efforts being made to end the war. Rising petrol prices have caused by the war have become a signature issue of the midterm elections, with polls showing voters likely to punish Republicans for the effect on the cost of living.

article_title: Most Israelis think settlements policy should change to avoid more sanctions, poll finds
article_content:
The UK government’s decision to impose a ban on trade in goods from illegal settlements was not decisive in how Israelis voted in their general election, but a majority think the Israeli government’s settlements policy should change if it is going to lead to further sanctions, a new poll of Israelis shows.
There had been fierce criticism of the UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s decision in September to impose a trade ban and wider sanctions on illegal settlements, with some claiming it would drive Israeli voters into the arms of Benjamin Netanyahu.
A survey last month by Israeli social research group aChord shows overall support for foreign sanctions on violent settlers in the West Bank, but there was little support for the UK’s ban on trade with goods from illegal settlements, with many fearing it would end up being extended across Israel.
The survey is unique in showing how much the tougher line on Israel adopted by Britain and some foreign states was affecting the thinking of Israeli voters, and the extent to which Israelis thought it was a response to Israel’s actions or born of hostility to Israel, or even antisemitism.
The survey showed that three-quarters of supporters of the bloc backing Netanyahu said UK sanctions and trade ban policies towards Israel did not affect their vote at all, and to the small extent that they changed anyone’s vote, they shifted voters both ways, leaving no detectable net effect.
Just over three-quarters of all those surveyed (76) – had heard of the UK government announcement on settlements, even if 18 % had only heard the broad headline. Four-fifths of those that were aware of the announcement knew that the policy applied to the West Bank, and not the whole of Israel.
Israel’s relations with the west were “important or very important” to 60% of the supporters of the Change bloc of parties backing Gadi Eisenkot in deciding their vote. But even then these relationships came fifth in importance in a proffered group of six motives for voting. Only 30% of supporters of the Netanyahu bloc said relations with the west mattered in the same way.
But 71% of voters for the opposition Change bloc said the Israeli government should adapt its settlements policy to avoid an escalation of sanctions. Only 14% of Netanyahu bloc voters agreed, most saying instead that the government should continue the policy “whatever the price”.
A plurality of the public – 50% – said the settlement and construction policy in the West Bank should be adjusted to avoid sanctions escalation and international isolation, with 71% of Eisenkot bloc supporters agreeing to this proposition. Support for a change in the policy is strongest among supporters of the Arab parties.
The finding prompted Hannah Weisfeld, the director of the British-Jewish organisation Yachad, to claim the research “illustrates that the Israeli public certainly recognises that if there is not a policy shift in relation to settlement enterprise, the international community is likely to try to create an incentive to shift things from the outside. If anything, that highlights the importance of UK and other allies taking action that targets the occupation.”
The survey also showed that concerns about foreign sanctions are highest when voters feel they will suffer a high personal price. Only 36% of all those surveyed agreed that the settlement policy should continue even if sanctions on banks that finance construction in illegal settlements led either to higher interest rates, difficulties in transferring money abroad, or using credit cards abroad. The poll suggests that the more people feel they will be damaged personally, the more they oppose the settlement policy.
A majority of all Israelis surveyed (52%) support sanctions on individual violent settlers, so long as the sanctions are imposed only on those acting violently, but 70% of Netanyahu bloc supporters oppose foreign sanctions in all circumstances.
There is much less widespread support for the policy of banning the import of goods from the illegal settlement, with 63% of all those surveyed opposing the ban and 26% either supporting the measure outright, or saying they would if it were underlined that the ban would not apply to goods from outside settlements.

article_title: Путін панікує перед виборами у США: конгресмен пояснив причину
article_content:
Путін панікує перед виборами у США: конгресмен пояснив причину
На думку американського законодавця, Кремль прагне домогтися поступок від України до можливої зміни більшості в Конгресі США.
Російський диктатор Володимир Путін поспішає досягти вигідної Москві домовленості щодо України, оскільки проміжні вибори у США можуть обмежити можливості Дональда Трампа впливати на політику підтримки Києва.
Таку оцінку висловив конгресмен-демократ від Каліфорнії, член Комітету Палати представників зі збройних сил Джордж Вайтсайдс в авторській колонці для The Hill.
За його прогнозом, республіканці можуть втратити контроль над Палатою представників за результатами голосування 3 листопада. Вайтсайдс вважає, що це посилить можливості Конгресу протидіяти тиску на Україну після початку роботи нового складу в січні.
Саме цим автор пояснює спроби Вашингтона й Москви прискорити домовленості та схилити Київ до поступок.
Окрему увагу конгресмен приділив українським ударам по російських нафтопереробних заводах. На його думку, ця кампанія створює серйозні проблеми для Кремля, а прагнення припинити атаки свідчить про їхню ефективність.
Вайтсайдс розкритикував домовленість Трампа з Путіним щодо постачання російського дизельного пального на американський і світовий ринки. Він вважає, що такий крок забезпечує Москві додаткові доходи під час війни.
Автор також послався на повідомлення медіа про погрози обмежити обмін розвідданими з Україною, можливе ненадання попереджень про російські ракетні удари та обмеження роботи терміналів Starshield. Ці дії він розцінює як інструменти примусу Києва до поступок.
За оцінкою Вайтсайдса, зміна більшості в Конгресі може створити можливості для законодавчого захисту обміну розвідданими, багаторічної військової допомоги Україні та збереження заморожених російських активів.
Конгресмен закликав Україну та європейських союзників зберігати стійкість до кінця року. Він переконаний, що затяжна війна проти України зі стабільним фінансуванням становитиме для Путіна дедалі більшу проблему.

article_title: Переговори України та РФ за посередництва США в Абу-Дабі: Німеччина та Британія пояснили свій скептицизм
article_content:
Переговори України та РФ за посередництва США в Абу-Дабі: Німеччина та Британія пояснили свій скептицизм
Очільники оборонних відомств двох країн наголосили, що мир має бути прийнятним для України, а Європа повинна брати участь у переговорах.
Міністри оборони Німеччини та Великої Британії Борис Пісторіус і Вес Стрітінг скептично оцінили перспективи майбутніх переговорів України, США та Росії в Абу-Дабі.
Про це вони заявили на спільній пресконференції в Берліні 2 листопада, повідомляє Укрінформ.
Пісторіус пояснив свою позицію досвідом попередніх років: за його словами, після численних дискусій і переговорів російські бомбардування та атаки на Україну лише посилювалися.
Він також наголосив, що проблема полягає не в Зеленському, а подальших дій тепер мають ужити американський президент і Путін.
На переконання глави Міноборони ФРН, тривалий і справедливий мир, який гарантує суверенітет та територіальну цілісність України, неможливий без участі європейців. Саме від європейських держав очікують участі в реалізації майбутніх домовленостей.
Стрітінг підтримав оцінку німецького колеги. Він зазначив, що партнери прагнуть дипломатичного прориву, однак завершення війни має відбутися на прийнятних для України умовах.
«Не може бути жодного рішення щодо України без України», — наголосив британський міністр.
Він додав, що європейські країни безпосередньо зацікавлені в результатах переговорів, адже братимуть участь у забезпеченні гарантій безпеки. Стрітінг також підкреслив, що саме Путін повинен припинити розв’язану ним агресивну війну.
Нагадаємо, Стів Віткофф повідомив, що переговори на робочому рівні між Україною та Росією за посередництва США відбудуться 10–11 листопада в Абу-Дабі.
Нагадаємо, що раніше йшлося про переговори без Китаю: чому Пекін усунувся від самітів щодо України
На тлі відсутності зовнішнього тиску на Кремль з боку Пекіна та відсутності власної дипломатичної гри, мирні переговори ризикують перетворитися на черговий тупиковий сценарій.

article_title: Migration is a moral issue for Burnham – but is he trying to please everyone?
article_content:
While out on the campaign trail in Makerfield, Andy Burnham gave a glimpse into where he might land on Labour’s plans for immigration reform, which had already been decried by the left of the party as unfair while described on the right as electorally necessary.
Asked what he thought of Reform’s attack on “open borders Andy” – Nigel Farage’s early attempt to define him as soft on migration – the then Manchester mayor dismissed the charge as “ridiculous” and went on the defensive.
“I’m not like that. You know me. I was in the Home Office under Tony Blair, and actually, it was my job to return people. That was my specific role,” he said while out knocking on doors in the constituency.
“I used to have to travel to governments around the world and persuade them to take back planes of people who had come here with no basis to stay, so you know, I’ve never have been shy of getting to grips with these difficult issues.”
But Burnham wasn’t just pitching to the Reform-inclined voters he needed to win the seat; he was already charting whatever path he might need to take if he made it to Downing Street.
While he was supportive of attempts by the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, to limit legal and illegal migration, which had been criticised by some senior Labour figures as un-British, Burnham wanted to reframe the changes.
“I think there’s a different way of thinking about it that might in the end get you to a better position, and one that restores public confidence,” he said.
The prime minister’s political allies say he regards migration as a moral issue, showing people who’ve lost faith in politics that the government does have control over the UK’s borders and is prepared to do something about it.
But he also wants to tell a positive story about the contribution of migration to the country, they say. Weeks after arriving in No 10, the Guardian revealed that social care workers could be exempted from the plans as he looked for ways to relieve pressure on the sector.
In an interview with ITV this week, Burnham again tried to make the case. “When you have planned migration, it’s difficult to say if it’s too high or too low,” he said, arguing that migrants help plug “gaps in the economy”.
In the end, Mahmood’s reforms came with a significant carve-out for almost 300,000 care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) after five years.
In a further compromise to those on the Labour benches feeling squeamish, those deemed to be making a “strong contribution” to the UK – high earners, those with strong British connections or who work in health and teaching – will also be able to settle in five years.
But that Burnham delivered the bulk of Mahmood’s hardline reforms should not come as a surprise. The prime minister, steeped in the politics of the “red wall”, understands better than many the salience of the issue with voters.
The most rigorous of the new rules first drawn up a year ago by the Home Office – retrospective changes for many migrants, and forcing small boats arrivals to face up to 30 years before applying for settlement – are still there.
How they land with the public (which polling suggests supports a doubling of the waiting time for most migrants to 10 years) now depends in part on whether ministers can convince them it’s about people making a contribution, rather than a U-turn forced by their own side.
The Conservatives and Reform, unsurprisingly, are already pushing the latter narrative, Farage describing the care workers carve-out as “the beginning of the capitulation” on borders.
Burnham is, equally predictably, arguing that it’s about fairness. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier,” he said.
“Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.”
But Burnham’s words did not come in the Commons chamber or at a press conference standing alongside Mahmood or even as part of his prolific social media output.
They were instead issued in a press release, after the government chose to push ahead with the sensitive policy announcement while he was out of the country – travelling to the Commonwealth leaders summit in Antigua.
The plans are still likely to face criticism from some on either wing of the Labour party – for going too far or not far enough – although plenty of former critics do now appear to be on board. But without an obvious vote to coalesce around, any major rebellion looks unlikely.
Mahmood’s bigger challenge will be convincing the public. She will need Burnham, who has praised her for “gripping this problem”, to help her to do so. But the prime minister will have to accept, on an issue as divisive as this, he won’t be able to please everyone.
author: Pippa Crerar Political editor

article_title: Shabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlash
article_content:
Shabana Mahmood rowed back on her most hardline plans to make care workers wait 15 years for settlement in the UK, but told MPs on Monday that many migrants would still face retrospective rule changes to make them wait a decade.
Under pressure from a cabinet backlash and health unions, the home secretary has offered a carve-out for care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years.
But most of the rigorous new rules drawn up by Mahmood’s office last year remain, including plans to force those who arrived in the UK by irregular means such as small boats to face up to 30 years before being able to apply for settlement.
The changes drew cries of betrayal from the Conservatives and the Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, who said it was “the beginning of the capitulation”.
But Mahmood told the Commons she would still enact sweeping changes that will mean many migrant workers will wait double the time they had expected for settlement.
She said settlement was “one of most valuable rights this country can offer. Until now it has been given almost automatically. From today it must be earned. Those who contribute will settle fastest. Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait much longer.”
In particular, the wait for those earning under £50,000 will double to 10 years. This was criticised by some Labour MPs who said vital workers such as research scientists and chefs would be caught by the changes.
The Law Society said the changing rules could threaten the rule of law, saying it “retrospectively undermines the legal certainty that individuals, families and employers rely on”.
Some MPs suggested they would continue to press the home secretary to rethink the retrospective nature of the changes – though the new policies do not require a vote in parliament, so MPs have limited means to block them.
Abtisam Mohamed, the Labour MP for Sheffield Central, said: “Retrospectively uprooting someone’s plans, sometimes made at the most vulnerable time in their lives, is unfair. I’ll be pressing for those already here to be protected.”
The former shadow home secretary Diane Abbott also criticised the retrospective changes. “You can come in legally, you can work legally and then have your residency rights turned upside down,” she said, warning of another potential Windrush scandal.
The Walthamstow MP Stella Creasy said there was a “partial recognition” of the contribution migrants made but there were thousands of people “facing 10 years of limbo with many businesses unclear if talent will stay or not as a result”.
She said: “The economic consequences of those people walking away from the UK will far outweigh any savings in entitlement to benefits, given many of them don’t claim anyway, so the home secretary still has work to do to make these reforms work for our national interest.”
Refugees will also face a longer wait of 10 years, with an additional 10-year penalty for those who do not enter legally – and those who do not find employment will face a wait of up to 30 years.
Andy Burnham, who promised voters in his Makerfield byelection that he would support Mahmood’s migration agenda, endorsed the plans and said the home secretary was “gripping this problem” by introducing the earned element.
“People want to see an immigration system based on control, contribution, and which rewards those who play by the rules,” the prime minister said. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier. Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.”
But migrant rights organisations accused the government of “moving the goalposts” for those who had played by the rules. “People who have built their lives around the government’s requirements deserve better than decisions that turn their own and their families’ lives upside down,” said Amnesty International.
The key climbdown from the home secretary was an exemption for care workers – something which the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had explicitly criticised. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, also repeatedly refused to say she backed proposals to prolong the qualifying period for settlement.
Under pressure from health unions to make an exception for care workers, the home secretary has moved to allow an estimated 280,000 care workers and their dependents to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years.
In the revised set of proposals, care workers earning more than £25,000 will be able to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years, a third of the time that was announced last year.
Home Office officials calculate that about 500,000 migrants will have to wait longer than the current five years. But critics of Mahmood’s softening point out that 1.4 million out of the 1.9 million migrants who came to Britain under the so-called “Boriswave” surge in legal migrants will still be eligible for indefinite leave after five years.
Highest earners – those earning more than £125,000 – will be able to settle within three years. Those earning more than £50,271 and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers will be able to settle after five years.
The exception will be the small number of refugees who enter through designated safe and legal routes such as the reopening of the scheme for Afghan women and girls and Palestinians. No other refugees will be eligible for settlement if they have accessed any public funds.
Mahmood met union general secretaries to map out the changes on Monday morning, before presenting them to MPs. The Unison general secretary, Andrea Egan, said it was welcome that Mahmood had not implemented her original plans, which were “morally bankrupt and a threat to public services”.
Egan said the obligations placed on care workers to qualify for the five-year path were still onerous. “The government must make sure it isn’t unjustly denied to them. Thousands of migrant care workers have had their employment patterns and pay disrupted by rogue employers,” she said. “The power of employers to threaten workers with deportation or disrupt their route to settlement must end.”
Business groups warned that the retrospective nature of the changes would still cause far-reaching damage in some sectors. The CBI said the exemption for some care workers meant the policy risked “being higher costs for the relatively small number of businesses using skilled worker visas, without addressing the problem the policy was originally designed to solve”.
Make UK said it would make it far more difficult for businesses to retain skilled workers and industries would “undoubtedly lose talent to countries that welcome skilled workers rather than moving the goalposts”.
The shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, said Mahmood’s decision to allow a carve-out for care workers who arrived on the visa before May 2025 would cost the country up to £10bn, a figure Mahmood has cited in support of her original plans. The home secretary said the longer wait for settlement for more than half a million people would mean a cut to the projected benefits bill.
Other Conservative MPs acknowledged that it was the previous government who had allowed numbers to rise so significantly. The backbencher Edward Leigh said to Philp that “anybody who was serving as a Home Office minister at that time should wear sackcloth and ashes”.

article_content:
Переговори України та Росії за посередництвом США в Абу-Дабі: Віткофф назвав дати й теми зустрічі
США стануть посередником на переговорах 10–11 листопада, а перед ними обговорять гарантії безпеки для України з європейськими партнерами.
Переговори між Україною та Росією на робочому рівні відбудуться 10–11 листопада в Абу-Дабі за посередництва США.
Про це спецпосланець президента США Стів Віткофф повідомив у соцмережі X.
За його словами, сторони зосередяться на післявоєнних безпекових домовленостях, деескалації, гуманітарних зусиллях та подальших кроках до миру.
«Сполучені Штати виступатимуть посередником у переговорах на робочому рівні між Україною та Росією 10–11 листопада в Абу-Дабі, просуваючи місію президента Трампа із завершення війни», — написав Віткофф.
Окремо він анонсував зустріч американських переговорників із представниками Франції, Німеччини, Великої Британії, Євросоюзу та НАТО. Вона відбудеться цього тижня у Брюсселі.
Учасники обговорять гарантії безпеки для України, післявоєнну безпекову архітектуру Європи та економічні можливості для підтримки української відбудови.
Віткофф висловив сподівання, що подальші переговори розвинуть результати попередніх зустрічей у Києві, Осло та Санкт-Петербурзі й наблизять укладення всеосяжної та тривалої мирної угоди.

article_title: Tennessee national guard trained guns on dying man after guard member shot him, video shows
article_content:
Tennessee national guard troops in Memphis last summer trained their handguns on a man as he lay dying on a sidewalk after a guard member shot him in the back, video released Monday by county prosecutors shows.
A Memphis police officer can be heard in the footage from an officer’s body camera calling for an ambulance and then asking the troops: “Hey, you guys got a medical kit or anything?”
The Shelby county district attorney’s office released the videos, which also include footage from stationary cameras and a cellphone from a bystander, as the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation continues its investigation into the 5 July shooting of Tyrin Johnson.
Johnson, 20, who had been armed, died at the scene from a single gunshot wound, according to investigators. An autopsy report shared by Johnson’s family found that he was shot in the back, contradicting police and national guard accounts that said he was facing the guard members with a gun when they fired at him.
The footage did not show Johnson’s initial encounter with the guard members or them firing at him.
The guard members were part of a federal taskforce created by Donald Trump, who last year sent troops and federal agents to Democratic-run cities that he described as overrun with crime. Tennessee’s Republican governor Bill Lee had deployed the guard to support the effort. The task force was involved in four fatal shootings between May and July.
District attorney Steve Mulroy said he has not yet decided whether to file charges in connection with the death.
A spokesperson for the Tennessee national guard did not immediately respond to email and phone messages seeking comment. Ed Yarbrough, an attorney for the two guard members, said they have no comment at this time.
Authorities said the troops were responding with local police to reports of gunshots at about 4am when they began pursuing an armed man fleeing on foot.
Footage from stationary street cameras shows a person in dark clothing firing shots through an empty parking lot at three people walking on a sidewalk. Two Memphis police officers hear gunshots nearby and start walking and then running in that direction, a body camera worn by one of the officers shows. The officers say on their radio that they are pursuing a man who is running and armed with a gun.
The video, which is blurry from the officer’s movement, captures yelling and the sound of a single gunshot, followed by several additional gunshot noises.
A Tennessee national guard report obtained by the Associated Press via a public records request said two guard members responded to the Memphis police radio call, left their vehicle and approached the suspect, who “rounded on them and pointed a tan handgun at them”. Both guard members fired their service weapons – M17 handguns – and Memphis police arrived shortly after, the report stated.
Police body camera footage shows guard members at the scene shouting “Hands!” and “Turn over!” as they point their handguns at a man lying on his back on the sidewalk.
André C Wharton, an attorney for Johnson’s family, noted that the videos do not show the moments immediately before the shooting, or the shooting itself.
“This investigation must stay focused on the moment the guardsman fired the fatal shot and whether that action was reasonable,” Wharton said.
Johnson was the father of a young child and was preparing to help lead the family construction business, his grandfather, Evaniel Johnson, said.
At least six guard members were on the scene immediately after the shooting, the body camera video shows. One can be seen moving a handgun that is on the ground until a police officer tells him to leave it alone. An officer calls for an ambulance over the radio, and a guard member begins to cut off the man’s shirt just before the video ends.

article_title: Україна в ООН закликала заарештувати Путіна: Мельник звернувся до держав
article_content:
Україна в ООН закликала заарештувати Путіна: Мельник звернувся до держав
Український дипломат закликав держави-учасниці Римського статуту виконати ордери на арешт шістьох російських високопосадовців.
Постійний представник України при ООН Андрій Мельник закликав країни виконати ордери Міжнародного кримінального суду на арешт російського диктатора Володимира Путіна та ще п’ятьох російських посадовців.
Про це він заявив на засіданні Генеральної Асамблеї ООН, присвяченому звіту МКС, повідомляє Укрінформ.
«Усі ці ордери МКС мають бути виконані», — наголосив Мельник.
Дипломат закликав держави-учасниці Римського статуту заарештовувати підозрюваних і передавати їх суду.
Йдеться про Путіна та Марію Львову-Бєлову, ордери щодо яких видали у справі про незаконну депортацію та переміщення українських дітей. Ще четверо фігурантів — Сергій Кобилаш, Віктор Соколов, Сергій Шойгу та Валерій Герасимов. Їх підозрюють у злочинах, пов’язаних з ударами по українській енергетиці.
Мельник наголосив, що Росія продовжує атакувати енергетичну інфраструктуру, намагаючись залишити цивільних без води, тепла та електрики перед зимою. За його словами, відповідальність має наставати незалежно від посади винних, а тривалий мир неможливий без правосуддя.
Окремо постпред закликав держави долучатися до роботи Спеціального трибуналу щодо злочину агресії проти України, який має доповнити роботу МКС.
Нагадаємо, що раніше США запровадили санкції проти президентки МКС, яка видавала ордер на арешт Путіна
